title_en: Yarmarka market and Yosef Yitzchak's arrest in Lubavitch
summary_en: Ten-year-old Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested at the Lubavitch market fair after defending Reb Dovid the butcher from a corrupt police sergeant.
story_body: During the two-day yarmarka market fair in Lubavitch on June 29-30, 1891, young Yosef Yitzchak encountered a police sergeant beating Reb Dovid the butcher with false accusations of theft. After defending the butcher, Yosef Yitzchak was arrested and locked in a dark cell, where he reviewed Mishnah by heart and prayed Minchah. He was released when officers realized he was the nephew of Rabbi Zalman Aharon Schneersohn, and the butcher was exonerated when the sergeant's actual theft was uncovered.

title_en: Arrest of Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi
summary_en: Chabad's founder Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi was arrested by czarist authorities, the first of repeated imprisonments of Chabad Rebbes.
story_body: In 1798, Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, the founder of Chabad, was arrested in czarist Russia for standing up for Judaism. This was the first in a series of imprisonments that Chabad Rebbes would endure under Russian oppression. The arrest became a foundational moment in Chabad history and a touchstone Yosef Yitzchak recalled while himself in prison.

title_en: Rayatz's second arrest over secular school accusations
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested a second time due to accusations from teachers at the secular school in Lubavitch.
story_body: In 1902, Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn faced his second arrest, brought about by accusations leveled by teachers at the secular school in Lubavitch. This arrest reflected ongoing tensions between traditional Chabad education and the secular educational system pushed by reformers. It was one of seven arrests he would experience over his lifetime under czarist and later Communist rule.

title_en: Rayatz's third arrest in Poalei Tzion conflict
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested a third time after a conflict with Poalei Tzion activists in Lubavitch.
story_body: In 1906, Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested following a confrontation with Poalei Tzion, a Labor Zionist organization active in Lubavitch. The clash reflected the broader ideological battles between traditional Chabad Chasidism and emerging Jewish political movements in early twentieth-century Russia. This was one of multiple arrests he endured under czarist rule.

title_en: Rayatz's St. Petersburg arrest over military exemption efforts
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested in St. Petersburg over his efforts to exempt rabbis from military service.
story_body: In 1906, Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested in St. Petersburg after working to secure exemptions for rabbis from compulsory military service in the Russian army. His advocacy for protecting Jewish religious leaders from conscription was viewed as obstructionist by czarist authorities. This was one of his early imprisonments under the czarist regime.

title_en: Rayatz's St. Petersburg arrest over rabbis' conference
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested in St. Petersburg following an informer's report about planning for a rabbis' conference.
story_body: In 1910, Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested in St. Petersburg after an informer alerted authorities about his role in planning a rabbinic conference. Such gatherings were viewed as politically threatening by czarist authorities monitoring Jewish religious leadership. This was the fourth in his series of arrests under the Russian regime.

title_en: Rayatz's Rostov arrest by Yevsektzia
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested in Rostov following accusations from the Yevsektzia, the Jewish section of the Communist Party.
story_body: In 1920, in Rostov, Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested after the Yevsektzia, the Jewish section of the Communist Party, leveled accusations against him. The Yevsektzia became a primary opponent of religious Jewish life in the early Soviet period, targeting Chabad activities. This marked the sixth of his seven arrests and his first under Communism.

title_en: Rayatz's St. Petersburg arrest and death sentence
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested in St. Petersburg and sentenced to death, eventually freed due to international Jewish pressure.
story_body: In 1927, Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested in St. Petersburg and held at the notorious Shpalerka Prison, where Soviet authorities sentenced him to death for his religious activities. World Jewry mounted significant international pressure on the Soviet government, ultimately securing his release. This seventh and final arrest marked the climax of his confrontations with anti-religious authorities in Russia.

title_en: Birth of Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, who would become the sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe, was born in Lubavitch on 12 Tamuz 5640.
story_body: On June 30, 1880 (12 Tamuz 5640), Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was born in Lubavitch to Rabbi Shalom Dovber (the Rashab) and Rebbetzin Shterna Sara. His birth followed a vivid dream in which his mother was reassured by three previous Lubavitcher Rebbes that she would bear a son. At his circumcision, his grandfather Rabbi Shmuel served as sandek and prophetically declared that the child would become a Rebbe.

title_en: Marriage of Rashab and Shterna Sara
summary_en: Rabbi Shalom Dovber Schneersohn married his cousin Shterna Sara, who moved from Ovruch to Lubavitch.
story_body: In 1875, Rabbi Shalom Dovber (the Rashab) married his cousin Rebbetzin Shterna Sara, fulfilling an engagement contract drawn up in 1865 when both were young children. Shterna Sara moved four hundred miles from her hometown of Ovruch, Ukraine, to Lubavitch following the marriage. The match had been suggested by Rabbi Menachem Mendel, who saw the two grandchildren together and declared them 'Bride and groom!'

title_en: Engagement contract of Rashab and Shterna Sara
summary_en: An engagement contract was written between the young Rashab and his cousin Shterna Sara at the urging of Rabbi Menachem Mendel.
story_body: In 1865, Shterna Sara visited Lubavitch from her hometown of Ovruch as a young girl. Seeing his two grandchildren standing together in his home, Rabbi Menachem Mendel (the Tzemach Tzedek) declared, 'Bride and groom!' That year, while both children were still young, their parents wrote a tena'im, the formal engagement contract that would lead to their marriage a decade later.

title_en: Rebbetzin Shterna Sara's dream of three Rebbes
summary_en: On Simchat Torah 1879, Rebbetzin Shterna Sara received a prophetic dream of three previous Rebbes promising her a son.
story_body: On Simchat Torah 1879, Rebbetzin Shterna Sara was distressed after her father-in-law Rabbi Shmuel overlooked her when bestowing blessings on the family. That night, she dreamed of a Jew who promised her a son if she would give eighteen rubles to charity. Rabbi Shmuel later identified the dream visitors as the first three Lubavitcher Rebbes: the Tzemach Tzedek, the Mitteler Rebbe, and the Alter Rebbe. Ten months later, she gave birth to Yosef Yitzchak.

title_en: Lubavitch's last synagogue closed by Soviets
summary_en: The last synagogue in Lubavitch was shuttered by Communist authorities in 1936.
story_body: In 1936, Communist authorities shuttered the last operating synagogue in the town of Lubavitch, ending centuries of organized Jewish religious life there. The closure followed the passing of Rabbi Yosef Leib Beriya, a scholar respected by Jews and non-Jews alike, who had maintained the synagogue. This marked the end of Lubavitch as a functioning Jewish community under Soviet rule.

title_en: Nazi seizure of Lubavitch
summary_en: German forces seized the town of Lubavitch and established a ghetto that September.
story_body: On July 21, 1941, Nazi forces seized the town of Lubavitch during their invasion of the Soviet Union. By September of that year, they had established a Jewish ghetto in the historic town. The Nazis targeted Lubavitch's residents with particular brutality because of its history as the center of Chabad Chasidism.

title_en: Massacre of Lubavitch's Jews
summary_en: 483 Jews of Lubavitch were murdered and the ghetto destroyed on November 4, 1941.
story_body: On November 4, 1941, Nazi forces murdered 483 Jews and destroyed the ghetto in Lubavitch, effectively ending the Jewish presence in the historic town. Only one Jewish resident remained in Lubavitch until the early 1960s. The Hebrew Standard of Australia later reported that the brutality of the extermination in Lubavitch 'supersedes anything the Red Army committee investigating Nazi atrocities have thus far come across.'

title_en: Rashab departs Lubavitch ahead of German advance
summary_en: Rabbi Shalom Dovber and his family departed Lubavitch on October 25, 1915, ending its century as Chabad's capital.
story_body: On October 25, 1915 (17 Cheshvan 5676), the Rashab and his family departed Lubavitch in the face of the advancing German army during World War I. With his departure, Lubavitch's 102-year run as the capital of the Chabad chasidic movement came to an end. The Rashab never returned to Lubavitch, though the yeshivah remained in the town for another two years.

title_en: Rayatz's final visit to Lubavitch
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz traveled to Lubavitch for the final time to pray at the graves of his predecessors.
story_body: In 1922, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn made his final pilgrimage to the town of Lubavitch to pray at the graves of the Lubavitcher Rebbes interred there. The visit came years after his father had left during World War I, and the town was no longer the spiritual capital it had once been. This was the last visit by a Lubavitcher Rebbe to the historic town.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe settles in Lubavitch
summary_en: Rabbi Dovber, the second Chabad Rebbe, settled in Lubavitch in summer 1813, beginning the town's era as Chabad's capital.
story_body: In the summer of 1813, Rabbi Dovber, the second Chabad Rebbe, settled in the town of Lubavitch. He was the first of four Chabad Rebbes to reside there, establishing the town as the capital of the Chabad chasidic movement for the next 102 years. His arrival followed the death of his father, Rabbi Schneur Zalman, who had passed away the previous year while fleeing Napoleon's invading army.

title_en: Death of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, founder of Chabad, passed away while fleeing Napoleon's invading army.
story_body: In 1812, Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, the founder of Chabad and first Lubavitcher Rebbe, passed away while fleeing from Napoleon's invading army through Russia. His son Rabbi Dovber succeeded him and the following year settled in Lubavitch, establishing the town as Chabad's capital. The Alter Rebbe's flight reflected his strong opposition to Napoleon's potential influence on Jewish life.

title_en: Bolshevik Revolution
summary_en: The Bolshevik revolution in Russia ushered in subdued religious life in Lubavitch and across the country.
story_body: In 1917, the Bolshevik revolution transformed Russia, bringing Communist rule that would dramatically constrain Jewish religious life. After the revolution, religious life in Lubavitch continued in a subdued fashion under increasing pressure from Soviet authorities. The revolution set the stage for decades of suppression of Chabad and other Jewish religious activities.

title_en: Passing of Rabbi Shmuel, the Rebbe Maharash
summary_en: Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn, the fourth Lubavitcher Rebbe, passed away in Lubavitch three days after Yom Kippur 1882.
story_body: In 1882, three days after Yom Kippur, Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn, the Rebbe Maharash and fourth Lubavitcher Rebbe, passed away in Lubavitch at the age of forty-eight. On the eve of Rosh HaShanah that year, he had cryptically told his wife that she would rise up thirty-two steps physically while he would rise spiritually, alluding to his impending passing. He had been Rebbe for a little more than sixteen years, leaving his youngest daughter just four years old.

title_en: Chabad elders convene to address succession
summary_en: Prominent Chabad rabbis gathered in Lubavitch to urge the Rashab and his brother to assume leadership after their father's passing.
story_body: On Shabbat, October 21, 1882 (8 Cheshvan 5643, Parashas Lekh Lekha), Chabad elders convened in the home of Rebbetzin Rivkah Schneersohn to address the future of the movement following Rabbi Shmuel's passing. Prominent rabbis including Rabbi Zalman Pinsker, Rabbi Dan Tumarkin, and Reb Chaim Yaakov Viderevitz attended. The two older sons, Rabbi Zalman Aharon and Rabbi Shalom Dovber, initially refused to sit with the rabbis, but eventually agreed to recite maamarim, tacitly stepping into their father's role.

title_en: Rabbi Shmuel becomes Rebbe Maharash
summary_en: Rabbi Shmuel became the fourth Lubavitcher Rebbe in Lubavitch following his father's passing, while his brothers established rival Chabad courts.
story_body: In 1866, following the passing of his father Rabbi Menachem Mendel (the Tzemach Tzedek), Rabbi Shmuel became the fourth Lubavitcher Rebbe in Lubavitch. His brothers established rival Chabad courts in nearby towns: Rabbi Yehuda Leib in Kopust, Rabbi Chaim Schneur Zalman in Liadi, and Rabbi Yisrael Noach in Nizhyn. For the next half a century, Chabad Chasidim would be divided between these different Chabad Rebbes.

title_en: Rashab fully accepts position of Rebbe
summary_en: On Rosh HaShanah 1893, Rabbi Shalom Dovber fully accepted the position of Rebbe, becoming the fifth Lubavitcher Rebbe.
story_body: On Rosh HaShanah in 1893, the Rashab, then thirty-two, fully accepted the position of Rebbe, becoming the fifth Lubavitcher Rebbe. He walked into services and took his father's seat near the holy ark, which had remained vacant since Rabbi Shmuel's passing eleven years earlier. With his acceptance of the position, Chasidim began to flock to Lubavitch in large numbers once again, beginning what the Rayatz called 'the era of the rebirth of Lubavitch.'

title_en: Rashbatz appointed teacher of Yosef Yitzchak
summary_en: Rabbi Shmuel Betzalel Sheftel (Rashbatz) was appointed by the Rashab to teach his son Yosef Yitzchak.
story_body: A few days after Rosh HaShanah 1893, the Rashab appointed Rabbi Shmuel Betzalel Sheftel, known as the Rashbatz, to teach his son Yosef Yitzchak. The Rashbatz had previously taught the Rashab himself at the behest of Rabbi Shmuel. He remained Yosef Yitzchak's teacher until 1900, and was renowned for his ability to clarify chasidic concepts through parables and his deep knowledge of chasidic teachings from previous generations.

title_en: Yosef Yitzchak's bar mitzvah
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn celebrated his bar mitzvah on Monday, Tamuz 5653, with Chasidim convening from throughout Russia.
story_body: On Monday, Tamuz 5653 (June 26, 1893), Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn celebrated his bar mitzvah in Lubavitch. He woke at 6:00 a.m., immersed in the mikveh, and prayed at the gravesites of his ancestors before reciting two of three maamarim he had memorized. The weeklong celebration drew Chasidim from throughout Russia, with the third maamar revealed only privately on the following Shabbat to a select group. His father blessed him that 'You should never be fearful of anything.'

title_en: Rashab writes ethical will for his son
summary_en: Concerned about his health, the Rashab wrote an ethical will outlining how his wife should educate young Yosef Yitzchak if he died.
story_body: In 1888, when he was just twenty-seven and his son Yosef Yitzchak was eight, the Rashab was deeply concerned about his health and decided to write an ethical will. The will outlined how he wished his wife to educate their son if he passed away. Based on the verse 'Educate a child in accordance to his way,' the document was eventually published in 1943 under the title Chanokh LaNaar.

title_en: Family returns to Lubavitch after extended absence
summary_en: After years abroad seeking medical care, the Rashab and his wife returned to spend an entire year in Lubavitch with their son.
story_body: In 1890, after years of being absent from Lubavitch while seeking medical treatment in Russia and abroad, the Rashab and his wife finally returned home. The Rayatz later wrote that this was 'almost the first in my life that my father spent entirely at home,' as the greater part of previous years had been spent abroad. However, in December 1890, the Rashab fell ill with a high fever for about two months.

title_en: Akedah ceremony at Lubavitch Ohel
summary_en: On Yosef Yitzchak's fifteenth birthday, the Rashab brought him to the Ohel and inducted him as a Jewish leader.
story_body: On the Rayatz's fifteenth birthday in 1895, the Rashab brought him to the Ohel in Lubavitch and declared he was bringing his son to the akedah, drawing on the biblical binding of Yitzchak. Standing before the open ark, the Rashab transferred to his son the sacred task of working for the public good, recounted 140 years of Lubavitcher Rebbes' communal work, and inducted him as a Jewish leader. From that day, the Rayatz stood by his father's side as his personal secretary and confidant.

title_en: Rashab summers in Bolivke with his son
summary_en: The Rashab began six summers of intensive mentorship with his son Yosef Yitzchak in Bolivke beginning in summer 1895.
story_body: In the summer of 1895, the Rashab traveled with his wife to the resort town of Bolivke, forty-five miles from Lubavitch. While the official reason was his weakened health, the true motive was to spend time mentoring his son. For six years until 1901, the Rashab took the Rayatz on two-hour daily walks, studying Talmud and chasidic maamarim, sharing personal stories, and preparing him for future leadership.

title_en: Rashab seeks medical care in Moscow
summary_en: Gravely ill, the Rashab traveled to Moscow for medical care and considered relocating to Eretz Yisrael.
story_body: In 1896, the Rashab was gravely ill and traveled with his wife to Moscow for medical care. Doctors gave him a bleak prognosis of just months to live. He suggested to his wife they travel to Eretz Yisrael to spend his last days there, saying their sixteen-year-old son could lead Chabad in his place. Rebbetzin Shterna Sara prevailed on him to remain in Lubavitch, and he ultimately recovered, living another twenty-four years.

title_en: Alter Rebbe urges refugees to farm
summary_en: At age eleven, Rabbi Schneur Zalman urged Prague refugees in Russia to become farmers for stable livelihood.
story_body: In 1756, at the age of eleven, the future Alter Rebbe, Rabbi Schneur Zalman, urged refugees arriving in Russia from Prague to become farmers as a means of earning a stable livelihood. This early act of communal service initiated the 140-year tradition of communal work by the Lubavitcher Rebbes that the Rashab would later recount to his son at the Ohel. The episode established a lifelong pattern of practical leadership concerned with Jewish material welfare.

title_en: Yosef Yitzchak begins formal education
summary_en: Four-year-old Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn began formal schooling with master educator Rabbi Yekusiel Aizik.
story_body: In 1884, when Yosef Yitzchak was four years old, he began his formal education in cheder. On his first day, his father and uncle Rabbi Zalman Aharon celebrated by tossing candies that they said came from the angel Mikhael, continuing a family tradition from the Tzemach Tzedek. His teacher, Rabbi Yekusiel Aizik, was a master educator descended from Chasidim of the Alter Rebbe, known for his enthusiastic storytelling about the Baal Shem Tov.

title_en: Family travels to Yalta for Rashab's health
summary_en: The Rashab and family traveled to Yalta for six months for his health, with five-year-old Yosef Yitzchak studying under Schneur Zalman Slonim.
story_body: In fall 1885, the Rashab and his family traveled almost one thousand miles south from Lubavitch to Yalta for six months, where the warm climate would benefit his health. Five-year-old Yosef Yitzchak accompanied them and studied under Rabbi Schneur Zalman Slonim from Hebron, who had come to Lubavitch for an extended stay. The family took daily walks together and the Rayatz later described it as an idyllic period spent with his parents.

title_en: Lag BaOmer dinner in Kharkiv
summary_en: The Rashab and family stopped in Kharkiv on Lag BaOmer, where local Chasidim organized a large welcome dinner.
story_body: In May 1886, returning from Yalta to Lubavitch, the Rashab and his family stopped in Kharkiv on Lag BaOmer. Local Chasidim organized a large dinner to welcome them, with rabbis, prominent Chasidim, and community members crowding the room to the rafters. When the Rashab taught a maamar, Chasidim crowded around to listen. During the event, young Yosef Yitzchak found his mother crying privately and conveyed her concerns about his father's health back to the Rashab.

title_en: Rashab exempted from army draft
summary_en: At age eighteen, the Rashab was exempted from the army draft after a medical examiner discovered he had tuberculosis.
story_body: In 1878, at the age of eighteen, Rabbi Shalom Dovber (the Rashab) was examined for the Russian army draft. The medical examiner discovered he had tuberculosis, leading to his exemption from military service. Professor Zacharov told the Rashab's younger brother Mendel that the Rashab had just two months to live, a prognosis that proved dramatically incorrect as he lived for another forty-two years.

title_en: Raza relocates to Vitebsk
summary_en: Rabbi Zalman Aharon Schneersohn relocated to Vitebsk, deferring leadership of Chabad to his younger brother the Rashab.
story_body: In the summer of 1893, Rabbi Zalman Aharon Schneersohn (the Raza) relocated from Lubavitch to Vitebsk, fifty miles away. The move possibly was meant to keep him out of the limelight, clearing the way for his younger brother the Rashab to emerge as Rebbe. The Raza had declared that 'My brother, the Rashab, was born a Rebbe and is a Rebbe' and may also have been motivated by financial difficulties. He continued to visit Lubavitch often and became a major influence on his nephew Yosef Yitzchak.

title_en: Last Chabad breakaway dynasty ends
summary_en: With the passing of Rabbi Shmaryahu Noach Schneersohn of Bobruysk in 1923, the last breakaway Chabad dynasty came to an end.
story_body: In 1923, Rabbi Shmaryahu Noach Schneersohn of Bobruysk passed away, marking the end of the last of the breakaway Chabad dynasties that had emerged after Rabbi Menachem Mendel's passing in 1866. At that point, all Chabad Chasidim accepted Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn as the sole Chabad Rebbe. This consolidation followed the establishment of Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim in Lubavitch, which had drawn students from across the various Chabad streams.

title_en: Death of Rabbi Yosef Leib Beriya
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Leib Beriya, the scholar who maintained Lubavitch's last synagogue, passed away in 1936.
story_body: In 1936, Rabbi Yosef Leib Beriya, a scholar respected by both Jews and non-Jews alike, passed away in Lubavitch. His death directly preceded the Soviet authorities' closure of the town's last synagogue, which he had maintained until his passing. His death marked the practical end of Lubavitch's organized Jewish life.

title_en: Rashab publishes diary entries after leaving Soviet Union
summary_en: After leaving the Soviet Union, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn began publishing his diary entries with chasidic history and lore.
story_body: In 1927, after leaving the Soviet Union following his arrest and death sentence, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn began publishing the diary entries he had been compiling since his youth in Lubavitch. He had been writing down stories, chasidic lore, and customs heard from Chasidim and his father from a young age, encouraged by his teacher Reb Nissan. These publications became foundational sources for chasidic history and tradition.

title_en: Nechama Dina Schneersohn is born
summary_en: Nechama Dina Schneersohn, future wife of the Rayatz, was born in Kishinev.
story_body: Nechama Dina Schneersohn was born on 17 Tishrei 5642 (October 24, 1881) in Kishinev to Rabbi Avraham Schneersohn, a second cousin of the Rebbe Rashab. She would later be selected as the bride for the Rashab's only son, the Rayatz.

title_en: Czar Alexander II assassinated
summary_en: Czar Alexander II of Russia was assassinated, ushering in a more repressive era for Jews.
story_body: The assassination of Czar Alexander II in 1881 brought his son Alexander III to the throne. The new czar rolled back his father's reforms and increased oppression of Russian Jews, setting the stage for the May Laws the following year.

title_en: May Laws restrict Russian Jewish life
summary_en: Czar Alexander III instituted the May Laws, severely restricting Jewish residency, economy, and education.
story_body: In 1882, Alexander III enacted the discriminatory May Laws, prohibiting Jews from leasing land outside the Pale, restricting high school and university attendance, and limiting mortgages. These laws were a major catalyst for mass Jewish emigration to America and the West.

title_en: BILU sends first Zionist settlers to Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: BILU, an early Russian Zionist group, sent its first settlers to Eretz Yisrael.
story_body: BILU was one of the earliest Russian Zionist organizations. In 1882 it dispatched its first settlers to Eretz Yisrael, marking the beginning of organized secular Zionist settlement and an emerging ideological challenge to traditional Jewish life.

title_en: Rashab assumes leadership of Chabad on Rosh HaShanah
summary_en: Rabbi Shalom Dovber Schneersohn formally assumed the position of Rebbe in Lubavitch on Rosh HaShanah.
story_body: On Rosh HaShanah 1893, the Rashab formally took on the mantle of Chabad leadership. He used the position to reassert Lubavitch's involvement in Russian Jewish communal affairs after years of relative quiet following the Maharash's passing in 1882.

title_en: Rayatz represents father at Kovno rabbinic conference
summary_en: At age fifteen, the Rayatz represented his father the Rashab at a conference of Jewish religious leaders in Kovno.
story_body: In 1895, at just fifteen years old, the Rayatz attended a conference of Jewish religious leaders in Kovno on behalf of his father, the Rebbe Rashab. He simultaneously began serving as the Rashab's private secretary, a role he would hold for 25 years.

title_en: Rashab visits gravesites of chasidic forebears
summary_en: Rashab visited the gravesites of the Baal Shem Tov, the Maggid, the Alter Rebbe, and the Mitteler Rebbe.
story_body: In the summer of 1896, troubled by the spiritual state of Russian Jewry, the Rashab traveled to Mezibuzh, Anipoli, Hadyach, and Nizhyn to pray at the graves of the Baal Shem Tov, the Maggid of Mezeritch, the Alter Rebbe, and the Mitteler Rebbe. Upon his return he prayed at the graves of his grandfather and father before establishing Tomchei Temimim.

title_en: Rayatz becomes engaged in Bolivke
summary_en: The Rayatz signed engagement contracts with Nechama Dina Schneersohn in Bolivke.
story_body: On 28 Sivan 5656 (June 9, 1896), the tena'im were signed in Bolivke, formally engaging the Rayatz to Nechama Dina. The Rebbe Rashab took on all wedding expenses despite his family's limited means, having chosen Nechama Dina over wealthier matches with large dowries.

title_en: Shterna Sara writes to family in Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: Rebbetzin Shterna Sara wrote to her Hebron cousins about the choice of Nechama Dina as the Rayatz's bride.
story_body: On 1 Elul 5656 (September 1, 1896), Rebbetzin Shterna Sara wrote to Rabbi Mordechai Dovber and Rabbi Schneur Zalman Schneersohn in Hebron, explaining that Nechama Dina was chosen for her piety despite the family forgoing significant dowry offers. She also asked them to pray for the family at the holy gravesites before Rosh HaShanah.

title_en: Rayatz attends Vilna rabbinic conference
summary_en: The Rayatz again represented his father at a conference of Jewish religious leaders, this time in Vilna.
story_body: Following his 1895 appearance in Kovno, the Rayatz traveled to Vilna in 1896 to once more represent the Rashab at a gathering of Jewish religious leaders, deepening his early immersion in Russian Jewish communal affairs.

title_en: Wedding of the Rayatz in Lubavitch
summary_en: The Rayatz married Nechama Dina in Lubavitch on a Friday afternoon, two weeks before Rosh HaShanah.
story_body: On 13 Elul 5657 (September 10, 1897), the Rayatz wed Nechama Dina in Lubavitch. The chuppah was held Friday afternoon in the courtyard of the main synagogue, with the Rayatz donning the customary Lubavitcher shtreimel. Chasidim streamed in from across Russia for the celebrations.

title_en: Founding meeting of Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim
summary_en: The Rashab gathered fifty guests at the wedding reception and announced the founding of Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim.
story_body: On 15 Elul 5657 (September 12, 1897), the day of the wedding reception, the Rashab unveiled his plan for a new yeshivah integrating Talmud with chasidic philosophy. Despite skepticism from many of the assembled rabbis and philanthropists, the Rebbe pressed forward, and this date became the official founding of Tomchei Temimim.

title_en: Studies begin at Tomchei Temimim in Lubavitch
summary_en: Tomchei Temimim opened its doors with Rabbi Shmuel Gronem as mashpia on the auspicious 18 Elul.
story_body: Studies began on 18 Elul 5657 (September 15, 1897), the joint birthday of the Baal Shem Tov and the Alter Rebbe. The Rashab personally selected the first students from among the yoshvim and appointed Rabbi Shmuel Gronem as the yeshivah's first mashpia, with detailed curriculum instructions.

title_en: Knesses Beis Yitzchak yeshivah opens in Slabodka
summary_en: Opponents of the Musar movement opened Knesses Beis Yitzchak yeshivah in Slabodka.
story_body: In 1897, scholars who objected to the systematic study of musar at Slabodka opened a rival yeshivah called Knesses Beis Yitzchak. The split reflected an ongoing controversy in Lithuanian yeshivas over whether ethics study should be integrated alongside Talmud.

title_en: Tomchei Temimim moves to Zembin
summary_en: After the High Holidays, Tomchei Temimim's students and their mashpia relocated from Lubavitch to Zembin.
story_body: Following the Tishrei holidays of 1897, the original cohort of Tomchei Temimim students relocated with Rabbi Shmuel Gronem to Zembin, a small town some 160 miles west of Lubavitch. The smaller setting reduced distractions, and over the year the original group grew to eighteen students.

title_en: Rayatz becomes director of Tomchei Temimim
summary_en: On 24 Elul 5658, the eighteen-year-old Rayatz was appointed director of Tomchei Temimim.
story_body: After Chasidim led by Rabbi Asher Grossman of Nikolayev urged the Rayatz to lead the yeshivah and the Rashab endorsed the idea, the Rayatz assumed the directorship on 24 Elul 5658 (September 11, 1898). He immediately took on fundraising, faculty management, and expansion of the institution.

title_en: Yeshivah named Tomchei Temimim on Simchat Torah
summary_en: During Simchat Torah hakafot, the Rashab formally named the yeshivah Tomchei Temimim.
story_body: On Simchat Torah 1898, as the seventh hakafah began around 4 a.m., the Rashab paused the dancing and announced that the new yeshivah would be named Tomchei Temimim, derived from the hakafot verse 'Tomekh temimim, hoshiya na.' Its students would forever be known as temimim.

title_en: Farbrengen on 19 Kislev decries Lubavitch maskil school
summary_en: At a 19 Kislev farbrengen, the Rashab bitterly denounced Baron Gunzburg for supporting an Enlightenment school in Lubavitch.
story_body: On 19 Kislev 5659 (December 3, 1898), the Rashab spoke about a major farbrengen, lamenting that Baron Gunzburg had refused his plea to 'give me Yavneh' and spare Lubavitch from a maskil-funded school. The school had nonetheless opened with 130 students.

title_en: Rashab writes letter denouncing Zionism
summary_en: The Rashab wrote a major letter sharply criticizing Zionism's secular nationalist program.
story_body: On 10 Tamuz 5659 (July 22, 1899), the Rashab penned a sharp critique of Zionism, denouncing proponents who sought to replace Torah-based Jewish identity with secular nationalism. The letter became a foundational statement of the Chabad position on the early Zionist movement.

title_en: Chamah's Enlightenment schools reach 150
summary_en: By 1900, the Society to Promote the Enlightenment (Chamah) had established 150 schools across Russia.
story_body: Founded in 1863 with backing from the Gunzburg family, Chamah's network of schools, which minimized Jewish instruction and promoted Russian-language secular education, had expanded to 150 institutions by 1900. The Rashab regarded the growth as a serious threat to traditional Jewish education.

title_en: Simchat Torah mission statement for Tomchei Temimim
summary_en: On Simchat Torah, the Rashab laid out the mission of Tomchei Temimim, calling its students 'soldiers of King David.'
story_body: On Simchat Torah night 1900, three years after the yeshivah's founding, the Rashab compared the temimim to soldiers of King David who set worldly concerns aside for a higher mission. He charged them with disseminating chasidic teachings and standing strong as Jewish leaders against the temptations of the era.

title_en: JCA pledges one million francs to Enlightenment schools
summary_en: The Jewish Colonial Association in Paris pledged one million francs to develop Enlightenment schools in Russia.
story_body: In 1900, the Paris-based JCA committed one million francs toward Enlightenment-oriented schooling for Russian Jews. The Rashab, assisted by the Rayatz, organized an international rabbinic lobbying effort that ultimately blocked a follow-up 600,000-franc allocation and redirected funds toward Jewish economic development.

title_en: Rayatz opens textile mill in Dubrovno
summary_en: The Rayatz opened a Shabbat-observant textile mill in Dubrovno using JCA funds.
story_body: In 1901, tasked by his father, the Rayatz spent a year setting up a textile mill in Dubrovno some sixty miles from Lubavitch. Built with JCA funds redirected from Enlightenment schools, the mill closed on Shabbat and eventually employed two thousand local Jews, removing the stigma of factory work.

title_en: Russo-Japanese War breaks out
summary_en: War broke out between Russia and Japan over control of Manchuria and Korea, drafting thousands of Jewish soldiers.
story_body: In 1904, conflict erupted between Russia and Japan, conscripting thousands of Jewish soldiers into the Russian army for two years before an inglorious Russian defeat. The Rashab and Rayatz launched a campaign to provide Passover supplies to the Jewish troops on the Far East front.

title_en: Knesses Beis Yitzchak hires Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz
summary_en: Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz was hired as rosh yeshivah of Knesses Beis Yitzchak in Slabodka.
story_body: In 1904, Knesses Beis Yitzchak in Slabodka hired Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz to lead the yeshivah. He would later relocate the yeshivah to Vilna in 1921 and to Kamenitz in 1926, becoming one of the most influential Lithuanian roshei yeshivah of the era.

title_en: Chinese Matzah Campaign for Russian soldiers
summary_en: The Rashab and Rayatz secured permission and supplies to ship Passover matzah to Jewish soldiers in the Far East.
story_body: Building on a limited 1904 attempt, in 1905 the Rashab and Rayatz mounted a far larger effort to provide Passover matzah and supplies to Jewish soldiers fighting on the Russo-Japanese front. Despite anti-Semitic government obstruction and immense logistical challenges, they obtained permission and distributed supplies across the Far East front.

title_en: Covert rabbinic strategy meeting in St. Petersburg
summary_en: The Rayatz attended a covert rabbinic strategy meeting in St. Petersburg to address the wave of pogroms.
story_body: In the summer of 1905, the Rayatz joined a clandestine meeting of prominent rabbinic leaders in St. Petersburg to develop a response to the pogroms erupting across Russia. He was subsequently dispatched to Western Europe to enlist German and Dutch statesmen and foreign bankers to pressure the Russian government.

title_en: Poalei Tzion attacks Tomchei Temimim
summary_en: Armed Poalei Tzion members confronted the Rayatz at the yeshivah and later shot at the building.
story_body: On March 22, 1906, Marxist Zionist Poalei Tzion members marched into Tomchei Temimim demanding the release of teenage student Berel Davzik. Three days later they returned with weapons, threw stones, and fired bullets at the yeshivah, narrowly missing Rabbi Moshe Klatzkin of Romanov. Students drove them off, but the Rayatz forbade reprisal.

title_en: Poalei Tzion raid the Rashab's summer home in Bolivke
summary_en: Six to eight armed Poalei Tzion members raided the Rashab's summer home in Bolivke, terrorizing his family.
story_body: A few months after the yeshivah attack, Poalei Tzion intruders broke into the Rashab's Bolivke summer home with revolvers drawn, destroying furniture and ransacking the house in front of the Rayatz's young daughters and their grandmother. The Rashab was forced to hire security guards; his brother the Raza eventually negotiated a settlement from Vitebsk.

title_en: Rayatz investigated over Lubavitch riots
summary_en: The Rayatz was investigated by Russian authorities in December 1906 over radical-youth riots in Lubavitch.
story_body: In December 1906, in the aftermath of the 1905 revolution's political tensions, the Rayatz was investigated about riots in Lubavitch by radical youth. He proved the rioters were not part of the yeshivah and was released after a brief detention.

title_en: Rashab acquires Beit Romano in Hebron
summary_en: After years of effort, the Rashab completed the purchase of Beit Romano and an adjacent property in Hebron.
story_body: By 1908, the Rashab had raised the funds and navigated the legal hurdles to acquire Beit Romano, a large mansion originally built by an affluent Istanbul Jew. Combined with an adjacent property, it would serve as the base for Toras Emes, the first chasidic yeshivah in the Jewish homeland.

title_en: Confidential pre-conference rabbinic meeting
summary_en: The Rashab asked the Rayatz to organize a confidential meeting of Chabad-aligned rabbis to set strategy.
story_body: In October 1908, anticipating the St. Petersburg rabbinic conference, the Rashab tasked the Rayatz with convening a small confidential meeting of Chabad-aligned rabbis to develop a consensus on government engagement and prepare for the forthcoming Duma elections.

title_en: Vilna pre-conference of leading rabbis
summary_en: Twenty-five leading rabbis met in Vilna to set the agenda for the upcoming St. Petersburg conference.
story_body: In May 1909, through coordination between the Rashab and Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski of Vilna, the Russian government permitted twenty-five leading rabbis to gather in Vilna. The Rayatz was named secretary of the meeting, which set the agenda for the 1910 national conference in St. Petersburg.

title_en: National rabbinic conference in St. Petersburg
summary_en: The government convened a national conference in St. Petersburg to resolve issues of community leadership and education.
story_body: In 1910, the Russian government held an unprecedented rabbinic conference in St. Petersburg with the Rashab among the organizers. Debates centered on whether community rabbis needed secular education; Rabbi Chaim Ozer's compromise prevailed. The conference concluded with a disrespectful meeting with Prime Minister Pyotr Stolypin.

title_en: Rayatz arrested in St. Petersburg over conscription advocacy
summary_en: The Rayatz was briefly imprisoned in St. Petersburg for advocating military exemptions for young men.
story_body: In 1910, czarist authorities arrested the Rayatz in St. Petersburg for his efforts to exempt young Jewish men from military service. As with his other arrests between 1911 and 1916, the detention was brief and ended with a stern warning when no incriminating evidence was found.

title_en: Toras Emes yeshivah founded in Hebron
summary_en: The Rashab sent students led by Rabbi Zalman Havlin to Hebron to establish Toras Emes, the first chasidic yeshivah in the Jewish homeland.
story_body: In 1911, the Rashab dispatched a group of outstanding Tomchei Temimim students led by Rabbi Zalman Havlin to Hebron to establish Toras Emes. As a branch of Tomchei Temimim, it was intended to invigorate chasidic study in Eretz Yisrael and produce a new cadre of Jewish leaders for the land.

title_en: Rayatz letter outlines Hebron yeshivah purpose
summary_en: The Rayatz wrote a long letter to Rabbi Havlin and his students laying out the purpose of the Hebron yeshivah.
story_body: On 3 Kislev 5672 (November 24, 1911), the Rayatz sent a detailed letter to Rabbi Zalman Havlin and his Hebron students. It articulated the mission of Toras Emes: invigorating chasidic study in Eretz Yisrael and producing new Jewish leadership for the land, parallel to Tomchei Temimim's mission in Russia.

title_en: Mendel Beilis blood libel trial
summary_en: Mendel Beilis was tried in Kiev on blood libel charges; defense attorney Oscar Gruzenberg won acquittal.
story_body: In 1913, Kiev Jew Mendel Beilis was accused of murdering twelve-year-old Andrei Yushchinksy for ritual purposes. The Rayatz, dispatched by the Rashab, enlisted leading attorney Oscar Gruzenberg, who orchestrated a masterful defense culminating in a Shema declaration. Beilis was acquitted, but the trial drew worldwide attention to Russian anti-Semitism.

title_en: World War I erupts in Europe
summary_en: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand triggered World War I; Germany declared war on Russia that summer.
story_body: In 1914, the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria ignited World War I. Germany declared war on Russia that summer and invaded the following year, setting the stage for the upheaval that would eventually force the Rashab to flee Lubavitch.

title_en: Rashab speaks against Kaiser Wilhelm on Simchat Torah
summary_en: On Simchat Torah, the Rashab denounced Kaiser Wilhelm as a heretic and refused to live under his rule.
story_body: On Simchat Torah 1915, the Rashab declared, 'I know the kaiser well from the thirty years that I have been traveling outside Russia. He is an apikores, and under his rule I cannot dwell.' He recounted a Berlin episode in which Wilhelm had ordered police to remove him and the Rayatz from a public speech.

title_en: Rashab departs Lubavitch for Rostov-on-Don
summary_en: On 16 Cheshvan, the Rashab and his family abandoned Lubavitch ahead of the German advance, relocating to Rostov-on-Don.
story_body: On 16 Cheshvan 5676 (October 24, 1915), after 102 years of four Chabad Rebbes calling Lubavitch home, the Rashab and his family departed for Rostov-on-Don, seven hundred miles south of Moscow. The library was packed into 35 crates and stored in Moscow; the Rashab brought the valuable manuscripts with him.

title_en: Rayatz arrested in St. Petersburg
summary_en: The Rayatz was again imprisoned in St. Petersburg for advocating military exemptions for young Jewish men.
story_body: In 1916, the Rayatz was arrested for the fourth time between 1911 and 1916, again connected to his efforts to exempt young Jewish men from military service. As before, the detention was brief and ended with a warning rather than charges.

title_en: Russian Revolution
summary_en: Czar Nicholas II abdicated and was later executed amid the Russian Revolution.
story_body: In 1917, after years of anti-Jewish policy and wartime turmoil, Czar Nicholas II abdicated, ending the Romanov dynasty. He was later executed. The October Bolshevik Revolution that followed ushered in the Communist era and a new chapter of persecution for Russian Jewry.

title_en: Rayatz at Moscow and Kharkiv assemblies
summary_en: The Rayatz took a leading part in assemblies of rabbis and laymen in Moscow and Kharkiv.
story_body: In 1917 and 1918, against the backdrop of revolution and civil war, the Rayatz played a prominent role in rabbinic and lay assemblies convened in Moscow and Kharkiv to grapple with the future of Russian Jewish communal life.

title_en: Bolsheviks take control of Rostov
summary_en: Bolshevik forces took control of Rostov in January, ending consideration of emigration from Russia for the Rebbe's household.
story_body: In January 1920, the Bolsheviks consolidated control over Rostov. The new regime's arrival ended discussions in the Rashab's household about relocating outside Russia entirely. The Rashab curtailed public activities to avoid drawing the regime's attention.

title_en: Rashab's prophetic Purim-eve conversation with the Rayatz
summary_en: In a candlelit study, the Rashab entrusted the Rayatz with combatting Soviet anti-religious oppression at the cost of self-sacrifice.
story_body: On 8 Adar 5680 (February 27, 1920), the Rashab summoned the Rayatz into his candlelit study. He foretold at least twenty-two years of dark clouds for Russian Jewry, predicted the eventual fall of the Soviet regime and specific fates for Lenin, Trotsky, and Stalin, and charged his son with self-sacrifice to defend Torah and Judaism.

title_en: Rashab's final Purim farbrengen in Rostov
summary_en: Defying Bolshevik curfew, the Rashab led a twelve-hour Purim farbrengen as police looked on without intervening.
story_body: At the 1920 Purim celebration in Rostov, the Rashab insisted on a full farbrengen despite the 9 p.m. curfew. When Bolshevik officers entered the room, the Rashab continued teaching a maamar on evil as a false reality. The officers stood silently and then departed, and the farbrengen continued until morning light.

title_en: Passing of the Rebbe Rashab in Rostov
summary_en: Rabbi Shalom Dovber Schneersohn, the fifth Lubavitcher Rebbe, passed away in Rostov after a brief illness.
story_body: Two weeks after the Purim farbrengen, the Rashab fell ill on a Friday and was diagnosed with typhoid. On the following Shabbat night, after blessing each of his granddaughters and the Rayatz, he whispered the words 'bekhol levavkha uvekhol nafshekha' of Shema and his soul ascended, thrusting the Rayatz into the leadership of Chabad.

title_en: R. Boruch Ber moves yeshivah to Vilna
summary_en: Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz relocated his Slabodka yeshivah to Vilna.
story_body: In 1921, Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz moved Knesses Beis Yitzchak from Slabodka to Vilna. He would later move it again to Kamenitz in 1926, where it became one of the great Lithuanian yeshivas of the interwar period.

title_en: Toras Emes reconstituted in Jerusalem
summary_en: Rabbi Zalman Havlin returned to Eretz Yisrael and reestablished Toras Emes in Jerusalem.
story_body: Following the Rashab's instruction before his passing, Rabbi Zalman Havlin returned to Eretz Yisrael in 1922 and reconstituted Toras Emes in Jerusalem, where it continues to flourish as a center of chasidic scholarship to this day.

title_en: Death of Vladimir Lenin
summary_en: Soviet leader Vladimir Lenin died at age 53 after repeated strokes, fulfilling the Rashab's 1920 prediction.
story_body: In January 1924, three and a half years after the Rashab's prediction to the Rayatz, Lenin died at age fifty-three following multiple strokes and medical complications. His death set off a power struggle from which Stalin would emerge dominant.

title_en: R. Boruch Ber moves yeshivah to Kamenitz
summary_en: Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz relocated his yeshivah from Vilna to Kamenitz.
story_body: In 1926, Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz moved Knesses Beis Yitzchak from Vilna to Kamenitz, where it would remain one of the leading Lithuanian yeshivas until the Holocaust.

title_en: Trotsky banished to Alma Ata
summary_en: Stalin banished Leon Trotsky to remote Alma Ata in Kazakhstan.
story_body: In 1928, fulfilling the Rashab's 1920 forecast that Trotsky would be exiled, Stalin banished his rival to Alma Ata. Two years later, Trotsky would be deported from the Soviet Union entirely.

title_en: Yevesektzia dismantled in Soviet purges
summary_en: Stalin dismantled the Yevesektzia, killing and exiling its Jewish Communist leaders.
story_body: In 1930, the Yevesektzia, the anti-religious Jewish section of the Communist Party that had been a primary persecutor of Soviet Jews, was dismantled. Many of its leaders and activists were killed or exiled in the purges, fulfilling another of the Rashab's 1920 predictions.

title_en: Trotsky deported from Russia
summary_en: Two years after his banishment to Alma Ata, Leon Trotsky was deported from Russia entirely.
story_body: In 1930, having been banished to Alma Ata two years earlier, Trotsky was deported from the Soviet Union altogether. He moved through European cities before eventually settling in Mexico, where he would be assassinated a decade later.

title_en: Trotsky assassinated in Mexico City
summary_en: A Stalinist agent assassinated Leon Trotsky at his home in Mexico City.
story_body: In 1940, three years after a Moscow trial sentenced him to death in absentia, Leon Trotsky was assassinated by a Stalinist agent at his home in Mexico City. The killing completed the arc of Stalin's elimination of his exiled rival, fulfilling the Rashab's twenty-year-old prediction.

title_en: Lubavitch yeshivah opens in Samarkand
summary_en: A Lubavitch yeshivah opened in Samarkand during World War II, signaling a relaxation of Soviet religious persecution.
story_body: In 1942, twenty-two years after the Rashab's prediction to the Rayatz, the Soviet government's active religious persecution eased during World War II. A Lubavitch yeshivah opened in Samarkand, and the Russian Orthodox Church was again permitted to operate publicly.

title_en: Death of Joseph Stalin
summary_en: Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin died five days after Purim.
story_body: On March 5, 1953, Joseph Stalin died of a stroke, five days after Purim. At the Purim farbrengen that year, the seventh Rebbe had alluded to the death of the czar; when news of Stalin's collapse emerged, Chasidim saw a connection to those remarks.

title_en: Seventh Rebbe sends students to Australia
summary_en: The seventh Rebbe dispatched a group of elite students to Australia to establish a new center of Chabad learning.
story_body: In 1966, the seventh Rebbe began applying the model pioneered by the Rashab and Rayatz, dispatching senior students from the central yeshivas to seed new institutions abroad. The Australia dispatch became the template for the global network of some fifty Chabad yeshivas today.

title_en: Death of Nechama Dina Schneersohn
summary_en: Nechama Dina Schneersohn, wife of the Rayatz, passed away on 10 Shevat.
story_body: On 10 Shevat 5731 (January 7, 1971), Nechama Dina Schneersohn died at age 89. She had been the Rayatz's partner through engagement in Bolivke in 1896, marriage in 1897, the founding of Tomchei Temimim, exile, and the eventual move to America.

title_en: Volozhin yeshivah established
summary_en: The modern yeshivah movement began with the founding of the yeshivah in Volozhin.
story_body: In 1803, the yeshivah in Volozhin was established, launching the modern Eastern European yeshivah movement. Over time, other major Lithuanian-style yeshivas would follow in Slabodka, Mir, Telz, and Novardok.

title_en: Chabad community founded in Hebron
summary_en: Chasidim who had earlier immigrated to Safed and Tiberias established a Chabad community in Hebron.
story_body: In 1823, Chasidim who had first settled in Safed and Tiberias moved to Hebron, founding the Chabad community there. Rabbi Dovber, the second Rebbe, purchased a property for a synagogue, and his daughter Rebbetzin Menucha Rochel later immigrated to join the community.

title_en: Lilienthal Enlightenment education conference
summary_en: Max Lilienthal organized a government-backed conference in St. Petersburg to secularize Jewish education in Russia.
story_body: In 1843, German Enlightenment activist Max Lilienthal, backed by education minister Sergei Uvarov, organized a St. Petersburg conference to overhaul Jewish education in Russia. The third Chabad Rebbe, the Tzemach Tzedek, played a pivotal role in blocking Lilienthal's plans.

title_en: Rebbetzin Menucha Rochel immigrates to Hebron
summary_en: Rebbetzin Menucha Rochel, daughter of the Mitteler Rebbe, immigrated to Hebron.
story_body: In 1845, Rebbetzin Menucha Rochel, daughter of the second Chabad Rebbe Rabbi Dovber, immigrated to Hebron. Her descendants maintained a close connection with the Rebbes in Lubavitch, traveling there regularly and anchoring the Chabad presence in Hebron for generations.

title_en: Russian government rabbinical schools established
summary_en: The Russian government established 'rabbinical schools' in Vilna and Zhytomyr to train crown rabbis.
story_body: In 1847, the czarist government opened state-run rabbinical schools in Vilna and Zhytomyr to formalize the crown rabbinate. The schools were heavily influenced by the Enlightenment, and their graduates were poorly regarded by the Jewish public; the schools eventually closed, but the crown rabbi institution persisted.

title_en: Chevrah Mefitzei Haskalah (Chamah) founded
summary_en: Wealthy Russian Jews founded Chevrah Mefitzei Haskalah to promote secular Jewish education and assimilation.
story_body: In 1863, backed by some of Russia's wealthiest Jews including the Gunzburg dynasty, the Society to Promote the Enlightenment (Chamah) was established. Its mission was to promote Jewish assimilation into Russian society, and by 1900 it had grown to 150 schools.

title_en: Knesses Yisrael yeshivah founded in Slabodka
summary_en: Rabbi Nosson Tzvi Finkel founded Yeshivas Knesses Yisrael in Slabodka, originally as a kollel for married men.
story_body: In 1877, Rabbi Nosson Tzvi Finkel established Knesses Yisrael in Slabodka as a kollel for married men. It soon became a full yeshivah and introduced systematic study of musar, sparking the controversy that would lead opponents to open the rival Knesses Beis Yitzchak in 1897.

title_en: May Laws expanded under Alexander III
summary_en: The May Laws were expanded, further tightening restrictions on Russian Jews.
story_body: In 1885, three years after their initial enactment, Czar Alexander III expanded the May Laws. The reinforced restrictions on residency, education, and economic activity accelerated mass Jewish emigration from Russia to the United States and other Western countries.

title_en: Death of Czar Alexander III
summary_en: Czar Alexander III died and was succeeded by his son Nicholas II, the last Russian czar.
story_body: In 1894, Alexander III died after thirteen years of repressive rule. His son Nicholas II succeeded him and continued the anti-Jewish policies of his predecessors, blaming Jews for Russia's troubles and presiding over both the Beilis trial and the eventual collapse of the Romanov dynasty.

title_en: Rashab buried in Rostov Jewish cemetery
summary_en: Rabbi Sholom DovBer Schneersohn, the fifth Lubavitcher Rebbe, was buried in Rostov hours after his Saturday night passing.
story_body: The casket was carried to the cemetery by yeshivah students and elders of anash, with the whole Jewish community of the city present. Standing at his father's fresh grave, the Rayatz publicly appointed three rabbis as a beit din and declared he was purchasing the plot conditionally, reserving the right to later reinter the Rashab in the ancestral burial ground in Lubavitch. The German invasion and the revolution had prevented the return to Lubavitch.

title_en: Yiddishes Tageblatt predicts end of Chabad
summary_en: Jonathan Mark's New York Yiddish newspaper wrote that the Rashab left no fitting successor in his son.
story_body: Following the Rashab's passing, Jewish newspapers worldwide predicted the end of Chabad. In the Yiddishes Tageblatt, Jonathan Mark opined that the Rashab's son lacked the aptitude to follow in his place. Seven years later, Mark reversed course and praised the new Rebbe in his book Gedolim Fun Unzer Tzeit.

title_en: Rayatz arrested by Cheka during morning prayers
summary_en: Three Cheka officers brought the Rayatz from the Rostov synagogue to a police station for interrogation about Judaism and Kabbalah.
story_body: During the year of mourning for his father, the Rayatz was confronted by three armed officers, two of them Jewish Yevsektzia members, who demanded he remove his tallit and tefillin and come with them. At the police station, fifteen armed officers sat around a conference table to intimidate him. When one threatened with his gun, the Rayatz replied that 'this toy' impresses only those with no faith — 'we have one G-d and two worlds.'

title_en: Yeshivah relocates from Kremenchuk to Rostov
summary_en: Facing starvation in Ukraine, Tomchei Temimim moved to Rostov to be near the new Rebbe.
story_body: During the war the yeshivah had been transferred from Lubavitch to Kremenchuk, but with key Jewish supporters fleeing the city, students were forced to ration bread to every other day. The Rayatz declared, 'I want Tomchei Temimim to be next to me,' and within two weeks roughly eighty boys arrived, many ill and in torn clothing. Rabbi Shmuel Gurary borrowed funds and sold personal property to keep the yeshivah afloat.

title_en: Rayatz falls ill with typhus in Rostov
summary_en: The Rayatz became too weak to lead evening services as the typhus epidemic struck his household.
story_body: On the night of 28 Marcheshvan 5681, the Rebbe could no longer lead services. In the following days his mother Rebbetzin Shterna Sara and his three daughters also fell ill. Doctors gave him little chance of surviving, with Professor Milsalavski telling Goldin that medically there was no cure.

title_en: Rayatz begins recovery from typhus on 19 Kislev
summary_en: The Rebbe's condition turned the corner on the Chasidic festival commemorating the Alter Rebbe's release from czarist prison.
story_body: After about three weeks of grave illness, the tide turned on 19 Kislev — the day marking Rabbi Schneur Zalman's 1798 release from prison and regarded as the New Year of Chabad Chasidism. Yeshivah students had been praying at the Rashab's ohel led by Reb Itche der Masmid, and a rabbinical court collected written pledges from students donating years of their lives, reportedly totaling thirty years.

title_en: Rayatz farbrengs for hours on Purim after fast collapse
summary_en: Though he fainted observing the Fast of Esther, the Rebbe recited a maamar for two and a half hours on Purim.
story_body: Still recuperating from typhus, the Rebbe asked his doctor whether he could farbreng and say a maamar on Purim. The doctor allowed it but instructed him to limit the maamar to fifteen minutes. The next day the Rebbe spoke for two and a half hours and remained with the Chasidim for more than three additional hours.

title_en: Vitebsk cheder show trial halted by 5,000 protesters
summary_en: Thousands of local Jews protested a Yevsektzia staged trial of the traditional cheder in Vitebsk.
story_body: Five thousand local Jews came out shouting to stop the trial and threatening to close the cinema where it was being held, while thousands more assembled in local synagogues. Uneasy Yevsektzia members called off the trial after physical threats, but they regrouped soon after. A second trial was held in which the cheder was sentenced to be liquidated.

title_en: Yevsektzia stages show trial against Lubavitch yeshivah
summary_en: A trial in Rostov demanded the closure of Tomchei Temimim and conscription of its students into the workforce.
story_body: The Yevsektzia 'testified with lies' and forcefully demanded that the yeshivah be closed and that its students be added to the army of workers. During this period they also forced their way into the Rebbe's home, seizing household goods, clothing, and silver inherited from his father. Three students and the Rebbe's future son-in-law Rabbi Shmaryahu Gurary were imprisoned for five days.

title_en: Chafetz Chaim transfers yeshivah back to Poland
summary_en: Rabbi Yisrael Meir Kagan, in his early eighties, moved his Radin yeshivah out of Soviet Russia.
story_body: Having transferred the yeshivah to Russia in 1915 at the start of World War I, the Chafetz Chaim moved it back to Poland in 1921. Stopping in Minsk, he told the local rabbi Nissan Telushkin that he had no strength left to battle the malicious government and 'the evil renegades' forcing yeshivah students to desecrate Shabbat. Later in life he reportedly regretted leaving.

title_en: Cheka issues release document for Rayatz
summary_en: The secret police formally attested to the release of Rabbi Schneersohn weeks after the interrogation.
story_body: Following the previous summer's interrogation in Rostov, the Cheka issued a document attesting to the Rebbe's release. It was just one act in a years-long drama of conflict with the Yevsektzia that would culminate in arrest and exile six years later.

title_en: Chicago Sentinel reports starving Lubavitch students
summary_en: The American Jewish newspaper described starvation among yeshivah students who had evacuated Lubavitch for Rostov.
story_body: The Sentinel reported that 'the yeshivah students who have evacuated Lubavitch for Rostov-on-Don are starving.' The financial pressures, famine, and disease prompted some students to leave the yeshivah and return home. Once one of the great centers of European Jewish scholarship, the yeshivah was whittled down to just forty students in Rostov.

title_en: Rayatz reflects in letter on assuming leadership
summary_en: On 10 Shevat 5682 the Rayatz wrote of his shock at reading his father's instruction that he assume the leadership.
story_body: The Rayatz revealed that his eyes 'darkened' when he read that the leadership of the community was placed on him. He became deeply ill from the weight of the responsibility but was restored to life and committed to following his father's sacred instructions. Decades later, 10 Shevat would become the date of his own passing in 1950.

title_en: Tomchei Temimim relocates to Poltava
summary_en: Forty students traveled four hundred miles by horse and wagon to a more hospitable Ukrainian city.
story_body: Unable to obtain authorization to travel by train, the students made the long trip by wagon. The Rebbe appointed Rabbi Yechezkel (Chatche) Feigin as administrator of the central yeshivah in Poltava. The local Chabad community of some twenty thousand Jews was diverse and better organized, and the Yevsektzia had less influence there.

title_en: Rayatz writes to Agudath Israel about home schooling
summary_en: The Rebbe wrote to Agudath Israel leaders in the United States about ongoing local harassment of religious home schooling.
story_body: After the Rabbinical Committee blocked a 1923 proposal by the People's Commiserate of Justice to close loopholes permitting religious home instruction, the Rebbe acknowledged the partial victory. Despite the formal ruling allowing private religious instruction for up to six children, local authorities continued to harass teachers. The letter is preserved in Igrot Kodesh.

title_en: Secret covenant of ten in Moscow
summary_en: The Rayatz convened nine Chasidim to form a clandestine network to preserve Judaism under Soviet rule.
story_body: In the winter of 1924, with decrees against Torah students and Jewish schools intensifying, nine temimim gathered in Moscow and the Rebbe completed the quorum of ten. They swore an oath to defiantly fortify Judaism under the Soviet regime, even to the point of mesirat nefesh. The known members included Elchonon Dov Morozov, Bentzion Shemtov, Simon Yakovshvili, and Yerachmiel Binyaminson; classes were held in cold, windowless dungeons dug into the ground.

title_en: Rebbe's home in Rostov searched by Yevsektzia
summary_en: Yevsektzia officers searched the Rebbe's house and threatened arrest, prompting the eventual move to Leningrad.
story_body: Returning from meetings in Moscow, the Rayatz was met outside Rostov by his secretary Rabbi Morozov with ominous news that the Yevsektzia had searched his house. The search ended at four a.m., and only intervention by influential locals prevented arrest. Soon afterward, the Rebbe relocated to Leningrad.

title_en: Rabbinical Committee secures JDC funding
summary_en: The American Joint Distribution Committee began diverting funds to 'cultural work' supporting the Rebbe's network.
story_body: Funding was critical to the Rabbinical Committee's success, and Dr. Joseph Rosen, the JDC representative in Russia, directed money to the Rebbe for educational projects. The 'cultural work' label was code for religious education and the activities of the committee of rabbis. Allocations also supported home-based industry job training for urban Jews.

title_en: Leningrad Jewish Religious Community gains state recognition
summary_en: LERO became the formally recognized central Jewish communal body in Leningrad under Lev Gurewicz.
story_body: Gurewicz, a Zionist lawyer with limited Jewish education, led LERO and harbored ambitions to unite all of Russian Jewry in a national congress. In the summer of 1925 he met the Rebbe for the first time and proposed a partnership. The Rebbe was lukewarm, sensing risks that would later prove justified.

title_en: JDC report counts 15,000 children in secret schools
summary_en: A confidential aide-memoire described the underground Jewish education system operating across the USSR.
story_body: The confidential report sent to the JDC in New York stated that some fifteen thousand children were being educated in a growing number of secret schools. In Moscow alone, three hundred children studied in groups of three, hiding in cellars and venturing to the woods in summer. Each teacher was paid thirty rubles a month, with another thirty rubles paid to a watchman keeping lookout for authorities.

title_en: Korosten rabbinical conference in Ukraine
summary_en: Nearly one hundred rabbis gathered in Korosten; Rayatz was unanimously elected honorary chairman.
story_body: The Rebbe was skeptical the conference would be productive but believed the noble intentions of organizer Rabbi Zev Kipnis would prevent harm. He dispatched Bentzion Shemtov to ensure an agenda strengthening Jewish education. When the Rebbe's telegram was read aloud, all the rabbis stood in respect — but the esteem displayed alarmed the Communist authorities, who had hoped the conference would divide Russian Jewry.

title_en: Ten religious members resign from LERO board
summary_en: The traditionalist minority quit LERO after the reformist majority secretly implemented religious changes.
story_body: The board of LERO had twenty-four members split between those wanting to retain classic Jewish education and those wishing to modernize. After reformers were exposed implementing unilateral changes, the ten religious members resigned in October 1926 accusing LERO of acting unethically. Weeks later they petitioned the government for recognition of a new religious organization.

title_en: Rayatz writes to Katzenellenbogen urging caution
summary_en: The Rebbe asked the chief rabbi of Leningrad not to act unilaterally on plans for a national conference.
story_body: Gurewicz had been traveling Russia falsely claiming the Rebbe's endorsement for a national congress. In a personal handwritten letter to Rabbi David Tevel Katzenellenbogen dated 23 Cheshvan 5687, the Rayatz wrote that the idea required further consideration and urged consultation with other rabbinic leaders. The chief rabbi was being misled by LERO's leadership.

title_en: Morozov's Zionist daughters arrested in Leningrad
summary_en: Rachel and Sara Morozov were arrested for belonging to the Zionist organization Dror.
story_body: Rabbi Elchonon Morozov's two daughters were drawn from religious observance by the lure of secular Zionism. They were arrested on February 9 for activities in Dror, weeks before their father was also seized. When they learned their father was being mistreated in prison, they declared a hunger strike until his conditions improved.

title_en: Rabbi Elchonon Morozov arrested
summary_en: The Rebbe's chief secretary and key underground coordinator was jailed, initially accused of smuggling books abroad.
story_body: Morozov was held with the worst political prisoners, creating an ominous atmosphere among the Chabad community. Before being taken, he secretly handed the list of underground yeshivas and schools to his eleven-year-old son, who hid it without the police noticing. In May 1927 he was indicted for helping Jews cross the border illegally and sentenced to three years exile in Krasnoyarsk.

title_en: Yevsektzia raid foiled at Moscow hotel
summary_en: A Yevsektzia officer's attempt to arrest the Rayatz at a Moscow hotel was thwarted by a senior OGPU official.
story_body: The Rebbe had traveled to Moscow under tight secrecy to meet JDC representatives. After being smuggled between hotels, he met with Mark Semyonovitch Bashkov, an OGPU executive board member he had encountered on the train. When Yevsektzia officer Krotov burst in with armed men, Bashkov produced his credentials — and the would-be arresters 'stood like blocks of wood, as if thunderstruck' and fled.

title_en: Rayatz holds defiant Purim farbrengen in Leningrad
summary_en: The Rebbe screamed defiance at the Yevsektzia during a fiery Purim gathering filled with informants.
story_body: Rabbi Zalman Duchman described the farbrengen as 'terrifying.' The Rayatz shouted, 'Who is the Yevsektzia? A rabbi's son? A butcher's son? I am not frightened by them!' He urged Chasidim to spread Judaism with self-sacrifice, telling one follower: 'Zalman, if they ever build a bonfire and confront you with the choice of yielding your child to their schools or casting yourself into the flames, let yourself be cast into the flames!'

title_en: Shemtov arrested after Korosten conference work
summary_en: Bentzion Shemtov was arrested in Korosten and held in Kharkiv for a month until Passover.
story_body: The secret police had discovered Shemtov's activities and his role at the Rabbinical Conference. After release at Passover, he was detained again in June on the same day the Rebbe was arrested in Leningrad. He was held for another thirty days and grilled about the clandestine Chabad system before being released pending trial.

title_en: Leningrad conference announced for October
summary_en: Just after Passover, the Leningrad community publicly scheduled its long-debated national Jewish congress.
story_body: Despite the Rebbe's opposition, LERO pressed ahead with plans for an October conference. The plan was secretly backed by the Yevsektzia, who saw it as a chance to create alternative leadership and divert JDC funds away from the Rebbe's network. With Moscow and Minsk withholding approval, the scheme faltered — making drastic action against the Rebbe a matter of time.

title_en: Shemtov marries Esther Golda in Siberian exile
summary_en: After three years exile in Siberia, Bentzion Shemtov married his fiancée in a remote village near the Trans-Siberian railroad.
story_body: Esther Golda Futerfus made the long trek to Siberia in summer 1930 to join her fiancé. The wedding was held in Yanivskiek, about fifty miles from the railroad; lacking a mikveh, she hacked through an icy river to immerse. With no ring, Shemtov fashioned one from a silver fork, and exiled chasidic rabbi Shmuel Levitin officiated.

title_en: Yevsektzia dismantled by Stalin
summary_en: Stalin disbanded the Jewish section of the Communist Party; many of its leaders were later killed in the purges.
story_body: Established in 1917 to fortify Bolshevik control over Jewish masses, the Yevsektzia had been the Rayatz's primary adversary throughout the 1920s. After 1930 many of its leaders, including Semyon Dimenstein and Moshe Litvakov, were killed or exiled in the Great Purge. After the Yevsektzia was disbanded, government actions against synagogues and religious leaders actually became harsher.

title_en: Rebbetzin's third Rebbe predecessor dies in Bobruysk
summary_en: Rabbi Shmaryahu Noach Schneersohn of Bobruysk, last leader of the rival Chabad dynasties, passed away.
story_body: After the 1869 passing of the third Rebbe Rabbi Menachem Mendel (Tzemach Tzedek), four of his sons established themselves as competing Rebbes in other towns while his youngest, Rabbi Shmuel, became Rebbe in Lubavitch. Those rival dynasties petered out without successors. With Rabbi Shmaryahu Noach's passing, the last of those branches ended and his Chasidim gravitated to the Rebbe Rayatz.

title_en: Habima theater troupe departs Russia for tour
summary_en: The Hebrew-language Habima Theater left the Soviet Union on a government-sanctioned tour and never returned.
story_body: Established in 1917 with state recognition, Habima had been a Yevsektzia target since Dimenstein protested its 1919 grant from the Soviet ministry of culture. The whole troupe departed in 1926 and relocated to Tel Aviv. In 1958 Habima became the official national theater of Israel.

title_en: Yakovshvili arrested in Moscow
summary_en: Armed men burst into Simon Yakovshvili's home, accusing him of counterrevolutionary activity.
story_body: Yakovshvili was offered freedom in exchange for confirming the counterrevolutionary status of one hundred named Jews; he refused. He was flogged repeatedly and ultimately given a death sentence. Minutes before execution, an edict from fellow Georgian Lavrentiy Beria — head of Stalin's secret police — spared his life, though he served nearly a decade in the gulag.

title_en: Morozov killed by firing squad
summary_en: The Rebbe's longtime secretary was executed after refusing to deny his true identity to interrogators.
story_body: Having hidden since 1930 under the false identity Berke Pesner, Morozov was finally caught in 1938 along with his son Shmuel. Police tortured Shmuel to confirm his father's identity; Morozov cried out, 'Shmuel, tell them that I am your father!' Police told Morozov his crime was being 'a representative of the Lubavitcher Rebbe, who is G-d's representative in Russia.'

title_en: Rabbi Moshe Feinstein immigrates to United States
summary_en: The rabbi of Lyuban, Belorussia, received an exit visa through American relatives' lobbying.
story_body: Like dozens of other rabbis, Reb Moshe had stayed in Russia trying to preserve a core of observant Jews despite Yevsektzia oppression. He later became dean of Mesivta Tifereth Jerusalem and one of the greatest Jewish legal scholars of the twentieth century. He recalled discovering a family connection to Chabad — his great-grandmother Rochel had been a classmate of the Tzemach Tzedek in the Alter Rebbe's cheder.

title_en: Rabbi Yechezkel Feigin killed in Warsaw synagogue fire
summary_en: The Rebbe's longtime secretary perished when Nazis burned a Warsaw synagogue with Jews trapped inside.
story_body: Passport issues had prevented Feigin from leaving Riga with the Rebbe in 1939 for the United States. In December 1941, Nazis brought most of the city's Jews into a synagogue and set it ablaze, forcing other Jews to watch. According to some reports, Rabbi Yitzchak Gurevitz removed the Torah scroll from the ark and danced with Feigin as they burned alive; when news reached the Rebbe in 1945, he fainted from grief.

title_en: Yeshivah branch established in Samarkand
summary_en: During wartime evacuation, a branch of Tomchei Temimim opened in remote Uzbekistan.
story_body: As Chabad Chasidim fled the German invasion to Central Asia, a branch of the yeshivah was established in Samarkand. Within a short period another branch opened in Tashkent. These wartime outposts later became the nucleus that sustained Jewish life in the region for decades.

title_en: Rabbi Aryeh Leib Kaplan killed on Yom Kippur
summary_en: The Slabodka-trained rabbi who heeded the Rayatz's advice to remain in Russia was murdered by anti-Semitic thugs.
story_body: Kaplan had been planning to immigrate to Palestine in 1922 when the Rayatz advised him to stay and help Russian Jews: 'If you protect the children of G-d, G-d will watch over your children.' He served as a rabbi near Kiev until his 1939 arrest and exile to Uzbekistan, where on the train he met Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson. His children all later escaped to Israel and the United States.

title_en: Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch founded by Rayatz
summary_en: The Rayatz established Chabad's central educational organization, the first network of Jewish day schools in the U.S.
story_body: While other postwar Orthodox leaders focused on yeshivas as citadels of scholarship for a small nucleus, the Rebbe campaigned for fundamental change in general Jewish life worldwide. Merkos became the engine for that mission, predating other national Jewish educational organizations such as Torah Umesorah. The work would later expand into the global shluchim network.

title_en: Chabad mass escape from Soviet Union on Polish passports
summary_en: Roughly one thousand Chabad Chasidim fled the USSR using forged Polish documents in a clandestine operation.
story_body: Among those who escaped were Bentzion Shemtov, the Yakovshvili family (who changed their name to the more Polish-sounding Jacobson), and many activists from the underground network. After surviving the war in Tashkent and elsewhere, they masquerade as Polish refugees. Most were later resettled by the Rebbe to communities around the world.

title_en: Shemtovs sent to build Chabad in England
summary_en: Following their escape from Russia, the Rebbe dispatched Bentzion Shemtov and family to develop the Chabad community in England.
story_body: Having survived three years in Siberia and decades of underground activism, Shemtov was sent on a new mission to the United Kingdom. He worked to build the Chabad community there before later moving to Israel, where he founded Machon Levi Yitzchak to publish the seventh Rebbe's talks in Hebrew. He passed away in 1975 at age seventy-two.

title_en: Simon Jacobson dies in Toronto
summary_en: The Georgian-born underground rabbi died at age 53, broken by years of torture in the Soviet gulag.
story_body: After immigrating to Toronto in 1952 with his family, Jacobson was appointed rabbi of the local Chabad congregation. His grandson Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Jacobson recalled, 'he was worn out from years of suffering.' He passed away in June 1953, followed by his wife two years later, leaving three orphaned sons.

title_en: Yiddish school network peaks at 1,100 schools
summary_en: The state-run Yiddish school system reached its peak with around 130,000 students.
story_body: The Yevsektzia championed Yiddish as the language of the 'Jewish proletariat' while abolishing Hebrew study and Zionist culture. By 1929 there were 1,100 such schools across the Soviet Union. Jewish religion, history, Hebrew, and tradition were excluded from the curriculum, and many religious parents sent children to non-Jewish schools to avoid the anti-religious propaganda.

title_en: Jews begin settling in Birobidzhan
summary_en: Stalin's Jewish province on the Chinese border opened for settlement, with Yiddish street signs but banned religious practice.
story_body: To promote secular Jewish socialism, the Soviet government created a Jewish autonomous province in remote Siberia.
