Religious practice was banned and the Jewish population never rose above forty-five thousand. Only after the fall of the Soviet Union did Judaism return to Birobidzhan, when Rabbi Mordechai Scheiner became the community's rabbi in 2002.

title_en: Tomchei Temimim yeshivah founded in Lubavitch
summary_en: The Rashab established the flagship Chabad yeshivah with a small select group of outstanding scholars.
story_body: Among the first students chosen was Elchonon Morozov, born 1877, who excelled to the point that the Rashab selected him as the personal study partner for his son the Rayatz. Tomchei Temimim was a revolutionary accomplishment close to the Rashab's heart — both the key to continuity of chasidic teachings and an incubator for new Jewish leadership. It would remain the last bastion of Jewish scholarship functioning in the Soviet Union.

title_en: England severs diplomatic relations with Russia over espionage
summary_en: Britain cut diplomatic ties with the Soviet Union after exposing Russian spies operating in the United Kingdom.
story_body: At the end of May 1927, Conservative Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin presented Parliament with deciphered Soviet telegrams proving espionage activities by the All-Russian Co-operative Society. The break in diplomatic relations heightened Soviet paranoia. Together with the assassination of ambassador Voykov, it provided pretext for Stalin's wave of internal repression that swept up the Lubavitcher Rebbe.

title_en: Latvia signs trade agreement with the Soviet Union
summary_en: Latvia signed a commerce treaty with Soviet Russia that still required ratification by the Latvian parliament.
story_body: Though Latvia needed the deal more than the Soviets, the Bolsheviks wanted it as a step in peeling the Baltic states away from the West. Internal Latvian opposition meant the trade agreement had to be ratified by the Saeima. Mordechai Dubin's swing vote later became leverage to pressure Moscow into releasing the Rebbe and granting him an exit visa.

title_en: Soviet ambassador Pyotr Voykov assassinated in Warsaw
summary_en: A Russian monarchist killed Soviet ambassador Pyotr Voykov at the Warsaw train station in retaliation for his role in the czar's execution.
story_body: Voykov, who was Jewish and had been active with Stalin in the Bolshevik party, had been denied accreditation by Canada but accepted as ambassador to Poland. His assassination unleashed Stalin's accusations of a foreign monarchist network tied to Britain, leading to mass executions of former nobles and clergy in the Soviet Union.

title_en: Stalin unleashes wave of executions after Voykov assassination
summary_en: Stalin ordered the execution of former nobility and clergy across Russia and empowered the GPU with extrajudicial emergency tribunals.
story_body: In response to the Voykov assassination and the British diplomatic break, Stalin claimed a foreign monarchist plot and unleashed widespread repression. Party organizations affirmed the executions at hundreds of factory meetings, and the GPU received emergency authority to expedite cases. The Yevsektsia seized the moment to move against the Lubavitcher Rebbe, their most fiery religious adversary.

title_en: GPU arrests Rebbe Rayatz at his Leningrad apartment
summary_en: Just after midnight on June 15, 1927, armed GPU agents burst into Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn's Leningrad apartment and arrested him.
story_body: Officers Mikhail Nachmanson and Grigory Lulov, both from Chabad families, led a contingent of armed men in a search lasting an hour and a half. The Rebbe recited grace slowly to allow family members to conceal incriminating documents. Despite his daughters' pleas and his mother Shterna Sara's tearful outburst, he was taken at 2:20 a.m. to the notorious Shpalerka prison.

title_en: Rebbe's secretary Chaim Lieberman arrested after burning documents
summary_en: GPU agents arrested Rabbi Chaim Lieberman, the Rebbe's secretary, just after he finished burning records of the secret school system.
story_body: Warned by Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson that the GPU had raided the Rebbe's home, Lieberman immediately burned all financial records and correspondence related to the underground Jewish school network. The fire had not yet consumed everything when officers knocked at his door, but they found nothing usable. He was arrested anyway and interrogated.

title_en: Rebbe begins hunger strike in Shpalerka prison demanding tefillin
summary_en: After being struck and having his tefillin confiscated, the Rebbe refused food until they were returned.
story_body: Following his arrival at Shpalerka, the Rebbe insisted on his right to pray with tefillin and was beaten and pushed down a ladder by a guard. His belt buckle gashed his stomach. When the prison warden told him to forget the 'foolishness,' the Rebbe began a hunger strike that lasted until Friday before sunset.

title_en: Rebbe interrogated by GPU officers in Shpalerka prison
summary_en: Two nights after his arrest, Nachmanson, Lulov and two others interrogated the Rebbe and threatened him with execution within 24 hours.
story_body: The interrogators rested their hands on weapons laid on the table, accusing the Rebbe of counterrevolutionary activity, leading Soviet Jewry, influencing American bourgeois Jews through the JDC, and operating a network of religious institutions. The Rebbe rebuffed them, citing Soviet law that did not ban religious teaching. As the session ended, Lulov declared, 'In twenty-four hours, you will be shot.'

title_en: Rebbe receives tefillin and challah in Shpalerka prison
summary_en: After 72 hours of fasting, a Jewish guard delivered the Rebbe's tefillin and books, and challah from home arrived before sunset.
story_body: Friday before Shabbat, the Rebbe finally received his tefillin and sefarim. He refused the prison's non-kosher meals and demanded food from home. Just before sunset, three loaves of uncut challah were delivered to his cell, breaking his hunger strike.

title_en: Rebbe undergoes second GPU interrogation in Shpalerka
summary_en: The Rebbe insisted he was a teacher of chasidic philosophy uninvolved in politics, and confirmed his opposition to the planned Leningrad Jewish conference.
story_body: Recovered GPU file no. 898 shows the Rebbe maintained the same position before and after the revolution. He affirmed his opposition to the Yevsektsia-supported conference of Russian Jewish kehillot, which had become the immediate flashpoint for his arrest.

title_en: Rebbe's first postcard from prison delivered to family
summary_en: A Shabbat postcard from the Rebbe reached his family declaring he was well, despite the beatings he had endured.
story_body: On Shabbat June 25, the family received the Rebbe's first written word from Shpalerka. Although he had been repeatedly beaten and was in excruciating pain, his message was upbeat. He requested sefarim including Likkutei Torah and Chumash Bemidbar.

title_en: Rebbe's death sentence commuted to Solovki exile
summary_en: Madam Peshkova's intercession and international outcry caused the GPU to replace the Rebbe's death sentence with ten years' exile in Solovki.
story_body: On Wednesday June 29, an official informed Rabbi Eliyahu Chaim Althaus that the firing-squad verdict had been commuted to exile in the remote Solovki Islands prison camp. The family was told to bring food and say goodbye. A crowd gathered outside the prison as Lulov tried one last time to extort a public retraction from the Rebbe, who refused.

title_en: Rebbe released for home visit and exiled to Kostroma (3 Tamuz)
summary_en: After nineteen days in Shpalerka, the Rebbe was permitted six hours at home before boarding a train into three-year exile in Kostroma.
story_body: Continued lobbying by Madam Peshkova overturned the Solovki decree, and the sentence was reduced to three years in Kostroma. The Rebbe refused to leave on Thursday because the journey would violate Shabbat; he was kept until Sunday morning July 3. At Leningrad station thousands of Jews formed an honor guard as he gave a defiant speech declaring that only Jewish bodies, not souls, are subject to foreign rule.

title_en: Rebbe notified of unconditional release from Kostroma exile (12 Tamuz)
summary_en: When the Rebbe came for his weekly check-in at GPU headquarters in Kostroma, an officer informed him that orders had arrived from Moscow freeing him.
story_body: Sustained pressure from Madam Peshkova, telegrams to President Kalinin and Premier Rykov, and international protests forced Moscow to overturn the exile. On Tuesday July 12, the Kostroma GPU station was closed for a local holiday, but an officer told Althaus the release papers had arrived. The seventh Rebbe would later establish 12 Tamuz as an annual festival of liberation.

title_en: Rebbe returns to Leningrad from Kostroma exile
summary_en: Two days after his release, the Rebbe arrived back in Leningrad, despite the GPU's threat to re-arrest him.
story_body: Word of the liberation spread quickly across the Soviet Union; in Kharkiv, Rabbi Hillel Levin received a telegram and Chasidim gathered at Rabbi Aharon Tomarkin's home to celebrate. In Leningrad, Stanislav Messing had opposed the release and threatened to arrest the Rebbe again. The Rebbe recited HaGomel that first Shabbat before relocating to Malakhovka outside Moscow.

title_en: Riga Jewish community formally invites Rebbe as chief rabbi
summary_en: On 23 Menachem Av, the Riga Jewish community formally invited the Rebbe to serve as its chief rabbi, providing legal cover for an exit visa.
story_body: Mordechai Dubin, a Chabad chasid and member of the Latvian Saeima, presented the invitation to Russian officials, who initially rejected it. Simultaneously Dr. Oscar Cohn delivered an invitation from Frankfurt's Jewish community. Dubin then leveraged his swing vote on the unratified Latvia-Soviet trade agreement to extract the exit visa from Moscow.

title_en: Feigin writes urgent appeal to American Chasidim for funds
summary_en: Rabbi Yechezkel Feigin cryptically pleaded with Eliyahu Simpson and Yisrael Jacobson in America to wire funds for the Rebbe's relocation and the secret school system.
story_body: Using code language about 'illness' and 'expert doctors' to evade censors, Feigin warned that miracles do not happen every day and the Rebbe had to be moved to Riga immediately. His letter conveyed both the cost of imprisonment and the ongoing financial demands of keeping underground institutions afloat.

title_en: JTA publishes report from Riga on cause of Rebbe's arrest
summary_en: The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported that the Rebbe's arrest stemmed from his opposition to the planned conference of Soviet Jewish kehillot.
story_body: The JTA's Riga dispatch said that 'well-informed circles in Moscow' traced the arrest to the Lubavitcher Rebbe's resistance to the Leningrad conference set for October 21, 1927. The conference's initiators, it reported, decided to discredit the Rebbe before Soviet authorities to remove his opposition.

title_en: Rebbe celebrates last Simchat Torah with Russian Chasidim
summary_en: The Rebbe spent his final holiday in the Soviet Union surrounded by Chasidim who packed his Leningrad synagogue beyond capacity.
story_body: Despite the risk of arrest, Chasidim flocked from across the country. The room, with a normal capacity of six hundred, swelled with hundreds more. The Rebbe urged each Chasid to influence their community, declaring 'I will be with you.' At the train station thousands lined the platform, and one Chasid, Rabbi Meir Simcha Chein, wept, 'The Rebbe is going, and we are left here.'

title_en: Rebbe writes letter to anash and temimim in Russia (19 Kislev)
summary_en: From outside Russia, the Rebbe wrote to his Chasidim 'in the country of my birth' saying he had been forced to leave.
story_body: Marking the Chabad festival of 19 Kislev, the Rebbe addressed his followers in the Soviet Union, recounting the Yevsektsia's persecution of his efforts to strengthen Torah. 'I was forced to leave Russia,' he wrote. 'My heart and soul are with the anash and temimim in our country.'

title_en: Rebbe declares 12 Tamuz a festival of liberation in public letter
summary_en: On the first anniversary of his release, the Rebbe published a letter establishing 12 Tamuz as a yearly festival for all who love Torah.
story_body: Written from his new residence, the letter framed the anniversary as a celebration not only for the observant but for 'all those who merely bear the name Jew,' since every Jewish heart is bound with God and Torah. Since then, 12 Tamuz has been marked annually in Jewish communities across the world.

title_en: Rebbe writes letter blaming Voykov reprisals for clergy crackdown
summary_en: In a letter dated 19 Iyar 5688, the Rebbe described how Soviet authorities struck out at religious leaders to avenge Voykov's assassination and the British expulsion.
story_body: The Rebbe explained that the 1927 wave of repression against clergy of all faiths was tied to two international shocks: the rupture with England and the killing of the Soviet ambassador in Warsaw. The Yevsektsia, he wrote, exploited the moment to act against him.

title_en: Soviets shut down yeshiva in Nevel
summary_en: Authorities closed the American-subsidized yeshiva in Nevel a year after the Rebbe's arrest.
story_body: The Nevel yeshiva, located in a Chabad enclave about 120 miles from Lubavitch, had been an important center of religious learning. Its closure, reported by the JTA on November 2, 1928, was part of the ongoing campaign against Jewish religious education in the Soviet Union.

title_en: Rebbe writes reflection on the meaning of his 1927 imprisonment
summary_en: In a letter dated 17 Iyar 5694, the Rebbe wrote that suffering for an ideal develops a person's abilities and transforms weakness into strength.
story_body: Years after the ordeal, the Rebbe reflected that his eighteen days, eleven hours, and fifteen minutes in Shpalerka should be marked down to the minute. Every moment of suffering for the strengthening of religion, he wrote, brings tremendous reward and infinite fortitude of mind.

title_en: Mikhail Nachmanson arrested by Soviet authorities
summary_en: One of the two officers who arrested the Rebbe was himself arrested on his birthday and sentenced to a labor camp in Kolyma.
story_body: Nachmanson, a Nevel-born Chabad-family Chasid turned Bolshevik who had risen to head regional NKVD departments, was transferred to Lubyanka Prison and given an extrajudicial five-year sentence. He was released in 1941, re-arrested in 1950, freed in 1953 after Stalin's death, and amnestied in 1956 — yet remained a committed Communist until the Soviet Union's collapse.

title_en: Grigory Lulov executed by Supreme Soviet verdict
summary_en: Grigory Lulov, the second GPU officer who arrested the Rebbe, was shot by order of the Supreme Soviet.
story_body: Born in Riga in 1899, Lulov had joined the Communist party in 1916 and the Cheka in 1919. He received the Order of Lenin and an 'Honorary Worker of the Cheka-GPU' badge in 1937. Arrested at the end of 1938, he was executed on January 21, 1940, during Stalin's purges of the security organs.

title_en: Stanislav Messing executed in Soviet purges
summary_en: Stanislav Messing, the Jewish Communist head of the Leningrad GPU who had opposed the Rebbe's release, was shot.
story_body: Messing had threatened to countermand any order from Moscow freeing the Rebbe and to arrest him again if he returned to Leningrad. A decade later he himself was swept up in Stalin's purges. Some accounts say he came from a chasidic family.

title_en: Di Yisurim Fun Lubavitcher Rebben published in Riga
summary_en: An anonymous Yiddish narrative of the Rebbe's Soviet imprisonment, later identified as the work of journalist Elimelech Josselsohn, was published in Riga.
story_body: Josselsohn, a religious Zionist who had studied in Jerusalem before returning to Riga to write for Frimorgen, captured the mood and climate of the turbulent era. The book was translated into English for the first time in volume 6 of Likkutei Dibburim (Kehot, 2012).

title_en: Rayatz records Rashab's prediction of Soviet collapse
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak recorded in his diary the prediction his father, the Rebbe Rashab, had made three weeks before his passing.
story_body: The Rashab told his son there would be difficult times requiring actual self-sacrifice, but that the Communist government would eventually disintegrate. The fall of the Soviet Union in the early 1990s, and the flourishing of Chabad activity in its wake, was understood by Chasidim as the fulfillment of this prophecy.

title_en: Solovki Islands monastery converted to first Soviet political prison camp
summary_en: The fifteenth-century monastery on the Solovki Islands in the White Sea was converted into the Soviet Union's first political prison camp.
story_body: Solovki operated as a notorious labor camp from 1921 until the onset of war in 1939. It was the site to which the GPU first sentenced the Lubavitcher Rebbe before international pressure forced commutation to internal exile in Kostroma.

title_en: Agudas Chassidei Chabad established in New York
summary_en: Chabad synagogues across North America united under Agudas Chassidei Chabad.
story_body: Founded by figures including Max Kramer, the organization was still in its infancy when news of the 1927 arrest reached America. It eventually became Chabad's world headquarters and the home of the priceless library the Rebbe brought from Russia.

title_en: Chabad network smuggles 1,000 Chasidim across Polish border
summary_en: The underground Chabad network orchestrated the audacious escape of one thousand Chasidim from the Soviet Union into Poland using false passports.
story_body: Drawing on the clandestine infrastructure that had survived the arrests, imprisonments, and executions of the previous two decades, the network exploited a brief postwar window to extract Chasidim and their families. Those who escaped, along with their children, provided the leadership that fueled a global Jewish renaissance after the war.

title_en: Golda Meir attends Rosh HaShanah at Moscow's Choral Synagogue
summary_en: Israel's first ambassador to Russia was greeted by thousands of Jews on the second day of Rosh HaShanah outside the Moscow synagogue.
story_body: Meir had been disappointed by the small attendance on the first day, but the second day's enormous crowd — which she later told Italian reporter Oriana Fallaci had been orchestrated by Chabad — moved her deeply. She said it was 'the one time in my life that I considered becoming religious,' and recounted the moment to soldiers during the 1973 Yom Kippur War.

title_en: Six-Day War triggers Russian Jewish identity awakening
summary_en: Israel's victory inspired young Soviet Jews to explore their heritage, fueling a religious awakening nurtured by the Chabad underground.
story_body: Many young Russian Jews, including future Knesset Speaker Yuli Edelstein, became students of Chabad rabbis who had continued teaching despite decades of harassment. The same year, the Soviets broke diplomatic relations with Israel, ending Lishkat Hakesher's open activities in Russia and pushing them underground in cooperation with Chabad.

title_en: First public menorah lighting in Moscow's Red Square
summary_en: Chabad held the first public menorah lighting in Moscow's Red Square as the underground network emerged into the open.
story_body: With the Soviet system collapsing, the seventh Rebbe in New York began dispatching young rabbis and rebbetzins to rekindle Jewish life in Russia. They linked up with the clandestine activists who had operated for decades. Chabad rabbis went on to reclaim historic synagogues, open schools, and rebuild Jewish life across the former Soviet Union.

title_en: Seventh Rebbe dispatches shluchim to rebuild Jewish life in Russia
summary_en: From New York, the seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe began sending young rabbis and rebbetzins to reestablish Chabad institutions in the former Soviet Union.
story_body: The new shluchim joined with veterans of the clandestine network who had operated under the Soviets. Together they opened schools, restored historic synagogues, and established cultural and social-service centers. Today Chabad is the premier force in Jewish life in the former Soviet Union.

title_en: Yitzchak Shamir addresses Tel Aviv memorial for seventh Rebbe
summary_en: Former Israeli Prime Minister Yitzchak Shamir recounted discovering Chabad's clandestine Soviet network as a young Mossad operative.
story_body: Speaking at a Tel Aviv memorial for the seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe, Shamir said that on his early-1950s mission to Russia, 'we were surprised to discover that in every city across Russia, there was an existing clandestine Jewish network being directed by the Rebbe in New York.' The discovery led to a long partnership between the Mossad and Chabad's underground.

title_en: Rabbi Dovid Meir Rabinowitz immigrates to United States
summary_en: Rabbi Dovid Meir Rabinowitz, a devoted Chabad chasid, immigrated to the United States in 1896 and settled in Boston.
story_body: Rabinowitz pioneered traditional Judaism and Jewish education in Boston. In 1927, his daughter received a two-word telegram from the Rebbe's family — 'Tatte arestirt' — and he dispatched his sons Asher and Peretz to Washington, where they enlisted Justice Louis Brandeis to lobby on the Rebbe's behalf.

title_en: Wooden synagogue built in Kostroma
summary_en: The small wooden synagogue of Kostroma's tiny Jewish community was constructed in 1907.
story_body: By the time the Rebbe arrived in exile in 1927, the synagogue had been closed by Soviet authorities. Services moved to the large home of local shochet Yerachmiel Kugel, where the Rebbe and his entourage stayed. In recent years the Jewish community in Kostroma has undergone a rebirth.

title_en: Rabbi Eliyahu Simpson immigrates to the United States
summary_en: Rabbi Eliyahu Simpson, a chozer of the Rashab's discourses, immigrated to the US and served as rabbi of the Chabad synagogue in Boro Park.
story_body: In 1927, Simpson was among the American Chasidim who scrambled to secure funds for the Rebbe's relocation. After the arrival of the Rebbe Rayatz in 1940, he became one of his secretaries and a key figure in the development of Chabad in the United States.

title_en: Roza Melamed, last witness to Sixth Rebbe's Kostroma exile, dies in Beer Sheva
summary_en: Roza Melamed, who was twelve when her family hosted the Rebbe in Kostroma in 1927, died at the age of 99.
story_body: The daughter of the Kostroma shochet Yerachmiel Kugel, Melamed recalled the Rebbe constantly studying Torah and asking the children daily how they were doing. He blessed her with long life and prayed she never know the suffering he had endured. She lived to fulfill the blessing, dying in Beer Sheva.

title_en: Yuli Edelstein addresses International Conference of Chabad Shluchim
summary_en: Israeli Knesset Speaker Yuli Edelstein paid tribute to the Chabad underground in Moscow that had inspired his return to observance.
story_body: A former Soviet refusenik who was sentenced on false charges to a Siberian prison camp for three years, Edelstein credited Rabbi Getche Vilensky and Rabbi Mottel Lipshitz of the Moscow Chabad underground as his inspiration on his journey to Jewish observance.

title_en: United States extends diplomatic recognition to Soviet Union
summary_en: US diplomatic recognition of the Soviet Union, which had been withheld since the Bolshevik revolution, finally came in 1933.
story_body: The absence of US recognition was a key part of Soviet diplomatic isolation in 1927, alongside the British rupture. That isolation made the Latvia trade deal — and Mordechai Dubin's leverage — crucial to securing the Rebbe's exit visa.

title_en: Israel establishes Lishkat Hakesher to support Soviet Jewry
summary_en: Israel's prime ministerial office set up Lishkat Hakesher, the secret liaison bureau directed at strengthening Jewish life in the USSR.
story_body: Headed first by Shaul Avigur from 1953 to 1970, Lishkat Hakesher worked closely with Chabad's clandestine network in Russia. Its open activities ended after the Six-Day War when the Soviets cut ties with Israel, but it later became the global coordinator of the Soviet Jewry movement.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in Riga, Latvia after exile from Soviet Russia
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn arrives in Riga, Latvia, after being forced to leave Soviet Russia.
story_body: Two days after Simchat Torah, the Rebbe's train from Leningrad crossed into Latvia. At 7:00 a.m. on 25 Tishrei, 5688 the train pulled into Riga, where thousands gathered at the station and surrounding plaza. The Rebbe and his family slowly navigated the crowd to a local hotel, eventually moving to an apartment in an upscale Jewish neighborhood.

title_en: Rebbe composes letter to Chasidim on train from Russia
summary_en: On the train leaving Russia, the Rebbe writes to his Chasidim that distance cannot break their essential bond.
story_body: Heartbroken by the boisterous Leningrad send-off, the Rebbe composed a letter to the Chasidim while still on the train. He wrote that 'the essential connection between us cannot be broken, nor does the fact that distance stands between us break that bond.' The letter was dated 24 Tishrei, 5688.

title_en: Rebbe declines invitation to relocate to Warsaw
summary_en: Responding to the Warsaw community's invitation to settle there, the Rebbe declines for unstated reasons.
story_body: Shortly after his arrival in Riga, the Warsaw community wrote inviting the Rebbe to relocate there. He responded that 'their request could not be fulfilled for various reasons,' possibly because of visa or citizenship difficulties. He added that he hoped to visit them soon.

title_en: Rebbe writes to Zevin urging protest against Leningrad Jewish conference
summary_en: From Riga the Rebbe writes Rabbi Shlomo Yosef Zevin urging Russian Chasidim to undermine the planned Leningrad Jewish conference.
story_body: Despite the suffering he endured in Russia for opposing the Leningrad Jewish conference, the Rebbe dispatched a detailed action plan from Riga to disrupt it. The conference, organized by the Leningrad Jewish community and surreptitiously supported by the Yevsektzia, targeted nine key cities including Moscow and Kutaisi. The plan succeeded and the conference was never convened.

title_en: Rebbe directs Rabbi Yakovshvili to study shechitah and work in Kutaisi
summary_en: From Riga the Rebbe instructs Rabbi Simon Yakovshvili to travel to Kutaisi and learn shechitah while building Jewish education there.
story_body: The Rebbe wrote to Rabbi Simon Yakovshvili directing him to travel to Kutaisi in Soviet Georgia and study the art of shechitah. He told him to defer pursuing a shidduch and to consult with Avraham Levik Slavin and Schneur Zalman Altshuler on educational projects, requesting regular updates on all accomplishments.

title_en: Rebbe praises Shimon Bliner for establishing Mishnah and chasidic classes in Moscow
summary_en: From Riga, the Rebbe writes to the Chasid Shimon Bliner praising his establishment of underground Mishnah and chasidic philosophy classes in Moscow.
story_body: The Rebbe wrote, 'I enjoyed reading that you established classes in Mishnah and chasidic philosophy. I read the names of those involved; please share with them my blessing.' This was one of many letters showing the Rebbe's intimate involvement in underground Russian Jewish activity from his Riga base.

title_en: Vaad Magen UMekhaseh founded to protect Russian Jewry
summary_en: Two weeks after arriving in Riga, the Rebbe convenes prominent rabbis to create the Committee for the Protection and Care of Russian Jewry.
story_body: The first meeting included Rabbi Yosef Rosen (the Rogotchover Gaon), Berlin chief rabbi Dr. Meir Hildesheimer, and Rabbi Mendel Zak. The committee laid out a plan to enlist major Jewish groups like the JDC and Alliance Israélite Universelle. Renowned rabbis including the Chafetz Chaim and Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski joined the effort.

title_en: Rebbe writes Rizik recounting departure from Russia
summary_en: In a forthcoming letter to Baruch Rizik in Rostov, the Rebbe shares the anguish of leaving Russia six weeks earlier.
story_body: The Rebbe described thousands filling the Leningrad station, 'full of emotion,' surging toward the train. He wrote of passing 'eighteen hours with anguish in the heart, pain in the soul, the darkness of the night, the ringing of the wheels of the train only adding to the sense of sadness.' His spirits lifted when Latvian Chasidim boarded the train an hour from Riga and sang the joyous melody from his Lubavitch chuppah three decades earlier.

title_en: Rebbe writes Haffkine about strategizing against Yevsektzia
summary_en: The Rebbe writes scientist-philanthropist Waldemar Haffkine in German, urging a secret meeting of Jewish leaders to counter the Yevsektzia.
story_body: The Rebbe explained that being just outside Russia's border allowed him to continue his efforts more freely for Russian Jewry. He told Haffkine he had 'not given up on Russia' and now sought to enlist his help in arranging a private meeting of Jewish leaders to find a way to 'extinguish the power of the Yevsektzia.' He emphasized the effort must be conducted with the utmost secrecy.

title_en: Grodner Moment publishes feature on the Rebbe's activity in Riga hotel
summary_en: The Polish Yiddish daily Grodner Moment reports on the Rebbe's prayer, audiences, and Shabbat maamarim at his Riga hotel.
story_body: The paper described the Rebbe sitting 'day and night in a room designated for prayer and learning,' meeting all types of Jews in the afternoons. On Shabbat, large crowds flooded the hotel to hear the Rebbe recite a maamar, with his voice 'becoming stronger and more flowing, words streaming from his mouth, quotes from the Bible, Talmud, and Zohar woven and seasoned with parables.'

title_en: Rebbe sends second letter to Haffkine on Russian Jewry strategy
summary_en: The Rebbe follows up his earlier German-language correspondence with Haffkine pressing for action against the Yevsektzia.
story_body: The Rebbe again emphasized the need for a private meeting of prominent Jews to counter what he called 'the greatest danger and damage to the activities of Russian Jewry.' It appears, however, that the suggestion of such a private meeting did not prove successful in practice.

title_en: Detroit Jewish Chronicle praises Rebbe's impact on Latvian Jewry
summary_en: The Detroit Jewish Chronicle reports that the Rebbe's exile has been a boon for Orthodox Jewry in Latvia.
story_body: The paper wrote that 'the Lubavitcher Rebbe had brought a great deal of activity into the life of Orthodox Jewry in Latvia.' It concluded that 'Soviet Russia has thus, by expelling the Lubavitcher Rebbe, done a good turn to the Jews of Latvia.' The story was an early sign that the Rebbe's influence transcended his immediate community.

title_en: Rebbe visits Warsaw yeshivah and conducts long Purim farbrengen
summary_en: Four months after departing Russia, the Rebbe travels to Warsaw for two weeks, visiting the yeshivah and holding a marathon Purim farbrengen.
story_body: The Rebbe met with Warsaw's leading rabbis and communal leaders, deepening awareness of the plight of Russian Jewry, and spent time in yechidut with many Chasidim. The highlight was a long Purim farbrengen with the yeshivah students that began at 3:30 p.m. and did not end until 2:00 a.m. The Warsaw yeshivah had grown to 250 students by that year.

title_en: Hadoar publishes 'The New Book of Lamentations' on Soviet Jewish colonies
summary_en: The Hebrew US weekly Hadoar publishes an anonymous twelve-page letter describing the dire condition of Jews in Soviet agricultural colonies.
story_body: The letter, addressed to JDC Moscow head Dr. Rosen, denounced the Soviet plan to relocate Jews to communal farms as a Yevsektzia scheme 'to break down and destroy the Jewish spirit.' It documented hunger, cold, and religious oppression in the colonies. 'We plow and plant with tears and harvest with despair,' the writer warned.

title_en: Rebbe details ordeals in Russia in long letter from Riga
summary_en: The Rebbe writes a long letter detailing his suffering in Russia and his sense of loss after exile.
story_body: He wrote, 'I fled the bad, but I have not yet found the good.' He continued, 'I was driven from my country and forced to separate from my beloved brothers and friends.' The Rebbe expressed his desire 'to live in our country of Russia, where people are putting their lives on the line for Torah and observance in the midst of deprivation.'

title_en: Rebbe writes British Chief Rabbi Hertz pleading for Russian Jewry
summary_en: The Rebbe pleads with British Chief Rabbi Dr. Yosef Hertz to use his influence to fund Russian Jewish education.
story_body: Following the Rashag's earlier diplomatic visit to London, the Rebbe wrote, 'It is not a time for silence or to hold back on action. We must save Russian Jewry.' He told Hertz he knew 'of twenty thousand children in the USSR who wish to study Torah and are unable to – not because of the persecution, but rather the lack of money.'

title_en: Rebbe publishes first maamar since leaving Russia, in Yiddish
summary_en: Weeks before the High Holidays, the Rebbe publishes maamar Kinyan HaChaim in Yiddish, breaking with eighteenth-century Hebrew-only convention.
story_body: It was the first maamar printed not in Hebrew but in Yiddish since the eighteenth century, making chasidic teachings accessible to a broader public. In its introduction, the Rebbe addressed those who had drifted from chasidic roots: 'Remember your historical roots, your parents and grandparents.' He urged parents to 'instill these teachings in your children.'

title_en: Rebbe blesses Sylvia Reinen for translating maamar into Yiddish
summary_en: The Rebbe writes a special blessing for Sylvia Reinen, who translated the first post-Russia maamar into Yiddish.
story_body: In the letter to Alexander Sender Reinen, the Rebbe wrote, 'A special blessing to your wife for her efforts translating the discourse… It will be a great merit that those who don't understand another language are able to study it.' This marked the beginning of an effort to engage women with the intellectual depth of Chabad Chasidut.

title_en: Soviet education minister Lunacharsky targets the Rebbe in NYT
summary_en: Soviet Minister of Education Anatoly Lunacharsky declares war on 'Schneersohnovschina' in The New York Times.
story_body: Lunacharsky said, 'We shall combat the relics of the Middle Ages, the Schneersohnovschina.' The Times explained the term as 'the religious activities of the Lubavitcher Rebbe, who is now in exile in Latvia.' According to Lunacharsky, the solution lay in 'the fusion of the Jews in the great melting pot of the peoples who inhabit the Soviet Union.'

title_en: Cyrus Adler argues JDC should not support Rebbe's matzah campaign
summary_en: JDC leader Dr. Cyrus Adler writes Joseph Hyman opposing support for the Rebbe's emergency campaign to ship matzah into the USSR.
story_body: Adler warned that the Yevsektzia might block deliveries, embarrass the Russians, or that the Soviets might not agree to allow shipments. Years later, Adler regretted the decision, writing in 1932, 'I am not disposed to take the attitude to completely surrender all Jewish religious practice in Russia to the Soviets.'

title_en: Rebbe writes Teitelbaum warning that Russian schools face collapse
summary_en: The Rebbe writes JDC board member Rabbi Aron Teitelbaum that Russian Jewish schools are 'hanging between life and death.'
story_body: He told Teitelbaum, 'The institutions in Russia are hanging between life and death. There are daily requests for funding.' The Rebbe revealed he was taking personal loans to keep Russian institutions afloat, warning that denial of funding would bring victory to the Yevsektzia and demoralize underground activists.

title_en: Rashag reports to Meisel on Passover matzah campaign progress
summary_en: Rabbi Shemaryahu Gurary writes Rabbi Yisrael Meisel in Tel Aviv with extensive details on the international matzah-shipment campaign.
story_body: The Rashag described the daily struggle with Russian officials, who repeatedly stalled and shifted authority between Riga, Moscow, and Berlin. He praised Chief Rabbi Hertz's major public announcement in London and the strong support from French Chief Rabbi Levi and Russian immigrant donors in Paris. Committees had been formed across Europe and as far as Shanghai and Harbin.

title_en: International matzah campaign delivers 140,000 kilos to Soviet Jews
summary_en: The Rebbe's emergency campaign successfully ships 140,000 kilos of matzah into the famine-stricken Soviet Union before Passover.
story_body: Mordechai Dubin secured Soviet approval through diplomatic channels in Riga while production ran at full force in Riga, Dvinsk, and Berlin. Another 5,689 packages were mailed directly to families in four hundred communities. The campaign cost $88,000 (some $1.3 million today); the JDC contributed $10,000 thanks to Dr. Rosen's urging in Moscow.

title_en: Rabbi Feigin appeals to US Chasidim for fundraising help
summary_en: Rabbi Yechezkel Feigin writes Rabbis Simpson and Jacobson urging them to establish a US fundraising program for the Rebbe.
story_body: Feigin explained that historic sources of income in Russia were nonexistent in Riga. He described the Rebbe's spiritual suffering: 'There are few anash here. When the Rebbe says a maamar, there are not many who appreciate it.' He noted the Rebbe was burdened by many debts and was unable to establish a yeshivah due to lack of resources.

title_en: Rebbe writes Rabbi Munk requesting German translation of maamar
summary_en: The Rebbe writes Rabbi Meir Munk in Berlin asking him to arrange for a maamar to be translated into German.
story_body: This was the first time a chasidic discourse would be published in a European language other than Hebrew or Yiddish. The Rebbe wanted to engage German Jews, many of whom lacked a strong Jewish academic background, and give them the opportunity to appreciate concepts of chasidic philosophy. The Ramash later arranged for another translation in 1936.

title_en: Sixteen Jewish leaders arrested in Minsk for corresponding with the Rebbe
summary_en: The Detroit Jewish Chronicle reports the arrest of sixteen Jewish leaders in Minsk for the 'counterrevolutionary crime' of corresponding with the Rebbe.
story_body: According to the paper, the men 'had been hounded by the secret police for no other reason other than being in contact with the Lubavitcher Rebbe.' The arrests confirmed the very real danger to recipients of the Rebbe's prolific underground correspondence from Riga.

title_en: Rebbe delivers Simchat Torah talk demanding Jewish street outreach
summary_en: On Simchat Torah 1930 in Riga, the Rebbe lays out a vision of bold outreach and demands non-observant Jews not stay for dancing.
story_body: The Rebbe lamented that Latvia was 'Jewish only in appearance,' tasked Dubin's group with transforming Jewish education, and declared, 'You need to stand on the street corners and pull Jews into a synagogue to study.' He then sternly told those unwilling to put on tefillin to leave before hakafot — a directive later revealed to have foiled a Peretz Communist youth-club plot to disrupt the celebration.

title_en: Feigin writes Jacobson revealing Peretz plot against Simchat Torah
summary_en: Rabbi Feigin writes to Rabbi Jacobson in the US explaining how the Rebbe's harsh Simchat Torah words foiled a Communist youth-club plot.
story_body: Feigin disclosed that members of the local left-wing Peretz youth club had infiltrated the crowd intending to cut the electricity and violently break up the hakafot. 'When the Peretz leaders heard the Rebbe's strident words, they instructed their followers to leave.' When Feigin later informed the Rebbe, he replied, 'Now I know that I was justified in speaking that way.'

title_en: Agudas Chassidei Chabad founded in Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia
summary_en: Twenty-one Chasidim gather at the Rashag's home during the High Holidays and, with the Rebbe's approval, found Agudas Chassidei Chabad.
story_body: For the High Holidays of 1930, Chasidim from Poland and Lithuania came to celebrate with the Rebbe in Riga. A group of twenty-one Chasidim convened in the home of the Rashag, who suggested the new organization. With the Rebbe's approval, Agudas Chassidei Chabad took on the mandate of strengthening the Chabad community across the three-country region.

title_en: Rebbe visits Rokiškis and addresses gathering of women
summary_en: A large group of women requests that the Rebbe speak for them during his visit to Rokiškis, Lithuania — historically unprecedented for a chasidic Rebbe.
story_body: Rabbi Feigin recorded that 'in the wake of the request, the Rebbe spoke to a gathering of women.' Historically, chasidic Rebbes only addressed men in public; the Rokiškis talk was a deliberate step toward empowering women in Chabad. The same year, the Rebbe lamented the lowered standards of Jewish scholarship in modern integrated schools.

title_en: Rebbe relocates from Riga to Poland
summary_en: After six years in Latvia, the Rebbe relocates his court to Poland.
story_body: Throughout his Riga years the Rebbe's stationery read 'Riga, temporary.' Permanence remained elusive: 'The Rebbe resided in Riga for six years and during that extended time, no decision was made on his permanent place of residence,' wrote chasidic historian Rabbi Sholom Ber Levin. Poland too would only provide a home for a few years.

title_en: Ulmanis coup; Rabbi Hodakov appointed chief inspector of Jewish schools
summary_en: After the Ulmanis coup, Rabbi Mordechai Dubin orchestrates Rabbi Hodakov's appointment as chief inspector of Latvia's Jewish schools.
story_body: Prime Minister Kārlis Ulmanis disbanded political parties and parliament, but Dubin's personal bond with Ulmanis kept Agudath Israel functioning. Dubin arranged for Rabbi Chaim Mordechai Aizek Hodakov, the eighteen-year-old founding dean of Derech Eretz, to take over school inspection. Hodakov shifted historically secular Yiddishist schools toward Torah-based curriculum, replacing Sholem Aleichem with religious study and instituting prayer and yarmulkes.

title_en: Rebbe directs Rabbi Cheifetz to teach his daughter chasidic philosophy
summary_en: Asked whether women may study chasidic philosophy, the Rebbe answers emphatically yes and tells Rabbi Cheifetz to study maamarim with his daughter.
story_body: The Rebbe quoted his grandfather Rabbi Shmuel: 'amongst Chasidim there is no difference between a boy or a girl.' He lamented that this had been said fifty-five years earlier 'when the light of Chasidism was burning brightly,' adding that 'now this is an even greater imperative.' The directive catalyzed the formation of Achot Hatemimim, bringing teens and young women into serious study of chasidic texts.

title_en: Rebbe blesses founding of Society of the Sisters of the Temimim in US
summary_en: The Rebbe writes in English blessing the founding of an Achot Hatemimim women's group in America.
story_body: He wrote, 'In reply to your letter advising me of your excellent resolution to interest yourselves in the study of Chasidism… I was greatly gratified with your good decision.' He appointed a committee of three prominent American rabbis — Yisrael Jacobson, Yisrael Kazarnovsky, and Yochanan Gordon — to teach the group and advise on format and curriculum, instructing them to set up weekly classes.

title_en: Rebbe contrasts Chabad and Polish chasidism in letter on identity
summary_en: The Rebbe defines Chabad's identity in contrast to Polish chasidic groups, emphasizing personal avodah over the Rebbe-bond.
story_body: He wrote, 'One of the fundamental principles of Chabad is that it teaches its followers to be deeply engaged in the avodah of Chasidism. In contrast, for the Polish Chasidim, the main point is the connection to the Rebbe.' The letter framed Chabad's focus on internalizing Torah ideals through one's own effort, contrasting the Polish emphasis on the bond with the tzaddik.

title_en: Rebbe escapes German-occupied Poland to New York via Riga
summary_en: The outbreak of World War II compels the Rebbe to escape to New York, ending his European wanderings.
story_body: After escaping German-occupied Poland, the Rebbe made few public appearances during a short second stay in Riga before departing to the US. One of these was a rare public talk to Achot Hatemimim. The wandering ended in New York, where the Rebbe established Chabad's permanent base at 770 Eastern Parkway.

title_en: Beis Rivkah schools established in New York by Achot Hatemimim
summary_en: In the fall of 1941 the members of Achot Hatemimim of Greater New York establish the Beis Rivkah schools.
story_body: The schools grew directly out of the women's empowerment work the Rebbe had begun in Riga and continued in the US. With Beis Rivkah, the initiative to translate maamarim and form women's farbrengens evolved into a permanent institution for chasidic girls' education.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz passes away in New York
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn passes away after the last decade of his life in Brooklyn.
story_body: He had lived at 770 Eastern Parkway for the last decade of his life, having established Chabad's permanent base in the iconic Gothic-style building after his 1940 escape from Europe. The seventh Rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, succeeded him as leader of Chabad.

title_en: Seventh Rebbe launches tefillin campaign before Six-Day War
summary_en: In the weeks before the Six-Day War, the seventh Rebbe initiates the first of Chabad's public mitzvah campaigns.
story_body: The campaign entailed Jews donning tefillin in public venues, drawing directly from the Simchat Torah 1930 directive in Riga to 'stand on the street corners and pull Jews into a synagogue.' What had begun as a Western European innovation became the symbol of postwar Chabad outreach worldwide.

title_en: Rabbi Aaron Rakeffet visits Riga on covert Mossad mission
summary_en: Rabbi Dr. Aaron Rakeffet is dispatched to the Soviet Union as a covert Mossad agent and discovers a vibrant Riga community.
story_body: Rakeffet was surprised to find at the Riga synagogue a group of older Jews who had held on through Communism. After the service, he was told to wait until the government agents left, then 'they broke out vodka and cake, and we sat and had a farbrengen.' The Rebbe's six-year stay in Riga half a century earlier was still 'what kept them going all those years.'

title_en: Baal Shem Tov ascends to heaven on Rosh HaShanah and meets Messiah
summary_en: On Rosh HaShanah 1746 the Baal Shem Tov's soul ascends and the Messiah tells him to disseminate his teachings publicly.
story_body: According to the historic letter the Baal Shem Tov sent to his brother, using kabbalistic secrets his soul rose to heaven. He asked the Messiah, 'When will you come?' The answer: 'In the time when your teachings will become public and revealed in the world.' This principle later anchored the Chabad mission of spreading chasidic teachings to the world.

title_en: Alter Rebbe freed from czarist prison; chasidic teaching expands
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi is freed from czarist prison and begins teaching maamarim with deeper explanations.
story_body: The seventh Rebbe identified the 1798 release as the second transformational point in disseminating chasidic teachings. 'This began a new stage, when the teachings went chutzah, outside.' The 1897 founding of Tomchei Temimim and the later translation of maamarim into other languages built on the same trajectory.

title_en: Max Lilienthal opens first German-style Jewish secular school in Riga
summary_en: Max Lilienthal, an adherent of the German Haskalah, arrives in Riga and establishes the first German-style Jewish secular school in Imperial Russia.
story_body: At the time, there were fewer than a thousand Jews in Riga. According to Jewish Museum director Ilja Lensky, the community wanted a secular Jewish school, possibly under Russian government pressure for a less religious education system. From that beachhead Lilienthal attempted to transform Jewish education throughout Russia, and by 1927 secular-oriented Jewish schools dominated Riga.

title_en: Small Chabad community established in Riga
summary_en: A modest Chabad community takes root in Riga, with a few synagogues including one with three sanctuaries for Lubavitch, Liadi, and Kopust branches.
story_body: The Riga Chabad community grew slowly until enhanced by Russian emigration in the early twentieth century. In the Jewish ghetto, one Chabad synagogue housed three adjacent sanctuaries for the varied Chabad sub-groups. But there was no yeshivah to bring a youthful spirit to the city, a far cry from Lubavitch's vibrant ethos.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab founds Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim in Lubavitch
summary_en: Rabbi Sholom DovBer Schneersohn opens the first chasidic yeshivah, revolutionizing Jewish education.
story_body: Yehuda Geberer notes Chabad took the lead in this arena: 'The first who did this was the Rebbe Rashab with the opening of Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim in 1897.' With time, other chasidic groups followed Chabad's lead, establishing their own yeshivas. The seventh Rebbe identified the founding as a major stage in the dissemination of chasidic teachings.

title_en: Czernowitz Conference declares Yiddish 'glue' of Jewish life
summary_en: At the Czernowitz Conference, secular Yiddish leaders declare Yiddish to be 'the glue to hold Jewish life together.'
story_body: The Yiddish movement believed using Yiddish would be a barrier to assimilation, rejecting classic Jewish religious beliefs and observance. Many of its early schools were strongly anti-Zionist, though most later became supportive of Zionism. Yiddish schools spread across Russia, Europe, the US, and Canada, but most had closed by the early 1970s.

title_en: World Agudath Israel founded in Katowice, Poland
summary_en: Jewish religious leaders establish World Agudath Israel at a Katowice conference as a response to secularization and Zionism.
story_body: The Agudah unified many chasidic groups with the Lithuanian yeshivah community, though Chabad did not join. In Latvia, Agudath Israel became a major influential party, winning two Saeima seats in 1922 and 1925, falling to one in 1928, and regaining two in 1931. After the 1934 Latvian coup, multi-party elections did not resume until 1990.

title_en: Latvia declares independence from Russian rule
summary_en: The Latvians overthrow Russian rule and become independent, ushering in active Jewish political participation.
story_body: Latvian independence lasted until the German invasion in July 1941. The Rebbe later said that since 1918, an effort should have been made to establish Torah institutions. In an election held shortly after the Rebbe's 1927 arrival, Latvian Jews won six parliamentary seats divided among religious parties, Zionists, and the Bund.

title_en: Rabbi Mordechai Dubin establishes Derech Eretz School in Riga
summary_en: Latvian parliamentarian Rabbi Mordechai Dubin founds the Derech Eretz School, an Orthodox school teaching both religious and secular subjects.
story_body: The school laid the foundation for educational change in Riga. Its founding dean was an eighteen-year-old Rabbi Chaim Mordechai Aizek Hodakov. The opportunity to fulfill the Rebbe's later mission of transforming Jewish education in Latvia came in 1934, when Hodakov was appointed chief inspector of all Jewish schools.

title_en: Chabad yeshivah opens in Warsaw with twelve students
summary_en: While the Rebbe is still in Rostov, a Chabad yeshivah opens in Warsaw with twelve students on the first yahrzeit of the Rebbe Rashab.
story_body: The Rebbe referred to this time as 'days of light and days of joy,' even as the yeshivah in Rostov was being forcibly closed and the Chabad educational network in Russia went underground. He appointed a board of five members, instructing them to 'focus on discussions of ethical behavior, instilling a G-d-fearing spirit, and acquiring good character traits.' By 1928 the yeshivah had grown to 250 students.

title_en: Soviet Jewish agricultural-colony resettlement project launched
summary_en: The Soviet land-resettlement project is launched, relocating Jews to communal farms in Ukraine and Crimea.
story_body: Yevsektzia leader Semyon Dimenstein had advocated this in conferences as early as 1918. Authorities relocated Jewish families, sometimes forcibly, in the hope of 'productizing' Jews into farmers. Before they ended their support in 1938, the JDC invested $16 million ($238 million today) in helping the Communists move Jews to agricultural settlements.

title_en: Rebbe writes qualified endorsement of agricultural colonies to JDC
summary_en: While still in Russia, the Rebbe writes the JDC leadership in New York with a qualified endorsement of the Jewish agricultural colonies.
story_body: He wrote, 'It was gratifying to hear from Dr. Rosen about the establishment of the agricultural colonies,' but raised concerns about the 'lack of attention to religious institutions, mikveh, teachers, shochtim, rabbis, synagogues.' He encouraged the JDC to also help the thousands who could not work in agriculture. The letter was translated into English and read at the JDC board meeting.

title_en: Rebbe writes Agudas Harabonim urging religious infrastructure in colonies
summary_en: While still in Russia, the Rebbe writes the New York-based Union of Orthodox Rabbis urging them to lobby the JDC for religious institutions in the colonies.
story_body: He pressed US rabbis to ensure the JDC 'provide the agricultural colonies with the religious institutions necessary for every Jew.' Without publicly criticizing the JDC, the Rebbe believed Jews would be far better served by remaining in the cities near family and community.

title_en: Rebbe proposes home-based industries plan to JDC board
summary_en: The Rebbe writes the JDC board proposing home-based industries for Russian Jews as an alternative to agricultural resettlement.
story_body: He asked the JDC to provide Russian Jews with the tools, training, and financial support necessary to establish home-based factories and small businesses. This would give them greater economic freedom and allow the option of not working on Shabbat. The Rebbe argued such industries 'would provide the Jews with a respectable income and sense of dignity.'

title_en: Germany invades Latvia
summary_en: The German invasion ends Latvian independence and devastates the country's Jewish population.
story_body: Latvian independence, which had begun in 1918, lasted until the German invasion. Riga's chief rabbi Mendel Zak and his family were among those killed in the Holocaust. In 1945 Soviet troops would seize Latvia, making it part of the Soviet Union until 1991.

title_en: Soviet Union seizes Latvia
summary_en: Soviet troops seize Latvia, ending German occupation and making the country part of the USSR.
story_body: Latvia remained part of the Soviet Union until it regained independence in 1991. The vibrant Riga Jewish community the Rebbe had served in the late 1920s and early 1930s lived on in fragments under Soviet rule, as Rabbi Rakeffet would discover during his 1985 Mossad mission.

title_en: Latvia regains independence from Soviet Union
summary_en: Latvia regains its independence after almost half a century under Soviet rule.
story_body: The end of Soviet rule reopened Latvia to wider Jewish religious activity. Multi-party elections, which had not been held since the 1934 Latvian coup d'état, had only resumed in 1990, the year before formal independence.

title_en: Siyum HaShas held at MetLife Stadium
summary_en: Agudath Israel organizes the Siyum HaShas at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey with some ninety thousand in attendance.
story_body: The celebration marked the completion of the daf-yomi cycle of Talmud study. Today Agudath Israel — founded in 1912 — is a major religious party with seats in the Israeli Knesset and a significant presence in the US and European countries. The MetLife event reflected the global scope of Talmud study in the postwar era.

title_en: Drottningholm arrives in New York Harbor with the Sixth Rebbe aboard
summary_en: The Swedish liner Drottningholm pulled into New York Harbor at 4:00 p.m. carrying the Sixth Rebbe and his family after a perilous voyage from Gothenburg.
story_body: After a harrowing twelve-day crossing during which the ship was stopped by British warships and German submarines, the Drottningholm reached New York. Port regulations required passengers to wait aboard overnight. A delegation of US Chabad leaders boarded the ship to greet the Rebbe in his stateroom.

title_en: Sixth Rebbe disembarks at Pier 97 in Manhattan
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn disembarked at Pier 97 on West 57th Street, declaring that America would become a center of Torah.
story_body: Thousands welcomed the Rebbe as he came down the gangway in a wheelchair, bedecked in a shtreimel. When a reporter expressed skepticism, the Rebbe insisted 'America iz nisht aderesh — America is no different. It will become a center of Torah.' Later that day he addressed crowds at the Greystone Hotel, calling for rescue of Polish Jewry and the founding of a yeshivah.

title_en: Announcement of Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim Lubavitch in America
summary_en: On his first day in America the Sixth Rebbe declared that Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim Lubavitch would open the next day at the Oneg Shabbat Synagogue in Brooklyn.
story_body: Speaking at the Greystone Hotel, the Rebbe announced his vision to fortify Jewish education in the US and told the crowd the new yeshivah would launch at once. He pressed Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson that he would not sleep until Jacobson promised to open it. Jacobson began enlisting students the next morning.

title_en: Sixth Rebbe appeals to Leo Jung to complete a Manhattan mikveh
summary_en: Less than a week after arriving, the Rebbe wrote to Rabbi Dr. Leo Jung urging him to help finish a stalled new mikveh in Manhattan.
story_body: Rabbi Joseph Lookstein had told the Rebbe the project was stuck. On Purim, the Rebbe pressed Jung — a champion of aesthetically pleasing mikvehs — to push it to completion, signaling his intent to support broader Orthodox infrastructure beyond his own circle.

title_en: Studies begin at Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim in Brooklyn
summary_en: A week after the Rebbe's arrival, the new American Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim opened its doors in the basement of Congregation Oneg Shabbat in East Flatbush.
story_body: Rabbi Mordechai Mentlik was appointed dean. The first cohort was barely a minyan, drawn mostly from American students who had been studying chasidic philosophy with Rabbi Jacobson, plus a few alumni of the Otwock yeshivah. Benches and a makeshift kitchen were assembled in the cellar.

title_en: New York Released Time statute signed into law
summary_en: Governor Herbert Lehman signed the statute approving Released Time for religious instruction during the public school week in New York.
story_body: The law allowed public-school children to leave school one hour weekly for religious instruction at nearby venues. The Sixth Rebbe would seize on this in coming years, directing Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch to mobilize a citywide Jewish Released Time program against significant liberal-Jewish opposition.

title_en: Sixth Rebbe spends Passover in Lakewood, New Jersey
summary_en: The Rebbe took a Passover interlude in Lakewood, New Jersey, before returning to the Greystone Hotel in Manhattan.
story_body: While searching for a permanent residence, the Rebbe used the Greystone Hotel as his base. Some Chasidim later proposed Lakewood as a quieter location for his headquarters, but the Rebbe rejected suburban isolation in favor of a visible presence in urban Brooklyn.

title_en: 770 Eastern Parkway purchased by Agudas Chassidei Chabad
summary_en: Chabad purchased a three-story brownstone at 770 Eastern Parkway in Crown Heights to serve as the Rebbe's permanent residence and headquarters.
story_body: Rejecting Brownsville and suburban options, the Rebbe selected prestigious Crown Heights despite there being only three Chabad families in the neighborhood. The building, originally built as a doctor's home and clinic by architect Edwin Kline, had an elevator essential to the Rebbe's mobility. It would become the iconic '770,' replicated worldwide.

title_en: Sixth Rebbe moves into 770 Eastern Parkway
summary_en: Just after Chai Elul, the birthday of the Baal Shem Tov and the Alter Rebbe, the Sixth Rebbe took up residence in his newly acquired Crown Heights home.
story_body: Chasidim described overflowing joy at finally seeing the Rebbe in a permanent base. Avraham Pariz wrote of indescribable happiness on every face, though Avraham Hecht noted that the celebration was tinged with anxiety as European Jewry was being consumed by war even as American Chabad took root.

title_en: HaKriah VeHaKedushah monthly magazine launched
summary_en: The Sixth Rebbe launched HaKriah VeHaKedushah, a monthly Yiddish magazine calling for spiritual renewal and immediate teshuvah as a response to the war.
story_body: Published from late 1940 through the war's end, the magazine carried the Rebbe's call of 'L'alter leteshuvah, l'alter legeulah' — immediate repentance prompts redemption. A small English section was added in April 1941. Its message was that prayer and repentance would catalyze divine deliverance.

title_en: First Chabad yeshivah students arrive in Kobe, Japan
summary_en: The first group of Tomchei Temimim students reached Kobe, Japan in early 1941 after traversing the Soviet Union by trans-Siberian railway.
story_body: After Russian official Schlossberg — whose father had been a Chabad Chasid — arranged exit visas, the students traveled via Moscow and Vladivostok. The small Jewish community in Kobe, established 1912, opened its doors to them while they awaited US visas that would ultimately be revoked.

title_en: Rashag-led delegation meets First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt at the White House
summary_en: A Chabad delegation led by the Rashag met Eleanor Roosevelt to plead for emigration of the Bobover Rebbe and Chabad Chasidim trapped under Soviet rule.
story_body: Arranged by the Quaker-led American Friends Service Committee after Clarence Pickett's appeal to Mrs. Roosevelt, the delegation requested intervention with the Russian government. The effort failed: the Bobover Rebbe, who fled to Lvov, was beaten to death by German soldiers months later, and the Riga Chasidim were killed after the German invasion of Latvia.

title_en: Ramash and Chaya Mushka Schneerson board ship in Lisbon for America
summary_en: Menachem Mendel Schneerson and his wife Chaya Mushka boarded a ship in Lisbon bound for the United States after fleeing Nazi-occupied France.
story_body: After Paris fell, the couple fled to Vichy France. The US consulate in Nice was hostile to Jews, but they obtained visas in Marseille. Acquiring Spanish and Portuguese transit visas was difficult, but at the last minute permission came through and they sailed for America.

title_en: Ramash and Chaya Mushka arrive in the United States
summary_en: The future Seventh Rebbe and his wife reached the United States after an eleven-day Atlantic crossing from Lisbon.
story_body: The Sixth Rebbe greeted his son-in-law warmly and tasked him with chairing three new pillars of Chabad: Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch, Kehot Publication Society, and Machne Israel. Yitzchok Groner recalled the Ramash personally greeting each of the forty yeshivah students who waited at the dock.

title_en: Riga's Choral Synagogue burned with Jews locked inside
summary_en: Riga's Choral Synagogue was set ablaze by Nazi forces with many Jews locked inside, killing senior Chasidim including Yechezkel Feigin and Reb Itche der Masmid.
story_body: Among those murdered were some of the Sixth Rebbe's closest Chasidim and his secretary Rabbi Yechezkel Feigin. When the Rebbe received the report years later it triggered his heart attack of November 1944. A government memorial is held annually at the site of the ruined synagogue.

title_en: Bobover Rebbe Benzion Halberstam killed by German soldiers in Lvov
summary_en: Rabbi Benzion Halberstam, the Bobover Rebbe, was beaten to death by German soldiers shortly after the Nazi invasion of Russian-controlled Lvov.
story_body: Months earlier, the Rashag-led Chabad delegation to Eleanor Roosevelt had specifically pleaded for his emigration from the Soviet zone, but the intervention failed. His death came just after the German invasion in July 1941.

title_en: Japanese government relocates yeshivah students from Kobe to Shanghai
summary_en: Japanese authorities transferred all yeshivah students from Kobe to the international city of Shanghai, including some forty Chabad students and around 200 from the Mir Yeshivah.
story_body: Rabbi Meir Ashkenazi, Shanghai's Ashkenazi chief rabbi and a Chabad Chasid, arranged for the Mir to use the Beth Aharon Synagogue. The Chabad students rented a separate location and continued their Polish-style integrated study of Talmud and Chasidut, isolated from teachers and from the Rebbe in New York.

title_en: Canada allocates visas for 80 Polish refugee yeshivah students
summary_en: After Rabbi Oscar Fasman's lobbying, the Canadian Jewish Congress agreed to a small allotment of visas for Polish Jewish scholars in neutral countries, including nine Chabad students.
story_body: The Rebbe dispatched Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson to Canada to push for inclusion of the Chabad students. Only twenty-nine of the eighty visa holders ultimately departed Shanghai; the rest waited and were trapped in Asia for the war's duration, with some interned in the Philippines.

title_en: Polish refugee yeshivah students reach Montreal train station
summary_en: After sailing from Shanghai via San Francisco and traveling overland by train, the refugee yeshivah students arrived in Montreal on a Friday and were welcomed by the community.
story_body: Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson met them at the station with instructions from the Rebbe: they were to establish a yeshivah in Montreal. Their arrival had been hastened by the Rebbe's insistence that they take the very first ship despite the dateline-Yom Kippur dilemma.

title_en: Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim opens in Montreal
summary_en: At a community reception on Saturday night, Rabbi Jacobson surprised Montreal Jewry by announcing that Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim would open the next day.
story_body: Local leaders had wanted a single combined yeshivah, but Jacobson's unilateral move resulted in two institutions opening — Tomchei Temimim and Mercaz HaTorah. The Chabad yeshivah became the foundation for Montreal's growing network of Chabad schools, synagogues, and campus centers.

title_en: Mottel Altein sent to Pittsburgh's Nusach Ari Congregation
summary_en: On the morning of the Pearl Harbor attack, twenty-two-year-old Mottel Altein boarded a train to Pittsburgh on the Rebbe's instructions to take over a struggling Orthodox synagogue.
story_body: The night before, the Rebbe had summoned Altein and refused to delay the trip. Altein heard news of the Japanese attack en route. He arrived to find his telegram unopened at the synagogue and the president debating whether to relocate the shul and join the Conservative movement. The Rebbe's intervention kept it Orthodox.

title_en: Children's Passover parade in Crown Heights
summary_en: Yitzchok Groner and Moshe Kazarnovsky led roughly three hundred children carrying placards down Eastern Parkway in a public parade urging Jewish observance.
story_body: Organized at Rabbi Hodakov's direction, the parade passed beneath the Rebbe's second-floor window. The Ramash later reported the Rebbe's enthusiasm. The event marked a shift toward public Jewish celebration and became a precursor to the Lag BaOmer parades the Seventh Rebbe inaugurated in 1953.

title_en: Hebrew Parochial School opens in Chicago
summary_en: A new Jewish day school opened on Chicago's West Side that would evolve into the Arie Crown Hebrew Day School.
story_body: The Sixth Rebbe sent Rabbi Chaim Hodakov to help organize the school and urged Chicago Chasidim to support it. Chabad rabbis including Zalman Posner taught there. The school faced a financial crisis in 1946, which the Rebbe quietly resolved by activating his network of donors.

title_en: Yosef Rodal — first Shanghai student to marry — weds in Montreal
summary_en: Yosef Rodal, the oldest of the Shanghai refugee students, became the first of the group to marry, with the Rebbe personally providing funds for a diamond ring.
story_body: Rodal had lost most of his family in the Holocaust. The Rebbe, knowing the bride was a Canadian who expected a diamond, gave Rodal money to buy one. A delegation of New York rabbis attended the wedding. Most of the Shanghai cohort would settle in Montreal, marry, and become teachers, rabbis, and dayanim.

title_en: Sheina Schneersohn-Horenstein killed in Treblinka
summary_en: Sheina, the Sixth Rebbe's younger daughter, was killed at Treblinka on the second day of Rosh HaShanah.
story_body: Sheina and her husband Menachem Mendel Horenstein had been unable to leave Poland because the Horensteins were Polish citizens denied entry to Latvia. Their fate remained unknown until after the war. The Ramash withheld the confirmed dates from the ailing Rebbe; the Seventh Rebbe later recited Kaddish annually on the second day of Rosh HaShanah for Sheina.

title_en: Menachem Mendel Horenstein killed in Treblinka
summary_en: The Sixth Rebbe's son-in-law Mendel Horenstein was killed at Treblinka on 25 Cheshvan, seven weeks after his wife Sheina.
story_body: Mordechai Unrad, who had been in Mendel's barracks at Treblinka, confirmed the dates of death to the Ramash in August 1949. The couple had adopted their nephew Yaakov Yosef Lis, who also perished. The information was withheld from the Sixth Rebbe in his lifetime.

title_en: Vaad Hatzalah cuts off funding to Chabad students in Shanghai
summary_en: Beginning in December 1942, the Vaad Hatzalah rescue committee ceased life-saving disbursements to the Chabad yeshivah students stranded in Shanghai.
story_body: While the Mir Yeshivah and other yeshivos received generous stipends for food and clothing, the Chabad students were left to fend for themselves. Rabbi Chaim Shmuelevitz quietly tried to assist them. After the war, the policy became a lasting wound; in 1962 the Seventh Rebbe told Rabbi Gutnick that it had caused his father-in-law to weep.

title_en: Children of Tehran arrive in Palestine
summary_en: Some 1,228 Polish Jewish refugee children, most from religious families, arrived in Palestine after a long trek via Russia and Iran.
story_body: The quasi-governmental Jewish Agency, controlled by Mapai, placed the children on secular kibbutzim without religious teachers, kosher food, or Shabbat observance. Their forced secular indoctrination would prompt international Orthodox protest led by Chief Rabbi Herzog and the Sixth Rebbe.

title_en: Japanese authorities establish Jewish ghetto in Shanghai's Hongkou district
summary_en: Japanese occupation authorities confined Jewish refugees in Shanghai to a designated ghetto in the Hongkou district, administered by Sgt. Kano Ghoya.
story_body: Food became scarce and the Chabad yeshivah students, already cut off from Vaad Hatzalah funds, were barely surviving on a bit of rice per day. Aryeh Leib Brailovsky, prompted by an enigmatic dream of the Rebbe pleading for his hungry children, raised funds locally to sustain them.

title_en: Sixth Rebbe writes anguished letter to Jacob Klatzkin on Jewish leadership
summary_en: The Rebbe sent a long, bitter letter to philosopher Jacob Klatzkin lamenting media silence, government apathy, and Jewish leaders' failure during the Holocaust.
story_body: Responding to Klatzkin's call for public demonstrations with Torah scrolls, the Rebbe wrote that media 'sit behind a shade,' political leaders' ears are 'closed to our cries,' and that the time had come to call all Jews — irrespective of party — to fasting, prayer, and teshuvah. He compared the Jewish silence unfavorably to that of other faith communities.

title_en: Sixth Rebbe publishes letter protesting Jewish Agency treatment of Tehran Children
summary_en: Two weeks before Passover, the Rebbe issued a public letter in Jewish newspapers protesting the Jewish Agency's placement of refugee children in irreligious settings.
story_body: Responding to a request from the Gerrer Rebbe, he urged Orthodox groups to demand the children's transfer to a proper educational environment. He later organized over four hundred American rabbis in support of Chief Rabbi Herzog and proposed an international donations boycott of the Jewish Agency until it acceded.

title_en: Rabbis' March on Washington
summary_en: More than 400 Orthodox rabbis marched from the Capitol to the White House three days before Yom Kippur, demanding US government action to rescue European Jewry.
story_body: Organized by Peter Bergson with Vaad Hatzalah and Agudas Harabonim, the march was the only Jewish demonstration at the Capitol during the war. The Sixth Rebbe, unable to travel, sent a delegation of four — Mindel, Quint, Gurary, and Binyamin Levitin. President Roosevelt left the White House by a back exit on the advice of Wise and Roseman.

title_en: Tomchei Temimim Montreal dedicates former orphanage as new home
summary_en: After Sam Bronfman and other donors helped acquire a former orphanage, the Montreal yeshivah dedicated its new permanent facility.
story_body: Chief Rabbi Yehoshua Hirshorn called for the day to be marked as a Yom Tov for Montreal Jewry. By this point Bronfman, who had earlier tried to push the yeshivah to Toronto, had come to see its value. The yeshivah continued to expand, with the Rebbe corresponding regularly on curriculum and staffing.

title_en: Roosevelt creates the War Refugee Board
summary_en: President Roosevelt signed an executive order establishing the War Refugee Board three months after the Rabbis' March on Washington.
story_body: Created over the opposition of Secretary of State Breckinridge Long and pushed by Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau, the Board ultimately helped save many Jews — particularly in Hungary. But it came too late for the more than five million Jews already murdered.

title_en: Torah Umesorah founded by Rabbi Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz
summary_en: Rabbi Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz of Torah Vodaath was instrumental in establishing Torah Umesorah, the National Society for Hebrew Day Schools.
story_body: Torah Umesorah took the first tentative steps to open Orthodox day schools beyond New York. The Sixth Rebbe — already running a network of yeshivos in over a dozen cities — welcomed the new initiative rather than treating it as competition.

title_en: 1,000 European Jewish refugees arrive at Oswego, New York camp
summary_en: Roughly 1,000 European Jewish refugees, many concentration-camp survivors, were admitted to the United States and placed in a camp at Oswego in upstate New York.
story_body: The camp was the only one in the US for European refugees during the war, operated by the War Relocation Authority. The refugees were not given US immigration status. The Rebbe sprang into action to provide religious services and educational programming for them.

title_en: Sixth Rebbe's delegation visits Oswego refugee camp
summary_en: Eleven days after the refugees' arrival, the Rebbe sent Rabbis Hodakov and Kazarnovsky and Dr. Mindel to Oswego to assess their needs.
story_body: Over the following months Chabad supplied religious provisions, educational programs, and general assistance. When the refugees were released in 1945–46, a group of the children enrolled in the Chabad yeshivah in Brooklyn.

title_en: Sixth Rebbe suffers heart attack
summary_en: The Rebbe suffered a heart attack on 26 Cheshvan, triggered by a letter detailing the Nazi murder of his closest Chasidim in Riga.
story_body: Already weakened after the High Holidays and ordered to rest by his cardiologist, the Rebbe received the report describing how Reb Itche der Masmid, Rabbi Mordechai Cheifetz, Rabbi Yechezkel Feigin and others had been burned to death in a Riga synagogue. He slowly recovered over the following weeks but his health remained fragile.

title_en: HaKriah VeHaKedushah ceases publication
summary_en: The Sixth Rebbe's wartime monthly HaKriah VeHaKedushah ceased publication the month the war ended.
story_body: Founded in October 1940 to call American Jewry to teshuvah and spiritual mobilization during the war, the magazine ended its run after five years. Its closing the month of victory suggests its mission was deliberately tied to providing a spiritual response to the conflict.

title_en: Shanghai yeshivah students send report to Rashag exposing Vaad Hatzalah policy
summary_en: After the Japanese surrender restored communications, the Chabad students in Shanghai sent a detailed letter to the Rashag documenting Vaad Hatzalah's discriminatory funding policy.
story_body: The letter described how funds were cut off in December 1942 and only small humiliating amounts dispensed thereafter. It also noted that Vaad Hatzalah had initially refused funding to the Amshinover Rebbe. The revelations prompted New York rabbis to seek intervention from Chabad leaders in Israel.

title_en: Hebrew Parochial School Chicago financial rescue
summary_en: Facing mortgage default and closure, Chicago's Hebrew Parochial School was rescued overnight after board member Yankel Katz phoned the Sixth Rebbe.
story_body: When the board met to discuss closing, Katz left to find a payphone. The Rebbe told him to reconvene the meeting the next night. By the next evening a group of affluent donors the Rebbe had personally contacted were waiting at the gate, and within minutes the pledges to save the school were in place.

title_en: JDC sends 27 Chabad shochtim to Ireland for kosher meat production
summary_en: The JDC sponsored twenty-seven Chabad-affiliated kosher slaughterers to staff a Dublin meat plant supplying kosher meat to European Jewish refugees.
story_body: Working in partnership with the Sixth Rebbe in the postwar refugee period, the JDC arranged this large-scale shechita operation to feed survivors in displaced-persons camps in Italy and elsewhere. Rabbi Benjamin Gorodetsky helped coordinate.

title_en: Rabbi Meir Ashkenazi relocates from Shanghai to New York
summary_en: Shanghai's former Ashkenazi chief rabbi Meir Ashkenazi settled in Brooklyn after over two decades in China.
story_body: Once in New York, members of Vaad Hatzalah initiated a din Torah accusing him of having diverted Mir Yeshivah funds to Chabad students in Shanghai. Ashkenazi argued that taking a small percentage was justified given the mortal risk of collecting funds at a neutral embassy under Japanese occupation. The rabbinical court ruled in his favor.

title_en: Rabbi Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz passes away
summary_en: Rabbi Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, longtime principal of Torah Vodaath and architect of Torah Umesorah, passed away on 3 Elul.
