story_body: Shortly before his death he told a group of close friends gathered at his bedside about how the Sixth Rebbe had quietly saved Torah Vodaath from foreclosure during the war years — a secret he refused to take to the grave.

title_en: Israeli Frumkin Commission established to investigate immigrant children's education
summary_en: Under religious-community pressure, the Israeli government created the Frumkin Commission to investigate the secular indoctrination of refugee and immigrant children.
story_body: Chaired by Gad Frumkin — son of a Chabad Chasid who had welcomed the Rebbe during his 1929 Palestine visit — the commission found that accusations of forcible removal of peyos and interference with religious studies were true, and that policies aimed to recruit children to the Histadrut rather than support religious parties.

title_en: US Supreme Court upholds Released Time in Zorach v. Clauson
summary_en: The Supreme Court ruled 6–3 in favor of Released Time programs, rejecting challenges brought by liberal Jewish groups.
story_body: Justice William Douglas wrote that Released Time involved neither religious instruction in public-school classrooms nor expenditure of public funds. The ADL, American Jewish Congress, and American Jewish Committee had backed the lawsuit. Justice Felix Frankfurter dissented. The ruling vindicated the Rebbe's wartime push to organize the Jewish Released Time program.

title_en: First Lag BaOmer parade held on Eastern Parkway
summary_en: The Seventh Rebbe inaugurated the first Lag BaOmer children's parade on Eastern Parkway, building on the precedent of the 1942 Passover parade in Crown Heights.
story_body: The annual parades would become a hallmark of Chabad communities worldwide, expressing Jewish public pride in the streets. The format echoed the children's procession that Yitzchok Groner and Moshe Kazarnovsky had led past 770 a decade earlier.

title_en: Seventh Rebbe inaugurates worldwide tefillin campaign on eve of Six-Day War
summary_en: As Israel faced existential threat in 1967, the Seventh Rebbe launched a global tefillin campaign as a spiritual response to the danger.
story_body: The campaign echoed the Sixth Rebbe's wartime call for repentance as a means to invoke divine deliverance, and reflected Chabad's view — rooted in Kabbalah and Chasidism — that spiritual transformation precipitates physical salvation. It became one of the Seventh Rebbe's signature 'mivtzoim' (campaigns).

title_en: Rabbi Yosef Dov Soloveitchik appointed rosh yeshivah of Yeshivah University
summary_en: After his father Rabbi Moshe Soloveichik passed away, Rabbi Yosef Dov Soloveitchik was appointed rosh yeshivah of Yeshivah University with crucial backing from the Sixth Rebbe.
story_body: The YU board was divided, but the Sixth Rebbe wrote a letter calling Soloveitchik a 'gaon' whose appointment would 'restore the school's former glory.' He also personally lobbied board member Abraham Mazer. Soloveitchik's son Haym later said the Rebbe was 'the deciding factor' in the appointment.

title_en: Rebbe weeps over Chasidim murdered in the Holocaust
summary_en: In May 1945, as news of the Holocaust reached America, the Rebbe wept uncontrollably over photographs of his murdered Chasidim.
story_body: With the war in Europe ended and the scope of the Nazi genocide becoming clear, the sixth Rebbe sat in his office gazing at pictures of devoted followers like Rabbis Yechezkel 'Chatche' Feigin and Yitzchak 'Itche der Masmid' Horowitz. The fate of his daughter Sheina remained unknown. Rabbi Shmuel Levitin could not console him, and only the upbeat Rabbi Moshe Chaim Yehoshua Schneersohn-Twerski was finally able to lift his mood.

title_en: Kielce pogrom kills 42 Jews returning to Poland
summary_en: A year after the war's end, Polish residents murdered 42 Jews in a vicious pogrom in Kielce, signaling that survivors were unwelcome.
story_body: When Holocaust survivors returned to Poland to reclaim homes and businesses seized by neighbors, they met violent resistance. The Kielce pogrom drove home the reality that prewar Jewish life in Poland could not be revived, accelerating refugee flows to the United States, Canada, South America, Australia, and Mandatory Palestine.

title_en: Shanghai refugee yeshiva students arrive in the United States
summary_en: After years of wartime exile in Shanghai, the refugee students of Tomchei Temimim finally received visas and arrived on American shores.
story_body: Having fled Poland to Lithuania at the war's onset, the students were forcibly relocated through Russia and Japan to Shanghai, where they endured isolation and starvation. At the war's end they learned that almost all of their relatives had perished in the Holocaust. After a year waiting for American visas, they arrived in 1946 and became a key cadre for the sixth Rebbe's postwar vision.

title_en: Rebbe's letter to Shanghai students charges them with mission
summary_en: On 15 Av 5706 the Rebbe wrote to his Shanghai students, telling them divine providence had brought them to warm up 'tepid America' with chasidic passion.
story_body: Upon their arrival from Shanghai, the sixth Rebbe sent a poignant letter laying out a new vision for his refugee students. He framed their long odyssey from Poland through China to America as a divine mission to bolster Jewish life, instructing them not to be sidetracked by American bounty but to look for the positive in others and the deficiencies in themselves.

title_en: Telz students flee east with British passports
summary_en: Students from Poland's Telz Yeshiva, including 20-year-old Chaim Gutnick, fled east via Russia and Japan to Brisbane, Australia.
story_body: Holding British passports and Japanese transit visas from Chiune Sugihara, the Telz group made a long and hazardous journey by train and ship to Australia. Local Jewish leaders, anxious that idealistic students would disrupt the religious status quo, paid for their onward tickets to the United States, where Telz had reopened in Cleveland.

title_en: Telz Yeshiva reopens in Cleveland, Ohio
summary_en: Rabbis Mordechai Katz and Eliyahu Meir Bloch reopened the Telz Yeshiva in Cleveland in October 1941 with a nucleus of ten students who had come via Australia.
story_body: Telz roshei yeshivah Katz and Bloch had traveled to the US in 1940 to explore relocation options, settling on Cleveland. The ten students who escaped Poland eastward and crossed to America through Australia became the founding cohort of the American Telz Yeshiva, which became a major center of American Orthodoxy.

title_en: Rebbe instructs Chaim Gutnick to remain in Australia
summary_en: In early 1941 the sixth Rebbe directed Chaim Gutnick to stay in Australia and prepare the ground for postwar Jewish refugees.
story_body: Gutnick, the only Chabad follower among the Telz refugees, wrote to the Rebbe in Brooklyn asking him to arrange US admission. Instead the Rebbe charged him with a mission: 'Prepare the ground for the arrival of Jewish refugees so that it will be a place of Torah.' At a time when Allied victory was uncertain, Gutnick later called this 'the vision of a true Jewish leader.'

title_en: Rebbe tells Russian Chasidim to wait before fleeing
summary_en: On 8 Tevet 5706 the Rebbe responded in code to Russian Chasidim asking whether to attempt escape, telling them the situation was unclear and they should wait.
story_body: Rabbi Shmuel Levitin in New York relayed a coded message from his son-in-law Binyamin Gorodetsky in Uzbekistan. The Rebbe's actual words being too dangerous to wire, Levitin sent a telegram saying simply, 'Grandfather says it's better to stay put,' urging caution until the window for safe Polish-passport border crossings became clearer.

title_en: Group of 232 Chasidim cross Soviet border on December 2, 1946
summary_en: Fifty families totaling 232 Chasidim, including Rebbetzin Chana Schneerson, crossed from Russia into Poland during a tense two-hour border inspection.
story_body: Russian guards removed all passengers and inspected papers; Rabbi Berel Gurewicz was arrested while the rest were allowed to reboard. The Ramash (later the seventh Rebbe) later told Chasidim in Paris that during those exact two hours, the sixth Rebbe in Brooklyn sat reciting the Az Yashir prayer and finally exclaimed, 'They got through, they got through,' moments before a telegram arrived from Przemysl.

title_en: Rebbe sends celebratory letter to escapees from Russia
summary_en: On 15 Kislev 5707 the Rebbe wrote a letter overflowing with joy to anash and the students of Tomchei Temimim who had escaped from Russia.
story_body: Six days after the December 2 crossing, the Rebbe wrote, 'Blessed is the Lord, our G-d... who saved you and your family members.' He assured the refugees that 'all of our brothers and sisters will help you with love and affection' to find livelihoods and Jewish education for their children.

title_en: Rebbe appoints Binyamin Gorodetsky as European representative
summary_en: On 15 Kislev 5707 the Rebbe named Rabbi Binyamin Gorodetsky his European representative and instructed him to open an office in Paris.
story_body: Gorodetsky was tasked with assisting the refugees in France and other countries and facilitating their permanent resettlement. The Rebbe asked him to compile a detailed questionnaire on each refugee with photographs and ages. The bureau, known as 'the lishkah,' continues to operate from Paris to the present day.

title_en: Ramash leads Lag BaOmer farbrengen in Paris
summary_en: On Lag BaOmer 1947, while in Paris arranging his mother's emigration, the Ramash led a farbrengen recounting the Rebbe's mystical role in the December border crossing.
story_body: The future seventh Rebbe traveled to France in 1947 to reunite with his mother Rebbetzin Chana after twenty years of separation. At the Lag BaOmer gathering he told the story of how, on December 2, 1946, the sixth Rebbe had recited Az Yashir and proclaimed 'They got through' at the exact hour the refugees were detained at the border.

title_en: Rabbi Mendel Futerfas arrested ending the Great Escape
summary_en: Soviet secret agents arrested Rabbi Mendel Futerfas and other Chasidim aboard a passenger train, ending the organized exodus from Russia.
story_body: When remaining Chasidim attempted to cross on a regular passenger train, agents circulated onboard and arrested Futerfas at the border. The arrests began a roundup that ensnared other organizers including Sara Katzenelenbogen, forcing the Lvov network to scatter deep into Russia to evade the secret police. Futerfas would be sentenced to nine years in prison.

title_en: Rebbe's interrogation-day response to Futerfas
summary_en: On 17 Iyar 5707, the day Mendel Futerfas was brought into Soviet interrogation, the Rebbe sent his wife a letter answering an imagined telegram from her husband.
story_body: Futerfas later recounted that at his moment of crisis, he envisioned writing to the Rebbe and conjured the image of Simchat Torah 1927, the last time he saw him. On that same day his wife in England received a letter beginning 'Your telegram has been received,' dated 17 Iyar 5707. Only when reunited in 1963 did the couple piece together what had occurred.

title_en: Rebbe instructs Chasidim to stay in Poland to free prisoners
summary_en: On 8 Iyar 5707 the Rebbe wrote to Rabbi Shalom Mendel Kalmenson directing Zalman Serebryanski and Yitzchak Goldin to remain in Poland to help free three jailed Chasidim.
story_body: Berel Gurewicz, Berke Chein, and Tzipa Kozliner had been detained by local police in Lvov unaware of the larger escape network. The Rebbe coordinated a $7,000 bribe routed through a contact in Vilnius, written about in code as 'medicine' for those ill. The bribe led to improved conditions and reduced sentences for all three.

title_en: Berel Gurewicz freed in Poland before Passover
summary_en: Just before Passover 1948, Berel Gurewicz was freed in Poland as part of a prisoner exchange after maintaining his cover as a Polish citizen.
story_body: Bribed Soviet officials included Gurewicz in a Russia-Poland prisoner exchange. He then secretly crossed into Czechoslovakia, and with Vaad Hatzalah's help, he traveled to Paris to reunite with the family that had fled Russia without him.

title_en: Dr. Nissan Mindel sent on mission to England
summary_en: In September 1945 the Rebbe sent his secretary Dr. Nissan Mindel to England to survey postwar European Jewry and explore Chabad expansion.
story_body: Mindel's mandate was to 'collect detailed information on the economic and spiritual status of our fellow Jews in liberated Europe' and to scope options for Chabad's educational programs in the United Kingdom. The Rebbe wrote ahead to Jewish leaders and the British Chabad community asking them to assist him.

title_en: Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson dispatched to Paris and Prague
summary_en: In summer 1946 the Rebbe sent Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson to Paris and Prague to coordinate the escape of Russian Chasidim from Poland to the American zone.
story_body: Working with the Brichah underground, Jacobson organized clandestine border crossings from Poland into Czechoslovakia and secured papers permitting refugees to move into Germany's American zone. He was followed by other emissaries including the Rebbe's son-in-law, the Rashag.

title_en: Bentzion Shemtov sent to establish Chabad in London
summary_en: In October 1947 the Rebbe sent Bentzion Shemtov, one of the nine Chasidim of the 1924 oath, to establish Chabad in London.
story_body: Shemtov was among the trusted veterans of Chabad activism whom the Rebbe deployed in the postwar years to build infrastructure in Western communities. His mission in London laid groundwork for Chabad's enduring presence in the United Kingdom.

title_en: Rebbe sends first students to Brandeis University
summary_en: In 1949 the Rebbe dispatched two students, Shlomo Carlebach and Zalman Schachter, to Brandeis University in Chabad's first formal college campus outreach.
story_body: Telling them 'the time has come for us to reach out to college students,' the Rebbe inaugurated what would become a defining feature of Chabad activity. The seventh Rebbe would later expand this into a global Chabad House network beginning at UCLA in 1969; Carlebach and Schachter each eventually broke away from Chabad.

title_en: Rebbe writes Gurewicz before voyage to Australia
summary_en: On 23 Iyar 5709 the Rebbe wrote Nachum Zalman Gurewicz urging him to influence fellow passengers en route to Australia.
story_body: Before Gurewicz's departure from Europe, the Rebbe wished him mazel tov on his son's bar mitzvah, to be celebrated aboard ship docked at Port Said. The Rebbe instructed him to use the long voyage to influence others, particularly the young, to study Torah.

title_en: Rebbe rebukes Wilshanski to pursue outreach to Australian youth
summary_en: On 26 Iyar 5709 the Rebbe urged Reb Betzalel Wilshanski, age 52, to reach out to Australian youth even those uninterested in study.
story_body: Known for his scholarship from his Lubavitch yeshivah years, Wilshanski was learning to adapt as a public activist. The Rebbe exhorted him: 'Even those who apparently don't want to study, you should draw them closer by giving them reading material in their language. Don't get disillusioned in your efforts.'

title_en: Rebbe presses Gurewicz to lead change in Melbourne
summary_en: On 17 Elul 5709 the Rebbe responded to Gurewicz's lament about Melbourne's anemic Jewish life by declaring this was the very reason providence had brought him there.
story_body: Gurewicz had reported discouragingly on the state of Melbourne Jewry. The Rebbe wrote back emphatically: 'The time has come that he, along with his fellow Chasidim, should work with zealousness and joy to improve the situation. This is a mission that the divine providence has brought you there to fulfill.'

title_en: Tzemach Gurewicz brings family to Cuba
summary_en: In summer 1948 Tzemach Gurewicz, unable to obtain a US visa, took his family to Cuba hoping to find an onward route to New York.
story_body: Having endured five years in a Russian prison and the Great Escape, Gurewicz longed to reach his relatives in America. The Rebbe redirected his focus, telling him to build educational programs in Cuba first; only after he had done so would the Rebbe finally signal that the time had come for him to come.

title_en: Rebbe writes Rodshtein questioning Gurewicz's rush to America
summary_en: On 7 Marcheshvan 5709 the Rebbe wrote Rabbi Moshe Leib Rodshtein questioning why Tzemach Gurewicz was rushing to leave Cuba for the US.
story_body: Rodshtein had been working to secure visas for his nephew's family. The Rebbe responded, 'I do not understand why he is rushing to come here. So much can be done there in the sphere of spreading Torah and boosting Jewish education,' redirecting Gurewicz to communal labor in Havana.

title_en: Rebbe approves Gurewicz move from Cuba to New York
summary_en: On 19 Kislev 5709 the Rebbe told Rodshtein it was finally time for Tzemach to come to America, having praised his educational work in Cuba.
story_body: After Gurewicz set up educational programs in Cuba as the Rebbe had directed, the Rebbe relayed approval for him to move on. He would not arrive in New York until June 1950, after the sixth Rebbe's passing.

title_en: Rebbe encourages Meir Chaikin to stay in Stockholm
summary_en: On 13 Tamuz 5709 the Rebbe rejected Rabbi Meir Chaikin's idea of leaving disappointing Stockholm, framing his post as an honor of divine providence.
story_body: Disillusioned with Stockholm's lackluster religious community, Chaikin sought to relocate. The Rebbe wrote, 'You should consider your arrival in Stockholm a great honor that divine providence has chosen you to illuminate with the light of Torah in an unplanted field.'

title_en: Rabbi Aloy told to return to South Africa after election scare
summary_en: Following the 1948 victory of the Nationalist Afrikaner Party, Rabbi Yirmiyahu Aloy met the Rebbe in New York and was simply told, 'Fuhr aheim — go back home.'
story_body: Many Jews feared the Nationalist victory presaged another Holocaust. Aloy, who had emigrated from Lithuania to South Africa before the war, asked the Rebbe in private whether to leave. The Rebbe laughed and dismissed the concern; Aloy returned and emerged as one of South Africa's most prominent rabbis on the rabbinical court.

title_en: Rebbe rebukes Paris refugees for relying on JDC support
summary_en: In a letter to the Paris community the Rebbe wrote that it was 'inappropriate' and 'not the way of Chasidism' to sit idle while depending on JDC charity.
story_body: Many Chasidim transferred from DP camps to France, where the JDC generously supported them. The Rebbe pressed them toward self-sufficiency: 'Each one of you must make an effort to earn a livelihood... Exert yourselves and move quickly, be it in an institution of Torah, business, or employment.'

title_en: Colel Chabad founded by Rabbi Schneur Zalman
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi established Colel Chabad in 1788 to support early chasidic immigration from Europe to the Land of Israel.
story_body: Colel Chabad is the oldest continuously operating charitable organization in the Land of Israel. Its founding to assist Chabad immigrants from Europe predated by more than 150 years the Rebbe's postwar effort to refocus Chabad in Israel outward toward all Israeli Jews.

title_en: Sara Katzenelenbogen's husband Michoel assassinated
summary_en: In 1937 Russian authorities assassinated Michoel Katzenelenbogen, leaving his wife Sara to take over financing the clandestine Chabad educational network.
story_body: After her husband's murder Sara Katzenelenbogen became a primary organizer of underground Chabad education and later of the Great Escape. Eventually captured in Uzbekistan after being placed on the most-wanted list, she died of a heart attack in prison in 1952.

title_en: Sara Katzenelenbogen dies in Soviet prison
summary_en: Sara Katzenelenbogen, a primary organizer of the Great Escape, died of a heart attack in Soviet prison in 1952 after her capture in Uzbekistan.
story_body: Placed on Russia's most-wanted list for her role financing clandestine Chabad education and the 1946–47 escape, Katzenelenbogen was eventually arrested and never released. She was the mother-in-law of Shula Kazen, who escaped to the Pocking DP camp.

title_en: Berke Chein immigrates to Israel after Soviet imprisonment
summary_en: Berke Chein, whose death sentence had been commuted following a bribe arranged by the Rebbe, immigrated to Israel in 1961 after his Soviet imprisonment.
story_body: Chein had been arrested in Lvov for attempting to escape during the Great Escape and held by local police. The $7,000 bribe arranged by the sixth Rebbe through a Vilnius contact reduced his sentence; he was freed after three years and ultimately settled in Israel.

title_en: Tzipa Kozliner allowed to leave Russia
summary_en: Tzipa Kozliner, one of three Chasidim jailed in Lvov during the Great Escape, finally received Soviet permission to emigrate in 1970.
story_body: Kozliner had been detained by local police in Lvov in 1947 and her conditions improved after a bribe arranged by the Rebbe. She was released from jail well before her eventual emigration two decades later, part of the early Soviet Jewry exit waves.

title_en: Schneur Gutnick passes away in London
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Gutnick, rabbi of the London Chabad synagogue, passed away in 1931, leaving his eleven-year-old son Chaim an orphan.
story_body: Rabbi Yechezkel Abramsky took an interest in the young Chaim Gutnick after his father's death and encouraged his attendance at Telz Yeshiva in Poland. Chaim would later emerge as one of Australia's most influential rabbis.

title_en: Rabbi Moshe Chaim Yehoshua Schneersohn-Twerski immigrates to US
summary_en: Rabbi Moshe Chaim Yehoshua Schneersohn-Twerski, a descendant of the second Rebbe, immigrated to the United States in 1924.
story_body: Born in 1867, he settled on Eastern Parkway near what would become the sixth Rebbe's shul. A distant relative and close confidant of the sixth Rebbe, his naturally joyous disposition made him the one who could console the Rebbe after the Holocaust photographs incident of May 1945.

title_en: Nine Chasidim take oath with the Rebbe
summary_en: In 1924 nine Chasidim, including Bentzion Shemtov, took an oath with the sixth Rebbe that would mark them as trusted activists for decades.
story_body: The 1924 oath bound a small group of Chasidim to the Rebbe's mission during the harshest years of Soviet anti-religious persecution. Members of this group, like Shemtov, were later deployed in the postwar era to build Chabad infrastructure in Western countries.

title_en: Zalman Shazar immigrates to Palestine
summary_en: Zionist leader Zalman Shazar (born Schneur Zalman Rubashov to a Chabad family) immigrated to Palestine in 1924.
story_body: Born in 1889 in Mir near Minsk to a Chabad family, Shazar became active in the Zionist Poalei Tzion movement before settling in Palestine to take a leadership role in Zionist activities. He would later play a part in the planning of Kfar Chabad with the sixth Rebbe.

title_en: Sixth Rebbe departs Russia after Simchat Torah in Leningrad
summary_en: The sixth Rebbe departed Russia in 1927, the day after Simchat Torah in Leningrad, in a memory Mendel Futerfas would invoke from a Soviet interrogation cell two decades later.
story_body: Futerfas's last sight of the Rebbe was at the Simchat Torah gathering in Leningrad in 1927. When facing Soviet interrogation on 17 Iyar 5707, he conjured that image and mentally composed a letter requesting a blessing — to which, by mystical coincidence, the Rebbe in New York responded that very day.

title_en: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson exiled to Kazakhstan
summary_en: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson, father of the future seventh Rebbe, was jailed by Soviet authorities and exiled in 1939 to a remote village near the Chinese border.
story_body: His wife Rebbetzin Chana followed him into exile in Kazakhstan and was at his bedside when he passed away in Alma Ata in 1945. She later escaped Russia through the Great Escape, made it to Paris, and was reunited with her son the Ramash in 1947 after twenty years of separation.

title_en: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson passes away in Alma Ata
summary_en: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson died in Alma Ata, Kazakhstan in 1945 with his wife Rebbetzin Chana at his bedside, after years of Soviet exile.
story_body: Exiled in 1939 from his rabbinical post for religious activism, Levi Yitzchak endured years in a remote Kazakh village. After his death his wife eventually escaped Russia through the Great Escape, reaching a German DP camp and ultimately Paris.

title_en: Rebbe's letter to Rabbi Yosef Wineberg on global mission
summary_en: On 7 Shevat 5710 the Rebbe wrote Rabbi Yosef Wineberg summarizing his goal: a Tomchei Temimim student in every community and country.
story_body: The Rebbe's vision was articulated as: 'in every community and in every country, a student of Tomchei Temimim, a beacon of the Torah light in the ways of Chasidism.' Wineberg was assisting refugees with relocation, and this letter framed the broader strategic blueprint that the seventh Rebbe would expand into a global emissary network.

title_en: Ramash delivers first maamar, accepting the Chabad leadership
summary_en: On the first yahrzeit of the Rayatz, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson delivered his inaugural maamar in 770, formally assuming the role of seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe.
story_body: A year after the Rayatz's passing, Chasidim packed 770 in Brooklyn for the yahrzeit farbrengen, eager to see whether the Ramash would accept leadership. After he spoke on ahavat Yisrael, the elder chasid Rabbi Sender Nemtzov rose and called out for chasidut. The Ramash then delivered his first maamar, 'Basi Legani,' built on his father-in-law's final teaching, marking the start of his tenure as seventh Rebbe.

title_en: Rayatz releases his final maamar 'Basi Legani' for 10 Shevat
summary_en: The Rayatz released his final maamar, based on the verse 'I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride,' on the day of his passing.
story_body: The maamar, distributed for 10 Shevat 5710, would later become the foundational text for the seventh Rebbe's first maamar and for an annual teaching tradition. Every year on 10 Shevat, his successor expounded on a concept from this final maamar, building the seventh Rebbe's leadership directly on the foundation laid by his father-in-law.

title_en: Passing of the seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe in Brooklyn
summary_en: Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, the seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe, passed away in Brooklyn at age 92 and was interred alongside his father-in-law.
story_body: After 42 years of leadership during which he transformed Chabad into the largest Jewish movement in the world, the seventh Rebbe passed away on 3 Tamuz 5754. He was buried in Montefiore Cemetery, New York, next to the Rayatz. The Ohel has since become a pilgrimage site visited by close to a million Jews and non-Jews seeking prayer and inspiration.

title_en: Birth of Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn in Lubavitch
summary_en: The future sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe, Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, was born in Lubavitch, Russia.
story_body: Born on 12 Tamuz 5640, he would grow up to succeed his father, the Rashab, as the sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe. His birthday, 12 Tamuz, later coincided with his release from Soviet imprisonment in 1927, making the date a celebrated chasidic holiday.

title_en: Rayatz begins communal work as his father's personal secretary
summary_en: At age 15, Yosef Yitzchak began his communal career serving as personal secretary to his father, the Rashab.
story_body: This early role gave him intimate access to the affairs of the Chabad movement and prepared him for decades of communal leadership. He would handle correspondence, organizational matters, and represent his father in increasingly significant roles.

title_en: Marriage of Yosef Yitzchak to Nechama Dina Schneersohn
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn married Nechama Dina Schneersohn on 13 Elul 5657.
story_body: The union joined two branches of the Schneersohn family. Nechama Dina would stand by her husband through Soviet persecution, exile, and the eventual escape to America.

title_en: Rayatz appointed head of Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak was appointed to lead Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim, the central Chabad yeshiva founded by his father.
story_body: This role placed him at the helm of Chabad's flagship educational institution at age 18. Tomchei Temimim would become his lifelong project, with branches eventually established across Russia, Poland, and ultimately North America.

title_en: Rayatz travels to Vilna, Brisk, Lodz, and Koenigsberg
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak traveled across Eastern Europe to establish the Dubrovna factory.
story_body: The trip was part of his communal economic work, organizing infrastructure that could support Jewish life and community in the region. He visited major Jewish centers including Vilna, Brisk, Lodz, and Koenigsberg in pursuit of the project.

title_en: Rayatz travels to St. Petersburg for communal matters
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak traveled to St. Petersburg to handle communal matters on behalf of Russian Jewry.
story_body: St. Petersburg, as the imperial capital, was a key center for Jewish advocacy with government officials. The Rayatz repeatedly traveled there throughout the early 1900s, work that ultimately led to his being arrested four times between 1902 and 1911.

title_en: Rayatz organizes Passover fund for Russian troops in the Far East
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak helped organize a fund to provide Passover supplies for Jewish soldiers in the Russian army deployed to the Far East.
story_body: During the Russo-Japanese War, Jewish soldiers serving far from home faced enormous difficulty observing Passover. The Rayatz participated in organizing logistical and financial support to bring matzah and other holiday needs to these troops.

title_en: Rayatz lobbies German and Dutch bankers to stop pogroms
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak traveled to Germany and Holland to persuade bankers to use their financial leverage to stop pogroms in Russia.
story_body: Following the wave of pogroms that swept Russia in 1905-1906, the Rayatz sought international economic pressure as a tool for protecting Jewish communities. He approached prominent bankers in Germany and Holland, asking them to use their leverage with the Russian government.

title_en: Rayatz participates in organizing the Vilna Conference
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak helped organize the Vilna Conference addressing the state of Russian Jewry.
story_body: The Vilna Conference gathered rabbinic and communal leaders to address pressing challenges facing Russian Jewry. The Rayatz's involvement reflected his growing stature as a communal organizer.

title_en: Rayatz travels to Germany to confer with communal leaders
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak traveled to Germany for consultations with Jewish communal leaders.
story_body: His travels in 1909 continued his pattern of seeking international Jewish coordination on issues facing Russian Jewry. Germany hosted significant Jewish philanthropic and political networks that the Rayatz worked to engage.

title_en: Rayatz involved in preparing the Rabbinical Conference
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak helped prepare a major Rabbinical Conference addressing Russian Jewish religious affairs.
story_body: The conference was part of ongoing efforts to defend traditional Jewish practice in the face of Russian government interference. Between 1902 and 1911, his communal advocacy resulted in four arrests in Moscow and St. Petersburg.

title_en: Rayatz accepts position of sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe
summary_en: Following the passing of his father, the Rashab, in Rostov, Yosef Yitzchak accepted the role of sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe.
story_body: The Rashab left explicit instructions that his son succeed him, easing the succession. The Rayatz took on leadership during one of the most perilous periods in Russian Jewish history, as Bolshevik anti-religious campaigns intensified.

title_en: Rayatz establishes Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim in Warsaw
summary_en: The Rayatz established a branch of Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim in Warsaw and launched a program to strengthen Judaism in Soviet Russia.
story_body: With the original Lubavitch yeshiva network under attack from Soviet authorities, opening a Warsaw branch provided a relatively safe haven outside Russia. Simultaneously, the Rayatz launched an extensive underground network to sustain Jewish education and observance inside the USSR.

title_en: Rayatz forced to leave Rostov and relocate to St. Petersburg
summary_en: Forced from Rostov, the Rayatz relocated to St. Petersburg, intensified Jewish life efforts in Russia, and established Agudas Chassidei Chabad in the US.
story_body: Bolshevik pressure made Rostov untenable, but the Rayatz refused to abandon Russian Jewry. From St. Petersburg, he expanded the underground religious network. He also founded Agudas Chassidei Chabad in the United States as a base for international support.

title_en: Rayatz arrested, sentenced to death, exiled, and expelled from Russia
summary_en: After establishing yeshivas in Bukhara, the Rayatz was arrested by Soviet authorities, sentenced to death, exiled to Kostroma, and forced to leave Russia for Latvia.
story_body: Soviet secret police arrested the Rayatz for his clandestine religious work, initially sentencing him to death. International pressure commuted the sentence to exile in Kostroma and ultimately expulsion from the USSR. He departed for Riga, Latvia, where he would establish his next base of operations.

title_en: Rayatz campaigns to send matzah to Soviet Jews
summary_en: From his new base outside Russia, the Rayatz organized campaigns to supply matzah to Jews still trapped under Soviet rule.
story_body: With Passover observance increasingly difficult in the USSR, the Rayatz mobilized international networks to ship matzah eastward. The effort continued through 1929 and laid groundwork for ongoing covert religious support.

title_en: Rayatz visits Eretz Yisrael and the United States
summary_en: The Rayatz undertook a historic visit to Eretz Yisrael and the United States, his first time in both countries.
story_body: The journey took the Rayatz to the Holy Land, where he visited established and emerging Jewish communities, and then to America, where he met thousands of Jews and laid groundwork for future Chabad activity. The visits reshaped his geographic vision for the movement.

title_en: Rayatz departs the United States to return to Europe
summary_en: The Rayatz left the United States to return to Europe after his historic American visit.
story_body: He set sail on 21 Tamuz 5690, beginning a journey that would take him via Germany to recovery in Marienbad and finally home to Riga. The trip back marked the end of his groundbreaking visit to America, where he had established Agudas Chassidei Chabad's American presence.

title_en: Rayatz arrives in Bremen, Germany
summary_en: After leaving New York, the Rayatz arrived in Bremen, Germany.
story_body: Bremen, a major German port, served as his entry point back to Europe. From there he traveled to Berlin in time for Tisha B'Av.

title_en: Rayatz spends Tisha B'Av in Berlin
summary_en: The Rayatz observed Tisha B'Av in Berlin during his journey back to Riga.
story_body: Berlin in 1930 hosted a significant chasidic community, including many émigrés from Russia. The Rayatz's presence for Tisha B'Av brought together local chasidim for a meaningful observance of the fast day.

title_en: Rayatz arrives back in Riga after American journey
summary_en: The Rayatz returned to his Riga home on 15 Elul after his American trip and a recuperation stay in Marienbad.
story_body: Riga had become his European base following expulsion from the USSR. The arrival concluded his months-long voyage from New York via Bremen, Berlin, and Marienbad.

title_en: Rayatz visits Rakshik in Lithuania
summary_en: The Rayatz traveled to Rakshik, Lithuania, for nine days to receive local Chasidim.
story_body: Many Chasidim in the region could not travel to Riga, so the Rayatz brought himself to them. The visit from 1 Adar to 9 Adar gave Lithuanian Chabad communities a rare opportunity to meet the Rebbe.

title_en: Rayatz departs Riga to survey Warsaw yeshiva
summary_en: The Rayatz left Riga on 9 Tamuz to spend two weeks in Warsaw assessing the yeshiva and the possibility of relocating there.
story_body: Warsaw had become a major center of Chabad activity outside the USSR. The Rayatz wanted to evaluate the Tomchei Temimim branch in person and weigh whether to move his own residence to Poland.

title_en: Rayatz spends Shabbat in Otwock
summary_en: During his Warsaw trip, the Rayatz spent Shabbat 13 Tamuz in Otwock.
story_body: Otwock, a resort town near Warsaw, would later become the Rayatz's permanent residence. This early visit foreshadowed its future role as the Chabad center in Poland.

title_en: Rayatz travels to Marienbad for recovery
summary_en: The Rayatz left Warsaw on 23 Tamuz for an extended stay in Marienbad.
story_body: Marienbad's spas were a frequent destination for the Rayatz, who suffered chronic health issues. He stayed until 1 Elul before beginning his journey back to Riga.

title_en: Rayatz returns to Riga via Berlin
summary_en: After Marienbad and a short Berlin stop, the Rayatz arrived back in Riga on 7 Elul.
story_body: The travel pattern of Riga–Marienbad–Berlin–Riga became familiar over his Latvian years. He would not stay long, however, departing for Poland just two weeks later for the High Holidays.

title_en: Rayatz departs Riga for the High Holidays in Poland
summary_en: On 21 Elul, the Rayatz left Riga to spend the High Holidays in Poland.
story_body: Spending the High Holidays among the Chasidim of Warsaw and Otwock allowed the Rayatz to strengthen his Polish flock. He would remain in Poland through Cheshvan, dividing his time between Warsaw and Otwock.

title_en: Rayatz returns from Poland to Riga
summary_en: After dividing his post-holiday time between Warsaw and Otwock, the Rayatz returned to Riga on 10 Cheshvan.
story_body: The return concluded a months-long Polish stay. Latvia remained his official residence, even as his connections to Polish Chasidic life deepened.

title_en: Rayatz visits Lithuanian Chabad communities
summary_en: The Rayatz traveled through Lithuania, visiting communities including Glubok and Pastov.
story_body: From 30 Adar Alef to 9 Adar Bet, he brought himself to townlets where local Chabad Chasidim could meet him in person. He returned to Riga on March 17.

title_en: Marriage of Sheina Schneersohn to Mendel Horenstein in Landvarov
summary_en: The Rayatz's youngest daughter Sheina married Mendel Horenstein in Landvarov, Poland, on 10 Sivan.
story_body: The Rayatz left Riga before Shavuot to attend the wedding. Sheina and her husband would later be among the millions murdered in the Holocaust, while her sister Chaya Mushka escaped to America.

title_en: Rayatz travels to Druskenig for medical treatment
summary_en: After his daughter's wedding, the Rayatz traveled to Druskenig for about two months of medical treatment for his feet.
story_body: Chronic foot problems plagued the Rayatz throughout his life and shaped much of his travel schedule. The spa town of Druskenig provided extended treatment in the summer of 1932.

title_en: Rayatz travels to Ludmir via Brisk and Kovel
summary_en: Leaving Druskenig on 23 Av, the Rayatz traveled to Ludmir, stopping along the way in Brisk and Kovel.
story_body: Each stop on the journey allowed local communities to receive the Rebbe. The route through Brisk and Kovel passed through major centers of Polish Jewish life.

title_en: Rayatz returns to Riga via Warsaw and Vienna
summary_en: The Rayatz arrived back in Riga on 9 Elul after delivering maamarim in Warsaw and Vienna.
story_body: The Rayatz used travel stops to deliver chasidic discourses, strengthening the connection of remote communities. The trip closed a summer of extensive movement through Poland, Lithuania, and Austria.

title_en: Rayatz travels to Berlin for medical care
summary_en: The Rayatz traveled from Riga to Berlin on 12 Tevet for approximately two months of medical care.
story_body: His arrival in Berlin came just as Adolf Hitler's rise to power approached its peak; the Nazis would take control of Germany weeks later. The Rayatz nonetheless spent two months there receiving treatment before continuing his European travels.

title_en: Rayatz returns to Riga from Paris
summary_en: After traveling from Berlin to Paris in March 1933, the Rayatz returned to Riga on 23 Adar.
story_body: This trip wove together stops in Berlin, Paris, and Riga, reflecting both medical needs and communal obligations. Paris would later host a sanitorium that the Rayatz visited repeatedly.

title_en: Rayatz leaves Riga permanently
summary_en: The Rayatz departed Riga on July 4, 1933, leaving Latvia permanently though the move was not publicly announced.
story_body: After years based in Riga, the Rayatz quietly relocated his residence to Warsaw. He stopped first at the Warsaw yeshiva to lead a farbrengen, then continued to Marienbad before formally settling in Warsaw later that summer.

title_en: Rayatz leads farbrengen at Warsaw yeshiva en route to Marienbad
summary_en: Passing through Warsaw on his way to Marienbad, the Rayatz led a farbrengen at the yeshiva.
story_body: The Warsaw yeshiva, a flagship of Tomchei Temimim outside the USSR, would soon become the Rayatz's home base. His farbrengen on the way to Marienbad already signaled the deepening relationship.

title_en: Rayatz arrives in Marienbad for extended stay
summary_en: The Rayatz arrived in Marienbad on 13 Tamuz for a six-week health-focused stay.
story_body: His Marienbad stays were a fixed feature of his European years. He remained there until 29 Av before officially moving to Warsaw.

title_en: Rayatz officially relocates to Warsaw
summary_en: Leaving Marienbad on 29 Av, the Rayatz settled in Warsaw as his new permanent residence.
story_body: Warsaw replaced Riga as the seat of the sixth Rebbe. The move strengthened his ties to Polish Chasidim and centered Chabad operations in the heart of European Jewry.

title_en: Rayatz moves to Warsaw, Poland
summary_en: The Rayatz settled in Warsaw, Poland, as recorded in the canonical timeline of his life.
story_body: Although he had relocated in mid-1933, official chronologies record 1934 (5694) as the year of his Warsaw residency. From here he led the Chabad movement until his move to Otwock in 1936.

title_en: Rayatz visits Riga for nine days
summary_en: The Rayatz visited Riga from 12-20 Adar 5694, delivering maamarim and speaking to the women of the community.
story_body: Returning to the Latvian community he had lived among for years, the Rayatz used the visit to reconnect with his former host city. His talks to the women of the community were a notable feature of the visit.

title_en: Rayatz visits Glubok and Vilna
summary_en: The Rayatz left Warsaw on June 3 for a visit to Glubok in Lithuania, stopping in Vilna along the way.
story_body: He remained in Glubok through 6 Tamuz, an inspiring visit for the Chasidim of the region. The trip continued his pattern of bringing himself to communities that could not easily come to him.

title_en: Rayatz travels to Marienbad
summary_en: On 22 Tamuz the Rayatz departed Warsaw for another stay in Marienbad.
story_body: His annual summer trips to Marienbad for health treatment were a fixture of his Warsaw years. The 1934 trip was followed by a visit to Prague on the way home.

title_en: Rayatz visits Prague
summary_en: Returning from Marienbad, the Rayatz visited Prague on 15 Av before continuing to Warsaw.
story_body: Prague hosted a small but historic Jewish community. The Rayatz's visit allowed him to engage with local Jews before completing his journey back to Warsaw.

title_en: Rayatz begins publication of Hatomim journal
summary_en: The Rayatz launched Hatomim, a chasidic journal published from his base in Warsaw.
story_body: Hatomim became an influential publication for the Chabad world, featuring chasidic teachings, history, and contemporary content. It documented the movement's life in interwar Poland and amplified the Rayatz's voice.

title_en: Rayatz travels to Perchtoldsdorf sanitorium near Vienna
summary_en: On 6 Kislev 5695 the Rayatz traveled to the West End Sanitorium in Perchtoldsdorf for treatment by Dr. Max Gerson.
story_body: Dr. Max Gerson was a famous physician known for innovative dietary therapies. The Rayatz spent nearly half a year under his care, returning to Warsaw only in mid-April 1935.

title_en: Rayatz farbrengs in Vienna at Reb Klonimus Kalman Poppenheim's home
summary_en: During his Perchtoldsdorf stay, the Rayatz led a farbrengen at the home of Reb Klonimus Kalman Poppenheim in Vienna.
story_body: Poppenheim's home was a hub for Chabad life in Vienna. The farbrengen on 4 Tevet drew together local Chasidim, an important communal moment during the Rayatz's lengthy Austrian convalescence.

title_en: Rayatz returns to Warsaw before Passover
summary_en: The Rayatz arrived back in Warsaw on 12 Nisan, just in time for Passover.
story_body: His half-year stay in Austria had ended after a few additional days of communal meetings in Vienna. He returned home for the holiday with his family.

title_en: Rayatz relocates permanently to Otwock
summary_en: On 21 Elul, the Rayatz moved permanently to Otwock, and the central Tomchei Temimim yeshiva was transferred there from Warsaw.
story_body: Otwock's clean air and quiet streets suited the Rayatz's health needs while keeping him close to Warsaw. The yeshiva's transfer made the town a major center of Chabad life in interwar Poland.

title_en: Rayatz moves Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim and his residence to Otwock
summary_en: The Rayatz's official chronology records 1936 as the year his residence and the central yeshiva moved to Otwock.
story_body: Although the actual relocation occurred in 1935, the canonical timeline assigns it to 5696. Otwock became the Rayatz's home until his escape from Nazi-occupied Poland.

title_en: Rayatz returns to Perchtoldsdorf sanitorium
summary_en: The Rayatz returned to the Perchtoldsdorf sanitorium on 17 Tevet for additional medical treatment.
story_body: His ongoing health issues required regular treatment by Dr. Max Gerson. The Rayatz stayed in Austria until late February, returning home for his grandson's bar mitzvah.

title_en: Bar mitzvah of Shalom Ber (Berke) Gurary
summary_en: The Rayatz's grandson, Shalom Ber (Berke) Gurary, celebrated his bar mitzvah on 25-26 Shevat.
story_body: The Rayatz returned from Perchtoldsdorf specifically to attend the bar mitzvah. Berke was the son of the Rayatz's eldest daughter Chana and her husband Rabbi Shmaryahu Gurary.

title_en: Rayatz travels to Paris for medical treatment
summary_en: The Rayatz traveled to Paris on June 28 for treatment at the sanitorium in Ville-d'Avray.
story_body: Ville-d'Avray, a suburb of Paris, hosted a major sanitorium the Rayatz used over multiple summers. He remained in France until the end of August, also engaging with the local chasidic community.

title_en: Rayatz says maamar in the Paris chasidic community
summary_en: Before leaving Paris, the Rayatz delivered a maamar in the chasidic community on 8 Elul.
story_body: The maamar marked the conclusion of his summer stay and strengthened the Paris Chabad community ahead of the High Holidays. He then traveled via Vienna and Perchtoldsdorf back to Otwock.

title_en: Rayatz returns to Otwock after Paris and Austria
summary_en: Returning from Paris via Vienna and Perchtoldsdorf, the Rayatz arrived back in Otwock on 22 Elul.
story_body: The complex itinerary reflected the layered concerns of health, communal engagement, and family. He was home in time to lead the chasidim through the Tishrei holidays.

title_en: Rayatz departs Otwock for Vienna
summary_en: On December 27, the Rayatz left Otwock for Vienna and a week of treatment in Perchtoldsdorf.
story_body: This trip kicked off a multi-month journey that took him to Paris through February. Health remained the consistent driver of these long winter absences from Otwock.

title_en: Rayatz arrives in Paris for extended stay
summary_en: After a week in Perchtoldsdorf, the Rayatz arrived in Paris on 21 Tevet for a stay lasting until 7 Adar.
story_body: The extended stay combined treatment and engagement with Parisian Chabad. He would head back to Perchtoldsdorf before returning to Otwock in late March.

title_en: Rayatz returns to Otwock from Paris and Austria
summary_en: After his Paris-Perchtoldsdorf circuit, the Rayatz arrived back in Otwock on 11 Nisan, just before Passover.
story_body: The return home gave him a few weeks with family before the holiday. He would head out again to Perchtoldsdorf in mid-June for the summer.

title_en: Rayatz travels to Perchtoldsdorf for summer
summary_en: The Rayatz left Otwock on 6 Tamuz for a summer-long stay at the Perchtoldsdorf sanitorium.
story_body: He remained in Austria until late August. This was his last summer of regular Austrian treatment; Nazi annexation of Austria in March 1938 would cut off this route.

title_en: Rayatz returns to Otwock for holidays
summary_en: On 19 Elul, the Rayatz returned to Otwock from Perchtoldsdorf in time for the holidays.
story_body: Returning before Rosh Hashanah ensured he could lead the Tishrei observances with his chasidim. He would not return to Austria for treatment until just before the Anschluss.

title_en: Rayatz returns to Perchtoldsdorf
summary_en: The Rayatz traveled to Perchtoldsdorf on 24 Tevet for what would be his final visit before Austria fell to the Nazis.
story_body: He stayed until 6 Adar Alef before relocating to Paris. The timing proved providential, as the German annexation of Austria came just three days after his departure.

title_en: Rayatz departs Austria for Paris before the Anschluss
summary_en: The Rayatz left Austria for Paris on March 9, just three days before Germany annexed Austria.
story_body: The Anschluss on March 12, 1938 closed Austria as a safe destination for the Rayatz. Had he stayed longer, he could have fallen into Nazi hands. He continued his medical treatment in Ville-d'Avray, France.

title_en: Rayatz returns to Otwock from Paris for Passover
summary_en: After his Paris sanitorium stay, the Rayatz returned to Otwock on 12 Nisan in time for Passover.
story_body: Following his last extended treatment abroad, the Rayatz returned to Otwock for the holiday. Nazi Germany's tightening grip on Europe would soon end his ability to travel for health care.

title_en: Rayatz travels to Riga for health reasons
summary_en: The Rayatz visited Riga from 4 Shevat to 11 Nisan 5699 for health reasons.
story_body: With Austria closed and tensions rising across Europe, Riga remained accessible. The Rayatz spent over two months in Latvia before returning to Otwock for Passover, his last calm period before war.

title_en: Rayatz leaves Otwock for Warsaw after the start of WWII
summary_en: Four days after the German invasion of Poland, the Rayatz left Otwock for Warsaw.
story_body: On 21 Elul, with German forces racing into Poland, the Rayatz relocated from Otwock to Warsaw. The move began the harrowing months of his rescue from Nazi-occupied Warsaw, eventually engineered through US diplomatic channels.

title_en: Rayatz departs Warsaw after rescue from the Nazi army
summary_en: The Rayatz was rescued from Nazi-occupied Warsaw on 21 Kislev, departing for Riga.
story_body: An extraordinary multinational rescue effort, including high-level US diplomatic intervention, extracted the Rayatz from Warsaw. He left the besieged city on December 14, en route to Latvia and ultimately America.

title_en: Rayatz arrives in Riga after escape from Warsaw
summary_en: Following his escape from Warsaw, the Rayatz arrived in Riga on Sunday, December 18 (25 Kislev).
story_body: Latvia provided a way station while plans were finalized for the next leg of his journey. He would remain in Riga for several months before continuing to Sweden and onward to America.

title_en: Rayatz departs Riga for Stockholm
summary_en: On 24 Adar Alef, the Rayatz left Riga for Stockholm, Sweden.
story_body: The Stockholm transit allowed the Rayatz to board a transatlantic ship from neutral Sweden, the safest available route to the United States as the war engulfed Europe.

title_en: Rayatz boards transatlantic ship in Gothenburg
summary_en: The Rayatz boarded a ship in Gothenburg, Sweden, on 27 Adar Alef for his transatlantic journey.
story_body: Gothenburg was a major port for transatlantic crossings during the war. The voyage from Sweden to the US took nearly two weeks, taking him through dangerous wartime waters.

title_en: Rayatz arrives in the United States
summary_en: The Rayatz arrived in the United States on March 19, 1940 (9 Adar Bet), settling in Brooklyn and establishing Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim there.
story_body: His arrival in America launched a new chapter for Chabad. From Brooklyn's Crown Heights, the Rayatz reestablished Tomchei Temimim and began transforming American Jewry, founding institutions that his son-in-law would later expand into a global movement.

title_en: Rayatz founds HaKriah VeHaKedushah and Machne Israel
summary_en: The Rayatz began publication of the journal HaKriah VeHaKedushah and founded Machne Israel, a Chabad outreach organization.
story_body: HaKriah VeHaKedushah gave the Rayatz a public voice in wartime America, addressing both refugees and American Jews. Machne Israel became one of Chabad's central organizational arms, dedicated to strengthening Jewish observance and identity.

title_en: Rayatz expands American institutions and establishes Kehot Publication Society
summary_en: The Rayatz established Tomchei Temimim yeshivas in Montreal, Newark, Worcester, and Pittsburgh, and founded Kehot Publication Society.
story_body: Within two years of arriving in America, the Rayatz built a network of yeshivas across North America. Kehot Publication Society became the official publishing arm of the Chabad movement, producing thousands of works of Torah and chasidic teachings over subsequent decades.

title_en: Rayatz launches refugee relief, public school program, and Jewish farmer outreach
summary_en: The Rayatz opened a relief office for refugees with a Paris branch, established Shaloh for public-school Jewish education, and launched outreach to Jewish farmers.
story_body: In 1945, as the Holocaust ended, the Rayatz expanded Chabad's footprint into three new spheres: postwar refugee aid, religious instruction for Jewish children in American public schools, and connecting with isolated Jewish farmers. Each initiative reflected his vision of reaching every Jew, wherever they were.

title_en: Rayatz establishes Kfar Chabad in Israel for Russian refugees
summary_en: The Rayatz founded Kfar Chabad, a Chabad village in Israel, primarily as a settlement for refugees arriving from the Soviet Union.
story_body: Founded in the year of Israeli statehood, Kfar Chabad gave the chasidic refugees from the USSR a community of their own in the Holy Land. The village became and remains a major Chabad center in Israel.

title_en: Rayatz lays foundation for Jewish educational network in North Africa
summary_en: The Rayatz laid the foundation for a Chabad-run Jewish educational network in North Africa.
story_body: In the final year of his life, the Rayatz turned attention to the ancient but vulnerable Jewish communities of North Africa. The network that began in 1950 would expand to serve thousands of children in Morocco, Tunisia, and Algeria.

title_en: Passing of Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn in New York
summary_en: The Rayatz passed away on 10 Shevat 5710 and was interred in Montefiore Cemetery, New York.
story_body: After a decade in America rebuilding Chabad from the ashes of the Holocaust, the Rayatz passed away on January 28, 1950. His passing left the movement in a year-long state of uncertain succession before his son-in-law accepted leadership on the first yahrzeit.

title_en: Birth of Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, founder of Chabad chasidut, was born.
story_body: The Alter Rebbe established the Chabad school of chasidic thought, emphasizing intellectual engagement with mystical concepts. His magnum opus, the Tanya, became the foundational text of the movement.

title_en: Passing of Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi
summary_en: The Alter Rebbe, founder of Chabad, passed away in 1812.
story_body: His passing came during the chaotic retreat of the Russian population fleeing Napoleon's invasion. He was succeeded by his son, Rabbi Dov Ber, the Mitteler Rebbe.

title_en: Birth of Rabbi Dov Ber, the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: Rabbi Dov Ber, second Lubavitcher Rebbe, was born.
story_body: The Mitteler Rebbe succeeded his father as the second Lubavitcher Rebbe and was known for prolific chasidic discourses. He moved the movement's center to Lubavitch, the town that gave Chabad its alternate name.

title_en: Passing of Rabbi Dov Ber, the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe, second Lubavitcher Rebbe, passed away in 1827.
story_body: His passing led to the leadership of his son-in-law and nephew, Rabbi Menachem Mendel, the Tzemach Tzedek. The Mitteler Rebbe's extensive chasidic discourses remained an enduring legacy.

title_en: Birth of Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn, the Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek, third Lubavitcher Rebbe, was born in 1789.
story_body: Named for his classic work on Jewish law, the Tzemach Tzedek became a towering figure in 19th-century Russian Jewry. He led Chabad through major challenges to traditional Jewish life from the Russian government.

title_en: Passing of the Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek passed away in 1866.
story_body: After his passing, his sons divided into separate chasidic dynasties. His youngest son, the Rebbe Maharash, succeeded him as the fourth Lubavitcher Rebbe.

title_en: Birth of Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn, the Rebbe Maharash
summary_en: The Rebbe Maharash, fourth Lubavitcher Rebbe, was born in 1834.
story_body: The Maharash was known for his sharp intellect and the saying 'lechatchila ariber,' urging chasidim to overcome obstacles from above. He led Chabad during the Industrial Revolution and times of growing Jewish migration.

title_en: Passing of the Rebbe Maharash
summary_en: The Rebbe Maharash passed away in 1882.
story_body: His passing came during an era of accelerating change for Russian Jewry. He was succeeded after a transitional period by his son, the Rashab.

title_en: Birth of Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn, the Rashab
summary_en: The Rashab, fifth Lubavitcher Rebbe, was born in 1860.
story_body: The Rashab built Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim, transforming Chabad education. He led the movement through pogroms, World War I, and the early years of Soviet rule, dying in Rostov in 1920.

title_en: Passing of the Rashab in Rostov
summary_en: The Rashab passed away in Rostov in 1920.
story_body: His passing in Soviet Rostov launched the succession of his son, the Rayatz, as sixth Rebbe. The Rashab left explicit instructions for the succession, easing what could have been a fraught transition.

title_en: Birth of Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, the seventh Rebbe
summary_en: Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, the seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe, was born in 1902.
story_body: Born in Nikolaev to the Schneerson family of rabbinic descent, he later married the Rayatz's daughter Chaya Mushka. After a lifetime of preparation, he accepted leadership in 1951 and led Chabad until his passing in 1994.

title_en: Birth of Rabbi Yisrael Baal Shem Tov
summary_en: The Baal Shem Tov, founder of the chasidic movement, was born in 1700.
story_body: The Baal Shem Tov launched a religious revival emphasizing the divine spark in every Jew, joyful worship, and spiritual access for all. His teachings reshaped Eastern European Jewry and laid the foundation for Chabad and other chasidic dynasties.

title_en: Passing of the Baal Shem Tov
summary_en: The Baal Shem Tov passed away in 1760.
story_body: His passing left the leadership of the chasidic movement to his closest disciple, the Maggid of Mezeritch. The Baal Shem Tov's brief revolution had set in motion a generations-long spiritual transformation of Eastern European Jewry.

title_en: Passing of Rabbi Dovber, the Maggid of Mezeritch
summary_en: The Maggid of Mezeritch, successor to the Baal Shem Tov, passed away in 1772.
story_body: Under the Maggid's leadership, chasidism spread across Eastern Europe through a circle of brilliant disciples. Among them was Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, who would go on to found the Chabad branch of chasidism.

title_en: Birth of Rebbetzin Nechama Dina Schneersohn in Kishinev
summary_en: Nechama Dina Schneersohn, future wife of the Rayatz, was born in Kishinev to Rabbi Avraham Schneersohn.
story_body: Nechama Dina was the daughter of Rabbi Avraham Schneersohn, a second cousin of the Rebbe Rashab. Her birth date corresponds to 17 Tishrei 5642. She would later marry Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn (the Rayatz) and become rebbetzin of the sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe.

title_en: Assassination of Czar Alexander II of Russia
summary_en: Czar Alexander II was assassinated, ending his era of reforms and ushering in repressive policies under his son Alexander III.
story_body: Alexander II's assassination led directly to a wave of anti-Jewish repression. His son Alexander III rolled back his father's reforms and intensified oppression of Russian Jews. The assassination set the stage for decades of state-sponsored anti-Semitism.

title_en: Russian May Laws restrict Jewish residency and economic life
summary_en: Czar Alexander III instituted the discriminatory May Laws restricting Jewish residency, education, and commerce.
story_body: The May Laws prohibited Jews from leasing land outside the Pale of Settlement, restricted high school and university attendance, and limited mortgages on land. They were expanded in 1885 and became a major catalyst in Jewish emigration from Russia to America and other countries.

title_en: Rashab formally assumes position of Lubavitcher Rebbe
summary_en: On Rosh HaShanah, Rabbi Shalom Dovber Schneersohn (Rashab) formally assumed leadership as the fifth Lubavitcher Rebbe.
story_body: The Rashab began to reassert Lubavitch involvement in Russian Jewish communal affairs. He challenged the dominance of Enlightenment-aligned representatives like Baron David Gunzburg and asserted leadership on behalf of the chasidic community, drawing on the vast Chabad network across Russia.

title_en: Czar Alexander III dies; Nicholas II ascends Russian throne
summary_en: Alexander III died and was succeeded by his son Nicholas II, who continued and intensified anti-Jewish policies.
story_body: Nicholas II would be the last czar of Russia, ruling until his abdication and execution in 1917. He blamed Jews for Russia's problems in personal letters and presided over a period of severe pogroms and repression of Russian Jewry.

title_en: Rayatz represents father at rabbinic conference in Kovno
summary_en: At age fifteen, the Rayatz represented the Rashab at a conference of Jewish religious leaders in Kovno.
story_body: This was the Rayatz's first major communal role. He formally became active in community affairs that year and began serving as his father's private secretary, a role he would hold for the next twenty-five years until the Rashab's passing in 1920.

title_en: Engagement of Rayatz to Nechama Dina in Bolivke
summary_en: The Rayatz became engaged to his second cousin Nechama Dina Schneersohn in Bolivke, where the family was spending the summer.
story_body: The Rashab and his wife had chosen Nechama Dina over wealthier candidates with large dowries, following the Rayatz's preference for marrying a relative. The tena'im was signed on 28 Sivan 5646 in Bolivke. The Rebbe Rashab undertook all wedding expenses since the bride's family had limited means, and the celebration lasted a week.

title_en: Rashab visits ancestral gravesites before founding yeshivah
summary_en: The Rashab traveled to the gravesites of the Baal Shem Tov, the Maggid, the Alter Rebbe and the Mitteler Rebbe to pray for guidance.
story_body: Pained by the spiritual condition of Russian Jewry, the Rashab visited the gravesites in Mezibuzh, Anipoli, Hadyach, and Nizhyn. Upon returning to Lubavitch he also prayed at the gravesites of his grandfather the Tzemach Tzedek and his father the Maharash. With their blessing, he established the yeshivah the following year.

title_en: Shterna Sara writes cousins about Rayatz's bride and wedding delay
summary_en: Rebbetzin Shterna Sara wrote her cousins in Hebron describing the chosen bride and explaining the wedding was deferred a year.
story_body: Writing on 1 Elul 5646 to Rabbi Mordechai Dovber and Rabbi Schneur Zalman Schneersohn in Hebron, Shterna Sara praised Nechama Dina as 'charming and very observant' and explained that the family had given up major financial benefits to select the most proper young woman. She requested they pray for the family at the holy places before Rosh HaShanah.

title_en: Rabbinic conference in Vilna with Rayatz representing father
summary_en: The Rayatz again represented the Rashab at a conference of Jewish religious leaders, this time in Vilna.
story_body: Following his first conference in Kovno the previous year, the sixteen-year-old Rayatz attended this Vilna gathering. These meetings began his lifetime involvement with Europe's leading rabbinic figures and prepared him for his later leadership role in Russian Jewish communal affairs.

title_en: Wedding of the Rayatz and Nechama Dina in Lubavitch
summary_en: The Rayatz and Nechama Dina were married in Lubavitch two weeks before Rosh HaShanah.
story_body: Chasidim streamed to Lubavitch for the celebration. The Rayatz donned a shtreimel and recited Shehechiyanu before the ceremony. The chuppah was held Friday afternoon (13 Elul 5657) in the courtyard of the main synagogue, after which the crowd escorted the couple through town with singing and dancing.

title_en: Rashab unveils plan for Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim
summary_en: At a Sunday afternoon meeting of fifty distinguished wedding guests, the Rashab unveiled his plan for a revolutionary yeshivah integrating Talmud and Chasidic philosophy.
story_body: Held the day of the Rayatz's wedding reception (15 Elul 5657), the Rashab announced his plan to 'open a yeshivah for our youth, with proper administration, so that they can dedicate themselves exclusively to Torah study.' Most attendees expressed serious reservations about the feasibility. The day of this meeting is considered the founding date of Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim.

title_en: Tomchei Temimim begins studies in Lubavitch
summary_en: On 18 Elul, birthday of both the Alter Rebbe and Baal Shem Tov, studies began in Lubavitch under mashpia Shmuel Gronem.
story_body: The Rashab personally selected the first group of students, many of whom were already yoshvim studying informally in Lubavitch. Rabbi Shmuel Gronem was appointed mashpia with detailed instructions regarding curriculum. After the High Holidays the students relocated to Zembin, a smaller town with fewer distractions.

title_en: Knesses Beis Yitzchak yeshivah founded in Slabodka
summary_en: Opponents of musar study founded Knesses Beis Yitzchak as a rival to Slabodka's musar yeshivah.
story_body: A major controversy erupted in Slabodka between those who argued that study should focus exclusively on Talmud and those who supported teaching ethics through musar. Those opposed to musar opened Knesses Beis Yitzchak in 1897. In 1904 they hired Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz as rosh yeshivah.

title_en: Enlightenment activist Mordechai Ben Hillel scouts Lubavitch for a school
summary_en: Enlightenment activist Mordechai Ben Hillel scouted Lubavitch to explore opening a secular school targeting the chasidic stronghold.
story_body: Ben Hillel reported that Lubavitch was visited by thousands annually and that establishing a school there would influence all of Russian Jewry. With the support of Baron Gunzburg, the school opened with 130 students despite the Rashab's strong opposition. The Rashab would later lament Gunzburg's support at a major farbrengen.

title_en: Rayatz appointed director of Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim
summary_en: At age eighteen, the Rayatz assumed the position of director of Tomchei Temimim on 24 Elul 5659.
story_body: A group of Chasidim led by Rabbi Asher Grossman approached the Rayatz to take the role, citing his wisdom, motivation, and energy. After he demurred, they appealed to the Rashab, who endorsed the idea. The Rayatz immediately faced complex tasks of fundraising, hiring staff, and managing the yeshivah's growth.

title_en: Rashab names yeshivah 'Tomchei Temimim' on Simchat Torah
summary_en: During Simchat Torah hakafot at approximately 4 a.m., the Rashab named the new yeshivah Tomchei Temimim.
story_body: After dancing intensely around the bimah, the Rashab paused the singing and declared: 'The yeshivah that was established by the grace of G-d doesn't have a name. Now I am naming it Tomchei Temimim.' The name derived from the verses recited during the seventh hakafah. Students and alumni would henceforth be called 'temimim.'

title_en: Rashab declares mission of Tomchei Temimim as 'soldiers of King David'
summary_en: Three years after founding, the Rashab laid out a mission statement comparing the temimim to King David's devoted soldiers.
story_body: On Simchat Torah, the Rashab told the students they should 'divorce' themselves from worldly concerns and make spiritual development their priority. He charged them with disseminating chasidic teachings outward, recalling the Baal Shem Tov's vision of bringing redemption through spreading the wellsprings.

title_en: Jewish Colonial Association pledges 1 million francs for Haskalah schools
summary_en: The Jewish Colonial Association in Paris pledged 1 million francs to support Enlightenment schools in Russia.
story_body: Chamah's campaign to open secular schools expanded with this major funding pledge. The Rashab, with the Rayatz's help, organized an international lobbying effort with prominent rabbis in Russia and France to petition the JCA to withhold the funds. They succeeded in blocking a second allocation of 600,000 francs.

title_en: Rayatz opens textile mill in Dubrovno using diverted JCA funds
summary_en: The Rayatz spent a year setting up a textile mill in Dubrovno using JCA funds redirected toward Jewish economic opportunity.
story_body: With help from the Polyakov brothers, the Rashab convinced the JCA to divert Haskalah funds toward creating economic opportunities for Russian Jews. The factory, located sixty miles from Lubavitch, was closed on Shabbat and eventually provided gainful employment for two thousand local Jews, removing social stigma from factory work.

title_en: Yeshaya Berlin donates for refurbishment of Tomchei Temimim zal
summary_en: Philanthropist Yeshaya Berlin of Riga gave a large gift enabling refurbishment of the study hall and construction of a dining room.
story_body: With enrollment growing rapidly, the Rayatz approached Berlin for a major gift. The study hall known as the zal was refurbished and additional facilities were built. Berlin was a successful businessman married to a granddaughter of the third Rebbe and remained close to the Chabad Rebbes throughout his life.

title_en: Russo-Japanese War breaks out over Manchuria and Korea
summary_en: War broke out between Japan and Russia over control of the Far East regions of Manchuria and Korea.
story_body: Thousands of Jewish soldiers were enlisted in the Russian army and fought for two years before Russia's inglorious defeat. The Rashab was concerned about Jewish soldiers far from home with no food or matzah for Passover, prompting him to launch initiatives to provide for their religious needs.

title_en: Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz appointed rosh yeshivah of Knesses Beis Yitzchak
summary_en: Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz was hired as rosh yeshivah of Knesses Beis Yitzchak in Slabodka.
story_body: Rabbi Baruch Ber became one of the most influential Lithuanian rosh yeshivos of his era. He would later move the yeshivah to Vilna in 1921 and to Kamenitz in 1926, where it became known as the famed Kamenitz yeshivah.

title_en: Matzah campaign delivers Passover supplies to Jewish soldiers in Far East
summary_en: After failed efforts the previous year, the Rashab and Rayatz secured permission and shipped Passover supplies to Jewish soldiers throughout the Far East front.
story_body: Facing obstacles of an anti-Semitic regime, the need for a broad Jewish coalition, logistical nightmares of shipping thousands of miles, and securing funding, the Rashab and Rayatz intensified the effort. After much work, czarist permission was obtained and Passover supplies were distributed to soldiers dispersed across a vast geographical area.

title_en: Covert rabbinic meeting in St. Petersburg over Russian pogroms
summary_en: The Rayatz participated in a covert summer meeting of prominent rabbinic leaders in St. Petersburg to strategize against the wave of pogroms across Russia.
story_body: The 25-year-old Rayatz was dispatched to Western Europe to meet famous statesmen of Germany and Holland, persuading them and foreign bankers to apply pressure and economic sanctions on the Russian government. He proved himself as a modern shtadlan capable of advocacy on the international Jewish scene.

title_en: Poalei Tzion confronts Rayatz with weapons over student Berel Davzik
summary_en: Members of Marxist Zionist group Poalei Tzion confronted the Rayatz at the yeshivah with weapons, demanding student Berel Davzik be allowed to stay.
story_body: The Rayatz had telegrammed the parents of underage student Davzik, who had become active in Poalei Tzion. On Thursday night, group members marched in with weapons threatening the Rayatz, who responded fearlessly. Three days later they returned, shooting at the yeshivah and narrowly missing Rabbi Moshe Klatzkin of Romanov. Yeshivah students drove them off.

title_en: Poalei Tzion raids Rashab's summer home in Bolivke
summary_en: Six to eight armed Poalei Tzion members raided the Rashab's summer home in Bolivke, destroying furniture and ransacking the property.
story_body: Brandishing revolvers and exclaiming 'We'll show you!', the intruders frightened the Rayatz's young daughters and the Rebbetzin. They blocked the road to prevent police from arriving. The Rashab was forced to hire security guards. His brother the Raza, living in Vitebsk, eventually negotiated an agreement with Poalei Tzion.

title_en: Pyotr Stolypin appointed Russian interior minister and prime minister
summary_en: Pyotr Stolypin was appointed interior minister and prime minister under Czar Nicholas II.
story_body: Stolypin's anti-Semitic agenda would prompt the Rayatz's covert mission to St. Petersburg to subvert a planned decree against the Jewish community. Stolypin served until his assassination in 1911.

title_en: Rayatz investigated by authorities over Lubavitch radical youth riots
summary_en: The Rayatz was investigated due to riots in Lubavitch by radical youth, which he proved were not part of the yeshivah.
story_body: Coming after the 1905 revolution when political tensions ran high, this was one of four arrests of the Rayatz between 1911 and 1916. He proved the rioters were not connected to the yeshivah and was released with a stern warning. These detentions did not deter him from his communal work.

title_en: Rashab becomes owner of Beit Romano complex in Hebron
summary_en: After years of effort, the Rashab acquired the large Beit Romano property and an adjacent property in Hebron.
story_body: Originally owned by an affluent Jew from Istanbul, the mansion was put up for sale by his children. The Rashab raised the necessary funds and navigated complicated legal steps over several years to acquire it. The Rayatz was intimately involved. The combined property became the base for the new yeshivah and gave the Rashab a strong foothold in Hebron.

title_en: Confidential meeting of Chabad-aligned rabbis to plan rabbinic conference
summary_en: The Rashab asked the Rayatz to organize a confidential meeting of rabbis closely aligned with Chabad to strategize for the upcoming St. Petersburg conference.
story_body: With the Russian government convening a major rabbinic conference and the first Duma elections approaching, the Rashab needed to develop a consensus position. The agenda also included determining 'the manner and extent of our involvement in preparation for the elections in the forthcoming duma.'

title_en: Pre-conference meeting of 25 leading rabbis in Vilna
summary_en: Twenty-five leading rabbis convened in Vilna with government permission to set an agenda for the upcoming national conference.
story_body: The meeting was made possible through efforts of the Rashab in coordination with Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski of Vilnius. The Rayatz was named secretary of the meeting. The participants worked to develop a unified rabbinic position ahead of the contentious St. Petersburg conference.

title_en: National rabbinic conference convenes in St. Petersburg
summary_en: The Russian government hosted an unprecedented national conference of rabbis and community leaders in St. Petersburg.
story_body: Traditional rabbis, crown rabbis, and community leaders gathered to seek consensus on community leadership and education. The Rashab was named as one of the conference organizers, with the Rayatz at his side throughout. Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski's compromise position on secular knowledge for rabbis was adopted by majority. The conference concluded with a disrespectful meeting with Prime Minister Stolypin.

title_en: Rayatz imprisoned in St. Petersburg over military exemption efforts
summary_en: The Rayatz was imprisoned in St. Petersburg because of his efforts to exempt young men from Russian military service.
story_body: This was one of four arrests of the Rayatz between 1911 and 1916. All detentions were brief, since government inquiries found nothing incriminating. He was released each time with a stern warning, but these incidents spurred him to even greater communal efforts. He was imprisoned again in 1916 for the same cause.

title_en: Rashab considers opening Tomchei Temimim branch in Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: The Rashab began to seriously consider opening a branch of the yeshivah in Eretz Yisrael, focused on Hebron.
story_body: Jerusalem's historically religious character was being transformed by non-religious Zionist immigrants, while Hebron remained a spiritual oasis. To bolster the impoverished Chabad community there, the Rayatz established Chevronim, a special fund to help Hebron's Jews. The community leaders asked the Rashab to purchase Beit Romano.

title_en: Toras Emes yeshivah established in Hebron
summary_en: The Rashab sent a group of outstanding students led by Rabbi Zalman Havlin to Hebron to establish Toras Emes, the first chasidic yeshivah in the Jewish homeland.
