story_body: Considered a branch of Tomchei Temimim in Lubavitch, the new yeshivah aimed to invigorate the study of chasidic teachings in Eretz Yisrael and create a new cadre of Jewish leaders there. Just as the Rashab hoped Tomchei Temimim graduates would set a new direction for Russian Jewry, he hoped Toras Emes graduates would do so in the Holy Land.

title_en: Rayatz letter to Havlin outlining purpose of Hebron yeshivah
summary_en: The Rayatz wrote a long letter to Rabbi Havlin and his students in Hebron outlining the purpose of the new yeshivah.
story_body: Dated 3 Kislev 5672, the letter detailed the curriculum and vision for Toras Emes. The Rayatz was intimately involved in setting up the program, giving detailed instructions for curriculum and student acceptance, while expecting Rabbi Havlin would ultimately take full administrative responsibility.

title_en: Assassination of Russian Prime Minister Pyotr Stolypin
summary_en: Pyotr Stolypin, Russia's interior minister and prime minister, was assassinated.
story_body: Stolypin had been the target of the Rayatz's covert St. Petersburg mission to subvert his planned anti-Jewish decree. He had served Czar Nicholas II since 1906. Earlier in 1910, he had met disrespectfully with rabbinic leaders at the conclusion of the national rabbinic conference, blaming them for the Bund's anti-government activities.

title_en: Beilis blood libel trial in Kiev
summary_en: Mendel Beilis was tried in Kiev on trumped-up blood libel charges in a case that drew worldwide attention.
story_body: Beilis was accused of killing a 12-year-old boy whose body was found near the brick factory he managed. Prosecutors tried to link him and ritual murder to the Chabad community through his friendship with a man named Feivel Schneersohn. The Rashab and Rayatz played a major behind-the-scenes role, with the Rayatz enlisting attorney Oscar Gruzenberg to spearhead the masterful defense.

title_en: Rashab letter to Shmuel Treinin about Beilis trial
summary_en: The Rashab wrote to Shmuel Treinin explaining why he had decided against personally testifying at the Beilis trial.
story_body: Dated 17 Elul, the Rashab cited concerns that his testimony might draw too much attention and could strengthen the prosecution's case. He was also concerned about elucidating obtuse theological concepts in 'modern terms.' Despite not testifying, the Rashab remained deeply involved behind the scenes in trial preparations.

title_en: Rayatz letter to Havlin on entrepreneurial management approach
summary_en: The Rayatz wrote to Rabbi Havlin articulating Chabad's management approach of empowering individuals with full responsibility.
story_body: Dated 3 Kislev 5674, the letter stated: 'Our approach is to appoint individuals and entrust them with the management, and they are responsible for the projects given over to them.' This entrepreneurial model would become emblematic of Chabad expansion in the decades to come, used by both the Rayatz and the seventh Rebbe.

title_en: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand sparks World War I
summary_en: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria ignited the winds of war across Europe.
story_body: Germany declared war on Russia that summer and invaded the following year. The war disrupted the Toras Emes yeshivah in Hebron, as Russian students were considered enemy aliens under Ottoman rule and forced to return to Russia. The conflict would eventually force the Rashab to abandon Lubavitch.

title_en: Rashab abandons Lubavitch and relocates family to Rostov-on-Don
summary_en: The Rashab, his son, and their families departed Lubavitch on 16 Cheshvan, fleeing the advancing German army.
story_body: After 102 years as home to four Chabad Rebbes, the sun set on Lubavitch. The historic Chabad library was packed into thirty-five crates and placed in storage in Moscow, while the Rashab took valuable manuscripts with him. The Rashab told the Chasidim 'We hope to return... before Passover' but they never returned. They settled in Rostov-on-Don, 700 miles south of Moscow.

title_en: Rashab delivers Simchat Torah warning about Kaiser Wilhelm
summary_en: On Simchat Torah, the Rashab declared he knew Kaiser Wilhelm well from his European travels and could not dwell under his rule.
story_body: The Rashab told the Chasidim: 'I know the kaiser well from the thirty years that I have been traveling outside Russia. He is an apikores (heretic), and under his rule I cannot dwell.' He recalled how during a public speech in Berlin, the kaiser had stared at them sharply and had police remove them, the Rashab interpreting it as Wilhelm already plotting war.

title_en: Rayatz imprisoned again in St. Petersburg over military exemption
summary_en: The Rayatz was imprisoned in St. Petersburg again because of his efforts to exempt young men from Russian military service.
story_body: This was his fourth arrest. The Rayatz's far-reaching public activities and watchful defense of Russian Jewry's rights aroused the displeasure of the czarist regime. Government inquiries found nothing incriminating and he was released with a stern warning, only spurring him to greater efforts.

title_en: Russian Revolution ends czarist regime; Nicholas II abdicates
summary_en: Czar Nicholas II abdicated and was executed, ending the Russian czarist regime, and the Pale of Settlement decree was terminated.
story_body: The revolution brought enormous upheaval. The Pale of Settlement, originally established by Catherine the Great in 1791, was terminated. Following the Communist Revolution, Jews were granted freedom to live anywhere in Russia. The Bolshevik Revolution and subsequent civil war led to Communist consolidation of power, alarming the Rashab and his family.

title_en: Rayatz takes leading part in rabbinic assemblies in Moscow and Kharkiv
summary_en: The Rayatz took a leading role in major assemblies of rabbis and laymen convened in Moscow and Kharkiv.
story_body: These assemblies addressed urgent communal concerns during the chaotic period of revolution. The Rayatz participated again in 1918. By this time he had spent over two decades involved in essentially every major concern facing Russian Jewry as his father's secretary and emissary.

title_en: Bolsheviks take control of Rostov-on-Don
summary_en: The Bolsheviks took control of Rostov, prompting the Rashab to curtail his public activities.
story_body: Not wanting to draw the attention of the new regime, the Rashab asked Chasidim to limit visits to him for services, maamarim, or private audiences. Only a small group joined him for services afterward. The idea of relocating out of Russia entirely had been raised earlier but faded after the Bolshevik takeover.

title_en: Rashab summons Rayatz to discuss future under Communist rule
summary_en: In a candle-lit study, the Rashab told the Rayatz that the Jewish people were entering a period of dark clouds lasting at least 22 years.
story_body: On Friday 8 Adar, with Purim approaching, the Rashab summoned his son. Studying Pri Etz Chaim on Mordechai and Esther, the Rashab made extraordinary predictions about Lenin's strange death, Trotsky's exile and execution, Stalin adapting to the times, and the eventual fall of the Soviet regime. He charged the Rayatz with mesirat nefesh to spread Torah, which proved prophetic when the Rayatz's father passed weeks later.

title_en: Defiant Purim farbrengen in Rostov under Bolshevik police visit
summary_en: The Rashab led a 12-hour Purim celebration that continued despite a curfew and visits from Bolshevik police officers.
story_body: Despite government bans on meetings and a 9 p.m. curfew, the Rashab encouraged singing and sent for additional liquor. When three police officers entered during a maamar, the Rashab declared 'We have to say chasidut, and they will be batul' and continued teaching about evil as a false reality. The officers gazed silently and left. The farbrengen lasted until morning light.

title_en: Passing of the Rebbe Rashab in Rostov-on-Don
summary_en: Two weeks after Purim, the fifth Lubavitcher Rebbe passed away from typhoid after blessing his children and reciting Shema.
story_body: Diagnosed with typhoid on Sunday after a Friday onset of illness, the Rashab's condition deteriorated through the week. Late at night he asked to be moved to his study, telling Chasidim 'I am going to heaven, and I am leaving you my manuscripts.' After blessing each of his daughters and his son, he passed at dawn while whispering 'with all your heart and all your soul' from the Shema.

title_en: Toras Emes yeshivah reconstituted in Jerusalem
summary_en: Rabbi Zalman Havlin returned to Eretz Yisrael and reconstituted the Toras Emes yeshivah in Jerusalem.
story_body: Before his passing in 1920, the Rashab had instructed Havlin to return to Eretz Yisrael as soon as possible. The yeshivah, originally founded in Hebron in 1911 but disrupted by World War I, was now re-established in Jerusalem. Today it remains a flourishing center of Jewish scholarship.

title_en: Death of Soviet leader Vladimir Lenin
summary_en: Lenin died at age 53 after repeated strokes and medical complications.
story_body: His death fulfilled the Rashab's 1920 prediction that 'Lenin will die in a strange fashion.' As Lenin's health had deteriorated, Stalin had been consolidating power. The Rayatz noted the accuracy of his father's predictions about Soviet leaders in his diary entries.

title_en: Rayatz reflects on father's 1920 predictions in Moscow diary entry
summary_en: On 10 Adar Alef, while harassed in Moscow by the Yevesektzia, the Rayatz wrote in his diary about his father's prophetic predictions.
story_body: The Rayatz woke at 3 a.m. troubled by events in Moscow. After reflecting on the 1920 meeting with his father about the new regime and its leaders' fates, 'I went back to sleep, and my soul was relaxed.' These predictions endowed him with fortitude during the darkest times of Soviet persecution.

title_en: Trotsky banished from Russia to Alma Alta
summary_en: Leon Trotsky was banished to remote Alma Alta as Stalin consolidated power.
story_body: Trotsky's exile fulfilled the Rashab's 1920 prediction that 'Trotsky will be exiled.' He was deported from Russia entirely two years later and eventually relocated to Mexico after living in European cities. He would be assassinated in 1940 by a Stalinist agent.

title_en: Stalin dismantles the Yevsektsia
summary_en: Stalin dismantled the Yevsektsia (Jewish section of the Communist Party), killing and exiling many of its leaders and activists.
story_body: This fulfilled the Rashab's 1920 prediction that the Communist Jews who fought Judaism would be 'broken and their leaders killed.' A whole generation of Jewish Communists involved in Jewish affairs were liquidated in massive purges. The Yevsektzia had been the greatest threat to religious Jewry in the Soviet Union.

title_en: Trotsky deported from the Soviet Union
summary_en: Trotsky was deported from Russia entirely, two years after his initial banishment to Alma Alta.
story_body: After living in European cities, Trotsky eventually relocated to Mexico. In 1937 he was sentenced to death in absentia in a Moscow trial. He was assassinated by a Stalinist agent in his home in Mexico City in 1940.

title_en: Trotsky sentenced to death in absentia in Moscow trial
summary_en: Leon Trotsky was sentenced to death in absentia in a Moscow show trial.
story_body: By this point Trotsky was living in Mexico after years of exile. The sentence would be executed three years later when a Stalinist agent assassinated him in his Mexico City home, fulfilling the Rashab's prediction made in 1920 that Trotsky would be executed.

title_en: Trotsky assassinated by Stalinist agent in Mexico City
summary_en: Trotsky was assassinated by a Stalinist agent at his home in Mexico City.
story_body: His assassination completed the fulfillment of the Rashab's 1920 prediction that 'Trotsky will be exiled, and they will execute him.' The Rayatz had recorded his father's prophetic warnings in his diary years earlier, noting how remarkably they were coming to pass.

title_en: Stalin elevated to supreme military rank of generalissimo
summary_en: The Supreme Soviet elevated Stalin to the highest military rank of generalissimo.
story_body: Though Stalin rejected the new generalissimo uniform and continued referring to himself as a marshal, his military attire fulfilled the Rashab's 1920 prediction that 'Stalin will follow the spirit of the time as needed, and he will be adorned with epaulets.' At Yalta and Potsdam, Stalin had appeared in his marshal uniform.

title_en: Seventh Rebbe dispatches elite students to Australia
summary_en: The seventh Rebbe dispatched a group of elite students to Australia, beginning a global expansion model.
story_body: Following the model pioneered by the Rashab and Rayatz of sending selected students from flagship yeshivos to establish new centers, the seventh Rebbe set up new yeshivos around the globe. Today some fifty Chabad yeshivos exist worldwide, with senior students sent for one or two years to maintain scholarship standards in branches.

title_en: Death of Rebbetzin Nechama Dina Schneersohn
summary_en: Rebbetzin Nechama Dina, wife of the Rayatz, passed away on 10 Shevat 5731.
story_body: Born in Kishinev in 1881 to Rabbi Avraham Schneersohn, she had married the Rayatz in Lubavitch in 1897. As the rebbetzin of the sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe, she shared his lifetime of communal work through czarist persecution, Soviet exile, and eventual relocation to America. She passed away on the same Hebrew date as her husband, 10 Shevat.

title_en: Collapse of the Soviet Union
summary_en: The Soviet Union disintegrated after 70 years of Communist rule.
story_body: Its eventual collapse fulfilled the Rashab's 1920 prediction to the Rayatz that 'a country that persecutes Judaism will eventually fall.' This may have inspired the Rayatz to confront the Communists knowing their regime would end and Jewish life would be restored. Following the fall, Chabad returned to Rostov and reclaimed the building owned by the Rashab.

title_en: Rayatz delivers first maamar to Rivkin at end of shivah
summary_en: The Rayatz privately recited a chasidic discourse to Berel Rivkin in his father's Rostov study at the close of the shivah.
story_body: On the Shabbat that ended his week of mourning for his father, the Rayatz invited Berel Rivkin into the Rashab's study and recited a maamar his father had said on Purim, adding insights of his own. He asked Rivkin to keep it private, but news of the discourse soon spread among the Chasidim. It was his first step toward accepting the position of sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe.

title_en: Rayatz recites maamar publicly on first day of Passover
summary_en: After a private recitation arranged with Rivkin, Chasidim listened from outside the door as the Rayatz delivered a maamar for nearly an hour on Passover.
story_body: On the first day of Passover, the Rayatz again told Rivkin he wished to recite a maamar privately. Rivkin arranged for Chasidim to gather outside the door of the Rashab's study; they cracked open the doors and listened. A week later, at the end of Passover, the Chasidim entered the room itself while he spoke.

title_en: Yeshivah Tomchei Temimim relocates to Rostov
summary_en: Tomchei Temimim moved from Kremenchuk in Ukraine to Rostov in the winter of 1920 amid extreme food shortages.
story_body: After fleeing Lubavitch during the war, the yeshivah had landed in Kremenchuk, where students rationed bread to once every two days. The new Rebbe brought the yeshivah to Rostov, saying he wanted Tomchei Temimim next to him. Conditions remained dire, but Rabbi Shmuel Gurary borrowed funds and sold personal property to sustain it.

title_en: Rayatz falls ill from typhus in Rostov
summary_en: On 28 Marcheshvan, the Rayatz became too ill to lead evening services as the typhus epidemic intensified in Rostov.
story_body: The typhus epidemic struck the Rebbe's household; soon his mother Rebbetzin Shterna Sara and his three daughters also caught the disease. Doctors said his survival was unlikely. A rabbinical court convened and students pledged years of their own lives for the Rebbe's recovery.

title_en: Rayatz says maamar despite illness on Shabbat Toldot
summary_en: On Shabbat Parshat Toldot, between bouts of typhus, the Rayatz mustered strength to deliver a maamar.
story_body: Shortly after first falling ill, the Rebbe had enough strength to say a maamar on Shabbat Toldot. The illness then intensified, and his situation became grave; Professor Milsalavski said there was no medical cure, but believed the Rebbe might recover.

title_en: Rayatz begins recovery from typhus
summary_en: After roughly three weeks of grave illness, the Rebbe's condition began to improve on 19 Kislev.
story_body: Chasidim led by Reb Itche der Masmid prayed repeatedly at the Ohel of the Rashab, and Goldin telegrammed Chasidim in Lubavitch, Nizhyn, and Hadyach to pray at the graves of earlier Rebbes. The improvement coincided with 19 Kislev, the chasidic festival marking the Alter Rebbe's release from czarist prison in 1798.

title_en: Rayatz fasts and farbrengs on Purim despite illness
summary_en: Still recovering from typhus, the Rayatz fainted on the Fast of Esther but completed the fast and led a long Purim farbrengen the next day.
story_body: The doctor permitted the Rebbe a fifteen-minute maamar; he instead recited one for two and a half hours and sat with Chasidim for three more. Many yeshivah students were also ill, and the financial strain of medical bills was mounting. Reb Shmuel Gurary's death exacerbated the crisis.

title_en: Chicago Sentinel reports starving Lubavitcher students
summary_en: The Chicago-based Sentinel reported that yeshivah students who had evacuated Lubavitch for Rostov were starving.
story_body: By mid-1921, financial pressures, famine, and disease drove many students to leave Rostov for home. The grand yeshivah of Lubavitch had been whittled down to roughly forty students in Rostov, making it among the last bastions of traditional Torah scholarship in Russia.

title_en: Yevesektzia stages show trial against Lubavitch yeshivah
summary_en: The Yevesektzia organized a show trial in Rostov demanding the closure of Tomchei Temimim and conscription of its students into the labor army.
story_body: Following a similar staged trial against a Vitebsk cheder in January, the Yevesektzia targeted Lubavitch in Rostov. They forced their way into the Rebbe's home, seized inherited household goods and silver, and imprisoned three students plus the Rebbe's future son-in-law Shmaryahu Gurary for five days before he negotiated their release.

title_en: Chafetz Chaim moves yeshivah back to Poland
summary_en: Rabbi Yisrael Meir Kagan, in his early eighties, returned his Radin yeshivah from Russia to Poland.
story_body: Leaving Russia, the Chafetz Chaim stopped in Minsk and told local rabbi Nissan Telushkin that he had no strength left to battle the Communists and the renegades within. Later in life he reportedly regretted leaving, saying a Jew must be ready to sacrifice himself for Judaism.

title_en: Lubavitch yeshivah relocates to Poltava
summary_en: Forty students of Tomchei Temimim moved by horse and wagon from Rostov to Poltava, where local Chasidim agreed to underwrite the yeshivah.
story_body: Unable to secure rail authorization, the students traveled four hundred miles by wagon. Poltava had a strong, diverse community of about twenty thousand Jews and a less aggressive Yevesektzia. That summer the Rebbe appointed Rabbi Yechezkel Feigin as administrator.

title_en: Yevesektzia search of Rebbe's home in Rostov
summary_en: Returning from Moscow, the Rayatz found that Yevesektzia officers had searched his Rostov home and intended to arrest and exile him.
story_body: His secretary Rabbi Elchonon Morozov met him outside the city with the warning. After ten days back in Moscow he returned to Rostov, where the house was surrounded; an extensive overnight search nearly ended in arrest, prevented only by influential locals. The Rebbe then decided to relocate to Leningrad.

title_en: Rayatz establishes Rabbinical Committee for Russian Jewry
summary_en: Departing from historical decentralization, the Rebbe convened a national rabbinical body with himself as chair, advocating for rabbis under Yevesektzia pressure.
story_body: By 1922 the Rebbe was in contact with communities across Russia about schools, mikvaot, rabbis, and shochtim. The Rabbinical Committee leveraged the inconsistency between formally permissive Soviet law and the aggressive Yevesektzia, lobbied the Soviet Bar Association for clarification on religious schooling, and defended teachers in court.

title_en: Secret covenant of nine Chasidim in Moscow
summary_en: The Rayatz convened nine confidants in Moscow to swear an oath to sustain Judaism under Soviet rule even at the cost of their lives.
story_body: Building on a 19 Kislev 5684 address in Rostov calling for emissaries to every city, the Rebbe formalized a clandestine covenant the next winter. The nine became generals of an underground network of schools, yeshivot, synagogues, and mikvaot that lasted until the Soviet collapse. Among the known members were Elchonon Morozov, Bentzion Shemtov, Simon Yakovshvili, and Yerachmiel Binyaminson.

title_en: JDC begins diverting funds for Russian Jewish 'cultural work'
summary_en: The American Joint Distribution Committee began allocating funds to support the Rebbe's Rabbinical Committee, education, and religious activities.
story_body: JDC representative Dr. Joseph Rosen, who admired the Rebbe, helped overcome critics inside the Jewish community and pressure from Communist officials to direct money to the Rebbe's projects. The funds supported both home-based industrial training for urbanized Jews and underground religious activities.

title_en: Rayatz relocates from Rostov to Leningrad
summary_en: Following the near-arrest in Rostov, the Rebbe moved his court to a large apartment on the corner of Machovaya and Fantilamanskaya streets in Leningrad.
story_body: The apartment had belonged to a baron from Kass, the governor of Bessarabia, who was banished from Leningrad in June 1924 and signed the dwelling and much of its furniture over to the Rebbe. Without an official permit for prayer assemblies, Chasidim gathered in a large room similar to the Lubavitch hall. The city's chief rabbi was the respected David Tevel Katzenellenbogen.

title_en: LERO formally recognized in Leningrad
summary_en: The Leningrad Jewish Religious Community (LERO), led by Lev Gurewicz, received formal Soviet recognition.
story_body: Gurewicz, a Zionist with a law degree, would soon propose a national congress of Russian Jewish communities, secretly backed by the Yevesektzia, to create a lay-led structure that could supplant the Rebbe's leadership. The Rebbe met Gurewicz that summer and responded coolly to the idea.

title_en: Korosten conference of rabbis
summary_en: About one hundred rabbis convened in Korosten, Ukraine; though skeptical, the Rayatz was unanimously named honorary chairman.
story_body: Led by Rabbi Zev Kipnis, the conference was government-sanctioned as a divide-and-conquer maneuver to weaken the Rebbe ahead of the Leningrad community conference. The Rebbe secretly sent the young Bentzion Shemtov to steer the agenda. When his telegram was read, the rabbis stood in respect; alarmed authorities later arrested Shemtov and Kipnis.

title_en: Resignation of LERO religious minority in Leningrad
summary_en: Ten religious board members resigned from LERO after discovering reforms to Jewish education and religious practice being implemented behind their backs.
story_body: LERO had twenty-four board members split between traditionalists and modernizers; the majority secretly pushed reforms before being exposed. The ten resigning members convened at Leningrad's main synagogue, applied for recognition as a separate community, and confronted Rabbi Katzenellenbogen, who had been misled by Gurewicz.

title_en: Daughters of Elchonon Morozov arrested for Zionism
summary_en: Rachel and Sara Morozov were arrested in Leningrad on charges of belonging to the Zionist organization Dror.
story_body: While imprisoned, the sisters learned of their father Elchonon Morozov's own arrest and declared a hunger strike until his treatment improved. On the fifth day he was moved into a cell with Zionist prisoners.

title_en: Elchonon Morozov arrested in Leningrad
summary_en: The Rayatz's secretary and chief underground coordinator was arrested, initially accused of attempting to smuggle the Rebbe's books abroad.
story_body: Before being taken away, Morozov handed the list of underground yeshivot and schools to his eleven-year-old son. Jailed with hardened criminals, in May he was indicted for helping Jews cross the border illegally, sentenced to three years' exile, and deported to Krasnoyarsk. Rabbi Feigin called the arrest 'terrifying and ominous' for the network.

title_en: Rayatz nearly arrested at Moscow hotel
summary_en: A Yevesektzia officer hunted the Rebbe at his Moscow hotel; he was smuggled out the kitchen entrance and hidden at a second hotel.
story_body: Traveling secretly to meet JDC representatives, the Rebbe was spotted on the train by Mark Semyonovitch Bashkov, a senior OGPU member of Belorussian-chasidic descent. A friendly hotel manager warned the Rebbe at midnight and relocated him. Days later, Yevesektzia officer Krotov burst into the new room to arrest him, but Bashkov's OGPU credentials drove the agents off.

title_en: Fiery Purim farbrengen against the Yevesektzia
summary_en: At a mid-March Purim farbrengen in Leningrad, the Rayatz publicly mocked and defied the Yevesektzia in the presence of their spies.
story_body: The Rebbe screamed that the Yevesektzia did not frighten him and urged Chasidim to defy the regime to the point of self-sacrifice rather than send children to Communist schools. He told one Chasid that if confronted with the choice of a bonfire or yielding his child, he should accept the flames. Chasidim and informers alike sensed that retribution was imminent.

title_en: Bentzion Shemtov arrested in Kharkiv
summary_en: Following the Korosten conference, Shemtov was detained in Korosten and held in Kharkiv until Passover.
story_body: Secret police had uncovered his role at the conference and his organizing across Ukraine's Volhynia region. He was released after about a month, only to be arrested again in Kharkiv in June on the same day the Rebbe himself was arrested in Leningrad.

title_en: Leningrad conference of Russian Jewish communities announced
summary_en: Just after Passover, LERO announced that its national Jewish congress would convene that October.
story_body: Despite Gurewicz's traveling lobbying campaign, the major communities of Moscow and Minsk withheld approval, following the Rebbe's lead. The Yevesektzia, secretly backing the plan, intended to use the new lay-led structure to bypass the Rebbe and divert JDC funding away from his network.

title_en: Bentzion Shemtov arrested in Kharkiv same day as Rebbe
summary_en: Three months after his Passover-time release, Shemtov was arrested again in Kharkiv and grilled about the underground Chabad network.
story_body: He was held for thirty days and revealed nothing, then released pending trial. He later received a three-year sentence to Siberian exile. The Rebbe was arrested on the same day in Leningrad.

title_en: Bentzion Shemtov weds Esther Golda in Siberian exile
summary_en: Shemtov married Esther Golda Futerfus in the small Siberian village of Yanivskiek.
story_body: Esther Golda made the long trek from Moscow that summer. Without a mikveh, she immersed in an icy river; without a ring, Shemtov fashioned one from a silver fork. Exiled rabbi Shmuel Levitin officiated. Reb Mendel Futerfus, a legendary underground figure, had suggested the match.

title_en: Yakovshvili family escapes Russia as 'Polish' refugees
summary_en: After nine years in the gulag, Simon Yakovshvili and his family fled Russia using false Polish passports, changing their name to Jacobson.
story_body: Yakovshvili was part of the audacious escape of about one thousand Chasidim organized by the Chabad underground in late 1946 and early 1947. The Shemtov family escaped on the same route. In 1952 the Jacobsons settled in Toronto, where Simon served briefly as rabbi of the local Chabad congregation before his death in June 1953.

title_en: Shemtovs sent to England by the Rebbe
summary_en: After leaving Russia, Bentzion Shemtov was dispatched to England to help build the Chabad community there.
story_body: Shemtov later moved to Israel, where he founded Machon Levi Yitzchak to publish the seventh Rebbe's talks in Hebrew. He died in Israel in 1975.

title_en: Yakovshvili (Simon Jacobson) dies in Toronto
summary_en: Simon Yakovshvili, by then known as Jacobson, died in Toronto at age fifty-three from the effects of years of Soviet imprisonment.
story_body: He had served as rabbi of the local Chabad congregation after immigrating to Toronto in 1952. His wife followed him in death two years later, leaving three orphaned sons aged six, twelve, and fourteen.

title_en: Elchonon Morozov and son Shmuel killed by Soviet secret police
summary_en: After eight years hiding under the alias Berke Pesner, Morozov and his son Shmuel were arrested; both were killed.
story_body: Investigators tortured Shmuel to confirm his father's identity. Shmuel refused; Morozov, hearing him, cried out to identify himself and was told he was being put to death as the Rebbe's representative. He was killed by firing squad; Shmuel had already died under torture.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab dispatches rabbis to Soviet Georgia
summary_en: Responding to a request from community leaders in Kutaisi, the Rashab sent Shmuel Levitin and other rabbis to establish a yeshivah for Sephardic Jews.
story_body: The Georgian community was steeped in tradition but lacked rabbis and scholars. The Rashab sent Levitin, Slavin, Sasonkin, Perlow, and Zuber, among others. Decades later, when the underground emissary Simon Yakovshvili returned to Georgia, the region's Jewish life remained vibrant enough to alarm Yevesektzia leader Moshe Litvakov.

title_en: Tomchei Temimim founded in Lubavitch
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab established the Tomchei Temimim yeshivah in Lubavitch, beginning with a small group of outstanding students.
story_body: Elchonon Morozov was among the first students. He was chosen as the personal study partner for the Rashab's son, the future Rayatz, and later joined the yeshivah faculty before becoming the Rebbe's secretary.

title_en: Yevesektzia founded as Jewish section of the Communist Party
summary_en: Established to consolidate Bolshevik control over the Jewish masses, the Yevesektzia became the Rebbe's primary adversary.
story_body: Many of its members came from the secular Bundist workers' party, which was historically hostile to Jewish religious observance and Zionism. Led by Semyon Dimenstein, the Yevesektzia frequently exceeded Soviet policy in attacking synagogues, schools, and religious leaders.

title_en: Yevesektzia dismantled by Stalin
summary_en: Stalin dissolved the Yevesektzia, and many of its leaders were later killed or exiled during the Great Purge.
story_body: The dissolution did not soften the Soviet stance on religion. In the 1930s, after the Yevesektzia was gone, government actions against synagogues and religious leaders became harsher.

title_en: Rayatz arrested at synagogue in Rostov
summary_en: Three Cheka officers entered the synagogue and escorted the Rebbe, still in mourning for his father, to a police interrogation.
story_body: Brought before fifteen armed officers around a long table, the Rebbe was interrogated about Judaism and Kabbalah. When one officer threatened him with a pistol, the Rebbe replied that he had one G-d and two worlds, while they had one world and many gods. The Cheka eventually issued his release on August 8, 1921.

title_en: Vitebsk show trial against cheder canceled by protests
summary_en: Five thousand local Jews shut down a Yevesektzia show trial of a traditional Vitebsk cheder.
story_body: Thousands more gathered in synagogues to protest, and the Yevesektzia organizers were physically threatened. They later regrouped and staged a second trial that sentenced the cheder to liquidation.

title_en: Moshe Feinstein immigrates from Lyuban to United States
summary_en: After serving as rabbi of Lyuban, Belorussia, Rabbi Moshe Feinstein received an exit visa secured by US-based relatives.
story_body: He had remained in the Soviet Union trying to preserve a core of observant Jews under relentless anti-religious propaganda. He would later become dean of Mesivta Tifereth Jerusalem in the United States and one of the leading halachic authorities of the twentieth century.

title_en: Tomchei Temimim branch opened in Samarkand
summary_en: During World War II, a branch of the underground yeshivah was established in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, followed shortly after by one in Tashkent.
story_body: Between 1922 and 1940, the yeshivah had opened and closed in twenty-seven cities, often operating in multiple places at once, including remote Soviet Georgia. The Uzbekistan branches sustained Jewish life through and after the war.

title_en: Joseph Yitzchak Schneersohn convenes covenant on 19 Kislev in Rostov
summary_en: On 19 Kislev, the Rebbe charged Chasidim in Rostov to fan out to every city, establish places of study, and hire teachers.
story_body: Volunteers stepped forward and the Rebbe promised to make a pact with them. A few months later he formalized the secret covenant in Moscow with a quorum of ten.

title_en: Habima theater troupe leaves Russia
summary_en: The Hebrew-language Habima theater departed on a government-sanctioned international tour and never returned.
story_body: Habima had been founded in 1917 and received a government grant in 1919 over Yevesektzia leader Dimenstein's objections. After years of Yevesektzia harassment, the troupe relocated to Tel Aviv. In 1958 it became the official national theater of Israel.

title_en: Rabbi Yechezkel Feigin killed by Nazis in Warsaw
summary_en: Unable to obtain a passport to join the Rebbe in the United States, Feigin was burned alive in a Warsaw synagogue by the Nazis.
story_body: The Nazis brought most of the city's Jews into a synagogue and set it on fire, forcing other Jews to watch. By some accounts, Rabbi Yitzchak Gurevitz removed a Torah scroll from the ark and danced with Feigin as they burned. When the Rebbe received word of these deaths in 1945, he fainted from grief.

title_en: Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch founded in the United States
summary_en: The Rayatz established Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch, Chabad's central educational organization, in the United States.
story_body: Merkos seeded the first network of Jewish day schools in the United States, preceding similar national organizations such as Torah Umesorah. It would also lay groundwork for the postwar global shluchim movement.

title_en: Rabbi Aryeh Leib Kaplan arrested and exiled to Uzbekistan
summary_en: Rabbi Kaplan, who had heeded the Rebbe's advice to remain in Russia, was arrested and deported to Uzbekistan.
story_body: On the train into exile he met Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson, father of the seventh Rebbe, who was also being banished. They were placed in villages thirty miles apart and stayed in contact. Kaplan was killed by anti-Semitic thugs on Yom Kippur 1943; Rabbi Levi Yitzchak died in 1944 and is buried in Alma Ata.

title_en: Reburial of the Rebbe Rashab in Rostov
summary_en: When Rostov planned to destroy the old Jewish cemetery, Chasidim secretly transferred the Rashab's grave to a new Jewish cemetery.
story_body: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson gave detailed instructions to a group of ten Chasidim, who fasted and performed the transfer late at night despite the danger of police discovery. Twenty years after the Rashab's passing, his body was found whole and intact, shocking the participants. Shmuel Gurary was also reinterred next to him.

title_en: Yitzchak Goldin arrested for underground educational work
summary_en: Goldin was arrested for his role in the Chabad educational underground; an initial death sentence was commuted to exile in Kazakhstan.
story_body: Goldin had assisted the Rebbe during his illness in Rostov and helped administer Tomchei Temimim. He escaped Russia in 1946 and eventually moved to Brooklyn.

title_en: Bobruysk Chabad dynasty ends with passing of Rabbi Shmaryahu Noach
summary_en: Rabbi Shmaryahu Noach Schneersohn of Bobruysk, the last leader of the breakaway Chabad branches, passed away; his Chasidim gravitated to the Rayatz.
story_body: After the 1869 passing of the third Rebbe Menachem Mendel, four of his sons established themselves as Rebbes in other Russian towns alongside Rabbi Shmuel in Lubavitch. Those dynasties eventually petered out. With Shmaryahu Noach's death, Chabad Chasidim from Kopust, Bobruysk, and elsewhere united behind the new Lubavitcher Rebbe.

title_en: Soviet ministry approves grant to Habima theater
summary_en: Despite Yevesektzia leader Dimenstein's protest, the Soviet ministry of culture approved a grant to the Hebrew-language Habima theater.
story_body: Dimenstein argued the grant indulged 'the whim of the bourgeoisie' and pursued Hebrew culture as anathema to Jewish Communism. A public debate was held in Moscow in 1920. The episode illustrated that the Yevesektzia routinely exceeded Soviet government policy.

title_en: Chafetz Chaim transfers yeshivah from Poland to Russia
summary_en: Rabbi Yisrael Meir Kagan moved his Radin yeshivah from Poland to Russia at the beginning of World War I.
story_body: The yeshivah remained in Russia until March 1921, when the elderly Chafetz Chaim returned it to Poland after expressing despair over the Communist regime and Jewish renegades. He later voiced regret over the departure.

title_en: Government-sanctioned yeshivah opens at Moscow's Choral Synagogue
summary_en: During a brief period of Soviet tolerance, a small state-approved yeshivah opened in Moscow's Choral Synagogue.
story_body: The program was tiny and tightly constrained; by 1962 it had just six students. The Lubavitch underground network remained the primary engine sustaining Jewish learning under Communism.

title_en: Network of Yiddish state schools reaches peak in Soviet Union
summary_en: By 1929 there were 1,100 state-run Yiddish schools in the Soviet Union, serving roughly 130,000 students.
story_body: Promoted by the Yevesektzia as schools for the 'Jewish proletariat,' they excluded Hebrew, Jewish religion, history, and tradition. Many religious parents sent their children to non-Jewish schools instead to avoid the anti-religious propaganda.

title_en: Marina Rosche becomes nucleus for underground Moscow yeshivah
summary_en: In the late 1980s, as Communism weakened, students studied more openly at Moscow's Marina Rosche Chabad synagogue.
story_body: Students educated during those late-Communist years formed the nucleus sustaining Jewish life in Moscow until and after the Soviet collapse.

title_en: England severs diplomatic relations with Russia over espionage
summary_en: PM Stanley Baldwin presented deciphered Soviet telegrams to the House of Commons after the All-Russian Co-operative Society raid, ending UK-Soviet diplomatic relations.
story_body: At the end of May 1927, England severed diplomatic relations with Russia after a police raid on the All-Russian Co-operative Society in the UK uncovered Soviet espionage activities. Conservative Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin presented the House of Commons with deciphered Soviet telegrams as proof. This rupture helped trigger Stalin's broader crackdown on perceived enemies inside Russia, including religious leaders.

title_en: Latvia signs trade agreement with Soviet Union
summary_en: Latvia and the Soviet Union signed a friendship and commerce treaty that still required ratification by the Latvian Saeima, where Chabad MP Mordechai Dubin held a swing vote.
story_body: On June 2, 1927, Latvia and the Soviet Union signed a trade deal that was economically vital to Latvia but politically important to the diplomatically isolated Russians. Internal Latvian opposition meant the deal had to be ratified by the Saeima, where Chabad Chasid Mordechai Dubin held two seats. Dubin would later leverage his swing vote to pressure Russia into releasing the Rebbe.

title_en: Assassination of Soviet ambassador Pyotr Voykov in Warsaw
summary_en: Russian monarchist Boris Koverda shot Soviet ambassador Pyotr Voykov at the Warsaw train station, triggering Stalin's wave of executions and arrests.
story_body: In early June 1927, a Russian monarchist assassinated Soviet ambassador to Poland Pyotr Voykov at the Warsaw train station, citing Voykov's role in killing Czar Nicholas. Stalin responded with mass executions of former nobility and broader extrajudicial GPU powers. The Yevesektzia seized this atmosphere of repression to move against the Rebbe.

title_en: GPU arrests Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn in Leningrad
summary_en: Shortly after midnight, GPU agents Mikhail Nachmanson and Grigory Lulov burst into the Rebbe's Leningrad apartment, searched it for an hour and a half, and took him to Shpalerka prison.
story_body: Minutes past midnight on June 15, 1927 (14 Sivan 5687), GPU officers Nachmanson and Lulov, both from Chabad families, led a contingent of armed men into the sixth Rebbe's Leningrad apartment. After a tense search lasting an hour and a half during which the Rebbe insisted on first reciting grace and warned the officers they would regret the arrest, he was taken at around 2:20 a.m. to the notorious Shpalerka prison. By taking a wrong corridor inside the prison, the Rebbe miraculously avoided being grouped with twelve other clergy who were summarily shot that night.

title_en: Rebbe receives tefillin and food from home in Shpalerka
summary_en: After 72 hours of fasting and resisting beatings, the Rebbe was finally given his tefillin and books and received three loaves of uncut challah from his family.
story_body: On Friday June 17, 1927, after two nights and three days of imprisonment, a Jewish guard returned the Rebbe's confiscated tefillin and books. The Rebbe refused the prison's non-kosher meals and demanded food from home. Just before sunset, three loaves of uncut challah were delivered to his cell.

title_en: Second GPU interrogation of the Rebbe
summary_en: In a second interrogation documented in the GPU file, the Rebbe insisted he was a rabbi and teacher of chasidic philosophy, never involved in politics, and confirmed his opposition to the proposed Leningrad Jewish conference.
story_body: On June 21, 1927, GPU investigators questioned the Rebbe again. He stood firm that he had been a rabbi both before and after the revolution and was uninvolved in politics. When asked about the proposed conference for Russian Jewry being organized by the Leningrad community, he confirmed his opposition.

title_en: Rebbe's postcard from prison reaches family
summary_en: A Shabbat postcard from the imprisoned Rebbe arrived at his home, reporting he was 'well' despite beatings and requesting Likkutei Torah and Chumash Bemidbar.
story_body: On Shabbat, June 25, 1927, a postcard the Rebbe had written from Shpalerka was delivered to his family in Leningrad. Despite repeated beatings and excruciating pain, the message was upbeat. He asked his family to send him sefarim, including Likkutei Torah and a Chumash Bemidbar.

title_en: Solovki exile sentence reduced to three years in Kostroma
summary_en: After Madam Peshkova's further intervention, the Rebbe's ten-year Solovki sentence was replaced with a three-year exile to Kostroma on the Volga River.
story_body: On Thursday, after Madam Peshkova pressured the GPU again, the Rebbe was informed that instead of Solovki he would be exiled for three years to Kostroma. He saw the official document on the desk, with the original 'Death by firing squad' crossed out, replaced by 'Ten years in Solovki', and then by 'Three years in Kostroma.' Guards beat him repeatedly when he refused to stand to hear the sentence.

title_en: Rebbe released from Shpalerka and exiled to Kostroma
summary_en: After nineteen days in Shpalerka, the Rebbe was permitted a six-hour visit home and then boarded a train to begin three years of exile in Kostroma.
story_body: On Sunday, July 3, 1927 (3 Tamuz 5687), the Rebbe left Shpalerka prison after 18 days, 11 hours, and 15 minutes of imprisonment. He had refused to leave on Thursday because the train would have forced him to desecrate Shabbat; Madam Peshkova's intercession through Premier Rykov and GPU chief Menzhinsky won him a delay until Sunday. After meeting Chasidim at home, an honor-guard of Leningrad Jews lined his path to the train, where he gave a defiant platform speech declaring that 'only our bodies were sent into exile.'

title_en: Rebbe freed from exile in Kostroma
summary_en: On the day of his weekly required check-in with the Kostroma GPU, the Rebbe was informed that a telegram from Moscow had ordered his unconditional release.
story_body: On Tuesday, July 12, 1927 (12 Tamuz), the Rebbe came to the GPU headquarters in Kostroma for his mandated weekly appearance. An officer told him papers had arrived freeing him. The international outcry combined with Madam Peshkova's lobbying had overcome the opposition of Leningrad GPU chief Stanislav Messing. The Rebbe marked the day by teaching a maamar on Psalms 118:7, 'G-d aided me'; 12 Tamuz has since been celebrated annually as a Chabad festival of liberation.

title_en: Rebbe returns to Leningrad after exile
summary_en: Two days after being freed in Kostroma, the Rebbe arrived back in Leningrad despite fears that the local GPU might arrest him again.
story_body: On July 14, 1927, the Rebbe arrived back in Leningrad following his liberation from Kostroma exile. The news of his release spread quickly across the Soviet Union, sparking celebrations among Chasidim. On his first Shabbat back he recited the HaGomel blessing of thanksgiving for surviving prison.

title_en: Riga Jewish community invites Rebbe to be chief rabbi
summary_en: On 23 Menachem Av 5687, the Riga Jewish community sent a formal invitation for the Rebbe to become its chief rabbi, used as leverage to secure his exit visa.
story_body: On August 21, 1927 (23 Menachem Av 5687), the Riga Jewish community formally invited the Rebbe to become its chief rabbi. Mordechai Dubin, head of the Riga community and a member of the Latvian Parliament, presented the letter to Russian officials. Combined with Dubin's swing vote on the pending Russia-Latvia trade treaty, the invitation became the key lever for obtaining the Rebbe's exit visa.

title_en: Rebbe celebrates last Simchat Torah with Russian Chasidim in Leningrad
summary_en: Russian Chasidim packed a Leningrad synagogue, normally holding 600, far beyond capacity for the Rebbe's final Simchat Torah before leaving the Soviet Union.
story_body: In October 1927, the Rebbe celebrated his last holiday in Russia, Simchat Torah, with his Chasidim in Leningrad. Despite the risk of arrest, Chasidim flocked from across the country; the synagogue swelled with people packed into every corner. The Rebbe urged them, 'Don't fear anyone,' and consoled them, 'I will be with you,' while one Chasid wept, 'The Rebbe is going, and we are left here.'

title_en: Rebbe writes anniversary letter calling 12 Tamuz a festival of liberation
summary_en: A year after his release, the Rebbe published a letter declaring that 12 Tamuz is a 'festival of liberation' for all who love Torah and even for every Jew.
story_body: On June 3, 1928 (15 Sivan 5688), the Rebbe issued a public letter explaining that his liberation should be marked annually as a festival for those who love Torah and observe its commands, and indeed for every Jew, 'for the heart of every man of Israel is perfectly bound with G-d and His Torah.' This letter formalized the annual observance of 12 Tamuz across Jewish communities.

title_en: Yeshivah in Nevel closed by Soviet authorities
summary_en: The JTA reported the closure of the American-subsidized Chabad yeshivah in Nevel, roughly 120 miles from Lubavitch.
story_body: On November 2, 1928, the JTA reported that the yeshivah in Nevel — a vibrant Chabad town about 120 miles from Lubavitch — had been shut down by Soviet authorities a year after the Rebbe's arrest. Nevel had been a center of chasidic life with a Jewish population of nearly 5,900 in 1897. The local Jewish community was later annihilated by the Nazis during the Holocaust.

title_en: Mikhail Nachmanson arrested for counterrevolutionary activity
summary_en: GPU/NKVD officer Mikhail Nachmanson, who had arrested the Rebbe, was himself arrested on his birthday and sent to Lubyanka prison and later the Kolyma labor camp.
story_body: On September 9, 1936, his birthday, former GPU/NKVD officer Mikhail Nachmanson was arrested for counterrevolutionary activity and transferred to Lubyanka Prison in Leningrad. Without trial, he received an extrajudicial five-year sentence in Kolyma. He was released in 1941, rearrested in 1950, freed after Stalin's death in 1953, and given amnesty in 1956, yet remained a committed Communist until the end of his life.

title_en: GPU officer Grigory Lulov executed
summary_en: Grigory Lulov, one of the two GPU agents who arrested the Rebbe in 1927, was executed by verdict of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR.
story_body: On January 21, 1940, GPU officer Grigory Nikolaevich Lulov was executed following his arrest at the end of 1938. Born in Riga in 1899, Lulov had joined the Communist Party in 1916 and the Cheka in 1919, becoming an 'Honorary Worker of the Cheka-GPU' decorated with the Order of Lenin in 1937 before falling victim to the purges himself.

title_en: Chabad network smuggles 1,000 Chasidim out of the USSR on false passports
summary_en: The clandestine Chabad network orchestrated the audacious escape of about one thousand Chasidim across the Soviet border into Poland using forged Polish passports.
story_body: In 1946, the underground Chabad network — which had endured through decades of Soviet persecution — orchestrated the escape of roughly a thousand Chasidim across the border to Poland on false passports. They and their children went on to provide leadership for the global Jewish renaissance and to inspire a new generation of postwar Chasidim.

title_en: Golda Meir witnesses Chabad-organized Rosh Hashanah crowds in Moscow
summary_en: Israel's first ambassador to Russia, Golda Meir, was greeted at Moscow's Choral Synagogue by thousands of Jews on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, an event she later credited to Chabad.
story_body: In 1949, newly appointed Ambassador Golda Meir attended High Holiday services at Moscow's Choral Synagogue. On the first day of Rosh HaShanah she found only a small group of elderly Jews, but on the second day thousands filled the streets to welcome her. Decades later she told Italian reporter Oriana Fallaci that 'it was Chabad that orchestrated the welcome of thousands.'

title_en: Sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe arrives in Riga, Latvia from Russia
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn arrives in Riga two days after Simchat Torah following expulsion from the Soviet Union.
story_body: After enduring arrest and exile in Russia, the sixth Rebbe crossed into Latvia by train, arriving at 7:00 a.m. at Riga station. Thousands of Jews of every background filled the station and surrounding plaza to greet him. He and his family were eventually escorted to a hotel and later to an apartment in an upscale Jewish neighborhood.

title_en: Rebbe writes letter to Chasidim during train journey out of Russia
summary_en: On the train to Latvia, the Rebbe composes a letter to his followers affirming their unbroken spiritual bond.
story_body: Heartbroken at leaving Russia, the Rebbe wrote, 'The essential connection between us cannot be broken, nor does the fact that distance stands between us break that bond.' The letter, written during the journey, was preserved in Igrot Kodesh, volume 1.

title_en: Rebbe writes detailed letter to Baruch Rizik about leaving Russia
summary_en: Six weeks after his departure, the Rebbe describes the emotional farewell at the Leningrad station and his anguished overnight journey.
story_body: In a forthcoming letter to a Chasid in Rostov, the Rebbe described the thousands who filled the station 'full of emotion,' the eighteen-hour overnight train ride, and his prayer for the Jews left behind. The letter survives in Igrot Kodesh, volume 17.

title_en: Rebbe writes to Haffkine from Riga about Russian Jewry
summary_en: The Rebbe writes in German to scientist Waldemar Haffkine, explaining that Riga allows him broader reach to help Russian Jewry.
story_body: The Rebbe told Haffkine, 'I have not given up on Russia. My residence is just outside the border so I can continue my efforts for Russian Jewry.' He explained he could now correspond more freely and proposed strategies against the Yevsektzia.

title_en: Rebbe writes to Haffkine proposing secret meeting against Yevsektzia
summary_en: The Rebbe urges Haffkine to help arrange a confidential gathering of Jewish leaders to counter the Yevsektzia.
story_body: Calling the Yevsektzia 'the greatest danger and damage to the activities of Russian Jewry,' the Rebbe stressed the meeting must be done 'with the utmost secrecy.' The plan ultimately did not materialize.

title_en: First meeting of Vaad Magen UMekhaseh held in Riga
summary_en: Two weeks after arriving, the Rebbe convenes prominent rabbis to form the Committee for the Protection and Care of Russian Jewry.
story_body: The committee included Rabbi Yosef Rosen (the Rogotchover Gaon), Rabbi Meir Hildesheimer of Berlin, and Rabbi Mendel Zak of Riga. It later gained the backing of Rabbis Yisrael Meir Kagan and Chaim Ozer Grodzinski, and organized worldwide fasts and prayers for Soviet Jewry.

title_en: Rebbe writes to Rabbi Zevin urging opposition to Leningrad conference
summary_en: Just days after arriving in Riga, the Rebbe writes urging Chasidim to undermine the Yevsektzia-backed Leningrad Jewish conference.
story_body: The Rebbe wrote, 'Anyone with a G-d-fearing spirit should protest against the Leningrad conference and undermine those plotting against the values of Torah.' He dispatched a detailed nine-city action plan that successfully prevented the conference from convening.

title_en: Rebbe sends action plan to disrupt Leningrad conference
summary_en: The Rebbe dispatches an organizing plan covering nine key cities with instructions to Chasidim to undermine the Yevsektzia conference.
story_body: The plan focused on cities including Moscow, Leningrad, and Kutaisi in Soviet Georgia, with lists of contacts and detailed instructions. The plans succeeded and the conference was never convened.

title_en: Rebbe writes to Rabbi Yakovshvili about shechitah and Kutaisi
summary_en: The Rebbe instructs Rabbi Simon Yakovshvili to return to Kutaisi, learn shechitah, and coordinate Jewish education there.
story_body: Despite being in Riga, the Rebbe directed activity in remote Soviet Georgia. He instructed Yakovshvili to consult with Avraham Levik Slavin and Schneur Zalman Altshuler about educational projects and report back regularly.

title_en: Rebbe writes to Shimon Bliner praising Moscow Torah classes
summary_en: The Rebbe lauds Chasid Shimon Bliner for establishing underground classes in Mishnah and chasidic philosophy in Moscow.
story_body: The Rebbe wrote that he 'enjoyed reading' about the new classes and asked Bliner to share his blessing with all involved. The letter is preserved in Igrot Kodesh volume 16.

title_en: Grodner Moment reports on Rebbe's activities in Riga hotel
summary_en: The Yiddish daily reports on the masses flocking to the Rebbe's hotel for prayers, blessings, and Shabbat maamarim.
story_body: The paper described corridors 'packed with masses of people' awaiting audiences, and Shabbat afternoons when 'the hotel loses its mundane weekday state' as people flooded in to hear the Rebbe recite a maamar weaving Bible, Talmud, and Zohar.

title_en: Detroit Jewish Chronicle reports on Rebbe's impact in Latvia
summary_en: The American Jewish paper reports that Soviet Russia inadvertently helped Latvian Jewry by expelling the Lubavitcher Rebbe.
story_body: The paper wrote, 'The Lubavitcher Rebbe had brought a great deal of activity into the life of Orthodox Jewry in Latvia. And Soviet Russia has thus, by expelling the Lubavitcher Rebbe, done a good turn to the Jews of Latvia.'

title_en: Rebbe writes long letter detailing ordeals in Soviet Russia
summary_en: The Rebbe writes that Riga is only 'temporary' and details his suffering in Russia and longing for the country he was forced to leave.
story_body: He wrote, 'I fled the bad, but I have not yet found the good. I was driven from my country and forced to separate from my beloved brothers and friends.' His new stationery printed 'Riga' followed by the word 'temporary.'

title_en: Rebbe writes to Chief Rabbi Hertz of Britain about Russian Jewry
summary_en: The Rebbe implores the British chief rabbi to help save twenty thousand Russian children unable to study Torah for lack of funds.
story_body: Thanking Rabbi Hertz for welcoming his son-in-law Rashag, the Rebbe wrote, 'It is not a time for silence or to hold back on action. We must save Russian Jewry. What will future generations say if we do not answer their call in the time of crisis?'

title_en: First Yiddish maamar published in Riga in over a century
summary_en: The Rebbe publishes the maamar Kinyan HaChaim, the first chasidic discourse printed in Yiddish since the eighteenth century.
story_body: Published before the High Holidays, this was the Rebbe's first maamar since leaving Russia. Printing in Yiddish rather than Hebrew made chasidic teachings accessible to a wider lay audience, marking a major step in disseminating Chasidut.

title_en: Rebbe thanks Sylvia Reinen for translating maamar into Yiddish
summary_en: The Rebbe blesses Sylvia Reinen for her role translating a chasidic discourse, an early step in empowering women in chasidic learning.
story_body: Writing to her husband Alexander Sender Reinen, the Rebbe noted, 'It will be a great merit that those who don't understand another language are able to study it.' This was a foundational moment in opening chasidic study to women.

title_en: Soviet education minister Lunacharsky attacks Rebbe in NY Times
summary_en: Anatoly Lunacharsky publicly declares war on 'Schneersohnovschina' — the religious activities of the Lubavitcher Rebbe.
story_body: Lunacharsky told the Times, 'We shall combat the relics of the Middle Ages, the Schneersohnovschina.' The term was thereafter used by Soviet authorities to imprison Chasidim. He declared the Jewish solution lay in 'fusion of the Jews in the great melting pot.'

title_en: Rebbe writes to Rabbi Teitelbaum about dire Russian Jewish institutions
summary_en: The Rebbe describes Russian Jewish institutions 'hanging between life and death' and pleads for JDC funding.
story_body: Writing to JDC board member Rabbi Aron Teitelbaum, the Rebbe described schools on the verge of closing and personal loans to keep them afloat. He warned that withdrawing funding would hand victory to the Yevsektzia.

title_en: Cyrus Adler argues against funding Rebbe's matzah shipment
summary_en: JDC leader Cyrus Adler writes Joseph Hyman opposing support for the Rebbe's emergency matzah campaign for Soviet Jews.
story_body: Adler argued that 'the Yevsektzia might block the deliveries' and that the shipment might embarrass the Russians. He later reversed position in 1932, writing he was not disposed to surrender Jewish religious practice to the Soviets.

title_en: Rashag reports to Meisel on Passover matzah shipment to Soviet Union
summary_en: Rabbi Gurary documents the complex diplomatic and logistical struggle behind the international matzah campaign for Soviet Jewry.
story_body: The Rashag lamented Russian bureaucracy: 'Every day they say they have no answer. Then they say I must inquire in Moscow.' Ultimately, 140,000 kilos of matzah were shipped plus 5,689 packages, at a total cost of $88,000.

title_en: Rebbe launches international matzah campaign for Soviet Jewry
summary_en: Facing Soviet famine, the Rebbe coordinates a global emergency campaign to ship matzah into Russia before Passover.
story_body: The Rebbe enlisted Mordechai Dubin, the Rashag, and rabbis including Chaim Ozer Grodzinski, Yisrael Meir Kagan, and Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld. Despite Soviet obstruction, 140,000 kilos of matzah reached Russian Jews, proving the Rebbe could marshal global support without the Jewish establishment.

title_en: Feigin urges American Chabad to set up maamad fundraising
summary_en: Rabbi Yechezkel Feigin describes the Rebbe's spiritual isolation and financial crisis in Riga and urges US Chabad to organize support.
story_body: Feigin wrote, 'Spiritually, the Rebbe is suffering. There are few anash here.' He noted the Rebbe lacked resources to establish a yeshivah in Riga and faced mounting debts and medical needs.

title_en: Rebbe begins yearlong journey to Eretz Yisrael and America
summary_en: From his Riga base, the Rebbe undertakes an almost yearlong trip to the Holy Land and the United States.
story_body: The travels were aimed at inspiring communities and meeting Jewish leaders to help Russian Jewry. The visit was a turning point for establishing the Rebbe's international stature and for the future of American Chabad.

title_en: Detroit Jewish Chronicle reports arrest of 16 leaders in Minsk
summary_en: The paper reports that sixteen Jewish leaders were arrested in Minsk for the counterrevolutionary crime of corresponding with the Rebbe.
story_body: The Chronicle reported the leaders 'had been hounded by the secret police for no other reason than being in contact with the Lubavitcher Rebbe.' Communications between the Rebbe and Soviet Jews carried grave personal risk.

title_en: Simchat Torah 1930 — Rebbe's stern address foils Peretz disruption
summary_en: The Rebbe demands those not observing basics of tradition leave; only later it is revealed the Peretz Communist youth had infiltrated to disrupt the dancing.
story_body: On this Simchat Torah, the Rebbe also founded Agudas Chassidei Chabad of Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia, criticized Latvian Jewry as 'Jewish only in appearance,' and called on Chasidim to 'stand on the street corners and pull Jews into a synagogue to study' — the seed of public outreach that would later define Chabad.

title_en: Feigin reveals Peretz plot to Rebbe two days after Simchat Torah
summary_en: Rabbi Feigin informs the Rebbe that Peretz infiltrators had planned to cut electricity and break up the hakafot.
story_body: When the Rebbe heard the details, he said, 'Now I know that I was justified in speaking that way, though at the time I did not know what pushed me to say it.' The story was preserved in Feigin's letter to Jacobson.

title_en: Rebbe addresses women's gathering in Rokiškis, Lithuania
summary_en: A large group of women requests the Rebbe speak to them — an unprecedented event in chasidic history.
story_body: Historically chasidic Rebbes only addressed men publicly. In the same visit, the Rebbe lamented declining scholarship, criticized modern integrated schools, and praised the 'old-style cheder' while supporting Tze'irei Agudath Israel as a practical compromise.

title_en: Rebbe writes Rabbi Cheifetz endorsing women's chasidic study
summary_en: The Rebbe instructs Rabbi Mordechai Cheifetz to teach maamarim to his daughter, citing his grandfather's teaching.
story_body: Quoting Rabbi Shmuel that 'amongst Chasidim there is no difference between a boy or a girl,' the Rebbe lamented neglect of girls' chasidic education. This catalyzed the formation of Achot Hatemimim and serious women's chasidic study.

title_en: Ulmanis coup d'état in Latvia; political parties disbanded
summary_en: Prime Minister Kārlis Ulmanis dissolves the elected parliament and bans political parties, including Jewish ones.
story_body: Only Agudath Israel was allowed to function because of Mordechai Dubin's personal bond with Ulmanis. Multi-party elections did not return until 1990. Dubin used his expanded influence to engineer Hodakov's appointment as inspector of Jewish schools.

title_en: Hodakov appointed chief inspector of Jewish schools in Latvia
summary_en: Rabbi Chaim Mordechai Aizek Hodakov is named chief inspector of Latvia's Jewish schools, beginning reforms toward traditional Judaism.
story_body: Orchestrated by Dubin, the appointment let Hodakov replace secular curricula with Torah lessons. Yiddishist teachers staged a strike but failed. Hodakov instituted required prayer and yarmulkes, transforming the historically secular schools.

title_en: JTA reports Latvia's secular Jewish school union disbanded
summary_en: New York's JTA reports the secular Jewish Parents Union in Latvia disbanded, with all educational programs transferred to Agudath Israel.
story_body: The shift marked a major victory in the culture war between traditional Jewish education and the secular Yiddish identity movement in Latvia.

title_en: Women's Achot Hatemimim group founded in United States
summary_en: The Rebbe writes in English to a new women's group in America, appointing three prominent rabbis to teach them chasidic philosophy.
story_body: The Rebbe expressed gratification with their decision to study Chasidism and selected Rabbis Yisrael Jacobson, Yisrael Kazarnovsky, and Yochanan Gordon as their mentors. The model expanded the women's chasidic study initiative pioneered in Riga.

title_en: Rebbe relocates from Latvia to Poland
summary_en: Six years after arriving in Riga, the Rebbe moves his residence to Poland.
story_body: Riga had served as a base for years of travel and recovery, but Poland — home to a vast Jewish population and the growing Warsaw yeshivah — became the next station. The yeshivah was eventually based in the suburb of Otwock.

title_en: Rebbe escapes Nazi-occupied Poland and arrives in New York
summary_en: After a brief second stay in Riga, the Rebbe escapes Europe and establishes Chabad's permanent base in America.
story_body: The wandering that began with the 1927 exile from Russia ended at 770 Eastern Parkway in Brooklyn, the iconic Gothic-style building where the Rebbe spent the last decade of his life. He addressed Achot Hatemimim in Riga during the second interlude.

title_en: Sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn passes away
summary_en: The sixth Rebbe passes away in Brooklyn after a decade leading Chabad from 770 Eastern Parkway.
story_body: He had started from scratch three times: after his father's passing in 1920, in Riga in 1927, and in America in 1940. His passing set the stage for his son-in-law, the seventh Rebbe, to assume leadership and expand the initiatives launched in Riga.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab passes away in Rostov
summary_en: Rabbi Sholom DovBer Schneersohn, the fifth Lubavitcher Rebbe, passes away, leaving leadership to his son.
story_body: His passing forced his son Yosef Yitzchak to begin again from scratch — the first of three such restarts in his life. Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim, which the Rashab had founded in 1897, became a key inheritance.

title_en: Warsaw branch of Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim opens
summary_en: On the first anniversary of the Rashab's passing, twelve students inaugurate the Warsaw branch of the chasidic yeshivah.
story_body: The Rebbe called this 'days of light and days of joy.' He appointed an oversight board and instructed them to focus on ethics, G-d-fearing spirit, and character. By 1927 it had 157 students; by 1928, 250. It eventually relocated to Otwock and became the incubator for postwar Chabad rabbis.

title_en: Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim founded by Rebbe Rashab
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab establishes the first chasidic yeshivah, a revolutionary institution other chasidic groups would later emulate.
story_body: Historian Yehuda Geberer notes this was Chabad's leading response to 'the great crisis' — declining chasidic numbers in the interwar years. The yeshivah balanced talmudic study with chasidic philosophy, creating the model later expanded by the Rayatz across Poland and Lithuania.

title_en: Letter to JDC qualifiedly endorsing agricultural colonies
summary_en: The Rebbe acknowledges Dr. Rosen's colonies but warns of the missing religious infrastructure: mikvaot, teachers, shochtim, synagogues.
story_body: Reading at a JDC board meeting in English translation, the Rebbe asked, 'What about the thousands who cannot work in agriculture, or move from their homes?' He urged the JDC to help them through urban home-based industry instead.

title_en: Letter to Agudas Harabonim on agricultural colonies
summary_en: The Rebbe urges American Orthodox rabbis to lobby the JDC for religious infrastructure in the Soviet agricultural colonies.
story_body: He asked them to ensure the colonies were provided 'with the religious institutions necessary for every Jew,' arguing that without synagogues, mikvaot, and schools, the resettlements would sever Jews from their tradition.

title_en: Soviet land resettlement project launched to 'productize' Jews
summary_en: The USSR begins relocating Jewish families to communal farms in Ukraine and Crimea to transform them into farmers.
story_body: Driven by Semyon Dimenstein and the Yevsektzia, the project displaced traditional Jewish economic roles. The JDC financially supported the plan despite the Rebbe's warnings that it lacked religious infrastructure and served Soviet anti-religious ends.

title_en: 'The New Book of Lamentations' published in Hadoar
summary_en: An anonymous letter in the US Hebrew newspaper exposes the bleak conditions and anti-religious motives behind the Soviet colonies.
story_body: The writer charged that the Soviet government was using colonization 'to break down and destroy the Jewish spirit.' He described hunger, harsh winters, and Potemkin-village shows put on for visiting JDC officials.

title_en: Jews expelled from Borisov collective for refusing Shabbat milking
summary_en: Jews in new collective settlements in the Borisov region are removed as 'undesirables' for refusing to milk cows on Shabbat.
story_body: The case illustrated how the agricultural settlements pushed Jews to choose between livelihood and observance. The synagogue of communal farm town Krivoy Rog was converted into an arts hall where Yiddish ballads mocked traditional pieties.

title_en: Agudas Chassidei Chabad founded for Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia
summary_en: Twenty-one Chasidim meet at the Rashag's home during High Holidays to form a union of Chabad communities across the region.
story_body: Rashag proposed the organization with the Rebbe's approval. It took on the mandate of strengthening Chabad communities in Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia, providing institutional infrastructure for the dispersed movement.

title_en: First Bais Yaakov school founded by Sarah Schenirer in Poland
summary_en: Sarah Schenirer founds the first Bais Yaakov, pioneering formal Torah study for Orthodox women.
story_body: The Schenirer schools focused on basic Jewish literacy, traditions, and history but did not emphasize chasidic theology. The Rebbe's later Achot Hatemimim initiative would go further, promoting serious study of Tanya and chasidic discourses.

title_en: Czernowitz Conference declares Yiddish a Jewish national language
summary_en: Leaders at the Czernowitz Conference proclaim Yiddish 'the glue to hold Jewish life together.'
story_body: The Yiddish movement's secular philosophy rejected classic Jewish religious observance and aimed to build Jewish identity around language alone. It spread to Russia, Europe, and North America before fading in the late twentieth century.

title_en: World Agudath Israel founded at Katowice conference
summary_en: Jewish religious leaders establish Agudath Israel in Katowice, Poland, in response to secularization and Zionism.
story_body: The movement unified many chasidic groups with the Lithuanian yeshivah world, though Chabad did not join. Agudath Israel later won seats in the Latvian Saeima and became a major presence in Israel and the US.

title_en: Max Lilienthal opens first German-style Jewish school in Riga
summary_en: Adherent of the German Haskalah Max Lilienthal establishes Russia's first German-style Jewish secular school in Riga.
story_body: Riga's small Jewish community invited him seeking a secular Jewish school, possibly under pressure from the Russian government. From Riga, Lilienthal attempted to transform Jewish education throughout Russia, laying groundwork for the secular orientation the Rebbe later encountered.

title_en: Latvia declares independence from Russia
summary_en: Latvians overthrow Russian rule and establish an independent republic.
story_body: Independence enabled Jewish political participation and party activity; the Rebbe later noted that the community should have established yeshivot from this point on but failed to do so.

title_en: Soviet Union annexes Latvia at end of WWII
summary_en: Soviet troops seize Latvia, incorporating it into the USSR until 1991.
story_body: Latvia's first independence ended; the surviving Jewish community came under Soviet rule. Religious life persisted underground, sustained by the legacy of the Rebbe's six-year stay decades earlier.

title_en: Multi-party elections return to Latvia after 56-year hiatus
summary_en: Latvia holds its first multi-party elections since the 1934 Ulmanis coup.
story_body: After more than five decades without competitive elections, the move marked the beginning of political pluralism's return and preceded Latvia's full independence in 1991.

title_en: Agudath Israel siyum HaShas at MetLife Stadium
summary_en: Some ninety thousand attend the global celebration marking the completion of the daf yomi cycle of Talmud study.
story_body: Organized by Agudath Israel in New Jersey, the event reflected the movement's continuing global Orthodox influence more than a century after its founding.

title_en: Tefillin campaign launched before Six-Day War
summary_en: The seventh Rebbe initiates the first mitzvah campaign, urging Jews to don tefillin even in public venues.
story_body: Launched in the weeks before the Six-Day War, the campaign was the first of the Rebbe's public mitzvah initiatives. It traced directly back to the 1930 Simchat Torah talk in Riga, where the sixth Rebbe called for outreach on street corners — with the future seventh Rebbe present.

title_en: Beis Rivkah schools established by Achot Hatemimim in New York
summary_en: Members of Achot Hatemimim of Greater New York establish Beis Rivkah, the future flagship Chabad girls' school network.
story_body: The founding crowned years of women's chasidic study development that began with the Rebbe's Riga initiatives. Beis Rivkah grew into the Chabad system that today integrates chasidic philosophy into the standard women's curriculum.

title_en: Rabbi Chaim Mordechai Aizik Hodakov born in Beshankovich
summary_en: The future chief of staff to the seventh Rebbe is born in the Russian town of Beshankovich.
story_body: Hodakov's family moved to Riga when he was two, where he studied under Rabbi Yoel Barantchik of the Novardok Musar movement. He became an ardent Chasid when the Rebbe arrived in 1928 and later founded the Derech Eretz school at eighteen.

title_en: Rabbi Hodakov passes away after decades as Chabad chief of staff
summary_en: Rabbi Hodakov passes away after serving as the seventh Rebbe's chief of staff and secretary.
story_body: He had overseen Chabad's global growth, accompanied the Rebbe to America in 1940, and helped establish the first national Jewish school system in the US. His career spanned from chief inspector in 1930s Latvia to the postwar Chabad headquarters.

title_en: Dr. Nissan Mindel born in Riga
summary_en: Nissan Mindel, future secretary to two Lubavitcher Rebbes and translator of the Tanya, is born in Riga.
story_body: He met the Rebbe as a young man on the Rebbe's arrival from Russia. He earned a master's at Manchester and a doctorate in Semitic languages at Columbia, before serving as secretary in Otwock and accompanying the Rebbe on the 1940 voyage to America.

title_en: Dr. Nissan Mindel passes away
summary_en: Dr. Nissan Mindel, longtime Chabad secretary and English translator of the Tanya, passes away.
story_body: He served on the boards of Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch and Agudas Chassidei Chabad and wrote major works on chasidic history and philosophy in addition to his Tanya translation.

title_en: Rakeffet visits Riga as covert Mossad agent and finds living Chabad legacy
summary_en: Rabbi Aaron Rakeffet visits Riga and discovers a vibrant underground Jewish community still shaped by the Rebbe's 1927-1933 stay.
story_body: After services, older Jews ushered him upstairs once government agents left, then 'broke out vodka and cake' for a farbrengen with stories of the Rebbe. Rakeffet attests the richness absorbed during the Rebbe's six-year stay was 'still pulsating half a century later.'

title_en: Schneur Zalman of Liadi born
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, founder of Chabad Chasidism, is born.
story_body: He went on to author the Tanya and institute the maamad tradition of Chasidim supporting the Rebbe's court — a tradition stretched thin during the Rayatz's Riga years when Soviet Chasidim could no longer contribute.

title_en: Schneur Zalman of Liadi passes away
summary_en: The first Lubavitcher Rebbe and founder of Chabad Chasidism passes away.
story_body: His freedom from czarist prison in 1798 had launched a new stage of public chasidic teaching, a development the Rebbe Rayatz pointed to when expanding the dissemination of Chasidut to wider audiences in Riga.

title_en: Alter Rebbe freed from czarist imprisonment
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman is freed from czarist prison, beginning a new era of deeper public chasidic teaching.
story_body: The seventh Rebbe identified this as a major turning point in the dissemination of chasidic teachings — the moment when Chasidut began to reach 'chutzah,' outside. The arc continued through the 1897 yeshivah and the Riga-era translations.

title_en: Baal Shem Tov's soul ascent on Rosh Hashanah
summary_en: Rabbi Yisrael Baal Shem Tov experiences a mystical ascent and receives the Messiah's instruction to spread chasidic teachings.
story_body: Asked when he would come, the Messiah replied, 'In the time when your teachings will become public and revealed in the world.' This vision became the foundational principle of Chabad's mission of disseminating Chasidut, which the Rayatz expanded in Riga.

title_en: Baal Shem Tov's letter to his brother published
summary_en: A disciple publishes the Baal Shem Tov's letter describing his 1746 mystical ascent for the first time.
story_body: The letter, addressed to his brother and describing his encounter with the Messiah, became foundational text for the Chabad mission of spreading chasidic teachings outward.

title_en: Sholem Aleichem School (Yiddish day school) founded in Melbourne
summary_en: Originally called I.L. Peretz Sunday School, the Melbourne institution is founded; today it is the world's only full-time Yiddish day school.
