story_body: The school promotes Yiddish language and literature alongside 'veltkhe yiddishkayt' — a secular approach to Jewish history and ethics. It survives as the last vestige of a movement that flourished in interwar Europe and faded elsewhere.

title_en: Emancipation of Russian serfs
summary_en: The Russian Empire emancipates its serfs, giving peasants land that would later be seized for Soviet collectivization.
story_body: The land-ownership pattern that emerged was overturned by Soviet collectivization, which forced the creation of farming collectives, dropped productivity, and contributed to the famine the Rebbe later confronted with his matzah campaign.

title_en: Wedding of Chana Schneerson and Rabbi Shmaryahu Gurary in Rostov
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz's older daughter Chana married Rabbi Shmaryahu Gurary in a very modest ceremony in Rostov.
story_body: At the time, Rostov was suffering from typhus and famine, and the Yevsektzia had forcibly closed the Lubavitch yeshivah. The secret police broke into the Rebbe's home before the wedding and seized property including the wedding dress. With limited finances, only light refreshments of cake and drinks were served to guests.

title_en: Rashab flees Lubavitch in the face of German invasion
summary_en: The fifth Rebbe, Rabbi Sholom Dovber (Rashab), fled the town of Lubavitch as the German army advanced during WWI.
story_body: Chabad Rebbes traditionally wore the shtreimel only in Lubavitch. When the Rashab fled in the face of the German invasion in 1915, he ceased wearing it. The departure ended the historic Lubavitch chapter of Chabad, beginning years of wandering and persecution.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz assumes leadership of Chabad
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn assumed the position of sixth Rebbe of Chabad-Lubavitch.
story_body: The Rebbe Rayatz took over leadership after the passing of his father, the Rebbe Rashab. He would not wear the traditional shtreimel again until his daughter Chaya Mushka's wedding in 1928, a symbolic gesture marking a new era of Chabad.

title_en: Ramash meets Chaya Mushka for first time in Kislovodsk
summary_en: Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson (Ramash) met his future wife Chaya Mushka in the resort town of Kislovodsk, escorted by matchmaker Rabbi Eliyahu Chaim Althaus.
story_body: The Rebbe Rayatz confided to Althaus that summer that he wished to marry off his daughter to the Ramash, and asked him to act as shadkhan. Althaus escorted the twenty-one-year-old groom on the 600-mile trip from Yekaterinoslav to Kislovodsk. The Ramash stayed two weeks before returning to Rostov with the Rebbe.

title_en: Rebbe writes 'Hilkhot Mendel' letter to Chaya Mushka
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz wrote to his daughter alluding to the Ramash's recent visit and hinting he wanted to see her again.
story_body: A week after the Ramash returned to Rostov, the Rebbe wrote to Chaya Mushka, who remained in Kislovodsk, that he had been studying 'Hilkhot Mendel' (the subject of Mendel) for several hours each day. He noted that the Ramash had left with a pleasant impression of the Caucasus and would like another excursion in the mountains.

title_en: Lenin dies; St. Petersburg renamed Leningrad
summary_en: Vladimir Lenin died in January 1924, prompting the renaming of St. Petersburg to Leningrad.
story_body: The renaming of the former Russian capital came just before the Rebbe Rayatz was compelled to relocate there. The Rebbe later moved to Leningrad in May 1924 after being ordered by the political police to leave Rostov.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz relocates from Rostov to Leningrad
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz was forced to leave Rostov for Leningrad by order of the Soviet political police.
story_body: As he later described it, 'I was compelled to leave by the order of the political police.' His family followed shortly thereafter. The Ramash visited Leningrad regularly, also attending classes at the local university and being drawn deeper into the Rebbe's affairs.

title_en: Ramash hides from Bolsheviks in Luga
summary_en: Fearing detention by the Bolsheviks, the Ramash took refuge for several months in the home of Rabbi Chanoch Henoch Etkin in Luga, on the outskirts of Leningrad.
story_body: At the time the Ramash was engaged, the Bolsheviks began investigating him. He hid in Etkin's home for a few months, spending his time studying and learning Talmud daily with his host. Etkin had regular employment and was not harassed by the authorities.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz leaves Russia for Riga
summary_en: The Russian authorities granted approval for the Rebbe and his family to depart Russia for Riga, Latvia, after years of persecution.
story_body: The Rebbe insisted his future son-in-law also be permitted to leave. When officials asked, 'Can't you find another son-in-law?' the Rebbe famously replied, 'A son-in-law like him I can't find there.' The move ended the Russian chapter of Chabad leadership.

title_en: Ramash departs Riga for Berlin
summary_en: Two months after arriving from Russia, the Ramash departed Riga for Berlin, where he would attend lectures and university courses for years to come.
story_body: The day after he came to Berlin, the Ramash represented his future father-in-law at a convention of Agudath Israel. In Berlin he attended lectures by Rabbi Yechiel Yaakov Weinberg of the Rabbinical Seminary, and with Weinberg's help registered at Friedrich Wilhelm University for courses in geometry, physics, and higher mathematics.

title_en: Feigin's first appeal to Jacobson for wedding funds
summary_en: Rabbi Yechezkel Feigin secretly wrote to Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson in New York imploring American Chasidim for financial help for the upcoming royal wedding.
story_body: With the wedding approaching, the financial situation was dire. The Communist revolution had disrupted donations from Russian Chasidim, and few Chasidim lived in Western Europe. Feigin wrote, 'We must put our heads together and find a solution. In the end, a wedding must be made. But with what?'

title_en: Feigin's second appeal to Jacobson
summary_en: Six weeks before the wedding, Feigin wrote again to Jacobson urging him to enlist Rabbi Shalom Dovber Rivkin and launch an appeal to all Tomchei Temimim alumni.
story_body: Feigin explained that European Chasidim could not really help because of the suffering they had endured. 'Finances must come from your country,' he wrote, urging Jacobson to telegram or write to all the Temimim alumni and pleading with him to act swiftly.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz departs Riga for Warsaw wedding
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz left Riga by train for Warsaw, accompanied by his family and the groom, greeted by thousands at the train station.
story_body: Two rows of men stretching five hundred feet stood as an honor guard as the Rebbe entered the station. The crowd danced alongside as the train pulled away. Large crowds also gathered in the stations in Dvinsk and Vilnius to wish the Rebbe well during the journey.

title_en: Royal Wedding of Chaya Mushka and the Ramash in Warsaw
summary_en: The 'royal wedding' of the Rebbe Rayatz's daughter Chaya Mushka to Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson took place at Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim in Warsaw before 5,000 people.
story_body: The Rebbe wore his grandfather's shtreimel publicly for the first time since assuming leadership, symbolizing a new era of Chabad's rebirth in Western Europe. The Rebbe taught a maamar starting at 11:00 p.m. and again at 4:00 a.m. The wedding introduced the relatively unknown Ramash to the broader Jewish community, including Rabbi Meir Shapiro, who afterward told the Rebbe, 'You have taken a son-in-law who is a gaon.'

title_en: Ramash begins his Reshimot diary
summary_en: The Ramash made his first notation in what would become the Reshimot, a detailed private diary recording his interactions with the Rebbe Rayatz.
story_body: The diary included a wealth of chasidic lore, history, and customs, with anecdotes of all the Rebbes back to the Baal Shem Tov. Most of the Reshimot was written in Europe before WWII, with small sections added in Brooklyn in the early 1940s. The notations were discovered in his desk shortly after his passing and published posthumously by Kehot.

title_en: Ramash leads Sukkot farbrengen in Riga
summary_en: While the Rebbe was in the US, the Ramash led a Sukkot farbrengen in Riga that astonished the chasidic community.
story_body: Rabbi Eliyahu Chaim Althaus wrote that the Ramash spoke for hours saying words of Chasidut with teachings from the Sages: 'The critics and cynics have been silenced.' News spread so that on Simchat Torah, a huge crowd gathered, and Althaus reported people leaving the farbrengen saying they had never seen or heard anything like it.

title_en: Mordechai Schwei celebrates wedding in Finland
summary_en: Rabbi Mordechai Schwei, the sole Chasid in remote Finland, wrote to Zelig Slonim describing how he marked Chaya Mushka's wedding.
story_body: Despite his isolation, Schwei wrote, 'I shared in the joy with all the Temimim and the Rebbe.' His letter reflects how Chasidim around the world celebrated the wedding remotely as a moment of collective joy, even in the most distant outposts of the chasidic world.

title_en: Rebbe sends theological letter to Ramash on Chabad's distinctive focus
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz sent his son-in-law a lengthy letter exploring Chabad's distinctive emphasis on intellectual ideas and spiritual growth as opposed to other chasidic groups' focus on miracles.
story_body: The Ramash responded, 'From the depths of my heart, I thank you for this precious gift,' while also writing that he remained 'puzzled' that people still said 'In Chabad, we have no interest in miracles.' The letter was later published in Hatomim, volume 2.

title_en: Wedding of Sheina Schneerson and Mendel Horenstein in Landwarow
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz's youngest daughter Sheina married Rabbi Mendel Horenstein in Landwarow, Poland, with Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski officiating.
story_body: Landwarow was chosen because of visa issues, sitting just over the border from Vilnius. Rabbi Baruch Ber Leibowitz of Kaminetz Yeshivah was also present and had a scholarly discussion with the Ramash. After the wedding, the couple moved to Paris, and a few months later Chaya Mushka and the Ramash joined them there.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz stays in Berlin for medical treatment
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz began a two-month stay in Berlin for medical care, during which the Ramash was at his side as informal secretary.
story_body: Throughout the 1930s, as the Rebbe sought medical care in Berlin, Vienna, Paris, and Marienbad, the Ramash accompanied him. These extended periods together provided extensive opportunities for mentorship, conversation, and assistance with correspondence and other affairs.

title_en: Ramash and Chaya Mushka leave Berlin for Paris
summary_en: As the Nazi threat began to grow, the Ramash and Chaya Mushka left Berlin and after a brief interlude in Riga resettled in Paris.
story_body: In Paris, the Ramash pursued a degree in engineering. He continued attending classes at European universities and remained involved in the Rebbe's affairs from a distance, exchanging hundreds of letters with his father-in-law about Chabad theology, history, and practical matters.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz stays at Vienna sanitorium
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz began a six-month stay at the West End Sanitorium in Perchtoldsdorf on the outskirts of Vienna.
story_body: The Ramash spent these months at the Rebbe's side, providing extended opportunities for mentorship and conversation. The Rebbe entrusted his son-in-law with many private affairs during these stays, and the Ramash functioned at times as the Rebbe's secretary.

title_en: Hatomim magazine founded
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz founded the Hatomim periodical as a platform to promulgate Chabad teachings and reinforce the Tomchei Temimim yeshivah in Poland.
story_body: The magazine featured chasidic teachings, history, and scholarly essays. The Rebbe asked the Ramash, then in Paris, to review articles for the magazine, though few knew the Ramash was assisting with editing. It promoted Tomchei Temimim, then located in Poland, as a premier center of Jewish learning.

title_en: Polish government enacts currency restrictions
summary_en: Poland withdrew from the 'gold block' and instituted currency restrictions, making it problematic to transfer funds in and out of the country.
story_body: The restrictions hampered the Rebbe's ability to manage finances from Poland. In response, the Rebbe entrusted the Ramash in Paris with much of his financial affairs, having him open accounts and maintain records. The Rebbe instructed donors globally to send contributions directly to the Ramash in Paris.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz heads to New York
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz traveled to New York, while the Ramash hesitated to leave Paris to join him.
story_body: Feigin wrote to Jacobson asking him to encourage the Ramash to come to the US, noting his great ability to draw the younger generation closer to Jewish observance. The Ramash resisted, seemingly fearing it would detract from his studies, but Feigin argued he had completed his secular studies and could now dedicate himself totally to Torah.

title_en: Ramash and Chaya Mushka arrive in the United States
summary_en: After a harrowing escape from Paris via Vichy France and Portugal, the Ramash and his wife arrived in the United States.
story_body: The escape followed the German invasion of France a few months earlier. Upon arrival in the US, the Ramash's involvement in the Rebbe's affairs expanded greatly, and he soon took on multiple leadership roles in newly established Chabad institutions.

title_en: Kehot Publication Society founded
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz established Kehot Publication Society, a publishing house for the works of Chasidism and Judaism, appointing the Ramash as its chairman.
story_body: Kehot became the central publishing organ for Chabad-Lubavitch literature. Its founding marked the beginning of the Ramash's expanded public role in the movement, paving the way for him to eventually assume leadership as the seventh Rebbe.

title_en: Machne Israel founded
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz founded Machne Israel, Chabad's social service agency, with the Ramash as executive director.
story_body: Machne Israel was one of three corporations founded by the Rebbe in 1941, all with the Ramash in leadership positions. The trio of new organizations expanded the Ramash's involvement with American Chabad institutions and laid the foundation for the global Chabad outreach network.

title_en: Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch founded
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz founded Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch, Chabad's central education branch, with the Ramash as executive director.
story_body: Merkos took the lead in establishing the first national network of Jewish day schools and eventually began overseeing the global network of Chabad shluchim and institutions. It became one of the most consequential Chabad organizations, transforming American Jewish education.

title_en: Sheina Horenstein killed at Treblinka
summary_en: Sheina Horenstein, the Rebbe Rayatz's youngest daughter, was killed at Treblinka on the second day of Rosh HaShanah 5703.
story_body: With the outbreak of war, Sheina and her husband Rabbi Mendel Horenstein had traveled with their adopted son to Otwock to care for Rabbi Mendel's aging parents. Eventually they were all captured by the Nazis. Their fate was unknown for years until a Treblinka survivor described the details in 1950.

title_en: Rabbi Mendel Horenstein killed at Treblinka
summary_en: Rabbi Mendel Horenstein, son-in-law of the Rebbe Rayatz, was killed at Treblinka on 25 Marcheshvan, almost two months after his wife Sheina.
story_body: His adopted nephew Yaakov Yosef Liss was also killed by the Nazis in 1942. The couple had adopted Yaakov Yosef when his mother (Mendel's sister Sara) died a few days after giving birth to her second child. In 1950 the seventh Rebbe received details of their fate from a Treblinka survivor.

title_en: Ramash describes parental-love teaching to Edelman and Fogelman
summary_en: At 770 Eastern Parkway, the Ramash recounted to yeshivah students Dovid Edelman and Hershel Fogelman a teaching from the Rebbe about loving every Jew completely.
story_body: The Ramash had been chastised by elder Chasidim for warmly welcoming non-observant Jews rather than criticizing them. He asked the Rebbe if he was acting correctly. The Rebbe replied that just as a parent feels deeper love for a child missing a limb, G-d loves every Jew completely, but loves those who are missing observance even more. This philosophy clearly infused the Ramash's later leadership as the seventh Rebbe.

title_en: Kfar Chabad established
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz established Kfar Chabad, the Chabad village in Israel, instructing that its focus should be to reach beyond religious Jews to all Israelis.
story_body: Kfar Chabad became a hub for Chabad activity in the newly founded State of Israel. The Rebbe's directive that it reach all Israelis foreshadowed the broader outreach philosophy that the Ramash would later expand globally as the seventh Rebbe.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz receives US citizenship wearing shtreimel
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz received US citizenship, an occasion on which he wore his grandfather's shtreimel.
story_body: The Rebbe had begun wearing the shtreimel publicly at his daughter Chaya Mushka's 1928 wedding, after a fourteen-year hiatus since the Rashab fled Lubavitch. He continued wearing it on Shabbat, holidays, and other special occasions, including this citizenship ceremony.

title_en: Rabbi Zevin urges Ramash to become Rebbe
summary_en: After the passing of the Rebbe Rayatz, Rabbi Shlomo Yosef Zevin urged the Ramash to accept the mantle of leadership as the seventh Rebbe.
story_body: Zevin told him: 'Thank G-d, a scion has been saved from the family of our Rebbe, who was educated and mentored in the home of the Rebbe Rayatz. You were always hand in hand [with the Rebbe Rayatz], and he never withheld any good [Torah] from you.' Zevin had known the Ramash from Russia, where he was secretary of the Rabbinical Committee.

title_en: Seventh Rebbe's 25th wedding anniversary farbrengen
summary_en: On Shabbat 14 Kislev, the seventh Rebbe held a farbrengen marking his twenty-fifth wedding anniversary, with uncharacteristically personal reflections.
story_body: He noted that 'generally speaking, even regarding a private person, his wedding constitutes an all-encompassing event. For me, however, my wedding day brought me into more general and communal affairs.' He told those gathered that the wedding 'connected me to you, and you to me,' framing his marriage as a bond with the Chasidim.

title_en: Rabbi Shlomo Cunin sent as shliach to California
summary_en: Rabbi Shlomo Cunin was sent by the seventh Rebbe to California, an early and then-controversial example of Chabad shlichut.
story_body: Cunin recalls Chasidim in New York telling him he would not last long on the West Coast and insinuating he was only going because he could not get a job close to home. The concept of shlichut to communities lacking basic religious infrastructure was revolutionary in the 1950s and 1960s, even within Chabad.

title_en: Discovery of the Reshimot
summary_en: The seventh Rebbe's private diary, the Reshimot, was discovered in his desk shortly after his passing.
story_body: The diary, begun in 1928 and containing a wealth of chasidic lore, history, and customs, was later published as Torat Menachem: Reshimat HaYoman by Kehot Publication Society in 2006. It opened a window into the seventh Rebbe's decade-long spiritual dialogue with the Rebbe Rayatz.

title_en: Baal Shem Tov's soul ascends to Mashiach
summary_en: Per his famous letter, the founder of Chasidism's soul ascended on high and encountered the Messiah.
story_body: Rabbi Yisrael Baal Shem Tov wrote to his brother-in-law about a mystical ascent in which he asked the Messiah when he would come. The Messiah replied, 'When your wellsprings will spread to the outside' — a phrase that would later guide the Rebbe Rayatz's vision for spreading chasidic teachings to America.

title_en: First chasidic aliyah led by Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk
summary_en: Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk led the first chasidic immigration to Eretz Yisrael, founding settlements in Tiberias and Safed.
story_body: His protege Rabbi Schneur Zalman, the future founder of Chabad, escorted him until Mogilev-Podolski in southern Ukraine and considered continuing on himself, but his mentor instructed him to remain in Europe to spread chasidic teachings. This aliyah established a chasidic presence in the Holy Land that endured for generations.

title_en: Vilna Gaon issues first cherem against chasidim
summary_en: Rabbi Eliyahu of Vilna issued a ban of excommunication against the chasidic movement.
story_body: The Vilna Gaon, one of the most influential Jewish scholars of the eighteenth century, formally opposed the nascent chasidic movement with a cherem. He issued the ban again in 1781, and after his passing his students orchestrated accusations against Rabbi Schneur Zalman that led to the Chabad founder's imprisonment by the czar.

title_en: Vilna Gaon issues second cherem against chasidim
summary_en: The Vilna Gaon renewed his ban of excommunication against the chasidic movement.
story_body: Four years after the first cherem, the Vilna Gaon again formalized opposition to chasidism. The animosity between chasidim and their opponents shaped Jewish communal politics in Europe and the Holy Land for decades.

title_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman establishes Colel Chabad
summary_en: The Chabad founder created an international fund to support chasidic families settled in the Holy Land.
story_body: After Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk's passing, Rabbi Schneur Zalman established the fund to ensure the continuity of the chasidic community in Eretz Yisrael. Today, Colel Chabad remains the oldest continuously operating charity in Israel and is the country's largest provider of food security.

title_en: Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk passes away
summary_en: The leader of the first chasidic aliyah passed away in the Holy Land.
story_body: His successor, Rabbi Avraham Karlisker, also a student of the Maggid of Mezeritch, differed with Rabbi Schneur Zalman on a variety of issues, leading to disagreements within the Holy Land chasidic community.

title_en: Vilna Gaon students immigrate to Safed and Tiberias
summary_en: Opponents of the chasidic movement, the Perushim, made aliyah to Safed and Tiberias.
story_body: The arrival of the Vilna Gaon's students brought the European divisions between chasidim and their opponents into Eretz Yisrael, intensifying communal tensions in the Holy Land.

title_en: Colel Chabad formally named
summary_en: The fund created by Rabbi Schneur Zalman in 1788 received its formal name, Colel Chabad.
story_body: Initially established to support chasidic families in the Holy Land, the organization formalized its identity in 1817. Successive Chabad Rebbes used it to channel European Jewish support to the growing community in Eretz Yisrael.

title_en: Hebron Chabad synagogue established
summary_en: Rabbi Dov Ber, the second Chabad Rebbe, encouraged his Chasidim to relocate to Hebron, where they established a synagogue still standing today.
story_body: In response to disagreements within the chasidic community in Eretz Yisrael, the Mitteler Rebbe directed his followers to settle in Hebron. The synagogue they founded there in 1823 anchored the growing Chabad community in the patriarchal city.

title_en: Moses Montefiore's first visit to Palestine
summary_en: The prominent British Jewish leader Moses Montefiore made the first of seven trips to the Holy Land.
story_body: Montefiore, a confidant of Queen Victoria, would become one of the most influential nineteenth-century advocates for Jews worldwide. His trips to Palestine, Russia, Romania, Rome, and Morocco shaped Jewish diplomatic history.

title_en: Montefiore barred from Me'arat Hamakhpelah
summary_en: Despite the Turkish sultan's permission, local Muslim leaders blocked Sir Moses Montefiore from entering the Tomb of the Patriarchs.
story_body: Judith Montefiore wrote in her memoir of the 1838 attempt that a 'turbulent throng of Mussulmans' had gathered inside the mosque and a 'raving dervish' raged at the prospect of their entry. The couple decided it would be prudent to retreat without attempting further entrance.

title_en: Slonim family arrives in Hebron
summary_en: Rabbi Yaakov and Rebbetzin Menucha Rochel Slonim, the daughter and son-in-law of the Mitteler Rebbe, immigrated to Hebron.
story_body: Their arrival significantly bolstered the Chabad community in Hebron. Their descendants would play a central role in Hebron Jewish life, including the tragic 1929 massacre, when grandson Eliezer Don Slonim was killed.

title_en: Montefiore meets Czar Nicholas I in St. Petersburg
summary_en: Moses Montefiore traveled to St. Petersburg to urge the czar to improve conditions for Russian Jews.
story_body: Montefiore's intervention with Czar Nicholas I became a model the Rebbe Rayatz later invoked when urging JDC leaders to use their influence on behalf of Soviet Jewry. Montefiore returned to Russia for a second visit in 1876.

title_en: Rabbi Eliyahu Yosef Rivlin settles in Jerusalem
summary_en: Rabbi Rivlin, a Chasid of the Alter Rebbe, settled in Jerusalem and became rabbi of the local Chasidim.
story_body: His arrival helped establish an additional Chabad community in Jerusalem, complementing the Hebron settlement. His great-great-grandson Reuven Rivlin later served as Israel's president.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek synagogue founded in Old City
summary_en: A Chabad synagogue named for the third Rebbe was founded in the Jewish Quarter of the Old City of Jerusalem.
story_body: Land was purchased in 1850 with help from Sir Moses Montefiore, and a building was erected. It became the only synagogue in the Jewish Quarter not destroyed by the Jordanian occupation between 1948 and 1967, and remains a vibrant center on Chabad Street today.

title_en: Prince of Wales granted access to Hebron tomb
summary_en: The Turkish sultan ordered the ban on non-Muslim entry to Me'arat Hamakhpelah lifted for the Prince of Wales.
story_body: The visit was one of a very small number of rare exceptions to the centuries-long ban barring Jews and other non-Muslims from the Tomb of the Patriarchs. Even royal access did not extend to the actual cave beneath the Herodian structure.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek, third Chabad Rebbe, passes away
summary_en: Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn passed away, prompting a split among Chabad streams.
story_body: His passing led to multiple branches of Chabad emerging in Russia, including Kopust. The same division was mirrored within the Chabad community in Jerusalem and shaped Colel Chabad's governance for decades.

title_en: Marquis of Bute visits Me'arat Hamakhpelah
summary_en: The Marquis of Bute was one of the rare non-Muslims granted access to the Tomb of the Patriarchs.
story_body: His visit followed the Prince of Wales's 1862 access. These exceptional admissions were granted only at the insistence of the Turkish sultan and remained extremely rare.

title_en: Crown Prince of Prussia visits Hebron tomb
summary_en: The Crown Prince of Prussia gained access to the Tomb of the Patriarchs.
story_body: His visit was another of the rare exceptions to the Muslim ban on non-Muslim entry. Each such visit typically required direct intervention from the Turkish sultan.

title_en: Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld immigrates to Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: The future leader of the Eidah HaChareidis immigrated to the Holy Land.
story_body: Sonnenfeld, a student of the Ktav Sofer of Pressburg, worked closely with Rabbi Yehuda Leib Diskind, rabbi of Jerusalem's Ashkenazi community. He would later become a central voice opposing Zionist secularization in the city.

title_en: Montefiore's second visit to Russia
summary_en: Moses Montefiore returned to Russia three decades after his first meeting with the czar.
story_body: The visit continued his lifelong diplomatic effort on behalf of Russian Jews. The Rebbe Rayatz would later cite Montefiore's interventions as a model when urging American Jewish leaders to advocate with the Soviet regime.

title_en: Second story added to Jerusalem Chabad synagogue
summary_en: An additional level was constructed atop the Tzemach Tzedek synagogue in the Jewish Quarter.
story_body: A plaque dedicated by the Sassoon family of Mumbai marking the addition remains prominently displayed in the building today.

title_en: Rabbi Shmuel, fourth Chabad Rebbe, passes away
summary_en: Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn, the Rebbe Maharash, passed away in Lubavitch.
story_body: Shortly before his passing, an Alexandria Jew brought his grandson to Rabbi Shmuel along with first fruits, asking for a blessing. Rabbi Shmuel promised that one day the grandson would bring fruit to his own grandson — a blessing fulfilled when that grandson welcomed the Rebbe Rayatz to Alexandria in 1929.

title_en: Sons of Prince of Wales visit Hebron tomb
summary_en: The sons of the Prince of Wales were granted exceptional access to Me'arat Hamakhpelah.
story_body: Their visit followed their father's own admission two decades earlier. Such exceptions to the Muslim ban remained rare and tightly controlled.

title_en: Pittsburgh Platform issued by Reform movement
summary_en: The American Reform movement issued its founding principles, repudiating classical Jewish beliefs.
story_body: The platform questioned the divinity of the Torah and the obligation to observe mitzvot, foregrounding ethical living instead. The Rebbe Rayatz would later challenge this ideology directly in his American visit, arguing that fulfillment of practical mitzvot was the true key to connection with the Divine.

title_en: Yeshivas Rabbeinu Yitzchok Elchonon founded
summary_en: The yeshivah that would later become Yeshiva University was founded on New York's Lower East Side.
story_body: Initially based on the Lower East Side, the institution became Yeshivah College in 1928 and later Yeshivah University. At the time of the Rebbe Rayatz's 1929 visit, it had recently relocated to Washington Heights and was one of only a handful of Jewish schools in New York.

title_en: Eidah HaChareidis-precursor leadership transferred to Sonnenfeld
summary_en: Upon Rabbi Yehuda Leib Diskind's passing, Rabbi Sonnenfeld became head of Jerusalem's Ashkenazi community.
story_body: Sonnenfeld had worked closely with Diskind for years. His ascension positioned him to formalize the Eidah HaChareidis in 1921 and lead opposition to Zionist secularization.

title_en: Shaarei Zedek Hospital founded in Jerusalem
summary_en: Dr. Moshe Wallach founded Jerusalem's Shaarei Zedek Hospital with Shabbat observance and Jewish tradition built into its protocols.
story_body: Wallach, a religious German Jew known for piety and dedication to patients, would later sail home alongside the Rebbe Rayatz from Alexandria in 1929 and nurse the Rebbe back to health after he fell ill upon learning of the Hebron massacre. The hospital remains one of the premier medical centers in Israel.

title_en: Rabbi Avraham Yitzchak Kook becomes rabbi of Jaffa
summary_en: Rabbi Kook moved from Russia to Eretz Yisrael, becoming rabbi of Jaffa.
story_body: Kook, whose mother came from a Chabad family, was known for his scholarship and his efforts to bridge Jews of all backgrounds. He would later be appointed the first chief rabbi by the British Mandate in 1929.

title_en: Chabad purchases Hebron property under Rebbe Rashab
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab oversaw the purchase of a large Hebron property where Chabad opened a yeshivah.
story_body: Rabbi Shlomo Leib Eliazrov assisted the Rashab in the purchase of Beit Romano. The site of the new Hebron neighborhood traces back to this acquisition, which expanded Chabad's institutional presence in the city.

title_en: Henry Morgenthau visits Me'arat Hamakhpelah
summary_en: The Jewish US ambassador to the Turkish Empire was granted exceptional access to the Tomb of the Patriarchs.
story_body: Morgenthau's admission was among the rare instances when the Muslim ban was lifted at the sultan's insistence. Like other dignitaries before him, he was given access only to the Herodian structure, not the cave beneath.

title_en: Yeshivah Torah Vodaath founded in Williamsburg
summary_en: Torah Vodaath was established in Brooklyn's Williamsburg neighborhood.
story_body: At the time of the Rebbe Rayatz's 1929 visit, Torah Vodaath and Yeshivas Rabbeinu Yitzchok Elchonon were the principal yeshivot in New York. Only twelve percent of Brooklyn's Jewish children received any Jewish education in the 1920s.

title_en: Hebrew Theological College founded in Chicago
summary_en: The Hebrew Theological College, also called Beis HaMidrash LaTorah, was founded in Chicago.
story_body: It became a major center of Jewish learning. During the Rebbe Rayatz's 1930 visit to Chicago, its rosh yeshivah Rabbi Nachman Bar was personally challenged by the Rebbe to expand his impact beyond the yeshivah walls.

title_en: Mufti of Jerusalem organizes Balfour-protest riots
summary_en: Mohammed Amin al-Husseini organized Palestine riots to protest the Balfour Declaration.
story_body: Al-Husseini, later appointed mufti of Jerusalem by the British Mandate, would go on to instigate the 1929 Hebron massacre and lead the 1936 Arab Revolt. During World War II he traveled to Berlin, where he met with Hitler and other top German officials and encouraged the Holocaust.

title_en: Colel Chabad Jerusalem board pledges allegiance to Rebbe Rashab
summary_en: In Tevet 5680, Colel Chabad's Jerusalem-based board officially decided to place itself under the direction of the Lubavitcher Rebbe.
story_body: The decision marked a shift from the Kopust branch's sway over the organization back to the main Chabad-Lubavitch line. After the Rashab's passing, the board reaffirmed the pledge to the Rebbe Rayatz, though tensions over governance and finances persisted until the Rayatz visited in 1929.

title_en: Eidah HaChareidis formally established
summary_en: Rabbi Sonnenfeld formalized the traditional Orthodox Chareidi community in Jerusalem.
story_body: The Eidah HaChareidis emerged as a counterweight to Zionist and Reform-influenced communal structures. It continues to exist today as a distinct traditional Orthodox community.

title_en: Agudas Chassidei Chabad founded in the United States
summary_en: A national Chabad organization was founded in the US to coordinate the small but growing community.
story_body: Still in its infancy at the time of the Rebbe Rayatz's 1929 visit, the organization connected with roughly forty Chabad synagogues in New York City and many more across the country. Yehuda Lokshin was its director when the Rebbe wrote to him in January 1929 about plans to visit America.

title_en: JDC creates the Agro-Joint subsidiary
summary_en: The Joint Distribution Committee created a corporation to resettle Soviet Jews on communal farms in cooperation with the Communist regime.
story_body: Under Dr. Joseph Rosen, the program operated for fourteen years, ultimately transforming roughly 200,000 Soviet Jews from urban dwellers to peasants. The Rebbe Rayatz repeatedly questioned the wisdom of the project and pushed for the JDC to instead support home-based industries and religious life.

title_en: JDC begins curtailing funding to the Rebbe's Russian network
summary_en: After supporting the Rebbe's operations on and off, the JDC began winding down its support for his work in Russia.
story_body: The retreat from funding Jewish education and religious life under Soviet conditions deepened the financial crisis facing the Rebbe Rayatz's underground network. It would become the central motivation for his 1929 American journey.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes JDC philanthropists about settlements
summary_en: On 25 Sivan 5685, the Rebbe wrote to the JDC board expressing concerns over the Russian resettlement project.
story_body: This was among the Rebbe's earliest written interventions on the agricultural colonies. He raised concerns about religious services on the farms and the wisdom of forcibly moving Jews to Ukraine, and asked the JDC to support home-based industries instead.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes long letter to Felix Warburg
summary_en: On 27 Iyar 5686, the Rebbe wrote a detailed letter to JDC chair Felix Warburg about the Russian settlements.
story_body: Without expressing direct opposition, the Rebbe raised important questions about religious services and asked the JDC to provide three things: facilities and religious services in the settlements, training in home-based industries for urban Jews, and subsidies for rabbis. Warburg ultimately rejected the religious priorities.

title_en: Felix Warburg visits the Soviet Union
summary_en: The JDC chairman traveled to Russia, met the Rebbe and a delegation of rabbis twice, and toured the Jewish agricultural colonies.
story_body: Warburg was impressed by Communist-staged farm towns named after him, Warburg-4 and Warburg-5, and returned a champion of forced collectivization. He promised the Rebbe help that did not materialize, and his biographer Ron Chernow later described the settlements as 'a bizarre hybrid of Park Avenue charity and Marxist agriculture.'

title_en: Yeshivas Rabbeinu Yitzchok Elchonon becomes Yeshivah College
summary_en: The institution evolved from a yeshivah into Yeshivah College, the precursor to Yeshiva University.
story_body: The transition reflected the slow emergence of American Jewish higher learning. At the time, serious Jewish scholarship still required travel to Poland, Lithuania, or Eretz Yisrael.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes letter on Colel Chabad reforms
summary_en: On 13 Elul 5688, the Rebbe wrote that he viewed Colel Chabad as 'a sacred obligation' but required reform of its governance and finances.
story_body: The Rebbe made his acceptance of Colel Chabad's leadership conditional on a proper understanding of its finances. The reforms he requested were ultimately codified in a new charter in 1933.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes Rabbi Aharon Milovski about JDC efforts
summary_en: The Rebbe detailed his efforts to secure JDC funding for Russian Jewish religious life in a letter to Rabbi Milovski.
story_body: The letter laid out the funding crisis facing Chabad's underground network in Russia. It was part of the broader correspondence that culminated in the Rebbe's decision to travel to the United States.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes Rabbi Chaim Ozer about American trip
summary_en: On 4 Cheshvan 5689, the Rebbe wrote to Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski, who along with the Chafetz Chaim encouraged the American journey.
story_body: Rabbi Chaim Ozer, who corresponded regularly with the Rebbe, had discussed the matter with the Chafetz Chaim in Radin. Their joint encouragement helped solidify the Rebbe's decision to travel to America.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes Yehuda Lokshin about US visit plans
summary_en: On 20 Shevat 5689, the Rebbe sent the first written indication of his plans to travel to America to Chabad's New York director.
story_body: The Rebbe wrote that the JDC's budget cuts were causing him great anguish and that he had consulted with Rabbi Chaim Ozer and the Chafetz Chaim, who encouraged him to go. The chasidic community was informed of the plan a few months later.

title_en: Feigin writes Jacobson urging US Chabad to prepare for Rebbe's visit
summary_en: On 26 Shevat 5689, Rabbi Yechezkel Feigin asked Yisrael Jacobson to unite the US Chabad community in preparation for the Rebbe's arrival.
story_body: Feigin described the Rebbe's financial difficulties and health challenges, and urged Jacobson to set aside internal differences. 'Leave behind the differences of opinion between you,' he wrote, 'make an effort to come together.'

title_en: Rabbi Kook appointed first chief rabbi by British Mandate
summary_en: With the establishment of the Chief Rabbinate, Rabbi Kook assumed the position of chief rabbi.
story_body: His appointment formalized his stature as the leading Religious-Zionist rabbinic voice in Palestine. The Rebbe Rayatz met with him three times during his 1929 visit, more than with any other figure.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes Glizenstein about decision to visit Holy Land
summary_en: On 1 Tamuz 5689, the Rebbe wrote of his decision to visit the Holy Land in place of his customary visits to ancestral graves in Russia.
story_body: Since he could no longer travel to his fathers' graves in Russia, the Rebbe explained, he had decided to visit Eretz Yisrael to pray at the sacred sites. The letter framed the trip's spiritual rationale alongside its political and fundraising goals.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes Sonnenfeld about Eretz Yisrael visit
summary_en: On 2 Tamuz 5689, the Rebbe wrote to Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld seeking help with visa arrangements.
story_body: The Rebbe emphasized to the Eidah HaChareidis leader that the purpose of the trip was personal — 'to visit the holy sites' — and not political. He also wrote to Rabbi Kook with the same request, signaling his intent to avoid the Yishuv's political fault lines.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes Slonim and Eliazrov about visit
summary_en: On 3 Tamuz 5689, the Rebbe wrote to Chabad leaders in Eretz Yisrael informing them of his impending arrival.
story_body: The Rebbe hoped Chasidim would not overburden him given his delicate health, and stated that every possible effort would be made to avoid political entanglements. 'My visit is of a private nature,' he wrote.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz departs Riga for journey to Eretz Yisrael and the US
summary_en: On 23 Tamuz 5689, the Rebbe left Riga with his son-in-law the Rashag for a year-long overseas voyage.
story_body: The trip came just months after the Rebbe recovered from a heart attack. His daughter Chaya Mushka and her husband, the Ramash, joined them in Berlin for the train journey through Germany, Czechoslovakia, and Austria to the Italian port of Trieste.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz boards ship at Trieste
summary_en: On 25 Tamuz 5689, the Rebbe boarded a ship at Trieste bound for Alexandria, Egypt.
story_body: His daughter Chaya Mushka and son-in-law the Ramash accompanied him as far as the southern Italian port of Brindisi, where they returned to Berlin. The Rashag continued with the Rebbe on the voyage.

title_en: Ship stops at Brindisi en route to Alexandria
summary_en: On 27 Tamuz 5689, the Ramash and his wife disembarked at Brindisi to return to Berlin.
story_body: The Rashag continued with the Rebbe Rayatz on the voyage to Alexandria, where they were welcomed by Jewish community leaders and a delegation of Chabad rabbis from Jerusalem.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in Jerusalem
summary_en: After a nine-day journey from Riga, the Rebbe arrived at Jerusalem's train station to a crowd of five thousand.
story_body: More than ten percent of Jerusalem's Jewish population turned out to welcome him. That same afternoon he made his way through the Old City on foot to the Western Wall, where 1,500 gathered and hundreds more watched from rooftops. 'I cried hot tears,' he wrote his family. 'Standing next to the Wall of the Beit HaMikdash, everything changes.'

title_en: Anti-Kook flyers distributed at Rebbe Rayatz's Jerusalem arrival
summary_en: At the train station, flyers protesting the Rebbe's planned meeting with Rabbi Kook were distributed, sparking a brief fight.
story_body: The flyers, signed deceptively as 'Chabad Chasidim of Jerusalem,' attacked Rabbi Kook in disparaging terms. A scuffle broke out, broken up by the British police. The Rashag made a major diplomatic effort to mitigate the damage and finalize the meeting with Rabbi Kook.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz enters Me'arat Hamakhpelah in Hebron
summary_en: The Rebbe became the only known Jewish rabbinic leader in centuries to enter the Tomb of the Patriarchs.
story_body: Eliezer Don Slonim, whose unique relationship with local Arab leaders made the visit possible, escorted the Rebbe with six rabbis. The anti-Semitic mufti of Jerusalem telegrammed local authorities demanding the visit be blocked, but his message arrived after the Rebbe had finished. The Rebbe also dispensed charity to the local Arab poor as he left.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz departs Eretz Yisrael for the United States
summary_en: After a two-week visit, the Rebbe left the Holy Land via Egypt en route to America.
story_body: Fifteen busloads of Chasidim escorted the Rebbe from his Tel Aviv hotel to the Lod train station. 'The Rebbe was very emotional,' wrote Rabbi Shimon Glitzenstein, 'and gave his blessing to each and every person.' The Rebbe distributed a printed maamar so he could depart by sharing words of Torah.

title_en: Hebron massacre
summary_en: Arab mobs incited by Jerusalem's mufti murdered sixty-four Jewish men, women, and children in Hebron.
story_body: Just days after the Rebbe Rayatz's visit, riots erupted across Palestine using Jewish prayer at the Western Wall as a pretext. Many of those killed in Hebron were Chabad Chasidim, including the American yeshivah student David Shainberg, who had been deeply impressed by the Rebbe just days earlier.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in New York Harbor
summary_en: Hundreds of Chasidim and well-wishers greeted the Rebbe as he disembarked, escorted by New York police.
story_body: His ten-month sojourn in the US would take him from Boston to St. Louis, with most of his time spent in the Crown Heights and Brownsville sections of Brooklyn and three months in Chicago. The visit would also set the stage for his eventual relocation to America in 1940.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes Rabbi Kook from his voyage
summary_en: On 21 Elul 5689, the Rebbe wrote that he had become sick from anguish after hearing of the Hebron massacre.
story_body: Dr. Moshe Wallach, on the same ship, nurtured the Rebbe back to health. The Rebbe praised Wallach in laudatory terms as 'a wise man with fear of Heaven.'

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz delivers Rosh Hashanah maamar in Brownsville
summary_en: For the High Holidays, the Rebbe attended a large Brownsville synagogue where he prayed at great length and recited a maamar.
story_body: Years later Yehoshua Greenberg recalled that the shul was packed, with many gathered outdoors. 'The Rebbe's voice was booming,' he said, 'and even those outside heard him.' The maamar 'Zeh HaYom Techilat Maasekha' was later published.

title_en: Hyman issues confidential JDC memorandum on the Rebbe
summary_en: JDC director Joseph Hyman prepared a confidential memo for Dr. Cyrus Adler in advance of his meeting with the Rebbe.
story_body: Hyman raised concerns about transferring funds to Russia and asserted the JDC could help 'on the condition that there be no publicity and no noise. No brass bands.' He noted the Rebbe had created a reliable mechanism to secretly transfer funds and referred to him as 'our friend' without using his name.

title_en: Adler-Rebbe Rayatz meeting on JDC support
summary_en: Just after Rosh Hashanah, the Rebbe and Dr. Cyrus Adler met to discuss JDC support for Russian Jewish religious life.
story_body: Adler, a traditional Jew educated in Orthodox schools, was sympathetic to the Rebbe's mission. In his internal JDC memo, Adler noted the difficulties of Russian Jewish life and was open to legally transferring funds. At a second meeting a month later, he assured the Rebbe the JDC would help significantly and secretly — a commitment that was ultimately not honored.

title_en: Simchat Torah celebration in Crown Heights
summary_en: A few thousand people joined the Rebbe for a forty-eight-hour holiday celebration in Brooklyn.
story_body: Reform Rabbi Stephen S. Wise visited the Rebbe privately during the day, later telling his Manhattan students, 'It is worthwhile for you to visit the chakham, the wise leader of the Jewish people, in Brooklyn.' The celebration continued past sunset with editors, reform rabbis, yeshivah alumni, and Chasidim joining a long farbrengen and series of talks outlining a vision for American Jewry.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in Philadelphia
summary_en: The Rebbe began a month-long stay in Philadelphia, where he was welcomed by crowds of thousands.
story_body: During the visit, the Rebbe was honored at Independence Hall with an invitation to sit in George Washington's chair, calling the building 'the cradle of American democracy.' Local philanthropists Nathan and Jennie Faggen hosted a major fundraising dinner that raised over fifteen thousand dollars despite the recent stock market crash.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in Baltimore
summary_en: The Rebbe began a three-week visit to Baltimore, welcomed by a crowd of three thousand.
story_body: During the visit, the Rebbe was presented with the key to the city by the mayor, met with Maryland Governor Albert Richie, and delivered a maamar to roughly 1,500 people challenging the ethics-only theology of liberal Judaism. 'The key to connecting with the Divine,' he taught, 'is through fulfilling the commandments.'

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz meets Justice Louis Brandeis
summary_en: In late January, the Rebbe asked the Supreme Court justice to spearhead a coalition of major Jewish groups to help Soviet Jews.
story_body: Rabbi Kook had given the Rebbe a letter of recommendation. The Rebbe proposed an alliance with the JDC coordinating colonies while others facilitated emigration and supported religious life, with Brandeis as chair. 'Rabbi Schneersohn impressed me so much,' Brandeis later wrote, but he limited himself to behind-the-scenes work, and the broader coalition floundered.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in Chicago
summary_en: A boisterous crowd of fifteen thousand welcomed the Rebbe at LaSalle Street Station for a three-month stay.
story_body: It took police half an hour to make a path for the Rebbe to exit the station. During the Chicago visit, the Rebbe challenged the rosh yeshivah of Hebrew Theological College, Rabbi Nachman Bar, to expand his impact beyond the yeshivah by teaching weekly parashah classes to ordinary Jews — a class Rabbi Bar would teach for the next sixteen years.

title_en: Minsk rabbis arrested by Soviet secret police
summary_en: A group of rabbis was arrested in Minsk and accused of being a counter-revolutionary organization linked to the Rebbe Rayatz.
story_body: The GPU charged Rabbi Pevsner with receiving instructions from the Rebbe in the US about organizing illegal rabbinical seminaries and Hebrew schools. The arrests emboldened JDC leaders, led by Warburg, who opposed funding the Rebbe's activities — they refused further support, fearing association with him might damage their Russian standing.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes Rabbi Rothstein about US indifference
summary_en: On 28 Shevat 5690, the Rebbe described the cold attitude toward Russian Jewry he encountered in America.
story_body: The Rebbe wrote that the JDC, the Agudas Harabonim, and public opinion in the US were all indifferent to Russian Jews' plight. After months in America, however, he sensed a slight shift: 'The public is waking up slightly and is beginning to feel that something must be done.'

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes Rabbi Rabinowitz of disappointment in JDC
summary_en: On 2 Adar 5690, the Rebbe expressed great disappointment over the JDC's repeated broken promises.
story_body: 'I trusted naively the words of Dr. Rosen in Riga that the JDC would help,' the Rebbe wrote. The Wall Street crash had hurt fundraising, but he remained undeterred: 'We must break down the wall of indifference. The condition of Russian Jewry is very grave.'

title_en: Brandeis writes Israel Thurman about Rebbe's coalition proposal
summary_en: Justice Brandeis described the Rebbe's coalition idea and his admiration for him in a letter to Israel Thurman.
story_body: 'Rabbi Schneersohn impressed me so much,' Brandeis wrote. David Bressler subsequently attempted to create a joint initiative of the American Jewish Committee, the American Jewish Congress, and the JDC, but the proposal floundered without Brandeis taking a public leadership role.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in Detroit
summary_en: More than ten thousand thronged Michigan Central Station to welcome the Rebbe for a week-long visit.
story_body: A police escort conducted the Rebbe to his car, and a procession of more than ten thousand escorted him to Detroit's Emanuel Synagogue. During the visit the Rebbe gave individual audiences and made an unannounced visit to a local Chabad synagogue, where he addressed the Depression and urged congregants not to despair.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in St. Louis
summary_en: The Rebbe began a ten-day visit to St. Louis, the furthest western city of his American tour.
story_body: The Jewish Record reported the crowd was unprecedented in size: 'Such a large crowd consisting of thousands of men, women, and children has never been witnessed at any reception accorded to a Jewish leader visiting our city.' During the visit local women publicly pressed the Rebbe for help building a new mikveh, which he championed.

title_en: St. Louis mikveh fundraising dinner
summary_en: Plans for a new St. Louis mikveh were unveiled at a fundraising dinner held at Congregation B'nai Amoona.
story_body: Each attendee received a card with a picture of the Rebbe and a coin he had given for supporters of the mikveh. The Rebbe encouraged the local committee, gave coins to distribute, and remained in contact with the women after returning to Europe.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz meets President Herbert Hoover at the White House
summary_en: The Rebbe was received by the US president, accompanied by Rabbis Moshe Kramer, Chaim Fogelman, and Asher Rabinowitz.
story_body: The visit was arranged at the last minute. The Rebbe used it to express appreciation for the freedoms granted American Jews and for the US government's assistance to Jews living overseas. The Rashag also thanked the president for his support of Jews in Eretz Yisrael.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz departs the United States
summary_en: On 20 Tamuz 5690, the Rebbe sailed for Europe, leaving a crowd at the pier with a new vision for American Jewry.
story_body: He proclaimed it was time for American Jews to redefine their role: 'Until this point, you were in the role of givers, supporting Torah institutions in Europe. But now you also have to become takers — adapt the approach of disseminating Jewish learning and strengthening Judaism, and institute it in America. Make America a place of Torah.'

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz's ship docks in Bremen
summary_en: On 27 Tamuz 5690, the Rebbe arrived in Bremen, Germany after the transatlantic voyage.
story_body: He proceeded to Berlin with his daughter Chaya Mushka and son-in-law the Ramash, then spent three weeks recuperating at the spa town of Marienbad on doctors' orders before continuing home to Riga.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz returns to Riga
summary_en: After thirteen months abroad, the Rebbe arrived home to a packed train station of well-wishers.
story_body: As soon as the train pulled in, loud 'Baruch haba' calls reverberated through the air. Police created a corridor through the dense crowd to allow the Rebbe's entourage to exit. Chasidim from nearby Poland and Lithuania later flocked to Riga to join him for the High Holidays.

title_en: Soviet famine of 1931–33 begins
summary_en: Severe famine engulfed the Soviet Union, prompted by unsuccessful farm collectivization.
story_body: Despite the famine's severity, JDC chair Felix Warburg dismissed the Rebbe's appeal to send matzah to Russian Jews in 1932, insisting they had access to flour. His stance reflected misconceptions formed during his staged 1927 visit to the Jewish farm colonies.

title_en: Adler writes Hyman protesting JDC silence on Russian Judaism
summary_en: Dr. Cyrus Adler urged the JDC not to remain silent as Jewish religious life was destroyed in Russia.
story_body: 'I am not willing to take the attitude that every vestige of Judaism shall be destroyed in Russia with our silence, which means assent,' Adler wrote. He also signed a personal letter of support to the Rebbe on Dropsie College stationery, asking Hyman to send it if the JDC did not object.

title_en: Warburg writes Hyman rejecting JDC support for Russian Judaism
summary_en: JDC chairman Felix Warburg dismissed efforts to bolster Jewish religious life in Russia as 'stupidity' and 'a waste of time.'
story_body: Warburg also rejected the Rebbe's matzah campaign and expressed personal disdain, writing 'I have no confidence in Schneersohn.' His Reform commitments shaped his view that Jewish observance was peripheral and that integrating Jews into Soviet society was the priority.

title_en: New Colel Chabad charter formalized
summary_en: The governance and financial reforms the Rebbe Rayatz had requested were codified in a new Colel Chabad charter.
story_body: Among the changes: procedures to ensure monies received from overseas were properly recorded, and financial statements submitted to the board. Rabbi Shlomo Leib Eliazrov, appointed as chairman during the Rebbe's 1929 Jerusalem visit, oversaw the new structure.

title_en: Gerrer Rebbe attempts to visit Me'arat Hamakhpelah
summary_en: Rabbi Avraham Mordechai Alter, the Gerrer Rebbe, attempted to visit the Tomb of the Patriarchs but was blocked.
story_body: Crowds of Muslims blocked his access, continuing the centuries-old ban broken only briefly by the Rebbe Rayatz in 1929. The Gerrer Rebbe's attempted visit underscored how exceptional that earlier admission had been.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz considers second Eretz Yisrael visit
summary_en: The Rebbe considered returning to Eretz Yisrael to pray at the graves of the righteous, but the plan did not come to fruition.
story_body: He would remain the only Lubavitcher Rebbe to actually visit Eretz Yisrael. The second trip he contemplated would have continued his tradition of seeking divine blessing at the kivrei tzaddikim, especially in preparation for the High Holidays.

title_en: Arab Revolt against the British Mandate
summary_en: Jerusalem's mufti Mohammed Amin al-Husseini led a major Arab revolt against the British Mandate.
story_body: The revolt was one in a sequence of violent campaigns al-Husseini orchestrated, including the 1920 Balfour-protest riots and the 1929 Hebron massacre. He would later travel to Berlin during World War II to encourage the Holocaust.

title_en: JDC begins winding down Agro-Joint
summary_en: With the farming communities believed to have gained economic stability, the JDC began closing the Agro-Joint program.
story_body: Leaders did not anticipate the wave of Stalinist terror that would follow. Within a year, secret police would arrest close to two hundred Agro-Joint workers as members of a 'foreign organization,' bringing a tragic end to the JDC-Soviet partnership.

title_en: Stalin's purges target JDC Agro-Joint workers
summary_en: Soviet secret police arrested close to two hundred JDC Agro-Joint workers as 'foreign agents.'
story_body: Many were shot, others died in prison or remained jailed for long periods. Among those targeted were forty-one German physicians who had come to serve the settlements — seventeen were shot or died in Soviet camps. JDC director Rosen protested unsuccessfully. The JDC remained publicly silent about the catastrophe, continuing instead to paint a positive picture of Soviet life.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz sends Rabbi Shmuel Levitin to the United States
summary_en: The Rebbe dispatched the prominent scholar and devoted Chasid Rabbi Shmuel Levitin to inspire the American community.
story_body: Levitin was unable to return to Europe due to the outbreak of war and remained in the US, where he played a key leadership role in the US Chabad community until his passing in 1974. He was part of a wider mission of Rebbe-sent emissaries who acted as a living bridge between the Rebbe in Europe and his followers in America.

title_en: Hyman writes JDC assessment for American Jewish Yearbook
summary_en: JDC director Joseph Hyman published a glowing assessment of Agro-Joint's accomplishments without disclosing the Stalinist purges.
story_body: 'In less than a decade and a half,' Hyman wrote, 'the work of the Agro-Joint helped transform Russian Jewry from a downtrodden, almost helpless ghetto population into self-reliant and productive workers.' The piece did not reveal that close to two hundred staff had been killed, imprisoned, or deported and that all JDC assets in Russia had been seized.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz relocates to the United States
summary_en: The Rebbe permanently moved to America, settling in Crown Heights, Brooklyn.
story_body: His 1929 visit had set the stage for the relocation. He chose Crown Heights, which had hosted him a decade earlier, as his new center. The relocation would shape the future trajectory of Chabad and global Jewish life.

title_en: Soviet Union takes over Latvia
summary_en: Russian forces took over Latvia, seizing much of the Rebbe Rayatz's correspondence in Riga.
story_body: The Rebbe's letters to his wife from his 1929–30 voyage, primarily in Yiddish, were among the materials captured. The papers were eventually transferred to the Russian National Library.

title_en: Rabbi Itche der Masmid Gurewicz burned alive in Kherson
summary_en: The renowned Chabad emissary and scholar Rabbi Itche Gurewicz was murdered by the Nazis in the synagogue of Kherson, Ukraine.
story_body: Gurewicz had served as an emissary of both the Rebbe Rashab and the Rebbe Rayatz, and was renowned for his commitment to learning and scholarship. His martyrdom in November 1941 stands among the many tragedies of the Holocaust that claimed devoted Chasidim.

title_en: State of Israel formally declared
summary_en: The land formerly known as British Mandate Palestine became the State of Israel upon its declaration of independence.
story_body: The seventh Rebbe later asserted that the historical name Eretz Yisrael would be more appropriate. The Jordanian occupation of the Old City of Jerusalem began the same year and would last until 1967.

title_en: Six-Day War and liberation of Jerusalem's Old City
summary_en: Israel liberated Jerusalem's Old City, ending the Jordanian occupation.
story_body: After the war, the area in front of the Western Wall was cleared, creating the broad plaza of today. The first Jew to return to live within the walls of the Old City was Moshe Zvi Segal, who took up residence in the heavily damaged Tzemach Tzedek Shul that had survived the Jordanian occupation.

title_en: Agudas Chassidei Chabad of Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia founded in Riga
summary_en: European Chasidim convened in Riga after Rosh HaShanah 1930 to formally establish Agudas Chassidei Chabad of Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia.
story_body: Fearing the Rebbe Rayatz might relocate to the US, Chasidim who had flocked to Riga for the High Holidays met Saturday evening at the Rashag's home. The new organization aimed to unite the Chabad community, reinforce study of chasidic philosophy, and build a financial foundation enabling the Rebbe to relocate to Warsaw. They sent a letter to the Rebbe urging him to settle in Warsaw rather than America.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz declines move to America, decides to remain in Europe
summary_en: In a letter dated 18 Cheshvan 5691, the Rebbe Rayatz informed US Chasidim he would remain in Europe due to spiritual needs and his health.
story_body: After his US visit had raised hopes of relocation, the Rebbe wrote his American Chasidim explaining that European communal duties, the yeshivas, and weakness of health made a move premature. Quoting the talmudic principle of not demolishing one synagogue before building another, he implied that leaving Europe would weaken Chabad's work there. He left the door open to a future move with proper preparation.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz visits Warsaw to review Tomchei Temimim yeshivah
summary_en: On 9 Tamuz 5691, the Rebbe traveled to Warsaw for a deep internal review of Chabad's flagship yeshivah.
story_body: News of the visit electrified students in Warsaw, Vilnius, and Lodz. Thousands of Warsaw Jews welcomed the Rebbe at the yeshivah gates before Shabbat. He delivered maamarim, led a farbrengen marking his prison release, and held private yechidut sessions with each student over two days.

title_en: Yochanan Gordon immigrates to America on Rebbe's promise
summary_en: Yochanan Gordon immigrated to the US at Chanukah 5692 after the Rebbe promised his children would remain religious and study in his yeshivas.
story_body: Gordon had resisted joining his three brothers in America, fearing his children would abandon observance as theirs had. The Rebbe assured him the children would remain religious Jews and learn in his yeshivas. The pledge was fulfilled in 1940 when Gordon's son Shalom Ber became one of the first students at the Rebbe's Brooklyn yeshivah.

title_en: Riga yeshivah opens then closes within months
summary_en: The Riga Tomchei Temimim yeshivah, opened by Latvian Chasidim in 1932 to keep the Rebbe nearby, closed by 10 Marcheshvan 5693.
story_body: Following the success of the Warsaw visit, Riga Chasidim mobilized to establish their own yeshivah hoping it would anchor the Rebbe in Latvia. Students came from chasidic backgrounds via Lithuanian yeshivas, but the effort was short-lived. The Evening Post reported its closure in November, and Feigin later wrote that students were unable to secure military service deferments.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz enters Berlin clinic for medical treatment
summary_en: In January 1933 the Rebbe spent two months in a Berlin clinic seeking diagnosis for his deteriorating speech and weakness.
story_body: After his return from America the Rebbe's speech had slowly changed. Riga doctors urged him to Berlin's superior medical resources. The renowned Professor Leve and other experts could not identify the illness but recommended ongoing medical supervision. His son-in-law Menachem Mendel visited daily.

title_en: Reb Itche der Masmid arrives in New York as Rebbe's emissary
summary_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Horowitz, the first of the Rebbe's American emissaries, arrived in New York a few weeks before the High Holidays of 1933.
story_body: Celebrated for his diligence and piety, Reb Itche spent two years in the US teaching Chasidism and raising funds for the Rebbe's European work. The New York Chabad community borrowed money to gather $5,000 for his mission. He visited Boston and other cities, deeply impressing all who met him; the Rebbe later wanted to send him again but could not secure a visa.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz moves to Warsaw
summary_en: In September 1933, after securing Latvian citizenship, the Rebbe completed his relocation from Riga to Warsaw.
story_body: The Rebbe had delayed the move until obtaining a Latvian passport, which would later prove lifesaving during the Nazi invasion. He spent the summer at Marienbad, holidays at Otwock, and then settled in Warsaw to be near the flagship Tomchei Temimim yeshivah. Feigin wrote that the Rebbe "returned to his old self," delivering long maamarim again.

title_en: US recognizes Soviet Union; Rebbe's religious-freedom campaign fails
summary_en: The Rebbe launched a global campaign pressuring the US to condition Soviet recognition on religious freedom, but the Roosevelt administration declined.
story_body: Russian Foreign Minister Maxim Litvinov traveled to Washington to negotiate diplomatic recognition. The Rebbe drafted seven demands and mobilized leaders including Chaim Ozer Grodzinski, Nahum Sokolow, Rabbi Eliezer Silver, and US Senators Borah and King. The US declined to make recognition contingent on Jewish religious freedom, securing only a concession for visiting American citizens.

title_en: Rebbe diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in Vienna
summary_en: In November 1934 doctors in Vienna identified the Rebbe's mysterious illness as multiple sclerosis after nearly two years of uncertainty.
story_body: The Ramash accompanied the Rebbe to Vienna where experts finally diagnosed the autoimmune disease, though they had no cure. Conflicting advice created confusion until they met Dr. Max Gerson, a German-Jewish refugee whose holistic dietary approach appealed to the Rebbe. The Rebbe moved into Gerson's Westend Sanatorium in Purkersdorf in December 1934.

title_en: Rebbe writes long Yiddish history of early Chasidism
summary_en: From the Purkersdorf sanatorium the Rebbe wrote a 100+ page Yiddish letter to his daughter Chaya Mushka on the early history of Chasidism.
story_body: Known as Der Longa Brief, the letter offered a graphic portrait of shtetl spiritual life and the figures who spread chasidic teachings. It was composed while the Rebbe was under Dr. Gerson's care and is filled with rich prose about the genesis of the chasidic movement.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz relocates from Warsaw to Otwock
summary_en: Two years after moving to Warsaw the Rebbe relocated to nearby Otwock, a resort town better suited to his health.
story_body: Otwock's pine-scented air and quieter atmosphere benefited the ailing Rebbe, and the town boasted many tzaddikim and a chasidic ambiance. The Tomchei Temimim yeshivah soon followed the Rebbe there, and Otwock became one of Europe's great centers of Jewish learning until the Nazi invasion in 1939.

title_en: Latvian police raid four Chasidim running Russia aid operation
summary_en: In November 1935 Latvian police simultaneously raided the homes of four Russian Chasidim running the Rebbe's covert aid operation to Soviet Jews.
story_body: Moshe and Shmaryahu Gurary, Dovber Chaskind, and Yosef Rosenblum had been working full-time from Riga shipping food packages and transferring funds to Jews in Russia. All four were jailed and released on bail. Forced to choose between prison or expulsion, the Rebbe advised emigration to British Mandate Palestine, where they continued the operation from Tel Aviv.

title_en: Rebbe convenes senior students on Polish yeshivah challenges
summary_en: In 1936 the Rebbe gathered senior Tomchei Temimim students privately, urging them to deepen their classmates' connection to chasidic teachings.
story_body: Some students wanted to expand Talmud study and minimize chasidic philosophy, concerning the Rebbe who wished the Polish yeshivah to mirror the original Lubavitch model. He asked seniors to win over peers to the integration of nigleh and nistar. He confided his personal anguish: "In Russia I experienced self-sacrifice. Now I am experiencing it again with the move from Riga to Poland."

title_en: Rabbi Mordechai Cheifetz dispatched to US as Rebbe's emissary
summary_en: In 1938 the Rebbe sent Rabbi Mordechai Cheifetz to the US, where his farbrengens drew yeshivah students including Avraham Hecht.
story_body: Cheifetz led chasidic gatherings lasting almost till dawn at New York yeshivas such as Torah Vodaath. Avraham Hecht recalled, "He could melt a stone. He melted me." Cheifetz inspired Hecht and five friends to travel to Otwock to study. Returning to Poland, Cheifetz spent ten days with the ailing Rebbe at Shavuot, reporting on each US Chasid by name.

title_en: American students Berel Levy and Hecht enroll in Otwock yeshivah
summary_en: In 1938 Berel Levy, Avraham Barnetsky, and newly married Shlomo Zalman Hecht enrolled at the Otwock yeshivah, the first Americans there.
story_body: The Rebbe worried Americans accustomed to comfort would struggle with Otwock's austere conditions, but Levy wrote home that they felt little strangeness. Levy described hundreds of students from across Europe and hundreds of Chasidim arriving for yechidut. The Rebbe took personal interest, advising Levy on his English reading habits and suggesting he read New York Times briefs.

title_en: Rabbi Shmuel Levitin arrives in US as Rebbe's emissary
summary_en: In 1939 Rabbi Shmuel Levitin arrived in the US just before the High Holidays as the Rebbe's emissary; the war prevented his return.
story_body: Levitin, born in 1883, had been imprisoned by the Soviets for religious activities in Georgia before escaping Russia in 1937. He visited communities across America until war broke out. His wife was trapped in Europe and killed by the Nazis. Levitin emerged as a chasidic elder playing a major role in Chabad's American development.

title_en: Tomchei Temimim relocates to Otwock; network reaches 1,440 students
summary_en: On the eve of the war the flagship Tomchei Temimim yeshivah relocated from Warsaw to Otwock with a network of ten branches and 1,440 students.
story_body: From a single Warsaw branch with modest enrollment in 1930, the yeshivah grew into an educational empire spanning Poland and Lithuania. Otwock held 450 students, Warsaw 250, and Lodz 150, with the rest distributed among other branches. Many branches also spawned Chabad chadarim. The relocation forced by the war later led to new branches in Japan, China, and elsewhere.

title_en: Rabbi Zelig Slonim sent to Australia as Rebbe's emissary
summary_en: In 1939 the Rebbe dispatched Rabbi Zelig Slonim on his final long mission, traveling Australia and New Zealand.
story_body: Slonim had previously served as the Rebbe's emissary in England, Scandinavia, and South Africa. The Sydney Jewish News announced his arrival as a distinguished scholar endorsed by the chief rabbis of Palestine, the UK, and South Africa. He worked on projects including building a mikveh in Brisbane before departing Perth in March 1940 on a dangerous journey back to Eretz Yisrael.

title_en: Rabbi Yosef Goldstein opens yeshivah in Chmielnik
summary_en: At a 1931 Riga farbrengen the Rebbe charged newly married Yosef Goldstein to open a yeshivah in Chmielnik in southern Poland.
story_body: Goldstein, twenty-four, was startled when the Rebbe placed a hand on his shoulder and assigned him the mission. With friends including Rabbi Mottel Bryski, he founded a yeshivah that grew to over seventy students and spawned an elementary program. Chaim Meir Bukiet enrolled there at age eleven, transferring later to Warsaw and Otwock.

title_en: Rebbe dispatches Zalman Gurary to open yeshivah in Volhynia
summary_en: In 1931 the Rebbe sent the nineteen-year-old Rabbi Zalman Gurary to Volhynia to strengthen Torah study and open a yeshivah.
story_body: Locals laughed at Gurary, telling him Novardok had already failed there. The Rebbe had written ahead introducing his "outstanding student" to local Chasidim and synagogues. Gurary persevered, overcoming initial skepticism by emphasizing the goal of educating local students. The success reflected the Rebbe's broader strategy of empowering students as spiritual entrepreneurs.

title_en: Yevesektzia dismantled; Soviet state takes over anti-religious campaign
summary_en: In 1930 the Soviet government dismantled the Yevesektzia, just as the Rebbe Rashab had foreseen, and the state itself took over religious suppression.
story_body: Until 1930 the Rebbe and the Committee of Rabbis had often played government officials against Yevesektzia zealots. With its closure, government restraint ended and persecution became state policy. Stalin's later purges devoured Yevesektzia leaders themselves: Dimenstein was killed in 1938, Litvakov executed in 1937, and Frumkin died in a Kazakhstan prison camp after her 1938 arrest.

title_en: Leningrad rabbis arrested including Shimon Lazaroff
summary_en: In 1930 Soviet authorities arrested eleven Leningrad rabbis including community head Rabbi Shimon Lazaroff for running underground religious institutions.
story_body: The indictment named Lazaroff as head of the religious association Tzemach Tzedek, accusing him of organizing unlawful yeshivas and chadarim funded by foreign capitalists. Sentenced to ten years, he died in a prison camp in 1933. Despite arrests the underground system showed remarkable resilience, with yeshivas closing in one town and reopening in another.

title_en: Rebbe launches food-package operation to Soviet Jews
summary_en: In a January 1931 letter to Peter Wiernik, the Rebbe outlined a covert plan to send food and clothing packages to Soviet Jews as if from relatives.
story_body: Observant Jews who would not work on Shabbat were denied ration cards, and the Soviet famine of 1932-33 deepened the crisis. The Rebbe organized a global network of "relatives" sending packages from Europe, the US, and beyond. The Rashag coordinated, contacting Jewish leaders as far as Cape Town and Paris. The campaign operated covertly to avoid Soviet interference.

title_en: Riga library acquisition begins Rebbe's world-class collection
summary_en: In the summer of 1928 the Rebbe and librarian Chaim Lieberman began transforming his personal collection into a world-class research library in Riga.
story_body: The Rebbe envisioned a public library for research like the British Museum, requiring thousands of books, financing, a facility, and a catalog. The London paper HaOlam soon hailed the collection as a treasure of Jewish artifacts, citing one of the oldest printed siddurim from 1475 and 950 Haggadot. The Rebbe sought books from booksellers as far as Yemen, Australia, and Africa.

title_en: Chabad library shipped from Russia to Latvia
summary_en: When the Rebbe left Russia in 1927, he succeeded in exporting his library despite Soviet opposition.
story_body: A Soviet investigator who understood the value of Jewish books urged the government to block the export. Mordechai Dubin arranged a second investigator who lacked such knowledge and authorized the license. The library, augmented in 1925 by a 5,000-volume collection from Shmuel Weiner, traveled with the Rebbe to Latvia, separate from the bulk stored in Moscow that the Soviets had refused to return.

title_en: Chabad library arrives in America via Stockholm
summary_en: The majority of the Rebbe's library arrived in the United States in 1941 via Stockholm after his escape from Nazi-occupied Poland.
story_body: When the Rebbe fled to America at the war's onset, he worked to transfer the library. Most reached him via Stockholm in 1941. A portion was lost during the war and ended up in the Polish National Library, where it was discovered in 1983 and ultimately repatriated to Chabad's Brooklyn library in 1988.

title_en: Polish National Library collection identified as Rebbe's books
summary_en: In 1983 microfilm copies of the Polish National Library's collection of the Rebbe's books were discovered in Canada, sparking an investigation.
story_body: Two years later a Canadian student visiting the Warsaw library was given an actual manuscript of the Rebbe's that eventually reached Toronto rabbis. This sparked a diplomatic initiative that returned the collection to Chabad in 1988. It joined the library at Lubavitch World Headquarters in Brooklyn, now holding close to 300,000 items.

title_en: Agudas Chassidei Chabad established in America
summary_en: Agudas Chassidei Chabad was formalized in America in 1924, predating similar formal organizations in other countries.
story_body: Many Jews had emigrated from the chasidic heartland in Russia to new communities worldwide. Some were ardent Chasidim, others merely nostalgic. While America formalized Chabad in 1924, in many other countries the connections remained informal. The Rebbe encouraged his Chasidim to expand their vision and take responsibility for all Jews.

title_en: Soviet seizure of Rashab's library transferred to Russian National Library
