summary_en: In 1924 the Soviet government transferred the seized portion of the Rashab's library, stored in Moscow since 1915, to the Russian National Library.
story_body: After the Rebbe Rashab evacuated Lubavitch in 1915, the bulk of the combined libraries was stored in Moscow while priceless manuscripts were taken to Rostov. With the fall of the czarist government the Moscow books were seized. Authorities agreed to repatriate the collection in 1921 but reneged, again in 1925. The Rebbe Rayatz pursued the library's return throughout his life.

title_en: Rebbe sends Zelig Slonim on first mission to England
summary_en: In January 1926 the Rebbe dispatched Rabbi Zelig Slonim from Soviet Russia to England as his emissary to teach and inspire London Chasidim.
story_body: While locked in spiritual combat with the Yevesektzia, the Rebbe still attended to overseas Chasidim. Slonim's mission included finding positions for Chabad rabbis and shochtim. He worked to install Rabbi Mordechai Gutnick at London's Nusach Ari synagogue despite congregational opposition, and the Rebbe coached him to bypass recalcitrant leaders by appealing directly to members.

title_en: Rabbi Slonim sent to South Africa on multi-year mission
summary_en: In 1929 the Rebbe sent Rabbi Zelig Slonim from Eretz Yisrael to South Africa for what became a 2.5-year mission.
story_body: Feigin wrote that the Rebbe knew little of what was happening in South Africa and asked Slonim to explore employment opportunities for rabbis and shochtim, both to strengthen Jewish life and to facilitate emigration from Russia. Slonim visited communities throughout South Africa and Rhodesia, sending detailed reports back to the Rebbe.

title_en: Soviet legislation strips clergy of housing and employment rights
summary_en: 1929 Soviet legislation made Shabbat-observant Jews liable for rents up to ten times higher if not officially employed, targeting clergy of all religions.
story_body: The law curbed clergy's ability to serve congregations and devastated observant Jews. Reports of growing hunger trickled out, and the Rebbe attempted food shipments. In 1929 he had sent matzah for Passover, but Russian authorities now refused to authorize organized shipments, prompting his shift to the covert package strategy.

title_en: Rebbe begins sending yeshivah students as US emissaries
summary_en: In 1943, after relocating to America, the Rebbe began sending yeshivah students to American Jewish communities to teach chasidic philosophy.
story_body: The idea had originated in a 1938 letter from Otwock to Rabbi Dovid Rabinowitz, proposing that outstanding yeshivah students spend extended time in US communities on purely spiritual missions. The project did not materialize before the war but was realized in 1943 in America. The program continues today as a global Merkos Shlichus initiative.

title_en: Rebbe visits Glubok and witnesses miraculous healing of Ida Haberman
summary_en: In June 1934 the Rebbe returned to Glubok in Lithuania and was welcomed by thousands; he blessed ten-year-old Ida Haberman who regained her sight.
story_body: The local Yiddish paper Gluboker Lebn claimed the reception surpassed those given to the presidents of Czechoslovakia and Austria. Ida's father, not a Chasid, brought her to the train station fearing she was going blind. She regained her sight; later hidden during the Holocaust, she immigrated to the US. During the visit the Rebbe also navigated a local conflict over a rabbinic appointment.

title_en: Moshe Binyamin Kaplan flees Russia in Great Escape
summary_en: Moshe Binyamin Kaplan, a former underground yeshivah student, fled Russia in the 1946 Great Escape and reached a German DP camp.
story_body: From the DP camp Kaplan wrote to the Rebbe in Brooklyn wondering what bond he could have, having never met him. The Rebbe replied that he remembered him very well and that the bond was through learning each other's Torah. Years later Rabbi Shalom Ber Levin found among the Rebbe's possessions a 1935 photo of Kaplan, taken when he was eighteen and sent secretly from Russia to Poland.

title_en: Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson meets with the Rebbe in Otwock about US relocation
summary_en: On Saturday night, Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson met the Rebbe in Otwock, where the Rebbe resolved to relocate to the United States within about six months.
story_body: Five days before the German invasion of Poland, Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson met privately with the Sixth Rebbe in Otwock. The Rebbe announced his firm decision to move to the United States, citing the success of American students at the Polish yeshivah and Rabbi Shmuel Levitin's assessment that a Lubavitcher yeshivah could thrive in America. He told Jacobson, 'Arrange everything systematically. In about half a year, with G-d's assistance, we will come to America,' and signaled a turn inward toward teaching Chasidism and caring for Chasidim.

title_en: Six American students depart for Otwock yeshivah with Rabbi Jacobson
summary_en: Rabbi Jacobson personally escorted six American boys aboard the Isle de France from the US to study at the Otwock yeshivah.
story_body: On 24 Av 5699, Jacobson left New York with six American students bound for Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim in Otwock. They arrived just seventeen days before the outbreak of World War II. The Rebbe had assured the parents 'you have nothing to fear,' and the boys' presence later became central evidence that a Chabad yeshivah could succeed in America.

title_en: Farbrengen at Otwock yeshivah marking its 32nd founding anniversary
summary_en: Students of the Lubavitch yeshivah in Otwock held an all-night farbrengen on 16 Elul commemorating the founding of Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim 32 years earlier.
story_body: On the eve of Germany's invasion, students gathered through the night singing melodies and hearing chasidic stories to mark the yeshivah's founding. Avraham Garfinkel recalled the celebration ending at sunrise — none of them imagined that within hours their world would be shattered by war.

title_en: Germany invades Poland; bombs fall on Otwock and the yeshivah
summary_en: Germany launched its invasion of Poland at dawn, and within hours Luftwaffe bombers struck Otwock, including the new Lubavitch yeshivah building.
story_body: At 4:45 a.m. a German battleship shelled Gdańsk, and panzer columns crossed into Poland. By 8:00 a.m., as students prepared for morning prayers in Otwock, German planes were bombing the town. Ten children in the Jewish orphanage were killed, and the new yeshivah building was struck though no students died. The Rebbe later admitted to the American students, 'I did not foresee it.'

title_en: American students bid farewell to the Rebbe and flee Otwock for Latvia
summary_en: On the first day of the war, the six American students visited the Rebbe in Otwock, who blessed them and sent them to Mordechai Cheifetz's care in Riga.
story_body: After the American Consul urged them to leave, the boys stopped at the Rebbe's home before departing. The Rebbe, already in silk Shabbat garments, told them to head to neutral Latvia and asked Meir Greenberg to tell Mordechai Dubin to have the Latvian government request a permit for the Rebbe and family. When asked about possibly desecrating Shabbat, the Rebbe replied that the merit of the Baal Shem Tov and Rabbi Schneur Zalman — both born on 18 Elul — would suffice that they would not need to transgress.

title_en: Rebbe and family relocate from Otwock to Warsaw under Latvian diplomatic cover
summary_en: In early September the Latvian Embassy sent a car with diplomatic plates to ferry the Rebbe and his family from bombed Otwock to Warsaw.
story_body: With trains halted and roads under bombardment, the Latvian Embassy dispatched its diplomatic vehicle twice. Chaim Lieberman left with part of the family on Monday, and the Rebbe followed the next day, taking valuable historic manuscripts but leaving the bulk of his library behind in Otwock. A tearful crowd bade him farewell as he blessed them, saying 'A king guards his subjects.'

title_en: Rosh HaShanah under German bombing in Warsaw
summary_en: On the eve of Rosh HaShanah, German bombs destroyed Shmotkin's building where the Rebbe was staying, forcing the family to flee mid-day to a medical clinic.
story_body: At 5 p.m. on 29 Elul, bombs struck the Muranowska Street building. Thrown across the courtyard by a blast, the Rebbe's family briefly feared a gas attack. With sunset approaching, a Jewish wagon driver risked arrest to transport them to 8 Gegrnitche Street. The Rebbe prayed Maariv without a minyan in barely a half hour, exhausted and unable to stand, yet reassuring everyone around him.

title_en: Rebbe returns to Shmotkin's apartment two days before Yom Kippur
summary_en: On 8 Tishrei the Rebbe moved back to Shmotkin's apartment in Warsaw, where he led a small Yom Kippur service punctuated by thunderous explosions.
story_body: As bombs continued falling, the Rebbe recited maftir Yonah with overflowing emotion. The closing service was hastened and the shofar sounded before nightfall to let worshippers leave before further bombing. After breaking the fast on soup, the Rebbe led the family in singing a chasidic melody while Warsaw was bombarded around them.

title_en: Polish army in Warsaw surrenders hours before Sukkot
summary_en: On 14 Tishrei the Polish army in Warsaw surrendered to Germany just hours before the holiday of Sukkot began.
story_body: Even as skirmishes continued around the city, the Rebbe insisted that a sukkah be built. The bewildered building manager complied, and late that night the Rebbe recited the traditional blessings in the sukkah, saying, 'Never once have I missed sitting in the sukkah, and I won't this year.'

title_en: Rabbi Jacobson arrives back in New York to launch the rescue campaign
summary_en: After a harrowing roundabout journey via Hungary, Yugoslavia, Italy and France, Rabbi Jacobson reached New York and immediately began organizing efforts to save the Rebbe.
story_body: Jacobson had missed his original passage on the Queen Mary and crossed the Atlantic in a converted swimming-pool locker aboard an overcrowded ship, leading Rosh HaShanah services on deck. Back in New York he enlisted attorney Samuel Kramer and called Asher Rabinowitz late at night, dispatching him to Washington to find a way to contact the Rebbe — refusing to let Shabbat or Yom Kippur deter the mission.

title_en: Senator Wagner appeals to Secretary of State Hull regarding the Rebbe's fate
summary_en: New York Senator Robert Wagner wrote to Secretary of State Cordell Hull asking the State Department to locate Rabbi Joseph Isaac Schneersohn in Poland.
story_body: On the eve of Yom Kippur, Wagner relayed appeals from leading New York Jews seeking the Rebbe's whereabouts. Days later, House Foreign Affairs chairman Sol Bloom replied that communication with Poland had been disrupted but the department would advise when contact was reestablished. The exchange marked the entry of US government channels into the rescue effort.

title_en: Benjamin Cohen and Robert Pell strategize the Rebbe's rescue
summary_en: Senior White House aide Benjamin Cohen pressed State Department European-affairs head Robert Pell to seek the Rebbe through German contacts.
story_body: Cohen impressed on Pell the Rebbe's standing as 'one of the leading Jewish scholars of the world' and suggested approaching Helmuth Wohlthat, a German diplomat Pell had befriended at the 1938 Evian Conference. The same day Pell telegrammed US consul Raymond Geist in Berlin, asking him to discreetly enlist Wohlthat in arranging safe passage for the Rebbe to Riga.

title_en: Hitler enters occupied Warsaw
summary_en: Just over a month after invading Poland, Hitler arrived in Warsaw and was welcomed by a massive Nazi military parade down the capital's main avenues.
story_body: Thousands of German soldiers strutted through Warsaw as Hitler reviewed his conquest of Poland. The display dramatized the new occupation order under which the Rebbe was hiding, while Polish Jews — initially comparing it to Germany's relatively benevolent World War I occupation — soon discovered the true face of Nazi anti-Semitism.

title_en: Haaretz reports the Rebbe has perished
summary_en: The Israeli newspaper Haaretz, relaying a dispatch from London, reported that the Rebbe had died in war-torn Warsaw.
story_body: With the Rebbe's whereabouts unknown to Chasidim worldwide, false reports of his death circulated in the press. Two days later Haaretz relayed a Vilna dispatch saying he was alive, and on November 16 reported that Tel Aviv Chasidim had received a telegram from Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski confirming the Rebbe was alive in Warsaw.

title_en: Lieberman cables the Rebbe's Warsaw address from Riga
summary_en: Rabbi Chaim Lieberman cabled Jacobson from Riga with the message 'Rabbi healthy, situation gross, awfully dangerous,' supplying the address Bonifraterska 29.
story_body: Lieberman, having escaped Warsaw to Riga, transmitted the Rebbe's location and pleaded for accelerated immigration. Asher Rabinowitz wired Justice Brandeis with the address, who passed it to Cohen in the White House, then to Geist in Berlin, and finally to Lt. Col. Ernst Bloch leading the search in Warsaw.

title_en: German military unit locates the Rebbe and delivers exit visas
summary_en: Lt. Col. Ernst Bloch and his Abwehr unit forced their way into the Gurary apartment where the Rebbe was hiding and announced they had come to save him.
story_body: After weeks of searching ruined Warsaw, Bloch's soldiers — several of Jewish background — entered the apartment as the Rebbe's grandson Berke and others braced for execution. Instead, the soldiers handed out exit visas and travel papers. The mission had been authorized at the highest levels of the Abwehr under Admiral Wilhelm Canaris, working through Helmuth Wohlthat in Goering's office.

title_en: Pell confirms to Rhoade that the Rebbe has been found alive
summary_en: Robert Pell informed attorney Max Rhoade that German soldiers had located the Rebbe alive in Warsaw and placed him under the protection of a staff officer.
story_body: A cable from the US Embassy in Berlin confirmed: 'He has been ill and is recovering' and that a German officer 'has been assigned to look after him.' Rhoade relayed the news to Sam Kramer and the American Chasidim, who rejoiced — though the road to safety remained long, dangerous, and dependent on still-elusive US visas.

title_en: Rebbe and family depart Warsaw for Berlin on the last day of Chanukah
summary_en: Escorted by Lt. Col. Bloch and Abwehr soldiers, the Rebbe and his entourage left occupied Warsaw by truck and wagon for a peripheral train station to Berlin.
story_body: The central station had been bombed, so Bloch arranged transport to the city's outskirts. German soldiers along the route challenged the obvious group of religious Jews, and at one checkpoint rifles were aimed at the Rebbe; Bloch invoked the authority of Admiral Canaris and threatened arrest if they interfered. After a full-day journey, the group reached Berlin, staying at the Jewish Community Center and then a hotel for Shabbat.

title_en: Rebbe arrives safely in Riga after escape from Nazi Europe
summary_en: On 5 Tevet the Rebbe reached Riga from Berlin via Lithuania, greeted by ecstatic crowds; that night a telegram 'The Rebbe is free' reached New York.
story_body: The Rebbe was met by chasidic crowds at Vilnius and Kovno stations, where Eliyahu Vad of Dos Vort interviewed him about the state of the Jewish nation. At the Latvian border Bloch's escort departed. In New York Rabbi Jacobson did handsprings on the sidewalk in joy and hosted a farbrengen, then placed a transatlantic call to thank the Rebbe the next day.

title_en: Rebbe issues twin encyclicals on Polish Jewry's plight from Riga
summary_en: Within hours of arriving in Riga the Rebbe composed two letters — one to world Jewry and one to Chabad Chasidim — describing the devastation in Warsaw and demanding relief.
story_body: Writing on 5 Tevet, the Rebbe described Jews 'burned alive' and homes turned to graves, urged worldwide fundraising channeled through the JDC 'irrespective of political party or personal philosophy,' and called on Chabad communities globally to treat aid to Polish Chasidim as 'saving lives and redeeming captives.'

title_en: Rebbe writes JDC head Morris Troper urging mass emigration of Polish Jewry
summary_en: From Riga, the Rebbe wrote JDC European chairman Morris Troper urging a vast relief campaign and the inclusion of emigration in the JDC's mandate.
story_body: Calling it his 'sacred duty to give firsthand information,' the Rebbe lauded the JDC as the only Jewish institution still working in Warsaw. He pressed Troper to extend relief into emigration assistance — first for the most urgent cases and ultimately for 'the wholesale immigration of Polish Jewry to a quiet place under the sun, where they can live a normal Jewish life.'

title_en: State Department investigators meet Chabad leaders in New York
summary_en: Two senior State Department visa officials met Chabad leadership in New York to evaluate the claim that Chabad qualified as a religious hierarchy.
story_body: After Max Rhoade's relentless lobbying, the visa division finally accepted the principle that the Rebbe's entourage might be admitted as the leadership of a religious hierarchy rather than each requiring an individual congregational sponsor. The officials received a detailed briefing on Chabad's history, structure, finances, and US synagogue network — a precondition for issuing the long-delayed visas.

title_en: Rebbe breaks his hand in Riga
summary_en: On 6 Shevat the Rebbe fell and broke his hand, wearing a cast for three weeks and a bandage in the fourth.
story_body: The injury kept the Rebbe from writing until just days before his departure for the US. During the same period his mother Rebbetzin Shterna Sara underwent a twelve-hour stomach operation, and the Rebbe delayed his travel until she recovered.

title_en: US visas issued to the Rebbe and entourage in Riga
summary_en: The US Consulate in Riga issued immigration visas to the Rebbe and the rabbis of his entourage, clearing the final bureaucratic hurdle to America.
story_body: After months of pressure from Rhoade, Cohen, and a coalition of congressmen and senators, the visas were granted. Sam Kramer informed Henry Butler the same day. The Rebbe's daughters Sheina and Chaya Mushka and their husbands were not included; the Schneersons later escaped via France and Spain, while the Horensteins were killed in Treblinka.

title_en: JDC meets Chabad delegation on aid to refugees and the Vilnius yeshivah
summary_en: JDC officials met Agudas Chassidei Chabad representatives, offering limited discretionary funds for the Rebbe but refusing to subsidize US immigration or the Vilnius yeshivah.
story_body: Citing US law forbidding organizations from financing immigration, the JDC declined the larger requests but agreed to a discretionary grant 'in view of Rabbi Schneersohn's leadership' and approved funding for Passover matzah for rabbis in Russia. The Rebbe would have to rely on his own resources to sustain the Vilnius yeshivah and rescue Chasidim still in Poland.

title_en: Rebbe departs Riga for Stockholm before crossing the Atlantic
summary_en: Thousands of Chasidim gathered in Riga to bid farewell to the Rebbe, who refused to leave seven empty plane seats and held up the flight until they were filled.
story_body: Shraga Feivel Zisman organized a human chain to allow the Rebbe's mother to be carried on a stretcher to the ambulance. The Rebbe asked Rabbi Mordechai Cheifetz to tell the crowd, 'The great ocean is not a barrier but a connector.' Discovering empty seats on the plane, he refused to depart until others were brought aboard, declaring, 'I cannot leave, I need to save others.'

title_en: Rebbe boards the SS Drottningholm in Gothenburg bound for America
summary_en: Three days after leaving Riga, the Rebbe and his eleven-person entourage boarded the SS Drottningholm at the Swedish port of Gothenburg for the voyage to the United States.
story_body: The Drottningholm was the only ocean liner still operating between neutral Sweden and the US. Mechanical problems detained it overnight at Bergen, Norway, with German submarines patrolling below in preparation for the invasion of Denmark a month later. German U-boats stopped the ship twice and British warships three times during the crossing, but each time the refugees were allowed to continue.

title_en: Breckinridge Long memo instructs State Department to obstruct Jewish immigration
summary_en: Assistant Secretary of State Breckinridge Long circulated a memo urging consular officials worldwide to 'delay and effectively stop' Jewish immigration to the US.
story_body: Long instructed US representatives to 'put every obstacle in the way' of refugees and to 'postpone and postpone and postpone the granting of the visas.' The memo crystallized the bureaucratic anti-Semitism that had nearly prevented the Rebbe's own rescue and would doom countless others seeking refuge from the Nazis.

title_en: Soviet Union invades Latvia
summary_en: Soviet forces invaded Latvia, fulfilling the fears that had driven the urgency to extract the Rebbe from Riga only months earlier.
story_body: The Chasidim's warnings to US officials that the Rebbe and his entourage faced execution under a Soviet regime proved well founded. Latvia remained under Soviet control until regaining independence in 1991, validating the rescue coalition's insistence that Riga could only be a temporary haven and that America was the sole durable refuge.

title_en: Portion of the Rebbe's library reaches the United States
summary_en: A portion of the Rebbe's library, left behind in Otwock and entrusted to the US Embassy in Warsaw, arrived in the United States.
story_body: Yechezkel Feigin had urged Rabbi Jacobson to intervene with US officials to save the 127 cases of books and three cases of manuscripts the Rebbe had been forced to leave behind. Jacobson's efforts were partially successful — some of the collection reached the US embassy in Warsaw and was eventually transferred to America in June 1941.

title_en: Admiral Wilhelm Canaris executed by the Nazis
summary_en: Admiral Wilhelm Canaris, head of the Abwehr who had authorized the Rebbe's rescue, was hanged just weeks before the end of World War II.
story_body: Canaris had grown disillusioned with Hitler after witnessing atrocities in Warsaw, attempted a 1943 ceasefire with the Allies through intelligence chiefs in Spain, and was eventually implicated in a plot to kill Hitler. His execution on April 9, 1945, came only weeks before Germany's surrender.

title_en: Lt. Col. Ernst Bloch killed at the front in the final days of the war
summary_en: Ernst Bloch, the half-Jewish Abwehr officer who escorted the Rebbe out of Warsaw, was killed near Berlin only days before the war's end.
story_body: After leading the Rebbe's rescue, Bloch was promoted to colonel and later appointed a battalion commander in Russia in 1943. In February 1945 the SS forced his dismissal from the army due to his Jewish background. When the Red Army reached Berlin in April 1945, he returned to the front and was killed days before the German surrender.

title_en: Agudas Chassidei Chabad established in the United States
summary_en: Agudas Chassidei Chabad was founded to strengthen the bond between roughly 150 Chabad-associated immigrant congregations in America.
story_body: Led by Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson, the organization operated as a loose confederation of immigrant synagogues whose members were linked largely by sentimental attachment to Chabad rather than active chasidic practice. Though it had not matured into a major national body by 1939, it became the institutional vehicle through which the rescue of the Sixth Rebbe was organized.

title_en: Rebbe forced from Riga to St. Petersburg under Yevsektzia pressure
summary_en: In May 1924, threats from the Yevsektzia compelled the Sixth Rebbe to leave Riga and relocate to St. Petersburg.
story_body: It was one in a series of forced relocations the Rebbe later catalogued at his Riga farewell — Rostov to St. Petersburg, out of Russia in 1927, then Warsaw, Otwock, back to Riga, and finally America — each driven by danger or duty rather than personal choice.

title_en: Rebbe forced out of Russia after death sentence
summary_en: In October 1927 the Sixth Rebbe was forced to leave the Soviet Union after a death sentence at the hands of the anti-religious regime was commuted to exile.
story_body: The Rebbe's expulsion from Russia ended his direct leadership inside the Soviet Union but began two decades of relocations across Latvia, Poland, and eventually the United States while he continued to sustain an underground religious network back in the USSR.

title_en: Rebbe relocates from Riga to Warsaw
summary_en: In August 1933 the Sixth Rebbe relocated from Riga to Warsaw to be near the yeshivah and strengthen chasidic life in Poland.
story_body: The move placed him at the center of Polish chasidic life for the rest of the decade. He moved again to Otwock in 1934 for health reasons, where he remained until German bombs forced him back into Warsaw at the outbreak of World War II.

title_en: Rebbe relocates from Warsaw to Otwock
summary_en: Health concerns prompted the Sixth Rebbe to move from Warsaw to the suburban resort town of Otwock in 1934.
story_body: Otwock served as the seat of his leadership and the home of Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim until German bombing on September 1, 1939 destroyed any possibility of staying. Otwock is where Jacobson met him on the eve of the war and where he resolved to move to America.

title_en: Tsar Alexander I issues Jewish Statute regulating rabbinate
summary_en: Tsar Alexander I issued a statute on the Jews whose Sections 52-53 governed rabbinic fees and synagogue splits, later cited against the Mitteler Rebbe.
story_body: The 1804 statute declared the rabbinate an office of honor rather than a paying position, forbidding rabbis from collecting funds beyond their fixed communal salary (Section 52). Section 53 allowed a faction to build its own synagogue when communal unity broke down, but limited each town to one official communal leader. Two decades later, the informer Shimcha Kissin invoked Section 52 to accuse Rabbi DovBer Schneuri of illegal fundraising.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe's letter about distribution of Maamad funds
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer Schneuri wrote a letter in Tevet 5574 concerning the division of Maamad support funds among family members after his father's passing.
story_body: Following the passing of the Alter Rebbe, his son Rabbi DovBer documented the allocation of donor funds collected for the rebbe's household (the maamad). The letter assigned half-yearly living expenses and gifts to relatives. This document, smuggled to the informer Pinchas Schick of Shklov in 1822, became the central exhibit Shimcha Kissin used against the Rebbe a decade later.

title_en: Arbitration contract signed before the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: An arbitration agreement was concluded before Rabbi DovBer Schneuri of Lubavitch, showing his role as a recognized adjudicator.
story_body: The contract documents a binding arbitration before the Mitteler Rebbe in his role as a religious-legal authority. Such documents were later cited by Khovansky as evidence the Rebbe overstepped purely religious functions by handling civil disputes between Jews and Christians.

title_en: Mogilev community signs synagogue and mikvah trustee agreement
summary_en: Chassidim of Mogilev formalized an agreement appointing gabbaim for their synagogue and mikvah, ratified the same day in the local magistrate court.
story_body: On 11 Menachem-Av 5582, Chabad chassidim in Mogilev signed a formal trustee agreement governing their synagogue and mikvah. The agreement was deposited the same day at the Mogilev district peace court, giving it legal standing. The arrangement reflects the institutional organization of Chabad communal life that opponents like Kissin viewed as encroachment.

title_en: Shlomo of Layev sends 1000 rubles to the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: On 18 Shvat 5585, Shlomo of Layev forwarded a 1000-ruble contribution to Rabbi DovBer Schneuri.
story_body: The transfer documented a large single donation to the Rebbe's treasury earlier in 1825, months before Shimcha Kissin filed his denunciations. Such gifts later figured in Khovansky's calculations of the Rebbe's annual income, which the governor claimed reached 10,000-14,000 rubles per year.

title_en: First denunciation against Chabad by Shimcha Kissin
summary_en: Shimcha Kissin submitted a general denunciation portraying Chassidim as a destructive sect exploiting youth and seizing community institutions.
story_body: Kissin's first letter to Governor Khovansky targeted the Chassidic movement broadly without yet naming the Mitteler Rebbe personally for embezzlement. He alleged the sect ("Karliner") manipulated young men, controlled charity coffers, monopolized shechita, and ran printing presses producing books of miracle tales. The letter demanded the authorities suppress Chassidism, setting in motion the events that led to the Rebbe's arrest.

title_en: Second denunciation by Shimcha Kissin
summary_en: Kissin submitted a second letter, this one personally accusing Rabbi DovBer of misappropriating community funds.
story_body: Following his general broadside, Kissin escalated by leveling direct financial charges against the Mitteler Rebbe himself. The accusation centered on funds allegedly collected from communities and distributed among the Rebbe's relatives as personal gifts. This shifted the case from a religious-policy complaint to a criminal allegation of embezzlement under the 1804 Jewish Statute.

title_en: Third denunciation by Shimcha Kissin
summary_en: Kissin filed a third denunciation against the Mitteler Rebbe, completing his trio of accusations to Governor Khovansky.
story_body: The third installment of Kissin's denunciations reached Khovansky in July 1825. Together with the two earlier letters, it supplied Governor Khovansky of Vitebsk with the pretext to summon the Rebbe for interrogation in early autumn. Kissin's central exhibit remained the 1813 letter on Maamad distribution that he had obtained through Pinchas Schick of Shklov.

title_en: Khovansky orders police to bring the Mitteler Rebbe for interrogation
summary_en: Governor Khovansky dispatched police official Korbicki to Lubavitch to summon Rabbi DovBer to Vitebsk for interrogation.
story_body: Order No. 4767 instructed Korbicki, together with Chevkin and another officer, to travel via Lubavitch, Babinovichi, and Shklov to bring the Rebbe to Vitebsk. Khovansky framed the summons as a private meeting on "several matters" rather than an arrest warrant. According to Beis Rebbi, the Rebbe was actually taken from his home in Lubavitch immediately after Sukkot 5586.

title_en: Interrogation of R. Zalman Slonim about the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: Khovansky's investigators questioned R. Zalman Slonim as part of the case against the Rebbe.
story_body: Slonim was among the close chassidim summoned for testimony in Vitebsk. His interrogation preceded the Rebbe's own first interview by two days. Investigators sought corroboration of Kissin's claims about communal fundraising and money distribution among the Rebbe's relatives.

title_en: First interrogation of the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer Schneuri underwent his first interrogation in Vitebsk by Colonel Loginov and court counselor Markov.
story_body: On 7 Cheshvan 5586 the Rebbe answered the first round of questions from Khovansky's two appointed investigators. They focused on whether he had written and signed the 1813 financial document presented by Kissin, what portion of the funds went to relatives, and on what legal basis the money was collected. Two days later the Rebbe submitted written answers to their queries.

title_en: Second interrogation of the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe was questioned a second time and submitted further written answers the same day.
story_body: The investigators pressed the Rebbe with follow-up questions on 15 Cheshvan 5586. The same day he provided written responses, a pattern of careful, documented answers maintained throughout the inquiry. The next day Khovansky reassigned the third investigator to other duties, leaving Loginov and Markov to complete the case.

title_en: Third interrogation of the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: A third round of interrogation took place on 19 Cheshvan 5586, followed again by the Rebbe's written replies.
story_body: By the third interrogation, the questioning had narrowed onto specific financial details and the Rebbe's role in Jewish arbitration. The Rebbe acknowledged accepting cases of debt disputes between Christian and Jewish parties, which Khovansky later cited as exceeding the religious-only scope assigned to rabbis by Section 52 of the 1804 statute.

title_en: Interrogation of R. Aharon of Strashelye
summary_en: From 21-28 October, Khovansky's officials interrogated Rabbi Aharon of Strashelye in connection with the case.
story_body: Rabbi Aharon HaLevi of Strashelye, the Alter Rebbe's senior disciple turned rival rebbe, was drawn into the inquiry for over a week. His earlier letters with Rabbi DovBer were among the materials Kissin had appended to his denunciation. Despite their well-known dispute, R. Aharon's testimony did not yield material that strengthened the case against Rabbi DovBer.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe petitions Governor Khovansky for release
summary_en: On 6 Kislev 5586 the Rebbe submitted a written request to Khovansky asking to be freed from detention.
story_body: Having endured three rounds of interrogation and roughly a month of confinement, Rabbi DovBer formally petitioned Governor Khovansky for release. Six days later the investigators delivered their summary of the inquiry to Khovansky. The Rebbe's release on 10 Kislev followed shortly thereafter, marking the first of what would become three stages of liberation.

title_en: Liberation of the Mitteler Rebbe on Yud Kislev
summary_en: On 10 Kislev 5586 Rabbi DovBer Schneuri was released from detention and returned home to Lubavitch.
story_body: The first stage of the Mitteler Rebbe's liberation came when Khovansky freed him to return home after the initial interrogations concluded. This date became Yud Kislev, the Chassidic festival of redemption commemorating his release. The legal case, however, was far from over: Khovansky immediately referred the file to the Mogilev provincial authorities for full trial proceedings.

title_en: Case transferred to Mogilev provincial government for trial
summary_en: Khovansky sent the file with his findings to the Mogilev provincial government, demanding that the accused be judged with full severity.
story_body: Order No. 10265 forwarded the entire investigation, including Loginov and Markov's reports, to Mogilev's provincial government on 19 Kislev 5586. Khovansky concluded that the Rebbe collected 10,000-14,000 rubles annually for personal use and acted as a civil arbitrator, both in violation of Section 52 of the 1804 statute. Mogilev province routed the case to the Babinovichi peace court, which initiated further investigations in Kapust, Orsha, Shklov, and Mogilev.

title_en: Mogilev high court acquits the Mitteler Rebbe (11 Kislev 5587)
summary_en: On 11 Kislev 5587 the Mogilev provincial high court ruled to acquit Rabbi DovBer of all charges.
story_body: The second stage of liberation came when the Mogilev high court, after reviewing the Babinovichi peace court's findings from investigations in multiple towns, formally cleared the Rebbe of every accusation. The verdict closed the case at the provincial level, but it still required ratification by Governor Khovansky. He instead lodged an appeal to the Senate in St. Petersburg, prolonging the legal struggle by another year.

title_en: Formal acquittal verdict sent to Governor Khovansky
summary_en: The Mogilev high court formally notified Governor Khovansky of its final acquittal of the Rebbe.
story_body: On 24 Shvat 5587 the high court delivered written confirmation of its acquittal ruling to Vitebsk. Khovansky responded by requesting the full file with a summary, then attempted to delay through a series of procedural demands. Within weeks he resolved to escalate the case to the Governing Senate in Saint Petersburg.

title_en: Khovansky appeals the acquittal to the Senate in St. Petersburg
summary_en: Governor Khovansky filed an appeal to the Governing Senate in St. Petersburg challenging the Rebbe's acquittal.
story_body: Refusing to accept the Mogilev verdict, Khovansky on Rosh Chodesh Sivan 5587 lodged a formal appeal with the Senate. He simultaneously instructed the Mogilev court to forward the case file to Petersburg. Khovansky's hope was to have the Rebbe brought to the capital for renewed proceedings, but the appeal would ultimately fail.

title_en: Passing of the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer Schneuri, the Mitteler Rebbe, passed away on 9 Kislev 5588, the day before what would have been the first formal celebration of Yud Kislev.
story_body: The Mitteler Rebbe's histalkus occurred on 9 Kislev 5588, just days before the Senate's final ratification of his acquittal. Because his passing fell one day before what would have been the inaugural Yud Kislev celebration, the festival was not established as widely as it might otherwise have been. Different traditions place the Rebbe's liberation in 5586, 5587, or 5588, reflecting the three distinct stages of his juridical exoneration.

title_en: Senate confirms acquittal of the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: The Governing Senate in St. Petersburg upheld the Mogilev court's acquittal of the Rebbe, rejecting Khovansky's appeal.
story_body: On 21 Kislev 5588 the Senate dismissed Khovansky's appeal and confirmed the Mogilev high court's verdict. This third and final stage of liberation came only days after the Rebbe's passing on 9 Kislev. The Mogilev court received notification on 7 Shvat 5588, and the question of trial expenses remained the subject of further correspondence into 1828.

title_en: Senate responds to Khovansky on rabbinic appointments
summary_en: The Senate replied to Khovansky's recommendations regarding the appointment of rabbis, closing out the long arc of his anti-Chassidic initiatives.
story_body: Seven years after the Rebbe's acquittal, the Senate addressed Khovansky's lingering proposals about regulating rabbinic appointments. The Mogilev high court forwarded copies of his recommendations to the Senate in February, and Khovansky relayed the response to the Mogilev provincial government. The exchange marks a final administrative coda to the policy program Kissin's denunciations had originally tried to advance.

title_en: Alter Rebbe released from Petersburg by tsarist decree
summary_en: Civil governor Treviov issued a document permitting Rabbi Schneur Zalman to return from Petersburg to his home and continue his activities throughout White Russia without interference.
story_body: Following his second arrest and interrogation in Petersburg in 1801, Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi (called Zalman Bruchavitch in Russian documents) was freed by imperial order. The civil governor of White Russia, Treviov, issued him a formal document on July 13, 1801, granting him full freedom to resume his religious leadership of the Chasidim throughout the region as he had done before.

title_en: Jewish Constitution of 1804 signed by the Tsar
summary_en: Tsar Alexander I signed the Statute Concerning the Jews, regulating rabbinic appointments, taxes, and communal life across the Russian Empire.
story_body: On December 9, 1804, the Tsar signed the comprehensive Jewish Constitution that governed Jewish life in the Empire for decades. Its provisions—including section 50 mandating triennial rabbinic elections, section 52 forbidding rabbis to collect funds beyond fixed salaries, and section 53 permitting separate congregations only under strict conditions—later became the legal basis for repeated investigations of the Chabad Rebbes.

title_en: Passing of the Alter Rebbe during the French invasion
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi died in 1812 during his flight from the Napoleonic invasion of Russia.
story_body: After fleeing Liadi ahead of Napoleon's advancing army, the Alter Rebbe died in the course of the wartime journey. His passing left the Chasidim of White Russia without their guiding teacher amid the devastation of the war, setting the stage for his son's succession the following year.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe accepts leadership and a 35,000-ruble fund
summary_en: White Russian Chasidim called Rabbi Dovber Schneuri to succeed his late father, pledging to support him and rebuild his property destroyed in the war.
story_body: In 1813 the Jews of White Russia summoned Berke Shneur—Rabbi Dovber, the Mitteler Rebbe—to take his father's place as their rebbe. They promised to compensate the family for losses sustained when the enemy destroyed their assets and to provide dignified support through voluntary donations. He gathered 35,000 rubles, distributed among relatives, personal needs, and synagogue construction—an act later cited as evidence in the government's investigation of him.

title_en: Imperial amnesty manifesto of 30 August 1814
summary_en: The Tsar issued a general amnesty manifesto on August 30, 1814, pardoning offenses committed prior to that date.
story_body: This sweeping amnesty later became the formal grounds on which Governor-General Khovansky recommended not punishing the Mitteler Rebbe for his 1813 fundraising. Despite Khovansky's view that the collection violated the Jewish Constitution, the 1814 manifesto covered actions taken before its issuance.

title_en: Document confirming Mitteler Rebbe's standing issued in Vitebsk
summary_en: Duke Alexander of Württemberg, military governor of White Russia, issued the Mitteler Rebbe a document attesting to his good standing and right to travel and teach.
story_body: On March 3, 1816, the former military governor of White Russia, Duke Alexander of Württemberg, gave Rabbi Dovber Schneuri a formal document parallel to the one his father had received in 1801. It described him as an honest man enjoying the full respect of the Jewish community, traveling to teach ethics and beneficial conduct—though, as Khovansky later noted, it conferred no right to collect money.

title_en: Imperial decree restricting voluntary donations to signed lists
summary_en: An imperial decree of June 14, 1816, required all charitable collections to be backed by signed declarations of consent submitted to the provincial government.
story_body: This decree narrowed the definition of 'voluntary donations' under Russian law: only contributions from individuals who had registered written consent with the provincial government could be lawfully collected. Khovansky later cited this 1816 decree to argue that the Mitteler Rebbe's fundraising—lacking signatures or registered authorization—was illegal.

title_en: Communal fundraising campaign for Petersburg shtadlanim
summary_en: Chasidic leaders meeting in Lubavitch in 1824 apportioned 1,720 rubles between Mohilev and Vitebsk provinces to fund delegates intervening for Jewish causes in Petersburg.
story_body: Representatives of Mohilev and Vitebsk Jews gathered in the town of Lubavitch to coordinate a special levy for delegates traveling to Petersburg on behalf of the community. They assigned 1,030 rubles to Mohilev province (60%) and 690 rubles to Vitebsk (40%). Khovansky later used this episode as evidence that 'voluntary' donations under the Mitteler Rebbe's leadership were in fact compulsory levies imposed by a few leaders.

title_en: Simcha Kisin files denunciation against the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: Vitebsk resident Simcha Kisin submitted a denunciation to Governor-General Khovansky accusing the Chasidic 'sect' and Rabbi Berke Shneur of pressuring traditional Jews and illegally collecting funds.
story_body: In July 1825, the Jew Simcha Kisin of Vitebsk lodged a complaint with Governor-General Khovansky alleging that the Chasidim—whom he called 'Karliners'—were oppressing 'authentic Jews of the old faith,' and that their rebbe, Berke Shneur, was amassing wealth through dedicated emissaries. As evidence, Kisin produced an original Hebrew document of fund distribution along with a Russian translation and two letters from the Rebbe—the materials that launched the long investigation.

title_en: Investigation against the Mitteler Rebbe formally opened
summary_en: The case file against the Mitteler Rebbe was formally received for investigation on October 2, 1825.
story_body: After Kisin's denunciation, Khovansky assigned two of his officials to conduct a formal inquiry. The case was officially received on October 2, 1825, with the investigation findings presented to Khovansky on November 10 and forwarded to the Mohilev provincial administration on November 17—beginning the multi-year legal proceedings.

title_en: Case forwarded to the Babinovitsy peace court
summary_en: The Mohilev government transferred the investigation against the Mitteler Rebbe to the peace court of the town of Babinovitsy on December 19, 1825.
story_body: Following Khovansky's order, the Mohilev provincial administration sent the case materials to the peace court at Babinovitsy for further examination. The Babinovitsy court ultimately deliberated for six months before issuing its decision in June 1826.

title_en: Babinovitsy peace court rules on Mitteler Rebbe's case
summary_en: The peace court at Babinovitsy issued its decision in the Mitteler Rebbe's case on June 20, 1826, after further investigation.
story_body: After receiving the case in late 1825, the Babinovitsy peace court conducted additional inquiries and reached its decision on June 20, 1826. The case was then forwarded on August 3 to the First Department of the Mohilev Supreme Court for review—the body that would ultimately acquit the Rebbe.

title_en: Imperial amnesty manifesto of 22 August 1826
summary_en: A new imperial amnesty was issued on August 22, 1826, shortly after Nicholas I's coronation.
story_body: Nicholas I's coronation amnesty pardoned a wide range of prior offenses. Together with the 1814 manifesto, it became one of the two reasons Governor-General Khovansky cited for not pursuing punishment against the Mitteler Rebbe despite his contention that the 1813 fundraising had been unlawful.

title_en: Mohilev Supreme Court acquits the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: On November 29, 1826, the First Department of the Mohilev Supreme Court ruled to acquit Rabbi Dovber Schneuri of all charges of illegal fundraising.
story_body: The court concluded that the Mitteler Rebbe had been freely chosen by the Chasidim as their religious teacher, that the donations he received were voluntary and unforced, and that even Jews of other provinces sent contributions without compulsion. It held that no one could be forbidden from giving a legal donation or disposing of private property, and that the Rebbe's arbitration work did not amount to exercising judicial authority. The ruling cleared him of all wrongdoing.

title_en: Khovansky appeals the acquittal of the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: Governor-General Khovansky signed his appeal to the Governing Senate on May 15, 1827, in Vitebsk, challenging the Mohilev Supreme Court's acquittal of the Mitteler Rebbe.
story_body: Prince Khovansky, Governor-General of Vitebsk, Mohilev, Smolensk and Kaluga, prepared a lengthy report to the Senate's Fifth Department arguing that the lower court's reasoning was unfounded and that the Mitteler Rebbe had in fact violated multiple provisions of the 1804 Jewish Constitution. While conceding that the imperial amnesties of 1814 and 1826 precluded actual punishment, he recommended barring the Rebbe from continuing as rabbi of the Chasidim and proposed broader restrictions on rabbinic authority in Russia. The appeal was filed in Vitebsk on May 15, 1827.

title_en: Russian Jewish Statute restricting rabbinic fund collection
summary_en: Czar Alexander I's Jewish Statute prohibited rabbis from collecting funds from the community beyond their fixed salary.
story_body: The Russian Jewish Statute of 5565 (1804) regulated Jewish communal life and explicitly forbade rabbis from gathering money from their congregations beyond a fixed salary. This statute would later be invoked by opponents of Chabad and by Russian investigators questioning whether the Mitteler Rebbe's collection of ma'amad funds violated the law. The Senate ultimately ruled that the voluntary nature of the donations, combined with the Rebbe's non-official rabbinic status, placed him outside its prohibitions.

title_en: Alter Rebbe flees Liadi as Napoleon's army advances
summary_en: During Napoleon's invasion of Russia, the Alter Rebbe fled Liadi with his family, and the rebbe's house was destroyed by fire.
story_body: When Napoleon's army advanced into Russia in 1812, the Alter Rebbe and his family abandoned Liadi to escape the French. The entire Bais HaRav in Liadi was consumed by fire in the aftermath. This destruction left the family destitute and later prompted a special ma'amad collection organized to rebuild a home for the rebbe's family in Lubavitch.

title_en: Passing of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, founder of Chabad, passed away on 24 Tevet 5573 after fleeing the Napoleonic war.
story_body: The Alter Rebbe, Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, passed away on 24 Tevet 5573 (early January 1813 Gregorian) after fleeing Liadi during the Napoleonic war. His son, the Mitteler Rebbe, assumed leadership of Chabad and resettled the family in Lubavitch. A special ma'amad fund of 35,000 rubles was organized in the year following his passing to rebuild the rebbe's household.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe distributes ma'amad bais harav funds
summary_en: One year after his father's passing, the Mitteler Rebbe organized distribution of 35,000 rubles in ma'amad funds among his family.
story_body: In Tevet 5574, one year after the Alter Rebbe's passing, the Mitteler Rebbe arranged the distribution of the ma'amad bais harav fund. He appointed R. Pinchas Schick of Shklov to administer the distribution, with R. Shlomo Freides and R. Zalman Reuzes of Shklov as overseers. Of the 35,000 rubles collected, two-thirds went to descendants of the Alter Rebbe and one-third was used by the Mitteler Rebbe to build his own home, a synagogue in Lubavitch, and to purchase seforim.

title_en: Second informer letter submitted against the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: Simcha Kisin submitted a second informer letter against the Mitteler Rebbe and the chassidic movement in June 1825.
story_body: In late Sivan to Tammuz 5585 (June 1825), Simcha Kisin filed his second informer letter portraying the chassidic movement as greedy exploiters of naive young Jews who seized control of communal funds, charity boxes, shechita, and printing houses. He attached a 1814 distribution letter regarding the ma'amad bais harav as supposed evidence that the Mitteler Rebbe was amassing vast personal wealth. The denunciation demanded the persecution and destruction of the chassidic movement.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe denounced and brought to Vitebsk
summary_en: At the end of Tishrei 5587, the Mitteler Rebbe was informed against and immediately taken to the city of Vitebsk.
story_body: At the end of Tishrei 5587 (October 1826), informers' charges against the Mitteler Rebbe escalated and he was promptly brought to Vitebsk for investigation. There the case fell under the jurisdiction of General-Governor Khovansky of Vitebsk province. The arrest opened months of investigation into the ma'amad collection and the chassidic movement before the Rebbe's eventual full acquittal.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe writes petition to Governor Khovansky
summary_en: In Cheshvan or early Kislev 5587 the Mitteler Rebbe wrote a petition to Vitebsk's Governor Khovansky asking that he personally judge the case.
story_body: While held in Vitebsk between Cheshvan and the beginning of Kislev 5587 (October-November 1826), the Mitteler Rebbe composed a written petition to General-Governor Khovansky. He requested that the governor personally adjudicate his case, drawing on kabbalistic and chassidic principles the Alter Rebbe had earlier presented before Czar Paul. The petition built on the framework relating fear of Heaven to fear of an earthly king and argued that a king's vision penetrates more truthfully than that of any subordinate judge.

title_en: Passing of the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer Schneuri, the Mitteler Rebbe, passed away on 9 Kislev 5588.
story_body: The Mitteler Rebbe, Rabbi DovBer Schneuri, passed away on 9 Kislev 5588, just days before the Russian Senate's final verdict in his case. His passing came after a year of investigations stemming from Simcha Kisin's denunciation and his arrest in Vitebsk. The Senate's acquittal would arrive twelve days after his death.

title_en: Senate acquits Mitteler Rebbe of all charges
summary_en: On 21 Kislev 5588 the Russian Supreme Senate acquitted the Mitteler Rebbe and legitimated the ma'amad bais harav system.
story_body: On 21 Kislev 5588, just twelve days after the Mitteler Rebbe's passing, the Supreme Senate in Petersburg upheld the Mohilev high court's acquittal and rejected Governor Khovansky's appeal. The ruling accepted that ma'amad donations were voluntary and that the Rebbe was not an official salaried rabbi, placing the practice outside the 1804 Jewish Statute's prohibitions. This decision legalized ma'amad as the financial foundation supporting Chabad rebbes for generations to come.

title_en: Kehot publishes introduction analyzing the Mitteler Rebbe's petition
summary_en: Kehot published in 5707 an edition containing the Rebbe's introduction examining the authorship of the Mitteler Rebbe's petition to Khovansky.
story_body: In 5707 (1946-1947), Kehot Publication Society issued an edition featuring an introduction by the Rebbe examining the petition written to Vitebsk's General-Governor Khovansky. The introduction argued against attributing the petition to the Alter Rebbe, demonstrating from internal evidence and historical circumstances that it was authored by the Mitteler Rebbe during his Vitebsk arrest. The analysis became foundational to subsequent Chabad scholarship on the imprisonment and acquittal.

title_en: Third denunciation letter by Simcha Keysin against Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch
summary_en: Simcha Keysin submits his third denunciation letter to Governor Khovansky against Rabbi DovBer (the Mittler Rebbe) over collection of Maamad funds.
story_body: In July 1825, the mitnaged Simcha Keysin of Shklov submitted a third denunciation to the governor of Vitebsk, alleging that the Maamad funds collected from chassidim by Rabbi DovBer Schneuri were being used for personal pleasures rather than communal needs. The letter attached a document from 1813 detailing distribution of these funds, supposedly written by the Rebbe himself. This denunciation, along with earlier ones, triggered the criminal investigation of the Mittler Rebbe.

title_en: Simcha Keysin's letter to authorities denouncing the Chabad chassidim of Shklov
summary_en: Simcha Keysin writes to Russian authorities accusing the 'Karliner sect' (chassidim) of seizing synagogues, printing Asiatic-rite prayer books, and oppressing 'true Jews.'
story_body: In June 1825, Simcha Keysin submitted a denunciation to a high Russian official, complaining that the chassidic movement led by the late Rabbi Shneur Zalman and now his son Rabbi DovBer was expanding its influence, seizing parts of the main Shklov synagogue, controlling printing presses for chassidic-rite siddurim, and forcing 'true Jews' to use their kosher meat. He framed the chassidim as an illegitimate sect harming the Jewish community.

title_en: Document on distribution of Maamad funds written by Rabbi DovBer
summary_en: A handwritten document detailing the distribution of Maamad (support fund) monies is composed by Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch.
story_body: In 1813, Rabbi DovBer Schneuri composed a detailed accounting document about the distribution of Maamad funds collected from chassidim. The document was later entrusted to R. Pinchas Schick of Shklov, the treasurer, and after his death fell into the hands of his nephew. It eventually reached the mitnaged Simcha Keysin, who used it as the central piece of evidence in his 1825 denunciation against the Mittler Rebbe.

title_en: Conflict in Shklov over Karliner takeover of main synagogue
summary_en: Major friction erupts in Shklov after chassidim take over a room in the main synagogue; the mitnagdim prepare to file a complaint with the government.
story_body: In 1822, Simcha Keysin found 'great confusion' in Shklov when chassidim took control of a room in the city's main synagogue. The mitnagdim prepared a complaint to the high government, but R. Pinchas Schick of Shklov, a senior chassidic leader, intervened and pledged to persuade Rabbi DovBer to ease pressure on the mitnagdim. As surety, R. Pinchas handed Keysin the Rebbe's handwritten document about Maamad fund distribution.

title_en: Donation pledges to R. Aharon of Staroshele's Maamad fund
summary_en: Nissan Shlomovitch of Chertkov pledges 50 silver rubles annually to R. Aharon Halevi of Staroshele's Maamad fund.
story_body: On 12 June 1819 (Tammuz), Nissan Shlomovitch of Chertkov signed a pledge to give 50 silver rubles annually to Rabbi Aharon Halevi of Staroshele, the founder of the breakaway Strashelye branch of Chabad. He also contributed 25 rubles cash at that time. The records of these donations represent a fragment of Maamad-style fundraising for the parallel chassidic court that arose after the passing of the Alter Rebbe.

title_en: Rabbi DovBer travels abroad to Karlsbad for medical treatment
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch (the Mittler Rebbe) travels to the healing springs of Karlsbad for medical treatment.
story_body: In the summer of 1825 (Tammuz-Av 5585), Rabbi DovBer Schneuri traveled outside Russia to Karlsbad to seek treatment at its therapeutic springs. While he was away, Simcha Keysin's denunciations were being delivered to Governor Khovansky in Vitebsk, setting in motion the chain of events that would culminate in the Rebbe's arrest and trial later that year.

title_en: Governor Khovansky orders Rabbi DovBer brought to Vitebsk for interrogation
summary_en: Governor Khovansky in Vitebsk orders police officials to bring Rabbi DovBer from Lubavitch for criminal investigation.
story_body: In September 1825 (Tishrei 5586), Governor Khovansky of Vitebsk ordered the regional police to detain Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch and bring him to Vitebsk to face investigation arising from Simcha Keysin's denunciations. The escort traveled from Vitebsk to Lubavitch and detoured through Shklov so it could pick up two chassidic witnesses to bring along for questioning.

title_en: Khovansky assigns investigators to lead the inquiry against Rabbi DovBer
summary_en: Governor Khovansky formally transfers the investigation of Rabbi DovBer to designated state investigators.
story_body: On 2 October 1825 (2 Marcheshvan 5586), Governor Khovansky handed responsibility for the inquiry to his special officials, Colonel Loginov and Court Counselor Markov, to gather evidence on the alleged illegal collection of funds by Rabbi DovBer. This marked the formal opening of the state's criminal investigation against the Mittler Rebbe.

title_en: Rabbi DovBer asked to authenticate documents attached to denunciation
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer is asked to confirm whether the documents attached to the denunciation are in his own handwriting; two chassidim are also interrogated.
story_body: On 5 October 1825 (5 Marcheshvan 5586), investigators in Vitebsk asked Rabbi DovBer to confirm that the attachments to Simcha Keysin's denunciation were written in his own hand. The same day, two of his chassidim, R. Zalman Roizes of Slonim and R. Shlomo Freides of Shklov, were also brought before the investigators and interrogated as part of the gathering of evidence.

title_en: First interrogation of Rabbi DovBer in Vitebsk
summary_en: The first formal interrogation of Rabbi DovBer Schneuri begins before Russian state investigators in Vitebsk.
story_body: On 7 October 1825 (7 Marcheshvan 5586), Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch underwent his first official interrogation in Vitebsk in connection with Simcha Keysin's denunciations. The investigators questioned him about the collection and use of Maamad funds, the relations between chassidim and mitnagdim, and the authenticity of the documents Keysin had submitted as evidence.

title_en: Khovansky orders treasury to reimburse travel costs of escort to Lubavitch
summary_en: Khovansky directs the Vitebsk treasury to reimburse his adjutant and the police officers who escorted Rabbi DovBer from Lubavitch via Shklov.
story_body: On 7 October 1825, Governor Khovansky wrote to the Vitebsk Provincial Treasury ordering it to reimburse Lieutenant Chevkin, district police officer Korvitsky, and another officer for the costs of the round-trip carriage journey from Vitebsk to Lubavitch and on to Shklov to fetch Rabbi DovBer and witnesses. They had used 6 horses on the way out and 9 on the return, since two more chassidim were added in Shklov.

title_en: Second interrogation of Rabbi DovBer in Vitebsk
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer undergoes a second interrogation in Vitebsk on the same denunciation case.
story_body: On 15 October 1825 (15 Marcheshvan 5586), Rabbi DovBer was brought again before the state investigators in Vitebsk for a second interrogation. The session continued the inquiry into the collection of Maamad funds and the allegations made by Simcha Keysin, building the formal record that would later be reviewed by higher courts.

title_en: Third interrogation of Rabbi DovBer; investigators sent to Lubavitch and Strashelye
summary_en: Third interrogation of Rabbi DovBer; same day, special agents are dispatched to verify his statements in Lubavitch and to bring Rabbi Aharon of Staroshele in for questioning.
story_body: On 19 October 1825 (19 Marcheshvan 5586), Rabbi DovBer faced his third interrogation in Vitebsk. The same day, the authorities dispatched a special investigator to Lubavitch to verify the Rebbe's testimony against local realities, and sent a separate officer to Strashelye to bring Rabbi Aharon Halevi of Staroshele for questioning in the same broader inquiry into chassidic fundraising.

title_en: Interrogation of Rabbi Aharon Halevi of Staroshele
summary_en: Rabbi Aharon Halevi of Staroshele is interrogated in Vitebsk over a week-long period as part of the wider inquiry into chassidic fundraising.
story_body: From 21 to 28 October 1825 (21–28 Marcheshvan 5586), Rabbi Aharon Halevi of Staroshele, founder of the Strashelye chassidic court, was interrogated in Vitebsk by Russian state investigators. The questioning related to the parallel Maamad fundraising in his branch of Chabad and was part of the broader probe arising from Simcha Keysin's denunciations against Rabbi DovBer.

title_en: Rabbi DovBer submits request to Khovansky to be released home
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer formally petitions Governor Khovansky to release him from detention in Vitebsk and allow him to return home.
story_body: On 4 November 1825 (6 Kislev 5586), with his interrogations concluded, Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch submitted a written request to Governor Khovansky asking to be released from Vitebsk and allowed to return home. The petition came after weeks of questioning, and the governor granted the release a few days later.

title_en: Release of Rabbi DovBer on Yud Kislev (Chag HaGeula of the Mittler Rebbe)
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch is released from Vitebsk on 10 Kislev 5586, the date later marked as his personal Chag HaGeula.
story_body: On 10 Kislev 5586 (late November 1825), Rabbi DovBer Schneuri was released from his detention in Vitebsk. The date became established in Chabad tradition as Yud Kislev, the Chag HaGeula (Festival of Liberation) of the Mittler Rebbe, observed annually as a day of celebration, farbrengens, and study of his teachings.

title_en: Investigators submit summary of investigation to Khovansky
summary_en: The state investigators write up a summary of their interrogation findings and submit it, along with supporting documents, to Governor Khovansky.
story_body: On 10 November 1825 (12 Kislev 5586), the investigators handling the case against Rabbi DovBer wrote a comprehensive review of the interrogations and evidence gathered, and turned the file over to Governor Khovansky. This summary became the basis for the subsequent transfer of the case to the Mohilev provincial authorities for formal judicial proceedings.

title_en: Khovansky transfers case to Mohilev province for trial
summary_en: Governor Khovansky forwards the case file to the Mohilev provincial government so that the case can be tried in the appropriate provincial court.
story_body: On 17 November 1825 (19 Kislev 5586), Khovansky transferred the entire investigative file on Rabbi DovBer to the government of Mohilev province, since Lubavitch and Babinovich fell under that jurisdiction. He simultaneously assigned the chief prosecutor of Mohilev to supervise the trial that would follow.

title_en: Mohilev provincial government sends case to Babinovich peace court
summary_en: The Mohilev provincial government routes the file to the Babinovich peace court for completion of the pre-trial investigation.
story_body: On 19 December 1825 (21 Tevet 5586), Mohilev authorities determined that the pre-trial inquiry was not yet complete and sent the file to the peace court in Babinovich, the jurisdiction to which Lubavitch belonged. The Babinovich court was tasked with finishing the questioning of witnesses before the case could go to formal trial.

title_en: Case file arrives at Babinovich peace court
summary_en: The case file against Rabbi DovBer reaches the Babinovich peace court.
story_body: On 23 December 1825 (25 Tevet 5586), the case file concerning Rabbi DovBer's alleged illegal collection of Maamad funds was formally received at the Babinovich peace court. Weeks would pass before the court actually began processing it, in part because of bureaucratic delays in assigning supervision.

title_en: Chief prosecutor delegates oversight to Babinovich court inspector
summary_en: Mohilev's chief prosecutor delegates judicial oversight of the case to the inspector of the Babinovich district court.
story_body: On 9 January 1826 (13 Shevat 5586), the chief prosecutor of Mohilev province handed over day-to-day supervision of the case against Rabbi DovBer to the inspector of the Babinovich district court, since the trial venue had shifted. This step set the stage for the actual investigative work in Babinovich to begin.

title_en: Babinovich court begins work on the case
summary_en: The Babinovich peace court begins actively processing the case file against Rabbi DovBer.
story_body: On 13 January 1826 (17 Shevat 5586), nearly a month after receiving the file, the Babinovich peace court began actively working on the case against Rabbi DovBer. Within days the court would dispatch a police officer to Lubavitch with written questions for the Rebbe.

title_en: Officer sent to Lubavitch with written questions for Rabbi DovBer
summary_en: The Babinovich court dispatches a police officer with written questions for Rabbi DovBer in Lubavitch.
story_body: On 16 January 1826 (20 Shevat 5586), the Babinovich peace court dispatched a police officer to Lubavitch carrying a list of written questions for Rabbi DovBer. The Rebbe's written answers would have been used to fill out the formal court record without bringing him back to Babinovich in person.

title_en: Court issues investigation orders to Kapust, Orsha, Shklov and Mohilev
summary_en: Babinovich court instructs courts in Kapust, Orsha, Shklov and Mohilev to interrogate local chassidim about the Maamad funds.
story_body: On 12 February 1826 (17 Adar I 5586), the Babinovich peace court, dissatisfied with the evidence it could gather locally, sent instructions to courts in Kapust, Orsha, Shklov and the lower court of Mohilev. Each was ordered to interrogate the chassidim in its town about the collection and distribution of Maamad funds, expanding the geographic scope of the inquiry considerably.

title_en: Mohilev government fines Babinovich court over investigation conduct
summary_en: The Mohilev provincial government fines the Babinovich peace court for illegal leniencies in handling the investigation and orders speedier collection of chassidic testimony.
story_body: On 3 March 1826 (6 Adar II 5586), the government of Mohilev province imposed a fine on the Babinovich peace court, citing illegal leniency in how the investigation was being run. At the same time, it ordered the courts in Kapust, Orsha, Shklov and Mohilev to accelerate gathering chassidic testimony in the case against Rabbi DovBer.

title_en: Babinovich peace court rules on the case
summary_en: The Babinovich peace court issues its decision on the case against Rabbi DovBer.
story_body: On 20 July 1826 (27 Tammuz 5586), the Babinovich peace court formally issued its decision on the case after months of investigation. The ruling and supporting file were then prepared for transfer to the higher provincial court in Mohilev, which would issue the final verdict.

title_en: Case returned to Mohilev higher court with Babinovich recommendation
summary_en: Following the close of the investigation, the case file is returned to the Mohilev higher court along with the Babinovich peace court's recommendation.
story_body: On 3 August 1826 (12 Av 5586), with the local investigation complete, the file was sent back to the higher court of Mohilev province, accompanied by the recommendation of the Babinovich peace court. The higher court would now deliberate on a final, binding verdict in the case against Rabbi DovBer.

title_en: Mohilev higher court acquits Rabbi DovBer
summary_en: The Mohilev higher court rules to acquit Rabbi DovBer and forwards the verdict to the provincial chief prosecutor for review.
story_body: On 29 November 1826 (11 Kislev 5587), after completing its deliberations, the Mohilev higher court issued a verdict acquitting Rabbi DovBer of the charges that had been brought against him. The case file together with the ruling was passed to the chief prosecutor of Mohilev province for the legally required review and confirmation.

title_en: Mohilev chief prosecutor confirms the acquittal verdict
summary_en: The chief prosecutor of Mohilev province formally approves the higher court's acquittal of Rabbi DovBer.
story_body: On 1 February 1827 (16 Shevat 5587), the chief prosecutor of Mohilev province endorsed the higher court's ruling acquitting Rabbi DovBer of the charges brought via Simcha Keysin's denunciations. The approved verdict was then sent on to Governor Khovansky in Vitebsk for his confirmation.

title_en: Acquittal verdict forwarded to Khovansky for confirmation
summary_en: The approved acquittal verdict is sent from Mohilev to Governor Khovansky in Vitebsk for his final confirmation.
story_body: On 9 February 1827 (24 Shevat 5587), the verdict acquitting Rabbi DovBer, now approved by the Mohilev chief prosecutor, was forwarded to Governor Khovansky in Vitebsk. Khovansky was expected to confirm the ruling, but instead would choose to appeal to the Senate in St. Petersburg.

title_en: Khovansky appeals acquittal of Rabbi DovBer to the Senate in St. Petersburg
summary_en: Refusing to confirm the verdict, Khovansky escalates the case by appealing the acquittal of Rabbi DovBer to the Senate of the Empire in St. Petersburg.
story_body: On 15 May 1827 (Rosh Chodesh Sivan 5587), Governor Khovansky declined to confirm the Mohilev court's acquittal of Rabbi DovBer and instead lodged an appeal with the Senate in St. Petersburg. He also attached broader policy proposals affecting the status and rights of rabbis throughout Russia, which the Senate said it would consider separately.

title_en: Khovansky orders Mohilev court to send case file to the Senate with his appeal
summary_en: Khovansky writes the Mohilev higher court instructing it to forward the case file together with his appeal to the Senate.
story_body: On 31 May 1827 (Rosh Chodesh Sivan 5587), writing from Kaluga, Khovansky directed the first department of the Mohilev higher court to ship the 16-page case file (no. 553) along with his official opinion to the ruling Senate. This formally placed the acquittal of Rabbi DovBer in the hands of the highest judicial body of the Russian Empire.

title_en: Passing of Rabbi DovBer, the Mittler Rebbe
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer Schneuri, the Mittler Rebbe, passes away on 9 Kislev 5588.
story_body: On 9 Kislev 5588 (late November / early December 1827), Rabbi DovBer Schneuri, the Mittler Rebbe, passed away. His passing came mid-way through the Senate's appeal proceedings concerning the Khovansky case; the Senate did not yet know of his death when it issued its ruling on the case days later. The date 9 Kislev is now marked annually as his yahrzeit, just one day before his Chag HaGeula on 10 Kislev.

title_en: Senate confirms acquittal of the Mittler Rebbe
summary_en: The Senate in St. Petersburg confirms the Mohilev acquittal of Rabbi DovBer, closing the criminal proceedings.
story_body: On 28 November 1827 (21 Kislev 5588), the ruling Senate in St. Petersburg upheld the Mohilev higher court's acquittal of Rabbi DovBer, formally closing the criminal case that had been opened against him in 1825 following Simcha Keysin's denunciations. At the time of its ruling, the Senate was unaware that the Mittler Rebbe had passed away on 9 Kislev, just twelve days earlier.

title_en: Senate rejects most of Khovansky's proposed reforms on Jewish status
summary_en: In winter 5594, the Senate informs Khovansky that it has rejected most of his proposals regarding the legal status of Russian Jewry, accepting only a few details.
story_body: In the winter of 1834 (5594), after years of delay, the Senate responded to Governor Khovansky's policy proposals that had been attached to his 1827 appeal in the Mittler Rebbe's case. The Senate decided to reject most of his suggestions concerning the status and rights of rabbis and Jewish communities, accepting only a few minor points, while informing him that a comprehensive new statute on Jews was already being prepared.

title_en: New Russian statute on the Jews published
summary_en: The Russian Empire publishes its new statute regulating the status of the Jews, the second such code after the 1804/5 statute.
story_body: In 5595 (1835), the Russian government published a new statute on the Jews, the second comprehensive code of its kind after the original statute of 5565 (1804/5). The legislation governed key aspects of Jewish communal life, the role of rabbis, residence rights, and other matters that had been at the center of Khovansky's earlier proposals and of the legal pressures on the chassidic movement throughout the 1820s and 1830s.

title_en: Khovansky assigns investigators to Kisin's denunciation against the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: Governor-General Khovansky formally assigns Colonel Loginov, Court Counselor Markov, and Major Morozov to investigate Kisin's denunciation accusing Rabbi Dovber Schneuri of illegally collecting funds from chasidim.
story_body: On 2 October 1825 (document no. 4831), Khovansky formally tasked three officials with investigating the denunciation lodged in June 1825 by a Vitebsk Jew named Kisin against 'Berke Schneur,' the rebbe of the Chasidic sect, accusing him of extorting large sums from Jews loyal to the 'old faith.' Kisin had produced an 1813 Hebrew distribution document showing 35,000 rubles allegedly divided among the rebbe's relatives, and claimed the rebbe was violating the 9 December 1804 Jewish Statute (§52) forbidding rabbis from accumulating wealth. Khovansky ordered the investigators to verify the document's authenticity, examine the sources of the funds, and summon the rebbe for formal questioning.

title_en: Morozov dismissed from the investigation against the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: Two weeks after appointing three investigators, Khovansky dismisses Major Morozov, leaving Loginov and Markov alone to investigate the rebbe.
story_body: About two weeks after assigning Loginov, Markov, and Morozov on 2 October 1825 to investigate the denunciation against the Mitteler Rebbe, Khovansky relieved Morozov of the assignment (document 18). The investigation thereafter continued under Colonel Loginov and Court Counselor Markov alone, who carried it forward to its conclusion.

title_en: Reb Zalman Slonim testifies about the Mitteler Rebbe's maamad funds
summary_en: Reb Zalman Leizerovich Slonim of Shklov testifies to investigators about how the Mitteler Rebbe collected and distributed maamad funds after Napoleon's invasion.
story_body: On 5 October 1825, Reb Zalman Slonim of Shklov, a 53-year-old chasid who had been appointed by the Mitteler Rebbe (together with Pinchas Shick and Shlomo Freidin) to oversee distribution of maamad funds, gave sworn testimony. He recounted how in spring 1813 the rebbe arrived in Shklov with his family, gathered prominent chasidim, and described his impoverishment after the French looting and burning of his Liadi properties. Slonim confirmed that contributions were freely given by chasidim according to ability, that the 35,000-ruble distribution document was indeed in the rebbe's handwriting, and that another rebbe, Aharon of Starosselye, also received voluntary support nearby.

title_en: Prosecutor of Mogilev confirms receipt of Khovansky's order in the rebbe's case
summary_en: Provincial Prosecutor Smolaninov of Mogilev formally acknowledges Khovansky's directive to oversee the legal proceedings against the Mitteler Rebbe.
story_body: On 2 December 1825, Smolaninov, the General Prosecutor of Mogilev Province, sent report no. 2292 to Governor-General Khovansky in Vitebsk acknowledging receipt of Khovansky's 17 November order (no. 5850). The order had instructed him to supervise the provincial government's transfer of the investigation against Rabbi Dovber Schneuri to the appropriate court, and to ensure proper application of the law in handling the defendants. The acknowledgement was received in Vitebsk on 5 December 1825.

title_en: Mogilev provincial government transfers the rebbe's case to Babinavichi court
summary_en: The Mogilev provincial government reports to Khovansky that it has forwarded the investigation against the rebbe to the magistrate's court in Babinavichi district.
story_body: On 16 December 1825, the Mogilev provincial government (signed by Civil Governor Maksimov and Counselors Butovich, Kishkovich, and Chitozhribsky) reported to Khovansky on action taken in response to his 17 November order (no. 5849). The report summarized findings against Rabbi Dovber Schneuri — including the 35,000-ruble post-1812 collection, ongoing annual collections of 10,000-14,000 rubles, and his serving as arbitrator between Jews and Christians — all allegedly contrary to §§51-52 of the 1804 Jewish Statute. Per §110 of provincial law, the file (no. 872) was forwarded to the magistrate's court in Babinavichi district, which contained Lubavitch, for prosecution.
