title_en: Senate in Petersburg upholds acquittal of the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: The Governing Senate in St. Petersburg rejects Khovansky's appeal and affirms the Mogilev high court's acquittal of the Mitteler Rebbe.
story_body: On 28 November 1827, the Governing Senate in Petersburg issued its decision on Khovansky's 25 May appeal of the Mogilev high court ruling acquitting Rabbi Dovber Schneuri of charges of illegal fundraising. Reviewing testimony from the Babinavichi community, 5 other communities, and 160 sworn witnesses — all confirming that the 30,000-ruble post-1812 collection and ongoing support were given voluntarily, and that the rebbe served as a preacher rather than as a salaried, tax-collecting rabbi — the Senate found Kisin's denunciation legally unfounded. It ordered the rebbe fully acquitted and referred Khovansky's broader proposals on Russian rabbis to its First Department. The decree was received in Mogilev on 12 December 1827.

title_en: Mogilev high court forwards Senate acquittal decree to Khovansky
summary_en: The First Department of the Mogilev high court sends Khovansky a copy of the Senate's decree acquitting the Mitteler Rebbe.
story_body: On 11 January 1828, the First Department of the Mogilev high court (signed by Chief Judge Felix Marzhevsky and Counselor Porfiry Karpilavich) forwarded Khovansky a copy of the Senate's 28 November 1827 decree, which had reached the department on 2 January 1828. Because the Senate had sent its ruling directly to the Mogilev provincial government rather than to Khovansky (who had filed the appeal), the high court provided him with the official copy. The transmittal (no. 54) closed Khovansky's involvement in the case begun by his 18 September 1825 proposal (no. 4425).

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe arranges distribution of maamad funds after the Alter Rebbe's passing
summary_en: At the end of the first year after the Alter Rebbe's passing, the Mitteler Rebbe organizes distribution of 35,000 rubles in maamad funds among the Alter Rebbe's descendants.
story_body: In Tevet 5574 (December 1813–January 1814), one year after the passing of the Alter Rebbe on 24 Tevet 5573, the Mitteler Rebbe arranged the distribution of 35,000 rubles in maamad funds. The funds had been collected from chasidim to rebuild the household of the rebbe in Lubavitch after the original household in Liadi was destroyed by fire when the family fled Napoleon's invasion. The Mitteler Rebbe entrusted the distribution to Reb Pinchas Shick of Shklov, with Reb Shlomo Freidin and Reb Zalman Roizes Slonim of Shklov as oversight, allocating shares to his brothers, sisters, children, stepmother, and other relatives of the Alter Rebbe.

title_en: Arbitration agreement before the Mitteler Rebbe between Litoslavsky and Averba
summary_en: Landowner Ivan Litoslavsky and Yeshaya Averba sign an arbitration agreement to have a 7,000-ruble debt judged by the Mitteler Rebbe in Lubavitch.
story_body: On 24 May 1814, landowner Ivan Litoslavsky and Yeshaya Berkovich Averba of Surazh district, Vitebsk province, signed an agreement in Lubavitch placing their 7,000-ruble debt dispute before the Mitteler Rebbe for binding arbitration. The agreement, witnessed by the Vilna merchant Shmaryahu Benyaminovich Berkin, declared that both parties would accept the rebbe's ruling without appeal. The document was later submitted as evidence to prove that the rebbe had violated Russian law by acting as arbitrator between a Jew and a non-Jew.

title_en: Michael ben Shlomo of Nikolayev sends 1000 rubles to the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: A chassid from Nikolayev encloses 1000 rubles for the Mitteler Rebbe and promises more before Passover.
story_body: On 18 Shevat 5585, Michael ben Shlomo of Nikolayev wrote to the Mitteler Rebbe (Admur HaEmtzaei) enclosing 1000 rubles in support, with a promise to send the additional sum by mail before Passover. The letter is one of many surviving documents showing the network of financial support flowing from chassidim across the Russian Empire to the Rebbe's court.

title_en: Shimcha Kissin files an informer's complaint against the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: Vitebsk resident Shimcha Kissin denounces the Mitteler Rebbe to Governor-General Khovansky, triggering an investigation.
story_body: In July 1825, the Jew Shimcha Kissin of Vitebsk submitted a petition to Governor-General Khovansky accusing the chassidic sect ("Karliners") and its leader Rabbi Berke Schneur (the Mitteler Rebbe) of pressuring traditional Jews and collecting large sums via emissaries for the Rebbe's personal benefit. He attached a Yiddish distribution document and two letters as evidence. The complaint launched the entire investigation that culminated in the Mitteler Rebbe's arrest.

title_en: Khovansky orders Adjutant Vlasenko sent to fetch R. Aharon of Starashele
summary_en: Khovansky proposes that the treasury fund Adjutant Vlasenko's travel to Starashele to bring R. Aharon Halevi to Vitebsk for questioning.
story_body: On 19 October 1825, Governor-General Khovansky directed the Vitebsk treasury chamber to pay Adjutant Captain Vlasenko's travel expenses for a mission, accompanied by a policeman of the Mogilev province, to the town of Starashele. The trip was to bring R. Aharon Halevi of Starashele to Vitebsk to be questioned in connection with the Kissin informer affair. Five days later the treasury reported the cost at 119 rubles 52 kopeks.

title_en: Prosecutor General transfers oversight of the Mitteler Rebbe's case to Babinovich
summary_en: Mogilev Prosecutor General Smolaninov orders the Babinovich district court inspector to conduct the inquiry into the charges against the Mitteler Rebbe.
story_body: On 9 January 1826 (13 Shevat 5586), Mogilev Prosecutor General Smolaninov reported to Governor-General Khovansky that he had instructed the inspector of the Babinovich district court to examine the file on Rabbi Berke Schneur (Mitteler Rebbe) of Lubavitch and reach a swift, lawful decision. This formally moved the case from Khovansky's officials into the regular court system.

title_en: Babinovich Peace Court rules in favor of the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: The Babinovich peace court issues its decision in the case against the Mitteler Rebbe.
story_body: On 20 July 1826, the peace court of Babinovich rendered its decision in the case opened against the Mitteler Rebbe on the basis of Shimcha Kissin's denunciation. The court concluded that contributions to the Rebbe were freely given and could not be considered illegal, dismissing the charges. The verdict was the first of several rulings exonerating the Rebbe.

title_en: Mogilev High Court's First Chamber upholds the Mitteler Rebbe's acquittal
summary_en: The First Chamber of the Mogilev High Court rules that the Mitteler Rebbe is not guilty.
story_body: On 29 November 1826, the First Chamber of the Mogilev High Court ruled in the case of Rabbi Berke Schneur. It found that the donations he received were given voluntarily by his followers and that no criminal offense had occurred, agreeing with the earlier Babinovich verdict. The decision was later presented to Governor-General Khovansky, who disagreed and appealed it to the Ruling Senate.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe's case presented to Governor-General Khovansky
summary_en: The case file on the Mitteler Rebbe is forwarded to Governor-General Khovansky for review.
story_body: On 12 February 1827, the Mogilev High Court's decision in favor of the Mitteler Rebbe was forwarded to Governor-General Khovansky. Khovansky considered the acquittal unjust and prepared an appeal, with his own legislative proposals concerning Jewish rabbis, to be submitted to the Ruling Senate.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe's case submitted to the Ruling Senate
summary_en: Khovansky's appeal of the Mitteler Rebbe's acquittal reaches the Ruling Senate.
story_body: On 15 May 1827, Governor-General Khovansky's appeal in the case of Rabbi Berke Schneur was submitted to the Ruling Senate in St. Petersburg, together with his proposals concerning the conduct of Jewish rabbis. The Senate would deliberate for six months before issuing its final ruling later that year.

title_en: Ruling Senate exonerates the Mitteler Rebbe of all charges
summary_en: The Ruling Senate dismisses the case, declaring the Mitteler Rebbe innocent of all charges.
story_body: On 28 November 1827, the Ruling Senate decreed that Kissin's denunciation had no legal basis and that Rabbi Berke Schneur was not guilty of any criminal offense, ordering him fully cleared. Khovansky's accompanying proposals regarding Jewish rabbis were referred to the First Chamber of the Senate for separate review. The Senate's decree was communicated to the Mogilev provincial government, formally ending the legal proceedings.

title_en: Vitebsk treasury asks who should reimburse adjutant's travel costs
summary_en: The Vitebsk treasury chamber petitions Khovansky to determine from whom to recover the 119 rubles spent on Vlasenko's mission.
story_body: On 17 March 1828, following the Senate's exoneration of the Mitteler Rebbe, the Vitebsk treasury chamber wrote to Governor-General Khovansky asking how the 119 rubles 52 kopeks paid for Adjutant Vlasenko's 1825 trip to Starashele should be recovered. Since the Senate had found no one guilty, the funds would eventually have to be written off as a state expense. The exchange continued through September 1828.

title_en: Rebbe Menachem Mendel Schneerson urges Hendel Deutsch to search Russian archives
summary_en: At a yechidus in New York, the Lubavitcher Rebbe asks the Leningrad historian Hendel Deutsch to search for documents related to Lubavitch.
story_body: In 5736 (1976), R. Hendel Deutsch, a descendant of Chabad chassidim engaged in Russian historical research in Leningrad, visited New York. In a private audience, the Lubavitcher Rebbe proposed that he search for documents connected to Lubavitch in Soviet archives. Over the next decade Deutsch occasionally sent material to the Rebbe via his nephew R. Chaim Yitzchak Kugel.

title_en: Search begins for the Mitteler Rebbe's arrest file in Soviet archives
summary_en: During R. Shalom DovBer Levin's mission to Moscow, the Rebbe directs that Russian archives also be searched for the Mitteler Rebbe's arrest file.
story_body: In winter 5748 (early 1988), Rabbi Shalom DovBer Levin was dispatched to Moscow to search for the seforim collection of the Rebbeim. Before the trip he wrote to the Rebbe suggesting that R. Nissan Mindel also check the Tsarist government archives for documents related to the Mitteler Rebbe's arrest. The Rebbe replied that the search should extend to documents concerning the Alter Rebbe and the Tzemach Tzedek as well. On Erev Rosh Chodesh Shevat the team visited Hendel Deutsch in Petersburg, who suggested the Khovansky archive might be in Minsk.

title_en: Hendel Deutsch emigrates and is sent by ChaMa to search Russian archives
summary_en: After emigrating to the United States, R. Hendel Deutsch is dispatched by ChaMa to search Russian archives for Chabad historical documents.
story_body: In 5751 (1991), R. Hendel Deutsch emigrated from the Soviet Union to the United States. That year the ChaMa organization sent him back to continue searching Russian archives for documents related to Chabad history. He returned with many documents but, despite further guidance from R. Shalom DovBer Levin, did not locate the Mitteler Rebbe's arrest file.

title_en: R. Shalom DovBer Levin briefs Prof. Yirmiyahu Branover on the missing arrest file
summary_en: Prof. Yirmiyahu Branover visits New York, where Levin lays out a detailed search plan for the Mitteler Rebbe's arrest file via Shamir's archive access.
story_body: At the beginning of Tishrei 5753 (October 1992), Prof. Yirmiyahu Branover visited New York. R. Shalom DovBer Levin met with him and laid out his theory that the Khovansky-era arrest file of the Mitteler Rebbe could finally be located through the Shamir organization's newly authorized archive access in Russia. Levin then wrote a detailed memorandum identifying which provincial archives — particularly Minsk — should be searched.

title_en: Levin meets Igor and Boruch Gorin in Moscow's Marina Roshcha
summary_en: In Moscow, Levin instructs Shamir's archive researcher Igor to focus the search on Minsk for the Mitteler Rebbe's file.
story_body: On 2 Shevat 5753 (24 January 1993), R. Shalom DovBer Levin met in Marina Roshcha, Moscow, with Igor, who was working for Shamir to locate Chabad-related documents, together with Boruch Gorin. Levin explained why the search should now concentrate on Minsk and handed over a written summary. A few months later Wagner joined the project.

title_en: Levin and Wagner plan a Shamir trip to Minsk archives
summary_en: Meeting in Moscow, Levin and Wagner finalize a plan to search Minsk archives for the Mitteler Rebbe's arrest file.
story_body: On Erev Shabbat 20 Tammuz 5753 (9 July 1993), R. Shalom DovBer Levin met with Igor Wagner in Moscow to discuss the methodology of the document search. They agreed that immediately after Shabbat the team would travel to Minsk to look specifically for the file relating to the arrest and liberation of the Mitteler Rebbe.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe's arrest file located in Minsk
summary_en: After years of searching, the file from the Mitteler Rebbe's arrest is found and photographed in Minsk.
story_body: On 2 Nissan 5754 (14 March 1994), R. Boruch Schiff received notification from Minsk that the long-sought file had been located and photographed — some 120 pages of documents from the Khovansky chancellery covering the entire 1825-1828 affair. The find ended a search that had begun in 1976 with the Rebbe's instructions to Hendel Deutsch and intensified in winter 1988. The translated dossier became the basis for the published volume of the case.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe writes to R. Sh., R. Y., and R. M. about the investigations
summary_en: During the investigations the Mitteler Rebbe writes a confidential letter outlining strategy and pleading for chassidic unity in petitions to the authorities.
story_body: Around Adar–Nissan 5586 (spring 1826), in the midst of the Khovansky investigations, the Mitteler Rebbe wrote to three chassidim (R. Shmuel, R. Yosef Yitzchak, and R. Menachem Mendel) discussing the delicate political situation. He laid out a strategy whereby the rank-and-file chassidim themselves would petition the courts, attesting that chassidic and non-chassidic Jews lived in halachic unity, and pleaded with R. Tzvi of Polotsk not to separate himself from the chassidic community.

title_en: Lubavitch fair assembly raises funds for Jews expelled from villages
summary_en: Representatives from Mogilev and Vitebsk provinces gathered at the Lubavitch fair to organize aid and lobbying for Jews expelled from villages.
story_body: On Wednesday evening, 20 Adar I 5584 (20 February 1824), Jewish leaders from towns across the Mogilev and Vitebsk provinces convened at the annual Lubavitch fair to address the plight of fellow Jews recently expelled from village settlements and left without means of livelihood. They resolved to send delegates to St. Petersburg to lobby imperial officials, allocating 60% of the funding burden to Mogilev province and 40% to Vitebsk. Trustees were elected — Alexander Ziskind of Dubrovna and Moshe Yehuda Leibowitz Poponia of Shklov for Mogilev (acting in consultation with Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch), and Binyamin Beinish Nachumowitz of Vitebsk and Binyamin Beinish Zussamowitz of Polotsk for Vitebsk.

title_en: Vitebsk leaders ratify trustee list for expelled-Jews relief fund
summary_en: Vitebsk province delegates reaffirmed the 690-ruble apportionment and replaced a trustee who declined the role with Chaim Simcha Ginzburg.
story_body: Three days after the main Lubavitch assembly, on Motzaei Shabbat into Sunday, 23 February 1824 (Adar I 5584), Vitebsk-area delegates signed a follow-up agreement in Vitebsk. They reaffirmed the 690-ruble share owed by their province, broke down the contribution by district, and replaced Binyamin Beinish Nachumowitz — who declined the trusteeship — with the prominent Chaim Simcha Ginzburg. The agreement was copied by Mendel the scribe and signed by representatives from Vitebsk and Polotsk.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe writes coded letter on the state of Chassidut
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch wrote a cryptic letter to close Chassidim addressing a faction claiming the Alter Rebbe had no successor.
story_body: In 5576 (1816), early in his leadership, the Mitteler Rebbe sent a heavily coded letter to confidants — including Pinchas Shick of Shklov — about a group of Chassidim who circulated the claim that after the Alter Rebbe's passing there was no rabbi to fill his place and that Chassidut had ceased. The Rebbe acknowledged Pinchas's earlier 'prophecy' that this struggle would arise and pass, and observed that even as Chassidut was being denigrated, the practice of fundraising continued to spread. The letter was later seized from Pinchas Shick's estate and used by an informer as part of the case against the Rebbe.

title_en: First interrogation of the Mitteler Rebbe by the provincial commission
summary_en: The provincial investigative commission formally presented eleven questions to Rabbi DovBer Schneuri about an internal fund-distribution document.
story_body: On 7 October 1825 (7 Marcheshvan 5586), the commission established by the provincial governor delivered eleven written questions to the Mitteler Rebbe regarding a document — already confirmed to be in his own handwriting — that distributed 35,000 rubles among his relatives. The interrogators Colonel Loginov, Court Counselor Markov, and Major Morozov pressed him on the source of the funds, why he collected money from Chassidim beyond his official salary, the meaning of the 'shtar iska' (rabbinic workaround for interest-bearing loans), and the secrecy surrounding the document. They demanded answers without delay.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe submits written answers to the interrogators
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer Schneuri responded point-by-point to all eleven questions, detailing the family's 1812 losses and the structure of Chassidic donations.
story_body: On 9 October 1825 (9 Marcheshvan 5586), the Mitteler Rebbe submitted detailed written answers explaining that the 35,000 rubles in question were one-time donations gathered after the family's 60,000-ruble loss when the French burned their property in Liadi during the 1812 invasion. He described fleeing with his father to inner Russia, his father's death in Haditch, and the appeal of Belarus Jews who reached him in Kremenchug asking that he succeed his father as their rabbi. He insisted Chassidim's gifts are voluntary and never fixed taxes, protested that a translator had inflated the sum to 140,000 rubles, and asked to see the original Hebrew document to identify the error. He signed in Hebrew, with Yehuda Yaffe of Kopust signing the Russian version on his behalf.

title_en: Court inspector Kilikovsky reports delays in Mitteler Rebbe case
summary_en: District inspector Kilikovsky informed Governor-General Khovansky that the Babinovich peace court was mishandling the case against Rabbi DovBer.
story_body: On 23 January 1826 (27 Shvat 5586), Inspector Kilikovsky of the Babinovich district court reported to Governor-General Khovansky that the case against Rabbi Berke Schneur of Lubavitch had stalled. The file had arrived at the peace court on 23 December 1825 and sat unexamined; only on 15 January 1826 did officials review it, opting on 16 January to send written questions via a constable to the rabbi and the Jewish communities — bypassing proper procedure, which required summoning the rabbi for direct questioning. Kilikovsky reported the irregularity and noted that the secretary Zhuravkovich had already been dismissed by the Mogilev provincial administration for misconduct.

title_en: Petersburg Senate replies to Khovansky on rabbinic authority
summary_en: The Governing Senate told provincial authorities to enforce existing 1804 statutes against unregulated rabbinic donations and civil adjudication.
story_body: On 25 January 1834 (27 Shvat 5594), the Governing Senate in Petersburg responded to Governor-General Khovansky's three recommendations on rabbis. The first — that rabbinic pay require provincial approval — was deferred to the comprehensive Jewish statute then in deliberation at the State Council, citing an 1828 prohibition on new Jewish laws until the general code was complete. The second and third — barring extra donations to rabbis and barring them from civil adjudication — were not enacted as new law but issued as administrative directives to enforce Sections 49, 51, and 52 of the 1804 Jewish Constitution.

title_en: Mogilev Chassidim sign agreement for new synagogue and mikveh
summary_en: The Chassidic community of Mogilev empowered five trustees to build a synagogue on newly purchased land and operate the attached bathhouse and mikveh.
story_body: On 17 July 1822 (11 Menachem Av 5582), members of the community identified as 'Chassidim of the Lubavitcher Rebbe' in Mogilev signed a binding agreement appointing Wolf Rashel, Shlomo Dankin, and Aizik Cohen, together with community elders Yosef Cohen and Yeshaya Mirkin, as trustees to oversee construction of a new synagogue on land purchased from Rasse Oleshevskaya. The trustees received full discretion over revenues, seat sales, and accounting, with no obligation to render reports. Any shortfall during construction would be advanced personally or borrowed, then repaid from future income of the adjoining bathhouse and mikveh, the synagogue's ground-floor rentals, and seat sales.

title_en: Alter Rebbe flees Liadi with family ahead of French advance
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi abandoned his home, library, and possessions to flee deep into Russia rather than remain under French rule.
story_body: In 1812, as Napoleon's army advanced into Belarus and neared Dubrovna, Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi abandoned his spacious home, valuable library, and all possessions in Liadi, fleeing with his family and close followers — including his son DovBer — into the Russian interior out of loyalty to the Russian throne. The French subsequently looted and burned the family's property, inflicting a 60,000-ruble loss. The family wandered through Kursk province for about six months in severe destitution, a period that ended with the Alter Rebbe's passing in Haditch in Poltava province.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe undertakes fundraising journey through Ukraine and Lithuania
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer travelled across Volhynia, Ukraine, Little Russia, and Lithuania to raise funds to rebuild after the family's 1812 losses.
story_body: After his father's passing and the family's wartime ruin, in 1813 Rabbi DovBer travelled through the Volhynia, Ukraine, Little Russia, and Lithuania regions to gather support for rebuilding homes, a large synagogue for gatherings and discourses, and household necessities. Communities along the route — both Chassidic and non-Chassidic — convened assemblies and contributed substantial sums, and Belarus communities followed through on the pledges they had sent to him in Kremenchug. In total roughly 35,000 rubles were collected and distributed among family members for housing, clothing, books, and about six months of living expenses.

title_en: Second wave of Jewish expulsions from Russian villages begins
summary_en: Imperial policy launched a renewed campaign to expel Jews from rural villages across the Mogilev and Vitebsk provinces.
story_body: In 5582 (1822) the second wave of expulsions of Jews from villages began, displacing families across the Mogilev and Vitebsk provinces and leaving them without homes or means of livelihood. The crisis prompted the Lubavitch fair assembly of 1824, in which Chassidic leaders coordinated a province-wide relief fund and Petersburg lobbying effort under the guidance of the Mitteler Rebbe.

title_en: Acting court inspector reports on Mitteler Rebbe case progress
summary_en: Acting district court inspector Dobravolski reports to Governor-General Khovansky on the slow progress of the Mitteler Rebbe's case at the Babinovich peace court.
story_body: Following Khovansky's order while passing through Babinovich, the acting court inspector took charge of expediting the case against Rabbi DovBer Schneuri of Lubavitch. The inspector found that the case had reached the peace court on December 23, 1825, but progress had been slow. Inquiries sent to the Rebbe were lost in transit, forcing a second messenger to be dispatched. The court then resolved to take sworn testimony from Jewish communities in Orsha, Kopust and Shklov regarding their alleged 1813 invitation to the Rebbe to succeed his father.

title_en: Mohilev High Court relays Senate recommendations on rabbinic conduct
summary_en: The Mohilev High Court forwards to Khovansky its 1827 recommendations to the Senate on illegal fundraising by Rabbi DovBer Schneuri and the proper role of rabbis.
story_body: Seven years after Khovansky submitted his original recommendations to the Senate, the Mohilev High Court's criminal division relayed a copy back to him. The document recommended dismissing the Mitteler Rebbe from his rabbinic post since he could not read or write Russian, Polish, or German as required by section 10 of the Jewish statute. It further proposed barring rabbis from organizing fundraising drives and from adjudicating civil disputes between Jews, restricting them to compensation set under provincial supervision.

title_en: Mohilev court confirms Lubavitch community's power of attorney
summary_en: The Mohilev peace court formally registers and confirms a power of attorney from the Chabad community of Lubavitch on behalf of Jewish residents of Mohilev.
story_body: The power of attorney from the Chasidic community of the Rebbe of Lubavitch, representing the brotherhood of Jewish residents of Mohilev, was presented and entered into the register of the Mohilev peace court as number 51. Signed by Mohilev residents including Litman Avramovich Makrievich, Leib Pevzner, Chaim Shimenovich Bichavski, and Shilem Movshovich Shainin, it was certified by the court with the government seal and witnessed by the mayor and councilmen.

title_en: Corrected translation submitted in Mitteler Rebbe fundraising probe
summary_en: An accurate Russian retranslation of a disputed Hebrew passage from the Rebbe's records is submitted to the investigation committee, refuting claims of a 140,000 ruble sum.
story_body: During the Rebbe's interrogation, investigators relied on a mistranslated Hebrew passage to claim he had collected roughly 140,000 rubles, of which only 35,000 had been distributed. The Rebbe insisted the translation was falsified and requested access to the original. A new accurate translation was prepared by the Rebbe's translator, the chasid Yehuda Yaffe of Kopust, who certified its accuracy alongside the Rebbe before Court Counselor Markov. The corrected text showed the disputed phrase referred to a portion of the total 35,000 rubles, not an additional sum.

title_en: Khovansky reports Babinovich court mismanagement to Mohilev government
summary_en: Governor-General Khovansky proposes to the Mohilev provincial government that the Babinovich peace court be publicly punished for mishandling the Mitteler Rebbe's case.
story_body: Khovansky relayed the district court inspector's findings that the Babinovich peace court had failed to bring the Rebbe in for sworn interrogation as the law required, instead sending a policeman with questions who had not yet returned. The inspector attributed the delays to the court officials' incompetence and ignorance of proper procedure. Khovansky proposed publicly punishing the court for deviating from legal procedure and noted that the secretary Zhuravkovich had already been dismissed for misconduct, calling for a reliable replacement so the case could not be further stalled.

title_en: Senate ban on rabbinic fundraising and civil arbitration relayed
summary_en: Khovansky transmits to the Mohilev and Vitebsk governments the Senate's order forbidding rabbis from collecting voluntary donations or adjudicating civil disputes.
story_body: Acting on Khovansky's 1827 recommendation, the Senate had referred the matter to the Minister of the Interior, who cited an 1828 directive forbidding new specific laws about Jews until the general Jewish statute was finalized. Instead, the minister called for strict enforcement of the existing 1804 statute's sections 49, 51, and 52. The Senate adopted this view in late January 1834, instructing Khovansky to notify Jews of Mohilev and Vitebsk that they must not donate to rabbis or use rabbis to settle civil disputes, but instead refer such matters to the established courts.

title_en: Investigation continues with sworn testimony from Jewish communities
summary_en: Court inspector Kilikovski reports that the Babinovich court is gathering sworn testimony from Jewish communities in Orsha, Kopust and Shklov about their 1813 invitation to the Rebbe.
story_body: Inspector Kilikovski reported that on February 8 the policeman sent to question the Rebbe had returned admitting he had lost the Rebbe's responses on the road from Lubavitch to Babinovich. A second messenger was dispatched and brought back responses on February 10. The court then resolved to obtain sworn testimony from communities in Orsha and Kopust, and from chasidim in Shklov, to verify whether they had written to the Rebbe in Kremenchug in 1813 promising to compensate his losses from the French invasion and to support his family if he succeeded his father as their rabbi.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe's second interrogation on synagogue and book costs
summary_en: The investigation committee questions the Mitteler Rebbe in detail about the construction of the Lubavitch synagogue and the purchase of religious books.
story_body: The committee of investigators — Colonel Loginov, Court Counselor Markov, and Major Morozov — pressed the Rebbe to specify how much of the collected funds went to building the large Lubavitch synagogue and acquiring sacred books. Distrusting his answers, the governor would soon dispatch a special investigator to Lubavitch to verify the responses on the ground. The Rebbe's written replies were given the same day, with the on-site verification mission departing four days later.

title_en: Khovansky reports lost responses and orders fast case resolution
summary_en: Khovansky reports to the Mohilev government on the lost interrogation responses and demands the responsible parties be punished and the case completed urgently.
story_body: Following the latest district court inspector's report, Khovansky relayed that the policeman sent with questions to the Rebbe had lost the responses on the road from Lubavitch to Babinovich. He proposed punishing those responsible at the Babinovich peace court for sending a policeman instead of bringing the Rebbe in for proper interrogation. Khovansky also instructed the Orsha and Kopust town councils and the Mohilev lower court to expedite the requested testimony, and reiterated his earlier call for a competent secretary to be appointed.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe's answers on Lubavitch synagogue construction
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe details to the investigation committee that the Lubavitch synagogue cost 6,000 rubles, with thousands more spent on Torah scrolls, furnishings, and books.
story_body: In his written response to the committee's questions, the Rebbe specified that the large synagogue in Lubavitch had cost 6,000 rubles to build. Four Torah scrolls of the five books of Moses written on parchment cost 1,500 rubles, while crystal chandeliers, arks and other interior furnishings came to 500 rubles. Religious books reached roughly 3,000 rubles. The Rebbe stressed that since construction occurred over time, he could not state with certainty how much came from the collected funds versus later income.

title_en: Khovansky orders Mohilev prosecutor to oversee Rebbe's case
summary_en: Khovansky instructs the General Prosecutor of Mohilev province to closely supervise the handling of the Mitteler Rebbe's case and ensure rapid execution of court demands.
story_body: Building on his earlier reports about the disorder at the Babinovich peace court, Khovansky directly instructed the provincial General Prosecutor to ensure the proposals issued to Mohilev province were carried out. The order emphasized swift execution of the Babinovich court's requests, and parallel cooperation from the lower court of Mohilev province, all to be done promptly and without delay.

title_en: Investigator Morozov reassigned from Mitteler Rebbe investigation
summary_en: Khovansky removes Major Morozov from the Mitteler Rebbe investigation team to focus on an unrelated criminal probe, leaving Loginov and Markov to complete the inquiry.
story_body: About two weeks into the month-long investigation that ran from early Cheshvan to early Kislev, Major Morozov was reassigned to a separate criminal case involving misuse of treasury funds. Khovansky formally released Morozov from the joint inquiry and instructed Loginov and Markov to complete the entire investigation without him, urging them to make every effort to bring out the truth. The two remaining investigators carried the case forward together.

title_en: Mohilev General Prosecutor reports on Rebbe's case to Khovansky
summary_en: General Prosecutor Smolaninov reports to Khovansky that the Mohilev provincial government has done nothing to expedite the Mitteler Rebbe's case.
story_body: Smolaninov informed Khovansky that despite the demand for a quick legal resolution, the provincial government had taken no action. He summarized the latest developments: the lost interrogation responses, the second messenger who retrieved them on February 10, and the decision to gather sworn testimony from communities in Orsha, Kopust and Shklov. Smolaninov reported that he had personally ordered the district court inspector to ensure the required testimony was gathered promptly and that no further delay would be tolerated.

title_en: Third interrogation of the Mitteler Rebbe in Vitebsk
summary_en: In his third interrogation, the Mitteler Rebbe was questioned about a list of donations to R. Aharon of Strashelye found in his home, which he denied ever seeing.
story_body: Investigators presented the Mitteler Rebbe (Rabbi DovBer Schneuri of Lubavitch) with a list of yearly donations pledged by various people for the support of a rebbe, found among his papers. He testified that he had never seen the list and did not know how it had come into his home. It is presumed the list was actually seized at the home of R. Aharon of Strashelye, who was arrested around the same time, and was mistakenly attributed to the Rebbe.

title_en: Interrogation of R. Aharon of Strashelye in Vitebsk
summary_en: R. Aharon HaLevi of Strashelye, brought as a witness rather than a defendant, was interrogated in Vitebsk about donations collected for the Mitteler Rebbe.
story_body: Aharon Movshovich HaLevi of Drizin, age 58, testified that he did not recognize a list of donations collected for the support of a rebbe. He stated he supported himself and his family on contributions of up to 3,000 rubles a year from Jews. In a follow-up session on October 28 he confirmed knowing some donors named in the ma'amad lists, and authenticated a letter sent to Simcha Kissin jointly with the Mitteler Rebbe. He was released around Rosh Chodesh Kislev, after less than two weeks in custody.

title_en: Investigator Korbitsky sent to inspect Lubavitch synagogue and library
summary_en: Investigator Korbitsky was dispatched from Vitebsk to Lubavitch to verify the Mitteler Rebbe's testimony about the cost of building the synagogue and acquiring its sacred books and Torah scrolls.
story_body: Acting on Governor Khovansky's order, the private investigator Korbitsky traveled to Lubavitch on October 19, 1825 — his second such mission. He measured and inventoried the wooden synagogue (built in 1814–1815 by the landowner Kruger for about 4,000–5,000 rubles), priced its furnishings at roughly 1,258 rubles, and catalogued 611 books in four cabinets in the Rebbe's home. Local Jews swore the building was financed by donations from the Rebbe's followers, but could not provide further details; Korbitsky recommended further investigation of Kruger and the scribe of Yanovich.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe's petition to Governor Khovansky requesting release
summary_en: Days before his release, the Mitteler Rebbe submitted a short petition to Governor Khovansky pleading for a speedy decision in his case, citing his deteriorating health.
story_body: After the conclusion of his interrogations and shortly before his release, the Mitteler Rebbe wrote a brief memorandum to Governor Khovansky. He expressed confidence that justice would prevail and that the false denunciation against him would be exposed, but appealed to the governor's sense of fairness to expedite a decision because his fragile health was steadily worsening. A longer follow-up petition was later printed in the kuntres 'Bad Kodesh.'

title_en: Investigators submit summary of Vitebsk interrogations to Khovansky
summary_en: The investigators in Vitebsk submitted to Governor Khovansky a summary of the results of their interrogations of the Mitteler Rebbe and related witnesses.
story_body: On 12 Kislev 5586 the Vitebsk investigators compiled and submitted their formal review of the inquiry into the Mitteler Rebbe to the governor-general, Prince Nikolai Khovansky. The document incorporated the findings of Korbitsky's on-site investigation in Lubavitch concerning the synagogue and the Rebbe's library, alongside the responses given by the Rebbe and witnesses such as R. Aharon of Strashelye during the Vitebsk interrogations.

title_en: Mohilev provincial government orders continued interrogation of the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: The Mohilev provincial government reported to Governor-General Khovansky that the magistrate court of Babinovich had been fined for procedural irregularities in the Mitteler Rebbe's case and was ordered to resume formal interrogations without delay.
story_body: Civil Governor Maksimov and his councillors reported that the Babinovich magistrate court had bypassed proper procedure by sending a policeman with questions to the Rebbe instead of summoning him to a hearing — an evident leniency. A fine of 10 rubles was imposed on the responsible officials, and the court was ordered to investigate the Rebbe thoroughly on the charge of collecting large sums from his followers and to punish the accused with full severity. Oversight was placed in the hands of the district court inspector and the provincial prosecutor.

title_en: District court inspector reports delays in Mitteler Rebbe investigation
summary_en: District court inspector Kilikovsky reported to Khovansky that the case against the Mitteler Rebbe was stalled because the courts of Orsha and Mohilev had not yet returned the required investigation results.
story_body: Inspector Kilikovsky of the Babinovich district court informed Governor-General Khovansky that the case against Rabbi Berke Schneur of Lubavitch was being held up because the courts in Orsha and Mohilev had not delivered the inquiry results requested on February 12. The Mohilev provincial administration had issued an urgent reminder on March 3, and Kilikovsky himself had pressed the inspectors of those districts on February 24 and again on March 17.

title_en: Mohilev provincial report on continued investigations in Kapust, Orsha, and Mohilev
summary_en: The Mohilev provincial government updated Khovansky on continuing inquiries into the Mitteler Rebbe, including a policeman who lost the Rebbe's written answers and sworn testimony being gathered from Jewish communities in Orsha, Kapust, and Shklov.
story_body: The provincial government detailed how the Babinovich court had relied on a policeman who returned having lost the Rebbe's responses, then dispatched a second courier and ordered sworn testimony to be collected from the Jewish communities of Orsha, Kapust, and Shklov. The investigators sought to verify a claim that in 1813 the people of Kremenchug had invited Rabbi Schneur to succeed his father, promising to compensate his property losses from the French invasion and to support his entire family. Officials were fined for procedural lapses, and the courts were ordered to complete depositions and rule on the case as swiftly as possible.

title_en: District court inspector reports completion of Mitteler Rebbe inquiries
summary_en: Inspector Kilikovsky reported to Khovansky that the required investigations from various localities in the Mitteler Rebbe's case had finally reached the Babinovich magistrate court and been reviewed.
story_body: In a brief dispatch dated 17 Iyar 5586, Kilikovsky, inspector of the Babinovich district court, informed the governor-general that all the depositions and inquiries needed for the case concerning Rabbi Berke Schneur of Lubavitch's alleged unlawful activities had been received from the various localities. The materials had been added to the case file and surveyed, advancing the proceedings toward a decision.

title_en: Provincial prosecutor reports collected testimony in Mitteler Rebbe case
summary_en: The provincial prosecutor of Mohilev reported to Khovansky that the necessary depositions, including testimony of Chassidim in Shklov, had been forwarded to the Babinovich magistrate court for swift adjudication of the Mitteler Rebbe's case.
story_body: Prosecutor Smolaninov of Mohilev province informed Governor-General Khovansky that reports from the magistrate courts of Orsha and Kapust, as well as the lower court of Mohilev, had reached the Babinovich court, along with the depositions of Chassidim in Shklov needed for the case. He had sent a written demand urging Babinovich to rule promptly on the alleged unlawful actions of Rabbi Berke Schneur of Lubavitch, and informed the district court inspector accordingly.

title_en: War of 1812 destroys Rabbi Schneur's property in Lyady
summary_en: The enemy destroyed Rabbi Schneur Zalman's property during the war of 1812, causing losses estimated at 60,000 rubles.
story_body: During Napoleon's 1812 invasion of Russia, the property of Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi was destroyed by the enemy, with damages reaching 60,000 rubles according to his own account. He subsequently traveled from Kremenchug to Shklov collecting donations to cover these losses, and his associates continued the fundraising effort afterward. These collected funds, totaling 35,000 rubles, later became central evidence in the 1825 investigation against his son Rabbi DovBer.

title_en: Mogilev court ratifies Lubavitch synagogue-building regulation
summary_en: A regulation of the Chabad community of Rabbi DovBer (Berke Schneur) of Lubavitch authorizing trusted men to oversee synagogue construction without accountability was signed in the Mogilev peace court.
story_body: On July 17, 1822, the chassidic community of Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch formalized a takanah empowering specially trusted individuals to manage the construction of a synagogue, exempting them from any obligation to render accounts of income or expenses, both during construction and afterward. The document was written in Russian on three-ruble stamped paper and notarized as an official document before witnesses at the Mogilev peace court. This regulation later surfaced as evidence in the 1825-1827 investigation against the Mitteler Rebbe.

title_en: Mogilev and Vitebsk Jews fund delegation to Petersburg
summary_en: Jews of Mogilev and Vitebsk gubernias enacted a takanah in the Lubavitch region to collect funds for emissaries traveling to Petersburg on communal advocacy matters.
story_body: In 1824, a regulation was formulated in the Lubavitch area by Jewish leaders of Mogilev and Vitebsk to fund a delegation traveling to Petersburg for shtadlanut on public affairs. Mogilev was assessed 1,030 rubles and Vitebsk 690 rubles for the emissaries' expenses. The takanah also affirmed that the chachamim, elders, heads of thousands and heads of hundreds named in the document were of equal authority, and the document later became evidence in the case against Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch.

title_en: Simcha Kisin denounces Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch to authorities
summary_en: A Jew named Simcha Kisin submitted a denunciation to Governor-General Khovansky accusing Rabbi DovBer (Berke Schneur) of Lubavitch of illegally collecting funds from his followers.
story_body: In July 1825, Simcha Kisin delivered a formal denunciation to Prince Nikolai Khovansky, Governor-General of Vitebsk, Mogilev, Smolensk and Kaluga, alleging that Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch — the Mitteler Rebbe — was illegally raising money from his chassidim. This informer's report cited documents including a fund-distribution sheet and correspondence between the Rebbe and his associates. The denunciation triggered the formal criminal investigation that would lead to the Rebbe's arrest and eventual acquittal nearly two years later.

title_en: Khovansky orders investigation of Mitteler Rebbe's fundraising
summary_en: Governor-General Khovansky directed Colonel Loginov and Court Counselor Markov to investigate Kisin's denunciation against Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch.
story_body: On October 2, 1825, Prince Khovansky issued an order to Colonel Loginov and Court Counselor Markov to conduct a formal inquiry into the accusations brought by Simcha Kisin against the Mitteler Rebbe. They were instructed to determine the source of the sums Rabbi Schneur had distributed among his relatives, whether they came from communal taxes, who collected them, under what legal authority, and whether accountings had been rendered. The investigators summoned the Rebbe along with Lubavitch resident Lavut and the Shklov townsmen Zalman Reizin and Shimon Freidin.

title_en: Release of the Mitteler Rebbe on 10 Kislev 5586
summary_en: Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch, the Mitteler Rebbe, was freed from Russian arrest on 10 Kislev 5586, three days before the Loginov-Markov summary report was issued.
story_body: On 10 Kislev 5586 (approximately November 8, 1825) the Mitteler Rebbe was released from imprisonment, a date that became the annual chassidic festival of Yud Kislev. The summary report by investigators Loginov and Markov, compiling all the interrogations and seized documents, was written three days after this release. Although the Rebbe was freed in body, the case formally continued through the Russian courts for another fifteen months until his final acquittal.

title_en: Loginov and Markov submit summary report on Mitteler Rebbe case
summary_en: Colonel Loginov and Court Counselor Markov filed their comprehensive report to Khovansky compiling all interrogations and documents in the case against Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch.
story_body: On November 10, 1825, the investigators Loginov and Markov submitted their final report to Governor-General Khovansky summarizing every interrogation conducted in Vitebsk, the search at Lubavitch by officer Korbitsky, and every document supplied by the informer Kisin or seized from the Rebbe. The report addressed the disputed distribution of 35,000 rubles, the Rebbe's role as arbiter, his correspondence about chassidic affairs, and the synagogue-building takanah. It was received by Khovansky's office the following day and forwarded to the Mogilev gubernia administration a week later.

title_en: Khovansky forwards Mitteler Rebbe case to Mogilev gubernia
summary_en: Khovansky sent the Loginov-Markov investigation file to the Mogilev gubernia administration for legal processing.
story_body: On November 17, 1825, after reviewing the investigators' report, Prince Khovansky forwarded the case against Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch to the Mogilev gubernia administration under reference numbers 5849 and 5850. This transfer began the lengthy judicial phase, in which the matter would be routed first to the Babinovichi peace court and ultimately to the Mogilev High Court. Khovansky later cited this directive when pressing officials for updates on the case.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe case transferred to Babinovichi peace court
summary_en: Following standard legal procedure, the case file on Rabbi DovBer was sent from the Mogilev gubernia administration to the Babinovichi peace court.
story_body: On December 19, 1825, the case against Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch — concerning allegedly illegal fundraising from his chassidim — was transmitted to the peace court of the town of Babinovichi for adjudication. The court would begin substantive work on the file in mid-January 1826. This routing through a local peace court was the standard procedure before the matter could rise to the Mogilev High Court for review.

title_en: Babinovichi peace court begins hearing Mitteler Rebbe case
summary_en: The Babinovichi peace court started its formal review of the file concerning Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch's alleged illegal fundraising.
story_body: On January 13, 1826, the Babinovichi peace court opened its examination of the case against Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch. The court would labor over the file for more than six months before issuing its decision in July 1826. Its conclusions were then forwarded to the Mogilev High Court for review, eventually leading to the Rebbe's complete acquittal.

title_en: Babinovichi peace court issues decision on Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: The Babinovichi peace court reached its final decision in the case against Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch and submitted it for review by the Mogilev High Court.
story_body: On July 20, 1826, after roughly half a year of deliberation, the Babinovichi peace court concluded its work on the case concerning Rabbi DovBer's alleged illegal collection of funds from his chassidim. The decision was then presented for re-examination by the First Department of the Mogilev High Court. The High Court's inspector, Kilikovsky, reported the transfer to Prince Khovansky on July 31, 1826.

title_en: Mogilev High Court acquits the Mitteler Rebbe on 11 Kislev 5587
summary_en: The First Department of the Mogilev High Court ruled to acquit Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch of the charges of illegal fundraising from his followers.
story_body: On November 29, 1826 — 11 Kislev 5587 — the First Department of the Mogilev High Court issued its verdict in favor of Rabbi DovBer (Berke Schneur) of Lubavitch, finding that the charges of unlawful collection of money from his chassidim could not stand. The decision was reached without opposition from the gubernia prosecutor general. This judgment, while not formally confirmed by higher authorities for several more months, secured the Rebbe's freedom from criminal jeopardy.

title_en: Gubernia prosecutor approves Mitteler Rebbe acquittal verdict
summary_en: The gubernia prosecutor general of Mogilev formally approved the High Court's verdict acquitting Rabbi DovBer of Lubavitch.
story_body: On February 1, 1827, corresponding to 16 Shevat 5587, the Mogilev gubernia prosecutor general endorsed the High Court verdict that acquitted Rabbi DovBer of all charges in the illegal-fundraising case. Eight days later the court submitted the approved judgment to Governor-General Khovansky for final ratification. This prosecutorial concurrence removed the last administrative obstacle within the gubernia to formal recognition of the Rebbe's innocence.

title_en: Mogilev High Court reports Mitteler Rebbe acquittal to Khovansky
summary_en: Judges of the Mogilev High Court formally reported to Governor-General Khovansky that Rabbi DovBer had been acquitted and remained at liberty.
story_body: On February 9, 1827, the First Department of the Mogilev High Court — judges Felix Marzhevsky, Porfiry Karpilovich, and Matvei Dekterev — submitted their verdict in the case of the Mitteler Rebbe to Khovansky for approval. They reported that no objection had been raised by the gubernia prosecutor and that 'Mr. Berke Schneur remains at his liberty.' Khovansky would subsequently request the full case file with a summary, which the court forwarded on March 22, 1827.

title_en: Khovansky requests Mitteler Rebbe case file with summary
summary_en: Governor-General Khovansky returned the High Court verdict and demanded the full case file accompanied by a brief summary and survey.
story_body: On March 2, 1827, from Vitebsk, Khovansky directed the First Department of the Mogilev High Court to send him the verdict in the Mitteler Rebbe case together with the original file and a concise summary as soon as possible. The court initially responded on March 22 with the requested materials, but Khovansky pressed again on March 29 before being informed on April 13 that everything had already been dispatched. The case would eventually be escalated to the Senate in Petersburg on appeal.

title_en: Tolodos Avraham Chaim biography published
summary_en: Otzar Hachassidim publishes 'Tolodos Avraham Chaim,' the biography and writings of R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum of Plescenice, edited by R. Shalom Dovber Levin.
story_body: Issued in Brooklyn on 24 Teves 5758 (1998), the volume compiles the life story of the chossid R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum of Plescenice along with his correspondence with the Rebbe Rashab, R. Shmuel Dovber of Borisov, the mashpia R. Hendel Kugel and other senior chassidim. It also publishes his writings in halacha, Kabbalah, Chassidus, language and avodas Hashem, drawn from his archive in the Agudas Chassidei Chabad–Lubavitch library.

title_en: R. Yosef Kugel of Plescenice passes away
summary_en: The well-known chossid R. Yosef Kugel of Plescenice passes away around Adar 5636.
story_body: R. Shmuel Dovber of Borisov, writing to R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum on 26 Adar 5636 (1876), reacts with shock to the sudden news of the passing of 'our friend, the God-fearing R. Yosef.' Earlier letters from 5 and 18 Adar of that year had still sent regards to R. Yosef and his nephew R. Gershon Leib, showing how unexpected the loss was for the chassidic circle of Plescenice.

title_en: R. Gershon Yehuda Leib Kugel passes away in Vilna
summary_en: R. Gershon Yehuda Leib Kugel passes away on Sunday after nightfall, Parshas Nitzavim 5637, and is buried in Vilna on 18 Elul.
story_body: His son R. Shlomo recorded in manuscript 584 that his father R. Gershon Yehuda Leib died on Motzaei Shabbos Parshas Nitzavim 5637 (1877) and was honored with burial in Vilna on 18 Elul, after midday. The yahrzeit is observed on 18 Elul. With his passing and the earlier move of the mashpia R. Hendel Kugel to Lubavitch, leadership of the Plescenice chassidim passed to R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum arrested in Plescenice
summary_en: R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum is arrested in 1888 over forged documents issued by his assistant R. Chaikel Rapaport to spare Jewish youths from the tsarist army.
story_body: As elected elder of Plescenice, Rosenbaum delegated the local administrative office (upravа) to his assistant R. Chaikel Rapaport, entrusting him with his official seal. Rapaport used the seal to issue forged passports and 'false benefits' to save Jewish boys from military conscription; when the authorities discovered this, both men were arrested. Rosenbaum was first held in Borisov for most of 5648 (1888) before being transferred to Smolensk.

title_en: Rosenbaum transferred to Smolensk prison
summary_en: After about a year in Borisov, R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum is sentenced and transferred to a Smolensk penal company in the summer of 5648.
story_body: Following the trial in Borisov, Rosenbaum was sentenced to two years in the 'rastantnaya rota' in Smolensk for signing a document on behalf of an only son seeking exemption from the army. The warden of the Borisov prison personally escorted him out and wept, recognizing that this prisoner was an unusually learned and refined man. Rosenbaum remained in Smolensk from the summer of 5648 (1888) until the summer of 5650 (1890).

title_en: Rosenbaum writes from Smolensk prison about his arrest
summary_en: From prison in Smolensk on 27 March 1889, Rosenbaum laments his fate of sitting among 'night robbers and forest murderers' for a single forged signature.
story_body: In a letter dated 27.3.89 from his Smolensk cell, Rosenbaum describes the bitterness of being imprisoned in old age among violent criminals, his dignity stripped away. He explains that his only 'crime' was signing on behalf of a sole-son draftee, an act of mercy that had been twisted into an accusation of fraud. The letter offers a rare glimpse into his prison conditions and inner state during the tsarist incarceration.

title_en: Rosenbaum writes to R. Hendel from prison
summary_en: On 20 Iyar 5649 Rosenbaum writes from prison to the mashpia R. Hendel, recalling his Lubavitch youth and reporting on Plescenice chassidic life.
story_body: Writing on 20 Iyar 5649 (1889) from Smolensk, Rosenbaum reminisces with R. Hendel Kugel about his student days in Lubavitch alongside R. Chaim Yaakov Widerewitz, whom he had just learned was passing through nearby Smolensk en route to Vitebsk. In a separate letter dated 'Wednesday Parshas Masei 5649,' he rejoices that the shochet R. Reuven Liberman has established regular Chassidus learning in Plescenice and prays that the local chassidic community will flourish in his absence.

title_en: Rosenbaum released from Smolensk and flees Russia
summary_en: Warned of a new prosecution after Simchas Torah 5652/3, Rosenbaum secretly flees Plescenice via Warsaw to Frankfurt.
story_body: After his release, a sympathetic investigating magistrate quietly warned Rosenbaum that fresh charges were pending and hinted that he should escape abroad. On one of the days of Tishrei 5652/5653 (1891/2) he was tipped off that he would be re-arrested the day after Simchas Torah; he hosted a joyous farewell farbrengen for the Plescenice chassidim and vanished that night. He traveled first to Warsaw, where his brother lived, and then to Frankfurt, where he and his son ran a dairy shop for about a year.

title_en: Rosenbaum expelled from Germany, moves to Amsterdam
summary_en: Around 5653, a German police officer orders Rosenbaum to leave Frankfurt, and he relocates reluctantly to Amsterdam.
story_body: After roughly a year running a dairy shop in Frankfurt with his son, a police official informed Rosenbaum that he had no right to reside in Germany and ordered him out. He moved to Amsterdam, where he partnered in business with the chossid R. Abba Person of Koenigsberg, who had likewise been forced to leave Russia. Unable to find sustainable income there, he would soon be pushed, against his preference, to consider emigration to America.

title_en: Rosenbaum works as Torah journal editor in Berlin
summary_en: During 5653 Rosenbaum lives in Berlin while editing and proofreading a Torah-scholarly journal in the publisher's home.
story_body: A surviving undated letter from this period describes Rosenbaum as 'arranging and preparing the words of the wise for print,' lodging in the home of an unnamed rabbinic publisher in Berlin. He used the post to correspond with R. Tzvi Tietz, author of Zikaron Yehuda on Eichah, about the wording of the bris milah blessing 'tziva yedidus,' explaining why he had cut a passage from Tietz's submitted essay.

title_en: Rosenbaum moves from Berlin to Koenigsberg
summary_en: In summer 5653 Rosenbaum relocates from Berlin to Koenigsberg, where he weighs and rejects emigrating to America.
story_body: By 4 Parshas Tavo 5653 (1893) Rosenbaum was writing from Koenigsberg to R. Ze'ev Wolf and R. Chaim Gershon Kugel about the hardships of resettling in Berlin and then Koenigsberg. He recounts a long reply he received from R. Chaim Yaakov Widerewitz – chief rabbi of the Sephardic Congregation in America, who had emigrated in 5652 – warning that America was good for the strong but harsh for refined and delicate people. Identifying himself with the latter, Rosenbaum decided for the time being not to cross the ocean.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz recalls Rosenbaum's gift of the Tzemach Tzedek's tallis
summary_en: On 12 Tishrei 5696 the Rebbe Rayatz writes that R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum had sent his father, the Rebbe Rashab, the tallis in which the Tzemach Tzedek had prayed.
story_body: In a letter dated 12 Tishrei 5696 (1935), published in Igros Kodesh vol. 3, the Rebbe Rayatz tells R. Dovid Shifrin that 'many years ago' R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum had presented his father, the Rebbe Rashab, with the Tzemach Tzedek's tallis gadol. Rosenbaum had purchased the tallis with a generous sum from the meshulach R. Madil, recognized it physically as the one in which the Rebbe had prayed, and eventually sent it to Lubavitch rather than wear it himself.

title_en: Rosenbaum writes his will mentioning the Tzemach Tzedek's tallis
summary_en: In his 5671 will, Rosenbaum records that the Tzemach Tzedek's tallis is in his wife's keeping and that he is afraid to wear it.
story_body: Writing his will in 5671 (1911), Rosenbaum noted that he still possessed the tallis of the Tzemach Tzedek, acquired in full payment from the meshulach R. Madil after he personally identified it as the one in which the Rebbe had prayed. He admitted uncertainty whether the tzitzis on it were the originals or replacements made by R. Madil, and explained that out of awe he could not bring himself to wear another tzaddik's tallis in this world.

title_en: Rosenbaum's halachic letter on Birkas HaLevana through a window
summary_en: On 13 Elul 5648 Rosenbaum writes a halachic responsum questioning whether one may recite Birkas HaLevana through a closed glass window.
story_body: Dated 13 Elul 5648 (1888) and addressed to a scholarly correspondent, the letter explores whether one may bless the new moon through window glass when it is impossible to go outside or open the window – for example in winter or when sewage is being removed nearby. Rosenbaum weighs the Dvar Shmuel's prohibition against the Magen Avraham's ruling permitting the havdalah candle blessing through glass, and proposes distinguishing between covering the viewer's eye and covering the object viewed. He also requests that the addressee acquire him a fine Genoese esrog and three matching hadas branches for Sukkos.

title_en: Birth of R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum in Pleshenitz
summary_en: R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum, son of R. Dovber, of Pleshenitz was born approximately in the year 5600 (1840).
story_body: R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum was born around 5600 (1840) in Pleshenitz, Belarus. As a young married man he was already studying in the court of the Tzemach Tzedek, and later became a devoted chassid of the Rebbe Maharash. He earned a living as a businessman while maintaining an active Torah correspondence with leading rabbis of his generation.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum writes Yud-Tes Kislev Torah letter from Smolensk
summary_en: On 19 Kislev 5650, R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum sent a detailed Torah letter from Smolensk to R. Chanoch Hendel analyzing chassidic concepts.
story_body: On the morning of Yud-Tes Kislev 5650 (December 12, 1889), R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum wrote from Smolensk to his colleague R. Chanoch Hendel. The letter discussed a maamar said on Parshas Lech Lecha concerning the concept of 'goy gadol' and a new creation through good deeds. He raised questions about the conflicting interpretations of the Yerushalmi, the Zohar, Targum Yonatan, and Rashi on the verse 'Hashem yotzei mimekomo,' asking that his doubts be brought before the Rebbe (Maharash) for clarification.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum leaves Russia
summary_en: R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum departed Russia during the years 5652-5653 (1892-1893).
story_body: After decades of life as a Chabad chassid and businessman in the Russian Empire, R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum left Russia in the years 5652-5653. The departure came in the early years of the Rebbe Rashab's leadership, as significant numbers of Russian Jews were beginning to seek refuge in the West. He would spend several years in transit before reaching his final destination.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum settles in the United States
summary_en: In 5658 (1898), R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum arrived and settled in the United States.
story_body: Five to six years after leaving Russia, R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum arrived in the United States in 5658 (1898), where he established his residence. He was among the earlier Chabad chassidim to take up permanent residence in America, well before the major waves of Chabad emigration that followed the Russian Revolution. He would live out the last fifteen years of his life there.

title_en: Passing of R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum in America
summary_en: R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum passed away on 25 Kislev 5674 (December 24, 1913) in the United States.
story_body: R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum passed away on 25 Kislev 5674, the first night of Chanukah, corresponding to December 24, 1913. He died in the United States, where he had settled some fifteen years earlier. A chassid who had been close to both the Tzemach Tzedek and the Rebbe Maharash, his surviving Torah correspondence preserves valuable insights into the chassidic thought of late nineteenth-century Russia.

title_en: R' Yosef Kogel writes RA"Ch about R' Maharash's succession
summary_en: R' Yosef Kogel of Pleshchenitz writes to RA"Ch describing notes from the Tzemach Tzedek confirming his son R' Shmuel (Maharash) as successor.
story_body: Soon after the Tzemach Tzedek's passing, Chassidim in Pleshchenitz had accepted the Maharash's leadership. On 8 Av 5626 R' Yosef Kogel wrote to RA"Ch relaying news from R' Meir Amtsizer in Orsha, who had seen copies of tzettlach written by the Tzemach Tzedek to his son R' Shmuel — 'open your mouth and your words will illuminate hidden things' — confirming his succession. Kogel adds that most of the world is now drawn after the Maharash, telling 'wonders' about him.

title_en: Wedding of R' Menachem Tzvi b. R' Shmuel Dovber of Borisov in Lubavitch
summary_en: The wedding of R' Menachem Tzvi, son of the famed Chassid R' Shmuel Dovber of Borisov, takes place in Lubavitch in Adar.
story_body: In Adar 5631 the wedding of R' Menachem Tzvi son of R' Shmuel Dovber (RShD"M) of Borisov was held in Lubavitch. RA"Ch sent a gift to the father of the groom in advance, and RShD"M acknowledged it in a letter that also mentioned an unspecified request that RA"Ch wished him to bring before the Maharash.

title_en: R' Shmuel Dovber of Borisov acknowledges RA"Ch's wedding gift
summary_en: RShD"M of Borisov writes to RA"Ch thanking him for his gift and promising to intercede on his behalf with the Maharash.
story_body: On 26 Shevat 5631, in the run-up to his son's wedding in Lubavitch, R' Shmuel Dovber of Borisov wrote to RA"Ch thanking him for the gift and the blessing. He added that he would not be lax in raising RA"Ch's request before the Maharash, though the specific nature of the request is not preserved in the surviving correspondence.

title_en: RA"Ch hears a 'Tze'enah Ure'enah' maamar from the Maharash on Shavuos
summary_en: RA"Ch is in Lubavitch for Shavuos and hears the Maharash deliver the maamar beginning 'Tze'enah Ure'enah', later entering for yechidus.
story_body: RA"Ch wrote to his nephew R' Shmuel Rosenbaum that on Shavuos 5639, during the Maharash's lifetime, he was in Lubavitch and heard an important maamar beginning 'Tze'enah Ure'enah'. He entered yechidus to ask about it, received the Rebbe's holy reply, and noted that another Chassid had also asked a question on the same maamar — material RA"Ch promised to relate in a later letter.

title_en: R' Shmuel Dovber of Borisov writes RA"Ch on 'the fallen Sukkah of David'
summary_en: In Kislev RShD"M of Borisov writes RA"Ch that he has much to share about contemporary events and 'the fallen Sukkah of David'.
story_body: Dating from the period immediately after the Maharash's passing, a letter from R' Shmuel Dovber of Borisov to RA"Ch in Kislev 5643 hints at unsettled times among the Chassidim, alluding to the 'fallen Sukkah of David'. The letter signals that he has 'much, much to inform' RA"Ch about current events affecting Chabad.

title_en: RA"Ch writes from Smolensk prison on his contact with the Rebbetzin
summary_en: From his Smolensk imprisonment RA"Ch writes to his mechutan R' Hendel describing letters from Rebbetzin Rivkah on his behalf.
story_body: On 20 Iyar 5649 RA"Ch wrote from prison in Smolensk to the mashpia R' Hendel, reporting that R' Avraham Yitzchak Zarchi had visited him and told him of a letter the Rebbetzin (wife of the Maharash, Rebbetzin Rivkah) had sent before Pesach to R' Leib Berlin on RA"Ch's behalf. RA"Ch expressed his distress at troubling her and admiration at her humility.

title_en: RA"Ch writes from Smolensk prison about visiting Lubavitch after release
summary_en: Nearing the end of his sentence, RA"Ch writes R' Hendel from prison about routing his journey home through Lubavitch.
story_body: On Thursday of Parshas Tzav 5650, as his release approached, RA"Ch wrote to R' Hendel that he intended to ask his elderly father in Pleshchenitz for permission, or advice, on whether to travel home via Lubavitch. He notes his father is so weak that he can no longer add greetings in his own hand to family letters and counts the hours until they meet again in life.

title_en: RA"Ch immigrates with his family to the United States
summary_en: In 5658 RA"Ch and his family settle in America, where he goes into the diamond and jewelry trade in New York.
story_body: According to R' Dovid Shifrin's account, in 5658 RA"Ch arrived with his family in the United States and established himself as a dealer in diamonds and pearls at 444 Grand Street, 2nd floor, New York. His home became a gathering place for Torah scholars, and he maintained an ongoing correspondence with the Rebbe Rashab back in Russia.

title_en: Rashab writes RA"Ch directing the organization of NY anash
summary_en: On 24 Adar I 5662 the Rebbe Rashab replies to RA"Ch, instructing NY anash to meet thrice weekly for Chassidus study and to fix tefillah and mitzvah observance.
story_body: Responding to RA"Ch's report on the life of anash in New York, the Rebbe Rashab on 24 Adar I 5662 (Igrot Kodesh vol. 1, letter 114) acknowledged a $100 contribution and urged the immigrants to organize. He directed them to gather at least three times weekly — Thursday night, Shabbos, and motzaei Shabbos — for fixed study of Chassidus, and to make 'tikkunim' in the conduct of public prayer and mitzvah observance in their new setting.

title_en: RA"Ch's wife dies after long illness in New York
summary_en: In 5664 RA"Ch's wife of his youth passes away after roughly four months of severe illness, depleting much of his savings.
story_body: Writing on Rosh Chodesh Adar Sheni 5665, RA"Ch recounts that in the preceding year, 5664, his wife of his youth had died after lying on a sickbed for some four months, with over a thousand dollars spent on her care. Earlier that same year he had lost nearly two thousand dollars when goods from Germany failed to arrive, together amounting to roughly three-quarters of the savings he had built up in his old age.

title_en: R' Yehoshua Kostral writes RA"Ch a letter of consolation
summary_en: From San Remo, R' Yehoshua Kostral writes RA"Ch a letter of consolation on the loss of his wife and broaches the question of remarriage.
story_body: On 7 Shevat 5664, from San Remo, Italy, R' Yehoshua Kostral wrote to RA"Ch to console him on the death of his wife, lamenting that he hardly knew who shared RA"Ch's home in America — perhaps his younger son R' Yosef who had married there. He gently raised the question of remarriage, noting RA"Ch was not yet old enough to live alone.

title_en: RA"Ch describes year of financial and personal losses
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Adar Sheni 5665 RA"Ch writes describing the preceding year's losses — his wife's death and major business setbacks.
story_body: In a letter dated Rosh Chodesh Adar Sheni 5665, RA"Ch reflects on a punishing previous year: the death of his wife after a four-month illness on which he spent over a thousand dollars, and a separate loss of nearly two thousand dollars in his business when goods failed to arrive from Germany. Together, he writes, these consumed about three-quarters of all the savings he had accumulated in his later years.

title_en: R' Avraham Chaim's arrest and imprisonment in Smolensk
summary_en: R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum was sentenced to two years in prison in Smolensk for attempting to exempt a young man from the Russian army.
story_body: R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum spent two years imprisoned in Smolensk, Russia, after trying to help a Jewish youth avoid Tsarist military conscription. Despite the harsh conditions, he maintained an extensive correspondence on Torah, Kabbalah, Chassidus, grammar, and divine service. His letters from prison reveal both the difficulty of his confinement and his continued spiritual life.

title_en: R' Avraham Chaim writes from prison about Parshas Lech Lecha maamar
summary_en: From his Smolensk prison cell on the eve of 19 Kislev 5650, R' Avraham Chaim responded to R' Hendel Kugel about the Rebbe Rashab's Parshas Lech Lecha maamar.
story_body: In early Kislev 5650 (late 1889), R' Hendel Kugel sent R' Avraham Chaim a summary of a maamar the Rebbe Rashab had delivered on Parshas Lech Lecha. On the eve of 19 Kislev, R' Avraham Chaim wrote back from his prison in Smolensk, expressing how precious the teaching was but lamenting that the summary alone was insufficient. He asked that R' Avraham the chozer record full maamarim and mail them to him several at a time.

title_en: Wedding of Brachah Slava Rosenbaum to Shlomo Kugel
summary_en: R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum's daughter Brachah Slava married Shlomo, son of R' Gershon Yehudah Leib Kugel and grandson of the mashpia R' Hendel Kugel.
story_body: The wedding took place during Parshas Terumah 5639 (early 1879). R' Avraham Chaim invited his close friend R' Shmuel Dovber of Borisov, who responded on 25 Adar with a mazal-tov letter explaining why he had been unable to attend. The match linked the Rosenbaum family with the Kugel family of Pleshchenitsy.

title_en: Birth of Gil Kugel in Pleshchenitsy
summary_en: Gil Kugel, son of R' Shlomo Kugel and Brachah Slava, was born in Pleshchenitsy on 4 Nisan 5640.
story_body: Recorded by his father Shlomo Kugel on the inside cover of manuscript no. 584 in the library, Gil was the first of several children born to the couple in Pleshchenitsy. The family register lists births of multiple siblings across the 1880s and into 5651.

title_en: Birth of Shmuel Kugel
summary_en: Shmuel Kugel was born on 10 Teves 5641 to R' Shlomo Kugel and Brachah Slava.
story_body: His birth is recorded in the family register inside manuscript 584 owned by his father R' Shlomo Kugel of Kotzieli. The note lists him as the second son, born on Friday Parshas Vayechi.

title_en: Birth of Tzvi Hirsch Kugel
summary_en: Tzvi Hirsch Kugel, son of R' Shlomo and Brachah Slava, was born on 18 Teves 5647.
story_body: Recorded by his father in the family register on manuscript 584, Tzvi Hirsch was born on Friday Parshas Shemos. He was a grandson of R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum and great-grandson of R' Hendel Kugel.

title_en: Birth of Meir Shalom Kugel during grandfather's imprisonment
summary_en: Meir Shalom Kugel was born on 20 Sivan 5649 while his grandfather R' Avraham Chaim was imprisoned in Smolensk.
story_body: Born on Wednesday Parshas Korach, Meir Shalom's birth was reported to his imprisoned grandfather R' Avraham Chaim by the mashpia R' Hendel Kugel, who traveled to Pleshchenitsy upon hearing the news. R' Avraham Chaim responded from prison on Parshas Pinchas with a blessing letter to his son-in-law and daughter, including detailed questions about the birth, the mohel, and the celebration.

title_en: Birth of Chanah Kugel
summary_en: Chanah Kugel was born on Friday Parshas Tazria, 2 Nisan 5651, in Pleshchenitsy.
story_body: Recorded by R' Shlomo Kugel in his family register on manuscript 584, Chanah was the fifth child listed in the household. The register documents the family's growth across the 1880s and early 1890s in Pleshchenitsy.

title_en: R' Avraham Chaim describes Pesach in Smolensk prison
summary_en: On erev Shabbos of the second day of Chol Hamoed Sukkos 5649, R' Avraham Chaim wrote to R' Eliyahu Rivkin describing how he kept Pesach in prison.
story_body: R' Avraham Chaim recounted that the previous Pesach in Smolensk prison, the local Chassid R' Zarchi brought him all his needs for the first day of Pesach and visited with his wife on Yom Tov bringing him beloved foods. Throughout that winter of 5649, he was also able to hire others to perform his mandatory prison labor.

title_en: New harsh labor rules imposed on Smolensk prisoners
summary_en: After Pesach 5649, Smolensk prison authorities imposed new rules requiring every prisoner to rise at 4 a.m. and assemble for forced labor selection.
story_body: R' Avraham Chaim wrote to R' Hendel Kugel on 20 Iyar 5649 about a new harsh regime in the Smolensk prison: every prisoner had to rise at the bell at 4 a.m. and stand in formation while the warden selected work assignments — a wait of two or three hours during the best part of the day. R' Avraham Chaim himself had been assigned for five days to fence the property of the prison administration.

title_en: R' Shneur Zalman Rosenbaum's American shliach mission for Tomchei Tmimim
summary_en: R' Shneur Zalman Rosenbaum was sent by the Rebbe Rashab to America to fundraise for the Tomchei Tmimim yeshivos.
story_body: R' Avraham Chaim wrote on Rosh Chodesh Adar Sheni 5665 (1905) that his brother R' Shneur Zalman had arrived in New York as an emissary of the Lubavitcher Rebbe to raise funds for the yeshivos. R' Shneur Zalman traveled through New York, Philadelphia, New Haven, Hartford, Springfield, and Boston, and R' Avraham Chaim asked whether he should also visit Rochester. The mission supported the four-city yeshiva network that had been founded six years earlier.

title_en: R' Avraham Chaim donates lottery winnings to the Rebbe Rashab
summary_en: R' Avraham Chaim won 5,000 rubles in an American lottery and sent 1,000 to the Rebbe Rashab, who acknowledged it on 12 Tishrei 5667.
story_body: On 12 Tishrei 5667 (October 1906), the Rebbe Rashab wrote to R' Avraham Chaim from Lubavitch confirming receipt of 1,000 rubles along with a record of how the money was distributed. The Rebbe blessed him with success and the means to continue doing tzedakah. A month later, on 18 Marcheshvan, the Rebbe advised him to invest the remaining funds in a house that would produce income.

title_en: R' Avraham Chaim sends Tzemach Tzedek manuscript to the Rebbe Rashab
summary_en: On 11 Elul 5667, the Rebbe Rashab wrote from Würzburg requesting that R' Avraham Chaim send him the autograph signature of the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: Writing from Würzburg on 11 Elul 5667 (1907), the Rebbe Rashab thanked R' Avraham Chaim for a 100-mark donation and discussed two books to be sent. Most precious, the Rebbe wrote, was the handwriting of the Tzemach Tzedek, which he requested be sent by registered mail to Lubavitch. The Rebbe Rayatz later recounted this gift in a letter dated 12 Tishrei 5696.

title_en: Tomchei Tmimim fundraising crisis after 1905 Russian pogroms
summary_en: R' Avraham Chaim wrote letters in summer 5667 urging American Chassidim to support Tomchei Tmimim after Russian pogroms cut off traditional funding.
