story_body: In a summer 5667 (1907) letter to R' Gershon Kopilovitz, R' Avraham Chaim explained that some 500 yeshiva students studied at Tomchei Tmimim in Lubavitch under the direct supervision of the Rebbe Rashab. With Russian pogroms devastating the donor base, the yeshiva faced terrible shortages, and R' Avraham Chaim called on American supporters to commit to regular annual pledges.

title_en: Death of R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum's wife in America
summary_en: R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum's wife died in 5664 in America, leaving him with his youngest son Yosef.
story_body: R' Yehoshua Kastrel wrote a letter of condolence to R' Avraham Chaim in 5664 (1904), noting that he presumed Avraham Chaim was now living with his youngest son Yosef, who had married in America. Kastrel admitted he barely knew either the deceased wife or Yosef personally.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim hears 'Tze'enah uRe'enah' discourse from Rebbe Maharash in Lubavitch
summary_en: On Shavuot 5639 R. Avraham Chaim was in Lubavitch and heard the Rebbe Maharash deliver the maamar 'Tze'enah uRe'enah,' afterwards entering yechidus to ask about its content.
story_body: R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum traveled to Lubavitch for Shavuot 5639, during the lifetime of the Rebbe Maharash. He heard the discourse 'Tze'enah uRe'enah' on the source of Kerias Shema in the Giving of the Torah, and in yechidus asked the Rebbe how this fit with the standard Kabbalistic mapping of positive and negative mitzvos to the divine name. He preserved the Rebbe's brief answer in writing for future study.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim decides to sell his share of the liquor business
summary_en: In the summer of 5637 R. Avraham Chaim resolved to sell his portion of the yayin saraf (whiskey) enterprise he held jointly with his mechutan R. Hendel, sparking a dispute over how to divide it.
story_body: R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum had been a partner with the mashpia R. Hendel in a whiskey and tavern business in Pleshchenitz. In the summer of 1877 he decided to liquidate his share, but he and R. Hendel could not agree on terms of the split. Both wrote their arguments to the Rebbe Maharash, who ultimately issued a binding compromise.

title_en: Letter from R. Shmuel Dovber of Borisov conveying the Maharash's compromise ruling
summary_en: On 7 Elul 5637 R. Shmuel Dovber of Borisov wrote to R. Hendel transmitting the Rebbe Maharash's compromise between him and R. Avraham Chaim over their joint whiskey venture.
story_body: After spending three Shabbosos in Lubavitch alongside R. Avraham Chaim and his brother, R. Shmuel Dovber of Borisov was directly entrusted by the Rebbe Maharash to relay his ruling in the partners' dispute. The psak gave R. Hendel a binary choice: retain the krechma and let R. Avraham Chaim sell his mill to anyone (even a non-Jewish license holder), or relinquish the krechma in exchange for 300 rubles. The Rebbe also advised R. Hendel to consult three trusted men if he could not decide on his own.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim writes to R. Chaim Gershon Kogel from Smolensk prison
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Nissan 5649 R. Avraham Chaim wrote from his imprisonment in Smolensk to his old friend R. Chaim Gershon Kogel, thanking him for his words of comfort.
story_body: Throughout his imprisonment in Smolensk, R. Avraham Chaim received consoling letters from friends across the Chabad world. On Rosh Chodesh Nissan 5649 he replied to R. Chaim Gershon Kogel, telling him that despite the many waters that had passed between them, the love expressed in his letter had not been extinguished. He observed that a prisoner's spirit cools from the heat of his oppressor when he sees that distant friends share in his sorrow.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim invites R. Hendel to visit him in Smolensk prison
summary_en: On 20 Iyar 5649 R. Avraham Chaim wrote to R. Hendel reversing his earlier objection and inviting him to come visit during the warmer months.
story_body: In the winter R. Avraham Chaim had discouraged R. Hendel from making the trip to Smolensk prison, both because of the cold and so the travel funds could be sent home to his family. On 20 Iyar 5649 he wrote that the time was now better for them both, asking R. Hendel to inform him before setting out. During that visit R. Hendel brought a gift for one of the guards, which led to a marked improvement in R. Avraham Chaim's treatment.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim reports easing of prison conditions after gift to guard
summary_en: In a letter dated Sunday Parshas Pinchas 5649, partly written in Aramaic to evade the censor, R. Avraham Chaim described how passing the guard the gift R. Hendel had brought won him quiet treatment.
story_body: Fearing the censor's eye, R. Avraham Chaim switched mid-letter into Aramaic to recount his interaction with the prison official. He explained that he had appealed to the guard not to be forced like the other Jewish prisoners to bake and travel to the bathhouse on Shabbos, and the guard had given a half-promise to accommodate him. He noted wryly that those who appear friendly only while they enjoy a benefit do not stand with a man in his time of trouble.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim forbids his wife to visit him in Smolensk
summary_en: In a letter of Wednesday Parshas Masei 5649 R. Avraham Chaim told R. Hendel he had refused his wife's request to travel to Smolensk to see him.
story_body: R. Avraham Chaim's wife had written that she wished to come to Smolensk for public appearance's sake. He replied that he did not consent: it would mean abandoning the home and shop and placing a week's burden on their son Zalman, with little real benefit. The decision is recorded in his letter to R. Hendel from the week of Parshas Masei 5649.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim writes essay on sadness vs. bitterness to R. Chanoch Hendel
summary_en: On Monday Ki Tisa 5649 R. Avraham Chaim wrote a lengthy chassidic letter to his mechutan R. Chanoch Hendel distinguishing depressive sadness (atzvus) from holy bitterness (merirus).
story_body: Responding to news about R. Hendel's grandson, who was engaged in avodas haLev based on Tanya, R. Avraham Chaim explained that the same effort to fulfill 've'ahavta lerei'acha' protects from excessive bodily attachments. He taught that sadness over the state of Klal Yisrael can be transformed into bitterness drawn from gevuros dikedushah — which carries vitality and pleasure — whereas plain atzvus comes from the cold, dry element of earth without any moisture of kedushah. He warned that tears that overflow such bounds must be examined to see whether they are truly an offering to G-d or merely the yetzer's pretext to rob a person of joy.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim drafts his first will and sends it to the Rebbe Rashab
summary_en: In 5668 R. Avraham Chaim prepared a will and dispatched a copy to the Rebbe Rashab for his review.
story_body: Sensing the need to set his affairs in order, R. Avraham Chaim composed a will in 5668 and forwarded a copy to the Rebbe Rashab. The text of that first will has not survived, but the Rebbe's acknowledgement letter from Marienbad is preserved, praising him for arranging his matters as a G-d-fearing and prudent man should.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab replies from Marienbad acknowledging R. Avraham Chaim's will
summary_en: On 23 Tammuz 5668 the Rebbe Rashab wrote from Marienbad to R. Avraham Chaim affirming the propriety of his will and blessing him with long life, livelihood, and health.
story_body: Receiving the copy of R. Avraham Chaim's will at his home, the Rebbe Rashab — then in Marienbad on the advice of Professor Berlin for his own health — responded on 23 Tammuz 5668. He commended the chassid for arranging his affairs as a G-d-fearing and discerning person should, and blessed him with longevity, parnassah, success, and the ability to engage in Torah and avodah in peace. The Rebbe also mentioned that he himself awaited a complete recovery among all of Israel.

title_en: R. Avraham Chaim writes a private will for his son Yaakov
summary_en: On 2 Iyar 5671 R. Avraham Chaim wrote a detailed private will for his son Yaakov covering burial arrangements, distribution of his tallesim and estate, and a 1,050-shekel gift to the Rebbe Rashab.
story_body: In ten clauses R. Avraham Chaim instructed Yaakov to bury him in his New York chevra's plot — warning him not to be swayed by the New Haven offer — and forbade any public hesped or newspaper notice. He detailed his prepared linen tachrichim from Germany, his Shabbos and weekday tallesim (including one inherited from the Tzemach Tzedek that he was afraid to wear in the next world), and asked that the bottom of the casket be broken so his body would touch the earth, per the Zohar in Parshas Vayechi and Terumah. He also charged Yaakov to forward 1,050 shekels of his estate as tzedakah to the Rebbe Rashab through his brother R. Z., to say kaddish, daven before the amud, and learn mishnayos throughout the year.

title_en: Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum begins imprisonment in Smolensk
summary_en: Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum arrives at the Smolensk prison in the summer of 5648 and is permitted to bring sacred ritual items with him.
story_body: Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum, a Chabad chassid and scholar in halacha, kabbalah and Hebrew grammar, was sentenced to imprisonment in Smolensk. He arrived at the prison in the summer of 5648 (1888), where he was initially put to hard labor alongside violent criminals serving lifetime sentences of exile. Despite the harsh conditions, the authorities allowed him from the outset to bring ritual articles into his confinement.

title_en: Avraham Chaim writes from prison requesting etrog and lulav
summary_en: From the Smolensk prison on 13 Elul 5648, Avraham Chaim asks Rabbi Yehuda Leib Maskil LeEitan to procure a Yanover etrog, a beautiful lulav, and three matched myrtle branches for Sukkot.
story_body: On 13 Elul 5648 (August 20, 1888), Avraham Chaim wrote from prison to Rabbi Yehuda Leib Maskil LeEitan asking him to acquire Sukkot articles on his behalf when purchasing his own. He requested a Yanover etrog, a lulav beautiful in appearance and complete in form, and three matched hadassim, with delivery to reach him immediately after Yom Kippur. The letter shows that prison authorities permitted him to receive religious articles within months of his arrival.

title_en: Rabbi Zalman Aharon advocates for Avraham Chaim in Smolensk
summary_en: On the Rebbe's counsel in 5650, Rabbi Zalman Aharon Schneersohn travels to Smolensk to intercede with the governor and ease Avraham Chaim's prison conditions.
story_body: Acting on the Rebbe's instruction from the year 5650 (1889/1890), Rabbi Zalman Aharon Schneersohn (the Raza) traveled to Smolensk to advocate for his imprisoned relative. Although outright release was impossible, he persuaded the governor to exempt Avraham Chaim from hard labor and grant him a separate cell apart from the other prisoners. He also notified the leading members of the local community and Chabad chassidim so they could continue supporting Avraham Chaim, and his intervention paved the way for further leniencies.

title_en: Avraham Chaim attends Yom Kippur services during Smolensk imprisonment
summary_en: On Yom Kippur 5650, Avraham Chaim is permitted to leave the Smolensk prison to pray at a local synagogue but refuses an aliyah due to the congregation's lax observance.
story_body: On Yom Kippur of 5650 (October 5, 1889), Avraham Chaim was allowed out of prison to attend services at a Smolensk synagogue. He declined, however, to accept an aliyah to the Torah, citing that the congregants were Sabbath desecrators and Yom Kippur eaters and that several of the synagogue's Torah scrolls were halachically invalid. The account implies he prayed there regularly while imprisoned but withheld participation in public honors for these reasons.

title_en: Avraham Chaim permitted to build a sukkah in prison courtyard
summary_en: Before Sukkot 5650, the Smolensk prison warden grants Avraham Chaim permission to erect a sukkah in the prison courtyard.
story_body: In a letter written between Yom Kippur and Sukkot 5650 Avraham Chaim lamented that he would be cut off from the community for the first nights of the festival, unable to eat even a kezayit of bread in a sukkah. To his relief the warden then granted permission to construct a sukkah in the prison courtyard, as recorded in a letter by Rabbi Shmuel Rosenbaum. The concession reflected the warden's growing regard for him and was one of several leniencies that followed Rabbi Zalman Aharon's earlier intervention.

title_en: Avraham Chaim leaves prison for Yud-Tes Kislev farbrengen
summary_en: On 19 Kislev 5650, the Smolensk prison warden permits Avraham Chaim to spend the entire night at the chassidim's gathering place and to purchase oil for Chanukah lights.
story_body: By 19 Kislev 5650 (December 12, 1889) Avraham Chaim had so won over the Smolensk prison warden that he was released for the night to the local chassidim's meeting place, where he remained with fellow chassidim until morning. On the eve of the date he wrote that Rabbi Avraham Yitzchak Zarchi had visited him and that, with the warden's permission, he would travel into the city the next day to buy oil for the Chanukah candles. The leniency was a high point of the cumulative effect of Rabbi Zalman Aharon's advocacy earlier in the year.

title_en: Passing of Rabbi Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum on first night of Chanukah
summary_en: Rabbi Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum passes away on 25 Kislev 5674, the first night of Chanukah, after declining the standard deathbed confession in favor of Patach Eliyahu.
story_body: In his final years Avraham Chaim suffered paralysis of his left arm, losing movement and sensation. When a visitor brought him a Torah Or siddur with the order of viduy for a dying person, he refused it, calling it a 'misnagdic viduy,' and instead recited Patach Eliyahu, the kabbalistic introduction said before Friday Mincha, from beginning to end with great sweetness. He passed away on 25 Kislev 5674 (December 24, 1913), the first night of Chanukah, his yahrzeit observed on that date.

title_en: R' Avraham Chaim begins counting days to redemption from prison
summary_en: At the start of 5650, imprisoned R' Avraham Chaim began counting down the days until his anticipated release.
story_body: Immediately upon the entry of the year 5650 (autumn 1889), R' Avraham Chaim Rosin, held in the Smolensk fortress prison, began to count the days until his liberation. He expressed this hope in letters to acquaintances, calling the year tarn (תר"נ) a year of mattir asurim ('releaser of the bound'). The countdown framed his correspondence and poetry during the entire year of imprisonment.

title_en: Prison letter from R' Avraham Chaim to R' Zev Wolf Kugel
summary_en: On 25 Tishrei 5650, R' Avraham Chaim wrote from prison to R' Zev Wolf Kugel describing his hopes of release within roughly eight months.
story_body: Writing from the Smolensk prison on 25 Tishrei 5650, R' Avraham Chaim told the grandson of R' Hendel that he could not yet describe his physical state, but that he expected good news within about eight months. He played on the gematria of the Hebrew month-name letters and the phrase mattir asurim, encoding his redemption hope into the date itself.

title_en: Letter from prison to Rabbi Yehuda Leib of Pleshchenitsy
summary_en: On Sunday of Parshat Noach 5650, R' Avraham Chaim wrote from prison to Rabbi Yehuda Leib Maskil L'Eitan of Pleshchenitsy about his countdown to freedom.
story_body: On the Sunday of Parshat Noach 5650, R' Avraham Chaim sent a parallel letter to Rabbi Yehuda Leib Maskil L'Eitan, rabbi of Pleshchenitsy. He repeated his wordplay on the year tarn as encoding mar-dror — bitterness turning to liberation — and described the 240 days remaining of his sentence as days that would be sweetened into glory upon his release.

title_en: Tu B'Shevat prison letter to Rabbi Yehuda Leib of Pleshchenitsy
summary_en: On 15 Shevat 5650 R' Avraham Chaim wrote again from prison, expressing that each day brought his salvation closer.
story_body: On 15 Shevat 5650, R' Avraham Chaim wrote once more to Rabbi Yehuda Leib of Pleshchenitsy. He thanked God for life and health, saying his days now seemed long but only until they passed, and likened his situation to the riddle that 'today' is yesterday's tomorrow and tomorrow's yesterday.

title_en: Prison administration changes and conditions harshen at Smolensk
summary_en: At the end of winter 5650, the officers overseeing the Smolensk prison were replaced and the conditions for the prisoners grew significantly harsher.
story_body: Toward the end of the winter of 5650, new guards took over the Smolensk prison and tightened the regime. Prisoners were forbidden to smoke, were limited to coarse prison-issue clothing and straw-stuffed pillows, lost access to private samovars, and were restricted to two meals' worth of food at a time. R' Avraham Chaim recorded these privations in his letters.

title_en: Letter to R' Hendel describing harsh new prison regime
summary_en: On Thursday of Parshat Tzav 5650, R' Avraham Chaim wrote to the mashpia R' Hendel about the worsened Smolensk prison conditions and Passover concerns.
story_body: On Thursday of Parshat Tzav 5650, R' Avraham Chaim wrote to the mashpia R' Hendel describing in detail the new restrictions imposed by the changed prison administration. He worried especially about Passover, since the prohibition on private samovars made hot water for matzah impossible, and the prison ovens could not be koshered. He noted that only about two and a half months remained of his sentence.

title_en: R' Avraham Chaim plans release from Smolensk prison on Parshat Korach
summary_en: R' Avraham Chaim expected to be released from the Smolensk prison on Monday of Parshat Korach 5650, planning then to travel to Lubavitch.
story_body: In his Parshat Tzav letter, R' Avraham Chaim told R' Hendel that his planned day of departure from the Smolensk prison would be the Monday of Parshat Korach, in late spring 5650. He intended to travel directly to Lubavitch upon release, ending roughly a year of imprisonment.

title_en: Letter on the Four Sons of the Haggadah from Pleshchenitsy
summary_en: On 8 Marcheshvan 5644, R' Avraham Chaim wrote from Pleshchenitsy to R' Yehoshua Lipman explaining the order of the Four Sons by kabbalistic principles.
story_body: Writing from Pleshchenitsy on 8 Marcheshvan 5644, R' Avraham Chaim addressed his prospective in-law R' Yehoshua Lipman. The letter unfolds a kabbalistic exposition of the Four Sons of the Passover Haggadah, mapping them onto the four worlds Atzilut–Beriah–Yetzirah–Asiyah and the four 'fierce ones' of Reish Lakish, and asks Lipman to clarify three differing orderings found in Pri Eitz Chaim and the siddur. He closes by inviting Lipman to bring the agreed wedding-gift sum in person.

title_en: Notes on mezuzah on the right and Chanukah candle on the left
summary_en: On Chanukah 5666, R' Avraham Chaim recorded his own kabbalistic reasoning for placing the mezuzah on the right and the Chanukah lamp on the left.
story_body: Marked 'Chanukah 5666,' R' Avraham Chaim's note works through the seeming paradox that the mezuzah, identified with the lower sefirot vav-heh, is placed on the right, while the Chanukah lamp, identified with the higher chochmah-binah, is placed on the left. He resolves it via the doctrine that the recipient can outrank the giver in or chozer, citing the Gemara's eleven blessings for one who appeases a poor man and parallels in tefillin placement.

title_en: Chassidic aliyah to Eretz Yisrael led by R. Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk
summary_en: R. Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk and his group ascended to Eretz Yisrael in the summer, joined initially by the Alter Rebbe who turned back at Mohilov.
story_body: In the summer of 5537 (1777), R. Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk led a major group of Chassidim to settle in Eretz Yisrael. The Alter Rebbe accompanied them as far as Mohilov in Podolia, where the Chassidim pressed him to remain in Russia to lead their community. The parting was marked by great weeping, and the Alter Rebbe returned to Russia while the group continued on.

title_en: R. Israel of Polotzk's group arrives in Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: On 5 Elul 5537, the Chassidic group including R. Israel of Polotzk arrived in Eretz Yisrael and settled in Tzfat.
story_body: After a long and difficult journey, the group of Chassidim led by R. Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk and including R. Israel of Polotzk reached Eretz Yisrael on 5 Elul 5537. Hundreds of Constantinople Jews joined them on the way to visit ancestral graves. The new settlers established themselves in Tzfat, where they began building a synagogue and faced immediate financial hardship from the many poor who attached themselves to the group.

title_en: Alter Rebbe returns to Liozna after parting from R. Menachem Mendel
summary_en: According to the Rebbe Rayatz's writings, the Alter Rebbe arrived back in Liozna in mid-Shvat 5538 after his stay in Mohilov.
story_body: After parting from R. Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk at Mohilov, the Alter Rebbe remained there for some time, where he reviewed the entire Talmud for the sixteenth time, standing day and night. Per the Rebbe Rayatz's notes in 'Avot HaChassidut,' he reached Liozna in mid-Shvat 5538. Other sources (Beis Rebbi) state he stayed in Mohilov a year and a half, returning home no earlier than 5539.

title_en: R. Israel of Polotzk sent as shadar to raise funds in the Diaspora
summary_en: Soon after arriving in Eretz Yisrael, R. Israel of Polotzk was dispatched as an emissary to organize fundraising for the impoverished new community.
story_body: Within weeks of the group's arrival in Tzfat, the dire poverty of the settlers and the many poor who had attached themselves to the aliyah forced R. Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk to send R. Israel of Polotzk back to the Diaspora as a shadar. In a letter, R. Menachem Mendel wrote that if they received 10,000 monthly it still would not suffice. R. Israel left Eretz Yisrael in Marcheshvan 5538 and traveled through Constantinople to raise funds for the new chassidic settlement.

title_en: R. Avraham HaKohen of Kaliska writes from Tzfat about the new settlement
summary_en: At the end of Shvat 5538, R. Avraham HaKohen of Kaliska wrote to the Chassidim of Smilian from Tzfat describing the new settlement's status.
story_body: R. Avraham HaKohen of Kaliska, one of the leaders of the new chassidic settlement, sent a letter from Tzfat at the end of Shvat 5538 to his followers in Smilian. He reported on their safe arrival, the establishment of their community in Tzfat, and sent the letter via R. Shlomo Segal as a trusted messenger.

title_en: R. Israel of Polotzk writes shadar letter from Iași
summary_en: On 9 Iyar 5538, R. Israel of Polotzk wrote a fundraising letter from Iași describing the hardships and the journey of the aliyah group.
story_body: While on his shadar mission back from Eretz Yisrael, R. Israel of Polotzk wrote a detailed letter from Iași on 9 Iyar 5538. He described the financial catastrophe caused by the many poor who joined the aliyah, the burden of supporting them through Constantinople, and pleaded for support of the new chassidic yishuv. The letter explicitly denied that he or R. Menachem Mendel had encouraged the poor to make aliyah, noting they had pressed themselves onto the group.

title_en: R. Shlomo Segal sent as shadar from Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: R. Shlomo Segal was dispatched as a shadar in winter 5539 and returned to Eretz Yisrael at the end of summer the same year.
story_body: Following R. Israel of Polotzk's earlier mission, R. Shlomo Segal was sent as a shadar from the chassidic settlement to the Diaspora in winter 5539. According to the analysis correcting A. Yaari's chronology, R. Shlomo Segal carried letters from R. Avraham of Kaliska to the Chassidim and returned to Eretz Yisrael by late summer 5539.

title_en: Famine strikes Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: A severe famine struck Eretz Yisrael in 5539, described in letters as unprecedented in living memory.
story_body: In 5539 a devastating famine struck Eretz Yisrael, described in chassidic letters as 'a famine in the land such as never was before.' A summer 5540 letter referred back to 'two years of famine in the land,' confirming the hardship spanned multiple years. This famine deepened the financial crisis of the new chassidic settlement and intensified the need for shadar fundraising.

title_en: R. Avraham of Kaliska visits Tiberias for Rosh Chodesh Shvat
summary_en: R. Avraham of Kaliska traveled to Tiberias for Rosh Chodesh Shvat 5539 in response to repeated requests from the community there.
story_body: After receiving repeated appeals from both Jerusalem and Tiberias, R. Avraham HaKohen of Kaliska traveled to Tiberias for Rosh Chodesh Shvat 5539. The trip was part of ongoing efforts to consolidate the chassidic presence in the holy cities and respond to community needs. This visit is documented in a letter that researcher Yaari originally misdated to 5538.

title_en: R. Shlomo arrives in Tiberias from the Diaspora
summary_en: In Menachem Av 5539, a man named R. Shlomo arrived in Tiberias from the Diaspora bearing a letter for R. Yitzchak of Ciecierzec.
story_body: A letter from summer 5540 records that in Menachem Av 5539 an individual named R. Shlomo arrived in Tiberias from abroad, carrying a letter addressed to R. Yitzchak of Ciecierzec. This mention is significant for the chronology of early chassidic shadarim, as it may relate to the identity and movements of R. Shlomo Segal.

title_en: Passing of R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk
summary_en: R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, leader of the chassidic community in Tiberias, passed away on Rosh Chodesh Iyar 5548.
story_body: On Rosh Chodesh Iyar 5548, the chassidic leader R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk passed away in Tiberias. His passing prompted some Russian chassidim to consider reducing or stopping their financial support of the chassidic settlement in Eretz Yisrael. Leadership of the Chabad chassidim in Tiberias transferred to R' Avraham of Kalisk.

title_en: Alter Rebbe writes Igeret HaTanchumin urging continued EY support
summary_en: Following the passing of R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk, the Alter Rebbe wrote a letter of consolation urging chassidim not to reduce their support of the Eretz Yisrael community by even a single coin.
story_body: After hearing that some chassidim wished to reduce their support of the Tiberias community because the original support had been directed at honoring the deceased tzaddik, the Alter Rebbe wrote his Igeret HaTanchumin (letter 11). He pleaded that not a single coin be withheld, emphasizing the supreme importance of supporting Jewish settlement in Eretz Yisrael, and praised R' Avraham HaKohen as the worthy successor.

title_en: R' Tzvi Hirsch Harker continues to Tiberias on Alter Rebbe's instruction
summary_en: In summer 5549 the emissary R' Tzvi Hirsch Harker wanted to return to Russia to revive flagging support but the Alter Rebbe instructed him to continue to Tiberias.
story_body: By summer 5549 R' Tzvi Hirsch Harker was already on his way back to Tiberias when he saw that Russian chassidic support was dwindling. He wanted to return to Russia to rally support, but the Alter Rebbe instructed him to continue his journey, promising to personally take responsibility for increasing Russian chassidic support. From Zaslov mid-journey he wrote to anash describing the Alter Rebbe's great love and dedication.

title_en: R' Avraham of Kalisk letter endorsing Alter Rebbe's leadership
summary_en: On 11 Menachem Av 5550 R' Avraham of Kalisk wrote to chassidim abroad endorsing the Alter Rebbe's leadership over the chassidic community.
story_body: Continuing the practice begun by R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk before his passing, R' Avraham of Kalisk wrote regularly to Russian chassidim urging them to attach themselves to the Alter Rebbe. In this 5550 letter he described the Alter Rebbe as the great rabbi 'this Sinai' through whose light they would see eternal light and the treasury of life and peace.

title_en: R' Avraham of Kalisk letter (5551) praising Alter Rebbe
summary_en: In 5551 R' Avraham of Kalisk wrote praising the Alter Rebbe as a wondrous counselor and urging chassidim to seek his guidance in all matters.
story_body: R' Avraham of Kalisk continued his yearly campaign of letters endorsing the Alter Rebbe's leadership. In 5551 he wrote that the Alter Rebbe was beloved and treasured, a holy man of God, a wondrous counselor who would show chassidim the way of God, and that they should listen to him.

title_en: R' Avraham of Kalisk letter (9 Adar 5553)
summary_en: On 9 Adar 5553 R' Avraham of Kalisk wrote praising the Alter Rebbe as one whose mouth produces pearls.
story_body: In his 9 Adar 5553 letter, R' Avraham of Kalisk shortened his own writing because the chassidim had with them the holy Alter Rebbe, who waters mountains from his lofts, and from the fruit of whose deeds the land is satisfied.

title_en: R' Avraham of Kalisk letter (5554) on Alter Rebbe's burdens
summary_en: In a 5554 letter R' Avraham of Kalisk described how the Alter Rebbe was constantly besieged by people seeking guidance from morning to evening.
story_body: In this letter (interpreted as 5554 because it elaborates on the Takanot Laznia of 5553), R' Avraham of Kalisk described the Alter Rebbe as the divine leader upon whom bundles of troubles from people hovered all day, who was approached by every troubled person and creditor seeking guidance in matters great and small.

title_en: R' Avraham of Kalisk winter letter (5555)
summary_en: In winter 5555 R' Avraham of Kalisk again wrote endorsing the Alter Rebbe as the practical halachic authority and divinely beloved.
story_body: R' Avraham of Kalisk continued in winter 5555 with another letter to the Russian chassidim. He emphasized that for practical halachic guidance the chassidim had with them the great rabbi, beloved of God, the renowned holy one - the Alter Rebbe - whose honor was the honor of the Omnipresent.

title_en: Emissaries demand Alter Rebbe cancel old EY fund channels
summary_en: In winter 5563 emissaries of R' Avraham of Kalisk demanded the Alter Rebbe cancel all existing Eretz Yisrael fundraising arrangements and let them create new ones.
story_body: In winter 5563 emissaries arrived asking the Alter Rebbe to cancel all existing fundraising arrangements in Russia so they could circulate and create new arrangements through 'true friends' not called by the name Chabad. They claimed to act with R' Avraham of Kalisk's knowledge. The Alter Rebbe refused to avoid increasing strife but the dispute escalated.

title_en: Alter Rebbe's letter (51) defending fund management
summary_en: In late summer 5565 the Alter Rebbe wrote letter 51 explaining the breakdown of EY fund transfers and defending his actions.
story_body: In late summer 5565 the Alter Rebbe wrote a detailed letter explaining the events: the winter 5563 demands by emissaries, the gabbai R' Yaakov Smilyaner's intervention, the letter he sent to R' Avraham of Kalisk offering to transfer all collected funds, and how 5563-5564 funds remained undelivered because Kalisker's own emissaries had said he would refuse them.

title_en: R' Avraham of Kalisk appoints R' Mordechai of Lechovitch over Russian EY funds
summary_en: In winter 5565 R' Avraham of Kalisk formally appointed R' Mordechai of Lechovitch to handle EY fund collection in Russia, separating from the Alter Rebbe.
story_body: After two years of non-receipt of Russian funds, R' Avraham of Kalisk wrote general letters in winter 5565 complaining that he had received nothing from Russia and announcing the appointment of R' Mordechai of Lechovitch to manage the EY funds collected in Russia. R' Mordechai in turn appointed R' Aharon and R' Yisrael of Ostravna as general gabbaim. The split was triggered by malicious emissaries who had spread false rumors.

title_en: R' Mordechai of Lechovitch letter on new EY gabbaim
summary_en: On 11 Kislev 5566 R' Mordechai of Lechovitch wrote confirming R' Aharon and R' Yisrael of Ostravna as the trusted treasurers for EY funds.
story_body: R' Mordechai of Lechovitch wrote on 11 Kislev 5566 urging that whoever is for God should ensure their tzedakah is given to the appointed treasurers - R' Aharon of Ostravna and his colleague R' Yisrael. This formalized the new fund-collection structure established under R' Avraham of Kalisk's leadership outside the Alter Rebbe's network.

title_en: R' Shimon Shmerling's shlichus to Lubavitch for Hebron settlement
summary_en: In summer 5581 R' Shimon Shmerling traveled as Hebron's first shaliach to Lubavitch to establish the Chabad settlement in Hebron.
story_body: R' Shimon Shmerling, founder of the Chabad community in Hebron and its first emissary, traveled from Hebron to Lubavitch in summer 5581 specifically to coordinate the establishment of the Chabad settlement in Hebron. He is recorded in the Montefiore census as having immigrated in 5581, suggesting he and his family came to Eretz Yisrael around this time.

title_en: Bill of sale of four amot in Hebron for Chabad settlement
summary_en: In 5582 R' Shimon Shmerling signed the bill of sale of four amot of land in Hebron, formalizing the new Chabad settlement.
story_body: The 5582 bill of sale of four amot in Hebron marked a foundational step in establishing the permanent Chabad community in the city. R' Shimon Shmerling, one of the founders, was a signatory. In the same year, EY support funds from Russia were sent through R' Yitzchak of Radvil, son of R' Yechiel Michel of Zlotchov.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe sends R' Shmerling to establish Hebron settlement
summary_en: In Tishrei 5583 the Mitteler Rebbe dispatched R' Shimon Shmerling to establish the Chabad settlement in Hebron, instructing him to marry off his son en route.
story_body: According to tradition recorded in family histories, in Tishrei 5583 the Mitteler Rebbe sent R' Shimon Shmerling to found the Chabad settlement in Hebron. His son R' Moshe was engaged to Chana Devorah, and the Rebbe instructed him to travel via her town, not dismount the wagon, ask whether she would join them to Eretz Yisrael, arrange the wedding immediately, and bring her along - which he did.

title_en: Pekidim VeAmarkalim begin uniform EY fund distribution
summary_en: From 5585 onward the Pekidim VeAmarkalim of Amsterdam distributed all incoming EY funds among the four kollels in the holy cities.
story_body: Starting in 5585 the Chevrat Terumat HaKodesh in Amsterdam (Pekidim VeAmarkalim) systematically distributed all donations among the four kollels - Sephardim, Perushim, Chassidim, and Chabad. Funds were sent four times yearly, usually via Beirut. This system continued until disputes arose with the later-established HoD kollel.

title_en: Pekidim VeAmarkalim letter volumes 1826-1829
summary_en: The Pekidim VeAmarkalim of Amsterdam maintained extensive correspondence with kollel heads, with letters from 5586-5589 later published.
story_body: The Pekidim VeAmarkalim corresponded extensively with the kollel heads and gabbaim in every city, keeping copies in special letter ledgers. Fifteen large volumes are preserved at the Yad Ben Zvi library. The first three volumes covering 5586-5589 were printed between 5725 and 5739 in the series 'Igrot HaPekidim VeHaAmarkalim MeAmsterdam.'

title_en: Passing of the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe passed away in 5588, two years after sending support funds to Hebron through R' Ephraim Yitzchak Epstein and his son-in-law would later send in 5590.
story_body: The Mitteler Rebbe, R' Dovber Schneuri, passed away in 5588. He had instituted yearly support quotas for every chassid - rich and poor alike - for Eretz Yisrael through tzedakah boxes in every home. This obviated the need for special emissaries from Hebron to come rally Russian support.

title_en: Compromise on EY fund distribution: Chabad gets 9/101
summary_en: In 5589 a compromise was reached giving Kollel Chabad nine parts of 101 of the Ashkenazic kollels' share of Pekoam funds.
story_body: The Ashkenazic kollels' portion of Pekoam funds was divided into 101 equal parts, of which Kollel Chabad received 9 parts. This 5589 compromise remained the basis for Chabad's share even after the later HoD kollel was carved out in 5597, with Chabad still receiving 9/101 of the reduced Ashkenazic share.

title_en: EY support sent via R' Ephraim Yitzchak Epstein
summary_en: In 5590 support funds were sent to Eretz Yisrael through R' Ephraim Yitzchak Epstein and his son-in-law R' Yosef Yehuda Leib of Shiof.
story_body: The 5590 receipt records that the support funds for Eretz Yisrael were transmitted through R' Ephraim Yitzchak Epstein and his son-in-law R' Yosef Yehuda Leib ben R' Chaim of Shiof. According to the 5599 Montefiore census, both immigrated to Eretz Yisrael themselves in 5590 - two years after the Mitteler Rebbe's passing.

title_en: Agreement between Chabad and Sephardic communities in Hebron
summary_en: In 5590 a formal agreement was concluded between the Chabad and Sephardic communities in Hebron, signed by R' Shimon Shmerling among others.
story_body: In 5590 the two communities in Hebron - Chabad and Sephardic - reached a formal agreement, signed by R' Shimon Shmerling. The agreement governed the relationship between the two settlements at a time when both shared the burden of protection payments to the local ruler Abd al-Rahman.

title_en: Muhammad Ali sends Ibrahim Pasha to conquer Eretz Yisrael and Syria
summary_en: In 5591 the Egyptian ruler Muhammad Ali sent his son Ibrahim Pasha to conquer Eretz Yisrael and Syria.
story_body: In 5591 Muhammad Ali of Egypt dispatched his son Ibrahim Pasha to conquer Eretz Yisrael and Syria. Ibrahim Pasha conducted a successful military campaign and became the general governor of the conquered territory from 5593 until 5600, profoundly affecting the Jewish communities under his rule.

title_en: Letter to Tzemach Tzedek signed by R' Shimon Shmerling
summary_en: In 5591 R' Shimon Shmerling was a signatory on a letter from the Chabad community in Hebron to the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: R' Shimon Shmerling, one of the founders of the Chabad community in Hebron, signed the 5591 letter from Hebron to the Tzemach Tzedek. This was part of regular correspondence between the Hebron community and the Lubavitcher leadership in Russia, reporting on the situation and requesting continued support.

title_en: Ibrahim Pasha becomes governor of Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: From 5593 Ibrahim Pasha served as governor general of Eretz Yisrael and Syria under Egyptian rule.
story_body: Following the successful conquest, from 5593 until 5600 Ibrahim Pasha served as the general governor of the territory conquered by Egypt. His rule brought significant changes to the Jewish communities of Eretz Yisrael, though it would later be marred by the violent suppression of local rebellions including the events of 5594 in Hebron.

title_en: Abd al-Rahman rebellion against Egyptian rule
summary_en: In early summer 5594 the local ruler Abd al-Rahman of Hebron rebelled against Ibrahim Pasha, prompting an Egyptian military response.
story_body: In early summer 5594 Abd al-Rahman, the local ruler of Hebron who had previously collected protection money from both the Sephardic and Chabad communities, rebelled against Ibrahim Pasha. In Tammuz, Ibrahim Pasha brought his army to crush the rebellion - with catastrophic consequences for the Jewish communities of Hebron.

title_en: Hebron Arab rebellion against Egyptian forces, Jews killed
summary_en: On 9 Iyar 5594 the Arabs of Hebron and surrounding villages rebelled against the Egyptian commander, killing several Chabad chassidim.
story_body: On Sunday 9 Iyar 5594 the Arabs of Hebron and surrounding villages rebelled against the Egyptian deputy commander stationed there. Several Chabad chassidim were killed in the attack, while about 400 others were trapped inside the citadel (kala) for weeks until starvation forced their surrender. The community endured constant threats of being burned alive and was saved only through massive ransom payments demanded by local officials.

title_en: Earthquake in Hebron
summary_en: On 16 Iyar 5594 a major earthquake struck Hebron, collapsing many houses in the Jewish courtyard and forcing residents to flee to the fields for a week.
story_body: On Sunday 16 Iyar 5594 a great earthquake shook Hebron, collapsing several homes in the Jewish courtyard. The Jews fled their dwellings and stayed for a full week in the fields among armed Arabs - 'like sheep among wolves' - while aftershocks continued every hour. Lesser tremors continued for about four weeks afterward, leaving the community traumatized.

title_en: Ibrahim Pasha sacks Hebron - massacre and desecration
summary_en: On 28 Tammuz 5594 Ibrahim Pasha's army entered Hebron, conducting a brutal sack with killings, rapes, desecration of Torah scrolls and destruction of homes.
story_body: On Monday 28 Tammuz 5594 the deputy commander arrived with his army and conquered Hebron. Despite Jewish hopes, the soldiers were given license to plunder. Homes were burned and ransacked for hidden treasures; oil was spilled and vessels shattered. Many women were violated and Torah scrolls were burned, torn, and spread on the ground with Torah scrolls rolled in blood. Two women, a child by the mikveh, and Sephardic sages were killed.

title_en: Hebron Chabad community letter to Tzemach Tzedek on Hebron events
summary_en: On 8 Elul 5594 the heads of the Chabad community in Hebron wrote to the Tzemach Tzedek describing the year's catastrophes and pleading for emergency aid.
story_body: Following the earthquake, the rebellion, and the brutal sack of Hebron, on 8 Elul 5594 the community leaders - R' Chaim Avraham (son of the Alter Rebbe) and R' Nachum (son of the Mitteler Rebbe) - wrote to the Tzemach Tzedek detailing the year's horrors. They begged him to publicize their suffering, noting that prices had tripled and they were borrowing food and money at interest to keep starving Jews alive.

title_en: End of Ibrahim Pasha's rule in Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: Ibrahim Pasha's rule over Eretz Yisrael ended in 5600 after seven years as governor general.
story_body: After conquering Eretz Yisrael and Syria for his father Muhammad Ali, Ibrahim Pasha served as governor general from 5593 until 5600. His rule, which encompassed the catastrophic events of 5594 in Hebron, ended in 5600, returning the region to Ottoman control.

title_en: HoD residents protest EY fund distribution
summary_en: In Adar 5596 residents from Holland and Germany (HoD) protested the existing distribution arrangement, having established a separate fifth kollel in Eretz Yisrael.
story_body: In Adar 5596 the HoD residents (Holland and Deutschland), having established a separate fifth kollel in Eretz Yisrael, contested the distribution arrangement. Though their immigrants were few, they argued that since most Pekoam funds came from their home countries, they deserved a larger share than per-capita allocation would yield. The dispute would persist until 5608.

title_en: HoD kollel begins receiving Pekoam share
summary_en: From 5597 the HoD (Holland-Deutschland) immigrants in Eretz Yisrael were given their share among the kollels in the Pekoam distribution.
story_body: After many had begun immigrating from Holland and Germany to settle in Eretz Yisrael, from 5597 onward the Pekidim VeAmarkalim included them in the kollel distribution. The HoD share was carved out of the existing Ashkenazic portion, gradually evolving toward the formula codified in 5610.

title_en: HoD-Chabad distribution dispute resolved
summary_en: The dispute between Kollel Chabad and Kollel HoD over Pekoam fund distribution shares dragged on until 5608 when it was finally resolved.
story_body: The protracted dispute between Kollel Chabad and Kollel HoD over their respective shares of Pekoam funds, which had generated multiple rabbinical rulings both ways, finally ended in 5608. The Pekidim VeAmarkalim addressed the matter in numerous letters between the parties before the final compromise.

title_en: New EY fund distribution order established
summary_en: In 5609 a new distribution formula was instituted dividing Pekoam funds into 168 parts: 67 to the Sephardim and 101 to the Ashkenazic kollels.
story_body: From 5609 the distribution formula was fixed: after expenses, funds were divided into 168 parts. The Sephardic kollels received 67/168. From the remaining 101/168, the HoD kollel took a third, and the remaining two-thirds was divided into 101 parts, of which Kollel Chabad in Hebron received 9/101.

title_en: Pekidim VeAmarkalim compromise settlement document
summary_en: In 5610 the Pekidim VeAmarkalim summarized the distribution outcomes in a formal compromise settlement document.
story_body: The 5610 compromise document of the Pekidim VeAmarkalim summarized the evolution of Eretz Yisrael fund distribution from 5585 onward through the various adjustments favoring HoD, ending with the formula codified in 5609 that remained in force at the time of writing.

title_en: R' Chaim Shmuel Shmerling moves to Jaffa to found Chabad settlement
summary_en: In 5626 R' Chaim Shmuel Shmerling moved from Hebron to Jaffa and founded the Chabad settlement there.
story_body: R' Chaim Shmuel Shmerling, son of R' Moshe and grandson of R' Shimon Shmerling, moved to Jaffa in 5626 and founded the Chabad community there. His move extended the Shmerling family's role as founders of Chabad settlements - from his grandfather establishing the Hebron community to his own founding of the Jaffa community.

title_en: Passing of R' Chaim Shmuel Shmerling in Jaffa
summary_en: R' Chaim Shmuel Shmerling, founder of the Chabad settlement in Jaffa, passed away on 20 Adar I 5654 in Jaffa and was buried in Jerusalem.
story_body: R' Chaim Shmuel Shmerling passed away in Jaffa on 20 Adar I 5654 and was buried in Jerusalem. Twenty-eight years after founding the Jaffa Chabad community in 5626, his death marked the end of his role in extending the family's pioneering legacy across the Chabad settlements of Eretz Yisrael.

title_en: Passing of R' Yosef Yehuda Shmerling in Jerusalem
summary_en: R' Yosef Yehuda Shmerling, 'firstborn' grandson of R' Shimon Shmerling and signatory of the 5604 Pekoam letter as 'trustee of the kollel,' passed away in Jerusalem on 2 Elul 5655.
story_body: R' Yosef Yehuda Shmerling, born around 5581 at the time of his family's immigration to Eretz Yisrael, was known as 'Yosef Yehuda the firstborn.' He signed the 5604 letter to the Pekidim VeAmarkalim as 'trustee of the kollel.' He passed away in Jerusalem on 2 Elul 5655, continuing the Shmerling family's central role in the Chabad settlement of the Holy Land.

title_en: R' Shmuel Segal arrives in Holy Land from Rohatchov
summary_en: R' Shmuel Halevi Segal, later first rabbi of the Chabad community in Hebron, immigrated to the Land of Israel from Rohatchov.
story_body: Per the 1839 census, R' Shmuel Halevi, then 64 years old, made aliyah from Rohatchov in 5584 (1824). Prior to his immigration he had served as a moreh tzedek (mo"tz) in Rohatchov and was a signatory on a charity assessment there in winter 5570 with the Alter Rebbe. After his arrival he became the leading rabbinic figure of the Chabad community in Hebron.

title_en: Charity assessment in Rohatchov signed by Alter Rebbe
summary_en: A charity assessment in Rohatchov in winter 5570 was signed by the Alter Rebbe, with R' Shmuel listed as 'mo"tz'.
story_body: In the winter of 5570 (1810) a tzedakah assessment for the town of Rohatchov was issued, bearing the signature of the Alter Rebbe. R' Shmuel, later the maggid of Hebron, appears on it as 'mo"tz' (moreh tzedek), reflecting his earlier rabbinic role in that town.

title_en: First Chabad-Sephardi agreement in Hebron
summary_en: The Chabad and Sephardi communities of Hebron signed an agreement in 5590 addressing the heavy protection-money demands of Sheikh Abdul Rahman.
story_body: In 5590 the two Jewish communities of Hebron, Chabad and Sephardi, formalized an inter-communal agreement signed by R' Shmuel Halevi among others. The agreement documents the exorbitant 'protection' payments demanded by Sheikh Abdul Rahman, the local ruler known as 'the Black Rabbi.' This was the first of several such accords as the communities tried to share the burden imposed by the local strongman.

title_en: R' Menachem Aryeh arrives in Hebron from Rohatchov
summary_en: R' Menachem Aryeh, son of R' Shmuel Halevi, immigrated to the Holy Land from Rohatchov together with his 16-year-old son R' Yisrael Yosef.
story_body: According to the 1839 Hebron census, R' Menachem Aryeh (also called Nachum Aryeh Leib) made aliyah from Rohatchov in 5592 (1832) at age 40. He came together with his already-married 16-year-old son R' Yisrael Yosef. He later served as administrator of the Chabad kollel, dayan, and head of yeshiva, signing the 1834 Tzemach Tzedek correspondence and other communal documents.

title_en: Letter to Tzemach Tzedek from R' Shmuel of Tzfat
summary_en: R' Shemayah, a Chabad chassid in Tzfat, wrote to the Tzemach Tzedek in winter 5595 about plans to relocate to Hebron.
story_body: In the winter of 5595 R' Shemayah wrote to the Tzemach Tzedek explaining that after Pesach, once the rains stopped, he intended to settle in Hebron among his Chabad brethren. He noted that R' Shmuel Halevi specifically advised him to join the Hebron community. The letter is preserved in Migdal Oz and indirectly confirms R' Shmuel's role as the de facto rabbi of Hebron.

title_en: Hebron Chabad community letters and shadarut documents
summary_en: In 5594 the leaders of the Hebron Chabad community signed letters to the Tzemach Tzedek and shadarut commissions for fundraising abroad.
story_body: During 5594 (1834) R' Shmuel Halevi and his son R' Menachem Aryeh signed multiple official Hebron Chabad documents, including correspondence to the Tzemach Tzedek and credentials for emissaries (shadarim) sent to raise funds abroad. These documents form the earliest preserved record of the community's institutional activity, reflecting the burdens of supporting the Hebron yishuv under Sheikh Abdul Rahman's exactions.

title_en: Hebron census taken for Montefiore
summary_en: At Moses Montefiore's request, Hebron's Jewish community took a comprehensive census of its Sephardi and Chabad populations in 5599.
story_body: On Sunday during Montefiore's visit to Hebron in Tammuz 5599, the community delivered to him a census of the entire Jewish population, with Sephardim and Ashkenazi-Chabad counted separately. The census, preserved in the Montefiore Archive in London, became a primary source for the genealogy of the Hebron Chabad community. It records details of residents including R' Shmuel Halevi (age 64) and his son R' Menachem Aryeh (age 40).

title_en: Montefiore's second visit to the Holy Land begins
summary_en: Sir Moses Montefiore and his entourage began their second visit to the Holy Land, lasting from late Iyar to late Tammuz 5599.
story_body: Montefiore's second trip to the Holy Land lasted about two months, from the end of Iyar through the end of Tammuz 5599. The party first toured Tzfat, Tiberias, and surrounding villages. They then traveled to Jerusalem, where due to a plague and quarantine they pitched their tents on the Mount of Olives opposite the Temple Mount.

title_en: Hebron Chabad sends delegation to greet Montefiore in Jerusalem
summary_en: On 28 Sivan 5599 the Hebron Chabad community received Montefiore's letter and dispatched a delegation to Jerusalem with an invitation.
story_body: When Montefiore wrote from Jerusalem to the heads of the Hebron community about the purpose of his visit, the letter arrived in Hebron on 28 Sivan. That same day the Chabad community wrote a letter of invitation asking him to visit their city, sent through a special delegation of two community leaders who traveled to Jerusalem to escort him personally to Hebron.

title_en: Hebron delegates arrive at Montefiore's camp on Mount of Olives
summary_en: On the eve of Rosh Chodesh Tammuz 5599, the Hebron Chabad delegation reached Montefiore's encampment on the Mount of Olives.
story_body: The Hebron delegation arrived at Montefiore's camp on the Mount of Olives on the night of erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz 5599. Lady Judith Montefiore notes in her diary that the messengers came to thank them for coming to the Land of Israel and stayed overnight. Dr. Eliezer Halevi's memoirs likewise mention these Hebron visitors who came to greet them.

title_en: Montefiore departs Jerusalem for Hebron
summary_en: Two days after the Hebron delegation arrived, Montefiore's party set out from Jerusalem to Hebron in the early morning.
story_body: On Friday morning, two days after the Hebron delegation reached him, Montefiore and his entourage departed Jerusalem for Hebron. After a brief stop at Rachel's Tomb they continued on, arriving near Hebron toward evening. Hundreds of Hebron residents came out to meet them, dancing and singing Psalms in their honor, and escorted them to an olive grove near the city where they pitched their tents.

title_en: Montefiore prays at Chabad synagogue in Hebron
summary_en: On Shabbat during their Hebron visit, Montefiore prayed Mincha at the Chabad synagogue in the Jews' courtyard.
story_body: During the Shabbat of Montefiore's visit, his party remained in their tents in the field. For the prayer services they went into the synagogues in the Jewish courtyard, and at Mincha Montefiore prayed in the Chabad synagogue. The community would later memorialize this event in a formal deed transferring his prayer spot in the synagogue to him as an eternal possession.

title_en: Hebron Chabad issues four honorary deeds to Montefiore
summary_en: On 4 Tammuz 5599 the Hebron Chabad leaders signed and delivered four honorary deeds to Sir Moses and Lady Judith Montefiore.
story_body: The four documents were signed on 4 Tammuz by the leaders of the Hebron Chabad community and delivered to Montefiore that same day. They granted him and his wife places in the synagogue, appointed Sir Moses as patron and head of the Talmud Torah society, and appointed Lady Judith as patron of the Bikur Cholim and Hachnasat Kallah societies. The deeds bound the community to send accountings to her each year.

title_en: Ottoman expulsion of Egyptian governor from the Land of Israel
summary_en: In 5600 the Ottomans expelled the Egyptian ruler from the Land of Israel, after which Sheikh Abdul Rahman returned to terrorize Hebron.
story_body: After the Ottoman authorities drove the Egyptian governor out of the Land of Israel in 5600, Sheikh Abdul Rahman resumed his rule over Hebron and its surroundings. He intensified his oppression of the Jews, imposing separate ransom payments on each of the two Jewish communities. The situation forced the diaspora kollel administrators to formally allocate him a share in the kollel's distribution list under the name 'the Black Rabbi.'

title_en: Renewed Chabad-Sephardi agreement in Hebron
summary_en: A renewed inter-communal agreement was signed in Hebron in 5602 documenting separate ransom burdens imposed by Sheikh Abdul Rahman.
story_body: Following the Ottoman return to power and Abdul Rahman's renewed exactions, the Chabad and Sephardi communities of Hebron updated their inter-communal agreement in 5602. The new accord, signed by R' Shmuel Halevi and R' Menachem Aryeh among others, formalized the separate 'ransom for souls' that the sheikh demanded from each community. This necessitated allocating him a fixed share in the Chabad kollel's distributions abroad.

title_en: Power of attorney to litigate in Jerusalem
summary_en: In 5603 R' Shmuel Halevi signed a power of attorney authorizing litigation in Jerusalem on behalf of the Hebron Chabad community.
story_body: Among the official acts of R' Shmuel Halevi as head of the Hebron Chabad community was a formal power of attorney from 5603 authorizing representation in legal proceedings in Jerusalem. The document is part of a series of signed instruments from his tenure as rabbi and maggid of Hebron. It reflects the community's regular need to handle disputes outside the city through proxies.

title_en: Mohammed Pasha conquers Hebron from Abdul Rahman
summary_en: In 5606 the Ottoman governor of Jerusalem, Mohammed Pasha, conquered Hebron from Sheikh Abdul Rahman, with widespread looting following.
story_body: After a long internal war between Abdul Rahman and his brothers, Mohammed Pasha, the Ottoman governor of Jerusalem, marched on Hebron in 5606 and captured it from the rebellious sheikh. During the conquest the city was given over to murder and plunder until the governor signaled a halt; the looters did not distinguish between Jews and gentiles. The Sephardi rabbis described how 'sons of Belial' stripped the entire city, while later accounts emphasize that during this second plunder lives were spared and the looting lasted only half a day.

title_en: Letter to Rabbi Avraham Chaim Gagin
summary_en: R' Shmuel Halevi signed a letter to R' Avraham Chaim Gagin, Rishon LeTzion, in 5606.
story_body: In 5606 R' Shmuel Halevi, maggid of Hebron, signed an official letter addressed to R' Avraham Chaim Gagin (the AGaN), Sephardi chief rabbi of Jerusalem. The letter is preserved in Migdal Oz and is one of the last documents bearing his signature before his death sometime between 5609 and 5615. It illustrates the ongoing institutional relationship between the Hebron Chabad community and the Sephardi rabbinic establishment of Jerusalem.

title_en: Hebron Chabad families relocate to Jerusalem
summary_en: Beginning in 5607, several Hebron Chabad families migrated to Jerusalem due to oppression by local Muslim rulers.
story_body: Unable to bear the burden of Sheikh Abdul Rahman's exactions and post-conquest hardship, several Chabad families left Hebron for Jerusalem starting in 5607. They settled in the northern part of the Old City on a street the Arabs called 'Harat al-Wad,' which became known among Ashkenazim as 'Rechov HaChevronim' — the Hebronites' Street — for the very families who settled there. In 5609 they described their motives in a moving letter to Montefiore.

title_en: Letter from Hebron migrants to Montefiore
summary_en: In 5609 Chabad family heads who had relocated from Hebron to Jerusalem wrote to Montefiore describing their reasons for leaving.
story_body: Two years after relocating to Jerusalem, leaders of the migrant families wrote to Sir Moses Montefiore in 5609. They described the crushing oppression of the local rulers in Hebron and the influx of new arrivals which only intensified the burdens. They explained that the special share allocated to Abdul Rahman in the Chabad kollel's distributions consumed funds intended for their own livelihood, forcing them to thin out the Hebron community.

title_en: Death of R' Shmuel Halevi, first Chabad rabbi of Hebron
summary_en: R' Shmuel Halevi Segal, first rabbi of the Chabad community in Hebron, died between 5609 and 5615.
story_body: R' Shmuel Halevi Segal, who had served as maggid and de facto rabbi of the Hebron Chabad community since his arrival in 5584, died at some point between 5609 and 5615. In the 5609 census he is still listed among the community appointees, but in the 5615 census only his widow appears. His son R' Menachem Aryeh succeeded him as a leading figure of the community and served as a dayan.

title_en: British Consul Finn reports on Abdul Rahman's extortion
summary_en: On 28 August 1854 British Consul James Finn wrote to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe detailing Sheikh Abdul Rahman's extortion of Hebron Jewry.
story_body: In late summer 5614, British Consul James Finn in Jerusalem wrote to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe describing the Hebron Jews' suffering at the hands of Abdul Rahman. He reported a unique feature of the sheikh's extortion: collecting a fixed share of the seasonal halukkah donations from European Jewry on which the Hebron Jews depended. His name was entered in the kollel ledgers as a stipend recipient, and he would send representatives to collect three days before the scheduled distribution.

title_en: Yeshivat Magen Avot founded in Hebron
summary_en: The Chabad yeshiva 'Magen Avot' was founded in Hebron in 5649, predating Yeshivat Torat Emet by over two decades.
story_body: Yeshivat Magen Avot, a Chabad yeshiva in Hebron, was established in 5649. It functioned in Hebron until Yeshivat Torat Emet was founded in 5672. The Rebbe Rashab took particular interest in Magen Avot and reorganized it in 5663 in an effort to deepen Chassidic learning in the Holy Land.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab reorganizes Yeshivat Magen Avot
summary_en: In 5663 the Rebbe Rashab reorganized Yeshivat Magen Avot in Hebron in an attempt to revive Chassidic learning in the Holy Land.
story_body: Distressed by the near-total absence of Chassidut study in the Holy Land, particularly among younger married men, the Rebbe Rashab in 5663 personally undertook to reorganize Yeshivat Magen Avot in Hebron. He hoped this would address the spiritual gap he had observed among otherwise pious students. In a letter from Elul 5663 he explained that even ardent Torah scholars in the Land knew almost nothing of Chassidut and were utterly distant from it.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab writes about plans for new Hebron yeshiva
summary_en: In Cheshvan 5669 the Rebbe Rashab wrote that the existing Hebron yeshiva was inadequate and outlined plans for a new institution.
story_body: In a letter from Cheshvan 5669 the Rebbe Rashab explained that although a Chabad yeshiva already existed in Hebron, it was 'small and not what we truly intend.' He envisioned a yeshiva that would attract God-fearing avreichim devoted to Torah study under proper supervision. This vision would be realized three years later with the founding of Yeshivat Torat Emet.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab purchases Romano courtyard in Hebron
summary_en: In late summer 5668 the Rebbe Rashab purchased the Romano courtyard in Hebron from Avraham Romano, son of Markado Romano.
story_body: At the end of summer 5668 the Rebbe Rashab acquired the famous Romano courtyard in Hebron from Avraham, son of the late Markado Romano. The grand mansion had been built outside the Jewish ghetto in the 1870s and had hosted prominent visitors, including R' Chizkiyah Medini, the Sdei Chemed, who lived and died there. After the purchase the building would become a central Chabad property in Hebron.

title_en: Yeshivat Torat Emet founded in Hebron
summary_en: At the start of 5672 the Rebbe Rashab founded Yeshivat Torat Emet in Hebron, sending a mashpia and seven select Tomchei Temimim students.
story_body: The Rebbe Rashab established Yeshivat Torat Emet in Hebron at the beginning of 5672. To launch it he dispatched a dedicated mashpia along with seven of the finest students from Yeshivat Tomchei Temimim in Lubavitch. In a general letter to chassidim in winter 5672 he explained that the lack of a proper yeshiva in their kollel had left even those drawn to Torah study without support, and announced the new institution as the realization of the founders' true vision.

title_en: WWI forces Torat Emet shluchim back to Russia
summary_en: With the outbreak of World War I in 5674, the mashpia and student shluchim of Yeshivat Torat Emet returned from Hebron to Russia.
story_body: When World War I began in 5674 (1914), the mashpia and the student shluchim who had been sent from Lubavitch to staff Yeshivat Torat Emet in Hebron were forced to return to Russia. The yeshiva's original Hebron operation effectively shut down. The institution would later be reopened in Jerusalem, where it continues to operate today.

title_en: Hebron Romano land purchase deed
summary_en: In 1871 (5631) a deed was registered for a parcel of Hebron land purchased on behalf of Markado Romano of Istanbul.
story_body: In 1871 a deed in Arabic was executed recording the purchase of a Hebron parcel for 'Markado the Jew of Constantinople residing in al-Khalil' from Khalil, son of the late Ibrahim Abu-Amar Siyaj, for 4,000 grush. The Romano family used such purchases to begin building outside the walls of the Jewish quarter, breaking the ghetto pattern. The grand Romano mansion that resulted was constructed over the following years and completed in 5638.

title_en: Romano courtyard construction completed
summary_en: Construction of the Romano mansion in Hebron was completed in 5638, immediately triggering a major dispute.
story_body: After years of planning and building, Markado Romano's grand mansion in Hebron was completed in 5638. The completion immediately sparked a controversy when Romano had a dispute with one of the builders, who brought the matter before R' Eliyahu Mani, Sephardi rabbi of Hebron. When Mani ruled against Romano, Romano accused him of favoritism, igniting a years-long communal conflict that drew in the entire Holy Land Jewish community.

title_en: Peace agreement ends Hebron rabbinic dispute
summary_en: In Tammuz 5646 a peace agreement was signed ending the long Hebron rabbinic dispute, with R' Eliyahu Mani as chief rabbi and R' Rachamim Yosef Franko as Av Beit Din.
story_body: After years of bitter dispute over the Hebron rabbinate, prompted by Markado Romano's conflict with R' Eliyahu Mani, the Jerusalem rabbis brokered a reconciliation. In Tammuz 5646 a peace agreement was signed, with both R' Eliyahu Mani and R' Rachamim Yosef Franko among the signatories. The accord established Mani as the Sephardi chief rabbi of Hebron and Franko (the Charif) as Av Beit Din.

title_en: Romano courtyard registered to R' Rachamim Yosef Franko
summary_en: Around 1888 the Romano courtyard in Hebron was formally registered in the name of R' Rachamim Yosef Franko.
story_body: After Markado Romano's death in Damascus while returning from visiting his ill son in Istanbul, his Istanbul heirs decided to register the Hebron mansion temporarily in the name of R' Rachamim Yosef Franko. A deed from approximately 1888 records the transfer from 'Markado Effendi son of Ibrahim Romano the Istanbuli' to 'Rachamim Effendi Franko.' The arrangement was not a final sale, since the heirs themselves did not live in the Holy Land.

title_en: R' Chizkiyah Medini settles in Romano house
summary_en: When R' Chizkiyah Medini came to Hebron in 5661, the Romano family hosted him in their mansion, where he completed his Sdei Chemed.
story_body: R' Chizkiyah Medini, author of the Sdei Chemed, arrived in Hebron in 5661 and was housed by the Romano family in their stately mansion. He used the building, which contained a synagogue called the Istanbuli Beit Knesset, as his base for Torah study and teaching. There he completed his monumental Sdei Chemed before dying on 24 Kislev 5665. The 'Yeshivat Sdei Chemed' was later established in the same building in his memory.

title_en: Death of R' Chizkiyah Medini (Sdei Chemed)
summary_en: R' Chizkiyah Medini, author of the Sdei Chemed, died on 24 Kislev 5665 in the Romano mansion in Hebron.
story_body: R' Chizkiyah Medini died on 24 Kislev 5665 in the Romano mansion in Hebron, where he had lived and taught since his arrival in 5661. He passed away while still engaged in his Torah study and writing. His monumental halachic encyclopedia, the Sdei Chemed, was completed during his years in that house, and the yeshiva later established there was named in his honor.

title_en: World War I devastates Hebron's Jewish community
summary_en: The outbreak of WWI shook Hebron's Jewish settlement, cutting off charitable distribution funds and triggering hunger and disease.
story_body: When World War I broke out in 5674/1914, Hebron's Jewish community was severely shaken. Fears of Turkish military conscription, the cessation of chalukah funds reaching the yeshivot, and a collapse of incoming support from emissaries (shadarim) forced many Jews to flee. Hunger and disease drove residents to seek refuge wherever they could find it.

title_en: Turkish government expels Russian-citizen Jews from Hebron
summary_en: In Tevet 5675, the Ottoman government expelled Chabad Jews of Russian citizenship from the Land of Israel as nationals of an enemy power.
story_body: R' Avraham Chaim Naeh recorded in the preface to his Shnos Chaim that the expulsion took place in Tevet 5675 (December 1914). Because much of the Chabad community in Hebron held Russian citizenship, they were forced out by Turkey as enemy nationals. Many of the exiles concentrated in Alexandria (No-Amon), Egypt.

title_en: R' Mordechai Dovber Slonim, head of Kollel Chabad Hebron, passes away
summary_en: R' Mordechai Dovber Slonim, the appointed head of Kollel Chabad in Hebron, died on 5 Tevet 5676 amid the wartime collapse of the community.
story_body: While the chief rabbi Shila and the yeshiva director R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin had fled to Russia at the start of the war, R' Mordechai Dovber Slonim remained behind in Hebron. Unable to withstand the suffering of the war years, he passed away in good name on 5 Tevet 5676. With his death, only a remnant of Chabad's Hebron leadership survived.

title_en: Zionist Office census records 757 Jews in Hebron
summary_en: A census conducted by the Zionist Organization's Palestine Office in 5678 found 757 Jews in Hebron, roughly half the pre-war population.
story_body: After the British conquest, the Palestine Office of the Zionist Organization conducted a census in 5678 (1918). It tallied 256 Ashkenazim, 444 Sephardim, and 57 Maghrebi and Yemenite Jews — a total of 757 souls. This was roughly half the Jewish population recorded a decade earlier.

title_en: Cheshvan 5683 census finds only 413 Jews remaining in Hebron
summary_en: By Cheshvan 5683 a precise count found only 413 Jews in Hebron, with the Chabad community essentially gone.
story_body: Yisrael Kaplan reported in HaTor (issue 31) that a careful census in Cheshvan 5683 found just 413 Jews in Hebron — 306 Sephardim and 107 Ashkenazim. The Chabad kollel, once first in seniority and stature with 165 souls in 5678, had nearly ceased to exist; only nine remaining families received a meager distribution administered from Jerusalem.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz urges revival of Torah study among Hebron Chabad remnant
summary_en: On 4 Shevat 5689 the Rebbe Rayatz wrote urging that Tanya, Likkutei Torah and chassidic review be set up for the remaining Chabad community in Hebron.
story_body: Writing to R' Shmuel Yehuda Chaim on 4 Shevat 5689, the Rebbe Rayatz lamented how abandoned the Hebron settlement had become and called for fixed shiurim in Tanya and Likkutei Torah. He named the dedicated chassid R' Moshe Goldsmid as the one who would gladly take on this teaching, if only listeners could be assembled.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz visits Hebron during his 1929 Holy Land trip
summary_en: In Tammuz 5689 the Rebbe Rayatz visited Hebron, touring Chatzer Romano and meeting with the local Chabad community.
story_body: The Rebbe Rayatz visited Hebron in Tammuz 5689, just weeks before the massacre that would destroy the community. He visited the home of R' Yaakov Yosef Slonim, toured Chabad's Chatzer Romano property, repeated a maamar in the synagogue, and called on the Slabodka yeshiva. The visit is described in Sefer HaToldos vol. 4 and in Sefer Chevron.

title_en: 1929 Hebron massacre destroys the Jewish community
summary_en: In Av 5689 Arab rioters massacred Jews in Hebron; survivors fled and the centuries-old Jewish settlement came to an end.
story_body: Just days after the Rebbe Rayatz's visit, the 1929 Hebron massacre fell upon the Jewish community. R' Moshe Goldsmid, the spiritual anchor of Chabad's tiny remnant, was among those slaughtered, hy"d. The surviving Jews abandoned Hebron, ending the Jewish settlement in the city.

title_en: Chabad chassidim begin migrating from Hebron to Jerusalem
summary_en: In 5607 Chabad families began migrating from Hebron to Jerusalem, founding the Chabad presence in the holy city.
story_body: Suffering under pressure from local landlords and the harsh treatment of gentile neighbors, Chabad families began leaving Hebron for Jerusalem in 5607 (1847). They rented homes in the northern Old City along Harat al-Wad — which Ashkenazim soon nicknamed 'Chevronim Street' (Hebron Street) — laying the foundation for the Chabad community in Jerusalem.

title_en: Ewald reports 16 Hebron Jewish families have relocated to Jerusalem
summary_en: A letter by F.C. Ewald dated October 4, 1847 reported 16 Jewish families totaling 53 souls had moved from Hebron to Jerusalem.
story_body: F.C. Ewald wrote on October 4, 1847 (published in London's Jewish Intelligence, January 1848) that since his previous report on the persecuted Jews of Hebron, 16 families had left and settled in Jerusalem, forming their own community of 53 souls. The letter is the earliest external attestation of the Hebron-to-Jerusalem migration of Chabad chassidim.

title_en: Jerusalem Chabad community petitions Montefiore for a synagogue
summary_en: In 5609 the founding Chabad settlers in Jerusalem wrote to Moses Montefiore describing their flight from Hebron and asking for funds to purchase a synagogue building.
story_body: The early Chabad settlers in Jerusalem, numbering some 30 baalei batim, sent a letter to Sir Moses Montefiore in 5609. They described their forced migration from Hebron two years earlier, the absence of a fixed beis midrash and mikveh, and asked for support to acquire a property they had found, available on a 12,000-grush mashkanta. Twelve heads of the community, led by R' Eliyahu Yosef Rivlin, signed the appeal.

title_en: R' Eliyahu Yosef Rivlin makes aliyah to Jerusalem
summary_en: The Gaon R' Eliyahu Yosef Rivlin, future overseer of Kollel Chabad in Jerusalem, immigrated to the Land of Israel in 5608.
story_body: The 5615 census records R' Eliyahu Yosef Rivlin as having immigrated in 5608 (1848). Rabbinic approbations to his Ohalei Yosef (Jerusalem 5626) note he 'pitched his tent of Torah in Jerusalem for some eighteen years' until his passing on 12 Tammuz 5625. He became one of the lead signatories on the founding documents of Jerusalem's Chabad community.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe directs Chabad chassidim to settle in Hebron
summary_en: Between 5581 and 5583 the Mitteler Rebbe instructed his chassidim in the Holy Land to relocate from Tzfat to Hebron.
story_body: Having earlier settled in Tzfat between 5560 and 5565, Chabad chassidim were directed by the Mitteler Rebbe to move to Hebron during 5581-5583. Hebron became the principal Chabad center in the Holy Land for the next century. A handful remained in Tzfat until the 1837 earthquake.

title_en: Chabad chassidim relocate from Tiberias to Tzfat
summary_en: Between 5560 and 5565 the early Chabad chassidim of the Holy Land moved their main settlement from Tiberias to Tzfat.
story_body: Chabad chassidim relocated from Tiberias to Tzfat in the years 5560-5565, establishing Tzfat as their principal center until the Mitteler Rebbe later redirected them to Hebron. The move set the stage for two decades of Chabad presence in Tzfat before the 1837 earthquake.

title_en: 1837 Galilee earthquake kills Chabad chassidim in Tzfat
summary_en: The 24 Tevet 5597 earthquake in Tzfat killed members of the small surviving Chabad community there, including R' Shemaya and R' Lapidot Chalavna with his son.
story_body: Even after most Chabad chassidim had relocated to Hebron, a handful remained in Tzfat. The catastrophic Galilee earthquake of 24 Tevet 5597 (January 1, 1837) killed several of them, including R' Shemaya and R' Lapidot Chalavna and his son Shalom Aharon. After the earthquake only a few Chabad families lingered in Tzfat for another two years.

title_en: R' Leib Baal HaYisurin passes away in Tzfat
summary_en: R' Leib Baal HaYisurin, who moved to Tzfat in his final years, died there on 15 Cheshvan 5597.
story_body: R' Leib Baal HaYisurin, one of the early Chabad chassidim in the Holy Land, relocated to Tzfat in his final years. He passed away there on 15 Cheshvan 5597, only weeks before the great earthquake claimed the lives of others of the small Chabad community in the city.

title_en: R' Uri Ornstein leaves Tzfat for Hebron
summary_en: R' Uri Ornstein, the last prominent Chabad chassid in Tzfat, moved to Hebron in 5599.
story_body: R' Uri Ornstein lived in Tzfat until 5599 (1839), when he too relocated to Hebron. His departure essentially ended the Chabad presence in Tzfat for the next several decades; no Chabad chassidim are recorded there from 5600 through 5630.

title_en: Yeshiva Toras Emes founded in Hebron
summary_en: The Chabad yeshiva Toras Emes was established in Hebron at the start of 5672, surviving roughly two and a half years until WWI shut it down.
story_body: The yeshiva Toras Emes was founded in Hebron in early 5672 (late 1911). It operated for some two and a half years until the outbreak of World War I forced the mashpia-director and students — Russian subjects in an enemy state — to return to Russia. The yeshiva would lie dormant for seven years until being refounded in Jerusalem.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab instructs Havlin to revive Toras Emes at first opportunity
summary_en: On Purim 5680 in Rostov, the Rebbe Rashab directed R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin to return to the Holy Land and refound the Toras Emes yeshiva at the first possible opportunity.
story_body: Before his passing, the Rebbe Rashab spoke with R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin on Purim 5680 in Rostov, instructing him that as soon as travel became possible he must return to the Land of Israel — without regard to obstacles — to resume directing Yeshiva Toras Emes as before. The instruction is preserved in a 5684 letter of the Rebbe Rayatz (Igros Kodesh vol. 1, no. 134).

title_en: R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin departs Rostov for the Holy Land
summary_en: In mid-Elul 5681 R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin set out from Rostov with his family for the Land of Israel to refound the Toras Emes yeshiva.
story_body: Sent by the Rebbe Rayatz to renew Toras Emes, R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin departed Rostov with his family in mid-Elul 5681. The Rebbe wrote on 16 Elul 5681 to Shila on Havlin's behalf and on 19 Cheshvan 5682 reported having received word that Havlin was in Tiflis awaiting passage from Batum. The journey ended up taking nearly four months.

title_en: R' Havlin arrives in Jerusalem to refound Toras Emes
summary_en: R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin reached Jerusalem on Friday 6 Tevet 5682, refounding the Toras Emes yeshiva there.
story_body: After a circuitous four-month journey from Rostov through Tiflis, Batum and Constantinople, R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin arrived in Jerusalem on erev Shabbos 6 Tevet 5682. R' Menachem Mendel Naeh recorded his arrival in a 15 Tevet letter to the Rebbe. Toras Emes was reestablished in Jerusalem, where it continues to operate.

title_en: R' Chaim Shmuel Schmerling migrates from Hebron to Jaffa
summary_en: R' Chaim Shmuel Schmerling's move from Hebron to Jaffa in 5626 founded the Chabad — and largely the Ashkenazi — settlement there.
story_body: The Chabad settlement in Jaffa, and to a significant degree the broader Ashkenazi community there, originated with R' Chaim Shmuel Schmerling's relocation from Hebron in 5626 (1866). He founded the public institutions of the Ashkenazi community and lived in Jaffa for nearly thirty years.

title_en: R' Chaim Shmuel Schmerling passes away in Jaffa
summary_en: Founder of Jaffa's Ashkenazi institutions, R' Chaim Shmuel Schmerling died there on 2 Adar 5654.
