Their formal role marked early institutional recognition of the Chabad community within Jerusalem's Ashkenazi communal landscape.

title_en: Jerusalem census lists Yehoshua Natkin and Zalman Epstein as trustees
summary_en: The 5626 census recorded Yehoshua Natkin of Jacobstadt and Zalman Epstein as trustees of Kollel Chabad.
story_body: Periodic Jerusalem censuses recorded the leadership of Kollel Chabad as it evolved. The 5626 entry identified two trustees serving the community, illustrating the continuity of the kollel administrative structure across decades. Such records form a primary source for reconstructing Chabad institutional history in Jerusalem.

title_en: Jerusalem census records trustees of Kollel Chabad
summary_en: The 5635 census listed Avraham Statzeres, Aharon Lipkin, and the scribe Yeshaya Orenstein as Kollel Chabad trustees.
story_body: Avraham Statzeres, born in Navaradok in 5565, had made aliyah in 5621. Aharon Lipkin, born in Tolzin in 5593, had made aliyah in 5607. Yeshaya Orenstein, born in Eretz Yisrael in 5595, served alongside them as the scribe of the trusteeship.

title_en: Yehudah V'Yerushalayim published mentioning Aharon Lipkin's role
summary_en: R. Yoel Moshe Solomon's 1878 work described how funds from England for Jerusalem's kollelim flowed through Aharon Lipkin for Chabad.
story_body: In Yehudah V'Yerushalayim, Yoel Moshe Solomon recounted that money received from England by the General Vaad of Jerusalem's kollelim was distributed to each kollel separately. The Chabad portion was delivered to R. Aharon Lipkin, identified as their trustee. The account confirms Lipkin's continuing leadership role through the 1870s.

title_en: Yitzchak Sharion arrives in Jerusalem
summary_en: R. Yitzchak Sharion arrived in Jerusalem in 5649 and later recorded the kollel's leadership in his memoirs.
story_body: Upon his arrival in Jerusalem in 5649, Sharion noted that Kollel Chabad had two trustees, the senior of whom hailed from Kherson in southern Russia and was known as 'the Khersoner.' Sharion's memoirs, published in Jerusalem in 1943, became a key source for the kollel's mid-19th-century history.

title_en: HaChavatzelet supplement names Kollel Chabad trustees
summary_en: A 23 Shvat 5649 supplement to HaChavatzelet identified Yitzchak Yaakov Shabtai and B.M. Reizes as Kollel Chabad's trustees.
story_body: Issue 19's supplement carried the signature 'Yitzchak Yaakov Shabtai and B.M. Reizes, trustees of Kollel Chabad in the Holy City.' Although Sharion had not remembered the names of the trustees of his era, this published notice preserved them. Soon thereafter Michel Baruch Reizes would emerge as senior trustee.

title_en: Moshe Wittenberg makes aliyah to Jerusalem from Vitebsk
summary_en: R. Moshe Wittenberg made aliyah from Vitebsk to Jerusalem in 5642, later assuming a central financial role for Kollel Chabad.
story_body: Wittenberg was a known upright and reliable man, a Torah scholar and prominent Chabad chassid. After settling in Jerusalem, his stature led the Rebbeim and senior charity overseers abroad to propose elevating him to manage Kollel Chabad funds for Eretz Yisrael. His arrival from Vitebsk would prove foundational for the kollel's modern financial structure.

title_en: Mordechai Shlonk appointed as Kollel Chabad trustee
summary_en: R. Mordechai Shlonk was appointed as a Kollel Chabad trustee in 5647 by order of the Kapuster Rebbe.
story_body: In his Tumat Yesharim pamphlet of 1913, Shlonk wrote that he had served as a kollel trustee for 26 years. His appointment in 5647 came by directive of the Kapuster Rebbe alongside Michel Baruch Reizes. Shlonk's long tenure made him a key continuity figure during the leadership transitions of the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

title_en: Position of 'ba'al ha'adres' created with Moshe Wittenberg appointed
summary_en: Beginning in 5648 the kollel added a 'ba'al ha'adres' role; R. Moshe Wittenberg was the first appointee.
story_body: Wittenberg agreed to take the role only on condition that every community abroad send its R'Meir Baal HaNess charity funds directly to Jerusalem rather than through itinerant shadarim. This was meant to eliminate excessive expense and occasional waste. Most communities thereafter mailed their contributions directly to him.

title_en: Death of R. Moshe Wittenberg
summary_en: R. Moshe Wittenberg, ba'al ha'adres of Kollel Chabad, died on 27 Nissan 5659.
story_body: HaChavatzelet reported that on the third day of Chol HaMoed Pesach 5659 the renowned philanthropist Moshe ben Reuven Wittenberg, born and raised in Vitebsk, passed away childless. He had loved Jerusalem and made it his home for about eighteen years. After his death R. Manish Verovlanski and R. Mordechai Shlonk were jointly appointed to the address role.

title_en: R. Manish Verovlanski appointed ba'al ha'adres by the Rebbe Rashab
summary_en: R. Manish Verovlanski of Lazna was named ba'al ha'adres of Kollel Chabad in 5660 on the Rebbe Rashab's instruction.
story_body: The Rebbe Rashab wrote to R. Mendel Slonim on 3 Menachem Av 5660 expressing his preference that funds be sent to Verovlanski because this would establish proper order. The Rebbe Rashab later wrote that Verovlanski's appointment came by his own selection. Verovlanski served only three years before his death.

title_en: Death of R. Manish Verovlanski; Dov Ber Efrat appointed as ba'al ha'adres
summary_en: On 21 Cheshvan 5663 R. Manish Verovlanski died and R. Dov Ber Efrat was appointed in his place.
story_body: Following Verovlanski's death the kollel's leadership convened unanimously on Friday and chose R. Dov Ber Efrat as his successor. By tradition the appointment required approval from the network of overseas overseers, so confirmation by telegram was sought before printing new envelopes. R. Yehuda Leib Menuchin, the kollel bookkeeper, wrote that the appointment had been by full consensus.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter on Kollel Chabad bookkeeping
summary_en: A 16 Kislev 5663 letter from the Rebbe Rashab referred to R. Yehuda Leib Menuchin as the kollel's bookkeeper.
story_body: The Rebbe Rashab wrote that R. Leib Menuchin was at the time serving as bookkeeper of the kollel. The reference establishes Menuchin's formal position within the institutional structure of Kollel Chabad in Jerusalem at the start of the 20th century.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab appoints R. Menachem Mendel Nae as Kollel Chabad bookkeeper
summary_en: On 6 Kislev 5666 the Rebbe Rashab informed R. Nae of his appointment as the kollel's accountant.
story_body: The Rebbe instructed Rabbi Nae to request his predecessor R. Leib Menuchin to transfer all accounting documents addressed to the Rebbe's son. Nae was directed to send subsequent financial reports to designated central overseers including R. Chaim Bagin. The appointment came at a time of reorganization of the kollel's senior administration.

title_en: Death of R. Dov Ber Fradkin
summary_en: R. Dov Ber Fradkin, son of the author of Torat Chesed, died on 17 Adar Sheni 5665.
story_body: Fradkin had been added to the roster of kollel trustees as an honorary member, signing letters of the kollel out of respect for the institution's prestige. His role brought distinction without operational responsibilities, as he was not directly engaged in the kollel's affairs. His death further consolidated the active leadership around Shlonk, Efrat, Menuchin, and Ornstein.

title_en: Death of R. Michel Baruch Reizes
summary_en: R. Michel Baruch ben David Reizes, trustee of Kollel Chabad, died on 4 Nissan 5666.
story_body: Reizes had come to Jerusalem from Poltava in Russian Ukraine. He had served as senior trustee of Kollel Chabad in the late 19th century, in succession to the Khersoner. His death is recorded in Avnei Zikkaron volume 12.

title_en: Death of R. Yehuda Leib Menuchin
summary_en: R. Yehuda Leib Menuchin, former bookkeeper of Kollel Chabad, died on 10 Menachem Av 5667.
story_body: Menuchin had served as the kollel's bookkeeper in the early years of the 20th century until his role was transferred to R. Menachem Mendel Nae in late 5666. After his death, the active leadership of the Jerusalem kollel narrowed to Shlonk and Efrat as the address holders, with Yeshaya Ornstein as scribe and Nae as bookkeeper.

title_en: Death of R. Yaakov Ornstein
summary_en: R. Yaakov Ornstein, scribe of Kollel Chabad, died on 22 Sivan 5668.
story_body: Ornstein was succeeded by R. Moshe Ornstein, who first appears in the kollel's correspondence on 14 Menachem Av 5669 alongside trustees Dov Ber Efrat and Mordechai Shlonk. His death marked a generational transition in the scribal office of the kollel.

title_en: Yonah Wolf Mendelsohn sent from Hebron to America as shadar
summary_en: R. Yonah Wolf Mendelsohn was sent from Hebron to America in 5639 as emissary of the city's Jewish community.
story_body: HaChavatzelet of 11 Cheshvan 5639 reported the shedarut as undertaken 'by the community of Israel residents of Hebron from the Sephardic and Ashkenazi congregations.' No indication ties it to the broader Kollel Chabad system. The article noted that Hebron's communities had never authorized the Jerusalem rabbinate to send emissaries on their behalf.

title_en: Direct postal collection replaces traveling shadarim
summary_en: From 5648 onward Kollel Chabad shifted from collecting support via traveling shadarim to direct postal transfer.
story_body: Funds were no longer entrusted to traveling emissaries but were mailed by each community directly to the 'ba'al ha'adres' in Jerusalem. The reform aimed to reduce avoidable expense and risk of misappropriation associated with the older shadar model. R. Moshe Wittenberg was appointed as the first ba'al ha'adres to oversee the new system.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab selects R. Meir Leib Horowitz as kollel emissary
summary_en: On 19 Shvat 5666 the Rebbe Rashab announced he had chosen R. Meir Leib Horowitz as shaliach for the holy task.
story_body: The Rebbe Rashab held that emissary travel remained essential to invigorate R'Meir Baal HaNess collections, despite the move to postal collection. He explained in several Shvat 5666 letters that personal travel was needed to gather accumulated sums and to strengthen future giving by appointing local collectors. Horowitz was selected as 'shaliach mitzvah' for this great mitzvah.

title_en: Bichawski publishes circular defending the adres system
summary_en: The general overseas gabbai R. Chaim Aharon Bichawski printed a circular titled 'Tshuva LeDorshei HaAdres' in 5668.
story_body: Bichawski urged donors not to wait for the arrival of traveling emissaries before remitting R'Meir Baal HaNess funds. Communities should send their contributions directly several times per year, and to avoid depriving the emissary of his livelihood, pay him a percentage of the sums collected and forwarded. The circular reflected the gradual shift away from purely shadar-based fundraising.

title_en: Kollel Chabad publishes detailed fundraising accounts
summary_en: In Kislev 5671 Kollel Chabad's trustees printed an itemized account of their etrog-trade-linked support in HaModia.
story_body: The supplement to HaModia presented a detailed list of remittances from hundreds of towns abroad for fiscal year 5670. Most communities were marked as having sent funds directly to Jerusalem rather than through shadarim. About one hundred towns were listed as collected by R. Ber Reich and roughly forty by R. Hirsch Tomerkin, indicating the surviving network of itinerant emissaries.

title_en: Agreement uniting Kollel Chabad with other Jerusalem kollels signed
summary_en: Heads of the Perushim, Volhynia, and Chabad kollels signed a ten-point agreement in Jerusalem on 14 Iyar 5632 unifying fundraising from Russia and Siberia.
story_body: After the earlier 5628 (1868) understanding failed to specify each kollel's share, leaders of all Ashkenazi kollels in the Holy Land negotiated a detailed pact dividing donations from Russia and Siberia—four parts to Perushim and Volhynia and one-fifth to Chabad. The document established joint signatories on receipts, banned unilateral fundraising letters, and required all monies to pass through four designated rabbis. It was signed for Kollel Chabad by Shimon Menashe Chaikin, Levi Yitzchak Slonim, Shneur Zalman Pundiminsky, and Yehuda Leib Slonim, all based in Hebron.

title_en: Rashab founds Va'ad HaChevroni to protect Hebron Chabad community
summary_en: In summer 5665 the Rebbe Rashab founded the Va'ad HaChevroni abroad to defend Hebron's share of Kollel Chabad funds against Jerusalem's growing dominance.
story_body: After the kollel's center shifted from Hebron to Jerusalem, the Hebron Chabad community declined economically as Jerusalem-based administrators favored their own city. The Rashab established the Va'ad HaChevroni to advocate for Hebron's rights abroad and demanded that a Hebron representative be included among the official signatories receiving kollel funds. He saw protecting Hebron as essential to maintaining the legacy of his predecessors who had specifically chosen Hebron.

title_en: Rashab publishes kuntres defending Hebron's primacy in Kollel Chabad
summary_en: At the start of 5667 the Rashab released a lengthy kuntres explaining why Hebron deserves priority over Jerusalem in Chabad's communal support.
story_body: The Rashab argued that although Jerusalem possesses greater inherent holiness, the present spiritual quality of Hebron was higher because Jerusalem had become contaminated by sinners while Hebron remained pure under vigilant rabbinic leadership. He cited the Mitteler Rebbe and Tzemach Tzedek's deliberate choice of Hebron and urged Torah scholars to settle there. He also announced plans for a new society called Chevronim to strengthen Hebron, though the previous year's troubles had delayed its launch.

title_en: Kollel Chabad reorganized with Va'ad HaMoetza after WWI
summary_en: At the end of Tevet 5680 Chabad anash in Jerusalem elected three administrators and a four-member advisory council to lead Kollel Chabad pending the Rebbe's involvement.
story_body: With the Hebron Chabad community dissolved by war and Russian income cut off after the Revolution, only the local administrators remained of the old kollel structure. By secret ballot, anash chose three memunim and a four-member Va'ad HaMoetza, explicitly declaring the kollel under the patronage of the Lubavitcher Rebbe and stipulating that all decisions were temporary until contact with the Rebbe could be restored. This arrangement lasted nine years until the Rayatz formally accepted the kollel's presidency.

title_en: R' Azriel Zelig Slonim sent as Kollel Chabad emissary to America
summary_en: On 24 Adar Sheni 5684 the Kollel Chabad administrators signed a contract dispatching R' Azriel Zelig Slonim to the United States as the kollel's fundraising emissary.
story_body: Three administrators—R' Yisrael Asher Liba, R' Mordechai Kazarnovsky, and R' Moshe Ornstein—signed the agreement preserved in the kollel's letter ledger. The mission reflected the post-war effort to rebuild Kollel Chabad's finances after Russian funding had collapsed. Shadar missions to America became increasingly important during the interwar period.

title_en: Rayatz establishes Shulchan HaNesius over Kollel Chabad
summary_en: On 7 Marcheshvan 5691 the Rayatz issued letters formalizing the Shulchan HaNesius committee to oversee Kollel Chabad alongside the existing Va'ad HaMoetza.
story_body: Having previously appointed R' Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezrov as his personal representative when he accepted the kollel's presidency, the Rayatz now created a Shulchan HaNesius to ensure direct supervision of the kollel's affairs. The committee included rabbis Eliezrov, Menachem Mendel Naeh, Chaim Kam, Yisrael Asher Liba, and Mordechai Reuven Rokeach. Its regulations were sent in a separate document no longer extant.

title_en: Rashab founds Torat Emet yeshiva as independent Chabad institution
summary_en: In 5672 the Rebbe Rashab established the Torat Emet yeshiva as a separate institution outside the umbrella of Kollel Chabad.
story_body: Until then Kollel Chabad had served as the overarching organization for all Chabad activity in the Holy Land, with private institutions operating under its supervision. The Rashab broke this pattern by founding Torat Emet as an independent yeshiva, marking the beginning of a new institutional model for Chabad in Eretz Yisrael.

title_en: Torat Emet yeshiva opens in Jerusalem
summary_en: In 5682 the Torat Emet yeshiva opened a branch in Jerusalem, maintaining its status as an institution independent of Kollel Chabad.
story_body: Following the model established by the Rashab when he originally founded Torat Emet in 1912, the yeshiva's Jerusalem branch operated outside the Kollel Chabad framework. This continued the trend of creating standalone Chabad institutions rather than placing all activity under the kollel umbrella.

title_en: Rayatz founds Achei Tmimim yeshiva in Tel Aviv
summary_en: In 5698 the Rayatz established the Achei Tmimim yeshiva in Tel Aviv as a Chabad institution independent of Kollel Chabad.
story_body: Continuing the pattern set by his predecessor, the Rayatz founded Achei Tmimim in Tel Aviv and later added a Tomchei Tmimim division. Both operated separately from Kollel Chabad's Jerusalem-based framework, shifting Chabad's institutional center of gravity in the Holy Land away from the older kollel structure.

title_en: Rayatz founds Agudat Chabad of Eretz Yisrael in Tel Aviv
summary_en: In the summer of 5701 the Rayatz established Agudat Chabad of Eretz Yisrael in Tel Aviv as a new umbrella organization for Chabad institutions.
story_body: Under the Rayatz's direct supervision, Agudat Chabad expanded into a new umbrella organization rivaling the older Kollel Chabad structure based in Jerusalem. This created tension over whether oversight of chassidus study programs in Jerusalem belonged to the Tel Aviv-based Agudat Chabad or to Kollel Chabad.

title_en: Rayatz orders Kollel Chabad to follow Agudat Chabad directives
summary_en: On 19 Menachem Av 5704 the Rayatz wrote to Kollel Chabad's leadership directing them and Yeshivat Tzemach Tzedek to obey Agudat Chassidei Chabad of Eretz Yisrael.
story_body: Disputes between Kollel Chabad and Agudat Chabad over jurisdiction—particularly over chassidus shiurim in Jerusalem—had been escalating between the two organizations. The Rayatz resolved the conflict by formally subordinating Kollel Chabad and Yeshivat Tzemach Tzedek's administrators to Agudat Chabad's directives. The ruling consolidated authority over Chabad activity in the Holy Land under the newer Tel Aviv-based body.

title_en: R' David Levanon, head of Kollel Chabad, passes away
summary_en: On 4 Nissan 5706 R' David Levanon, longtime co-administrator of Kollel Chabad, passed away and was succeeded by R' Yitzchak Avigdor Ornstein.
story_body: Levanon had served as co-signer on Kollel Chabad correspondence from 5688 through 5706, paired first with R' Yisrael Asher Liba and later with R' Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezrov. After his death on 4 Nissan, his administrative role was filled by R' Yitzchak Avigdor Ornstein, continuing the kollel's leadership structure.

title_en: R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk migrates from Safed to Tiberias
summary_en: In 5541 R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk left Safed for Tiberias after sustained harassment by the Sephardic pakid over communal tax payments.
story_body: Unable in 5540 to pay the annual fee demanded by the Sephardic pakid for Safed's communal needs, R' Menachem Mendel suffered repeated threats including imprisonment in iron chains. Though relief funds arrived through the emissary R' Shlomo Zalman HaKohen, the persistent torment caused him to fall ill for months and ultimately drove him to relocate to Tiberias. He found refuge in the house formerly occupied by R' Shlomo of Lvov, who had recently fled abroad.

title_en: R' Shlomo of Lvov, author of Mercavat HaMishneh, dies in Salonika
summary_en: On 21 Tammuz 5541 R' Shlomo of Lvov, author of Mercavat HaMishneh, died in Salonika after being driven from Tiberias and Acre.
story_body: R' Shlomo had settled in 5539 in Tiberias's finest house on the strength of a letter from Istanbul recommending him for honor and a worthy dwelling. He was eventually expelled, wandering through Sha'farem, Acre, and other locations, suffering bodily and financial harm at each stop. He finally fled abroad to Salonika where he died, his vacated Tiberias house becoming the residence of R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk.

title_en: R' Avraham of Kalisk and remaining Chassidim move from Safed to Tiberias
summary_en: In 5543 R' Avraham of Kalisk and remaining Chassidim of Safed were forced to leave the city after the Sephardic pakid's escalating hostility.
story_body: The pakid of Safed, hating that R' Avraham refused to eat from his shochet, expelled him forcefully, dragging many devoted Chassidim out with him. Some settled in the village of Pekiin, while R' Avraham himself moved to Tiberias where R' Menachem Mendel arranged a fine residence for him. The migration completed the relocation of the Chassidic community from Safed to Tiberias.

title_en: R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk completes his house and synagogue in Tiberias
summary_en: By winter 5546 R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk completed a three-story house in Tiberias containing a beautiful synagogue.
story_body: After years of struggle with the Sephardic pakid who initially refused permission for a separate Ashkenazi prayer space, R' Menachem Mendel built a permanent three-story house with an integrated synagogue. The Sephardic pakid who had tormented him died suddenly after attempting to extort funds, and the new pakid was peaceful. The synagogue served as a center of prayer and Torah study for the Chassidic community in Tiberias.

title_en: Plague strikes Safed, Tiberias and surrounding regions
summary_en: In 5546 a severe plague struck Safed and nearby cities, eventually reaching Tiberias where R' Menachem Mendel and his community sequestered themselves to survive.
story_body: The plague first ravaged Safed and surrounding areas, sending many Chassidim fleeing to Tiberias where R' Menachem Mendel arranged their needs. When the outbreak finally reached Tiberias from Purim through several days into Iyar, R' Menachem Mendel locked himself with over a minyan of followers inside his new courtyard rather than fleeing the city. Other Tiberias residents followed his example, sealing themselves into their homes; the surrounding villages including Pekiin were spared entirely.

title_en: Two R' Aharons emigrate to Eretz Yisrael; ship sinks near Crimea
summary_en: Two Chassidim named R' Aharon emigrated to Eretz Yisrael with R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk's caravan, surviving a shipwreck near Crimea.
story_body: In summer 1777 (תקל"ז), R' Aharon b"R Yitzchak Aizik (Aharon the Great) and R' Aharon b"R Meir of Smilyan (Aharon the Small) joined R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk's caravan to Eretz Yisrael. Their ship sank near Crimea, but both survived. They settled first in Tzfat and later moved to Tiberias.

title_en: R' Aharon the Great departs as shadar to chu"l
summary_en: R' Aharon b"R Yitzchak Aizik (Aharon the Great) left Eretz Yisrael as a shadar to the diaspora in 1785.
story_body: According to Sheluchei Eretz Yisrael, R' Aharon the Great departed for the diaspora as an emissary in 1785 (תקמ"ה), carrying a letter of mission from R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk and R' Avraham of Kalisk. He remained abroad for three years collecting funds and strengthening ties with the Chassidic communities.

title_en: R' Aharon the Great returns to Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: R' Aharon the Great returned to Eretz Yisrael in mid-Adar I 1788 after three years abroad as a shadar.
story_body: R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk's last letter, written in Nisan 1788, reports that 'the ship arrived, thank G-d, with the aforementioned shadar and his companions... they came in peace in the middle of Adar I.' This confirmed R' Aharon the Great's return to Eretz Yisrael after his shadar mission.

title_en: R' Yaakov of Smilyan becomes chief gabbai in chu"l
summary_en: R' Yaakov of Smilyan began his role as chief gabbai in the diaspora for Eretz Yisrael Chassidim in 1781.
story_body: R' Yaakov of Smilyan started his work as the chief gabbai abroad collecting funds for the Chassidic settlement in Eretz Yisrael in 1781 (תקמ"א). This role was foundational for the organized fundraising system that supported Chabad and other Chassidic groups in the Holy Land.

title_en: R' Shneur Zalman of Liadi reconciles with R' Aharon
summary_en: R' Shneur Zalman wrote an undated letter to his Chassidim reporting reconciliation with R' Aharon and others after a dispute.
story_body: In an undated letter (likely from 1783), R' Shneur Zalman of Liadi described investigating a dispute and finding that his beloved companions, including R' Tzvi b"R Mendel Segal and R' Aharon the Great, remained loyal to him. After two weeks together, the misunderstanding was resolved and their mutual love was renewed.

title_en: R' Aharon's confessional letter to R' Shneur Zalman
summary_en: R' Aharon the Great wrote a remorseful letter to R' Shneur Zalman in 1787 begging forgiveness for slighting him.
story_body: After returning to Eretz Yisrael, R' Aharon the Great was rebuked by R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk for having spoken against R' Shneur Zalman during his shadar mission. From Tiberias he wrote a tearful confession asking R' Shneur Zalman to forgive him so that he could be readmitted to R' Menachem Mendel's presence.

title_en: R' Shlomo Zalman HaKohen letter mentions passing of R' Menachem Mendel
summary_en: R' Shlomo Zalman HaKohen of Vilna wrote a summer 1788 letter mentioning the passing of R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk.
story_body: In summer 1788, R' Shlomo Zalman HaKohen of Vilna addressed a letter to the diaspora referencing the passing of R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk. The letter was also addressed to 'R' Aharon the Small,' confirming the latter's role 'attending the Rebbe' at that time.

title_en: R' Moshe Meisels asks Mitteler Rebbe about aliyah
summary_en: R' Moshe Meisels consulted the Mitteler Rebbe about emigrating to Eretz Yisrael in 1814-1815.
story_body: Between 1814 and 1815, R' Moshe Meisels asked the Mitteler Rebbe about settling in Eretz Yisrael. The Rebbe advised against the move at the time and said he would not allocate Chassidic charity funds beyond fifty gold coins for travel expenses for him and R' Baruch Mordechai, rabbi of Bobruisk.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe directs Chassidim to make aliyah
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe instructed several of his Chassidim, including R' Moshe Meisels, to emigrate to Eretz Yisrael in 1816-1817.
story_body: In 1816-1817 (תקע"ו-ז), the Mitteler Rebbe directed several of his Chassidim to settle in Eretz Yisrael. R' Moshe Meisels was among them, and he initially settled in Tzfat after making aliyah.

title_en: R' Leib of Sena emigrates to Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: R' Leib of Sena (Chitrik) made aliyah in 1821 according to the Montefiore census of 1839.
story_body: The Montefiore census of 1839 records that R' Leib of Sena, known as Chitrik, emigrated to Eretz Yisrael in 1821 and settled in Hebron. He may have stopped in Istanbul on his journey, where he made acquaintances who later helped forward correspondence to Europe.

title_en: First Hebron Chabad shadar journey rejected by Tzfat kollel
summary_en: In summer 1821, the head of the Tzfat Chassidic kollel obstructed a Hebron shadar mission to the diaspora.
story_body: In summer 1821 (קיץ תקפ"א), the head of the Tzfat Chassidic kollel, R' Gershon Margolies, opposed a shadar sent on behalf of the new Hebron Chabad community to the diaspora. He intercepted some of the propaganda letters intended to support the new Chabad settlement in Hebron.

title_en: R' Moshe Meisels moves from Tzfat to Hebron
summary_en: R' Moshe Meisels relocated from Tzfat to Hebron in winter 1823, joining the new Chabad community there.
story_body: In the winter of 1823 (חורף תקפ"ג), R' Moshe Meisels moved from Tzfat to Hebron, becoming one of the leading administrators of the new Chabad settlement there. He signed many of the community's communal documents over the following two decades.

title_en: First Chabad-Sephardic agreement in Hebron
summary_en: The first agreement between the Chabad and Sephardic communities in Hebron was concluded in Tammuz 1825.
story_body: In Tammuz 1825 (תמוז תקפ"ה), the Chabad and Sephardic communities of Hebron reached their first formal agreement governing shadar territories and fundraising. The text of this initial agreement has not survived, but it predated the more detailed 1830 agreement.

title_en: Hebron Chabad sends shadar R' Yitzchak Ashkenazi to Babylonia
summary_en: The Chabad community of Hebron sent R' Yitzchak b"R Shlomo Ashkenazi as a shadar to Babylonia and Basra in summer 1827.
story_body: In summer 1827 (קיץ תקפ"ז), the Chabad community of Hebron sent R' Yitzchak b"R Shlomo Ashkenazi to 'the cities of Babylonia and Basra and their surroundings.' Though the shadar was a Sephardic Jerusalem resident, he was dispatched by the Ashkenazi Chabad community, reflecting their isolation from traditional Russian funding streams.

title_en: New Italy/Spain shadarus compromise in Hebron
summary_en: A new compromise on shadar missions to Italy and Spain between Hebron's Chabad and Sephardic communities took effect on Rosh Chodesh Elul 1829.
story_body: On Rosh Chodesh Elul 1829 (ר"ח אלול תקפ"ט), a new compromise between the Chabad and Sephardic communities in Hebron came into effect regarding shadar missions to Italy and Spain. This compromise resolved disputes that had not been settled in the first 1825 agreement.

title_en: Second Chabad-Sephardic agreement in Hebron
summary_en: The second formal agreement between Hebron's Chabad and Sephardic communities was concluded in Elul 1830.
story_body: In Elul 1830 (אלול תק"צ), the Chabad and Sephardic communities of Hebron concluded their second formal agreement. It specifically covered shadar missions to Germany, Italy, Spain, and neighboring countries, building on the earlier 1825 understanding.

title_en: Pogroms and earthquake strike Hebron
summary_en: Hebron suffered pogroms and an earthquake in summer 1834, prompting urgent appeals from the Chabad community.
story_body: In summer 1834 (קיץ תקצ"ד), pogroms and an earthquake devastated Hebron. The Chabad community wrote desperate letters to their supporters abroad, which the Pekidim u'Amarkalim of Amsterdam later reproduced in printed circulars to encourage greater donations.

title_en: R' Natan Amram departs Hebron as shadar
summary_en: R' Natan Amram left Hebron on Erev Shavuot 1835 as a shadar to Italy and Turkey on behalf of the Chabad and Sephardic communities.
story_body: On the eve of Shavuot 1835 (ערב חג השבועות תקצ"ה), R' Natan Amram departed Hebron as a joint Chabad-Sephardic shadar. Although a request had been made to also include Germany, Holland, France, and England, those territories remained off-limits per the Pekidim u'Amarkalim agreement.

title_en: R' Natan Amram arrives in Livorno
summary_en: R' Natan Amram arrived in Livorno at the end of Av 1835 to begin his fundraising mission in Italy and Turkey.
story_body: At the end of Av 1835 (שלהי מנ"א תקצ"ה), R' Natan Amram reached Livorno, beginning a five-year shadar journey through many cities in Italy and Turkey on behalf of the Hebron Chabad community in partnership with the Sephardic kollel.

title_en: Hebron Chabad letter on famine and war
summary_en: Hebron's Chabad leaders wrote a letter on 13 Shevat 1846 describing severe famine and war that prevented food imports.
story_body: On 13 Shevat 1846 (י"ג שבט תר"ו), Chabad leaders in Hebron wrote a desperate appeal describing a heavy famine in the Holy Land. War between local rulers had been ongoing for nearly a year, preventing the import of grain, leaving women and children begging for bread. The letter was later reproduced by the Pekidim u'Amarkalim in their fundraising circulars.

title_en: R' Moshe Meisels passes away in Hebron
summary_en: R' Moshe Meisels, author of 'Shirat Moshe' on the 613 commandments and a Chabad leader in Hebron, passed away on 24 Menachem Av 1849.
story_body: R' Moshe Meisels, author of 'Shirat Moshe' on the 613 commandments, passed away in Hebron on 24 Menachem Av 1849. A longtime trustee of the Vilna community who later spied for Czar Alexander I against Napoleon and met Napoleon personally twice, he settled in Tzfat circa 1816 and moved to Hebron in 1823, where he became one of the leading administrators of the Chabad kollel.

title_en: Joint Hebron sages letter printed in HaMagid
summary_en: A joint letter signed by Hebron's Sephardic and Ashkenazi Chabad sages was printed in HaMagid following its dating in Tevet 1870.
story_body: In Tevet 1870 (טבת תר"ל), the leading rabbis of Hebron - both Sephardic and Chabad Ashkenazim - signed a joint appeal describing the community's plight. The letter was published as a supplement in HaMagid on 15 Adar I 1870, urging Jewish donors to contribute generously to support the suffering Holy Land communities.

title_en: Death of R' Shimon Menashe; R' DovBer Efrat appointed rabbi of Hebron
summary_en: Rabbi Shimon Menashe of Hebron passed away on 29 Sivan 1893, and R' DovBer Efrat was appointed in his place.
story_body: Rabbi Shimon Menashe of Hebron died on 29 Sivan 1893 (כ"ט סיון תרנ"ג). R' DovBer Efrat, who had already arrived in Hebron from Moscow following the 1891 expulsion of Jews from that city, was appointed to succeed him as rabbi of the Ashkenazi community in Hebron.

title_en: Expulsion of Jews from Moscow
summary_en: Russian authorities expelled the Jews of Moscow in 1891, forcing Chabad rabbis R' DovBer Efrat and R' Chaim Yaakov Widerwitz to flee.
story_body: In 1891 (תרנ"א), the Czarist government issued the Moscow expulsion decree, forcing Jewish residents to leave the city. The two Chabad rabbis serving Moscow at the time, R' DovBer Efrat and R' Chaim Yaakov Widerwitz, both had to depart. Widerwitz emigrated to America, while Efrat made aliyah to Hebron where his grandmother and the Slonim family lived.

title_en: R' DovBer Efrat arrives in Hebron
summary_en: R' DovBer Efrat arrived in Hebron at the end of 1891 after leaving Moscow due to the expulsion decree.
story_body: R' DovBer Efrat, grandson of Rebbetzin Menucha Rachel Slonim, arrived in Hebron at the end of 1891 (שלהי תרנ"א) after the Moscow expulsion forced him out of Russia. He joined his extended Slonim family already settled there.

title_en: R' DovBer Efrat issues shochet certification in Hebron
summary_en: R' DovBer Efrat issued a kosher slaughter certification on 13 Kislev 1891 shortly after arriving in Hebron.
story_body: On 13 Kislev 1891 (י"ג כסלו תרנ"ב), R' DovBer Efrat gave a relative a shochet u'bodek certification. The document opens with his statement that the Almighty had granted him to come to the Holy City and notes the duration of his residence there, confirming his arrival shortly before.

title_en: HaChavatzelet announces R' DovBer Efrat's rabbinic appointment
summary_en: The newspaper HaChavatzelet published the announcement of R' DovBer Efrat's appointment as rabbi of Hebron on 9 Tammuz 1893.
story_body: On 9 Tammuz 1893 (ט' תמוז תרנ"ג), the newspaper HaChavatzelet reported that R' DovBer Efrat, formerly one of the rabbis of Moscow, had been chosen as the new rabbi of the Ashkenazi community in Hebron. The notice described him as a 'distinguished guest' passing through Jerusalem.

title_en: R' Eliezerov writes blessing letter to new Hebron rabbi
summary_en: R' Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov (Shil"a) sent a blessing letter to R' DovBer Efrat on 15 Av 1893 from his shadar journey.
story_body: On 15 Av 1893 (ט"ו רחמים תרנ"ג), while serving as a shadar abroad, R' Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov (Shil"a) wrote a heartfelt blessing letter to R' DovBer Efrat congratulating him on his appointment as rabbi of Hebron. The letter wished him strength to lead with justice and uprightness.

title_en: R' DovBer Efrat leaves Hebron rabbinate for Jerusalem
summary_en: R' DovBer Efrat left the Hebron rabbinate after nine years to remarry and settle in Jerusalem in summer/Elul 1902.
story_body: After nine years as rabbi of Hebron's Ashkenazi community, R' DovBer Efrat left in summer 1902 (קיץ תרס"ב) and settled in Jerusalem in Elul of that year after taking a new wife there. He explained in HaChavatzelet that the heavy burden of communal duties had become too much for him in his advancing age.

title_en: R' DovBer Efrat appointed Chabad administrator in Jerusalem
summary_en: Following the death of R' Manish Wirowlianski on 21 Cheshvan 1902, R' DovBer Efrat was appointed Chabad kollel administrator in Jerusalem.
story_body: On 21 Cheshvan 1903 (כ"א מ"ח תרס"ג), R' Manish Wirowlianski, the administrator of the Chabad kollel in Jerusalem, passed away. The Jerusalem Chassidim appointed R' DovBer Efrat in his place, a role he held for nearly a decade until his death.

title_en: R' Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov becomes rabbi of Hebron
summary_en: R' Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov (Shil"a) was accepted as permanent rabbi of Hebron at the beginning of Iyar 1903.
story_body: At the beginning of Iyar 1903 (תחילת אייר תרס"ג), R' Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov was accepted as the permanent rabbi of Hebron, succeeding R' DovBer Efrat who had moved to Jerusalem. On 25 Iyar, R' DovBer Efrat printed a notice in HaChavatzelet redirecting all donations to be sent to the new rabbi.

title_en: R' DovBer Efrat passes away in Jerusalem
summary_en: R' DovBer Efrat, longtime Chabad rabbi and administrator in Hebron and Jerusalem, passed away on 1 Tammuz 1912.
story_body: R' DovBer Efrat passed away on 1 Tammuz 1912 (א' תמוז תער"ב) in Jerusalem. He had served nine years as rabbi of Hebron and nearly ten more years as administrator of the Chabad kollel in Jerusalem after the death of R' Manish Wirowlianski.

title_en: Montefiore's second visit to Eretz Yisrael with community census
summary_en: Moses Montefiore visited Eretz Yisrael and ordered a detailed census of every Jewish community in every city.
story_body: This was one of six Montefiore visits to the Holy Land. On each (except 5617, too close to the previous) he commissioned censuses listing every Jew by community, plus the community's institutions and leaders. The originals are preserved in his London archive, with photocopies in the Jerusalem library.

title_en: Hebron Chabad petitions Montefiore for a Jewish hospital in Jerusalem
summary_en: Hebron Chabad leaders wrote to Montefiore in Menachem Av 5609 urging the urgent construction of a Jewish hospital in Jerusalem.
story_body: The letter warned that without a Jewish hospital, sick Jews would be forced to seek care at the missionaries' hospital. The writers also asked that the Jerusalem doctor be authorized to travel to Hebron when called, since the town was too small to support its own physician at that time.

title_en: Montefiore's third visit and Hebron Bikur Cholim record
summary_en: Montefiore's 5615 census recorded Hebron's Bikur Cholim society as providing 'doctor, medicines and lodging' for the sick.
story_body: There was still no resident physician in Hebron, so the society either transported patients to Jerusalem or brought the Jerusalem doctor down. The Bikur Cholim entry is one of the earliest documented Hebron Chabad welfare institutions.

title_en: Montefiore's fourth visit to Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: Montefiore returned to Eretz Yisrael in 5617 without commissioning a new census.
story_body: This visit followed close on the 5615 census, so the existing records were considered sufficient. The visit is the only one of Montefiore's six tours of the Holy Land not associated with a fresh communal survey.

title_en: Montefiore's fifth visit; Hebron now has a resident physician
summary_en: The 5626 census recorded Hebron's first resident Jewish doctor, R. Yisrael Nachum of Chernobyl, age 66, who had immigrated in 5622.
story_body: Bikur Cholim was by then paying 4,000 grush a year for the doctor's salary plus 2,000 in other expenses. The census also showed the Chabad synagogue had built a small upstairs room for a Talmud Torah and study hall, with plans drawn for a full second floor.

title_en: Montefiore's sixth and final visit to Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: Montefiore's 5635 visit produced one final round of community censuses for the Yishuv.
story_body: Like its predecessors, the 5635 census recorded each community's institutions and leadership separately. The records remain a primary source for the demography of the mid-19th century Yishuv, with the originals in London and a working card index compiled by Yehoshua Mondshine.

title_en: Beis Menachem synagogue purchased in Jerusalem
summary_en: The Chabad community in Jerusalem bought the building that became the Beis Menachem synagogue and immediately added a small upper room.
story_body: The upstairs space served as a study hall for talmidei chachamim and a children's Talmud Torah. A full second floor was already part of the long-term plan, as shown by the synagogue stamp on later Montefiore censuses, but the plan would take more than two decades to execute.

title_en: Eliyahu Sasson of Bombay donates 200 pounds for Jerusalem synagogue expansion
summary_en: HaChavatzelet of Tammuz 5639 reported Eliyahu Sasson's 200-pound donation to expand the Jerusalem Chabad synagogue in memory of his wife.
story_body: Overcrowding had forced worshipers into the courtyard, especially on the High Holidays, with reports of illness from the summer sun. Sasson's gift, secured through intermediary Shneur Zalman Mendelovitz, would fund a full second floor named Knesset Eliyahu in honor of the donor.

title_en: Cornerstone laid for Beis Menachem second floor
summary_en: The cornerstone for the second floor of the Beis Menachem synagogue was laid in 5639, with plans drawn by the architect Schick.
story_body: Binyamin ben Shlomo Yechezkel, a Sasson family relative, set the first stone. The community elder Shneur Zalman Mendelovitz prayed for the donor's late wife Leah bat Parchi and blessed the entire Sasson family in Bombay, London and Calcutta. The plaque on the upper floor names the building Knesset Eliyahu.

title_en: Sir Eliyahu Sasson dies with synagogue construction unfinished
summary_en: Sir Eliyahu Sasson, the Bombay donor of the Jerusalem Chabad synagogue's second floor, died on 12 Iyar 5640.
story_body: HaChavatzelet reported that the shell of the new floor stood complete, but interior plaster, windows and doors were still missing. Work had been suspended for months due to lack of funds, and the obituary implied the family would need to complete what he had started.

title_en: Rabbi Dovber Efrat of Hebron remarries in Jerusalem
summary_en: Around Tishrei 5663 the Rabbi of Hebron, R. Dovber Efrat, married in Jerusalem and remained there, leaving Hebron Chabad without a rabbi.
story_body: Through the winter of 5663 the Hebron Chabad community debated whether to import a new rabbi from elsewhere or appoint one of its own members. By early summer they decided on Rabbi Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov, a respected local scholar then living in Hebron.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab approves Eliezerov as Rabbi of Hebron
summary_en: On 21 Iyar 5663 the Rashab wrote to the Sdei Chemed in Hebron formally approving Rabbi Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov as Rabbi of the Hebron Chabad community.
story_body: The Rashab had earlier received a petition from Hebron residents demanding a rabbi from outside the city; though he disagreed, he had stepped back rather than impose his choice. When the community itself converged on Eliezerov, he sent an immediate telegram of approval and a long letter the next day to Eliezerov himself.

title_en: Eliezerov publishes public appeal for Hebron Chabad institutions
summary_en: In Elul 5663 the new Rabbi Eliezerov and the Sdei Chemed issued a printed appeal warning that the Hebron community was on the brink of collapse.
story_body: The flyer described Hebron Jews silently bearing extreme poverty, without the energetic shadarim that other communities sent abroad. The signers begged donors to support the Magen Avos yeshiva, the children's Talmud Torah, and homes of shelter for the destitute who could not afford rent.

title_en: Hebron Tomchei Tmimim mashpia and students depart Lubavitch
summary_en: Mashpia Shneur Zalman Havlin received written instructions from both Rebbeim before leaving Lubavitch for Hebron on 2 Cheshvan 5672.
story_body: The Rashab told Havlin his sole focus in Hebron must be the yeshiva itself, apart from supervising Chabad properties. The Rayatz, as head of Tomchei Tmimim, formally appointed Havlin to the central vaad and as the local mashpia and representative, instructing him to commission an official institutional seal bearing the Tomchei Tmimim name.

title_en: Hebron yeshiva renamed Toras Emes
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Kislev 5672, one day after the students arrived in Hebron, the Rayatz announced the new yeshiva would be called Toras Emes rather than Tomchei Tmimim.
story_body: The Rayatz sat down to write a twelve-page letter the moment the safe-arrival telegram came in. The name change reflected a strategic decision to separate the new institution from the central Tomchei Tmimim treasury, so it would draw its own donors rather than burden the Lubavitch yeshiva network.

title_en: Toras Emes declares full financial independence from Tomchei Tmimim
summary_en: A Chanukah 5672 kuntres signed by Havlin and Eliezerov declared that Toras Emes Hebron had no fiscal connection whatsoever to Tomchei Tmimim Lubavitch.
story_body: The pamphlet warned supporters not to confuse the two institutions or shift donations between them, since each had its own vaad and shadarim. The Rashab issued a parallel general letter to Anash announcing Toras Emes and listing the dedicated emissaries he was sending to raise its funds.

title_en: Rayatz launches Toras Emes yeshiva in Jerusalem
summary_en: On 19 Cheshvan 5682 the Rayatz wrote to Havlin directing him to establish the yeshiva first in Jerusalem rather than Hebron.
story_body: Havlin selected a property in the Brand courtyard in the Beis Yisrael neighborhood (today the Karlin shtibel). The Rayatz prescribed four daily hours of Chassidus on the Tomchei Tmimim model, with the rest of the day devoted to nigleh in a strict schedule.

title_en: Toras Emes purchases land in Givat Shaul
summary_en: On 22 Sivan 5685 the Rayatz endorsed Havlin's plan to buy land in Givat Shaul for a permanent Toras Emes building.
story_body: Havlin had raised an initial $3,000 toward the project, with the Rayatz's earlier approval. By 2 Shevat 5686 the land had been acquired and the Rayatz wrote back with congratulations, calling it a mazal tov.

title_en: Toras Emes architectural plans approved by Rayatz
summary_en: On 7 Tevet 5687 the Rayatz received and approved the detailed building plans for the Toras Emes yeshiva on its new Givat Shaul plot.
story_body: He authorized Havlin to publicize the plans and solicit Anash and the broader Jewish community to fund the construction, promising spiritual reward to all donors. Despite the campaign and the cleared land, the building was never actually built.

title_en: Toras Emes flees Givat Shaul after 1929 riots
summary_en: Following the 5689 Arab riots the Toras Emes yeshiva abandoned Givat Shaul and relocated inside Jerusalem proper.
story_body: Havlin's son wrote on 13 Elul 5689 that the yeshiva had been forced out of its location outside the city and was now suffering severe overcrowding. The Rayatz ruled that the remote Givat Shaul site was unsafe and a more secure location had to be found.

title_en: Toras Emes destroyed in 1936 Arab violence
summary_en: During the 5696 disturbances the Toras Emes building was destroyed and burned by Arab attackers.
story_body: Despite earlier discussions about relocating, the yeshiva had remained at its post-1929 location until the 5696 violence forced its hand. From there the yeshiva moved permanently to the Bukharian quarter, where it remained for the rest of Havlin's life.

title_en: Midrash Shmuel yeshiva opens in Old City Jerusalem
summary_en: On 15 Elul 5704 the Chabad yeshiva Midrash Shmuel, named for the Rebbe Maharash, began classes in the Old City of Jerusalem.
story_body: The yeshiva was led by Rabbi Yitzchak Avigdor Ornstein as the Rayatz's representative, with Rabbis Alexander Yudasin and Yitzchak Naeh on the standing administration. Its stated mission was to anchor a Chabad center in the Old City for serious learners, teaching Shas, poskim and Chassidus in the path of Chabad's rebbeim.

title_en: Rayatz formally christens Midrash Shmuel and pledges Pesach support
summary_en: On 17 Iyar 5705 the Rayatz wrote to Rabbi Yudasin confirming Midrash Shmuel's founding, its name in honor of his grandfather the Maharash, and his 50-shekel Pesach donation.
story_body: The Rayatz had earlier written on Rosh Chodesh Adar 5705 asking Rabbi Ornstein for a full roster of students with ages, conduct, and family details. The Iyar letter expressed his blessing on Yudasin for the merit of helping establish the institution.

title_en: Midrash Shmuel closes with fall of Old City Jerusalem
summary_en: The Midrash Shmuel yeshiva ended when the Old City of Jerusalem fell during the War of Independence in 5708.
story_body: The yeshiva had run for roughly four years in the Chabad synagogue inside the Old City. The last documented references in the Rayatz's correspondence date to 16 Cheshvan 5708, only months before the Jewish Quarter was overrun and its institutions ceased to function.

title_en: R' Leib Chitrik begins service as Hebron Kolel Chabad administrator
summary_en: R' Yehuda Leib Chitrik of Sienna begins signing as a trustee of Hebron Kolel Chabad, a role he holds through 1844.
story_body: R' Leib Chitrik was among the earliest administrators of Hebron's Chabad community. From 1827 he signed emissary credentials and community letters on behalf of Kolel Chabad in Hebron, continuing in that role until 1844. The 1827 emissary document identifies him as 'Yehuda Leib son of Wolf, trustee of the holy city of Hebron.'

title_en: Hebron Ashkenazi and Sephardic communities sign formal agreement
summary_en: The two communities of Hebron sign a formal agreement, with R' Leib Chitrik among the Ashkenazi signatories.
story_body: In 1830 the Sephardic and Ashkenazi communities of Hebron concluded a formal accord governing communal matters. R' Leib Chitrik, a senior trustee of Kolel Chabad, was one of the Ashkenazi signatories. The agreement was one of several inter-community arrangements that shaped Hebron's Jewish life in the 19th century.

title_en: HaChavatzelet reports Montefiore estate distribution in Hebron
summary_en: HaChavatzelet reports that trustees of Moshe Montefiore's estate continue funding Hebron, with the Ashkenazi share distributed at 40 piasters per person.
story_body: After Moshe Montefiore's death at 101, his estate's trustees continued to send funds to the Holy Land. The 15 Av 5647 (1887) issue of HaChavatzelet described how Hebron's portion was split between the Sephardic and Ashkenazi communities by population, with a three-man Ashkenazi committee dividing the money at 40 piasters per soul.

title_en: Kolel Chabad holds lottery for two Montefiore-fund beneficiaries
summary_en: Kolel Chabad trustees draw lots for two Jerusalem members to receive that year's share of the Montefiore estate fruits.
story_body: On 19 Sivan 5662 (June 24, 1902), the trustees of Kolel Chabad notified the Vaad Klalli that a lottery — held before them and other notables — had selected R' David Gilel and R' Noach son of R' Chaim Ber to enjoy that year's distribution from Sir Moshe Montefiore's estate. Names of winners were sent to the London executors, who paid each recipient directly.

title_en: Hebron Sephardic and Ashkenazi communities agree on Montefiore split
summary_en: Hebron's two communities reach an agreement on how to divide their share of the Montefiore estate funds.
story_body: In 5666 (1906) the Sephardic and Ashkenazi communities of Hebron formalized how the Montefiore estate funds reaching the city would be divided between them. A receipt preserved in the SY"L Archive documents that on 22 Elul 5666 (September 12, 1906) one beneficiary received five pounds sterling as his share of the estate's fruits.

title_en: R' Sh.Y.L. Eliezerov leaves Hebron for Europe and Russia
summary_en: Hebron Ashkenazi chief rabbi Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov leaves Hebron for what was announced as a several-month fundraising trip abroad.
story_body: On 26 Marcheshvan 5664 (November 15, 1903), Hebron Ashkenazi rabbi Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov departed his city to travel abroad on behalf of Hebron's institutions, especially the Magen Avot yeshiva. R' Yaakov Yosef Slonim's farewell address in HaChavatzelet spoke of a few months' absence, but the trip in fact lasted over two years. Eliezerov went first to Lubavitch to consult the Rashab on improving Hebron's material and spiritual state.

title_en: Rashab appoints R' Eleazar Moshe Madiyevsky to head Hebron committee
summary_en: On 15 Shvat 5664 the Rashab writes asking R' Eleazar Moshe Madiyevsky to head a Russia-based committee for Hebron.
story_body: On 15 Shvat 5664 (February 1, 1904), the Rashab dispatched R' Sh.Y.L. Eliezerov to R' Eleazar Moshe Madiyevsky with a personal letter asking him to head a new Russia-based committee dedicated to improving conditions in Hebron. The discussions stretched on for a year and a half before the Vaad Chevroni was finally constituted in the summer of 1905.

title_en: Eliezerov reports cholera outbreak in Caucasus from Samarkand
summary_en: Writing from Samarkand on 3 Tevet 5665, Eliezerov reports a cholera outbreak in the Caucasus disrupting his mission.
story_body: From Samarkand in Bukhara on 3 Tevet 5665 (December 11, 1904), Eliezerov wrote to his brother-in-law R' M.M. Naeh that this trip had been the hardest of his four missions combined. He had agreed to take on the Caucasus mission for the Sephardic community but cholera had broken out there, forcing him to plan a return route via Baku and Georgia if possible, otherwise straight back to Lubavitch as the Rashab had instructed.

title_en: Eliezerov spends Shavuot with the Rashab in Lubavitch
summary_en: R' Sh.Y.L. Eliezerov spends Shavuot 5665 in Lubavitch, after which the Rashab dispatches him with letters of recommendation to Riga.
story_body: On Shavuot 5665 (June 9, 1905), Eliezerov was in Lubavitch, where the Rashab gave him letters of recommendation to the wealthy chassidim of Riga. The trip was tied to the purchase of Hatzer Romano in Hebron and other matters strengthening the Chabad settlement there. He then returned to Lubavitch to help organize the Vaad Chevroni in Tammuz.

title_en: Vaad Chevroni established in Lubavitch
summary_en: After a year and a half of discussion, the Vaad Chevroni — a Russia-based committee for Hebron's welfare — is established in Tammuz 5665.
story_body: In Tammuz 5665 (summer 1905), the Vaad Chevroni was finally established in Lubavitch under R' Eleazar Moshe Madiyevsky, with the Rashab's encouragement. R' Sh.Y.L. Eliezerov had spent Shavuot in Lubavitch and remained to help organize the committee, whose purpose was to attend continuously to improving Hebron's material and spiritual conditions.

title_en: Eliezerov returns to Hebron after over two years abroad
summary_en: R' Eliezerov returns to Hebron at the end of winter 5666, ending a mission that had lasted more than two years.
story_body: HaChavatzelet of 9 Nisan 5666 (April 3, 1906) reported that Rabbi Shlomo Leib Eliezerov, Ashkenazi av beit din of Hebron, had arrived in Jerusalem on Rosh Chodesh Nisan returning from his trip to Russia, and continued to Hebron on 3 Nisan. Soon after, the Sephardic community issued him a formal release certifying his fourth mission had been the most profitable yet.

title_en: Kolel Chabad purchases building adjacent to Beit Menachem synagogues
summary_en: A printed appeal from Tammuz 5667 announces the purchase of a large adjacent courtyard to save Jerusalem's Chabad synagogues from being shut.
story_body: In Tammuz 5667 (July 1907), Kolel Chabad of Jerusalem issued a printed appeal explaining that the Beit Menachem synagogues — founded fifty years earlier by the Tzemach Tzedek opposite the Hurva ruin — were about to be sealed because the adjoining three-story courtyard with its shops was about to be sold to a Muslim buyer. One of the signatories donated 4,000 rubles personally and the community borrowed another 12,000 rubles to buy the courtyard and dedicate its income to needy Chabad scholars in perpetuity.

title_en: Yeshivat Torat Emet founded in Hebron with seven Tomchei Tmimim students
summary_en: Seven elite Tomchei Tmimim students are sent to Hebron to found the Torat Emet yeshiva there.
story_body: Seven select students of Tomchei Tmimim — among them Alter Simchovitz, Hillel Pevzner, Tzvi Hirsch Katzav, Yechezkel Feigin, Menachem Krasik, Avraham Eli Asherov, and Yisrael Zalman Asnas — were dispatched in 1911 to found Yeshivat Torat Emet in Hebron. Nine additional students from Hebron and Jerusalem joined them. R' Shimon Glitzenstein later recalled enrolling in the yeshiva's first year, at the end of summer 5672.

title_en: R' Shimon Glitzenstein enrolls at Yeshivat Torat Emet in Hebron
summary_en: R' Shimon Glitzenstein joins Yeshivat Torat Emet at the end of summer 5672, replacing Alter Simchovitz who had returned to Lubavitch.
story_body: At the end of summer 5672 (1912), R' Shimon Glitzenstein enrolled at Yeshivat Torat Emet in Hebron in its first year of operation. He replaced R' Alter Simchovitz, who had returned to Lubavitch over the course of that summer. Glitzenstein would later document the yeshiva's early years in writings published in Bitaon Chabad.

title_en: Torat Emet opens Jerusalem branch under R' Tzvi Pesach Frank
summary_en: Torat Emet opens a Jerusalem branch with R' Tzvi Pesach Frank — later a chief rabbi of Jerusalem — as its rosh metivta.
story_body: Following discussions about absorbing Jerusalem avreichim into the yeshiva, Torat Emet opened a Jerusalem branch in 5674 (1913–14). The Frierdiker Rebbe's letter of 3 Kislev 5674 to R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin asked for accounts of the new branch. The rosh metivta of the Jerusalem branch was R' Tzvi Pesach Frank, who would later become one of Jerusalem's leading rabbinic authorities.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe issues detailed organizational plan for Torat Emet
summary_en: On 10 Shvat 5682 the Frierdiker Rebbe writes R' Sh.Z. Havlin a lengthy letter prescribing how to organize Torat Emet in three divisions.
story_body: On 10 Shvat 5682 (February 8, 1922), the Frierdiker Rebbe sent R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin a long and detailed letter laying out how to organize Yeshivat Torat Emet into three divisions, defining the student types, the rashei yeshiva to be hired, and the order of study. Havlin then recruited R' Moshe Aryeh Leib Shapira as a rosh metivta and R' Shimon Glitzenstein as secretary — both alumni of Torat Emet's original Hebron cohort — who would serve in these roles for decades.

title_en: R' Moshe Dovber Rivkin appointed senior teacher at Torat Emet
summary_en: R' Moshe Dovber Rivkin, newly arrived in Jerusalem from abroad, is appointed a senior teacher at the expanding Torat Emet.
story_body: In summer 5684 (1924) Torat Emet expanded and needed an additional rosh metivta. Just then R' Moshe Dovber Rivkin made aliyah and settled in Jerusalem. The Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to him on 2 Elul approving his joining the yeshiva, and to Havlin on Erev Rosh Chodesh Marcheshvan 5685 instructing that distinguished students be placed under his guidance. He served in that role for about three years before relocating to America.

title_en: Havlin and Rivkin travel to USA to fundraise for Torat Emet
summary_en: In Nisan 5688 R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin and R' Moshe Dovber Rivkin depart the Holy Land for America via Riga to fundraise for Torat Emet.
story_body: In Nisan 5688 (April 1928), R' Shlomo Zalman Havlin and R' Moshe Dovber Rivkin departed the Holy Land for the United States. They stopped first in Riga to consult with the Frierdiker Rebbe on the details of their mission. From then on Havlin spent extensive time in America raising funds for the yeshiva's deficit, while Rivkin remained in the US and joined Yeshivat Torah Vodaas as a rosh metivta.

title_en: About 1,000 Chabad chassidim emigrate from Soviet Russia
summary_en: In the years 5706–5707 around one thousand Chabad chassidim leave the Soviet Union.
story_body: Over 5706–5707 (1946–1947) approximately a thousand Anash escaped Soviet Russia. After two years in displaced-persons camps in Germany and Austria and an extended stay in Paris, they began to settle permanently in various countries. A portion made aliyah to the Land of Israel on the instruction of the Frierdiker Rebbe.

title_en: Chabad refugees settle in Lod and in newly named Kfar Chabad
summary_en: In 5709 two groups of Chabad refugees from Russia settle in the Land of Israel — one near Lod's train station, the other in the renamed Kfar Chabad.
story_body: Mainly in the year 5709 (1949), Chabad refugees arriving in the Land of Israel settled in two groups. One took over abandoned houses near the Lod train station; the other moved into the abandoned village of Safriya, renamed Kfar Chabad. Agudat Chabad of the Holy Land also received a dedicated building in the Lod compound to house a new Chabad yeshiva.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe advises on Lod yeshiva and refugee student placement
summary_en: On 19 Adar 5709 the Frierdiker Rebbe writes R' Zushe Vilimovsky directing that newly arrived students go to the Tel Aviv yeshiva for now.
story_body: On 19 Adar 5709 (March 20, 1949), the Frierdiker Rebbe replied to R' Zushe Vilimovsky, the manager designated for the Lod yeshiva, that arriving Anash students should be placed in Tomchei Tmimim in Tel Aviv. He suggested that the Lod building be reserved so it could later serve as the site of the new Tomchei Tmimim branch when conditions were right.

title_en: Chasidim arrive in Eretz Yisrael, settle in Tzfat
summary_en: The first major group of Chasidim arrived in Eretz Yisrael in Elul 5537 and settled in Tzfat rather than Tiberias.
story_body: When the early Chasidic aliyah reached the Holy Land in Elul 5537, the group settled initially in Tzfat, not Tiberias. This is corrected by the author against a folk tradition that placed the arrival in Tiberias. The Tiberias community was only established several years later.

title_en: Some Chasidim move from Tzfat to Tiberias
summary_en: About three and a half years after settling in Tzfat, part of the Chasidic community relocated to Tiberias in 5541.
story_body: The branching of the Chasidic yishuv from Tzfat to Tiberias took place in 5541. This created the Tiberias-based Chasidic community that would be led for decades by R' Avraham of Kalisk and R' Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk. Both Galilean cities would remain centers of Chasidic settlement.

title_en: R' Meir of Bychov's earliest known signature, from Tiberias
summary_en: R' Meir of Bychov's signature first appears on a letter written in Tiberias in winter 5546.
story_body: The earliest documentary trace of R' Meir of Bychov is his signature on a Tiberias letter from winter 5546, signed 'Meir son of R' Yaakov of Bychov.' This places him in the Chasidic yishuv of Tiberias by that date. He would later become one of the leading shadarim of the community.

title_en: R' Yoel Smolyaner sent on shlichut to Russia
summary_en: R' Yoel Smolyaner was dispatched from Eretz Yisrael to Russia in the winter of 5549 as the shadar for 5550.
story_body: In winter 5549 R' Yoel Smolyaner left the Holy Land as the official emissary to the Chasidic communities of Russia for the year 5550. A Tiberias letter from Rosh Chodesh Iyar 5549 already noted that his correspondence had reached Constantinople and that he was diverting via Trieste. His mission was unusually long and he did not return until Nissan 5551.

title_en: R' Meir of Bychov departs on his first shlichut
summary_en: R' Meir of Bychov set out on his first emissary mission abroad in the summer of 5549.
story_body: The author corrects the standard reference work 'Shluchei Eretz Yisrael,' showing that R' Meir of Bychov's first shlichut began in summer 5549 (not 5551 as commonly cited). Evidence includes a letter of Erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz 5549 from R' Shmuel Gronem introducing R' Meir as the bearer. R' Meir returned to Eretz Yisrael in Menachem Av 5551.

title_en: Plague and quarantine begin in Tiberias
summary_en: An epidemic struck Tiberias in Adar 5551, prompting the closure of the city gates for several months.
story_body: The Chasidic letters from Tiberias describe a plague and quarantine that began in Adar 5551 and continued until the city gates were reopened in Tammuz. The community wrote of severe financial distress during the lockdown, when 'silver had no outlet.' The arrival of the shadar R' Meir of Bychov shortly after the gates reopened brought desperately needed relief.

title_en: Tiberias plague quarantine ends as city gates reopen
summary_en: The city gates of Tiberias were reopened in Tammuz 5551 after months of plague quarantine.
story_body: After the Adar–Tammuz 5551 plague quarantine, Tiberias's gates were reopened in Tammuz. The Chasidic community wrote letters of thanksgiving to its overseas supporters describing the lifting of the closure. The timely arrival of the shadar R' Meir of Bychov soon after was seen as a divine deliverance.

title_en: R' Yoel Smolyaner returns to Eretz Yisrael after delayed shlichut
summary_en: R' Yoel Smolyaner arrived back in Eretz Yisrael on 10 Nissan 5551 after his long delayed emissary mission.
story_body: Sent abroad as the shadar for 5550, R' Yoel Smolyaner only returned to Eretz Yisrael on 10 Nissan 5551, well behind schedule. R' Avraham of Kalisk explicitly addressed 'the reason for the delay' in correspondence with the overseas overseers. His late arrival amid the Tiberias plague was contrasted with the more timely return of his successor R' Meir of Bychov.

title_en: R' Meir of Bychov returns from his first shlichut in Av 5551
summary_en: R' Meir of Bychov returned to Eretz Yisrael as the shadar of 5551 in Menachem Av of that year.
story_body: Having departed in summer 5549, R' Meir returned to Eretz Yisrael in Menachem Av 5551 as the shadar 'of this year.' His on-time return, immediately following the lifting of the Tiberias plague quarantine in Tammuz, was greeted as a salvation by the Chasidic community. A general letter from the Tiberias Chasidim and a separate letter from R' Avraham of Kalisk both announced his arrival.

title_en: R' Meir of Bychov's second shlichut
summary_en: R' Meir of Bychov undertook a second emissary mission for the Tiberias Chasidim in 5561.
story_body: Years after his first shlichut, R' Meir of Bychov was dispatched again from Tiberias to the diaspora Chasidic communities in 5561. The details are documented in 'Shluchei Eretz Yisrael' pages 624–626. He would go out a third time only two years later.

title_en: R' Meir of Bychov's third shlichut
summary_en: R' Meir of Bychov went out on his third emissary mission in 5563.
story_body: R' Meir of Bychov was sent abroad as a Tiberias shadar for a third time in 5563. This was his last documented shlichut before his appointment as a leader of the Tiberias kollel. Records of the mission are summarized in 'Shluchei Eretz Yisrael.'

title_en: R' Baruch of Mezhibuzh appoints leaders of Tiberias Chasidim
summary_en: After R' Avraham of Kalisk's passing in 5570, R' Baruch of Mezhibuzh appointed R' Tzvi Hirsch Segal of Harki and R' Meir of Bychov to lead the Tiberias Chasidic community.
story_body: Following the death of R' Avraham of Kalisk in 5570, the leadership of the general Chasidic community of Tiberias was reorganized by R' Baruch of Mezhibuzh. He asked the community to unify behind R' Tzvi Hirsch Halevi, with R' Meir of Bychov serving alongside him. The appointment letter, preserved in Yagdil Torah, asked the community to 'be one bound bundle in love, brotherhood, peace and friendship.'

title_en: R' Yosef Yehuda Leib m'Shyuf and R' Ephraim Yitzchak Epstein make aliyah from Shklov
summary_en: R' Yosef Yehuda Leib m'Shyuf and his father-in-law R' Ephraim Yitzchak Epstein made aliyah from Shklov to settle in Chevron in 5590.
story_body: In 5590, R' Ephraim Yitzchak Epstein traveled from Shklov to Chevron with his wife, son Zalman, daughter, son-in-law R' Yosef Yehuda Leib m'Shyuf, and their four-year-old son Yaakov Zevulun. Hearing of their journey, the Tzemach Tzedek entrusted them to deliver the Russian Chabad support funds to the Chevron community. They arrived in Kislev 5591 after road troubles delayed them past Rosh Hashanah.

title_en: Russian Chabad support funds arrive in Chevron
summary_en: The Russian Chabad support funds for 5590 reached Chevron in Kislev 5591, carried by R' Ephraim Yitzchak Epstein and R' Yosef Yehuda Leib m'Shyuf.
story_body: Originally expected by Rosh Hashanah 5591, the emissaries were delayed and arrived in Chevron only in Kislev 5591. A 14 Kislev 5591 letter from the Chevron Chabad community thanked the Tzemach Tzedek for arranging the early dispatch despite the late delivery. The same letter records that 'the road went wrong and an hour of emergency caused them to be delayed.'

title_en: Pogroms and earthquake devastate Tzfat
summary_en: Tzfat was struck by two pogroms and a major earthquake during 5594–5598, devastating the Jewish community including the family of R' Uri of Slonim.
story_body: In the disasters of 5594–5598 ('the two pillages and the earthquake'), Tzfat's Jewish population was repeatedly attacked and then struck by the Galilee earthquake of 1837. R' Uri of Slonim lost his father, three of his children, and all his property. The killing of his daughter Tzipa Leah is confirmed by the 'List of Tzfat Casualties' published years later.

title_en: Montefiore census of Tzfat after the disasters
summary_en: Sir Moses Montefiore conducted a census of the Tzfat Jewish community in Erev Shavuot 5599 during his visit.
story_body: On his visit to Tzfat at Erev Shavuot 5599, Montefiore registered the surviving Jewish residents after the earthquake and pogroms. R' Uri of Slonim, a Chabad chasid, was registered with the Perushim kollel since there was no Chabad kollel in Tzfat at the time. He signed a contemporaneous letter from the remaining Perushim community as 'Uri Chabad.'

title_en: First Chevron Chabad letter to Montefiore signed by R' Yosef Yehuda Leib
summary_en: On 28 Sivan 5599 the Chevron Chabad community sent the first of six summer letters to Sir Moses Montefiore.
story_body: Six letters were sent by the leaders of the Chevron Chabad community to Montefiore during summer 5599, the first dated 28 Sivan 5599. R' Yosef Yehuda Leib son of R' Chaim signed all of them. Notably, he already signed using the phrase 'son of the late' two days before the actual death of R' Chaim the Jerusalem shochet, demonstrating that the Jerusalem shochet was not actually his father.

title_en: Death of R' Chaim ben R' Moshe m'Shklov, first Ashkenazi shochet of Jerusalem
summary_en: R' Chaim ben R' Moshe m'Shklov, the first shochet of the Ashkenazi community in Jerusalem, died on Rosh Chodesh Tammuz 5599.
story_body: The chevra kadisha records of Jerusalem give the death date of R' Chaim ben R' Moshe m'Shklov as Rosh Chodesh Tammuz 5599 (not 5591, as one secondary source has it). He served as the first shochet for the Ashkenazi community of Jerusalem. The author uses this correct date to demonstrate that he could not have been the father of R' Yosef Yehuda Leib m'Shyuf, who had already signed as 'son of the late' two days before this date.

title_en: Montefiore census of Chevron
summary_en: Sir Moses Montefiore conducted a census of the Chevron Jewish community on 4 Tammuz 5599.
story_body: On 4 Tammuz 5599 Montefiore registered the Jews of Chevron during his visit. The Chevron Chabad community optimistically registered R' Uri of Slonim as a resident, though he was still in Tzfat at the time and only intended to move. The inaccurate details in his Chevron entry (wrong children's names, ages, and aliyah year) reflect that the community recorded him in absentia.

title_en: Chabad chasidim move from Chevron to Jerusalem
summary_en: R' Ephraim Yitzchak Epstein, R' Yosef Yehuda Leib m'Shyuf, and other Chabad settlers moved from Chevron to settle in Jerusalem in 5607.
story_body: An 5609 letter from the Chevron Chabad community to Montefiore explicitly says 'two years ago we settled in Jerusalem,' dating their move to 5607. This established the Chabad presence in Jerusalem alongside Chevron. R' Uri of Slonim, who had been an emissary in Chevron, also relocated to Jerusalem around this time.

title_en: Death of R' Yaakov Zevulun m'Shyuf at age 42
summary_en: R' Yaakov Zevulun m'Shyuf, son of R' Yosef Yehuda Leib, died in 5628 at age 42.
story_body: Born around 5586 and brought to Eretz Yisrael as a four-year-old in 5590, R' Yaakov Zevulun m'Shyuf died in 5628 at age 42. He was the eldest son of R' Yosef Yehuda Leib m'Shyuf, who had made aliyah from Shklov to Chevron with his father-in-law's family.

title_en: Death of R' Uri Ornstein of Slonim
summary_en: R' Uri Ornstein of Slonim, son-in-law of the 'Keren Orah,' died in Jerusalem on 17 Adar 5639.
story_body: R' Uri Ornstein, a Chabad chasid who had made aliyah from Slonim, served two terms as a Chevron Chabad emissary totaling twelve years. He died in Jerusalem on 17 Adar 5639. His wife Zisil, daughter of R' Yitzchak of Karlin, died seven years later on 12 Adar II 5646.

title_en: Death of Zisil Ornstein, daughter of R' Yitzchak of Karlin
summary_en: Zisil Ornstein, wife of R' Uri Ornstein and daughter of R' Yitzchak of Karlin, died on 12 Adar II 5646.
story_body: Recorded in 'Avnei Zikaron' volume 12, Zisil's death is noted as 12 Adar II 5646. She was the daughter of R' Yitzchak the rabbi of Karlin and outlived her husband R' Uri by seven years. Together they had been part of the Slonim contingent that settled in the Chabad communities of Eretz Yisrael.

title_en: SILA writes to Rebbe Rashab about Bukhara shlichut
summary_en: On 14 Tevet 5667, SILA (R' Shneur Zalman Ladier) wrote to Rebbe Rashab seeking permission for a Bukhara emissary mission.
story_body: Less than a year after returning to Chevron, R' Shneur Zalman Ladier ('SILA') wrote to the Rebbe Rashab on 14 Tevet 5667 explaining that disputes over Kolel Chabad leadership and personal pressures made permanent settlement in Eretz Yisrael impossible. He asked permission to undertake another shlichut, this time for the Sephardi community to Bukhara. He estimated the mission would take eight months.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab approves SILA's Bukhara shlichut
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Adar 5667 Rebbe Rashab approved SILA's request for the Bukhara shlichut.
story_body: The Rebbe Rashab responded on Rosh Chodesh Adar 5667 that 'the matter is necessary for him and cannot be postponed.' He also approved SILA's parallel travel to Lubavitch to discuss community affairs in person. The Rebbe blessed his journey with 'good and true reasons.'

title_en: SILA departs Lubavitch for Bukhara
summary_en: SILA departed Lubavitch for Bukhara on 8 Iyar 5667, traveling via Moscow with an acquaintance from Samarkand.
story_body: After spending Pesach and several weeks in Lubavitch consulting with the Rebbe Rashab, SILA left for Bukhara on 8 Iyar 5667. A letter from the Rebbe Rashab that day notes 'today our relative R' Shneur Zalman traveled to Bukhara via Moscow.' He was accompanied by a Samarkand resident who had been waiting for him in Moscow.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab inquires after SILA in Bukhara
summary_en: On 7 Adar II 5668 the Rebbe Rashab wrote to SILA in Bukhara asking how much longer his mission would take.
story_body: Still in Bukhara nearly a year after his arrival, SILA received a letter from the Rebbe Rashab on 7 Adar II 5668 expressing his strong desire that SILA return home. The Rebbe asked for a detailed report on his welfare and the duration of his remaining stay. SILA would not return to Chevron until Shevat 5669.

title_en: SILA returns to Chevron from Bukhara
summary_en: SILA returned to his home in Chevron in Shevat 5669 after his extended Bukhara shlichut.
story_body: Winter 5669 saw SILA in Lubavitch, and he reached his home in Chevron in Shevat 5669. The Rebbe Rashab welcomed him back with letters of 26 Shevat 5669 expressing relief at his safe arrival via Odessa and Jaffa. Rebbe Rayatz's 8 Adar 5669 letter reports that the family had been anxious during the journey's 20-day delay.

title_en: SILA's sixth Russia journey to advance Chevron Chabad projects
summary_en: In late 5670 SILA traveled to Russia to transfer Chevron property to the Rebbe Rashab's name, restore the minyan at the Avraham Avinu synagogue, and establish the Toras Emes yeshiva.
story_body: SILA's sixth Russia trip pursued three major Chevron Chabad initiatives: registering a Chevron property in the Rebbe Rashab's name, renewing the minyan at the historic Avraham Avinu synagogue, and founding the Toras Emes yeshiva. He remained in Lubavitch for most of 5671 and much of 5672 working on these projects. The Toras Emes yeshiva would become a landmark institution of Chabad education in Eretz Yisrael.

title_en: WWI begins; Russian Jews expelled from Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: With the outbreak of World War I in summer 5674, all Russian citizens were expelled from Eretz Yisrael, sending SILA on another shlichut to Bukhara.
story_body: The summer 5674 outbreak of WWI brought the Ottoman expulsion of Russian subjects from Eretz Yisrael. SILA, a Russian citizen, was forced to leave and used the opportunity for another emissary mission to Bukhara. He reportedly opened a yeshiva in Samarkand during his exile, where he is documented in Kislev 5677.

title_en: Founding of Yeshivat Tzemach Tzedek in Jerusalem
summary_en: Kolel Chabad founded Yeshivat Tzemach Tzedek in the Chabad synagogue of the Old City of Jerusalem in 5680, soon after WWI ended.
story_body: Following WWI, the managers of Kolel Chabad established Yeshivat Tzemach Tzedek in the Chabad synagogue in Jerusalem's Old City in 5680, with Yeshivat Midrash Shmuel founded subsequently. By this period most of the Chabad community had relocated to the New City and prayed primarily at the 'Ohel Yitzchak' synagogue. R' Avraham Zalman remained living inside the Old City synagogue throughout the war years.

title_en: Chabad Old City synagogue faces wartime closure
summary_en: On 10 Iyar 5704, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to Agudat Chasidei Chabad in Eretz Yisrael urgently appealing to save the Chabad Old City synagogue from closure during WWII.
story_body: With WWII straining the Jewish yishuv, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote on 10 Iyar 5704 that maintaining the Chabad synagogue in Jerusalem's Old City required 4–5 pounds per month to hire men for the minyan. He instructed Agudat Chasidei Chabad to take responsibility, allocating one pound monthly and securing matching contributions from Kolel Chabad, the Gemach, and Toras Emes. The Rebbe wrote separately to each institution.

title_en: Six Tel Aviv yeshiva students granted permission to study in New York
