story_body: Manuscript 1064, written close to the Alter Rebbe's lifetime, lists 'Hilchasa Rabsa LeShabsa' under the year 5557. These laws did not appear in the first three editions of his Siddur (printed in Shklov and Kapust during his lifetime) but were later printed on separate folios. They form one of the latest precisely dated kuntreisim of the Alter Rebbe's middle period.

title_en: Alter Rebbe's Siddur first printed in Shklov
summary_en: The Alter Rebbe's Siddur was first printed in Shklov in 5563, incorporating his Psakei Hasiddur including Seder Mechiras Chametz and revised Hilchos Tzitzis and Tefillin.
story_body: The Siddur was the vehicle by which many of the Alter Rebbe's later halachic rulings reached print, often differing from his earlier Shulchan Aruch. The Tzemach Tzedek noted that 'the Siddur was written a long time after the Shulchan Aruch.' Two more editions appeared during the Alter Rebbe's lifetime in Kapust.

title_en: Passing of R. Pinchas Horowitz, the Baal Haflaah, in Frankfurt
summary_en: R. Pinchas Horowitz, the Baal Haflaah, rabbi of Frankfurt-am-Main, passed away on 24 Tammuz 5565 after more than thirty-three years in the position.
story_body: The Baal Haflaah had taken his Frankfurt seat at the start of 5532, after passing through Brod. His son R. Zvi Hirsch Halevi Horowitz eulogized him in Sefer Lachmei Todah, noting that he had taught Torah in Frankfurt 'more than thirty-three years.' His earlier praise of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch is one of the key indicators dating the Alter Rebbe's halachic work.

title_en: Great fire in Liadi destroys Alter Rebbe's autograph Shulchan Aruch
summary_en: The great fire in Liadi in 5570 (1810) destroyed the autograph manuscript of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch along with other writings such as his teshuvah on mechiras chametz.
story_body: The fire consumed the Alter Rebbe's own handwritten Shulchan Aruch and other manuscripts that consequently never reached print. Among the lost works is the kuntres explaining all the details of the bill of sale for chametz, referenced in his general letter on the subject. The Tzemach Tzedek later searched for this teshuvah but could not locate it.

title_en: First edition of Alter Rebbe's Hilchos Pesach printed
summary_en: In 5574 (1814) the first printed edition of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch Hilchos Pesach appeared, including the nusach of Seder Mechiras Chametz and the general letter to the chassidim.
story_body: Printed years after the great Liadi fire and after the Alter Rebbe's own passing, this edition preserved the public-facing portions of his rulings on selling chametz. The accompanying kuntres explaining the details of the sale was not included; it had not been printed in the Siddur or the Shulchan Aruch and is presumed lost in the Liadi fire of 5570.

title_en: Sefer Lachmei Todah published in Offenbach
summary_en: R. Zvi Hirsch Halevi Horowitz published Sefer Lachmei Todah in Offenbach in 5577 (1817), containing his eulogy for his father R. Pinchas Horowitz of Frankfurt.
story_body: The volume preserves the son's hesped describing the Baal Haflaah's more than thirty-three years of teaching Torah in Frankfurt. This precise phrasing allows historians to pin the Baal Haflaah's tenure to between summer 5531 and summer 5532. Lachmei Todah thus indirectly anchors the dating of the Alter Rebbe's editing of Hilchos Tzitzis and Pesach.

title_en: First edition of Tanya printed in Slavita
summary_en: The Tanya of the Alter Rebbe was first printed in Slavita in 5556–5557 (1796–1797).
story_body: Tradition suggests that the partners R' Shalom Shachna (the Alter Rebbe's son-in-law) and R' Mordechai HaLevi Horowitz jointly printed the first edition of Tanya in Slavita. They remained occupied with that print shop throughout their lives. This edition is the foundational text of Chabad Chasidic teaching.

title_en: Tanya printed in Shklov
summary_en: Tanya was printed in Shklov in 5566 (1806).
story_body: The Shklov print shop, operated by R' Mordechai HaLevi Horowitz, produced this edition of Tanya. It was one of several editions of the Alter Rebbe's writings issued in Russia before 1826.

title_en: Tanya and Shulchan Aruch HaRav printed in Shklov
summary_en: Another edition of Tanya and the Shulchan Aruch HaRav were printed in Shklov in 5574 (1814).
story_body: The year after the Alter Rebbe's passing, his sons brought his Shulchan Aruch to press in Shklov. This edition appeared alongside a new printing of Tanya at the same print shop.

title_en: Siddur of the Alter Rebbe printed in Kapust
summary_en: The Alter Rebbe's Siddur was printed in Kapust in 5576 (1816).
story_body: The Kapust print shop, also associated with R' Mordechai HaLevi Horowitz, published the Alter Rebbe's siddur. Kapust would later become an important Chabad center.

title_en: Shulchan Aruch HaRav printed in Sadilkov with haskamos
summary_en: The Shulchan Aruch of the Alter Rebbe was printed in Sadilkov in 5586 (1826), after the printer received haskamos for this edition.
story_body: R' Mordechai HaLevi Horowitz, after years of printing in Kapust and Shklov, traveled to Sadilkov to produce this edition of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch. He secured rabbinic approbations specifically for this printing.

title_en: Passing of R' Zusha of Anipoli
summary_en: R' Zusha of Anipoli passed away on 2 Shevat 5560 (28 January 1800).
story_body: R' Zusha, a leading disciple of the Maggid of Mezeritch, had earlier given a haskamah for the first edition of Tanya. His passing came roughly half a year before R' Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev issued his haskamah for the Slavita Talmud and Tur.

title_en: R' Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev gives haskamah for Slavita Shas and Tur
summary_en: On 13 Tammuz 5560 (5 July 1800), R' Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev gave his haskamah for printing Shas and Tur in Slavita.
story_body: R' Shalom Shachna (son-in-law of the Alter Rebbe) and R' Mordechai of Orsha (the Alter Rebbe's brother) traveled to obtain this approbation. R' Levi Yitzchak praised them as 'two men of Ephraim' bringing the Shas and Turim to press. This signaled the formal start of the large Slavita printing project.

title_en: Passing of R' Shalom Shachna, son-in-law of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: R' Shalom Shachna, the Alter Rebbe's son-in-law and partner in the Slavita print shop, passed away in 5567 (1807).
story_body: From 1800 until his death, R' Shalom Shachna had occupied himself with printing the Talmud and Tur in Slavita on behalf of the Alter Rebbe, partnering with the Rebbe's brother R' Mordechai of Orsha. He likely also collaborated on printing the original Tanya in 1796–1797.

title_en: Alter Rebbe begins composing Shulchan Aruch with the Maggid
summary_en: By 5533 (1773), the Alter Rebbe had completed Hilchos Tzitzis and Hilchos Pesach of his Shulchan Aruch under the Maggid's encouragement.
story_body: The Maggid of Mezeritch repeatedly urged the young Shneur Zalman to compile a Shulchan Aruch. The project began during Shabbos Tachkemoni at the Maggid's court, where he completed the laws of Tzitzis and Pesach. The complete work would not be printed until decades after his passing.

title_en: First arrest of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: On 30 Tishrei 5559 (10 October 1798), Belorussian governor Zhgulin reported to Governor-General Lopukhin that the Alter Rebbe's papers and books had been seized.
story_body: During the Alter Rebbe's first arrest, his books and writings were sealed in a box and a trunk with the governor's seal and sent on for investigation. The authorities suspected the writings might contain material against the government. This was the first of two such confiscations during his lifetime.

title_en: Alter Rebbe returns from Petersburg and settles in Liadi
summary_en: On 11 Menachem Av 5561 (21 July 1801), the Alter Rebbe traveled from Petersburg directly to Liadi after his second arrest.
story_body: Following his second arrest and release, the Alter Rebbe moved his residence from Liozna to Liadi. This marked the start of a new era — longer maamarim with multiple layered explanations — that became the hallmark of Chabad teaching.

title_en: Passing of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: The Alter Rebbe, Shneur Zalman of Liadi, passed away in 5573 (1812–1813).
story_body: Throughout his life, the Alter Rebbe had refused to print his other works, including the Shulchan Aruch. Only after his passing did his sons bring the Shulchan Aruch to press. His maamarim, recorded by various scribes, formed the basis of subsequent Chabad teachings.

title_en: First long maamarim of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: On Rosh Hashana 5550 (1789) the Alter Rebbe delivered 'Mashbi'in Oso Tehi Tzadik', followed on Erev Shabbos Shuvah by 'Shuvah Yisrael' — among his first lengthy maamarim said publicly.
story_body: According to Sefer HaSichos 5703, these were the earliest of the long-format Chasidic discourses delivered by the Alter Rebbe in public. They preceded the major shift toward extended discourses with multiple layered explanations that came after his return from Petersburg in 1801.

title_en: Alter Rebbe's writings begin spreading widely
summary_en: According to HaYom Yom, in 5551 (1791) the Alter Rebbe's writings in revealed and hidden Torah began spreading broadly.
story_body: This pre-dated the first printing of Tanya by several years. By summer 5552 (1792), the work had already become publicly known under the name 'Tanya', and by 5553 (1793) the Alter Rebbe was citing and discussing it in his Tishrei–Kislev maamarim.

title_en: Earliest dated Alter Rebbe maamar manuscripts
summary_en: Starting in 5553 (1793), dated manuscripts of the Alter Rebbe's maamarim are extant for every successive year through 5572 (1812).
story_body: The earliest dated discourse in the surviving manuscripts is from the beginning of 5553. From this year onward, dated discourses exist continuously, marking the year in which Chabad teaching began to spread broadly in writing alongside the public release of Tanya.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek defines the scope of Torah Or
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek wrote that Torah Or contains the Alter Rebbe's maamarim from 5556 (1795/6) through the end of 5572 (1812).
story_body: In a letter, the Tzemach Tzedek explained that Torah Or specifically draws from the Alter Rebbe's maamarim of this period because it was during these years that the Chabad explanations of his thought were elaborated in depth. The Mitteler Rebbe similarly dated the regular flow of public discourses as beginning around 1795/6.

title_en: Earliest reported Alter Rebbe maamarim
summary_en: Rebbe Rayatz transmitted that the Alter Rebbe delivered certain maamarim as early as 5528 (1768).
story_body: These earliest discourses may have been brief teachings or repetitions of the Maggid's Torah. No fixed practice of writing down discourses existed yet, which is why none of them reached us in dated manuscript form. A regular practice of delivering discourses appears to have begun around 1783 with his settling in Liozna.

title_en: Manuscript of Alter Rebbe's discourses copied by Zalman Leib of Liubavitch
summary_en: In 5594 (1834), Zalman Leib b. R' Yid of Liubavitch-Riskin copied a major manuscript of the Alter Rebbe's discourses arranged by Torah portion.
story_body: The manuscript (Ms. 633) is notable for its careful headings identifying the dates and circumstances when each discourse was delivered, including maamarim from as early as 5554 (1794). It represents a serious early effort to catalog the chronology of Chabad maamarim.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab prepares Vilna edition of Tanya
summary_en: In Elul 5659 (September 1899), Rebbe Rashab wrote the first of his letters to R' Asher Grossman of Nikolayev directing corrections for the Vilna Tanya edition.
story_body: Rebbe Rashab entrusted R' Asher, a chossid and shochet from Nikolayev, with proofreading the Tanya against early manuscripts and prints for the new Rom press edition. The Rebbe personally reviewed the proposed corrections and resolved unresolved questions, finalizing the text for the new edition.

title_en: Vilna edition of Tanya printed by Tomchei Temimim
summary_en: In 5660 (1899/1900), the Vilna Tanya appeared as the official edition of Tomchei Temimim, published by the Rom press.
story_body: The print run included 3,400 standard copies and 1,400–1,600 quality 'regal' paper copies. The cover declared the edition was issued by Tomchei Temimim, and the proceeds beyond expenses were dedicated to supporting the yeshiva's students. This was the first major scholarly edition of Tanya.

title_en: R' Asher Grossman signs introduction to Vilna Tanya
summary_en: On the first day of Chanukah 5660 (18 December 1899), R' Asher Grossman signed the bibliographic introduction to the new Vilna Tanya in Vilna.
story_body: His introduction details the painstaking emendation process — collating manuscripts held by descendants of the Tzemach Tzedek — and credits R' Moshe Weiler of Krislave for collecting numerous addenda to Iggeres HaKodesh. The introduction was attributed publicly only after Rebbe Rashab insisted R' Asher's name be added.

title_en: Dedication poem in Vilna Tanya for Rebbe Rashab
summary_en: Dated 19 Kislev 5660 (11 December 1899), R' Asher composed an acrostic poem honoring Rebbe Rashab and placed it on the final page of the Vilna Tanya.
story_body: The poem's first letters spelled out 'Shalom DovBer ni' and the closing letters 'b'Rabi Shmuel ziya'. When the first copy reached Rebbe Rashab on 22 Tevet, he was displeased: he had not approved the poem and instructed that copies not be sold until R' Asher signed the dedication openly. The page was later torn from most copies.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab reports completion of Vilna Tanya proofing
summary_en: On 15 Teves 5660 (7 January 1900), Rebbe Rashab wrote to his son the Rayatz that, after one more careful review of the printed Tanya, he found eight typographical errors.
story_body: Eight replacement pages were reprinted on a separate sheet and inserted at the back of the volume, with a buyer's notice instructing readers to substitute the corrected pages for the original ones at pages 14, 21, 33, 43, 76, 140, 143, and 152.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letters about the dedication page incident
summary_en: On 22 and 24 Teves 5660 (14–16 January 1900), Rebbe Rashab wrote to the Rayatz and to R' Asher demanding that the unauthorized dedication poem be openly signed as a personal addition.
story_body: Rebbe Rashab made clear that he was distressed by the addition and would not allow distribution until the poem was clearly attributed to R' Asher rather than appearing as part of the book itself. The matter was resolved by tearing the page from nearly all copies.

title_en: Kehot edition of Tanya with full correction list
summary_en: In 5714 (1954), Kehot published a new edition of Tanya into which the Lubavitcher Rebbe incorporated R' Asher Grossman's correction sheets.
story_body: The Rebbe stated in his preface that the new edition included corrections that R' Asher had recorded on his personal copy of Tanya after the Vilna printing — material that had reached the Kazarnovsky family through R' Asher's son-in-law. The Rebbe noted that the Rayatz had endorsed using this correction sheet.

title_en: Maamarei Admur HaZaken HaKtzarim editing project begins
summary_en: In 5741 (1981), work began on compiling Maamarei Admur HaZaken HaKtzarim, the Liozna-period short maamarim of the Alter Rebbe.
story_body: The Rebbe directed the editor to arrange the discourses by the order of Torah verses, then by Sages' sayings. The volume included a 'General Survey of the Short Maamarim' and a tentative chronological list through 5561 (1801). The Rebbe expressed reservation about exact dating, given that scribes had not been precise.

title_en: Updated chronological list of Alter Rebbe's maamarim
summary_en: In 5752 (1992), R' Yosef Yitzchak Keller completed an updated chronological list of the Alter Rebbe's maamarim, published in Kerem Chabad issue 4.
story_body: The list reflected research drawn from the additional volumes of maamarim issued during the intervening decade, incorporating newly identified headings with dates for both Liozna and Liadi discourses. It expanded considerably on the original 1981 list.

title_en: Likkutei Torah expanded chronology of maamarim
summary_en: A more complete chronological list of Likkutei Torah maamarim was printed in the Kehot 5759 (1999) edition supplement.
story_body: This was the most refined dating effort to date for the maamarim included in Likkutei Torah, building on the prior work of R' Yosef Yitzchak Keller and the editorial team behind subsequent volumes of Maamarei Admur HaZaken.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab recounts history on 19 Kislev
summary_en: On 19 Kislev 5675 (6 December 1914), Rebbe Rashab told over the history of the Alter Rebbe's maamar-recording tradition.
story_body: Speaking on the chag of redemption, Rebbe Rashab described how the Mitteler Rebbe's primary haNochos came from the post-Petersburg period rather than from Liozna. The transcript was preserved in Toras Shalom and provides a key source for the chronology of Chabad maamarim.

title_en: Alter Rebbe arrested and sent from Lozna to Petersburg
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi was sent from Lozna to Saint Petersburg on 4 Kislev for his second arrest.
story_body: At the beginning of winter 5561, the Alter Rebbe was arrested for the second time on charges connected to his leadership of the Chassidic movement. On 4 Kislev 5561 (November 21, 1800) he was transferred from Lozna to the imperial capital of Saint Petersburg. His arrival there was confirmed roughly a week later in correspondence between the Russian general procurator and the governor of Belarus.

title_en: General Procurator confirms Alter Rebbe's arrival in Petersburg
summary_en: General Procurator Obolininov wrote to the governor of Belarus confirming the Alter Rebbe's arrival and demanding any further papers be sent.
story_body: On 11 Kislev 5561 (approximately November 28, 1800), General Procurator Obolininov sent a letter to Severin, governor of Belarus, confirming that Rabbi Schneur Zalman had been delivered to Petersburg. The procurator complained that no account books, documents, or correspondence had accompanied the prisoner, and ordered the governor to conduct a search and forward anything that could be found, including writings hidden with associates.

title_en: Tsar orders Alter Rebbe's case transferred to the Senate
summary_en: An imperial order assigned the Alter Rebbe's case to the Senate's third department, the political secret police.
story_body: On 22 Kislev 5561 (November 27, 1800 Old Style), an order was issued in the Tsar's name directing that the proceedings against Rabbi Schneur Zalman be handed to the Senate. The Senate in turn assigned the investigation to its third department, the political secret police of Tsarist Russia, where the broader inquiry into the Chassidic movement and the future legal status of the kahal communities was being examined.

title_en: Russian police search Alter Rebbe's home and seize 103 books
summary_en: Police searched the Alter Rebbe's home in Lozna and confiscated 103 books and 14 manuscript collections.
story_body: On 24 Kislev 5561 (November 29, 1800 Old Style), Russian police searched Rabbi Schneur Zalman's home in Lozna in search of writings against the monarchy. They removed 103 books and 14 manuscript collections to Petersburg as evidence. The remaining volumes were sealed in the house under a special seal, with the leaders of the Lozna community signing a written undertaking to keep them locked and untouched.

title_en: Alter Rebbe's seized writings handed to Senate's third department
summary_en: Obolininov forwarded the Alter Rebbe's seized books and manuscripts, with a Russian summary, to Olenin of the Senate's third department.
story_body: On 18 Tevet 5561 (December 22, 1800 Old Style), General Procurator Obolininov transferred the confiscated books and manuscripts of the Alter Rebbe to Olenin, prosecutor of the Senate's third department. The materials were accompanied by a Russian-language report prepared by the Jewish translators Leib ben Noach and Yehuda ben Feivish, who certified that they had found nothing in the writings opposed to Jewish law, the monarchy, or the welfare of the country.

title_en: Tanya circulates widely in handwritten copies among chassidim
summary_en: Around 5552 the Alter Rebbe's kuntreisim that became the Tanya were already in widespread manuscript circulation among chassidim.
story_body: Around the year 5552 (1792), the kuntreisim that would later be printed as the Tanya were disseminated widely among Rabbi Schneur Zalman's chassidim. The work spread through many handwritten copies made by different scribes, leading to an accumulation of textual errors. This proliferation of corrupted copies eventually persuaded the Alter Rebbe to authorize a definitive printed edition of the work.

title_en: Marriage testimony for Mitteler Rebbe's daughter and R' Yaakov Yisrael of Cherkas
summary_en: A signed testimony document followed the marriage of Rabbi Yaakov Yisrael of Cherkas to a daughter of the Mitteler Rebbe.
story_body: On 7 Shevat 5571 (February 1, 1811), a 'zichron edut' testimony document was drawn up concerning the marriage of Rabbi Yaakov Yisrael of Cherkas to a daughter of Rabbi Dovber, the Mitteler Rebbe. The document records the name of the Mitteler Rebbe's wife as Shaina daughter of R' Yaakov, providing one of the few clear sources for identifying his father-in-law by name.

title_en: Great fire destroys Alter Rebbe's house in Lyadi
summary_en: A sudden fire consumed the Alter Rebbe's home in Lyadi while he was traveling in Volhynia, destroying valuable books and manuscripts.
story_body: At the end of winter 5570 (early 1810), a small spark ignited a sudden blaze in the Alter Rebbe's large house in Lyadi while he was on a journey through the Volhynia provinces. Within minutes the entire roof and interior were engulfed, and nothing could be saved — not the costly seforim, household possessions, jewelry, nor pledged valuables that had been kept in the home. Most painful was the loss of the Rebbe's own manuscript glosses on the four sections of Shulchan Aruch.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe sends circular letter about the Lyadi fire
summary_en: Rabbi Dovber wrote a general letter to chassidim describing the devastation of the Lyadi fire.
story_body: In Nisan-Iyar 5570 (April-May 1810), shortly after the great fire in Lyadi, the Mitteler Rebbe sent a circular letter to the wider community of chassidim describing the loss. He underscored particularly the destruction of his father's manuscripts of glosses on the four sections of Shulchan Aruch, alongside books, household goods, and pledged valuables that had been kept in the house. He warned chassidim of the terrible blow this would be to his elderly father when he returned.

title_en: Alter Rebbe flees Lyadi with family ahead of Napoleon's invasion
summary_en: On Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul the Alter Rebbe and his family fled Lyadi to Krasna as the French army approached.
story_body: On Friday, Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5572 (around August 7, 1812), as Napoleon's army advanced on White Russia, Rabbi Schneur Zalman traveled with his entire household to Krasna. The following Friday they had to flee further from the French. The Mitteler Rebbe recorded that they escaped with only two wagons carrying twenty-eight souls — leaving all heavy possessions behind, despite the elderly Rebbe's frailty and the harshness of the journey.

title_en: Alter Rebbe arrives in Piena after months of wartime wandering
summary_en: After months on the road as a refugee, the Alter Rebbe reached the town of Piena on Erev Shabbat Vayishlach.
story_body: On Erev Shabbat parashat Vayishlach 5573 (December 1812), Rabbi Schneur Zalman reached the town of Piena, exhausted and elderly. The Tzemach Tzedek records that the harshness of the winter, the cold, and the constant displacement were far beyond what the aged Rebbe could bear physically. Yet he had refused under any circumstance to remain even one day under French rule, declaring he would not live under Napoleon's government.

title_en: Passing of the Alter Rebbe in Piena
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi passed away in Piena on the night of 24 Tevet.
story_body: On Motzei Shabbat parashat Shemot, the beginning of 24 Tevet 5573 (around January 8, 1813), at approximately 11 o'clock at night, the Alter Rebbe passed away in the town of Piena. His grandson the Tzemach Tzedek described the event as the ark of holiness being taken captive — the light of Israel and the anointed of Hashem summoned to the heavenly academy. He died as a wartime refugee, having refused to remain under Napoleonic rule.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe settles in Lubavitch as the new Chabad center
summary_en: Following the end of the Napoleonic war, the Mitteler Rebbe settled in Lubavitch and made it the center of the Chabad movement.
story_body: Shortly after the Alter Rebbe's passing and the conclusion of the Napoleonic war in 5573 (1813), Rabbi Dovber, the second Rebbe of Chabad, established himself in the small White Russian town of Lubavitch. He built a residence and a large beit knesset there. For the next 102 years Lubavitch served as the central seat of the worldwide Chabad movement under successive Rebbes — and from this town the movement took its enduring name.

title_en: Family homes in Lyadi reported burned in war's aftermath
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe wrote that a trustworthy source had reported the family's homes in Lyadi had been burned.
story_body: In the winter of 5573 (early 1813), shortly after the Alter Rebbe's passing, the Mitteler Rebbe wrote that he had heard from a trustworthy person that the family's houses in Lyadi had been consumed by a wartime fire. Any seforim or remnants of the Alter Rebbe's own manuscript writings that had remained in the Lyadi home were lost in this second fire — possibly including the last surviving fragments of his glosses on Shulchan Aruch.

title_en: Passing of Esther Miriam, daughter of the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: Esther Miriam, a daughter of the Mitteler Rebbe, passed away in Tammuz 5579.
story_body: In Tammuz 5579 (July 1819), Esther Miriam, a daughter of the Mitteler Rebbe, passed away. Her matzeva, identified only relatively recently, describes her as 'the modest and honored woman,' a phrasing suggesting she was already married at the time of her death. According to one reconstruction she may have been a first wife of Rabbi Aharon of Kremenchug, before he later married Chaya, daughter of Rebbe Nachman of Breslov.

title_en: R' Aharon Alexandrov brings Torah Or to press
summary_en: Rabbi Aharon Alexandrov brought the sefer Torah Or, edited by the Tzemach Tzedek, to the printing press.
story_body: In 5597 (1837), Rabbi Aharon ben Moshe Chaim Alexandrov brought the sefer Torah Or to press. This volume of the Alter Rebbe's chassidic discourses was edited and arranged for publication by the Tzemach Tzedek, who attested on the title page that the Alter Rebbe himself had reviewed and corrected many of these maamarim during his lifetime in his own hand and language.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek answers responsum to R' Aharon of Kremenchug
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek wrote a halachic responsum on Orach Chaim addressed to his cousin Rabbi Aharon of Kremenchug.
story_body: On 22 Sivan 5598 (June 1838), Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn — the Tzemach Tzedek — wrote a responsum on Orach Chaim, printed as siman 102 in his Shu't Tzemach Tzedek, in reply to a question from his relative Rabbi Aharon of Kremenchug. R' Aharon was a grandson of the Alter Rebbe through his daughter Freida, and was a son-in-law of both the Mitteler Rebbe and of Rebbe Nachman of Breslov.

title_en: Polish non-Jew brings Shu't Maharik with Alter Rebbe's glosses to America
summary_en: A Polish non-Jew arrived in America carrying a copy of Shu't Maharik bearing handwritten glosses by the Alter Rebbe.
story_body: In the summer of 5746 (1986), a Polish non-Jew arrived in the United States carrying a copy of Shu't Maharik (Lvov 5558) with handwritten glosses by the Alter Rebbe in its margins. He claimed to have inherited the volume from his grandfather. The book was acquired by a Chabad chassid and returned to the Chabad library — joining the small group of surviving books bearing the Alter Rebbe's own hand to escape the Lyadi fires.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab forced to flee Lubavitch as German army approaches in WWI
summary_en: At the start of 5676 (1915), as the German army approached Lubavitch, the Rebbe Rashab and his household were forced to leave the town, hoping to return after the war.
story_body: World War I brought the front lines near Lubavitch, the longtime seat of Chabad. The Rebbe Rashab departed with his family, expecting the displacement to be temporary. In fact, this marked the end of Lubavitch's era as the center of the Chabad movement; the town's chassidic infrastructure would never be restored.

title_en: Tomchei Temimim yeshiva students leave Lubavitch for safer towns
summary_en: In 5678 (1918) the yeshiva students left Lubavitch to study in other towns farther from the war zone near the front.
story_body: With Lubavitch sitting close to the WWI front, the yeshiva could no longer operate safely there. The students dispersed to study in interior towns. This was a key step in the institutional unraveling of Lubavitch as Chabad's center.

title_en: Passing of Rebbe Rashab in Rostov
summary_en: In 5680 (1920) the Rebbe Rashab passed away in Rostov-on-Don, far from his original home in Lubavitch.
story_body: Displaced by the war and unable to return to Lubavitch, the Rashab eventually settled in Rostov, where he passed away in 1920. His son and successor, the Rebbe Rayatz, would lead Chabad through Soviet repression. The Rashab's resting place in Rostov became an important pilgrimage site.

title_en: Court of the Rebbes in Lubavitch burned to the ground
summary_en: In 5681 (1921) the entire courtyard complex of the Rebbes in the town of Lubavitch was destroyed by fire.
story_body: After WWI and the upheavals of the Russian Revolution, the historic court of the Chabad Rebbes in Lubavitch was consumed by fire in 1921. The buildings that had served as the seat of the dynasty for over a century were lost. The town ceased to function as a Chabad center from this point onward.

title_en: First documented mention of the town of Lubavitch
summary_en: The earliest known document referencing the town of Lubavitch dates to 5281 (1521), placing its founding to roughly 500 years ago.
story_body: Lubavitch sat in the contested borderlands between Russia and Poland. Its first appearance in surviving records is from 1521. By tradition, the town was founded by a hidden tzaddik named R' Meir, and the name Lubavitch (from the Russian for love) reflected his character.

title_en: Vasili III of Russia cedes Smolensk-region towns including Lubavitch to Poland
summary_en: In 5281 (1521) Tsar Vasili III signed an agreement transferring several Smolensk-area towns, including Lubavitch, to Poland.
story_body: Lubavitch lay on the disputed frontier between the Russian and Polish states, which repeatedly fought over the region. Vasili III's 1521 accord briefly placed Lubavitch under Polish rule. The town's borderland status shaped its mixed Russian-Polish-Belarusian character for centuries.

title_en: Ivan the Terrible signs treaty transferring Smolensk-area towns to Poland
summary_en: In 5316 (1556) Ivan the Terrible signed an agreement similar to Vasili III's, again transferring border towns including the Lubavitch area to Poland.
story_body: The borderlands containing Lubavitch repeatedly changed hands between Russia and Poland in treaty negotiations. Ivan IV's 1556 accord echoed the 1521 transfer. The recurring border shifts left a complex political legacy in the region.

title_en: Lubavitch area joins the Russian Empire with the First Partition of Poland
summary_en: In the summer of 5532 (1772), with the First Partition of Poland, the Lubavitch region was annexed to the Russian Empire.
story_body: The First Partition of Poland in 1772 absorbed huge swaths of formerly Polish-Lithuanian territory into Russia. Lubavitch, sitting on the border, became Russian. The town would remain near the Russia-Belarus border under tsarist rule for the next century and a half.

title_en: Hendel Deutsch publishes Russian booklet documenting Lubavitch history
summary_en: In 5754 (1994) Mr. Hendel Deutsch compiled and published a small Russian-language booklet titled 'Lubavitch — Center of Chabad Chassidus, Documentary Sketches.'
story_body: Deutsch gathered surviving documents and general information about the town across the centuries. His booklet was published in Russian in 1994, providing a documentary basis for later historical accounts of Lubavitch's pre-Chabad and early-Chabad history.

title_en: Chabad center established in Liozna under the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: In 5543 (1783) Liozna became the seat of the Alter Rebbe's leadership and the center of the emerging Chabad movement.
story_body: The Alter Rebbe, R' Shneur Zalman, founded the Chabad branch of Chassidus and led the movement from Liozna for the first phase of his nesius. Liozna sat near Lubavitch in White Russia. It would serve as the Chabad center for nearly two decades.

title_en: Approximately fifty Jewish families recorded living in Lubavitch
summary_en: A list of about fifty Jewish families living in Lubavitch was recorded in 5544 (1784), later published in the Hendel Deutsch booklet.
story_body: Lubavitch was a small town, roughly 1.5 by 1.5 kilometers, but it served as a regional commercial hub. The 1784 list of about fifty Jewish families documents the local community well before Chabad's leadership moved there. The list was later reprinted in Deutsch's 1994 documentary booklet.

title_en: Chabad center moves from Liozna to Liadi
summary_en: In 5561 (1801) the Alter Rebbe moved the Chabad center from Liozna to the neighboring town of Liadi.
story_body: After about eighteen years in Liozna, the Alter Rebbe relocated to Liadi in 1801. Liadi would remain the Chabad center until his passing in 1812. The towns of Liozna, Liadi, and Lubavitch all sat near one another on the Russian-Belarusian frontier.

title_en: Liadi destroyed by fire as Alter Rebbe flees Napoleon's advance
summary_en: In 5573 (1813) the Alter Rebbe's home in Liadi was burned together with all its contents during the wartime upheaval.
story_body: After the Alter Rebbe's passing in late 1812, news arrived that the family's homes in Liadi had been destroyed by fire — described as the 'returning flame' of war. The Mittler Rebbe, then in Kremenchug, decided he could not return to Liadi. Many of the Alter Rebbe's manuscripts were lost in this fire.

title_en: Mittler Rebbe establishes the Chabad center in Lubavitch
summary_en: At the end of summer 5573 / start of 5574 (1813) the Mittler Rebbe settled in Lubavitch, making it the new center of the Chabad movement.
story_body: After his father's passing and the destruction of Liadi, the Mittler Rebbe spent half a year in Kremenchug before relocating to White Russia. He chose Lubavitch as his new seat, immediately at the beginning of his leadership. Lubavitch would remain the Chabad center for the next century, giving the movement its enduring name.

title_en: Construction begins on the Mittler Rebbe's great synagogue in Lubavitch
summary_en: In 5574 (1814) the Mittler Rebbe began constructing a large wooden synagogue in his courtyard in Lubavitch, a project that continued for a year or two.
story_body: After purchasing a wooden house from the local nobleman Krauer, the Mittler Rebbe built a sizable synagogue in the courtyard. According to the tsarist investigator Korbitsky's later report, it measured roughly 21 by 13 meters; the Rebbe Rayatz recorded much larger dimensions. The site reportedly stood where the Alter Rebbe had studied with R' Yissachar Ber decades earlier.

title_en: Mittler Rebbe sends three foundational letters to Anash including Kuntres HaHispaalus
summary_en: In 5574 (1814), his second year of nesius, the Mittler Rebbe sent three sequential letters to the chassidim, the second of which became Kuntres HaHispaalus.
story_body: Manuscript evidence in the Library identifies the date as 5574 for all three letters. The first served as introduction, the second became the famous Kuntres HaHispaalus on the levels of emotional response in avodah, and the third was later printed as Shaar HaYichud (Kuntres HaHisbonenus). They were published in reverse order across the following decades.

title_en: Mittler Rebbe prints Siddur with Chassidus and Biurei HaZohar in Kapust
summary_en: In 5576 (1816) the Mittler Rebbe published a Siddur with discourses from his father (Pirush HaMillos) and the volume Biurei HaZohar in Kapust.
story_body: Drawing on his own manuscript collection and copies circulating among chassidim, the Mittler Rebbe assembled the Alter Rebbe's discourses on the siddur and on the Zohar. Both volumes were printed in Kapust in 1816. These remain core published texts of the Alter Rebbe's Chassidus.

title_en: Shaar HaYichud printed in Kapust as part of Ner Mitzvah V'Torah Or
summary_en: In 5580 (1820) the third of the Mittler Rebbe's 1814 letters was printed in Kapust as Shaar HaYichud in the volume Ner Mitzvah V'Torah Or.
story_body: Although written in 1814, the third letter was the first of the three to reach print. It appeared in 1820 under the title Shaar HaYichud as part of the published Ner Mitzvah V'Torah Or in Kapust. Kuntres HaHispaalus and the introductory letter would only follow in print decades later.

title_en: Investigator Korbitsky files court report on Mittler Rebbe's court and library
summary_en: In 5586 (1825) the tsarist investigator Korbitsky submitted a report to the court describing the synagogue, books, and ritual objects in the Mittler Rebbe's courtyard in Lubavitch.
story_body: Korbitsky's report catalogued the synagogue's dimensions, Torah scrolls, menorahs from Petersburg, candlesticks, curtains, and a library of 611 books in four cabinets available for loan to townspeople. The report is a primary source for understanding the Mittler Rebbe's court at Lubavitch in this period. It was later cited in the published account of the Mittler Rebbe's arrest and release.

title_en: Fire at Beshen destroys over forty manuscripts of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: A fire in 5584 (1824) at the home of R' Beshen destroyed over forty volumes of the Alter Rebbe's own handwriting that were held there.
story_body: According to the Rebbe Rayatz citing his grandfather the Rebbe Maharash, the Alter Rebbe would entrust his manuscripts to the chassid R' Yisrael Yaffe of Kapust, who circulated them among chassidim for study and copying. A vast cache held at R' Beshen's home was lost in the 1824 fire. Only two volumes from 5566-5567 that were on loan to the Mittler Rebbe survived intact.

title_en: Mittler Rebbe travels to Haditch to visit Alter Rebbe's grave
summary_en: At the start of 5588 (1827) the Mittler Rebbe set out from Lubavitch on a long journey to prostrate himself at his father's grave in distant Haditch.
story_body: The Mittler Rebbe undertook the demanding trip to Haditch, where the Alter Rebbe was buried, in the autumn of 1827. He would not reach Lubavitch alive on the return. The trip ended in his own passing in Nezhin.

title_en: Passing of the Mittler Rebbe in Nezhin
summary_en: On 9 Kislev 5588 (late 1827) the Mittler Rebbe passed away in Nezhin on his return journey from Haditch and was buried there.
story_body: After visiting his father's grave in Haditch, the Mittler Rebbe fell ill on the way home. He passed in Nezhin on 9 (or 10) Kislev 5588, ending fifteen years of nesius. His resting place in Nezhin became, with Haditch and Rostov, one of the key Chabad pilgrimage sites in the former Russian Empire.

title_en: Tsarist decree shuts down Hebrew printing presses in Russia
summary_en: The 1836-1837 (5597) decree of Tsar Nicholas I ordered the closure of Hebrew printing presses in Russia and inspection of existing Jewish books.
story_body: Under Nicholas I, the regime moved against Jewish printing, closing presses and requiring every existing Jewish book in private hands to be inspected and stamped by an authorized rabbi-censor. The decree drove Hebrew printing — including Chabad printing — underground. Several Chabad works appeared in the following years from a clandestine press with falsified imprints.

title_en: Kuntres HaHispaalus printed as introduction edition in Warsaw
summary_en: In 5628 (1868) the introductory letter of the Mittler Rebbe's 1814 trilogy was printed in Warsaw as the preface to Kuntres HaHispaalus.
story_body: Although written in 1814, the introductory letter was the last of the three to see print. It appeared in Warsaw in 1868 as the preface to a new edition of Kuntres HaHispaalus. With this, all three of the 1814 letters to Anash were finally in circulation.

title_en: Tikkunei Zohar printed in Kapust by Yehuda Yaffe
summary_en: The Tikkunei Zohar was printed in Kapust in 5570 at the press of Yehuda son of A.S. Feivush Yaffe.
story_body: This authentic Kapust edition of the Tikkunei Zohar carried a censor's approval dated 1810. Years later, a clandestine reprint forged a title page dated 5585 (1825) but copied this same 1810 censor approval, revealing the forgery. The Yaffe family press was a leading Hebrew printer in White Russia during the early nineteenth century.

title_en: Passing of the Alter Rebbe (24 Tevet)
summary_en: Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, founder of Chabad, passed away on 24 Tevet 5573 in Pyena after fleeing the advancing French army.
story_body: After abandoning his home in Liadi during Napoleon's 1812 invasion, the Alter Rebbe died in flight, leaving his household possessions consumed by fire. His son and successor, the Mitteler Rebbe, remained in Kremenchug for a period before being persuaded to return to White Russia. The destitute state of the Rebbe's family after the war later became central to the Mitteler Rebbe's collection of Ma'amad funds.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe and Tzemach Tzedek settle in Lubavitch
summary_en: At the end of 5573 and beginning of 5574, the Mitteler Rebbe and his nephew/son-in-law the future Tzemach Tzedek established their court in the town of Lubavitch.
story_body: After the disruptions of the Napoleonic war and the passing of the Alter Rebbe, the Mitteler Rebbe accepted the chassidim's invitation to return from Kremenchug to White Russia. The town of Lubavitch was chosen as the new center of the Chabad movement, and would remain its seat for over a century until 1915.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe organizes Ma'amad fund distribution
summary_en: In Tevet 5574 the Mitteler Rebbe organized the distribution of 35,000 rubles collected to rebuild the Rebbe's household after the war.
story_body: Following his father's passing, the Mitteler Rebbe needed to rehabilitate the family after the destruction of the Liadi home. He entrusted the distribution to senior chassid Reb Pinchas Shick of Shklov, with Reb Shlomo Freides and Reb Zalman Roizes as overseers. Two-thirds went to relatives of the Alter Rebbe; one-third was used by the Mitteler Rebbe to build his home and synagogue in Lubavitch. This very distribution letter was later seized by the informer Simcha Kissin and used in the 1825 denunciation.

title_en: Shulchan Aruch HaRav (Hilchot Pesach) printed in Shklov
summary_en: An edition of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch covering the Laws of Passover appeared in Shklov in 5574.
story_body: This volume bore an authentic Kapust rabbinical censor's stamp with the signature of Rabbi Nachum Yaffe of Kapust beside it. The genuine stamp would later help historians distinguish authentic Russian-Jewish printings from the wave of forgeries that followed the 1837 ban on Hebrew presses.

title_en: Mikdash Melech printed in Sudilkov
summary_en: The kabbalistic work Mikdash Melech was printed in Sudilkov in 5580.
story_body: Like the Shklov Shulchan Aruch HaRav, this edition bore the authentic Kapust censor's stamp accompanied by Rabbi Nachum Yaffe's signature. It is one of only three known volumes preserving both the genuine stamp and the rabbi's handwritten name, contrasting with later forgeries that copied only the stamp.

title_en: Imrei Binah printed in Kapust
summary_en: Imrei Binah was printed in Kapust in 5581.
story_body: This volume is one of three known editions to bear both the authentic Kapust censor's stamp and Rabbi Nachum Yaffe's accompanying signature. Such authentic Kapust printings serve as the comparison standard against which later clandestine forgeries can be detected.

title_en: Simcha Kissin submits denunciations against Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: In Tammuz-Av 5585 the informer Simcha Kissin handed three denunciation letters about the Mitteler Rebbe to Governor Khovansky in Vitebsk.
story_body: Kissin's denunciation portrayed the Chassidic movement as exploiting youthful followers for money and seizing control of communal funds, slaughter, and printing. He attached a copy of the Mitteler Rebbe's 1814 Ma'amad distribution letter, attempting to prove that the Rebbe had amassed roughly 140,000 rubles. The Mitteler Rebbe was traveling abroad at the Carlsbad spa at the time and would be summoned upon his return.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe taken to Vitebsk for interrogation
summary_en: On Isru Chag Sukkot 5586 (October 1825) the Mitteler Rebbe was taken to Vitebsk, seat of Governor Khovansky, to face the investigators.
story_body: Governor Nikolai Khovansky ruled the provinces of Vitebsk, Mohilev, Smolensk and Kaluga. He ordered the police to bring the Rebbe immediately after the holiday. The case opened with the Rebbe verifying that the attached documents were in his hand, and his confidants Reb Zalman Roizes and Reb Shlomo Freides were summoned for parallel questioning.

title_en: Reb Aharon of Staroselye interrogated in Vitebsk
summary_en: Between 21 and 28 Cheshvan 5586 Reb Aharon of Staroselye was brought to Vitebsk and interrogated as part of the same case.
story_body: On 19 Cheshvan a special officer had been dispatched to summon Reb Aharon, a leading disciple of the Alter Rebbe who led his own circle in Staroselye. His interrogation extended the inquiry beyond the Mitteler Rebbe's immediate circle, signaling that Khovansky was probing the Chassidic movement more broadly.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe submits release request to Governor Khovansky
summary_en: On 6 Kislev 5586 (4 November 1825) the Mitteler Rebbe formally petitioned Governor Khovansky for release to his home.
story_body: With the active interrogation phase concluded, the Rebbe asked to be released pending the formal trial. The petition was granted four days later, sending the Rebbe home while his case moved into the provincial court system.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe released on Yud Kislev
summary_en: On 10 Kislev 5586 the Mitteler Rebbe was released from his Vitebsk interrogation and allowed to return home.
story_body: Though strictly only an interim release pending trial, this date became commemorated in Chabad as Yud Kislev, the festival of the Mitteler Rebbe's redemption. The eventual judicial acquittal would unfold in three further stages over the next two years; the Mitteler Rebbe himself never lived to see the final Senate confirmation.

title_en: Khovansky transfers case to Mohilev provincial government
summary_en: On 19 Kislev 5586 Governor Khovansky forwarded the case file to the Mohilev provincial government for trial.
story_body: Since Lubavitch lay in the Babinovichi district of Mohilev province, jurisdiction now passed there. The provincial authorities in turn sent the file to the Babinovichi peace court, which dispatched officers to Lubavitch and ordered parallel inquiries in Kapust, Orsha, Shklov and Mohilev to verify the Rebbe's account of how Ma'amad funds were collected.

title_en: Mohilev High Court acquits the Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: On 11 Kislev 5587 the Mohilev provincial high court cleared the Mitteler Rebbe of all charges.
story_body: Inquiries in Kapust, Orsha, Shklov and Mohilev had confirmed that chassidim had voluntarily invited the Rebbe to return from Kremenchug and pledged to support him. The court concluded that Ma'amad contributions were voluntary gifts to a non-salaried rabbi, not communal taxes, and so did not violate the 1805 Jewish charter. The verdict was sent to the prosecutor general and then to Governor Khovansky for confirmation.

title_en: Passing of the Mitteler Rebbe (9 Kislev)
summary_en: Rabbi Dovber Schneuri, the Mitteler Rebbe, passed away on 9 Kislev 5588.
story_body: His passing came twelve days before the Senate in Petersburg confirmed his judicial acquittal. The proximity of his passing to Yud Kislev — what would have been the first major celebration of his redemption — meant that the day was never widely established as a festival during his lifetime, contributing to historical confusion about whether the release occurred in 5586 or 5587.

title_en: Senate in Petersburg confirms acquittal of Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: On 21 Kislev 5588 the Petersburg Senate rejected Governor Khovansky's appeal and confirmed the Mitteler Rebbe's full acquittal.
story_body: Khovansky had appealed in 1827, arguing that uncollected Ma'amad contributions were destabilizing and could divert tax revenue. The Senate sided with the Mohilev court, ruling Ma'amad legal as voluntary support for a non-salaried rabbi. The decision arrived twelve days after the Rebbe's passing and permanently legitimized Ma'amad as the financial basis of the Chabad dynasty.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek accepts leadership of Chabad
summary_en: Following the passing of the Mitteler Rebbe in 5588, Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch, the Tzemach Tzedek, assumed the leadership of Chabad.
story_body: He was nephew and son-in-law of his predecessor, and had lived in Lubavitch alongside him since 1813. For nearly four decades he led Chabad from Lubavitch, traveling each year to a different region of chassidic communities, and writing the more than one thousand responsa of the Tzemach Tzedek series.

title_en: Rabbi Yissachar Ber Hurwitz appointed rabbi of Lubavitch
summary_en: From 5592 Rabbi Yissachar Ber Halevi Hurwitz served as the town rabbi of Lubavitch.
story_body: He held the post throughout most of the Tzemach Tzedek's tenure, and was later succeeded by Rabbi Avraham son of Avigdor HaKohen. The town rabbinate was distinct from the Rebbe's role; the Tzemach Tzedek himself was never the salaried communal rabbi of Lubavitch.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek purchases land for his Lubavitch courtyard
summary_en: Around 5594 the Tzemach Tzedek bought the plot of land in Lubavitch on which he built his home.
story_body: The parcel later became the site of the great Tomchei Temimim study hall. His first house stood at the northwestern corner of the courtyard with the synagogue beside it; both were destroyed in the great fire of 1856-1858, after which a much larger compound was rebuilt.

title_en: New Russian Jewish charter promulgated
summary_en: A new Russian statute regulating Jewish life was published in 5595, replacing the 1805 charter.
story_body: The Senate had informed Governor Khovansky that his earlier proposals for regulating the rabbinate would be subsumed under a wider planned overhaul. The 1835 charter became the legal framework under which the Tzemach Tzedek and other Russian Jewish leaders operated, including the rules that conditioned the great surveillance campaign against him in the 1840s.

title_en: Russian decree restricting Hebrew printing presses
summary_en: In 5597 the tsarist government shut down most Jewish presses across Russia, requiring all subsequent Hebrew printing to receive a rabbinical censor's stamp.
story_body: The decree triggered a wave of clandestine printing inside Russia in which presses imitated the look of older Kapust and other authentic editions, often forging both title pages and the rabbinical censor's stamp. At least five such forgeries imitating the late Kapust press were printed after this decree, four of them works of Chabad Chassidut, suggesting the underground printer was himself a Chabad chassid.

title_en: Maskilim denounce Tzemach Tzedek; police search his home
summary_en: In 5601 maskilim denounced the Tzemach Tzedek for opposing the government's plan to compel Jewish children to study secular subjects.
story_body: A special officer was sent to Lubavitch, interrogated the Rebbe, and searched his home. The shock caused the Rebbe to fall ill and take to his bed. The episode opened years of continuous secret surveillance and culminated in his being summoned to the 1843 Petersburg rabbinical conference.

title_en: Petersburg Rabbinical Conference on Jewish education
summary_en: During the summer of 5603 the Tzemach Tzedek participated in the Petersburg conference on Jewish education called by the Russian government.
story_body: The conference, proposed by the maskilim and convened by the Minister of Education, aimed to pressure leading rabbis to consent to government 'enlightenment' schools for Jewish youth. The Rebbe initially pleaded that his post-interrogation illness made travel impossible, but ultimately agreed that his attendance was essential to block undesirable resolutions. Following the conference he was granted the imperial title of Honorary Citizen for life.

title_en: Russian government removes surveillance on Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: In the spring of 5607 the Russian government lifted the continuous secret-police surveillance imposed on the Tzemach Tzedek after the 1841 denunciation.
story_body: After roughly six years of constant watch, the authorities concluded that there was no fault to be found in the Rebbe's conduct. The decision closed the chapter of harassment that had begun with the maskilim's denunciation and the police search of his home.

title_en: Great fire destroys Tzemach Tzedek's courtyard in Lubavitch
summary_en: Between 5616 and 5618 a great fire in Lubavitch destroyed the Tzemach Tzedek's home, the synagogue, and much of his library and manuscripts.
story_body: The Rebbe relocated to the estate of a local nobleman outside town while the courtyard was rebuilt on a more spacious scale. A letter from his son Rabbi Chaim Schneur Zalman (later the Rebbe of Liadi) survives, dated 8 Iyar, appealing to chassidim to contribute toward the rebuilding effort. The expanded compound included an enlarged synagogue and dedicated prayer halls within the Rebbe's own house.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek falls severely ill
summary_en: In Kislev 5620 the Tzemach Tzedek fell gravely ill in his rebuilt Lubavitch home.
story_body: The illness came shortly after the courtyard's reconstruction and his return from the nobleman's estate. He continued to lead the movement for several more years until his passing in 1866.

title_en: Passing of the Tzemach Tzedek (13 Nissan)
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek passed away on 13 Nissan 5626 in Lubavitch, where he is buried.
story_body: He was the first Chabad Rebbe to live in Lubavitch from start of leadership to his last day. His will forbade any structure of brick or wood over his grave, but his family built a roofless wall around it out of fear that gentiles would dig in search of buried gold. A study hall was later added on its southern side. His passing precipitated the succession crisis that would split Chabad into several branches.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek born in Liozna
summary_en: Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn (the Tzemach Tzedek) was born on the eve of Rosh Hashanah 5550.
story_body: The third Chabad Rebbe, known as the Tzemach Tzedek after his magnum opus of responsa, was born on Erev Rosh Hashanah 5550. He was the grandson of the Alter Rebbe and would later become son-in-law of the Mitteler Rebbe. This birth date is used as the baseline for dating his earliest halachic activity.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek asks Alter Rebbe a Yevamot question
summary_en: A note on tractate Yevamot in manuscript 1024 records the young Tzemach Tzedek asking his grandfather the Alter Rebbe about a difficult halacha.
story_body: In manuscript 1024 (folio 133a), later printed in Tzemach Tzedek Milu'im vol. 5 §59, the young Menachem Mendel records a question on tractate Yevamot that he asked 'before my grandfather and teacher the Gaon.' The note must therefore predate the Alter Rebbe's passing on 24 Tevet 5573, showing the Tzemach Tzedek was already engaged in halachic study during his grandfather's lifetime.

title_en: Alter Rebbe passes away on 24 Tevet
summary_en: Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, the Alter Rebbe, passed away on 24 Tevet 5573.
story_body: The founder of Chabad Chassidus passed away on 24 Tevet 5573, ending the period during which his grandson the Tzemach Tzedek studied directly under him. After this date, the Alter Rebbe's brother Maharil of Yanovitch became the principal halachic respondent in the Chabad community, while the young Tzemach Tzedek continued his studies.

title_en: Get from 5573 discussed in later responsum
summary_en: A responsum in Even HaEzer §391 of the Tzemach Tzedek discusses a divorce document written in 5573.
story_body: Among the earliest cases recorded in the Tzemach Tzedek's responsa is a discussion in Even HaEzer §391 about a get written in 5573. This is one of the few extant records of his halachic activity from the period before he began responding to questions regularly in 5578.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek begins responding to halachic questions
summary_en: Around 5578, at age 28, the Tzemach Tzedek began answering halachic questions on a regular basis.
story_body: While he had written occasional novellae earlier, the Tzemach Tzedek began responding to halachic queries with regularity around 5578, while his great-uncle Maharil of Yanovitch was still the primary respondent in the Chabad community. Responsum §349 in Yoreh Deah and others can be dated to this year, marking the beginning of his fifty-year career as a posek.

title_en: Earliest extant dated Tzemach Tzedek responsum
summary_en: The earliest precisely dated responsum reaching us, printed in Yoreh Deah §8, was written in 5579.
story_body: Internal evidence in the responsum (which refers to 'last year, 5578') places its composition in 5579. The original autograph has not survived; only a copy in manuscript 1041 with the Tzemach Tzedek's own glosses remains, with a header noting it was 'copied from volume 3 with annotations.' This is currently the oldest dated piece of his responsa literature in our hands.

title_en: Volume 1 of Tzemach Tzedek's responsa bound
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek bound the first volume of his collected responsa around 5579.
story_body: In his early years the Tzemach Tzedek bound his question-and-answer correspondence into numbered volumes (chelek 1, 2, 3, etc.). Volume 1, containing responsa from his earliest period, was bound around 5579. This volume, like most of the first fourteen, was later lost or destroyed in a fire in Lubavitch.

title_en: Volume 3 of Tzemach Tzedek responsa bound
summary_en: Volume 3 of the Tzemach Tzedek's bound responsa was completed around 5581.
story_body: Volume 3, containing responsa such as Even HaEzer 2 §145 (explicitly written in 5581), was bound around that year. Like most of the early numbered volumes, the original is lost; we know its contents only through summaries the Tzemach Tzedek later copied into other manuscripts when preparing a mehadura batra reorganized by the sections of the Shulchan Aruch.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe forwards Chernobyl agunah case to Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: In summer 5583 the Mitteler Rebbe transferred a difficult agunah case from the Chernobyl beis din to his son-in-law and Maharil.
story_body: The Mitteler Rebbe, his father-in-law, directed the young Tzemach Tzedek along with his great-uncle Maharil to examine an agunah case (Even HaEzer §§347–348) referred to him by the Chernobyl beis din. In the resulting responsum the two write that 'it was our master's command... and although we know our small worth, that we have not reached the stature to take up the name and respond from afar, nevertheless one does not refuse a greater.'

title_en: Volume 7 of Tzemach Tzedek responsa bound
summary_en: Volume 7 of the Tzemach Tzedek's responsa, manuscript 233, contains responsa written between 5582 and 5585.
story_body: Manuscript 233 is one of only three early bound volumes of the Tzemach Tzedek's responsa that survives. It collects question-and-answer exchanges from 5582 to 5585. Together with manuscripts 1019 and 1050 it provides our chief evidence for the structure of the lost volumes 1–14.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek responsa to R. Avraham Sheines of Shklov
summary_en: Responsa Even HaEzer §§297–298, written in 5585, were sent to R. Avraham Sheines of Shklov to settle a dispute among major rabbis.
story_body: According to Beis Rebbi (p. 120), R. Avraham son of R. Tzvi Sheines of Shklov brought before the Tzemach Tzedek a dispute among R. Aharon Halevi of Strashelye, R. Gershon of Shklov, R. Nechemiah of Dubrovna, the author of Beis Ephraim, and others. The Tzemach Tzedek's responses are recorded in Even HaEzer §§297–298, dated 5585.

title_en: Maharil of Yanovitch passes away
summary_en: Rabbi Yehuda Leib (Maharil) of Yanovitch, the Alter Rebbe's brother, passed away in early 5586.
story_body: Maharil of Yanovitch had served as the primary halachic respondent for the Chabad community after the Alter Rebbe's passing in 5573. With his death at the start of 5586, the responsibility shifted increasingly to his great-nephew the Tzemach Tzedek, who had already been building a responsa practice for roughly eight years.

title_en: Volume 13 of Tzemach Tzedek responsa bound
summary_en: Volume 13, manuscript 1019 — a book of summaries of earlier responsa — was bound around 5591.
story_body: Manuscript 1019 (volume 13) is a survivor of the early numbered series. It contains short summaries of responsa written in earlier volumes, citing them as chelek 1, 2, 3, 4, etc. Although undated internally, the responsa it digests can be matched to known dates, placing its compilation around 5590–5591.

title_en: Responsum 353 with conditional psak formula
summary_en: In responsum §353, written in 5592, the Tzemach Tzedek refuses to rule alone on a serious matter and demands two or three other prominent poskim concur.
story_body: The Tzemach Tzedek wrote in §353 (5592) that 'because of the gravity of the matter, I do not want anyone to rely on me alone, but only with the concurrence of two famous poskim or at least one famous moreh hora'ah, and if [the case develops further], then... it appears to me to permit her, if three great poskim concur.' The responsum is a paradigmatic illustration of his halachic humility, the dominant feature of his style.

title_en: Volume 14 of Tzemach Tzedek responsa bound
summary_en: Volume 14 was bound around 5593 and is lost; later manuscripts repeatedly reference it.
story_body: Volume 14 contained a published responsum (Even HaEzer §48) explicitly written in 5593, and manuscripts 1050 and 1021 cite it repeatedly with notes such as 'copied here with corrections from chelek 14.' The volume itself, along with most of the volumes numbered 1–14, did not reach us — many believed lost in a fire in Lubavitch.

title_en: Dispute between R. Shimon Zarchi and R. Yosef Ashkenazi of Yakobstadt
summary_en: In 5596 R. Yosef Ashkenazi disputed several rulings of R. Shimon Zarchi, rabbi of Yakobstadt, and both sides wrote to the Tzemach Tzedek for arbitration.
story_body: R. Shimon Zarchi, author of Nachalas Shimon and rabbi of Yakobstadt, and R. Yosef Ashkenazi, author of Ohel Yosef and then a rosh metivta in Yakobstadt, clashed in 5596 over several halachic matters. They submitted their reasoning to the Tzemach Tzedek, who responded with multiple rulings adjudicating between them (Orach Chaim §§43, 75; Yoreh Deah §217; Choshen Mishpat §85).

title_en: R. Yosef Ashkenazi appointed dayan in Novi Aleksandrovsky
summary_en: R. Yosef Ashkenazi, author of Ohel Yosef, was appointed dayan in Novi Aleksandrovsky in 5597.
story_body: After his disputes with R. Shimon Zarchi the previous year, R. Yosef Ashkenazi was appointed in 5597 to serve as moreh tzedek in the town of Novi Aleksandrovsky, leaving his position as rosh metivta in Yakobstadt.

title_en: Latest dated responsum in Mehadura Batra Even HaEzer manuscript
summary_en: Manuscript 1050, the Even HaEzer mehadura batra, contains a final dated responsum from 5603.
story_body: In later years the Tzemach Tzedek began reorganizing his responsa according to the sections of the Shulchan Aruch, possibly to prepare them for print. Manuscript 1050 — labeled in his own hand 'Responsa Even HaEzer, mehadura batra, chelek 2' — was bound around the time of its latest dated responsum, 5603.

title_en: Latest dated responsum in Mehadura Batra Orach Chaim manuscript
summary_en: Manuscript 1017, the Orach Chaim mehadura batra, was bound around 5612, the date of its latest responsum.
story_body: Manuscript 1017 contains the Tzemach Tzedek's reorganized Orach Chaim responsa, drawing on lost volumes 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 14 (the source volumes likely lost in the Lubavitch fire). Its latest internal date, 5612 (folio 276a), establishes the rough binding date.

title_en: Fire in Lubavitch destroys responsa manuscripts
summary_en: A fire in Lubavitch between 5616 and 5618 destroyed many of the Tzemach Tzedek's bound responsa volumes.
story_body: Compilers' notes at the end of the printed Tzemach Tzedek responsa state that 'our holy master wrote many responsa on this, and in the last fire, woe to us, the book was burned and only this responsum remained.' The Rebbe's notes, citing manuscripts datable to 5608–5616, place the fire between roughly 5616 and 5618. The disaster accounts for the loss of most of volumes 1–14.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's Even HaEzer §41 written between Chanukah and Sivan 5619
summary_en: Responsum Even HaEzer §41 references 'Sivan 5618... Chanukah 5619 past,' placing its composition between Chanukah and Sivan 5619.
story_body: Internal evidence in Even HaEzer §41 — its opening refers to 'Sivan 5618 past... Chanukah 5619 past' — locates the responsum between Chanukah 5619 and Sivan 5619, late 1858 to spring 1859. This and Yoreh Deah §42 establish that the entire manuscript 2143 ('Book 5619') was written in that year, the latest extant Tzemach Tzedek responsa volume.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek becomes gravely ill
summary_en: In Kislev 5620 the Tzemach Tzedek became gravely ill, an illness that lasted more than six years.
story_body: Beis Rebbi records that the Tzemach Tzedek 'became very ill in the month of Kislev 5620 and was ill for more than six straight years.' During this period he transferred most halachic answering to his son R. Yisrael Noach (Maharin), who would present harder cases back to his father.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek responsum delivered by his son Maharin
summary_en: Orach Chaim §85, dated 5622, was delivered through R. Yisrael Noach (Maharin), reflecting the Tzemach Tzedek's late-life delegation of halacha to his son.
story_body: From around 5620 onward, chassidim brought their questions through attendants who relayed them to the bedridden Tzemach Tzedek. He appointed his son R. Yisrael Noach (Maharin) to answer most halachic queries, occasionally forwarding harder ones to his father. Orach Chaim §85 (5622) is one of the late responsa explicitly mediated by Maharin.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek chiddushim in half Shevat 5623
summary_en: A chiddush in Chiddushim folio 232d is dated to mid-Shevat 5623.
story_body: Among the very few late writings from the Tzemach Tzedek's years of illness is a chiddush dated mid-Shevat 5623 (early February 1863). It is one of fewer than a half-dozen dated pieces preserved from after his collapse in Kislev 5620.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek summer 5623 responsum on Yoreh Deah
summary_en: Yoreh Deah §337 was written in summer 5623.
story_body: Yoreh Deah §337, written in summer 5623, is one of the few responsa preserved from the years after the Tzemach Tzedek became gravely ill. Most halachic work had passed to his son Maharin by this point; this responsum is among the small set still authored personally.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek winter 5624 responsum on Orach Chaim
summary_en: Orach Chaim §114, written in winter 5624, is among the latest extant Tzemach Tzedek responsa.
story_body: Orach Chaim §114 was composed in the winter of 5624, after more than four years of the Tzemach Tzedek's illness. Such late responsa appear only sporadically; the vast majority of halachic work during this period was answered by his son Maharin, with the Tzemach Tzedek consulted only on the most difficult cases.

title_en: Vilna mitnagdim alter Tzemach Tzedek's text on the Gra
summary_en: In 5644 mitnagdim at the Vilna press altered a passage in Tzemach Tzedek's Piskei Dinim that called a Vilna Gaon argument 'no proof'.
story_body: Piskei Dinim III, 69c originally read of an argument of the Vilna Gaon, 'this is no proof.' At the Vilna printing in 5644, soon after the passing of the Rebbe Maharash and during an interregnum in the Chabad leadership, type-setters substituted 'and I in my poverty have not merited to understand his holy words.' The Frierdiker Rebbe later recounted to the Rebbe that as soon as the forgery was discovered in Lubavitch, the offending pages were reprinted with the original wording, though some falsified copies could not be recalled.

title_en: Tzar's decree closes Jewish printing presses in Russia
summary_en: On 5 Marcheshvan 5597 (27 October 1836), the Russian Minister of the Interior announced the Tzar's decree to inspect all Jewish books in Russia, burn suspicious ones, and close all Hebrew printing presses except two — one in Vilna and one in Zhitomir.
story_body: The decree, recounted by the Rebbe Rayatz, ordered a sweeping inspection of Jewish books throughout Russia, with suspicious volumes to be burned. By Tevet 5597 all Hebrew presses in Russia were shuttered, leaving only the Romm partnership press in Vilna operating. This crippled Chasidic publishing for decades and is cited as a major reason why so few of the Tzemach Tzedek's writings were printed in his lifetime.

title_en: Kapust press closes mid-printing of Torah Ohr
summary_en: Following the Tzarist closure of Hebrew presses in Tevet 5597, the Kapust press was shut down having only completed the first volume of Torah Ohr by the Alter Rebbe.
story_body: When the Russian government closed nearly all Jewish printing houses in early 5597, the Kapust press was among those shuttered. It had managed to print only the first part of Torah Ohr, the Alter Rebbe's chasidic discourses; the second volume's publication was delayed for over a decade. This loss shaped the trajectory of Chabad publishing for generations.

title_en: Likutei Torah printed in Zhitomir
summary_en: In 5608 the second volume of the Alter Rebbe's discourses, edited by the Tzemach Tzedek, was printed at the newly licensed Zhitomir press under the title Likutei Torah.
story_body: After the Zhitomir press received government approval in 5607 (1847), publishers turned to printing the long-delayed second volume of Torah Ohr. It appeared in 5608 (1848) under the new title Likutei Torah, becoming one of the foundational works of Chabad chasidic literature. The Tzemach Tzedek had spent decades collecting, editing, and annotating the manuscripts that made up the volume.

title_en: Wedding of Maharil of Kapust, son of the Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: On 14 Cheshvan 5585, the Tzemach Tzedek's son Rabbi Yehuda Leib (later the Maharil of Kapust) married the daughter of Rabbi Shlomo Freides of Shklov, who gave 40 volumes of his transcripts of the Alter Rebbe's teachings as dowry.
story_body: The Mitteler Rebbe recorded delivering a discourse 'at the wedding of my grandson Yehuda Leib, 14 Cheshvan 5585.' Rabbi Shlomo Freides, a major chronicler of the Alter Rebbe's teachings, presented forty volumes of his transcripts as the dowry. The Tzemach Tzedek subsequently annotated and expanded these manuscripts, though most were later lost in the great Lubavitch fire.

title_en: Great fire of Lubavitch destroys Tzemach Tzedek manuscripts
summary_en: A great fire swept through Lubavitch in 5617, burning much of the town including the Tzemach Tzedek's home and many of his unpublished manuscripts in both nigleh and chasidus.
story_body: The fire devastated Lubavitch including the Tzemach Tzedek's residence and the homes of chasidim who held his manuscripts on loan. Twenty volumes were lost at the home of Rabbi Avraham, the local moreh tzedek, including the missing siman additions to the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch. The Rebbe lamented he no longer had the strength in his old age to rewrite them. Sources variously date the fire to 5616, 5617, or 5618.

title_en: First volume of Tzemach Tzedek's responsa printed
summary_en: In 5631 the first volume of the Tzemach Tzedek's responsa — Even HaEzer — was published, beginning the multi-decade project of releasing his halachic writings.
story_body: Five years after the Tzemach Tzedek's passing, editors completed the first volume of his responsa, covering Even HaEzer. The series would take another thirteen years to complete and was given the name Tzemach Tzedek (gematria of Menachem Mendel). From the publication of these volumes onward, the Rebbe himself became known as 'the Tzemach Tzedek.'

title_en: Yoreh Deah responsa of the Tzemach Tzedek printed
summary_en: In 5634 the three volumes of the Tzemach Tzedek's Yoreh Deah responsa were printed, including supplementary teshuvos on niddah and mikvaos as omissions in the third volume.
story_body: The Yoreh Deah set appeared in 5634 as part of the ongoing publication of the Tzemach Tzedek's halachic corpus. After printing the second volume, three additional responsa on the laws of niddah and mikvaos were discovered and added as 'omissions' at the end of the third volume — an early instance of the pattern of supplements and addenda that would characterize the entire series.

title_en: Chiddushim on the Talmud of the Tzemach Tzedek printed
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek's chiddushim on the Talmud were printed in 5638 as part of the ongoing release of his halachic writings.
story_body: Published roughly in the middle of the multi-decade Tzemach Tzedek printing project, the chiddushim on Shas included editorial cross-references to teshuvos prepared for the Choshen Mishpat volume — suggesting that volume was already ready for press, though Russian censors refused to permit its publication.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek responsa and Piskei Dinim series completed
summary_en: In 5644, eighteen years after the Tzemach Tzedek's passing, the final volumes — Orach Chaim responsa and two volumes of Piskei Dinim — were printed, completing the original series.
story_body: After 13 years of editorial work and printing, the series was completed in 5644. Newly discovered teshuvos and chiddushim were appended to the Piskei Dinim volume. The publishers gave the entire series the name 'Tzemach Tzedek' (gematria of Menachem Mendel), and from this point the Rebbe himself was named after his book. Choshen Mishpat responsa were blocked by Russian censors who opposed rabbinic adjudication.

title_en: Rashab seeks to print Choshen Mishpat responsa
summary_en: In 5654 the Rebbe Rashab wrote to his mechutan Rabbi Meshulam Reich about printing an additional volume of Tzemach Tzedek responsa that would include the censored Choshen Mishpat material.
story_body: The Choshen Mishpat responsa had been blocked by Russian censors decades earlier. In 5654 the Rashab attempted to revive the project, corresponding with his mechutan about publication, but the effort did not come to fruition. Further attempts followed in 5660 and 5668, with the Rashab noting in the latter year that the volume was 'already arranged and copied, ready for printing' — yet still it did not appear.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek additions printed in Vilna Shulchan Aruch
summary_en: A new Vilna edition of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch was printed in 5665, including additional Tzemach Tzedek responsa across all four chelkei Shulchan Aruch that had been discovered in the intervening twenty years.
story_body: Between 5645 and 5665, additional responsa of the Tzemach Tzedek covering all four sections of Shulchan Aruch came to light. Rather than issue a separate supplement, the editors of the 5665 Vilna edition of Shulchan Aruch HaRav incorporated them as an appendix to that printing — making the new Vilna edition an essential reference for halachic researchers.

title_en: Derech Mitzvosecha and early Tzemach Tzedek chasidic works printed
summary_en: Beginning in 5671, the Tzemach Tzedek's chasidic works — Derech Mitzvosecha, Derech Emunah (Sefer HaChakirah), Yahel Ohr, and the first volume of Or HaTorah — were printed in the generation after his passing.
story_body: Some 45 years after the Tzemach Tzedek's passing, his chasidic writings began to appear in print. The works printed between 5671 and 5678 included Derech Mitzvosecha (on mitzvos), Derech Emunah (philosophical investigation), Yahel Ohr (on Tehillim), and the first volume of Or HaTorah. The majority of his chasidic corpus — the Or HaTorah series — would only see print in the seventh generation.

title_en: Russian Revolution ends restriction on Jewish presses
summary_en: The condition where only two Hebrew printing houses operated in all of Russia, imposed in 5597, continued until the 1917 Russian Revolution.
story_body: The Rebbe Rayatz noted that the Tzarist limitation of only two Jewish presses in Russia — in Vilna and Zhitomir — persisted from the 5597 decree until the 1917 revolution. This 80-year bottleneck was a major reason chasidic publishing remained sparse through the eras of the Maharash and Rashab. After the revolution Hebrew publishing in Russia briefly opened up before new Soviet restrictions emerged.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz dates Tzemach Tzedek manuscript
summary_en: In Teves 5670 the Rebbe Rashab wrote a letter reconsidering the authorship of a small manuscript whose cover bore the inscription 'Adkaru lei yoma d'tilga,' concluding it was likely the Tzemach Tzedek's handwriting rather than the Mitteler Rebbe's.
story_body: In Kuntres Etz HaChaim the Rashab had cited the inscription with uncertainty about which Rebbe had written it. In his Teves 5670 letter he reconsidered and concluded it was more likely the Tzemach Tzedek's hand. The manuscript was later catalogued as item 29 in the Rayatz's collection but was lost during World War II along with many other bichlach.

title_en: Mailufim volume of Tzemach Tzedek edited by the Rebbe
summary_en: In 5706 the Rebbe (then Ramash) edited, at the direction of his father-in-law the Rayatz, a Milu'im volume of Tzemach Tzedek responsa including the previously censored Choshen Mishpat material.
story_body: Eighty years after the Tzemach Tzedek's passing, the previously blocked Choshen Mishpat responsa finally appeared in print. The Milu'im volume edited by the future Rebbe included Choshen Mishpat teshuvos, supplements across all four chelkei Shulchan Aruch, additions to the chiddushim on Shas, and further omissions discovered during typesetting.

title_en: New edition of Piskei Dinim with supplements
