summary_en: A new edition of the Tzemach Tzedek's Piskei Dinim was printed in 5732, with newly discovered piskei dinim and responsa from manuscripts added at the end.
story_body: By the 1970s additional Tzemach Tzedek material continued to surface from manuscript collections. The 5732 edition of Piskei Dinim incorporated these additions, continuing the century-long pattern of supplements, omissions, and milu'im that complicated finding any given responsum in the corpus.

title_en: Shaar HaMilu'im IV of Tzemach Tzedek printed
summary_en: In 5738 the fourth Shaar HaMilu'im volume was printed, gathering responsa, chiddushim, and piskei dinim that had been discovered in the years since the previous milu'im publication.
story_body: By 5738 a further wave of newly surfaced material had accumulated, warranting another supplementary volume. From 5738 onward additional finds were published primarily in the Yagdil Torah journal printed in New York between 5737 and 5746, which became a major venue for ongoing Tzemach Tzedek scholarship.

title_en: Rebbe directs reprinting Chabad works in square script
summary_en: At a Shabbos Kedoshim / Rosh Chodesh Iyar 5749 farbrengen, the Rebbe directed that all older Chabad publications previously typeset in Rashi script be reprinted in newly set square (meruba) letters for easier study.
story_body: Older Chabad works had long been reproduced via photo-offset of original printings in small Rashi script, hindering study. At the Rosh Chodesh Iyar 5749 farbrengen the Rebbe instructed that these works be reset in square letters. This launched the project to prepare a new edition of the entire Tzemach Tzedek series, integrating all the supplements, omissions, and milu'im accumulated over the previous century.

title_en: Complete new edition of Tzemach Tzedek published
summary_en: In 5754 a complete and reset edition of the Tzemach Tzedek series was published, integrating all supplements, omissions, and milu'im in newly typeset square letters.
story_body: Five years after the Rebbe's 5749 directive, the new comprehensive edition of the Tzemach Tzedek appeared. It consolidated 110 years of supplements, omissions, additions, and milu'im (including Choshen Mishpat) into a unified typeset series, finally resolving the longstanding difficulty of locating a given responsum scattered across multiple appendices.

title_en: Shaar HaMilu'im V from Moscow archives printed
summary_en: In 5769 photographs of seven additional bichlach arrived from the Moscow archives, and Shaar HaMilu'im volume V was compiled from them and printed.
story_body: Decades after the original supplements series began, photocopies of seven more manuscript volumes from Russian state archives reached the Chabad library. The material was edited into Shaar HaMilu'im V and published in 5769. A list of seven additional volumes still held in Russian archives was printed at the back of this volume.

title_en: Alter Rebbe's second arrest as collection catalyst
summary_en: Beginning in 5561 — the year of the Alter Rebbe's second arrest and journey to Petersburg — the future Tzemach Tzedek began systematically collecting and transcribing the Alter Rebbe's discourses.
story_body: The Rebbe Rayatz recorded that when the Alter Rebbe was taken to Petersburg in 5561, the future Tzemach Tzedek began assembling transcripts of his grandfather's teachings. By the time the Alter Rebbe returned in the summer of that year, the Tzemach Tzedek had over 1,100 bogen of transcripts. By the Alter Rebbe's passing in 5573, the collection exceeded 10,000 bogen — over a hundred large volumes — forming the foundation of the Chabad manuscript library.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's homes rebuilt after fire
summary_en: During 5619 (1858–1859) the Tzemach Tzedek's homes in Lyubavichi were rebuilt after the fire that had destroyed them.
story_body: Following the fire that consumed the Tzemach Tzedek's home in Lyubavichi (which also destroyed many of his responsa written between 1848–1856), he had moved temporarily into the local landowner's courtyard. During the year 5619 the buildings for him and his sons were reconstructed. The family then prepared to return to their newly built homes at the start of the following Hebrew year.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek moves into rebuilt home in Lyubavichi
summary_en: At the start of the Hebrew year 5620 (autumn 1859), the Tzemach Tzedek moved back into his newly rebuilt home in Lyubavichi.
story_body: After spending time in the courtyard of the town's landowner following the fire, the Tzemach Tzedek and his sons returned to live in their newly rebuilt buildings in Lyubavichi at the beginning of 5620. Shortly afterwards, in Kislev of that same year, he became seriously ill. The episode is recorded in Beis Rebbi, part 3, chapter 6.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek falls seriously ill in Lyubavichi
summary_en: In Kislev 5620 (late 1859) the Tzemach Tzedek became gravely ill shortly after returning to his newly rebuilt home.
story_body: Only weeks after moving back into the rebuilt buildings in Lyubavichi at the start of 5620, the Tzemach Tzedek fell seriously ill in the month of Kislev. The illness is noted as a major episode in his later years, recorded in the family chronicle Beis Rebbi (part 3, chapter 6).

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek travels to Rogachev, Zhuravichi and Dribin
summary_en: In the winter of 5590 (1829–1830) the Tzemach Tzedek traveled to the towns of Rogachev, Zhuravichi and Dribin to deliver Chassidic discourses.
story_body: Although the Tzemach Tzedek generally remained in Lyubavichi writing Chassidus, he periodically traveled to outlying towns to deliver maamarim publicly and to receive Chassidim in yechidus. This particular winter tour is reconstructed from headings on his maamarim, which routinely recorded the date and place of delivery. The journey is among the earliest documented in the registry of his discourses.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek travels to Bobruisk, Paritch and Rogachev
summary_en: In the winter of 5591 (1830–1831) the Tzemach Tzedek visited the towns of Bobruisk, Paritch and Rogachev.
story_body: Reconstructed from the headings of his Chassidic discourses, this winter tour brought the Tzemach Tzedek to important Chassidic centers in White Russia. Such trips combined public maamarim, private yechidus, and the strengthening of local Chassidic communities. The journey is documented in the chronological registry of his maamarim.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek travels to Ula, Polotsk, Ushatch and Chashniki
summary_en: In the winter of 5592 (1831–1832) the Tzemach Tzedek made a circuit through Ula, Polotsk, Ushatch and Chashniki.
story_body: This northern circuit of the Tzemach Tzedek is recorded in the maamarim he delivered along the way, which were dated and inscribed with their location of delivery. The trip extended his presence into Vitebsk-region towns and helped consolidate Chabad influence in the area. The journey appears in the chronological registry of his discourses.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek travels to Shklov and Tzarei
summary_en: In the winter of 5593 (1832–1833) the Tzemach Tzedek visited Shklov and Tzarei.
story_body: Shklov was historically a stronghold of the Misnagdic camp, making the Rebbe's visit there significant for Chabad–Misnagdic relations. The trip is documented through the dated headings of maamarim he delivered in those towns. It forms part of the chronological registry of his discourses reconstructed from manuscript sources.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek tours Borisov, Minsk, Korenitz, Vilna and Polotsk
summary_en: In the summer of 5595 (1835) the Tzemach Tzedek made an extensive tour reaching as far as Vilna.
story_body: This summer journey was unusually broad, taking the Tzemach Tzedek into Lithuania proper, including Minsk, Vilna, and Polotsk. According to the report of Captain Yurkovsky six years later, during this stay in Minsk the Rebbe delivered public sermons and explained passages from Kabbalah and the Talmud. The trip is reconstructed from the headings of his maamarim.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek tours Ukraine; visits graves of Alter Rebbe and Mitteler Rebbe
summary_en: In the summer of 5596 (1836) the Tzemach Tzedek made a far-reaching tour through Ukraine, visiting the graves of his grandfather and father-in-law and attending his son's wedding.
story_body: This extensive summer journey took the Tzemach Tzedek through Bayov, Shklov, Zhlobin, Bobruisk, Hlusk, Paritch, Chernigov, Nezhin (to prostrate at the grave of his father-in-law the Mitteler Rebbe), Priluk, Kremenchug, Chernobyl, Brahin, Haditch (to prostrate at the grave of his grandfather the Alter Rebbe), Panitch, and Hornostaypil (for the wedding of his son R. Yosef Yitzchak). The trip is documented through the dated headings of maamarim he delivered in each town. It is one of the most extensive recorded journeys of his nesi'us.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek travels to Bayov, Rogachev, Dubrovna and Smiljan
summary_en: In the summer of 5597 (1837) the Tzemach Tzedek traveled to Bayov for a wedding, then on to Rogachev, Dubrovna and Smiljan.
story_body: This summer journey began with a wedding in Bayov, continued through Rogachev to Dubrovna and Smiljan, and ended with a return to Dubrovna. The route is reconstructed from the dated headings of maamarim that the Rebbe delivered along the way. It exemplifies how the registry of his discourses preserves not only Torah content but also family events and biographical detail.

title_en: Rayatz prepares chronological registry of Rashab's discourses
summary_en: In 5681 (1921) the Rebbe Rayatz prepared a chronological registry of his father the Rashab's discourses from his nesi'us years 1883–1920.
story_body: This was the first systematic chronological list of the maamarim of a Rebbe organized by year of delivery. The Rayatz prepared it together with a general overview of the discourses of the Rashab's forty-year nesi'us. The methodology established here became the model for later registries of other Rebbeim's maamarim.

title_en: Publication of Sefer HaToldot Admur Maharash with maamar registry
summary_en: In 5707 (1947) the Rebbe Rayatz published Sefer HaToldot Admur Maharash, which included his chronological registry of the Maharash's discourses.
story_body: The Rebbe Rayatz expanded the registry methodology he had developed earlier for his father's maamarim, applying it to the maamarim of his grandfather, the Rebbe Maharash. The work was printed as a booklet in 1947 as part of Sefer HaToldot Admur Maharash. It would later be supplemented in 1981 with more than two hundred additional maamarim discovered in manuscript.

title_en: Rebbe publishes index of Rayatz's maamarim and sichos
summary_en: In 5728 (1968) the Rebbe edited and published a chronological index of the maamarim and discourses of his father-in-law the Rayatz.
story_body: Titled 'Maftech Sifrei Maamarei v'Drushei Admur Mohorayatz,' the booklet built on the registry tradition of organizing maamarim by year of delivery. The Rebbe personally edited the material and gave it to print. The work serves as an essential research tool for tracing the Rayatz's Chassidic discourses across his nesi'us.

title_en: Shaglov publishes index of the Rebbe's maamarim, sichos and letters
summary_en: In 5740 (1980) R. Yosef Yitzchak Shaglov prepared and printed an index of the Rebbe's maamarim, sichos and letters.
story_body: The volume, titled 'Maftech Maamarim Sichos uMichtavim,' continued the line of chronological registries begun by the Rayatz for earlier Rebbeim. By the early 1980s registries had been compiled for all the Rebbeim except the Tzemach Tzedek, whose maamarim posed special chronological difficulties because most were preserved undated in volumes organized by Tanach and Chazal rather than by year.

title_en: Publication of Rashimat Maamarei DACh of Maharash and Rashab
summary_en: In Iyar 5741 (May 1981) the Rashimat Maamarei DACh of the Maharash and Rashab was published, incorporating over two hundred newly identified maamarim.
story_body: R. Naftali Greenberg compiled supplements to the existing registries based on manuscripts in the Rebbe's library, identifying more than two hundred Maharash maamarim missing from the 1947 list. The Rebbe directed that all material be published quickly together with his own subsequent annotations. The volume was edited together with R. David Moshe Olidort and appeared in Iyar 5741.

title_en: Keller completes registry of Alter Rebbe's maamarim
summary_en: In 5752 (1992) R. Yosef Yitzchak Keller completed the chronological registry of the Alter Rebbe's discourses, published in Kerem Chabad.
story_body: Building on a 1981 preliminary list appended to Maamarei Admur HaZaken — HaKetzarim, R. Yosef Yitzchak Keller completed a comprehensive registry of the Alter Rebbe's maamarim, organized by year of delivery up through the Liadi period. The completed registry was published in the journal Kerem Chabad. The success of this project led directly into preparing a parallel registry for the Tzemach Tzedek.

title_en: Publication of Rashimat Maamarei DACh of the Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: In 5754 (1994) the Rashimat Maamarei DACh of the Tzemach Tzedek was published, organizing his maamarim chronologically for the first time.
story_body: The work was based on a card catalog compiled beginning in 5741 (1981) by R. Avraham Boruch Yunik, drawing on dated discourse headings in Or HaTorah, R. Hillel of Paritch's hanachos, the Maharash's hanachos, and the Tzemach Tzedek's own manuscript volumes. R. Yosef Yitzchak Keller completed and prepared the work after finishing the Alter Rebbe registry. It overcame the unique difficulty that the Tzemach Tzedek's maamarim were preserved by topic rather than by year.

title_en: Alexander I signs first comprehensive Jewish charter of Russia
summary_en: On 9 December 1804 (20 Kislev 5565) Tsar Alexander I signed the first detailed 'Jewish charter' regulating the status of Jews in Russia.
story_body: Following the partitions of Poland in 1772 that brought large Jewish populations under Russian rule, no comprehensive legal status had been established for them. The first detailed charter was prepared during 5564 (1804) and signed by Alexander I on 9 December that year. It would later be replaced by Nicholas I's expanded charter of 1835.

title_en: Nicholas I signs expanded Jewish charter
summary_en: On 13 April 1835 (26 Nissan 5595) Tsar Nicholas I signed an expanded 'Jewish charter' replacing the 1804 law.
story_body: Nicholas I's reign brought a stream of new decrees affecting Russian Jewry. A more elaborate Jewish charter was prepared during 5595 and signed on 13 April 1835. The text was printed in Hebrew that same year as 'Chok al Odot Yehudim' in Vilna and Grodno.

title_en: Nicholas I orders special ministerial committee on Jewish affairs
summary_en: At the end of 1840 (start of 5601) Tsar Nicholas I ordered the establishment of a special ministerial committee to fundamentally 'reform' Jewish life.
story_body: The committee included Minister of Interior Stroganov, Minister of Education Uvarov, Minister of Finance Vrontchenko, and Bludov of the legislative ministry, chaired by Count Kiselev; the head of the Third Section, General Dubelt, was later added. Uvarov took on the mission of 'enlightening' the Jews and allied with the Maskilim to compel the opening of state-style Jewish schools. He appointed Dr. Max Lilienthal of Riga as his intermediary with the Jewish population.

title_en: Maskilic denunciation of Tzemach Tzedek published in German-Jewish press
summary_en: On 5 February 1841 (26 Shevat 5601) an article in 'Israelitische Annalen' denounced the Tzemach Tzedek as the chief opponent of government educational reform.
story_body: The article, published in the German-Jewish weekly Israelitische Annalen issue 6, was sent from Vilna by Maskilim and named 'Mendel of Lyubavichi' as the leader of the Chassidim of Vitebsk and Mogilev. It claimed the Chabad movement was working to obstruct the government's educational plans and called for excluding Chassidim from communal leadership. The article was then submitted by Maskilim to Minister of Education Uvarov to provoke official action.

title_en: Uvarov requests intelligence on the Tzemach Tzedek from Stroganov
summary_en: On 28 March 1841 (18 Nissan 5601) Minister of Education Uvarov wrote to Interior Minister Stroganov requesting information on 'Mendel of Lyubavichi.'
story_body: Acting on the German-Jewish article and Maskilic agitation, Uvarov asked Stroganov whether the Ministry of Interior held any information on Mendel of Lyubavichi, his personality and the extent of his influence over the Jews and especially the Chassidim. This launched a year-long secret investigation involving the Third Section, the governor-general of Vitebsk-Mogilev, and gendarmerie officers across three provinces. The correspondence became the documentary backbone for the build-up to the 1843 Rabbinical Conference.

title_en: Uvarov requests Third Section investigation of Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: On 30 March 1841 (20 Nissan 5601) Uvarov wrote a confidential letter to Count Benckendorff, head of the Third Section, requesting an investigation of the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: Two days after his letter to Stroganov, Uvarov turned to the head of the secret police with the same request. He cited the Israelitische Annalen article and its respected editor Dr. Jost as warranting confidence in the report. Uvarov asked Benckendorff to collect detailed information on the Tzemach Tzedek's character, conduct, opinions, contacts and influence over the Jews, formally initiating the Third Section's investigation.

title_en: Stroganov confirms Tzemach Tzedek's great influence among Jews
summary_en: On 7 April 1841 (28 Nissan 5601) Minister of Interior Stroganov replied to Uvarov confirming the Tzemach Tzedek's strong influence over Jews in White Russia and Lithuania.
story_body: Stroganov reported he had no specific file on 'the Lyubavichi rabbi' but acknowledged that 'the Jewish rabbi Mendel of Lyubavichi who dwells in White Russia and belongs to the Chassidim sect, is truly respected by the Jews and has great influence on them, especially on the inhabitants of White Russia and Lithuania.' The confirmation gave official weight to the Maskilim's claims and intensified the case for direct surveillance.

title_en: Benckendorff orders provincial investigations of Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: On 5 April 1841 (26 Nissan 5601) Count Benckendorff ordered Governor-General Dyakov and gendarmerie commander Freigang to gather covert intelligence on the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: Acting on Uvarov's 30 March request, Benckendorff dispatched orders to Governor-General Dyakov of Vitebsk-Mogilev and to General Freigang, commander of the Fourth District of the gendarmerie. They were instructed to discreetly investigate the character, conduct, opinions, contacts and influence of the Jew Mendel of Lyubavichi. The order set in motion the parallel investigations that would shape the Third Section's eventual report.

title_en: Freigang orders gendarmerie officers to investigate Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: On 12 April 1841 (3 Iyar 5601) General Freigang instructed gendarmerie officers in Mogilev, Vitebsk and Minsk to investigate the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: Following Benckendorff's directive, Freigang relayed orders to Colonels Kutsinsky and Wojciech and Captain Yurkovsky. Wojciech of Mogilev would personally travel to Lyubavichi to interview the Rebbe under cover of investigating the local synagogue. The coordinated three-province inquiry generated the most detailed contemporary external descriptions of the Tzemach Tzedek's personality, household and influence.

title_en: Colonel Wojciech reports on his investigation of the Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: On 29 May 1841 (21 Sivan 5601) Colonel Wojciech submitted his report on his visit to the Tzemach Tzedek in Lyubavichi.
story_body: Earlier, during the February fair in Lyubavichi, Wojciech had entered the Rebbe's home on the pretext of inquiring about the synagogue, finding him studying from a book and conversing in halting Russian. He described the Tzemach Tzedek as over fifty, physically weak, living in poverty with six sons and two daughters, registered as a third-guild merchant but leaving trade to his family. Wojciech concluded the Rebbe was a 'simple man with limited intellect,' morally above reproach, who declined the title of rabbi inherited from his ancestors and wished only to live quietly with his books.

title_en: Dyakov reports to Benckendorff on Tzemach Tzedek's character and influence
summary_en: On 9 June 1841 (2 Tammuz 5601) Governor-General Dyakov reported to Benckendorff on the Tzemach Tzedek's residence, conduct and standing among the Jews.
story_body: Dyakov identified the man in question as Mendel Schneersohn, registered as a third-guild merchant in Babinovichi but residing permanently in Lyubavichi since 1813. He described the Rebbe as approximately fifty years old, of weak health and rarely leaving his home, possessing good character and conduct with no opinions contrary to the laws. Dyakov noted that Jews — Chassidim and even Misnagdim — turned to him from many places to resolve religious questions, and that he was honored as a descendant of great rabbis, including his grandfather of Liadi who 'was known in Petersburg due to some matter.'

title_en: Freigang submits combined gendarmerie report on Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: On 12 June 1841 (5 Tammuz 5601) General Freigang submitted a consolidated report from three provinces on the Tzemach Tzedek to Count Benckendorff.
story_body: Freigang summarized the parallel reports of Colonel Kutsinsky from Vitebsk, Colonel Wojciech from Mogilev and Captain Yurkovsky from Minsk. The reports broadly agreed that the Tzemach Tzedek lived simply and modestly, was regarded by his followers as a great scholar and held strong influence over them, while showing no signs of disloyalty. Yurkovsky's Minsk report uniquely recounted the Rebbe's 1835 visit to Minsk and noted that 'Zalman, the grandfather of Mendel of Lyubavichi' had been summoned to Petersburg around 1802 on suspicion of belonging to a harmful sect but was cleared and returned home shortly afterwards.

title_en: Benckendorff reports findings on Tzemach Tzedek to Uvarov
summary_en: On 18 June 1841 (11 Tammuz 5601) Count Benckendorff reported the consolidated investigation findings on the Tzemach Tzedek to Minister of Education Uvarov.
story_body: Having received the field reports through Dyakov and Freigang, Benckendorff forwarded the intelligence to Uvarov and requested a decision on next steps. The Third Section had now built a documentary file on the Tzemach Tzedek's character, family, conduct, and influence over the Jews of Vitebsk, Mogilev and Minsk. This concluded the surveillance phase and set the stage for the next move — pressuring the Rebbe to participate in the Rabbinical Conference.

title_en: Rabbinical Conference convenes in Petersburg
summary_en: From 18 Iyar to Elul 5603 (May–September 1843) the Rabbinical Conference summoned by the Russian government was held in Petersburg, with the Tzemach Tzedek in attendance.
story_body: After the Third Section's 1841 investigation and Dr. Max Lilienthal's personal visit to Lyubavichi, the government insisted on the Tzemach Tzedek's attendance to neutralize his anticipated opposition to its educational reforms. The Rebbe brought along one of his sons and a Chassid, and packed some thirty seforim with paper to record chiddushim during his stay. The conference's deliberations were kept secret — Beis Rebbi records that the Tzemach Tzedek refused to disclose what transpired, saying he 'had not been given permission to reveal' them.

title_en: Benckendorff reports on Mendel Schneersohn to Education Minister Uvarov
summary_en: Third Section head Benckendorff sent the Education Minister a report on Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn of Lubavitch, suspected of opposing government plans for the Jews.
story_body: On 25 June 1841 (18 Tammuz 5601), Count Benckendorff, head of the Third Section (secret police), forwarded a gendarmerie report on the Tzemach Tzedek to Education Minister Uvarov. The report described Schneersohn as the head of the Chassidic sect in Vitebsk and Mogilev, allegedly opposing the government's plans for Jewish education. Benckendorff requested the document be returned when no longer needed.

title_en: Uvarov orders covert surveillance of the Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: Education Minister Uvarov directed that secret surveillance be placed on Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch despite finding no unlawful conduct.
story_body: On 7 July 1841 (Rosh Chodesh Av 5601), Count Uvarov replied to Benckendorff that although Schneersohn had not committed unlawful acts and seemed harmless, secret surveillance should still be imposed on him. This was especially needed while the government implemented its new Jewish education plans. The two papers about Mendel were returned with the directive.

title_en: Third Section orders Mogilev gendarmes to spy on the Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: The Third Section ordered Colonel Voytsekh of the Mogilev gendarmerie to conduct covert surveillance of Rabbi Mendel Schneersohn of Lubavitch.
story_body: On 21 July 1841 (15 Av 5601), the head of the Third Section formally instructed Colonel Voytsekh of the gendarmerie in Mogilev province to secretly monitor Mendel Schneersohn's conduct and views. The order cited suspicions that he and his followers opposed the government's plans for the Jews. This launched what would become a six-year covert surveillance operation.

title_en: Lilienthal urges harsh suppression of Chassidic opposition
summary_en: Dr. Max Lilienthal wrote to the Education Ministry urging the government to suppress Chassidic opposition to Jewish education reforms.
story_body: On 11 March 1841 (Rosh Chodesh Nissan 5601), shortly after being appointed to oversee Jewish education, Dr. Max Lilienthal wrote to official Dukst-Dushinsky in the Education Ministry. He reported that his negotiations with the Chassidim of Minsk and Vitebsk revealed they would mount strong and consistent opposition. He urged the government to intervene and crush them in the harshest manner possible.

title_en: Lilienthal requests permission to write the Tzemach Tzedek officially
summary_en: Lilienthal requested official permission to write a formal letter to the Tzemach Tzedek concerning Jewish education reforms.
story_body: On 17 March 1841 (7 Nissan 5601), six days after his initial letter, Lilienthal again wrote to the Education Ministry. He asked for permission to address Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch in a formal capacity to learn his position on the proposed reforms. The official Dukst-Dushinsky replied that Lilienthal could write only as a private individual, not officially.

title_en: Lilienthal visits the Tzemach Tzedek in Lubavitch
summary_en: Dr. Max Lilienthal traveled to Lubavitch to meet personally with the Tzemach Tzedek about joining the planned Petersburg rabbinic commission.
story_body: In 5602, Lilienthal reported to the Education Ministry that he had sent a warm letter to the Rebbe and then traveled to Lubavitch to meet him. He described the Rebbe as about forty-five years old, not tall, and of utterly simple bearing. Lilienthal proposed that the Tzemach Tzedek join the planned rabbinic commission in Petersburg, but the Rebbe initially refused, citing his fragile health since the search and interrogation he had endured.

title_en: Chaim Ginzburg lobbies for the Tzemach Tzedek to attend Petersburg commission
summary_en: Chassidic activist Chaim Ginzburg wrote to Lilienthal that all Chassidim wanted the Tzemach Tzedek as their representative at the Petersburg commission.
story_body: On 10 February 1843 (22 Adar I 5603), the activist R. Chaim Ginzburg wrote to Dr. Lilienthal that the entire Chassidic community wanted the Tzemach Tzedek to travel to Petersburg as their representative. Although the Chassidim had initially selected R. Yitzchak Aizik of Orsha as their delegate, opinion shifted toward the Rebbe himself. The letter helped shape the government's eventual invitation.

title_en: Lilienthal officially invites the Tzemach Tzedek to the Petersburg commission
summary_en: Dr. Lilienthal formally notified the Tzemach Tzedek that he was invited to the rabbinic commission in Petersburg.
story_body: On 19 February 1843 (Rosh Chodesh Adar II 5603), Dr. Lilienthal formally notified Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch of his invitation to the Petersburg commission on Jewish education. Three days later Lilienthal wrote to the Education Ministry recommending the Tzemach Tzedek as the most important rabbi among the Russian Jews. He argued that the Rebbe's agreement with government policy would carry binding weight for the Chassidim of Vitebsk, Mogilev, Chernigov, Kiev, Kherson, and Minsk.

title_en: Uvarov instructs Governor-General to summon the Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: Education Minister Uvarov instructed Governor-General Diakov to invite Mendel Schneersohn to the Petersburg rabbinic commission.
story_body: On 14 March 1843 (24 Adar II 5603), Count Uvarov wrote to Pyotr Diakov, Governor-General of Vitebsk, Smolensk, and Mogilev provinces. He advised that one of the Chassidic rabbis must be included on the commission, given the Chassidim's prominence in Belorussia and Lithuania. He requested Diakov to notify Mendel Schneersohn to travel to Petersburg, calling him a man of moral merit and sound mind.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek requests travel permits for his assistants to Petersburg
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek petitioned Governor Diakov to allow him to bring R. Shmaria Paytelson and his son R. Yehuda Leib as assistants to Petersburg.
story_body: On 17 April 1843 (29 Nissan 5603), the Tzemach Tzedek wrote to Governor Diakov from Vitebsk. He requested that his travel pass be expanded to include Shmaria son of Mordechai Paytelson, needed to translate since he spoke only Yiddish, and his son Leib Schneersohn, needed to assist due to his weak health. He attached the passports and asked to be permitted to arrive in time for the commission's opening.

title_en: Petersburg rabbinic commission convenes
summary_en: The Petersburg rabbinic commission on Jewish education opened, with the Tzemach Tzedek among its members.
story_body: On 6 May 1843 (18 Iyar 5603), the rabbinic commission convened in Petersburg. The Tzemach Tzedek traveled there with R. Shmaria Paytelson as his translator and his son R. Yehuda Leib for medical assistance. The commission continued through August 1843 (Elul 5603), discussing Jewish educational reforms in great secrecy; the Rebbe later said the details could not be revealed.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek receives Honorary Citizen status from Tsar Nicholas I
summary_en: Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch received the certificate of Honorary Citizen, signed by Tsar Nicholas I.
story_body: In 5602 (1842), the Tzemach Tzedek received the title of Honorary Citizen by certificate signed by the Tsar. This title was a recognition of social standing under Russian estate law. It would later play a role in the lifting of his secret surveillance and in his recognition by the regime.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek receives Hereditary Honorary Citizen status
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek received the certificate of Hereditary Honorary Citizen for himself and his descendants.
story_body: In 5605 (1845), the Tzemach Tzedek received the elevated status of Hereditary Honorary Citizen. Per the Hayom Yom and other sources, this enhanced his standing in Russian society. The title was tied to his subsequent acquisition of an estate in his name.

title_en: Count Orlov writes to Governor Golitsyn about lifting Tzemach Tzedek surveillance
summary_en: Count Orlov, new head of the Third Section, wrote to Governor Golitsyn proposing to lift covert surveillance of the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: On 20 January 1847 (15 Shvat 5607), Count Orlov, who had succeeded Benckendorff as head of the Third Section, wrote to Prince A.M. Golitsyn, Governor-General of Vitebsk, Mogilev, and Smolensk. He noted that Schneersohn lived quietly, was uninvolved in conflicts, and had received the title of Honorary Citizen. Orlov asked Golitsyn for his opinion on whether the surveillance imposed in 1841 could now be lifted.

title_en: Governor Golitsyn endorses lifting Tzemach Tzedek's surveillance
summary_en: Governor-General Golitsyn replied to Orlov endorsing the removal of covert surveillance from the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: On 7 March 1847 (2 Nissan 5607), Prince Golitsyn replied from Vitebsk to Count Orlov. He reported that State Councillor Gamalin had confirmed Schneersohn's title as Honorary Citizen and that the six-year gendarmerie surveillance found his conduct exemplary. Golitsyn formally endorsed lifting the secret watch that had begun in 1841.

title_en: Orlov asks Uvarov to consent to lifting Tzemach Tzedek surveillance
summary_en: Count Orlov wrote to Education Minister Uvarov seeking his approval to halt the Tzemach Tzedek's covert surveillance.
story_body: On 14 March 1847 (9 Nissan 5607), Count Orlov wrote to Count Sergey Uvarov, the Education Minister. He summarized Golitsyn's report and asked Uvarov, whose 1841 letter had triggered the surveillance, to formally consent to its removal. He noted that the local government's report seemed sufficient grounds to end the watch.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's covert surveillance is officially lifted
summary_en: Education Minister Uvarov consented to the formal termination of the secret surveillance on the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: On 19 March 1847 (14 Nissan 5607), the Education Ministry issued document number 2643. Count Uvarov informed Count Orlov that he fully agreed to terminate the gendarmerie's covert surveillance on Honorary Citizen Rabbi Mendel Schneersohn. The six-year covert watch that had begun on 21 July 1841 was thus officially closed.

title_en: Mendelstam visits the Tzemach Tzedek to push new curriculum
summary_en: Maskil Arye Leib Mendelstam came to Lubavitch to urge the Tzemach Tzedek to approve new cheder textbooks.
story_body: In the winter of 5608 (1848), Arye Leib Mendelstam, who had replaced Lilienthal at the Education Ministry, arrived in Lubavitch. He sought the Rebbe's approval for newly edited anthology textbooks meant for use in chadarim. The Tzemach Tzedek explained at length why these compilations should not be introduced into traditional Jewish elementary schools.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek refuses to travel to Minsk to meet Mendelstam
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek wrote on 13 Adar I that he could not travel to Minsk and would not retreat from positions agreed at the 1843 commission.
story_body: On 13 Adar I 5608, the Tzemach Tzedek replied to Mendelstam's invitation to come to Minsk for further talks. He wrote that he could not travel under any circumstance and that nothing in the curriculum agreed at the 1843 commission should be diminished. He reiterated that the structure they had set for Torah study was an absolute necessity for the children.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek again rejects Mendelstam's educational program
summary_en: On 24 Nissan the Tzemach Tzedek wrote again to Mendelstam, firmly maintaining his earlier rejection of the new curriculum.
story_body: On 24 Nissan 5608, the Tzemach Tzedek replied to Mendelstam's letter of Rosh Chodesh Nissan, received on 9 Nissan. He explained that after a month of deliberation, his view remained the same as what he had already conveyed on 13 Adar I and at the original commission. He pressed Mendelstam to accept his answer, written, he said, in truth and love.

title_en: Government publishes Rambam excerpts under guise of Rebbe's approval
summary_en: The Petersburg government published abridged Rambam halacha booklets for chadarim, framed as if with the Tzemach Tzedek's approval.
story_body: In 5610 (1850), the Russian government in Petersburg printed condensed study booklets, 'Some Laws from the Yad Hachazaka of the Rambam,' for use in chadarim. The title page falsely implied the Rebbe's approval by referencing his responsa. This contradicted the Tzemach Tzedek's clear opposition to teaching such anthologies, which he considered useless to the children.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek acquires the Sederin estate as Hereditary Citizen
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek formally acquired the Sederin estate, securing Hereditary Honorary Citizen status for himself and his descendants.
story_body: In 5612 (1852), Bet Rebbi records that the Tzemach Tzedek secured from the government the inherited citizenship title (Potomstvennoe) for himself and his descendants. As part of this status he purchased the Sederin estate in the Bobruisk area of Minsk province, registered in his name. Reports linked the elevation to his role in encouraging Jewish agricultural settlement.

title_en: Rashab sends Tzemach Tzedek's citizenship certificates to attorney Gruzenberg
summary_en: Rabbi Sholom Dovber of Lubavitch sent the Tzemach Tzedek's Russian citizenship documents to defense attorney Oscar Gruzenberg during the Beilis trial.
story_body: On 3-4 Marcheshvan 5674 (late October/early November 1913), the Rashab wrote to Oscar Gruzenberg, lead defense counsel in the Mendel Beilis blood libel trial. Having read in the newspapers Gruzenberg's reference to the Tzemach Tzedek, he sent him the Hereditary Honorary Citizen certificate issued by Tsar Nicholas I, along with the earlier Honorary Citizen certificate. The Rashab believed these documents would help demonstrate the integrity of Russian Jewish leadership in the Tsar's eyes.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek visits Vilna and delivers Chassidic discourses
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek visited Vilna, where he delivered Chassidic discourses and received people in yechidus.
story_body: In the summer of 5595 (1835), the Tzemach Tzedek visited Vilna. The visit was documented by Shmuel Yosef Fuenn, a maskil of that generation, who described the Rebbe delivering a Chassidic discourse with eyes closed and an expression of awe. Fuenn recorded that the Rebbe did not raise his hand, modulate his voice, or pause, as if a holy spirit spoke from his throat.

title_en: Birth of Rebbe Maharash in Lubavitch
summary_en: Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn, the fourth Chabad Rebbe (Maharash), was born in Lubavitch on 2 Iyar 5594.
story_body: Rabbi Shmuel was the youngest son of the Tzemach Tzedek and would become the only Chabad Rebbe born, living his entire life, and passing away in Lubavitch. His birth on 2 Iyar 5594 (1834) coincides with the day Chasidim later mark as a special date connected to him. He would later succeed his father as the fourth Rebbe of the Chabad-Lubavitch dynasty.

title_en: Passing of the Tzemach Tzedek; Maharash assumes Chabad leadership
summary_en: On 13 Nissan 5626 the Tzemach Tzedek passed away in Lubavitch, and his son Rabbi Shmuel (Maharash) accepted leadership of the Chabad movement there.
story_body: After the Tzemach Tzedek's passing on 13 Nissan 5626 (1866), his younger son Rabbi Shmuel became the fourth Rebbe in Lubavitch. His brothers — also prominent rabbis — established branches of Chabad in towns such as Kopust, Liadi, Nizhin, and Ovruch. The succession defined the geographical structure of post-Tzemach-Tzedek Chabad in Tsarist Russia.

title_en: Maharash's first dated chassidic discourse manuscript
summary_en: The earliest dated chassidic discourse hanacha in Maharash's hand is from Parshat Beshalach, Motzaei Menucha, 5613.
story_body: Among the manuscripts inherited and produced by Maharash, the first dated hanacha (transcript) in his own handwriting is titled 'Beshalach, Motzaei Menucha, 5613.' These transcripts recorded discourses of his father, the Tzemach Tzedek, and would form a core part of the Chabad manuscript collection later catalogued by his descendants.

title_en: Young Maharash buys Hebrew books from a Lubavitch bookseller
summary_en: In Elul 5605, a bookseller visited Lubavitch and the young Rabbi Shmuel asked his father, the Tzemach Tzedek, for 30 rubles to buy books.
story_body: According to a memoir of the Rebbe Rayatz, during the Tzemach Tzedek's monthly tests of his son and other cheder students, prizes were monetary, which Rabbi Shmuel saved together with a weekly ruble to buy seforim. In Elul 5605 (1845) a bookseller came to Lubavitch and the young Maharash requested 30 rubles from money his father held for him; his father gave him the sum plus 10 rubles as a gift, allowing him to buy a substantial collection of books.

title_en: Second great fire destroys the Lubavitch courtyard
summary_en: In the summer of 5628 the entire Lubavitch courtyard and its houses burned down again, forcing reconstruction.
story_body: Two years after Maharash took up leadership, in summer 5628 (1868), the Chabad courtyard in Lubavitch suffered another major fire, destroying the houses and many of the Tzemach Tzedek's seforim and manuscripts. This created a legal-halachic dilemma because the Tzemach Tzedek's will had stipulated that none of his descendants live in his house — only Torah study or a beis midrash should occupy the site.

title_en: Maharash builds the Large Hall on the Tzemach Tzedek's house site
summary_en: In 5632 Maharash built the 30-by-30-cubit Ulam HaGadol on the site of his father's burnt house, designated for prayer during large gatherings.
story_body: After the 1868 fire, Maharash addressed his father's halachic will by erecting in 5632 (1872) a large hall (30 cubits square) on the site of the Tzemach Tzedek's former house. The hall served for Yamim Noraim prayers and major chassidic gatherings, where in later years the Rebbe Rayatz's bar mitzvah and his wedding to Rebbetzin Nechama Dina would also be held.

title_en: Wedding of Maharash's son Raza in the Small Hall
summary_en: At the start of winter 5634, the wedding of Maharash's son Rabbi Zalman Aharon (Raza) was held in the newly built Small Hall in Lubavitch.
story_body: Maharash had stipulated when building the Small Hall (Ulam HaKatan) on the site of the former beis midrash that he could use it for any purpose he wished. At the start of winter 5634 (1873), because the Large Hall was unheated, the wedding feast of his son Raza was held in the Small Hall with klezmer music, with Maharash citing that original stipulation.

title_en: Passing of Rabbi Baruch Shalom Schneersohn
summary_en: Rabbi Baruch Shalom, eldest son of the Tzemach Tzedek, passed away on 16 Shevat 5629 and was buried near his father's grave in Lubavitch.
story_body: Rabbi Baruch Shalom — 'safek bechor' (a doubtful firstborn) per a note by his brother Maharash — passed away on 16 Shevat 5629 (late January 1869), four years after his father the Tzemach Tzedek. He was interred about 4.5 cubits from his father's grave inside the ohel built in Lubavitch. The dating of his birth and death is used in halachic literature to discuss Ashkenazi customs regarding naming a child after a living relative.

title_en: Passing of Rebbe Maharash in Lubavitch
summary_en: Rabbi Shmuel of Lubavitch (Maharash) passed away on 13 Tishrei 5643 and was buried in the ohel he had built for his father, the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: Maharash died in Lubavitch on 13 Tishrei 5643 (late September 1882), having served continuously since 1866 despite chronic weakness in his final years. He was laid to rest in the ohel he had constructed years earlier for his father the Tzemach Tzedek. His yahrzeit remains observed as a major day in the Chabad calendar.

title_en: Bar Mitzvah of the Rebbe Rayatz in the Large Hall
summary_en: The bar mitzvah celebration of Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn (Rayatz) took place in the Large Hall of the Lubavitch courtyard in 5653.
story_body: According to Rayatz's own memoirs, the Large Hall built by his grandfather Maharash hosted his bar mitzvah celebration in 5653 (1893). The same hall had hosted the wedding of his aunt Chaya Mushka to Rabbi Moshe HaKohen Hornstein, and would also host his own wedding four years later.

title_en: Wedding of the Rebbe Rayatz to Rebbetzin Nechama Dina
summary_en: The wedding of Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn to Rebbetzin Nechama Dina was held in the Large Hall in Lubavitch in Elul 5657.
story_body: Rayatz married Rebbetzin Nechama Dina in Elul 5657 (August/September 1897) in the Large Hall of his grandfather Maharash's Lubavitch courtyard. This was the third major family simcha hosted in that hall, after Maharash's daughter Chaya Mushka's wedding and Rayatz's own bar mitzvah in 5653.

title_en: Rayatz letter recounting Maharash's construction of the Large Hall
summary_en: At the beginning of Kislev 5661 (November 1900), Rayatz wrote letter no. 4619 documenting Maharash's reasoning for building the Large Hall over the Tzemach Tzedek's home site.
story_body: In a letter dated to the beginning of Kislev 5661, the Rebbe Rayatz preserved family tradition about why Maharash, fearing the future neglect of his father's will, deliberately built the 30-by-30-cubit hall as a place of prayer and Torah on the site of the Tzemach Tzedek's home. This letter is among the primary sources for the early architectural history of the Lubavitch chatzer.

title_en: Passing of Rebbetzin Rivka, wife of Maharash
summary_en: Rebbetzin Rivka, wife of Rebbe Maharash, passed away on 10 Shevat 5674 and was interred beside her husband at the Lubavitch ohel.
story_body: Rebbetzin Rivka, daughter of Rabbi Aharon of Aleksandrov and wife of Maharash, died on 10 Shevat 5674 (1914) — a date later doubly significant in Chabad history. She was laid to rest near her husband Maharash adjacent to the Tzemach Tzedek's ohel in Lubavitch. A separate ohel in the cemetery housed graves of earlier rebbetzins of the Chabad dynasty.

title_en: Pidyon HaBen of Rabbi Baruch Shalom with the Alter Rebbe's discourse
summary_en: On Erev Chanukah 5566, a pidyon haben was performed for the infant Baruch Shalom, son of the Tzemach Tzedek, at which the Alter Rebbe delivered a chassidic discourse.
story_body: The Alter Rebbe delivered a chassidic discourse at the pidyon haben feast for his grandson Baruch Shalom on Erev Chanukah 5566 (December 1805). The discourse is preserved in Maamarei Admur HaZaken 5566. Because Baruch Shalom was a 'safek bechor' (doubtful firstborn), the pidyon was performed from doubt — a notable halachic detail in the family record.

title_en: Birth of Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson
summary_en: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson, father of the seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe, was born in 5638.
story_body: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson, son of Baruch Schneur Schneersohn and father of the Rebbe Menachem Mendel (the seventh Chabad Rebbe), was born in 5638 (1877/78). He descended from Rabbi Baruch Shalom, eldest son of the Tzemach Tzedek, through Baruch Schneur — a lineage Maharash's family tradition noted explicitly.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's wedding in Parshat Toldot
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek married Rebbetzin Chaya Mushka around Parshat Toldot 5564.
story_body: The wedding of the future Tzemach Tzedek to Rebbetzin Chaya Mushka took place during Parshat Toldot 5564 (Cheshvan, late 1803). This dating is used in the family chronicle to argue against an earlier proposed birth year of 5564 for their son Baruch Shalom, since a child born to them could only have arrived after the wedding.

title_en: Passing of R' Shalom Shachna, father of the Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: Rabbi Shalom Shachna, father of the Tzemach Tzedek, passed away in the summer of 5567.
story_body: Rabbi Shalom Shachna died in the summer of 5567 (1807), as established in the Igrot Kodesh of the Alter Rebbe. The dating became halachically relevant because the Tzemach Tzedek's son Baruch Shalom was born in 5566, before his namesake grandfather's death — a fact that complicates the Ashkenazi custom against naming a child for a living relative.

title_en: Passing of R' Baruch, father of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: R' Baruch, father of the Alter Rebbe of Chabad, passed away in 5552.
story_body: Rabbi Baruch, father of Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi (the Alter Rebbe), died in 5552 (1791/92). His name was carried by his great-grandson Baruch Shalom, eldest son of the Tzemach Tzedek, in line with the Ashkenazi practice of naming a child after a deceased relative.

title_en: Rayatz letter to Rabbi Eliyahu Chaim Althoyz on recording chasidic history
summary_en: On 17 Marcheshvan 5696 the Rebbe Rayatz wrote letter no. 810 to R' Eliyahu Chaim Althoyz urging him to record his memories of Lubavitch and Kremenchug.
story_body: On 17 Marcheshvan 5696 (November 1935), Rayatz pressed the chasid R' Eliyahu Chaim Althoyz to set aside time to write down what he had heard from his father and uncle about their time in Lubavitch and what he remembered from Kremenchug, particularly about the elder chasidim known as 'the bears.' The letter is part of Rayatz's larger campaign to recruit chasidim to preserve oral chasidic history.

title_en: Rayatz follow-up letter to Althoyz pressing for chasidic memoirs
summary_en: On 3 Shevat 5698 the Rebbe Rayatz wrote letter no. 975 again urging R' Eliyahu Chaim Althoyz to record short notes on the elder chasidim he had known.
story_body: Roughly two years after his first request, Rayatz wrote to Althoyz on 3 Shevat 5698 (February 1938) reiterating that he should write at least short notes — names, nicknames, appearances, and occupations — of the elder chasidim he had seen in childhood, youth, and adulthood, asking especially about 'the bears' (di berelech).

title_en: Rayatz letter mentioning Mohar'mtz Landau
summary_en: On 3 Sivan 5695 Rayatz wrote a letter addressed to a relative identified as Mohar'mtz Landau, descended from the Tzemach Tzedek's son Baruch Shalom.
story_body: In a letter of 3 Sivan 5695 (June 1935), Rayatz addressed an elder relative as 'sh'ber bsari' (my flesh-relation), with the surname Landau noted at the top. Chabad historian Rabbi Levin conjectures this is Moshe Tzvi Landau, son of Dan Landau (a son-in-law of Rabbi Baruch Shalom), illustrating how scattered branches of the Tzemach Tzedek's descendants were tracked through Rayatz's correspondence.

title_en: Rebbe's sicha of Parshat Miketz on naming customs
summary_en: On Parshat Miketz 5743 the Rebbe explained the differences between Sefardic and Ashkenazi customs regarding naming children after living relatives.
story_body: In a sicha delivered on Parshat Miketz 5743 (December 1982), printed in Hisvaaduyos vol. 43, the Rebbe Menachem Mendel addressed the differing customs between Sefardim and Ashkenazim regarding naming a child after a living grandparent. A follow-up question about whether this related to his own grandfather Baruch Schneur being named in his great-grandfather Baruch Shalom's lifetime was sent to him; he replied that he had not heard a tradition on the matter.

title_en: Rayatz visits Chasid R. Chaim Dover Vilensky in Lubavitch
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn saw the Chasid R. Chaim Dover Vilensky in Lubavitch during the summer of 5653.
story_body: The Rayatz later recalled having seen the noted Chasid R. Chaim Dover Vilensky of Kremenchug two or three times, the last being in Lubavitch in the summer of 5653 (1893). Decades later he sought to commemorate this Chasid by gathering material from Vilensky's son for the Hatamim journal.

title_en: Rayatz writes to R. Michael Vilensky to commemorate his father
summary_en: On 3 Tammuz 5699 the Rayatz wrote to R. Michael Vilensky asking him to compose a biography of his father for the Hatamim journal.
story_body: The Rayatz wrote to R. Michael Vilensky requesting that he prepare a memorial article about his father, the Chasid R. Chaim Dover of Kremenchug, for the ninth volume of Hatamim then being edited. World War broke out shortly afterward, the issue never appeared, and Vilensky's reply never reached its destination.

title_en: Rayatz arrives in the United States after escaping Europe
summary_en: At the end of winter 5700 the Rayatz was rescued from Nazi-occupied Europe and arrived in the United States.
story_body: After the outbreak of war disrupted Chabad publishing in Warsaw, the Rayatz was rescued from Europe and reached the United States in late winter 5700 (March 1940). From New York he soon resumed correspondence about projects interrupted by the war, including the commemorations of past Chabad Chasidim.

title_en: Rayatz renews request to R. Michael Vilensky from New York
summary_en: On 23 Adar Sheni 5700 the Rayatz wrote again from America asking R. Michael Vilensky to record his father's biography for Hatamim.
story_body: Having received Vilensky's address through the Kiryat Sefer editorial board, the Rayatz wrote once more from New York asking for biographical material about R. Chaim Dover Vilensky for the Hatamim journal. He hoped to revive publication of the journal in America, but the plan never materialized.

title_en: R. Chaim Liberman writes to Mendel Rosenbaum for father's biography
summary_en: On 22 Iyar 5700 the secretary R. Chaim Liberman wrote in Yiddish to Mendel Rosenbaum requesting a biography of his father, the Chasid R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum.
story_body: Acting on behalf of the Rayatz, secretary Chaim Liberman wrote to Mendel Rosenbaum, recently arrived in America, asking him to compose a full biography of his father R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum. The letter explained that former Lubavitch yeshiva students were producing collections devoted entirely to Chabad Chasidism and Chasidim of past generations.

title_en: R. Michael Vilensky sends completed questionnaire on his father
summary_en: On 15 Kislev 5708 R. Michael Vilensky finally sent in his written answers to the questionnaire about his father's life.
story_body: After nearly a decade of repeated requests, R. Michael Vilensky completed and dispatched his replies to a special questionnaire that the Rebbe's secretariat had prepared to help him record his father's biography. He apologized that the answers were heavy on quantity but light on quality, and that he had no written notes from which to work.

title_en: Passing of Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn (Rayatz)
summary_en: The sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe, Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, passed away on 10 Shevat 5710 in New York.
story_body: The Rayatz passed away on 10 Shevat 5710, a few days after writing to R. Michael Vilensky asking for letters that the Rebbe Rashab had sent to his father. His passing left ongoing biographical projects unfinished and ushered in the leadership of his son-in-law, the Rebbe Menachem Mendel Schneerson.

title_en: Hatamim archive found after Rebbe's passing on 3 Tammuz 5754
summary_en: After 3 Tammuz 5754, when the Rebbe's writings were reviewed, the long-lost Vilensky and Rosenbaum biographical files were discovered.
story_body: More than sixty years after the Rayatz first requested it, the file containing R. Michael Vilensky's answers about his father, together with the dossier on R. Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum, was found among the Rebbe's papers. The material was reviewed after the Rebbe's passing on 3 Tammuz 5754 and later published in Pardes Chabad and Toldos Avraham Chaim.

title_en: Hatamim journal published in Warsaw
summary_en: From 5695 to 5699 (1934-1939) the Hatamim journal was published in Warsaw by the alumni of Tomchei Temimim.
story_body: The Hatamim collection devoted to Chabad Chasidism appeared in Warsaw during the years 5695-5699. It included a regular section on biographies of prominent Chasidim of past generations, for which the Rayatz commissioned several memorial articles. Publication ceased with the outbreak of World War II.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's sons recommend R. M.Z. Neimark to Horki community
summary_en: On 15 Tevet 5620 the sons of the Tzemach Tzedek wrote to the Horki community urging them to retain R. Mushulam Zalman Neimark.
story_body: The sons of the Tzemach Tzedek sent a letter to the leaders of the Horki community asking them to strengthen the salary of R. Mushulam Zalman Neimark, their moreh tzedek, lest he look elsewhere. They emphasized that competent halachic authorities expert in Chasidus were rare in those times.

title_en: Passing of R. Yehoshua, Rabbi of Horki
summary_en: In the summer of 5602 the Chasid R. Yehoshua, Rabbi of Horki, passed away.
story_body: During the early years of the Tzemach Tzedek's leadership, the Rabbi of Horki was the Chasid R. Yehoshua. He passed away in the summer of 5602 and was succeeded by R. Yehoshua Eliyahu ben R. Yosef, who served at least until 5610 (1850).

title_en: R. Mushulam Zalman Neimark moves from Horki to Starodub rabbinate
summary_en: Around 5622 R. Mushulam Zalman Neimark left the rabbinate of Horki to assume the rabbinate of Starodub.
story_body: After serving in Horki from approximately 5610, R. Mushulam Zalman Neimark transferred to Starodub around 5622, where he served until about 5646. He was succeeded in Horki by the Chasid R. Chaim Shimon Dov Zivov, author of Shivim Temarim. He later also served in Vitebsk and Nevel.

title_en: Arrest of R. M.Z. Neimark and 80 Jews of Starodub
summary_en: In 5641 R. Mushulam Zalman Neimark and eighty Jews of Starodub were arrested following an informer's denunciation over efforts to exempt Jewish children from Russian military conscription.
story_body: Acting under the guidance of the Rebbe Maharash, R. Mushulam Zalman Neimark of Starodub had worked to secure exemptions for Jewish children from service in the Russian army. After the maskil Dov Lazarov denounced him, he and eighty Starodub Jews were arrested. The yeshiva in Starodub was shut by the police and even the Rebbe Maharash himself was nearly indicted, with Chasidim interrogated about their travels to Lubavitch.

title_en: Starodub Jews remain imprisoned for two years
summary_en: From 5641 to 5643 R. M.Z. Neimark and the arrested Starodub Jews remained in prison while community efforts sought their release.
story_body: The arrested Starodub Jews remained imprisoned for two years (5641-5643). The Rebbe Maharash sent a short letter of encouragement to Neimark in prison, dispatched his secretary R. Levi Yitzchak Idelevitz to Starodub to assess the situation, and corresponded in code with the prisoners. Activists in Riga, Velizh, Starodub and Kiev coordinated to retain top defense attorneys in Kiev.

title_en: Trial acquits Rabbi Zalman Neimark and Chassidim in Staradub
summary_en: After two years awaiting trial, Rabbi Zalman Neimark and other Chassidim were acquitted in the Staradub case in the winter of 5643.
story_body: Rabbi Zalman Neimark and a group of Chassidim from Staradub had been imprisoned and held over for trial for two years. The trial finally took place in the winter of 5643 (1883), ending with their full acquittal. Shortly after the verdict, Rabbi Neimark left Staradub and was soon invited to serve as rabbi of Vitebsk.

title_en: Rabbi Zalman Neimark appointed rabbi of Vitebsk
summary_en: Following the death of Rabbi Zalman Ostrovner around 5646-7, Rabbi Zalman Neimark was appointed rabbi of Vitebsk.
story_body: After Rabbi Zalman Ostrovner died in Vitebsk in approximately 5646-7 (1886-7), the community appointed Rabbi Zalman Neimark in his place. He served there only about two years before being invited to a different community in White Russia.

title_en: Rabbi Zalman Neimark becomes rabbi of Nevel
summary_en: In early summer 5648, Rabbi Zalman Neimark left Vitebsk and took up the rabbinate of Nevel, where he served until his death.
story_body: After two years in Vitebsk, Rabbi Zalman Neimark accepted the position of rabbi in Nevel in White Russia. A responsum he wrote from Nevel on 9 Nisan 5649 references a fire 'last summer,' indicating he had already settled there by the start of summer 5648 (1888). He continued to serve as rabbi of Nevel until his death.

title_en: Fire in Nevel scatters Rabbi Neimark's books
summary_en: A fire struck Nevel in summer 5648, leaving Rabbi Zalman Neimark's books displaced thereafter.
story_body: In a letter dated 9 Nisan 5649, Rabbi Neimark wrote from Nevel that 'last summer there was the present fire here, since which time the books have been moved from corner to corner.' The fire occurred in summer 5648 (1888) and continued to disrupt his study and books long afterward.

title_en: Rabbi Zalman Neimark of Nevel dies
summary_en: Rabbi Zalman Neimark, rabbi of Nevel, died on 28 Menachem Av 5653, and was succeeded by his son Rabbi Yechezkel Feivel.
story_body: After serving as rabbi of Nevel from 5648 onward, Rabbi Zalman Neimark died on 28 Menachem Av 5653 (10 August 1893), as recorded in the introduction to Eshel Avraham. His son, Rabbi Yechezkel Feivel, took his place as rabbi of Nevel.

title_en: R' Shlomo Kugel lives in Kiskoriene near Pleshchenitsy
summary_en: In 1836 R' Shlomo Kugel lived in the village of Kiskoriene near Pleshchenitsy in the Minsk region, beginning the Chassidic presence in the area.
story_body: According to a 5716 memoir by Mariasha Badana Putrefas, in 1836 (5596) a Jew named R' Shlomo Kugel lived in the village of Kiskoriene near Pleshchenitsy in the Minsk gubernia. Known as R' Shlomo Kiskoriener, his sons Hendel, Yosef and Gershon later spread Chassidut from the surrounding villages into the strongly mitnagdic town of Pleshchenitsy.

title_en: R' Yosef Kugel of Pleshchenitsy dies
summary_en: The Chassid R' Yosef Kugel of Pleshchenitsy died around Adar 5636, mourned in a letter by R' Shmuel Dovber of Borisov.
story_body: R' Yosef Kugel, brother of the mashpia R' Hendel Kugel, was one of the leading Chassidim of Pleshchenitsy. He died around Adar 5636, prompting R' Shmuel Dovber of Borisov to write to R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum on 26 Adar 5636 (22 March 1876) lamenting 'sudden news from Rebbi Z.R. of his camp of the passing of our beloved, God-fearing and trembling R' Y.'

title_en: R' Gershon Yehuda Leib Kugel dies
summary_en: R' Gershon Yehuda Leib Kugel, son of R' Hendel Kugel and father of R' Shlomo, died after Shabbat Parshat Nitzavim 5637.
story_body: As recorded by his son R' Shlomo in manuscript 584, R' Gershon Yehuda Leib Kugel died after the conclusion of Shabbat Parshat Nitzavim 5637 (September 1877). He was buried in Vilna on 18 Elul 5637 after midday, with his yahrzeit observed on 18 Elul.

title_en: R' Gershon Yehuda Leib Kugel buried in Vilna
summary_en: R' Gershon Yehuda Leib Kugel was buried in Vilna on 18 Elul 5637.
story_body: After dying just after Shabbat Parshat Nitzavim 5637, R' Gershon Yehuda Leib Kugel was buried in the Jewish community of Vilna on 18 Elul 5637 (28 August 1877). His yahrzeit was set for 18 Elul.

title_en: Wedding of R' Shlomo Kugel and Bracha Slava Rosenbaum
summary_en: R' Shlomo Kugel married Bracha Slava, daughter of R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum of Pleshchenitsy, during Parshat Terumah 5639.
story_body: R' Shlomo, son of R' Gershon Yehuda Leib Kugel, married Bracha Slava, daughter of R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum of Pleshchenitsy, in the week of Parshat Terumah 5639 (February 1879). R' Shmuel Dovber of Borisov, unable to attend in person because he was in Lubavitch, sent a mazal-tov letter on 25 Adar 5639.

title_en: Birth of Gil Kugel
summary_en: Gil Kugel, son of R' Shlomo Kugel, was born on Tuesday 4 Nisan 5640 in Pleshchenitsy.
story_body: As recorded in the Kugel family register (manuscript 584), R' Shlomo Kugel's son Gil was born on Tuesday, 4 Nisan 5640 (16 March 1880) in Pleshchenitsy. The entry was kept by his father along with the dates of all five of his children's births.

title_en: Birth of Shmuel Kugel
summary_en: Shmuel Kugel, son of R' Shlomo, was born on Friday 10 Tevet 5646 in the week of Parshat Vayechi.
story_body: R' Shlomo Kugel recorded the birth of his son Shmuel on Friday, 10 Tevet 5646 (18 December 1885), during the week of Parshat Vayechi. The note appears in the family register in manuscript 584.

title_en: Birth of Tzvi Hirsch Kugel
summary_en: Tzvi Hirsch Kugel, son of R' Shlomo, was born on Friday 18 Tevet 5647.
story_body: R' Shlomo Kugel recorded that his son Tzvi Hirsch was born on Friday, 18 Tevet 5647 (13 January 1887), in the week of Parshat Shemot. The entry appears in his family register in manuscript 584.

title_en: R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum arrested
summary_en: R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum of Pleshchenitsy was arrested in 5648 and remained imprisoned until late 5650.
story_body: In 5648 (1888) R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum, leader of the Pleshchenitsy Chassidic community after R' Hendel Kugel moved to Lubavitch, was arrested. He remained imprisoned, including in Smolensk, until late 5650 (1890), writing several letters from prison to his friends and family during that period.

title_en: Birth of Meir Shalom Kugel during Rosenbaum's imprisonment
summary_en: Meir Shalom, fourth son of R' Shlomo Kugel, was born on 20 Sivan 5649 while his grandfather R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum was imprisoned in Smolensk.
story_body: R' Shlomo Kugel recorded the birth of his son Meir Shalom on Wednesday, 20 Sivan 5649 (19 June 1889). The birth came while the child's grandfather R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum was imprisoned in Smolensk; R' Hendel Kugel traveled to Pleshchenitsy for the brit, and R' Avraham Chaim sent congratulations from prison on Sunday Parshat Pinchas.

title_en: R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum released from prison
summary_en: R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum was released from prison at the end of 5650 after roughly two years of imprisonment.
story_body: After his arrest in 5648, R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum remained imprisoned until the end of 5650 (1890). During this period he wrote numerous letters, including one on Thursday Parshat Tzav 5650 in which he discussed plans to travel via Lubavitch upon release, and another describing his elderly father counting the moments until they would meet again.

title_en: Birth of Chana Kugel
summary_en: Chana, daughter of R' Shlomo Kugel, was born on the eve of Shabbat Tazria, 2 Nisan 5651.
story_body: R' Shlomo Kugel recorded in his family register the birth of his daughter Chana on the eve of Shabbat Parshat Tazria, 2 Nisan 5651 (11 March 1891). The entry appears in manuscript 584 in the Lubavitch library.

title_en: Mazkir R' Reuven Liberman writes letter on state of Pleshchenitsy
summary_en: On the eve of Shabbat Parshat Chukat 5670, R' Reuven Liberman wrote to R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum lamenting how Pleshchenitsy had declined.
story_body: R' Reuven Liberman, leader of the Pleshchenitsy Chassidim after R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum's emigration, wrote on the eve of Shabbat Parshat Chukat 5670 (1910) describing how the town's glory had vanished. He contrasted the flourishing time when Rosenbaum lived there with its present decline, and longed to see him again even for a moment.

title_en: Death of R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum in America
summary_en: R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum, the former leader of Pleshchenitsy Chassidim, died in the United States on 25 Kislev 5674.
story_body: Born around 5600, R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum had spent his youth at the court of the Tzemach Tzedek and later became a leading Chassid of the Maharash and the leader of the Pleshchenitsy Chassidic community. After emigrating and settling in America in 5658, he died there on 25 Kislev 5674 (24 December 1913), as recorded in the Rebbe's footnote in Sefer HaSichot Kayitz 5700.

title_en: R' Reuven Liberman, last of the Pleshchenitsy Chassidim, dies
summary_en: R' Reuven Liberman, last of the great Chassidim of Pleshchenitsy, died on Shabbat 28 Nisan 5687 at age seventy.
story_body: R' Reuven Liberman, who had served as shochet and leader of Chassidic life in Pleshchenitsy since R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum's emigration, died on Shabbat 28 Nisan 5687 (30 April 1927) at age seventy. His son R' Chaim Liberman, then secretary to the Rayatz, traveled from Leningrad immediately after Pesach to attend the funeral, writing afterward that 'such men are gone from us now in every respect.'

title_en: Rayatz and R' Chaim Liberman arrested in Leningrad
summary_en: The Rayatz and his secretary R' Chaim Liberman were arrested in Leningrad on the eve of 15 Sivan 5687.
story_body: On the eve of 15 Sivan 5687 (14-15 June 1927), the Sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe (Rayatz) and his secretary R' Chaim Liberman were both arrested in Leningrad. After some time in the Leningrad prison, they were sent into exile separately—the Rebbe to Kostroma and Liberman to Tambov.

title_en: Liberation of the Rayatz on Yud-Beis Tammuz
summary_en: The Rayatz was freed from Soviet exile on 12-13 Tammuz 5687, the date later commemorated as Yud-Beis Tammuz.
story_body: After being arrested on 15 Sivan 5687 and exiled to Kostroma, the Rayatz was freed on 12-13 Tammuz 5687 (12-13 July 1927). The date became the great Chabad festival of liberation; later that fall, in the latter part of Tishrei 5688, he left Russia entirely and settled in Riga.

title_en: Rayatz leaves Russia and settles in Riga
summary_en: At the end of Tishrei 5688 the Rayatz left the Soviet Union and settled in Riga, Latvia.
story_body: After his liberation on 12-13 Tammuz 5687, the Rayatz remained in Russia for several more months. At the end of Tishrei 5688 (October 1927) he left Soviet Russia and settled in Riga, while his secretary R' Chaim Liberman remained behind in exile in Tambov.

title_en: R' Chaim Liberman departs Tambov for Riga
summary_en: R' Chaim Liberman left Tambov on 1 May 1928 (11 Iyar 5688) after the Rayatz secured his release.
story_body: After roughly a year of imprisonment and exile, R' Chaim Liberman was released and obtained an exit permit—largely through the efforts of the Rayatz from Riga and the intervention of Latvian Sejm deputy Mordechai Dubin. A photograph in the library archive shows his last day in Tambov, marked '1 May 1928,' corresponding to 11 Iyar 5688. He stopped briefly in Moscow on the advice of fellow Chassidim R' Yaakov Maskalik and R' Shmuel Levitin not to delay his departure.

title_en: R' Chaim Liberman arrives in Riga
summary_en: R' Chaim Liberman arrived in Riga from his Soviet exile on 19 Iyar 5688, where the Rayatz had awaited him.
story_body: R' Chaim Liberman arrived in Riga at 10 PM on 19 Iyar 5688 (9 May 1928), eight days after leaving Tambov. The Rayatz wrote that day that 'today one of my secretaries, Mr. Liberman, is arriving here,' describing how Mordechai Dubin had worked for some six months to obtain his exit permit after his arrest at the same time as the Rebbe.

title_en: Mariasha Putrefas writes Pleshchenitsy memoir
summary_en: Mariasha Badana Putrefas, a native of Pleshchenitsy, wrote a memoir of the Kugel family and Chassidic life there in 5716.
story_body: In 5716 (1956), Mariasha Badana Putrefas, a native of Pleshchenitsy, wrote a Yiddish memoir recounting the beginnings of Chassidut in the town. Her account—covering R' Shlomo Kugel of Kiskoriene, his sons Hendel, Yosef and Gershon, and the arrival of Chassidut in the mitnagdic town—was later translated into Hebrew by R' Y. Mondshine and published in Kfar Chabad issue 883.

title_en: Rosenbaum imprisoned in Smolensk; permitted religious articles in jail
summary_en: Beginning summer 5648, the chassid Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum was incarcerated in Smolensk prison and allowed to bring sacred items into the jail.
story_body: In the summer of 5648 (1888), the Chabad chassid Reb Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum was sent to prison in Smolensk. From his arrival the authorities permitted him to bring religious articles into the cell. He would remain there nearly two years, conducting an extensive correspondence with chassidim and family members.

title_en: Rosenbaum writes from Smolensk prison requesting an etrog for Sukkot
summary_en: On 13 Elul 5648 Rosenbaum wrote from prison to Rabbi Yehuda Leib Maskil L'Eitan of Pleschenitz asking him to acquire a fine Yanover etrog, lulav, and three hadasim.
story_body: Writing from the Smolensk jail on 13 Elul 5648, Reb Avraham Chaim asked the rabbi of Pleschenitz to purchase a Yanover etrog of fine appearance, a complete lulav, and three properly meshulash hadasim. He requested they reach him immediately after Yom Kippur so he could fulfill the mitzvah of the Four Species inside the prison.

title_en: Rosenbaum writes Rosh Chodesh Nissan letter from jail to R' Chaim Gershon Kugel
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Nissan 5649 the imprisoned Rosenbaum thanked R' Chaim Gershon Kugel for words of comfort and friendship that eased his suffering in captivity.
story_body: From his cell in Smolensk on 1 Nissan 5649, Reb Avraham Chaim wrote to R' Chaim Gershon Kugel acknowledging the warmth of his letter. He noted that an imprisoned man's spirit is consoled when even distant friends share in his pain. The exchange preserved one of several friendships Rosenbaum maintained from prison.

title_en: Rosenbaum forbids wife from visiting him at Smolensk prison
summary_en: Around Parshat Masei 5649 Rosenbaum wrote to R' Hendel explaining that he had refused his wife permission to travel to Smolensk and visit him, citing the burden on home and business.
story_body: In a letter dated the week of Parshat Masei 5649 to the mashpia Reb Hendel, Reb Avraham Chaim explained why he had rejected his wife's plan to visit him in prison. He felt the trip would force abandonment of their home and store and would burden their son Zalman with running everything for a week without yielding any real benefit.

title_en: Sister-in-law travels to Smolensk to visit Rosenbaum in prison
summary_en: In Elul 5649 Rosenbaum's bride-sister-in-law came to Smolensk to visit him, prompting him to send a letter asking her fiancé to purchase a fine tallit katan on his behalf.
story_body: During Elul 5649, Rosenbaum's sister-in-law (the bride) traveled to Smolensk to see him. In replying to her, he addressed her fiancé Reb David, asking him to purchase a tallit katan of the highest quality from Kiryat Chana David before the new year. The request reflected both his ritual concerns and his confidence in his future relative's taste.

title_en: Rosenbaum counts months to release in Rosh Hashanah-period letter
summary_en: On 25 Tishrei 5650 Rosenbaum wrote to R' Zev Wolf Kugel calculating that roughly eight months remained until his release and reading the year tav-resh-nun as a hint of redemption.
story_body: From the Smolensk jail on 25 Tishrei 5650, Reb Avraham Chaim told the young R' Zev Wolf Kugel that he could not yet share substantive news, but in about eight months he hoped to bring glad tidings. He interpreted the 240 days remaining of his sentence as the gematria of 'mar' (bitterness) that would be transformed into 'dror' (freedom), invoking the blessing 'matir asurim.'

title_en: Rosenbaum permitted to build a sukkah in Smolensk prison courtyard
summary_en: For Sukkot 5650 the warden granted Rosenbaum the unusual privilege of building a sukkah inside the prison courtyard.
story_body: Although Rosenbaum initially feared he would not even be able to eat a kezayit of bread in a sukkah and lamented his isolation from the community, the prison warden ultimately granted him permission to erect a sukkah in the prison yard for Sukkot 5650. The episode showed the warden's growing regard for him and was preserved in a letter by R' Shlomo Rosenbaum.

title_en: Rosenbaum receives leave to visit chassidim for 19 Kislev farbrengen
summary_en: On the night of 19 Kislev 5650 the warden allowed Rosenbaum to leave the prison and spend the night farbrenging with the chassidim in town.
story_body: After R' Raza Schneerson's intervention with the Smolensk governor improved Rosenbaum's prison conditions, on the night of 19 Kislev 5650 the warden permitted him to leave the jail entirely. He spent the whole night at the chassidic gathering with anash, and the following day received leave to go into town to purchase oil for Chanukah lights.

title_en: R' Raza Schneerson travels to Smolensk to plead for Rosenbaum
summary_en: On the Rebbe Maharash's posthumous instruction, in 5650 R' Raza Schneerson came to Smolensk and intervened with the governor to ease Rosenbaum's prison conditions.
story_body: Acting on the late Rebbe Maharash's counsel from the previous years, in 5650 R' Raza Schneerson traveled to Smolensk and presented himself to local leaders and chassidim on Rosenbaum's behalf. Although he could not obtain Rosenbaum's release, his intervention with the governor freed him from hard labor, secured him a separate cell, and won him kindly treatment from the warden including a private stove and a chest of books.

title_en: Rosenbaum's 15 Shevat letter from prison anticipating freedom
summary_en: On 15 Shevat 5650 Rosenbaum wrote to the rabbi of Pleschenitz that every passing day brought salvation closer, comparing memory of past days to a riddle about yesterday and tomorrow.
story_body: From Smolensk on 15 Shevat 5650, Reb Avraham Chaim told R' Yehuda Leib Maskil L'Eitan that he had no real news but that 'salvation draws nearer day by day.' He framed the long days behind bars with a Hebrew riddle: 'What was tomorrow and will be yesterday?'—answer, 'today'—expressing faith that he would yet see redemption.

title_en: Prison conditions sharply worsen at end of winter 5650 in Smolensk
summary_en: Around the end of winter 5650 the staff at Smolensk prison changed and stringent new restrictions were imposed on prisoners' clothing, food, bedding and use of fire.
story_body: At the close of winter 5650 the prison administration was replaced and Rosenbaum wrote to R' Hendel describing harsher rules: only government-issued uniforms, straw pillows instead of feather, no private samovars, food rationed to two meals only, no chests or utensils beyond a single pot and spoon. He worried particularly about Pesach, when reliance on the common kettle would force compromise on chametz and warm food.

title_en: Rosenbaum released from Smolensk prison around Parshat Korach 5650
summary_en: Rosenbaum left Smolensk prison about Monday of Parshat Korach 5650, ending nearly two years of incarceration, and planned to travel directly to Lubavitch.
story_body: After almost two years of imprisonment in Smolensk, Reb Avraham Chaim was released around the Monday of Parshat Korach 5650. In his last prison letter he announced the date of his expected freedom and his intention to journey at once to Lubavitch to see the Rebbe Maharash's son and successor circle.

title_en: Rosenbaum flees Russia after warning of renewed arrest
summary_en: In Tishrei 5652 a friendly investigator warned Rosenbaum that new charges were being prepared, prompting him to host one final Simchat Torah farbrengen and slip out of Pleschenitz that night.
story_body: On one of the days of Tishrei 5652-3, Reb Avraham Chaim was secretly told that fresh proceedings were being readied against him and that he must flee abroad. On Simchat Torah he hosted a great gathering for all the local chassidim, farbrenging joyously all day, and at nightfall vanished from town. Opponents who heard of his flight gave chase but failed to overtake him.

title_en: Rosenbaum reaches Frankfurt and opens a dairy shop
summary_en: After Shabbat in Warsaw with his brother, Rosenbaum traveled to Frankfurt where one of his sons joined him and they opened a dairy-products store, staying about a year.
story_body: Following his flight from Pleschenitz, Reb Avraham Chaim spent Shabbat in Warsaw at his brother's home. He then proceeded to Frankfurt, where one of his sons joined him and together they opened a shop selling dairy foods. They remained in Frankfurt about a year until German authorities expelled him.

title_en: Rosenbaum expelled from Germany and relocates to Amsterdam
summary_en: A German police official informed Rosenbaum he could not remain in Germany, and although he refused to consider America he moved instead to Amsterdam.
