Participation was limited to government-approved rabbis and assistants, fueling fears among the traditional rabbinate that the gathering would yield religiously hostile resolutions endorsed by the state.

title_en: R. Chaim Ozer warns of risk from crown-rabbi assembly
summary_en: On 27 Adar II 5660, R. Chaim Ozer Grodzinski wrote to R. Eliezer Moshe Madeyevsky urging vigilance over the planned crown-rabbi assembly.
story_body: Chaim Ozer asked Madeyevsky to investigate the matter inside the Interior Ministry and to ensure that the assembly's recommendations could not damage traditional Jewish life. He requested a personal meeting in Vilna on Madeyevsky's return to coordinate strategy.

title_en: Twenty-five crown rabbis convene in Nikolaev
summary_en: On 2 Iyar 5660, twenty-five government-appointed rabbis met in Nikolaev under official authorization, alarming the traditional rabbinate.
story_body: Fear spread that the assembly would adopt resolutions hostile to traditional Judaism backed by the imprimatur of the Interior Ministry. The Slonimer Rebbe Shmuel Weinberg and R. Yosef Slifer urgently dispatched R. Eliezer Yosef Klatzky to the Rebbe Rashab, who endorsed the immediate organization of a counter-assembly of traditional rabbis and rebbes.

title_en: Vilna rabbinical assembly convenes under Rebbe Rashab
summary_en: After nine years of effort, Rebbe Rashab succeeded in convening an officially-authorized rabbinical assembly in Vilna in Iyar 5669.
story_body: Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak later described it as 'the great Vilna assembly, the like of which had not been held in a hundred years.' Authorized by the Interior Ministry strictly for matters of religious strengthening, it nevertheless adopted a resolution to the ministry connecting religious decline to the economic catastrophe of the Pale of Settlement.

title_en: WWI expulsion order ends the Pale of Settlement in practice
summary_en: A special order in 5675 required Jews to abandon any locality within 24 hours of the approaching front, effectively dismantling the Pale of Settlement.
story_body: Most Pale provinces were declared front-zone areas in which Jewish residence was forbidden, and deportees were assigned to five interior provinces: Voronezh, Tambov, Penza, Crimea, and Yekaterinoslav. The decree was later rescinded, but by then German forces had occupied the original Jewish areas, leaving nowhere to return. The formal abolition came with the fall of the tsarist regime in 1917.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab pushes for rabbinical assembly on JCA funding crisis
summary_en: On 1 Sivan 5661, Rebbe Rashab wrote to R. Avraham Avli Perlson urging him to press leading rabbis to convene over the JCA donations being directed to Maskilic schools in Russia.
story_body: The JCA (Jewish Colonization Association) had begun channeling funds to schools of the Mefitzei Haskalah society, threatening traditional Jewish education in Russia. Rebbe Rashab considered the matter so urgent that he sought to organize a rabbinical assembly to formulate a response. He worked behind the scenes through R. Avraham Avli Perlson, asking the great rabbis (such as the Telshe Rav) to take ownership of the cause publicly while he supported them from the background.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab laments rabbinic inaction against Russian religious decline
summary_en: On 14 Tevet 5662 the Rebbe Rashab wrote that the absence of rabbinic mobilization while the Maskilim worked aggressively was 'terrifying,' and that he could rely only on R. Menachem Mendel Chein for assistance.
story_body: After repeated failed attempts to convene a rabbinical assembly in summer 5661, the Rebbe Rashab expressed bitter frustration in a letter to R. Eliezer Moshe Modayevsky. He reported informing R. Chaim Ozer Grodzinski of Vilna that the rabbis should no longer rely on him and must act independently, while he himself stood ready to travel for any assembly that would actually convene. Although R. Chaim Ozer was passionate about the cause, the Rebbe felt the man lacked the power to effect internal change.

title_en: Eighty rabbis invited to Grodno religious assembly
summary_en: By early winter 5664 (around 5 Kislev), serious preparations were underway for an official assembly of approximately eighty Orthodox rabbis in Grodno, formally convened by R. Eliyahu Akiva Rabinovich of Poltava.
story_body: After years of failed attempts, real preparations finally materialized in 5664 to convene an assembly of Orthodox rabbis under government authorization in Grodno. R. Eliyahu Akiva Rabinovich of Poltava served as the official convener, and the proposal had the backing of R. Chaim Soloveitchik of Brisk. The Rebbe Rashab proposed a preliminary smaller gathering of senior rabbis to define an agenda before the main assembly.

title_en: Maskilic press attacks planned Grodno rabbinical assembly
summary_en: Throughout Cheshvan-Kislev 5664, the Hebrew newspaper Ha-Melitz (issues 228, 242, 255) and the Russian Novosti published protests and articles attacking the planned Grodno Orthodox rabbinical assembly.
story_body: When word of the planned Grodno assembly reached Haskalah circles, they launched a press campaign to discredit it, publishing protests in Ha-Melitz, Novosti, and other outlets. The Rebbe Rashab described the Hebrew papers as 'shouting and barking,' while R. Eliyahu Akiva Rabinovich answered the attacks in the journal Ha-Peles (Tevet 5664). The Maskilim also planted false reports that prominent rabbis like the Lodzer Rav Maizel and rabbis of Dvinsk and Plotsk were withdrawing from the assembly.

title_en: Denunciations sent against Grodno rabbinical assembly
summary_en: By 17 Kislev 5664, two written denunciations had reached the Grodno governor's office, sent from Kovno and Bialystok, accusing the assembled rabbis of seeking to bring 'darkness' upon the world.
story_body: Opponents of the Orthodox rabbinical assembly escalated their resistance by sending official denunciations to Grodno authorities. Rebbe Rashab condemned the audacity, noting that beyond the threat to the assembly itself, the rabbis were being publicly disgraced before the gentiles. Despite this, the bureaucratic process for authorization continued; the governor had requested files on each registered participant and the permit was expected within roughly two weeks.

title_en: Baron Ginzburg intervenes to block Grodno assembly
summary_en: In Tevet 5664 (early January 1904), Baron Naftali Hertz Ginzburg met with the Russian Minister of the Interior on behalf of Haskalah circles, successfully derailing authorization for the Grodno rabbinical assembly.
story_body: When press attacks and denunciations failed to block the Grodno assembly, Haskalah leaders dispatched Baron Naftali Hertz Ginzburg to lobby the Minister of the Interior directly. According to Ginzburg's report, he had turned the minister against the assembly by arguing that the invitees were rabbis from minor towns. Rebbe Rashab lamented in letters dated 3-8 Tevet that this exposed how far the power of those opposed to Orthodox interests had grown.

title_en: Russian government approves Knesset Yisrael Orthodox organization
summary_en: In the winter of 5668 the Russian government formally authorized the Orthodox organization Agudat Knesset Yisrael, headed by R. Chaim Ozer Grodzinski.
story_body: After years of failed assemblies, the Charedi community achieved a major institutional milestone when the Russian government recognized Agudat Knesset Yisrael in winter 5668. R. Chaim Ozer Grodzinski of Vilna headed the organization, which became the legal framework that would later make a Vilna rabbinical assembly possible under its statute (paragraph 39). R. Eliezer Gordon of Telshe was deeply involved in the new body.

title_en: Postponed Lag BaOmer rabbinical assembly in Vilna
summary_en: R. Eliezer Gordon of Telshe scheduled a general rabbinical assembly for Lag BaOmer 5668 in Vilna under the auspices of Knesset Yisrael, but it had to be postponed when it was realized that the proper governmental authorization had not yet been obtained.
story_body: Acting with great urgency, R. Eliezer Gordon scheduled a general rabbinical assembly for Lag BaOmer 5668 in Vilna, conflating it with the affairs of the newly authorized Knesset Yisrael. Rabbis across the region had already begun gathering in district capitals to consult, but it became clear that a general assembly required the Minister of the Interior's permission rather than the local governor's. The organizers were forced to publicly announce the postponement via newspapers and telegrams.

title_en: Marienbad summer conference of Chassidic Rebbes
summary_en: In the summer of 5668 the Rebbe Rashab, the Gerrer Rebbe, and other leaders convened a conference in Marienbad to coordinate preparations for the planned rabbinical gatherings in Vilna and Petersburg.
story_body: Outside the reach of Russian government scrutiny, leading Orthodox figures including Rebbe Rashab and the Gerrer Rebbe (R. Avraham Mordechai Alter) met in the Bohemian spa town of Marienbad. They discussed the preparations for the upcoming Vilna assembly and the Petersburg Rabbinical Conference. The Gerrer Rebbe asked Rashab to clarify the situation in Petersburg through the special emissary being sent to the capital.

title_en: Lubavitch convenes preparatory assembly of Chabad rabbis
summary_en: In mid-Cheshvan 5669 the Rebbe Rashab convened an assembly of Chabad rabbis and lay leaders in Lubavitch, establishing a permanent bureau to prepare for the upcoming Vilna rabbinical assembly.
story_body: As preparations for the Vilna assembly intensified, the Rebbe Rashab gathered Chabad rabbis and community activists in Lubavitch itself for a strategic conference. The gathering established a standing committee to handle the preparatory work for the Vilna assembly. The Chabad assembly also decided to seek the Gerrer Rebbe's approval to send two Chabad representatives, R. Menachem Mendel Chein of Nezhin and R. Shmaryahu Leib Medalia of Vitebsk, to participate in the upcoming assembly of Polish rabbis.

title_en: Permit secured for Vilna rabbinical assembly via Ministry of Interior
summary_en: By 3 Kislev 5669 the Rebbe Rashab obtained Russian government authorization for a 25-rabbi consultative assembly in Vilna, leveraging Dr. Krebs's questions about preparations for the Petersburg Rabbinical Conference.
story_body: When Dr. Krebs, the 'Learned Jew' at the Ministry of the Interior, circulated preparatory questions for the upcoming Petersburg Rabbinical Conference, the Rebbe Rashab seized the opportunity. Through the wealthy Petersburg askan R. Shmuel Michel Treinin, a petition signed by Yitzchak Liubinsky was submitted requesting permission for twenty-five named Orthodox rabbis to meet in Vilna to consult on the upcoming conference's religious questions. The director of the relevant department signed the permit, ending years of failed attempts to obtain authorization.

title_en: Assembly of Polish rabbis convenes
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Kislev 5669 an assembly of Polish rabbis convened to address the same governmental questions about religious affairs that prompted the Vilna gathering.
story_body: Russian-ruled Poland organized its own rabbinical assembly on Rosh Chodesh Kislev to respond to the preparatory questions for the Petersburg Rabbinical Conference. Two Chabad representatives, R. Menachem Mendel Chein of Nezhin and R. Shmaryahu Leib Medalia of Vitebsk, attended at the invitation of the Gerrer Rebbe. They reported the assembly's discussions and decisions back to the Rebbe Rashab, who immediately relayed the details to his son, the Rayatz, who was overseeing preparations for the Vilna assembly.

title_en: Preliminary rabbinical conference in Baranovich
summary_en: From 9-11 Iyar 5669 a preliminary closed conference of senior rabbis convened in Baranovich, immediately prior to the main Vilna assembly, to align agendas and positions.
story_body: Following the Rebbe Rashab's longstanding insistence that any major rabbinical assembly be preceded by a smaller preparatory conference of selected senior figures, a three-day gathering was held in Baranovich. This allowed the leading Orthodox rabbis to clarify positions, narrow disagreements, and agree on what would be proposed publicly before the broader twenty-five-rabbi convention in Vilna began two days later.

title_en: Historic Vilna rabbinical assembly convenes
summary_en: From 12-20 Iyar 5669 (May 3-11, 1909) twenty Orthodox rabbis convened the major Vilna rabbinical assembly, described as the first such united gathering in approximately one hundred years.
story_body: After nearly a decade of failed attempts, the official Vilna rabbinical assembly finally took place over ten days in Iyar 5669, with the Gerrer Rebbe (R. Avraham Mordechai Alter) joining for part of the proceedings. Twenty of the twenty-five authorized rabbis attended. The assembly resolved to dispatch traveling rabbis and preachers to towns across Russia to strengthen religious observance, organize Torah study circles, and establish local educational committees (Vaadei Chinuch) of pious learned men to supervise schooling. The Rayatz, designated by the Rebbe Rashab to handle all operational details, prepared the formal protocol that was submitted via the governor to the Ministry of Interior's religious affairs department.

title_en: Maskilic counter-assembly convenes in Kovno
summary_en: Around the time of the Vilna rabbinical assembly, the Maskilim and government-appointed rabbis (rabbanim mi-ta'am) convened their own authorized 'Assembly of Jewish Public Activists' in Kovno, producing a roughly two-hundred-page volume of proposals that was submitted to the Ministry of Interior.
story_body: Determined not to cede the field to the Orthodox rabbinate, the modernist faction and government-appointed rabbis organized a parallel assembly in Kovno called the 'Assembly of Jewish Public Activists.' They recorded all their proposals in a volume of roughly two hundred pages, submitted it to the Ministry's religious affairs department, later published a printed collection of the speeches and proposals, and established a standing bureau to prepare for the Petersburg Rabbinical Conference.

title_en: Petersburg Rabbinical Conference elections in Russian provinces
summary_en: Beginning in Tishrei 5670, elections were ordered across Russian provinces to select two delegates per province for the upcoming Petersburg Rabbinical Conference, prompting the Rebbe Rashab to publish kol koreh broadsides and personally travel to campaign.
story_body: After the holidays in Tishrei 5670, the government ordered elections for delegates to the Petersburg Rabbinical Conference, with two representatives to be chosen per province through a multi-stage process. The Rebbe Rashab immediately issued a kol koreh, dispatched R. Moshe Rosenblum to coordinate with the gedolim, and obtained additional kol koreh letters from R. David Friedman of Karlin and R. Chaim Ozer Grodzinski. Thousands of copies were distributed to synagogues. Dr. Krebs at the Ministry of Interior actively lobbied against electing Orthodox rabbis, citing precedents where ministers had selected only one or two religious rabbis to past commissions.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab elected delegate from two Russian provinces
summary_en: In late 5669/early 5670 the Rebbe Rashab personally traveled to Mogilev and Chernigov to campaign and was elected as a delegate to the Petersburg Rabbinical Conference from both provinces.
story_body: Departing from his usual practice, the Rebbe Rashab personally undertook campaign travel to the cities of Mogilev (whose province included Lubavitch) and Chernigov to ensure that pious rabbis were selected as delegates to the Petersburg conference. He stood as a candidate himself and was elected from both provinces, an event later recorded in Zikaron LiVnei Yisrael as 'the campaign' he undertook. He acknowledged the burden weighed heavily upon him but felt he could not refuse.

title_en: Petersburg Rabbinical Conference of 1910
summary_en: From 4 Adar II to 6 Nisan 5670 (March 15 to April 15, 1910) the official Russian Rabbinical Conference convened in Petersburg for approximately one month, with Dr. Krebs serving as the government representative.
story_body: After two years of intensive preparation, the official Rabbinical Conference (Ravvinskaya Komissiya) convened in Petersburg under the auspices of the Ministry of the Interior's religious affairs department. The conference was the culmination of years of effort by Rebbe Rashab and the Orthodox rabbinate, who had finally succeeded in ensuring that this iteration of the periodic government rabbinical commission would consist primarily of pious Orthodox rabbis from across the empire, including the Polish provinces. The conference proper lasted about a month, with follow-up work continuing through the end of 5670.

title_en: Schneersohn elected as delegate from shtetl Nevel
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab was elected as a delegate from the shtetl of Nevel in the Vitebsk gubernia, despite efforts by secularists to block his selection.
story_body: During preparations for the Petersburg Rabbinical Conference, electors in the shtetl of Nevel (Vitebsk gubernia) unanimously voted to send the Rebbe Rashab (Rabbi Sholom DovBer Schneersohn) as their delegate. Secular activists tried to introduce a break in the voting and lobby against his candidacy, but failed. Nevel was the locality from which he was officially chosen.

title_en: Election of two delegates from Chernigov gubernia
summary_en: Rabbi David Tzvi Chen and Yitzchak Schneersohn were elected as the two delegates from the city of Chernigov for the upcoming Rabbinical Conference.
story_body: The city of Chernigov elected two delegates to the rabbinical conference: Rabbi David Tzvi (the Rad"tz) Chen, the religious rabbi of the city, and Mr. Yitzchak Schneersohn, the government-appointed rabbi (Rabbiner). The Rebbe Rashab wrote on the night of 25 Cheshvan that the government rabbi of Chernigov was not aligned with their camp, while the Rad"tz had only been chosen from Chernigov itself, with further district elections still pending.

title_en: District elections in Chernigov gubernia
summary_en: Elections of delegates in the remaining districts of Chernigov gubernia were held, with Rabbi Menachem Mendel Chen elected from Nezhin.
story_body: The week after the elections in the city of Chernigov, the remaining districts (uyezds) of the Chernigov gubernia held their elections. Attached to the Rebbe Rayatz's letter dated the night of 27 Cheshvan was the list of elected delegates, which included Rabbi Menachem Mendel Chen, son of the Rad"tz, chosen from his town of Nezhin. He would later play a major role in the conference.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab travels to Chernigov for delegate selection
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab traveled personally to Chernigov to lead the campaign for selecting two observant rabbis as gubernia representatives to the conference.
story_body: The Rebbe Rashab journeyed to Chernigov, accompanied by his son (the future Rebbe Rayatz), to manage the campaign for delegate selection. Knowing his own nephew Yitzchak Schneersohn was a candidate but not sufficiently God-fearing, he insisted that in matters of holiness, family ties carry no weight. He met with each rabbi and delegate individually to hear their views before sharing his own.

title_en: Compromise agreement on Chernigov delegates
summary_en: Yitzchak Schneersohn proposed and reached an agreement with the Rebbe Rashab to split the two Chernigov gubernia delegate seats — one for each camp.
story_body: On the morning of the assembly, Yitzchak Schneersohn came to the Rebbe Rashab's home immediately after prayers and proposed a compromise to avoid conflict: each side would get one delegate. The Rebbe's candidate Rabbi Mendel Chen of Nezhin would be elected, alongside one candidate from the opposing camp. The Rebbe, calculating the uncertainty of his less reliable supporters, accepted on the spot. Both delegates were subsequently elected from Chernigov gubernia.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab travels to Mohilev for delegate elections
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab personally traveled to Mohilev to campaign for the selection of observant delegates, staying at the home of philanthropist Reb Yehoshua Rozinkin.
story_body: The Rebbe Rashab journeyed to Mohilev to lead what was termed in local parlance a 'campaign' for delegate elections. The wealthy Reb Yehoshua Rozinkin built a new brick home for him with all new furnishings and even new silk bed coverings. Dignitaries of the city greeted the Rebbe at the train station with a carriage drawn by horses, as was customary for nobility.

title_en: Encouraging election results reported in Tevet
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab wrote that the bitter inter-party election struggle was producing favorable results, with the majority of those being elected being observant rabbis.
story_body: In Tevet, the Rebbe Rashab wrote to Rabbi Shilo (Hareshil"a) that the conflict between the parties was very intense, but that — God willing — the observant camp would prevail in the elections with a majority of kosher delegates. He noted that even the few elected were accomplishing much, and that opponents were also working hard from outside, requiring great effort on their part to rouse and act.

title_en: Election of 42 delegates to the Petersburg Rabbinical Conference
summary_en: Forty-two delegates were elected from the various gubernias of Russia for the Petersburg Rabbinical Conference, most of them God-fearing rabbis.
story_body: The election campaign concluded with 42 delegates chosen from across the gubernias of Russia, the majority of whom were observant rabbis. The Rebbe Rashab himself was elected as one of seven members of the conference's organizing committee. This represented a major victory for the religious camp after intensive campaigning.

title_en: Petersburg Rabbinical Conference convenes
summary_en: The Petersburg Rabbinical Conference began on 4 Adar Sheni and ran for about a month until 6 Nissan, with the Rebbe Rashab effectively leading the proceedings.
story_body: The Conference lasted approximately one month from 4 Adar Sheni to 6 Nissan 5670. The Rebbe Rashab dominated as the true leader, setting the tone and effectively directing the assembly despite formally remaining in the background. Because sessions had to be conducted in Russian and his fluency was limited, his views were articulated by Rabbi Mendel Chen of Nezhin, who excelled in Russian oratory, Talmudic learning, and piety. Henrich Sliozberg later wrote in his memoirs that the young Rebbe rarely spoke much, but every word demonstrated mastery over the masses; he was as immovable as stone on religious matters.

title_en: Three-way split on Russian rabbinic status at Petersburg Conference
summary_en: The Petersburg Rabbinical Conference split into three factions over what educational requirements should apply to officially recognized rabbis in Russia.
story_body: The central debate at the conference concerned the legal status of rabbis in Russia, who had not been government-recognized as spiritual leaders. The majority, led by Rabbi Chaim Ozer Grodzinski of Vilna, favored limited secular education and Russian language proficiency, with the rabbi also managing birth certificates. A twelve-member modernist minority led by the lawyer H. Sliozberg demanded broader secular education and refined Russian. An eight-member minority led by the Rebbe Rashab insisted that rabbis need only know Torah, with a separate clerk handling birth certificates. The conference elected a committee of three, including the Rebbe, to draft conclusions for the Interior Ministry's Religious Department.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab publishes 'Cheshbon Katzar' on Petersburg Conference
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab published a pamphlet 'Cheshbon Katzar' giving a detailed account of the Petersburg Rabbinical Conference and explaining the minority's reasoning.
story_body: At the conclusion of the conference, the Rebbe Rashab printed a booklet titled 'Cheshbon Katzar from the Petersburg Rabbinical Conference at the Rabbis' Assembly, 5670.' In the introduction he wrote that he wished to present to his brethren a short accounting of the conference's actions and clarify the various decisions and their reasoning. The pamphlet was published over the course of the summer of 5670.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab and Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik return to Petersburg
summary_en: In Iyar, the Rebbe Rashab and Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik returned to Petersburg, where communal needs required them to remain until late Sivan.
story_body: During the month of Iyar 5670, the Rebbe Rashab and Rabbi Chaim Soloveitchik of Brisk returned together to Petersburg. The state of communal affairs required them to remain in the capital through the end of Sivan. On the second day of Shavuot, Rabbi Chaim joined the Rebbe Rashab for the festive holiday meal, where they discussed words of Torah.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab travels to Petersburg in Cheshvan 5671
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab journeyed to Petersburg in Cheshvan 5671 to make final corrections to the Petersburg Conference protocol before its submission to the Interior Ministry.
story_body: After the official protocol was prepared, Baron David Gunzburg signed it and prepared to submit it, but fell ill with his final illness. The question arose of who would deliver the protocol to the head of the Religious Affairs Department at the Interior Ministry, and several corrections were still required. The Rebbe Rashab traveled to Petersburg in Cheshvan 5671 to handle these matters; the protocol was apparently submitted at that time.

title_en: Lawyer Ibsen completes memorandum on rabbinic status
summary_en: The Petersburg lawyer Ibsen finished preparing a memorandum on the status of rabbis in late Iyar 5671 after persistent prodding by the Rebbe Rashab.
story_body: The Rebbe Rashab had commissioned the Petersburg lawyer Ibsen to prepare a separate memorandum (doklad), apparently concerning rabbinic status, for submission to the Religious Affairs Department. The work dragged on until late Iyar 5671. Throughout the winter, the Rebbe repeatedly pressed Ibsen to finish, working through his son, Rabbi Shmuel Gourary, and Rabbi Menachem Mendel Chen. After completion, additional corrections were needed before submission to Chanan, head of the Religious Department.

title_en: Beilis affair derails planned rabbinic conference
summary_en: A second government-organized rabbinic conference scheduled for the winter of 5674 was derailed by the outbreak of the Beilis blood libel trial.
story_body: The Russian government had been preparing for a follow-up rabbinic conference to be held in the winter of 5674 (1913-1914). However, the Beilis blood libel affair erupted and threw the Jewish world into turmoil. The matter dragged on through the end of 5674, when World War I broke out, and the second rabbinic conference never materialized.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab convenes Moscow rabbinic assembly
summary_en: After the February 1917 Russian Revolution, the Rebbe Rashab worked to organize a religious united front, culminating in a Moscow rabbinic assembly in early Elul.
story_body: Following the collapse of the Tsarist regime and establishment of the Provisional Government in the winter of 5677, elections were planned for Jewish community councils and a general Jewish Congress to organize Jewish communal life. The Rebbe Rashab fought to organize a religious front against anti-religious factions. He pushed for an assembly of Torah giants in Russia, which Rabbi Chaim Ozer wanted to instead achieve through founding Agudas Yisrael branches. The assembly was ultimately convened in early Elul in Moscow, where the proposal to found a permanent rabbinical association was rejected by the participants.

title_en: Russian deportation of Jews from border provinces
summary_en: As the World War I front advanced into Russia in 1915, the Russian government ordered Jewish residents to leave their towns within 24 hours, displacing them to interior provinces.
story_body: During WWI, as the front line approached Jewish population centers in Russia, the government decreed that Jews must abandon their homes within 24 hours. This was carried out fully during the summers of 5675 and 5676, with Jews stripped of property and expelled from their towns. The refugees were assigned to five interior gubernias: Voronezh, Tambov, Penza, Crimea, and Yekaterinoslav. Although the decree was later rescinded, the Germans had by then captured the original Jewish areas, leaving the refugees stranded.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab founds religious aid committee in Petrograd
summary_en: In late winter 5676, after a rabbinic assembly in Petrograd, the Rebbe Rashab founded a religious committee to provide for the spiritual needs of WWI Jewish refugees.
story_body: The interior gubernias to which refugees had been displaced were outside the former Pale of Settlement and lacked synagogues, chadarim, mikvaot, and other religious institutions. The Rebbe Rashab traveled to Petrograd immediately after Purim 5676 to address this, organizing a special committee through an assembly of rabbis and activists. The committee, headed by Reb Shmuel Michel Trainin, worked to establish chadarim and Talmud Torahs, mikvaot, and to supply tefillin, tzitzit, and siddurim in the refugee locations.

title_en: R' Yaakov Landau dispatched as covert envoy to refugee towns
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab secretly sent Rabbi Yaakov Landau of Kornitz to assess the spiritual conditions of displaced Jews in Russia's interior.
story_body: The Rebbe Rashab dispatched Reb Yaakov Landau of Kornitz (later rabbi of Bnei Brak) as a covert emissary to survey the religious state of the Jewish refugees. Landau departed shortly after Purim 5676 for a month-long journey and was forbidden to reveal his mission to anyone. He returned about a week before Pesach and delivered his report to the Rebbe on the night of bedikat chametz at Rostov, having returned for Shabbat HaGadol as the Rebbe had commanded.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab campaigns for rabbinic exemption from conscription
summary_en: In summer 5676 the Rebbe Rashab began intensive efforts to obtain government exemption from military conscription for rabbis, shochtim, cantors and other religious functionaries.
story_body: In March 1916 (Adar Sheni 5676), the Russian Interior Minister sent a circular to provincial governors ordering police to identify serving rabbis and forward the lists for conscription review. Recognizing the catastrophe that would befall Jewish religious life if rabbis and shochtim were drafted, especially during wartime displacement, the Rebbe Rashab traveled to Petrograd to consult with local rabbis and activists. A memorandum was prepared for the Interior and War Ministers; though Mr. Markon delayed signing it through Pesach, Baron Alexander Gunzburg and lawyer Sliozberg eventually submitted their own memorandum on rabbinic exemption to the Interior Minister.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab travels to Petrograd to finalize rabbi exemption
summary_en: On 4 Iyar 5676 the Rebbe Rashab traveled (or prepared to travel) again to Petrograd to finalize lobbying for rabbinic and shochet exemption from military service.
story_body: On the 4th of Iyar 5676, the first day of Parshat Behar, the Rebbe Rashab prepared to journey again to Petrograd. The purpose was to bring to completion the lobbying efforts with government ministers to exempt rabbis and shochtim from military service. He returned home for the festival of Shavuot.

title_en: Partial rabbinic exemption granted by Russian government
summary_en: The Russian government agreed to exempt or extend exemption deferments for fifty rabbis on the lists, a small fraction of those awaiting decisions.
story_body: After persistent lobbying, the government granted exemption or extended deferments for approximately fifty rabbis on the conscription lists. This represented only a small fraction of those awaiting decisions, and it remained unclear whether the exemption came by direct Imperial decree or only by ministerial decision. The Rebbe Rashab immediately wrote to Reb Shmuel Michel Trainin to clarify the details and try to bring the matter before the Tsar.

title_en: Rabbis face conscription crisis over registration deadlines
summary_en: During summer 5676, rabbis who had missed initial conscription appearances faced refusal of their exemption status from military officials.
story_body: As the summer of 5676 progressed, the conscription appearance date arrived for rabbis. Most rabbis assumed they were not required to report, since provincial governors had already been instructed to submit lists of practicing rabbis. Military officials in Yekaterinoslav and apparently Minsk concurred, issuing exemption certificates pending clarification. However, other officials ruled that rabbis who failed to appear at the original call-up had forfeited their exemption. The Rebbe Rashab enlisted the prominent Petrograd lawyer Oskar Gruzenberg, who learned from Deputy Interior Minister Baltz that such rabbis would face trial for non-appearance but retained their underlying exemption rights.

title_en: Russian decree on conscription of displaced rabbis
summary_en: A second Russian government circular extended conscription registration requirements to displaced rabbis from border towns, complicating their exemption process.
story_body: While the initial conscription circular addressed only resident rabbis, a follow-up order extended the registration requirements to rabbis who had been displaced in summer 5675 from the border districts. These cases had to be processed through officials at the rabbis' original places of residence, from which they had been deported, severely impeding orderly clarification. Throughout summer 5676, the Rebbe Rashab continued to advocate for their status.

title_en: Petition over young rabbis' exemption status
summary_en: On 19 Tammuz 5676 the Rebbe Rashab protested to Reb Shmuel Michel Trainin that young rabbis under age 25 had been removed from the exemption list.
story_body: Reb Shmuel Michel Trainin reported through Reb Shmuel Gourary that the Director of the Religious Department had removed rabbis under age 25 from the exemption list. The Rebbe Rashab wrote that he could not understand why these rabbis should be excluded, since they had been certified by local police as serving rabbis. He argued that those who attained the rank of horaah at young ages were especially elevated, having dedicated all their days to Torah, and should not be excluded.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab begins effort to exempt rabbis from Russian army service
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab launched a sustained campaign during summer 1916 to secure military draft exemptions for Russian rabbis and shochtim.
story_body: From Sivan 5676 (mid-1916) through Tevet 5677, the Rebbe Rashab worked from Rostov to coordinate efforts through his agents in Petrograd — primarily R. Sh. M. Trainin, later joined by R. Eliezer Ginzburg of Moscow — to obtain draft exemptions for rabbis and ritual slaughterers (shochtim). Letters were written to government ministers, and attorney Oscar (Israel) Grosenberg was engaged. The effort was complicated by distinctions between holders of blue and white identity cards.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab requests consultation meeting in Petrograd
summary_en: On 18 Tammuz 5676 the Rebbe wrote to R. Sh. M. Trainin urging an organizational meeting to advance the rabbis' exemption.
story_body: In letter 1056 the Rebbe Rashab stressed that without a face-to-face gathering of activists, nothing would move forward. He asked the committee to decide whom to invite, when, and where, and to send invitation letters.

title_en: R. Eliezer Ginzburg of Moscow joins exemption effort
summary_en: On 20 Elul 5676 the Rebbe Rashab formally pulled R. Eliezer (Leib) Ginzburg of Moscow into the Petrograd rabbinical committee work.
story_body: The Rebbe wrote to Trainin asking that Ginzburg be summoned to Petrograd. Ginzburg eventually traveled there after Yom Kippur and made multiple trips, including a planned visit to Rostov to consult with the Rebbe in person.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab travels to Petrograd during February Revolution
summary_en: In Shevat 5677 the Rebbe Rashab traveled to Petrograd and remained there through Purim, during which the February Revolution toppled the Tsarist regime.
story_body: Having promised in mid-Tevet to travel within two weeks, the Rebbe arrived in Petrograd in Shevat and stayed until after Purim. During this period the February Revolution broke out, the Tsarist regime fell, and the democratic Provisional Government was established. No letters of his from Shevat-Adar 5677 survived.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab inquires about rabbis' exemption under Provisional Government
summary_en: On 22 Iyar 5677 the Rebbe wrote to Trainin expressing concern about renewed debate over rabbis' military status under the new democratic regime.
story_body: After the Provisional Government took power in winter 5677, discussion reopened on church-state separation and rabbinic conscription. The Rebbe wrote that he had long feared the question would resurface and was surprised no one had updated him from Petrograd.

title_en: Russian rabbis officially receive military exemption
summary_en: By Erev Rosh Hashanah 5678 the rabbis' draft exemption was officially confirmed and publicized in the Kiev press.
story_body: In letter 1071 the Rebbe Rashab announced the news, noting publication in Kiev newspapers that all rabbis — regardless of seniority or grade — held equal exemption rights. He praised the recognition of rabbinic status itself as a great good.

title_en: Rabbis assembly convenes in Moscow
summary_en: At the close of Av 5677 a rabbis' assembly met in Moscow and resolved to elect a committee preparing the All-Jewish Congress.
story_body: The assembly chose a committee to organize voting for Jewish community councils that would in turn elect the All-Jewish General Congress. It was decided the committee would sit in Petrograd alongside the general elections commission; the committee later relocated to Kharkov when Petrograd proved impractical.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab caught in Moscow during October Revolution
summary_en: Traveling toward Petrograd at the end of Marcheshvan 5678, the Rebbe was forced by the October Revolution to halt in Moscow and return to Rostov.
story_body: Invited by the Ministry of Religions for consultations in Petrograd, the Rebbe also planned to meet R. Chaim Ozer Grodzinski there to discuss a general rabbis' assembly. While en route the Bolshevik October Revolution broke out; he stayed Shabbos in Moscow and afterward returned to Rostov.

title_en: Elections to the All-Jewish General Congress
summary_en: Religious lists succeeded in the January 1918 (Shevat 5678) elections to the All-Jewish General Congress, but the Congress never convened.
story_body: Chabad's bloc 'Achdut' — number 3 on the ballot — was formed by merging with the religious lists 'Netzach Yisrael' and 'HaMasoret VeHaCheirut,' with the Rebbe's approval. In some places the Orthodox ran separately as 'Adas Yisrael' with a platform he composed. Despite electoral success, the subsequent consolidation of Bolshevik rule prevented the Congress from ever meeting.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab stays at Slavyansk healing waters
summary_en: From 9 Tammuz to 10 Elul 5678 the Rebbe stayed at the Slavyansk healing waters under harsh wartime travel conditions.
story_body: Amid the Russian Civil War, when travel was nearly impossible, the Rebbe made the one known journey of the period to the Slavyansk spa, arriving the eve of 9 Tammuz 5678 and remaining through 10 Elul. He wrote of overcrowded train cars, the unavailability of seat reservations, and dread about the return trip.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab dispatches secret emissary to Vitebsk and Lubavitch
summary_en: In Shevat 5679 the Rebbe sent a special emissary to Vitebsk, Petrograd and Moscow to learn the fate of his family and chassidim under Soviet rule.
story_body: By Rosh Chodesh Adar Sheni 5679 the emissary had still not returned. The Rebbe described in letter 1103 how he had heard nothing from his sister and brother-in-law in Vitebsk for nine months, that the Lubavitch courtyard and homes had been confiscated, libraries and furniture seized or smashed, and that the synagogue had been turned into a clubhouse 'out of vengeance.'

title_en: Passing of Rebbe Rashab in Rostov
summary_en: On Motzaei Shabbos Vayikra, the night of 2 Nissan 5680 at 3:30 AM, the Rebbe Rashab passed away in Rostov.
story_body: After years of organizing his father's manuscripts during the civil war, the fifth Lubavitcher Rebbe — Sholom Dovber Schneersohn — passed away in the early hours of 2 Nissan 5680 (March 21, 1920) and was buried in Rostov-on-Don. His son and successor, the Rebbe Rayatz, assumed the leadership of Chabad.

title_en: R. Shneur Zalman Slonim arrives at Lubavitch
summary_en: In summer 5645 (1885), the Rebbe Rashab's cousin R. Shneur Zalman Slonim arrived in Lubavitch from Hebron.
story_body: R. Shneur Zalman, son of R. Mordechai Dov Slonim of Hebron, came to Lubavitch and remained a substantial time. He later accompanied the Rebbe Rashab to Yalta for the winter and, on returning to Eretz Yisrael, was tasked with locating Chassidic manuscripts there.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab winters at Yalta healing waters
summary_en: Throughout the winter of 5646 (1885–1886) the Rebbe Rashab stayed at the Yalta healing waters, accompanied by R. Shneur Zalman Slonim.
story_body: The Rebbe traveled to the Crimean resort of Yalta for medical reasons and remained the entire winter. His cousin R. Shneur Zalman Slonim was with him throughout the stay, returning to Eretz Yisrael at the start of summer 5646.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab writes to R. Shabsai Shaftil seeking Alter Rebbe manuscripts
summary_en: On 11 Sivan 5646 the Rebbe Rashab wrote to the famed mashpia R. Shabsai Shaftil inquiring about the holy autograph manuscripts of the Alter Rebbe.
story_body: In letter 555 the Rebbe expressed his intense longing for the writings of the Alter Rebbe and asked Shaftil to update him on their status. The fate of these particular manuscripts remained unknown; a year later Shaftil sent him a manuscript of the Mitteler Rebbe instead.

title_en: Recovery of Mitteler Rebbe manuscripts via Yisrael Yaffe descendants
summary_en: After more than two years of searching, R. Shneur Zalman Slonim located descendants of the printer R. Yisrael Yaffe of Kopust and recovered substantial Mitteler Rebbe manuscripts.
story_body: Tasked by the Rebbe Rashab in 1886 to find descendants of R. Yisrael Yaffe, R. Shneur Zalman Slonim located them in Eretz Yisrael after over two years of investigation. Among the recovered manuscripts were large portions of the Mitteler Rebbe's Pirush HaMilos and unpublished sections related to Amrei Binah and Shaar HaTefillin, which the Rebbe Rashab acquired.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab writes to R. Avraham Dovid Lavut requesting manuscript
summary_en: On 8 Tishrei 5648 the Rebbe Rashab thanked R. Avraham Dovid Lavut for a holy autograph page and asked for the responsa manuscript of the Tzemach Tzedek's son.
story_body: The Rebbe wrote to the noted Chabad gaon Lavut — author of Kav Naki and Shaar HaKollel — expressing joy at receiving a page of holy autograph manuscript via Lavut's grandson R. M. A. Sh. He further requested that the grandson send the autograph responsa of R. Y. L. (Maharil) for the same reasons of preservation.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab employs scribe R. Shmuel Rabinovich to copy manuscripts
summary_en: On Monday of Parshas Vayakhel 5651 the Rebbe Rashab instructed his scribe R. Shmuel Rabinovich on which Chassidic discourses to copy.
story_body: The Rebbe sent a list specifying which texts to copy fully and which to merely examine, requesting the completed copies. He also arranged that R. Yitzchak Noach the shochet would obtain certain Maamarim from R. Baruch Tumarkin for copying, sent ten rubles, and asked Rabinovich to advise on the total fee.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab discusses division of father's books with son Rayatz
summary_en: On 18 Tevet 5670 the Rebbe Rashab wrote to his son the Rayatz about identifying books inherited from his father, the Rebbe Maharash.
story_body: In letter 282 the Rebbe Rashab described how the books from the Rebbe Maharash's private study could be identified by their bindings, and referenced an old list of how the books were divided among the brothers, which R. Nissan Skvolla still held. The autograph manuscripts had gone entirely to him as successor.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter to Rashaz Slonim about manuscripts in geniza
summary_en: On 8 Elul 5646, Rebbe Rashab writes to Rashaz Slonim instructing him to discreetly safeguard small-format manuscripts belonging to him found in a geniza.
story_body: This letter (Igros #556) marks the early phase of Rebbe Rashab's lifelong project of collecting manuscripts of his ancestors. He repeatedly emphasized that manuscripts in small format belonged to him personally. The correspondence with Rashaz Slonim about manuscript acquisition would continue for over 25 years.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter about firm pricing for manuscript acquisition
summary_en: On 22 Adar 5648, Rebbe Rashab cautions Rashaz Slonim against showing excessive enthusiasm when buying manuscripts, urging measured pricing.
story_body: Rashaz Slonim had begun overpaying for manuscripts after recognizing the Rebbe's intense desire for them. In this letter (Igros #562), Rebbe Rashab teaches that internal passion must be limited externally so sellers don't inflate prices. The principle was that emotional restraint preserves the practical ability to keep acquiring.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab rebukes Rashaz Slonim for overpaying for a manuscript book
summary_en: On 11 Nisan 5650, Rebbe Rashab tells Rashaz Slonim that paying over 100 rubles for a manuscript was excessive and that such buying would deplete any fortune.
story_body: After receiving a manuscript book sent via Rashaz's father, Rebbe Rashab expressed astonishment at the price paid (Igros #39). He warned that buying at any price would not only exhaust all means but also prevent assembling the truly essential manuscripts. He reaffirmed his core principle: manuscripts are the very life of his soul, yet acquisition must remain within limits.

title_en: Death of R' Avraham Mertzbacher, owner of major Munich book collection
summary_en: On 21 Sivan 5645, R' Avraham Mertzbacher of Munich died, leaving his son a collection of 156 manuscripts, 4,332 antique books, and 43 incunabula.
story_body: Mertzbacher had built his renowned bibliophile collection from 1866-1885 through Rabbi Raphael Nathan Rabinowitz, who used the books for his Dikdukei Sofrim project. After his death, his son Dr. Isaac Mertzbacher sought to sell the collection, which would later attract Rebbe Rashab's interest as a potential Jewish library acquisition.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab travels to Worishofen for medical waters
summary_en: In winter 5661, Rebbe Rashab traveled to the healing springs of Worishofen, where he met Dr. Isaac Mertzbacher and learned of the available Munich collection.
story_body: During this medical trip abroad, Rebbe Rashab encountered the son of the late R' Avraham Mertzbacher, who wished to sell his father's library. This chance meeting sparked Rebbe Rashab's multi-year effort to purchase the Munich collection and create a Jewish library in observant hands.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab requests Rabinowitz catalog for Mertzbacher purchase
summary_en: On the 5th day of Chanukah 5661, Rebbe Rashab wrote from abroad asking his son to send him the Rabinowitz book catalog and his personal book list.
story_body: Following his meeting with Dr. Mertzbacher, Rebbe Rashab needed reference materials to evaluate the collection's worth (Igros #677). The Rabinowitz catalog was particularly valuable because its pricing was considered authoritative. This launched the years-long negotiations over the Munich library.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter to R' Yeshaya Berlin about Mertzbacher collection
summary_en: On 4 Shevat 5661, Rebbe Rashab estimated the Munich collection price at 35,000-40,000 rubles and tried to enlist R' Yeshaya Berlin of Riga as funder.
story_body: In this letter (Igros #691), Rebbe Rashab described the pricing methodology based on the Rabinowitz catalog. He noted that Baron David Ginzburg would acquire such manuscripts at any cost without hesitation. The goal was to keep this Jewish treasure in observant hands rather than letting it pass to secular collectors.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab requests catalog return after Mertzbacher silence
summary_en: On 26 Shevat 5661, Rebbe Rashab reported that Hirshenger of Munich had requested his catalog back on Dr. Mertzbacher's behalf, pressing for a decision.
story_body: The lack of response was puzzling the Munich seller. Rebbe Rashab needed Yeshaya Berlin's definitive answer—whether he intended to fund the purchase or had abandoned the idea (Igros #697). The acquisition negotiations were stalling.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab instructs son on guarding manuscripts during Kamenka trip
summary_en: On 27 Iyar 5661, Rebbe Rashab wrote to his son Rebbe Rayatz with detailed instructions for appointing guards over the manuscripts before traveling to a Kamenka wedding.
story_body: Rebbe Rashab took manuscript security with utmost gravity (Igros #737). He asked his son to appoint constant guards with full devotion to protecting the manuscripts, including from theft. He also asked the family matriarch to oversee security generally.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab follow-up letter on manuscript security
summary_en: On 20 Menachem Av 5661, Rebbe Rashab pressed his son for immediate confirmation on who had been appointed to guard the manuscripts.
story_body: Rebbe Rashab noticed his son had failed to mention manuscript security arrangements in previous letters (Igros #765). He demanded immediate reply on who was guarding them and where the keys had been entrusted. The intensity reflects how central the manuscript archive was to his life's work.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab proposes Riga as home for Mertzbacher library
summary_en: On the eve of 25 Adar 5662, Rebbe Rashab urged R' Yeshaya Berlin to purchase the Munich library and house it in 3-4 rooms of his Riga home for Torah study.
story_body: Rebbe Rashab clarified his vision: the priority was that an important Jewish library exist in observant hands, even if located in Riga rather than Russia or Lubavitch (Igros #782). He proposed dedicating 2-3 rooms for books and one for study. He also approached R' Yaakov Horowitz of Riga as a possible co-funder.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab vision of Torah library in Riga
summary_en: On 10 Menachem Av 5662, Rebbe Rashab argued that since secular Jews maintain great libraries for ulterior motives, a G-d-fearing man should spend a few thousand to enable Jewish study.
story_body: Rebbe Rashab pushed Yeshaya Berlin to dedicate part of his large Riga home to a Jewish library where observant Jews could come and learn. He emphasized this would be 'a benefit to him and a benefit to the world.' Despite extensive negotiations, the Mertzbacher acquisition ultimately fell through.

title_en: Husiatin firm prints Otzar Klei Chemdah manuscript catalog
summary_en: In 5666, the Husiatin partnership of R' L. Shvager and R' D. Frenkel printed a catalog called 'Otzar Klei Chemdah' listing rare manuscripts on parchment and paper for sale.
story_body: The booksellers and manuscript dealers issued this catalog to market rare manuscripts. Rebbe Rashab obtained a copy and marked 22 manuscripts with stars indicating those he wished to purchase, with handwritten notes on the descriptions. The catalog itself is preserved in the Chabad library.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter to son on Husiatin manuscript purchases
summary_en: On 11 Nisan 5667, Rebbe Rashab directed his son which kabbalistic manuscripts to prioritize from the Husiatin catalog, including Sefer HaKavanot and Livnat HaSapir.
story_body: The Rebbe identified specific manuscripts worth pursuing (Igros #961), suspecting Livnat HaSapir might be the autograph of R' Avraham Saba based on a marginal signature. Eighteen of the marked manuscripts were ultimately acquired and now hold catalog numbers 1972-1989 in the library. Each purchased volume bears Rebbe Rayatz's notation: 'This we bought.'

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter to son on manuscript security via R' Elchanan
summary_en: On 11 Adar 5674, Rebbe Rashab instructed his son to entrust manuscript security to R' Elchanan, who should sleep in the manuscript room with other yeshiva students.
story_body: Continuing his pattern of manuscript security instructions during his absences (Igros #428), Rebbe Rashab insisted on having designated guardians physically present overnight. The yeshiva students would sleep in the manuscript room to ensure continuous protection.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter to Rashaz Slonim acknowledging manuscript shipment
summary_en: On 22 Elul 5672, Rebbe Rashab confirmed receipt of a precious manuscript including Birkat Chatanim by the Mitteler Rebbe, calling it deeply meaningful.
story_body: After 25 years of correspondence with Rashaz Slonim about manuscript collection (Igros #344), Rebbe Rashab expressed his desire that Rashaz continue sending such precious materials regularly. The Birkat Chatanim manuscript was catalogued as #1194 and printed in Maamarei Admur Ha'emtza'i Droshei Chatuna Vol. 1, p. 146.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter acknowledging additional manuscript shipment
summary_en: On 14 Cheshvan 5674, Rebbe Rashab acknowledged with deep gratitude another shipment of manuscripts received complete from Rashaz Slonim.
story_body: In this letter (Igros #1044), Rebbe Rashab praised the shipment as a great matter and credited Rashaz with great merit for his role. The lifelong manuscript-collection partnership remained productive into the years just before World War I.

title_en: Arrest of Rebbe Rayatz with house search in Petersburg
summary_en: In 5687, Soviet authorities arrested Rebbe Rayatz in Petersburg, conducting a house search where investigators examined manuscripts and antique books in the library.
story_body: During the search, officials did not open the cabinets containing the Rebbeim's manuscripts but inquired whose handwriting they were. They showed particular interest in one cabinet of antique manuscripts including Livnat HaSapir by R' Avraham Saba and the Shemoneh Shearim by R' Shmuel Vital, plus first-edition printed books like the 1476 Ralbag and 1489 Ramban. The interest, however, was only superficial.

title_en: Library visitor publishes description in HaOlam London
summary_en: On 22 Elul 5688, the London journal HaOlam published a visitor's account of the Lubavitch library highlighting its manuscript treasures and incunabula.
story_body: The visitor described a 440-year-old manuscript by R' Avraham Saba (author of Tzror HaMor), Ralbag's 1476 Torah commentary, and a Ramban printed in Lisbon in 1489. The published descriptions help corroborate which volumes were in the collection at that time, including the eight-volume Shemoneh Shearim autograph by R' Shmuel Vital.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz organizes his father's manuscript archive
summary_en: In 5680, after his father's passing, Rebbe Rayatz organized Rebbe Rashab's manuscripts by year and prepared comprehensive indexes for the collection.
story_body: Rebbe Rayatz catalogued 1,173 maamarei Chassidus surviving in Rebbe Rashab's own handwriting and documented an estimated 700-800 additional maamarim recorded only by the chozrim. He preserved hundreds of original letters and acquired letters from their recipients, eventually amassing some 2,000 letters of his father by 1927. Twenty-five volumes of these maamarim were eventually published as Sefer HaMaamarim 5643-5680.

title_en: Letter showing Rebbe Maharash books still undivided among heirs
summary_en: In 5653, Rebbe Rashab's letter to R' Yitzchak Dovber Vilenski indicates that the printed books from Rebbe Maharash's estate had not yet been divided among the sons.
story_body: Following Rebbe Maharash's passing, the printed book collection remained in his house for over a decade before being divided. This letter is one of the data points indicating that division did not happen immediately after his passing.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter mentions books still stored in sacks
summary_en: On 19 Menachem Av 5655, Rebbe Rashab wrote that 'in my home the books are lying in sacks,' suggesting recent division but not yet shelved.
story_body: This letter (Igros #64) indicates that the division of inherited books from Rebbe Maharash's estate had likely occurred during 5655, but the Rebbe had not yet built cabinets and shelved them. The systematic library organization would begin in earnest by 5660.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter from Charkov on shelving books
summary_en: On 22 Tevet 5660, Rebbe Rashab wrote from Charkov to his son in Lubavitch asking whether the books had been placed on shelves and about a Petersburg book shipment.
story_body: By 5660, Rebbe Rashab had begun the active phase of completing missing volumes and organizing books in cabinets (Igros #90). This represents the beginning of the systematic Lubavitch library construction that would continue for two decades.

title_en: R' Shmuel Vital begins writing Shemoneh Shearim in Damascus
summary_en: In 5409, R' Shmuel Vital began writing in Damascus the eight-volume Shemoneh Shearim manuscript of his father R' Chaim Vital's teachings of the Arizal.
story_body: R' Shmuel Vital completed the eight-volume autograph of the Shaarim between 5409 and 5413 (1649-1653), noting his location and date in each volume. The set was acquired for the Lubavitch library and catalogued as numbers 1942-1949. It was one of the manuscript treasures that drew Soviet interest during the 1927 search.

title_en: Shmuel Wiener invited to Lubavitch to help organize the library
summary_en: The renowned bibliographer Shmuel Wiener was invited to Lubavitch to assist in organizing the Rebbe Rashab's library.
story_body: Around 5673 (1913), the famous bibliographer Shmuel Wiener was brought to Lubavitch specifically to help arrange the library. According to R' Chaim Liberman's account, Wiener was given two weeks off from his work, and the Rebbe Rayatz asked him to come for a short time to view the books. He ended up staying only about a week.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter on book duplicates and library organization
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab wrote to his son about handling duplicate books in the library and identifying volumes inherited from his father.
story_body: In Tevet 5674 (January 1914), the Rebbe Rashab wrote multiple letters to his son the Rebbe Rayatz about library matters. He addressed which duplicate books could be sold to R' Meir Lubak on behalf of R' M.G., emphasizing that books inherited from his father, the Rebbe Maharash, should not be sold. He requested a list of duplicates with prices be sent to the buyer.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter on book spacing in library shelves
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab wrote that library books should not be packed too tightly on shelves to prevent damage.
story_body: On 15 Tevet 5674 (January 13, 1914), the Rebbe Rashab wrote to his son expressing satisfaction with the library organization. He instructed that books should not stand crowded and crammed together, as this damages them by preventing air circulation. While they need not be as spaciously arranged as Wiener had set them, they should not be packed tightly.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter on cataloging library books by subject
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab requested a topical catalog be made of the library's contents.
story_body: On 21 Tevet 5674 (January 19, 1914), the Rebbe Rashab wrote to his son expressing his long-standing desire for a subject-based catalog of the library. He wanted a list showing which general topics appeared in which books, such as the category of Torah. He hoped Moshe Chaim could create such a list, and had originally wanted Wiener to do it.

title_en: Catalog of Rebbe Rashab's book collection compiled
summary_en: A catalog listing 5,642 entries from the Rebbe Rashab's book collection was compiled.
story_body: During 5675 (1915), a catalog was apparently prepared of the books in the Rebbe Rashab's library, listing 5,642 numbered entries representing approximately 12,000 volumes. The work began in early 5673 but the surviving list, which includes books printed up to 5670, was likely completed during 5675 since the books were placed in storage at the start of 5676. The catalog counted multi-volume sets like Shas as single entries.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter on starting library catalog
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab expressed satisfaction that work had begun on organizing books and making a catalog.
story_body: On Erev Rosh Chodesh Shevat 5673 (January 1913), the Rebbe Rashab wrote to his son expressing pleasure that the books had been organized and a catalog made. He instructed that a copy of the list should be sent to Shmuel Wiener, who had assisted the Rebbe in selecting valuable books for the library.

title_en: R' Meir Heilperin letter on book selection for Rashab
summary_en: Book dealer R' Meir Heilperin wrote about cataloging books for selection by the Rebbe Rashab.
story_body: On 16 Elul 5672 (August 29, 1912), book dealer R' Meir Heilperin wrote requesting that R' M. Rabinowitz catalog all available books, both new and old half-quires, not just rare ones, so he could select what the Rebbe Rashab needed. The letter suggests Heilperin had already visited Lubavitch and examined the library during summer 5672.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab purchases books in Königswart
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab purchased rare Prague-printed books from a synagogue caretaker in Königswart.
story_body: On 10 Tammuz 5668 (July 9, 1908), the Rebbe Rashab wrote from Marienbad about visiting the small nearby town of Königswart with R' N. Gur-Aryeh and R' Z. Persitz. They found an old synagogue with an ancient Torah scroll, and from the caretaker he purchased several Prague-printed books including Chok L'Yisrael, Mesorat HaBrit HaKatan, Gevul Binyamin, and Horeh Gever.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab forced to flee Lubavitch due to WWI
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab and his family were forced to flee Lubavitch as the German army approached.
story_body: At the start of 5676 (1915), during World War I, as the German army approached the Lubavitch area, the Rebbe Rashab and his household were forced to flee. The decision to leave Lubavitch was made during Tishrei 5676, with the primary concern being how to transport the book collection. The Rebbe took the manuscript collection with him to Rostov but stored the printed books elsewhere.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter on plans to send books to Nizhny
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab wrote of plans to send the library books to Nizhny for safekeeping.
story_body: On 27 Tishrei 5676 (October 5, 1915), the Rebbe Rashab wrote to R' Shmuel Michel Trainin that he might travel from Lubavitch within a few weeks with his entire household. He planned to send the books, which were numerous, for safekeeping and could not delay until the last moment. His initial plan was to send them to Nizhny, though they ultimately went to Moscow.

title_en: Library books transferred to storage in Moscow
summary_en: The Lubavitch library's printed books were packed and sent to storage in Moscow during WWI.
story_body: During Cheshvan 5676 (late 1915), all the printed books were packed into crates and sent for safekeeping, ultimately to Moscow rather than Nizhny as originally planned. The 5,430 numbered items (approximately 12,000 volumes) were placed in a secure storage facility protected against fire, water, and theft. The books were stored in the warehouses of the chassid R' Zalkind Persitz in the Kukurov district of Moscow.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab passes away in Rostov
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab passed away in Rostov on the night of 2 Nissan 5680.
story_body: On Motzaei Shabbos Vayikra, the early morning of Sunday 2 Nissan 5680 (March 21, 1920) at 3:30 AM, the Rebbe Rashab passed away in Rostov-on-Don. In his final years he had occupied himself extensively with arranging the manuscript collection of his ancestors. Shortly before his passing he told the surrounding chassidim 'I am going to heaven, the writings I leave to you.'

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz born in Lubavitch
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz, Yosef Yitzchak, was born in Lubavitch on 12 Tammuz 5640.
story_body: The Rebbe Rayatz, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, was born on 12 Tammuz 5640 (1880) in Lubavitch. He would later become the sixth Rebbe of Chabad. His birthday of 12 Tammuz would also become significant as the date of his liberation from Soviet imprisonment decades later.

title_en: Bar Mitzvah of Rebbe Rayatz in Lubavitch
summary_en: The bar mitzvah of the Rebbe Rayatz was held in the great hall of the Rebbes' courtyard in Lubavitch.
story_body: In summer 5653 (1893), the bar mitzvah of the future Rebbe Rayatz was held in the great hall of the Rebbes' courtyard in Lubavitch. The same great hall would later host his wedding four years later.

title_en: Wedding of Rebbe Rayatz and founding of Tomchei Temimim
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz married and was appointed director of the newly founded Tomchei Temimim yeshiva.
story_body: At the end of 5657 (1897), the wedding of the Rebbe Rayatz took place in the great hall of the Rebbes' courtyard in Lubavitch. Immediately after the wedding, the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva was founded, and he was appointed as its director. After the wedding, an additional room was built onto his father's house for his residence.

title_en: City authorities seize Lubavitch courtyard buildings
summary_en: After the last yeshiva students left Lubavitch, the city authorities took over the Rebbes' courtyard.
story_body: At the end of 5678 (1918), after the last Tomchei Temimim students left Lubavitch, the municipality seized the courtyard. The great hall was converted into the city theater, the Rashab's house became the court building, the Maharash's rooms became the city council, the Rayatz's rooms became municipal offices, and the brick house became the city school.

title_en: Fire destroys all buildings in Lubavitch courtyard
summary_en: All the buildings in the Rebbes' courtyard in Lubavitch burned down at the start of Nissan 5681.
story_body: In the early days of Nissan 5681 (April 1921), one year after the passing of the Rebbe Rashab and between his yahrzeit and that of the Tzemach Tzedek, fire destroyed all the buildings in the Rebbes' courtyard in Lubavitch. The fire consumed everything within half an hour, including the beis midrash with all its Torah scrolls, and spread to the market and many streets. When the Rebbe Rayatz visited in summer 5682, he was shocked by the desolate scene.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab letter on destruction in Lubavitch
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab wrote about the seizure and destruction of property in the Lubavitch courtyard.
story_body: On Rosh Chodesh Adar Sheni 5679 (1919), the Rebbe Rashab wrote about events in Lubavitch: the courtyard and houses had been confiscated and great destruction wrought. Book crates, cabinets, and furniture had been taken and much was broken. Valuable utensils worth great sums were left behind, and they had reportedly turned the brick house into a club out of spite.

title_en: MKva restoration funds sent to Lubavitch
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz sent funds to Lubavitch for the restoration of the destroyed mikvah.
story_body: At the start of 5682 (1921), after the mikvah building in Lubavitch had been destroyed in the fire, the Rebbe Rayatz sent the remaining community a sum of money for its restoration. At that time several chassidim still lived in Lubavitch and had moved the synagogue to the brick house.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz visits Lubavitch to pray at ancestral graves
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz visited Lubavitch on Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5682 to pray at the ancestral graves.
story_body: On Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5682 (August 24, 1922), the Rebbe Rayatz traveled to Lubavitch to pray at the holy graves of his ancestors. During his stay, he delivered a chassidic discourse in the synagogue located in the brick house. This was the only time he visited Lubavitch after assuming the leadership of Chabad.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz letter on visiting Lubavitch graves
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz wrote to his uncle about arranging repairs to the ohel in Lubavitch.
story_body: On 5 Cheshvan 5689 (September 19, 1928), the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to his uncle Rabbi Moshe Leib Ginsburg about restoration efforts at the ohel of the Tzemach Tzedek and the Rebbe Maharash. R' Yechiel Chazan had written that the ohel needed major repairs. The Rebbe asked how much the repairs would cost so he could help arrange them.

title_en: Nazi massacre of Lubavitch Jews
summary_en: The Nazis murdered 630 Jews of Lubavitch in a mass grave during World War II.
story_body: After the Nazis conquered Lubavitch during World War II, around 5701 (1941), they found 630 Jews remaining—men, women, and children. They dug a mass grave and in a single day shot them all to death. By 5700 (1940), only about 120 Jewish families had remained in the town, as many had left when the courtyard and yeshiva closed.

title_en: Rebbe inquires about ohel restoration in Lubavitch
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz wrote from 770 inquiring about the state of the ohel in Lubavitch.
story_body: On 5 Marcheshvan 5709 (November 7, 1948), while living in 770 in New York, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to R' Yonah Eidelkop inquiring about the ohel in Lubavitch. He asked about arrangements for repairs and indicated that he would cover all related expenses. He requested information on what repairs were needed.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes about Lubavitch ohel state
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz wrote to R' Moshe Yitzchak Zuskewitz asking about the state of the ohelim in Lubavitch.
story_body: On 4 Shevat 5709 (February 3, 1949), the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to R' Moshe Yitzchak Zuskewitz requesting detailed information about the ohelim of the Tzemach Tzedek and the Rebbe Maharash in Lubavitch. He asked whether they needed repairs, how much such repairs would cost, and through whom such work could be arranged. He requested that this be handled discreetly without mentioning his name.

title_en: R' David Gurevitch restores Lubavitch tombstones
summary_en: R' David Gurevitch traveled from Samarkand to Lubavitch to restore the destroyed tombstones.
story_body: In 5726 (1966), the first opportunity arose for chassidim to visit Lubavitch. R' David Gurevitch traveled from distant Samarkand to Lubavitch and re-erected the destroyed tombstones of the Tzemach Tzedek and the Rebbe Maharash. Many of the cemetery's tombstones had previously been stolen by locals for use as building foundations.

title_en: Tomchei Temimim Moscow students seek Rebbe's approval for Lubavitch house
summary_en: Students from Tomchei Temimim Moscow sought the Rebbe's approval to purchase a house in Lubavitch.
story_body: At the start of 5749 (late 1988), yeshiva students from Tomchei Temimim in Moscow contacted the Rebbe's secretariat requesting approval to purchase a house in the town of Lubavitch. Within a few days, they received the Rebbe's response along with several hundred dollars as his participation in the purchase. The Rebbe wanted to be personally involved in establishing a Chabad presence in Lubavitch.

title_en: Beis Chabad house purchased in Lubavitch
summary_en: A house was purchased in Lubavitch on 21 Marcheshvan 5749 to serve as a Beis Chabad.
story_body: On 20 Marcheshvan 5749 (November 1988), the yeshiva students traveled to Lubavitch to find a house for sale. After a day of searching, they found the only house available for purchase, and on 21 Marcheshvan it was purchased in the name of student Nachum Tamarin. They added the inscription '770 - Beis Chabad' on the gate. The Rebbe subsequently called it 'Beis Schneersohn.'

title_en: Ohel rebuilt in Lubavitch
summary_en: The ohel in Lubavitch was rebuilt by R' David Nachshon and R' Avi Taub.
story_body: In 5749 (1989), the ohel in Lubavitch was rebuilt anew by R' David Nachshon and R' Avi Taub. From that time onward, more chassidim began traveling to Lubavitch to visit the Rebbes' courtyard and pray at their gravesites.

title_en: First portion of Lubavitch courtyard purchased for museum
summary_en: R' Natan Gurary purchased part of the Rebbes' courtyard in Lubavitch to build a museum.
story_body: In 5756 (1996), R' Natan Gurary purchased part of the Rebbes' courtyard in Lubavitch in order to build a museum on the site. He would later purchase additional portions in 5758 (1998), and the final third portion in 5760 (2000).

title_en: Lubavitch museum building completed
summary_en: The museum building in the center of the Lubavitch courtyard was completed and opened to the public.
story_body: At the start of Nissan 5761 (2001), the construction of the museum building in the center of the Rebbes' courtyard in Lubavitch was completed. The museum was then opened to the public, marking the restoration of an active Jewish presence in the historic town.

title_en: Rayatz writes letter recalling lifelong passion for collecting books
summary_en: Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak (Rayatz) writes in a letter on Rosh Chodesh Iyar 5690 that he has been a collector of books since his youth.
story_body: In a letter dated Rosh Chodesh Iyar 5690 (Iggeres 3837), the Rebbe Rayatz reflects on himself, noting that there are those who learn from books, those who read books, and those who collect them — and that he has been a collector since his earliest years. This statement frames a lifelong project of acquiring and preserving Jewish books that paralleled his father Rebbe Rashab's library work in Lubavitch.

title_en: Rayatz writes to Yaakov Yosef Slonim about buying books in Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz writes the first of several letters to R. Yaakov Yosef Slonim arranging the purchase of rare seforim through dealers in the Holy Land.
story_body: On the Tuesday of Parashas Pinchas 5664, Rayatz sends Slonim a list of 47 books he is willing to buy from a Jerusalem dealer for 92 rubles and 40 kopeks, asking him to negotiate the prices down. He emphasizes interest specifically in old editions and requests that the seller send lists of antique seforim, not new ones. He also asks Slonim to obtain addresses of dealers in Algiers, where he had heard cheap acquisitions were possible.

title_en: Rayatz forwards Nachum Etrog's Jerusalem book list to Slonim
summary_en: On erev Shabbos Vayetze 5665, Rayatz sends R. Yaakov Yosef Slonim a long list of seforim he wants to purchase from the Jerusalem dealer Nachum Etrog.
story_body: Rayatz writes that he has obtained an extensive list from Nachum Etrog in Jerusalem and is sending it to Slonim with prices marked according to his own knowledge and his various catalogs. He explains his priorities: the chief interest is rare books from first printings, with Kabbalah works first, then responsa, then poskim. He also urges Slonim to search the genizah of Jerusalem — and especially Chevron — for manuscripts of the Chabad Rebbes, particularly the Mitteler Rebbe.

title_en: Rayatz sends Slonim third book list extending to letter mem
summary_en: On the 2nd of Adar Sheni 5665, the Rebbe Rayatz sends Slonim the continuation of book lists, now covering through letter mem.
story_body: This third surviving letter in the Slonim correspondence shows that Rayatz's book-acquisition project in the Holy Land was systematic and alphabetical. The lists were being worked through letter by letter, with only the first installment (alef to ches) preserved in detail and this letter extending the project through mem.

title_en: Rashab writes from Lubavitch that Rayatz's books are intact
summary_en: On 11 Nissan 5667, Rebbe Rashab writes to his son Rayatz from Lubavitch reassuring him that his personal book collection is intact and in order.
story_body: Both the Rashab and the Rayatz spent most of 5667 abroad. The Rashab returned to Lubavitch for Pesach and wrote on 11 Nissan that 'your books are intact and stand in order as they were.' He repeated the reassurance about Rayatz's separate personal library on 24 Nissan, underlining that father and son maintained distinct collections in the Lubavitch library.

title_en: Rashab inquires after Rayatz's manuscript and book purchases
summary_en: On 24 Nissan 5667, Rashab writes Rayatz again about books and asks for news of manuscript and book acquisitions, including from Husiatyn.
story_body: In addition to repeating that Rayatz's books in Lubavitch are still in their place, Rashab inquires about the status of manuscripts being sought from Husiatyn and asks whether the list sent to Eretz Yisrael has produced any response. This pattern of detailed book-purchase oversight runs through many of the Rashab-Rayatz letters of this period.

title_en: Rashab from Menton objects to merging Rayatz's books into his library
summary_en: While in Menton, France in winter 5670, Rashab responds to Rayatz's plan to add his personal books to his father's collection, expressing mixed feelings.
story_body: While the Lubavitch books were being arranged in cabinets during the winter of 5670, Rayatz wished to fill out his father's collection from his own private holdings. Rashab, writing from Menton, replies that while he enjoys the completion, he is concerned that books be available in Rayatz's own room for casual learning. The episode marks the formal occasion when Rayatz instructed his bookbinder to emboss his initials 'yud-shin' in gold on the spines of his volumes to distinguish his collection.

title_en: Rayatz asks Eliyahu Simpson for weekly written summaries of Rashab's maamarim
summary_en: On 20 Tammuz 5673, Rayatz writes from his travels to chozer R. Eliyahu Simpson asking for weekly written summaries of his father's Shabbos maamarim.
story_body: While traveling and unable to hear Rashab's discourses himself, Rayatz writes Simpson to send him each week a brief outline of the Shabbos maamar — the opening, the conclusion, and the connective content, rather than a full hanachah. He asks Simpson to coordinate with fellow chozrim Alter and Yerucham to ensure the reports arrive consistently at the address provided.

title_en: Lubavitch library packed and sent to storage in Moscow
summary_en: When the Rashab evacuated Lubavitch at the start of 5676, the library's print collection was crated and sent to the Kokorev warehouses in Moscow for safekeeping.
story_body: With the front of World War I advancing, the Rashab left Lubavitch carrying only his most-used books and the manuscript collection, sending the printed seforim to Moscow for storage. The crates were deposited at the warehouses of the wealthy chassid R. Zalkind Persitz. They would never return to family control: the warehouses were nationalized and the books transferred to state libraries, beginning the decades-long struggle to recover them.

title_en: Pavel Papov reports on the Schneersohn book collection in Moscow
summary_en: On March 1, 1920, Pavel Papov files a report on the Schneersohn collection stored at the Kokorev warehouses in Moscow.
