Chaim Ozer's leadership reserve at least one hundred for Tomchei Tmimim talmidim and their rashei yeshiva. This was part of a parallel track to the American visa effort.

title_en: Letter to Rabbi Herzog on Palestine certificates for Polish yeshiva students
summary_en: On 1 Iyar 5700 the Rebbe Rayatz again wrote to Chief Rabbi Herzog asking that a portion of the new certificates be placed at his disposal for Lubavitch students still in Poland.
story_body: With the British certificates being prepared for Polish yeshiva students, the Rebbe pressed Rabbi Herzog to reserve a known number for him personally to allocate to Tomchei Tmimim talmidim, some still in Poland and some already rescued. He also wrote the same day to R. Chanoch Hendel Havlin in Eretz Yisrael coordinating the request through R. Chaim Ozer.

title_en: Letter to Rabbi Meir Ashkenazi of Shanghai on transit visas
summary_en: On 27 Sivan 5700 the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to Rabbi Meir Ashkenazi, rabbi of Shanghai, exploring rescue of the Vilna students via transit visas through China.
story_body: With the Atlantic route closed, the Rebbe asked Rabbi Ashkenazi to obtain transit visas for the students so they could travel through Russia and on to Shanghai en route to America. This Far East route would soon prove the only viable corridor and would shape the entire rescue plan that followed.

title_en: Sugihara issues Japanese transit visas to Mir and Tomchei Tmimim students
summary_en: In summer 5700 Japanese consul Chiune Sugihara in Kovno issued transit visas to yeshiva students, including Tomchei Tmimim talmidim, on the advice of the Amshinover Rebbe.
story_body: Mir students from Holland first obtained Dutch visas to Curacao and then Japanese transit visas through Sugihara in Kovno. The Amshinover Rebbe, R. Shimon Shalom Kalish, urged the rest of the refugees to follow suit. After telegraphing the Rebbe Rayatz, the Tomchei Tmimim students did the same and obtained Japanese transit visas before the consulate closed when Lithuania was absorbed into the Soviet Union.

title_en: Soviet annexation of Lithuania closes Kovno consulates
summary_en: In summer 5700 Lithuania ceased to exist as an independent state and became part of the Soviet Union, forcing the Japanese consulate in Kovno to close.
story_body: Sugihara told the refugees he was being recalled because Lithuania was no longer independent and a Japanese consul existed in Moscow. Before leaving he reportedly entrusted his stamp to a yeshiva student so that hundreds more passports could still be stamped with transit visas after the consulate officially closed.

title_en: 52 US visas secured for Tomchei Tmimim students
summary_en: On 16 Elul 5700 the Rebbe Rayatz reported that 52 student visas and 47 rabbinic visas had been obtained for entry to the United States.
story_body: Writing to R. Yaakov Katz, the Rebbe announced the breakthrough that 52 entry permits for students and 47 for rabbis, their families and rashei yeshiva had been secured. The first list contained mostly senior Tomchei Tmimim talmidim from the Otwock branch and became the basis of the first rescue convoy through Russia and Japan.

title_en: US Interior Department forwards visa list to Moscow and Tokyo embassies
summary_en: On 31 October 1940 the US Interior Department notified the Rebbe Rayatz that the approved visa name list had been sent to the US embassies in Moscow and Tokyo.
story_body: Because of wartime conditions the visas could not be issued at the US embassy in Lithuania. Washington forwarded copies of the approved names to Moscow, where students could collect them in transit, and also to Tokyo as a fallback for any who failed to obtain them in Moscow.

title_en: Letter to R. David Meir Rabinowitz on Moscow visa pickup
summary_en: On 4 Marcheshvan 5701 the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to R. David Meir Rabinowitz of Boston that the Vilna students had been summoned to the US consulate in Moscow to receive their visas.
story_body: The Rebbe described receiving a cable from his students in Vilna reporting that each had been told to come to Moscow to collect his American visa, and pleaded for immediate fundraising to pay for steamship tickets and travel costs. The pidyon shvuyim campaign would dominate his correspondence for the next several weeks.

title_en: Letter to R. David Meir Rabinowitz on Rebbe's failing health
summary_en: On 16 Marcheshvan 5701 the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to R. Rabinowitz noting weeks of poor health while pressing the urgent need for student travel funds.
story_body: The Rebbe described laboring under physical weakness and emotional strain while writing to every direction asking for help. He noted that he had been compelled, against his will, to ask friends to assist financially with the rescue, which had drained him further.

title_en: Letter to Abraham Kvash with rescue advice
summary_en: On 12 Kislev 5701 the Rebbe Rayatz replied to R. Abraham Kvash advising him to prepare his papers and meanwhile take work, since he could not yet travel via Russia.
story_body: Kvash, who had fled Soviet Russia to Poland and could not legally travel back through Russia to Japan, had asked whether to even attempt the US visa interview. The Rebbe answered that he should do everything possible to be ready so that when an opportunity arose his visa would be in hand, and meantime arrange employment.

title_en: Cable from Vilna students on Polish passports and visa fees
summary_en: On 30 Kislev 5701 the Vilna students cabled the Rebbe Rayatz that they had submitted Polish passports for visas and expected approval on 6 Tevet.
story_body: The students reported that under the latest decree all costs had to be paid in US dollars, $118 per train ticket plus another $50 in mandatory expenses, deposited at the Soviet state bank. They asked for detailed instructions, intensifying the funding crisis at the New York office.

title_en: Cable from Vilna students on four-day visa validity
summary_en: On 2 Tevet 5701 the Vilna students cabled that the exit permit had been received, valid only four days, and that funds must be deposited at the Soviet state bank immediately.
story_body: Signed 'Rachamim Tmimim,' the urgent cable warned 'if not now, then never,' and requested that the New York office pay for everyone still missing funds. This precipitated emergency borrowing in New York to pay the Soviet bank within the narrow window.

title_en: Letter to R. Yaakov Schechter on dire pidyon shvuyim cash crunch
summary_en: On 14 Tevet 5701 the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to R. Yaakov Schechter in Pittsburgh that with only four days to wire funds the rescue would fail unless emergency loans were secured.
story_body: He related that the previous week he had been forced to send 5,040 dollars beyond earlier remittances, and that a fresh cable required two more ship tickets at 400 dollars. The pidyon shvuyim fund was empty, and the rescue depended on free-loan funding sourced from the Ladies Auxiliary and other supporters.

title_en: First three students depart Vilna for Russia
summary_en: By 16 Tevet 5701 the first three Tomchei Tmimim students had departed Vilna and were on their way to Vladivostok and Japan.
story_body: Writing to the mashpia R. Yehoshua Isaac Baruch, the Rebbe Rayatz expressed both relief at the first departures and frustration that the rest had not yet left. The journey crossed Russia to Vladivostok and continued by ship to Japan, financed by funds wired from New York.

title_en: Feigin informs Binyaminson of American visas for Vilna students
summary_en: On 17 Tevet 5701 secretary R. Yechezkel Feigin wrote to R. Yerachmiel Binyaminson that American visas had been obtained for Tomchei Tmimim students in Vilna with thirty expected soon.
story_body: Feigin reported that some students had already set out via Russia and the rest were prepared to depart shortly. The letter formalized internal communication about a rescue already underway after weeks of cables and emergency wires.

title_en: Gershon Chanowitz and five students depart Vilna
summary_en: On 22 Tevet 5701 R. Shmaryahu Gourary reported that Gershon Chanowitz had left Vilna together with five other students.
story_body: Writing to R. Moshe Leib Rotshtein in Chicago, Rashag also noted that Shmuel and Fruma Chanowitz cabled that they were leaving Vilna that week and needed $14 each for the leg from Vladivostok to Tokyo. The remaining students were expected to depart by the end of the month.

title_en: Rebbe reports thirty students en route and pays for thirty-eight more
summary_en: On 24 Tevet 5701 the Rebbe Rayatz reported that thirty students were already on the road and a further thirty-eight had just been booked for travel from Vilna to New York.
story_body: Beyond the first thirty for whom all costs had been paid, Rashag committed an additional $10,000 in loans to cover thirty more students and eight rabbis and rashei yeshiva so that no eligible person would be left behind under Soviet rule. The pace of departures and the accumulating debt drove ongoing cables to Chicago and Pittsburgh.

title_en: First party of 30 students reaches USA stage of journey
summary_en: On 28 January 1941 the first party of thirty Tomchei Tmimim students was confirmed to be on its way to the United States via Japan.
story_body: The annotation appended to the second mimeographed list of seventy-five names recorded that thirty students had already left for America and the remainder were expected to follow shortly. This was the moment the rescue tipped from preparation to active migration.

title_en: Gershon Chanowitz arrives in Vladivostok
summary_en: On 2 Shevat 5701 Gershon Chanowitz reached Vladivostok along with other Tomchei Tmimim students, with departure for Japan set for the following day.
story_body: Rashag wired Rotshtein that the group was scheduled to sail from Vladivostok to Japan on 31 January 1941. The Trans-Siberian crossing had taken roughly two weeks, after which the convoy waited a few days in port before boarding the ship to Japan.

title_en: Tomchei Tmimim students sail from Vladivostok to Japan
summary_en: On 31 January 1941 the first group of Tomchei Tmimim rescuees sailed from Vladivostok across to Japan, eventually reaching Kobe.
story_body: The two-day sea voyage from Vladivostok brought the students to a Japanese port where they were met by members of the small Japanese Jewish community and taken to Kobe. From Kobe most would continue onward to the United States, although a number would remain stranded in Asia for many months.

title_en: Birth of R. Abraham Kvash
summary_en: R. Abraham Kvash was born on 1 Kislev 5675 in Kamenets-Podolsk, Ukraine.
story_body: A future senior Tomchei Tmimim talmid, Kvash studied first in Kiev as a child before joining the underground Lubavitch yeshiva in Vitebsk in 1928. His biography becomes a thread in this chapter as the Rebbe Rayatz attempts to rescue him from Latvia where he would ultimately perish.

title_en: Soviet secret police close Tomchei Tmimim in Vitebsk
summary_en: In late winter 5691 the Soviet secret police shut down the underground Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva in Vitebsk, forcing a group of students to flee to Georgia.
story_body: A group including R. Moshe Rubinson, Abraham Kvash, Yosef Goldberg, Michael Rapaport and others escaped to Kutaisi in Georgia, where they continued studying until winter 5693. A subsequent crackdown in Georgia, framed as a border-crossing case, scattered the group again.

title_en: Arrest of R. Moshe Rubinson and his students in Berditchev
summary_en: On 19 Kislev 5698 R. Moshe Rubinson and his students were arrested in Berditchev and interrogated about contact with the Rebbe Rayatz.
story_body: Under interrogation Rubinson disclosed that his correspondence with the Rebbe Rayatz was conducted through a longtime acquaintance named Kvash who lived in Poland. The Kvash connection between the underground Soviet talmidim and the Rebbe also surfaced in the 1935 interrogation file of R. Shammai Vigon in Rostov.

title_en: Abraham Kvash writes to Ezras Torah about flight from Russia
summary_en: On Isru Chag Shavuos 5697 R. Abraham Kvash wrote to Ezras Torah recounting his five-year-old flight from Soviet Russia and his father's subsequent five-year Siberian exile.
story_body: Kvash described leaving Russia for Warsaw because he could find no place of Torah there, and that his father R. Aharon Kvasha had been arrested by the GPU on suspicion of complicity in his escape and for Jewish religious activity. R. Aharon was sentenced to five years in Siberia.

title_en: Abraham Kvash begins service as rabbinic intern in Riga
summary_en: On 28 Shevat 5700 / 7 February 1940 R. Abraham Kvash began service as a 'rabbinic intern' in the Riga rabbinate.
story_body: Per the Rebbe's instructions to prepare paperwork and meanwhile take employment, Kvash took a junior rabbinic position in Riga. He served there until the Nazi conquest of Latvia.

title_en: Abraham Kvash writes to Rebbe about visa interview
summary_en: On Motzaei Shabbat Chayei Sarah, 22 Marcheshvan 5701, R. Abraham Kvash wrote to the Rebbe Rayatz asking guidance on whether to attend his US visa interview.
story_body: In coded language Kvash explained that the consul required a full account of his life including his illegal flight from Russia to Poland, and asked whether it was worth pursuing the visa at all given that he could not travel through Russia. He also marked his approaching 26th birthday on 1 Kislev.

title_en: Jews of Latvia executed by Nazis; Abraham Kvash killed
summary_en: In Kislev 5702 the Jews of Latvia, including R. Abraham Kvash, were executed by the Nazis.
story_body: After Latvia was overrun by the Nazis, the Jewish community was murdered in Kislev 5702. Kvash, whom the Rebbe Rayatz had tried unsuccessfully to extract via the Vilna-Russia-Japan route because of his Soviet origin, was among those killed.

title_en: Rebbe announces Tomchei Tmimim students have received visas in Japan
summary_en: On 4 Nisan 5701, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote that his students in Japan had received their visas and were awaiting transit arrangements.
story_body: In a letter dated 4 Nisan 5701 (April 1, 1941), the Frierdiker Rebbe announced that his students who had escaped to Japan already held their visas and were only waiting for travel arrangements. He prayed that they would arrive safely and continue their Torah studies with fear of Heaven. This was part of the broader rescue effort to move Tomchei Tmimim students from Nazi-occupied Europe through Japan to America.

title_en: About forty Tomchei Tmimim students gathered in Japan awaiting US travel
summary_en: On 4 Iyar 5701, the Rebbe reported that about forty students were in Japan awaiting travel to the United States.
story_body: In a letter dated 4 Iyar 5701 (May 1, 1941), the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote that roughly forty of his students were now in Japan, anticipating their journey to America. He noted that countless pleas were arriving from Lithuania and Latvia to be rescued in time, and his office maintained constant correspondence with those communities.

title_en: Rebbe asks Rabbi Ashkenazi in Shanghai to obtain visas for Vilna students
summary_en: On 4 Nisan 5701, the Rebbe asked Rabbi Meir Ashkenazi of Shanghai to secure visas for students stranded in Vilna and Riga.
story_body: Writing to Rabbi Meir Ashkenazi in Shanghai, the Frierdiker Rebbe explained that he could not bring all his students to America and therefore needed Ashkenazi's help to obtain Shanghai transit visas for talmidim in Vilna, in newly Soviet-occupied territories, and from Riga, where the large yeshiva in Dvinsk had operated. He pleaded that the effort be undertaken with maximum urgency.

title_en: Telegram reports US consul has obtained nothing from Washington for refugees
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Sivan 5701, a telegram from Japan reported that the American consul had received no new instructions from Washington regarding the students' visas.
story_body: On 27 May 1941 (Rosh Chodesh Sivan 5701), students wired Rashag that the American consul in Yokohama had visited but had received nothing new from Washington and that the situation remained as before. Student Goldman had denied his Polish relatives on the application form and would receive his visa, while the Canadian visas had not yet arrived.

title_en: Rashag writes Tomchei Tmimim students about affidavits sent for US visas
summary_en: On 17 Sivan 5701, Rashag wrote to the students in Kobe explaining the affidavits Agudas Chassidei Chabad had dispatched on their behalf.
story_body: Rashag (Rabbi Shmaryahu Gourary) wrote on 17 Sivan 5701 (June 12, 1941) instructing the Kobe students to tell the consul that Agudas Chassidei Chabad guaranteed responsibility for them and that the affidavits were secondary. He listed by name the affidavits already sent for individual students and elder refugees, including telegraphed affidavits for Bornstein and Feder.

title_en: Yehonatan Gershon Balter forced to leave Kobe yeshiva for Eretz Yisroel
summary_en: On 3 Sivan 5701, student Yehonatan Gershon Balter was forced to leave the Kobe yeshiva and depart by ship for Eretz Yisroel.
story_body: On 3 Sivan 5701 (May 29, 1941), Yehonatan Gershon Balter was compelled to depart Kobe by sea. The yeshiva students escorted him to the ship with brotherly farewells, and he later reported reviewing Chassidus aloud aboard the vessel. He eventually reached Tel Aviv where he joined Yeshivas Achei Tmimim.

title_en: Balter arrives safely in Cape Town en route to Eretz Yisroel
summary_en: On 4 Tammuz 5701, Yehonatan Gershon Balter reached Cape Town, where he met local Anash and visited the Chabad shul.
story_body: On 4 Tammuz 5701 (June 29, 1941), Balter arrived safely in Cape Town. He spent only a few days there but met members of Anash and visited the small Chabad shul. He had planned to review Chassidus on Shabbos there, but a ship for Eretz Yisroel departed before Shabbos, requiring him to continue his journey.

title_en: Kobe students summary letter on US visa cancellations dated 8 Tammuz
summary_en: On 8 Tammuz 5701, the Kobe students summarized in writing that the Yokohama consul was issuing visas only to those who denied having relatives in occupied Europe.
story_body: A document preserved in the secretariat archive, dated 8 Tammuz 5701 (July 3, 1941), summarized the students' situation: the consul in Yokohama would grant visas to those who denied their relatives, but a July 2 telegram from the State Department appeared to nullify this. The document also discussed students changing their surnames (e.g., Rodal to Bodal) and securing new affidavits under those names.

title_en: Yud-Beis Tammuz farbrengen organized by Kobe Tomchei Tmimim students
summary_en: On 12-13 Tammuz 5701, the Tomchei Tmimim students in Kobe celebrated the Chag HaGeulah with a major farbrengen attended by leading refugee rabbanim.
story_body: For Yud-Beis and Yud-Gimmel Tammuz 5701 (July 7-8, 1941), the Kobe students organized a public farbrengen in addition to their internal seudah. They invited the refugee Vaad of leading rabbanim, who filled three rooms of the yeshiva to capacity. Talmidim explained the meaning of the day and reviewed Chassidus, and the Amshinover Rebbe participated and spoke several times.

title_en: Rashag reports efforts to secure US and Canadian visas for Kobe students
summary_en: On 12 Av 5701, Rashag wrote to Rabbi Mordechai Leib Rotstein that they were pursuing both US and Canadian visas for the Kobe students.
story_body: Rashag wrote on 12 Menachem Av 5701 (August 5, 1941) to Rabbi Rotstein, reporting that they were not sitting idly by but were working actively to secure American entry permits as well as Canadian visas for the students. He acknowledged the harsh new immigration restrictions and the worsening situation, awaiting new State Department forms.

title_en: Rashag begins seeking Paraguay visas for the Kobe students
summary_en: On 22 Av 5701, Rashag reported they were rushing to obtain Paraguayan visas for the students forced to leave Kobe.
story_body: On 22 Menachem Av 5701 (August 15, 1941), Rashag reported the urgent push to secure Paraguayan visas for the talmidim being expelled from Kobe. He noted that each Paraguay visa cost $60.

title_en: Rebbe cables Kobe committee to delay students' departure to Shanghai
summary_en: On 23 Av 5701, the Rebbe cabled the Jewish committee in Kobe to delay the students' departure to Shanghai pending visas to Paraguay and Canada.
story_body: On 23 Menachem Av 5701 (August 16, 1941), the Frierdiker Rebbe sent a telegram to the Jewish committee in Kobe asking them to delay the transfer of his Tomchei Tmimim students to Shanghai, as he had obtained Paraguayan and Canadian visas for them that were expected within days. The following day he cabled the Polish ambassador in Japan asking for Canadian visas for 38 students.

title_en: Rebbe cables Rabbi Abramsky and Dr. Schwarzbart in London for Canadian visas
summary_en: On 6 Elul 5701, the Rebbe telegraphed Rabbi Abramsky and Dr. Schwarzbart in London asking them to use their connections to obtain Canadian visas.
story_body: On 6 Elul 5701 (August 29, 1941), the Rebbe sent telegrams to Rabbi Abramsky and to Dr. Schwarzbart in London. He explained that 39 of his finest Tomchei Tmimim students were trapped in Kobe under the Jewish committee's supervision, all Polish citizens, and asked them to leverage their contacts to obtain Canadian visas — at least ten.

title_en: First refugee group including Tomchei Tmimim arrives in Shanghai from Kobe
summary_en: On 7 Elul 5701, 350 Polish-Jewish refugees including the Lubavitcher students arrived in Shanghai from Kobe.
story_body: Erev Shabbos Parshas Shoftim, 7 Elul 5701 (August 30, 1941), 350 Polish-Jewish refugees arrived in Shanghai from Kobe. Among them were the Mir Yeshiva headed by mashgiach Rabbi Yechezkel Levenstein and Rosh Yeshiva Rabbi Chaim Shmuelevitz, students of Chachmei Lublin, the Lubavitcher Yeshiva, and talmidim from Telz, Kamenitz, Kletzk, and Radin. A special reception committee met them at the port and transported them to prepared lodgings in shuls and batei medrash.

title_en: Tomchei Tmimim talmidim send detailed report to Rebbe from Shanghai
summary_en: On 18 Elul 5701, the student leaders in Shanghai sent a detailed report to the Rebbe describing their reception by Rabbi Ashkenazi.
story_body: On Chai Elul 5701 (September 10, 1941), the student-leaders Yitzchok HaKohen Hendel, Yosef Weinberg, Yosef Menachem Mendel Tenenbaum, and Yosef Rodal wrote to the Rebbe. They described how Rabbi Meir Ashkenazi welcomed them warmly upon arrival before Shabbos Tetzei, hosted them for a farbrengen, and planned another for Chai Elul itself.

title_en: Nine Tomchei Tmimim students sail from Shanghai toward Canada
summary_en: On Erev Yom Kippur 5702, nine Tomchei Tmimim students sailed from Shanghai en route to Montreal via San Francisco.
story_body: On Erev Yom Kippur 5702 (September 30, 1941), nine of the senior Tomchei Tmimim students who had received Canadian visas sailed from Shanghai. The ship traveled to San Francisco rather than directly to Canada; from there the students would travel by train across the United States to Montreal under special supervision to prevent them from disembarking on US soil.

title_en: Rashag confirms students arrived in San Francisco and depart for Canada
summary_en: On 29 Tishrei 5702, Rashag wrote that the students had reached San Francisco safely and would travel that evening through Chicago to Canada.
story_body: On 29 Tishrei 5702 (October 20, 1941), Rashag informed Rabbi Rotstein in Chicago that the students had arrived safely in San Francisco and would depart that evening for Canada via Chicago. He urged Rotstein to arrange to meet them on the train, since they would not be permitted to disembark in the city.

title_en: Nine Tomchei Tmimim students arrive in Montreal to establish yeshiva
summary_en: On 2 Cheshvan 5702, nine Tomchei Tmimim students arrived in Montreal, where they were tasked with founding a branch of the yeshiva.
story_body: On 2 Marcheshvan 5702 (October 23, 1941), the nine students reached Montreal. Rabbi Yisroel Jacobson came immediately, and a week later Rabbi Shmuel Levitin arrived from New York. The students wrote that the Rebbe had instructed them to establish Yeshivas Tomchei Tmimim in Montreal in the spirit of the original yeshiva in Lubavitch and Otwock, marking the founding of Lubavitch institutions in Canada.

title_en: Remaining Kobe students write farewell letter to Montreal-bound talmidim
summary_en: On 3 Cheshvan 5702, the talmidim remaining in Shanghai wrote to their fellow students traveling to Montreal expressing regret over their abrupt parting.
story_body: On 3 Marcheshvan 5702 (October 24, 1941), the students who remained behind wrote to those headed for Montreal. They lamented that the rapid departure had not allowed time for proper farewells or to discuss yeshiva matters, but trusted it was hashgachah pratis that they had not parted for long, and reported that Erev Yom Kippur and Yom Kippur passed with their accustomed order.

title_en: Rebbe responds with joy to news of his students' arrival in Montreal
summary_en: On 7 Cheshvan 5702, the Rebbe wrote that Rotstein's report about the students brought him more relief than all the world's medicines.
story_body: On 7 Marcheshvan 5702 (October 28, 1941), the Frierdiker Rebbe replied to Rabbi Rotstein. He wrote that the news had revived him physically and was better for his weakened health than any medicine. He prayed that Hashem would help the students settle and succeed in their learning and avodah shebalev, and use the opportunity Providence had granted them to enliven Anash.

title_en: Montreal students thank Rotstein and Chicago Lubavitchers for reception
summary_en: On 16 Cheshvan 5702, the newly arrived Montreal students thanked Rabbi Rotstein for the warm reception during their stopover in Chicago.
story_body: On 16 Marcheshvan 5702 (November 6, 1941), the students wrote from Montreal to Rabbi Rotstein in Chicago thanking him for the warm reception, the $25 stipend they had received via Rabbi Rubinstein, and the provisions prepared for the remainder of their journey. They confirmed they had settled and were beginning to establish Yeshivas Tomchei Tmimim in Montreal per the Rebbe's special directive.

title_en: Rebbe instructs Levitin to pursue 300 visas for students stranded in Shanghai
summary_en: On 10 Kislev 5702, the Rebbe wrote Rabbi Shmuel Levitin urging maximum effort to obtain visas for talmidim still stranded in Shanghai.
story_body: On 10 Kislev 5702 (November 30, 1941), the Rebbe wrote to Rabbi Shmuel Levitin, who had been sent to greet the students in Montreal. He noted that Rashag had forwarded the list of remaining Shanghai students to Levitin and Rabbi Yosef Albert, urging that no effort be spared to fill all 300 visas being sought. These additional visas were never granted, and the talmidim remained in Shanghai until the war's end.

title_en: Rotstein replies to Rodal with joy over Montreal arrival photographs
summary_en: On 13 Kislev 5702, Rabbi Mordechai Leib Rotstein wrote to student Yosef Rodal expressing joy at receiving photographs from the Montreal reception.
story_body: On 13 Kislev 5702 (December 3, 1941), Rabbi Rotstein replied to talmid Yosef Rodal. He wrote that receiving the letter and two photographs had brought him great joy at seeing the students together with the gedolim, and hoped Rodal had also sent the photos to the Rebbe, anticipating the nachas this would cause the leader of the generation.

title_en: Talmid Shmuel Avraham Chanovitz dies in exile in Shanghai
summary_en: On 9 Adar II 5703, Tomchei Tmimim student Shmuel Avraham Chanovitz passed away in exile in Shanghai.
story_body: Of the 38 students who reached Japan and then Shanghai, talmid Shmuel Avraham Chanovitz did not survive the exile. He passed away in Shanghai on 9 Adar Sheini 5703 (March 16, 1943). A memorial matzeivah was erected in his honor; the remaining 27 students reached the United States only in the summer of 1946.

title_en: WWII ends in summer 5705
summary_en: World War II ended in summer 5705 with the Allied victory over Germany and Japan.
story_body: In the summer of 5705 (1945), World War II ended with the victory of the United States and its allies over Germany and Japan. In Shanghai, the Japanese forces who had controlled the city for several years and confined Jews to a ghetto-like area were replaced by American troops. Among the American soldiers were many Yiddish-speaking Jews from New York's East Side and Manhattan, whose presence cheered the Chabad yeshiva students stranded there.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes to Aryeh Leib Kremer about visas
summary_en: On 24 Tammuz 5705, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to R. Aryeh Leib Kremer urging stronger measures to secure American visas for the students stranded in Shanghai.
story_body: On 24 Tammuz 5705 (Igrot Kodesh vol. 8, letter 2736), the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to R. Aryeh Leib Kremer in response to his letter about visas for the Tomchei Tmimim students stranded in Shanghai. The Rebbe instructed him to take stronger and more reliable measures, to immediately send the list of students to R. Yerachmiel Binyaminson, and announced that he himself would write to Binyaminson asking him to intervene with those who had influence in such matters.

title_en: Shanghai students send petition to Rebbe Rayatz
summary_en: On Chai Elul 5705, the Tomchei Tmimim students in Shanghai sent a heartfelt letter to the Rebbe Rayatz begging to be rescued from Shanghai's harsh climate.
story_body: On 18 (Chai) Elul 5705, the students wrote to the Frierdiker Rebbe pleading from the depths of their hearts to be saved quickly from Shanghai — described as a city of an abyss with harsh, oppressive air that drained their strength and caused various illnesses. They emphasized that the city was unsuitable for yeshiva students and bnei Torah, and begged to be brought close to the Rebbe and his chassidim to resume orderly study and inner avodah.

title_en: Students receive first telegram from Rebbe Rayatz erev Yom Kippur
summary_en: On erev Yom Kippur 5706, the Shanghai students received their first telegram from the Frierdiker Rebbe via R. Yaakov Yisrael Zuber, instructing them to apply for visas to America.
story_body: On erev Yom Kippur 5706, the students in Shanghai received the first telegram from the Frierdiker Rebbe via R. Yaakov Yisrael Zuber of Stockholm, instructing them to file visa applications and reporting his wish to bring them to the United States. After more than three years of no contact, this brought tremendous joy — a triple celebration — and the news was marked with farbrengens, niggunim, and dancing on motzaei Yom Kippur.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes 6 Tishrei letter on student visas
summary_en: On 6 Tishrei 5706, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to the Shanghai students confirming his telegram about visa applications and his efforts on their behalf.
story_body: In a letter dated 6 Tishrei 5706 (Igrot Kodesh vol. 9, letter 2766), sent alongside the telegram via R. Yaakov Yisrael Zuber of Stockholm, the Frierdiker Rebbe informed the students that a telegram had been sent to his contact about what they needed to do to obtain entry permits to the United States. He assured them that he was working on their behalf and prayed that G-d would fulfill their hearts' requests for good in both material and spiritual matters.

title_en: Students cable Rebbe on Chol HaMoed Sukkot
summary_en: On the fourth day of Chol HaMoed Sukkot 5706, the Shanghai students cabled the Rebbe Rayatz via R. Yaakov Yisrael Zuber explaining that visa applications were not yet possible.
story_body: On the fourth day of Chol HaMoed Sukkot 5706, the students sent a telegram in reply to the Frierdiker Rebbe via R. Y. Zuber, explaining that the American consul in Shanghai was not yet handling visa matters. They asked whether all formalities could be prepared in advance before applications could be filed locally, hedging against further delays.

title_en: Students send letter on 7 Tishrei that is returned
summary_en: On 7 Tishrei 5706 the students sent another letter to the Rebbe Rayatz, but it was returned and resent on Hoshana Rabbah.
story_body: On 7 Tishrei 5706, the Shanghai students sent another letter to the Frierdiker Rebbe, but to their great sorrow it was returned. They then resent it on Hoshana Rabbah via the postal service, which had just begun accepting direct mail to America again after years of wartime disruption.

title_en: Students send detailed letter on 23 Marcheshvan
summary_en: On 23 Marcheshvan 5706, parashat Chayei Sarah, the Shanghai students wrote a detailed report to the Frierdiker Rebbe describing their joy at receiving his telegram.
story_body: On the third day of parashat Chayei Sarah, 23 Marcheshvan 5706, the students wrote a fuller report to the Frierdiker Rebbe describing the telegram received via R. Y. Zuber on erev Yom Kippur instructing them to file visa applications. They expressed threefold joy: that this was the first news of his welfare in over three years, that it was the first telegram from him since their arrival in Shanghai, and most of all that he wished to bring them close to him in America.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes to Elchanan Glaser about Polish quota
summary_en: On 26 Tishrei 5706 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to R. Elchanan Glaser urging him to seek Congressman Dickstein's help in bringing the Shanghai students under Poland's immigration quota.
story_body: On 26 Tishrei 5706 (Igrot Kodesh vol. 9, letter 2772), the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote in Yiddish to R. Elchanan Glaser explaining that his best students from the Warsaw and Vilna Tomchei Tmimim yeshivos were now stranded in Shanghai after missing the last ship due to visa formalities. He noted that with strong advocacy in Washington it might be possible to bring them under the Polish quota, or quotas of other countries that were nearly unused, and asked if Congressman Dickstein could be enlisted to take a serious interest in the matter.

title_en: Students write Rebbe on 25 Marcheshvan
summary_en: On 25 Marcheshvan 5706, the Shanghai students wrote to the Rebbe Rayatz, sending the letter via an American soldier.
story_body: On 25 Marcheshvan 5706, the students again wrote to the Frierdiker Rebbe, sending the letter through an American serviceman because they were unsure whether their earlier postal letters had arrived. They reported that they still could not file visa applications in Shanghai but expected this might become possible within a week.

title_en: Students cable Rashag on first night of Chanukah
summary_en: On the first night of Chanukah 5706, Rabbi Meir Ashkenazi and the Tmimim cabled the Rashag from Shanghai about visa appointment dates with the American consul.
story_body: On the first night of Chanukah 5706, Rabbi Meir Ashkenazi and the Tmimim cabled the Rashag (R. Shmaryahu Gourary) in English, reporting that the visa department had scheduled their appointments with the consul between 20 and 31 December. They warned that all necessary papers had to arrive in Shanghai by the 20th, or the matter would be delayed by months.

title_en: Rashag writes to U.S. Embassy in Shanghai
summary_en: On 4 Shevat 5706, the Rashag wrote in English to the American Embassy in Shanghai, enclosing affidavits and a list of the students.
story_body: On 4 Shevat 5706, the Rashag wrote to the American Embassy in Shanghai per the advice of Mr. Eliot B. Coulter of the State Department, enclosing the required affidavits and a list of the names of the Tomchei Tmimim students stranded in Shanghai, China. He expressed hope that these documents would facilitate issuance of American visas so the immigration could take place as soon as possible.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes to students on 7 Shevat
summary_en: On 7 Shevat 5706 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote a letter of profound joy and blessing to his Shanghai students upon news of imminent rescue.
story_body: On 7 Shevat 5706 (Igrot Kodesh vol. 9, letter 2839), the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to his beloved students, thanking G-d for the great kindness shown to them in the merit of his holy forebears — especially his father, the Rebbe Rashab, who gave his soul for the building of Tomchei Tmimim. He expressed inexpressible joy at the news of their rescue and strong hope that they would soon arrive in America to spread Torah and yiras Shamayim from a settled material and spiritual situation.

title_en: Shanghai students receive visa application forms
summary_en: On 7 Shevat 5706, the Shanghai students received the visa application forms but could not yet return them without the affidavits.
story_body: On the same 7 Shevat 5706, the students wrote to the Frierdiker Rebbe that they had received the visa application blanks, but since they had not yet received the affidavits, they could not return them to the consulate — the applications required the names and addresses of those sending the affidavits, which they did not yet know. They asked for the Rebbe's blessing that they obtain the visas quickly and easily.

title_en: Students cable visa news on erev Shabbat Pekudei
summary_en: On erev Shabbat Pekudei, 5 Adar Sheni 5706, the students cabled the Rebbe Rayatz that UNRRA reported good prospects for visas soon.
story_body: On erev Shabbat Parashat Pekudei, 5 Adar Sheni 5706, the Shanghai students cabled the Frierdiker Rebbe in Yiddish that UNRRA was reporting good prospects of obtaining the visas soon, but expressing doubt whether all 29 of them would be able to travel together. The number reflected the 27 students plus the wives of the two who were married.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz blesses students on 8 Adar Sheni
summary_en: On 8 Adar Sheni 5706, the Frierdiker Rebbe replied with blessings that the students obtain their visas easily and find means to travel to America.
story_body: On 8 Adar Sheni 5706 (Igrot Kodesh vol. 13, letter 4901), the Frierdiker Rebbe replied to the Shanghai students' telegram that they were expected to receive the U.S. visas. He blessed them to receive them with ease and success in material and spiritual matters, that G-d would arrange a means of travel, and that they would arrive and become settled in a complete order of Torah study and avodah she-balev, and engage in spreading Torah and yiras Shamayim.

title_en: Montreal students form Ezras Achim relief group
summary_en: As the Shanghai students' departure approached, the rescued Tmimim in Montreal organized 'Ezras Achim' to raise relief funds for them.
story_body: As the Shanghai students' travel approached, the previously rescued Tomchei Tmimim students in Montreal organized 'Ezras Achim' to collect tzedakah for the needs of the students still in Shanghai waiting to come to America. The Frierdiker Rebbe replied on 24 Adar Rishon 5706 (Igrot Kodesh vol. 13, letter 4897) thanking them for arranging help for their brother-students of Tomchei Tmimim and blessing them to soon be reunited in a life of Torah.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz asks U.S. government to allow plane travel
summary_en: On 3 Nissan 5706 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to R. Yosef Fleischer of Chicago that he had asked the U.S. government to allow the Shanghai students to fly home.
story_body: On 3 Nissan 5706 (Igrot Kodesh vol. 9, letter 2883), the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to R. Yosef Fleischer, a Chabad askan in Chicago, that he had written to the U.S. government as president of Chabad chassidim, requesting the Secretaries of the Interior and War to grant the students permission to travel on a government airplane, since they were needed for teaching and ruling for the Chabad organization. He noted that the matter had to remain confidential.

title_en: Three Shanghai students arrive by plane
summary_en: In Tammuz 5706 three Shanghai Tmimim — Avraham Yitzchak Garfinkel, Nachum Preger, and Mordechai Meir Brziski — arrived in America by plane.
story_body: As reported in HaPardes (Tammuz 5706), three students arrived by plane from Shanghai a few weeks earlier: Avraham Yitzchak Garfinkel, Nachum Preger, and Mordechai Meir Brziski of Chmielnik. The Frierdiker Rebbe's efforts to bring all the students by airplane had not succeeded; only two or three made the trip by air while the rest traveled by U.S. military ship.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arranges welcome receptions on 2 Tammuz
summary_en: On 2 Tammuz 5706 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to Chabad askanim in America directing them to arrange splendid receptions for the Shanghai students.
story_body: On 2 Tammuz 5706 (Igrot Kodesh vol. 9, letter 2923), as soon as the Shanghai students set out from China, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to several Chabad askanim asking them to arrange a fine reception for the Tomchei Tmimim students along their travel route, with special emissaries to organize welcome events in as many towns as possible.

title_en: Rebbe writes Achei Tmimim heads on 3 Tammuz
summary_en: On 3 Tammuz 5706 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to heads of Achei Tmimim yeshivas in various American cities, instructing them to travel to arrange receptions for the arriving students.
story_body: On 3 Tammuz 5706 (Igrot Kodesh vol. 9, letter 2924), the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to the heads of Achei Tmimim yeshivas in several American cities asking them to travel to the towns the Rashag would suggest and arrange welcome celebrations for the Tomchei Tmimim students arriving from Shanghai.

title_en: Rebbe writes Chicago Anash on 15 Tammuz
summary_en: On 15 Tammuz 5706 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to Chicago Anash announcing the Shanghai students' arrival that week and asking them to arrange a splendid reception.
story_body: On 15 Tammuz 5706 (Igrot Kodesh vol. 9, letter 2928), the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to Anash in Chicago that, thank G-d, his beloved Tmimim from Tomchei Tmimim in Shanghai were arriving safely in America at the end of that week. He asked them to organize a splendid reception in their city, conducted in proper order.

title_en: Shanghai students reach San Francisco
summary_en: In Tammuz 5706 the group of Shanghai Tmimim arrived in San Francisco aboard an American military ship.
story_body: The students sailed from Shanghai on an American military ship — the only available option, as airfare was prohibitively expensive — and the voyage was uncomfortable, with military two-tier bunks and many travelers feeling unwell. They were joined by a large group of refugees including other yeshiva students, and the ship landed in San Francisco on the West Coast of the United States.

title_en: Reception receptions in Seattle, San Francisco, Los Angeles
summary_en: Upon arrival in America, the 29 Shanghai students were divided among three West Coast cities for receptions arranged by Tomchei Tmimim.
story_body: Tomchei Tmimim representatives sent from New York by the Rashag — among them R. Yosef Weinberg and R. Moshe Hecht — met the students upon disembarkation. The group of about thirty was divided three ways: ten traveled to Seattle, Washington (welcomed at the train station by Rabbi Shapira and others), ten remained in San Francisco, and ten went to Los Angeles, where R. Moshe Hecht hosted a large reception in a packed Moshav Zekenim hall, the first such welcome for yeshiva war refugees in America.

title_en: Group yechidus with Rebbe Rayatz on 27 Elul
summary_en: On Monday, 27 Elul 5706, the Shanghai students finally entered for a brief group yechidus with the ailing Frierdiker Rebbe in New York.
story_body: Upon arriving in New York, the students found the Frierdiker Rebbe in weakened health, and their yechidus was repeatedly postponed. As R. Shmuel Dovid Reitchik wrote, each day they were told they could enter 'tomorrow or the day after,' until finally on Monday before Rosh Hashanah — 27 Elul 5706 — the entire group entered together for a few minutes, during which the Rebbe spoke to them briefly.

title_en: Meir Hendel calls for Tomchei Temimim gathering in Radom
summary_en: On 19 Kislev 5701, Meir Hendel sent a postcard inviting senior Tomchei Temimim students near Radom to gather and establish a yeshiva branch in the city.
story_body: Hendel, a student of Tomchei Temimim Otwock who had failed to cross the border into Vilna, returned to his home city of Radom. He called for senior students such as Yaakov Falkenfeld to gather on Yud-Tes Kislev to found a Radom branch of the yeshiva, but heavy snow and cold prevented anyone from reaching him at that time. The plan would later materialize as a clandestine yeshiva in the Radom ghetto.

title_en: Yosef Goldstein flees from Chmielnik to Radom
summary_en: On Purim 5701, Yosef Goldstein fled his home in Chmielnik after learning the Germans were searching for him, eventually reaching Radom.
story_body: Once in the Radom ghetto, Goldstein was struck by the poverty and the sight of Jewish children and bochurim wandering without teachers or supervision. He concluded that a yeshiva was urgently needed, and together with Meir Hendel resolved to establish one. His arrival was a key catalyst for the underground Tomchei Temimim yeshiva in the Radom ghetto.

title_en: Underground Tomchei Temimim yeshiva founded in Radom ghetto
summary_en: At the start of 5701, Meir Hendel and Yosef Goldstein founded a clandestine branch of Tomchei Temimim in the Radom ghetto, ultimately gathering close to two hundred students.
story_body: Funding for the yeshiva came largely from the father of bochur Motl Bumelgrin, a wealthy and respected community member who took on its principal expenses. The roshei yeshiva and mashpi'im R' Berl Kornitzer and R' Baruch Friedman were brought in from Otwock, leaving their families behind to teach and inspire the students. Despite the dangers of underground life under Nazi occupation, the yeshiva continued operating until the end of summer 5702.

title_en: Yosef Weinberg reports on the Radom yeshiva to the Rebbe
summary_en: On 7 Cheshvan 5702, just after arriving in Montreal with rescued students, Yosef Weinberg wrote to the Frierdiker Rebbe describing the Radom yeshiva.
story_body: Weinberg reported receiving a postcard from Meir Hendel announcing that he had founded a yeshiva in Radom with roughly 150 students, with Hendel as rosh mesivta and Yaakov Yehuda Goldberg delivering a shiur to one class. The letter conveyed news of the underground yeshiva functioning in Nazi-occupied Poland to the Rebbe in North America.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe writes back about the Radom yeshiva
summary_en: On 14 Cheshvan 5702 the Frierdiker Rebbe replied with delight at the news of Meir Hendel's yeshiva in Radom and asked for assistance to be sent.
story_body: In Iggeret 1603, the Rebbe expressed his pleasure at the report and asked that blessings be conveyed to Hendel and his students. He instructed contacts in Japan, Shanghai, Warsaw and elsewhere to investigate sending parcels to Hendel, with the cost to be reimbursed.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe writes about Tomchei Temimim students in Poland
summary_en: On 7 Kislev 5702 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote of the mesirat nefesh of Tomchei Temimim students still in Poland, including one who had assembled around 150 students.
story_body: In Iggeret 1640 the Rebbe described how his students who remained in Poland were giving themselves over literally to Torah study and teaching others. He noted that they were keeping the Torah not merely amid poverty but amid hunger and cold, and that in one place a single student had gathered roughly 150 talmidim — a clear reference to Hendel's yeshiva in Radom.

title_en: R' Berl Kornitzer captured by the Germans in Radom
summary_en: In mid-summer 5702, the Germans seized R' Berl Kornitzer as he left the Radom synagogue wrapped in tallit and crowned with tefillin, and he was never seen again.
story_body: All efforts to free him failed, and his fate remained unknown. The yeshiva feared retribution because Kornitzer had been entrusted with gold coins received from the wealthy patron for the yeshiva's support, but news arrived that he had hidden the coins in his shoes and they were apparently not discovered. The incident shook the entire underground community in Radom.

title_en: Farbrengen in Radom ghetto on Rosh Chodesh Elul
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Elul 5702, Anash and the temimim of Radom held a farbrengen at which R' Baruch Friedman rebuked a participant for suggesting their suffering was God's will.
story_body: When one of the participants groaned that nothing could be done if it was the Holy One's will that Jews suffer, R' Baruch Friedman rose and emotionally protested that it was forbidden to say such a thing. The gathering took place under intensifying persecution, with the yeshiva continuing its learning despite the deteriorating conditions in the ghetto.

title_en: Aussiedlung of Radom ghetto and murder of R' Baruch Friedman
summary_en: In mid-Elul 5702 the Germans gathered the Jews of Radom in a large square for selection, sending R' Baruch Friedman and most of the ghetto to the gas chambers of Treblinka.
story_body: Yosef Goldstein, who survived because of his work permit, walked beside R' Baruch Friedman to the selection and described how the mashpia stood with eyes raised heavenward, hands clasped, completely detached from his surroundings. Friedman had refused to seek a work permit, certain that he would not be taken to labor; he had once said at a Simchat Torah farbrengen in Warsaw that the Rebbe had blessed him that he would not die without teshuvah. He was deported to Treblinka along with most of the ghetto's inhabitants.

title_en: Radom underground yeshiva ceases to exist
summary_en: By the end of summer 5702 the Radom yeshiva ceased to function, its students and faculty murdered along with the rest of the kehilla.
story_body: Yosef Goldstein later summarized that the yeshiva had operated from the beginning of 5701 until the end of 5702, after which all were destroyed and led as sheep to the slaughter together with the holy communities of Poland. R' Berl Kornitzer and R' Baruch Friedman were among those killed, along with most of the close to two hundred bochurim.

title_en: Shlomo Zilberberg writes to the Rebbe after surviving the war
summary_en: On 15 Shevat 5706, surviving talmid Shlomo Zilberberg wrote to the Frierdiker Rebbe from Poland reporting that he and several other talmidim had survived.
story_body: Zilberberg informed the Rebbe in Yiddish that he and a few other students remained alive after the cruel hands of the Nazis, and that they were currently in Poland. He pleaded with the Rebbe to have mercy upon them and acknowledge their survival.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe writes to Yehoshua Heshel Reizman
summary_en: On 13 Adar I 5706 the Frierdiker Rebbe replied to surviving talmid Yehoshua Heshel Reizman, encouraging him to strengthen Torah, Jewish education, and good middot.
story_body: Replying to a letter from 8 Kislev, the Rebbe expressed joy that Reizman had been saved from the Nazis and pleasure at his efforts together with his fellow temimim to strengthen Torah, kosher chinuch, good middot and ahavat Yisrael. He urged them to persist despite all obstacles and obstructions in their country.

title_en: Pinchas Klein sends list of surviving Tomchei Temimim talmidim
summary_en: On 19 Adar I 5706, Pinchas Klein wrote to Arye Leib Kremer in Montreal listing the Tomchei Temimim students still alive in Poland.
story_body: Klein asked that his name and that of his wife be brought before the Rebbe for blessings. He listed surviving talmidim including Yosef Goldstein, a shochet in Lodz; Heshel Reizman in Częstochowa; Feivel Griner; Yehoshua Wolf Abramtchak from Koszwin; the Zilberberg brothers; Fishel Gitelis from Kowel; Yaakov Katz from Chelm; and Motl Bumelgrin from Zwolen.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe replies to Shlomo Zilberberg
summary_en: On 4 Adar I 5706 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to Shlomo Zilberberg expressing joy at his survival and asking for details of him and his brother.
story_body: The Rebbe wrote that he was very pleased to hear that Hashem had saved Zilberberg and his brother through His great kindness, and requested a detailed account of what had happened to them and to the other surviving Anash. He blessed them to settle into a good family life with parnassah and fixed times for Torah study in nigleh and chassidut.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe writes to Yerucham Fishel Gitelis
summary_en: On 22 Iyar 5706 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to survivor Yerucham Fishel Gitelis in Iggeret 6643, expressing pleasure at his rescue.
story_body: The Rebbe noted his delight that Hashem in His great kindness had saved Gitelis from the Nazis, and blessed him with healing, strengthened health, and assistance in all his material and spiritual needs.

title_en: Secretariat writes to Sweden on behalf of Heshel Reizman and wife
summary_en: On 5 Menachem Av 5706 the Frierdiker Rebbe's secretariat wrote to Anash in Sweden requesting an additional affidavit for Heshel Reizman's wife.
story_body: Reizman had married Sheindel and was living in Czechy near Liptovský Mikuláš, with a Swedish visa already in hand and a passport expected soon. Since his wife had no visa of her own, the Rebbe's office — likely writing to Yaakov Yisrael Zuber — asked that an additional affidavit be sent on her behalf so the couple could travel together.

title_en: Yisrael Azriel Feldman aids Anash refugees in Steyer DP camp
summary_en: On 20 Menachem Av 5707, Yisrael Azriel Feldman wrote to the Rebbe from Steyer, Austria, reporting on his aid to Anash arriving from the Soviet Union.
story_body: Feldman, a former Tomchei Temimim Warsaw student who had fled to Russia and then to the Steyer DP camp, was serving as the camp's rav and av beit din. He built a mikvah and arranged an oven for baking matzot at the highest standard, helping Anash including R' Moshe Zalman Kaminetzky, R' Elimelech Perman, R' Zalman Teibel and R' Menachem Mendel Seitz. He noted that he and Pinchas Klein were the only Tomchei Temimim talmidim in the camp.

title_en: Feldman founds Tomchei Temimim in Steyer DP camp
summary_en: On 16 Sivan 5708, Feldman wrote to the Rebbe announcing he had founded a Talmud Torah and yeshiva called Tomchei Temimim in the Steyer DP camp.
story_body: Under his supervision the new institution comprised two classes of students. The founding extended the Tomchei Temimim network into postwar Austria, serving Jewish refugees in the displaced persons camp.

title_en: Yisrael Azriel Feldman arrives in the United States
summary_en: On Erev Shabbat 21 Iyar 5709, Yisrael Azriel Feldman arrived in the United States from the Steyer DP camp in Austria.
story_body: Feldman wrote to the Rebbe describing his background as a native of Różan, Poland and son of a shochet from the chassidim of Uman, his studies in Tomchei Temimim Warsaw in 5694-95, and his sojourn in Russia before reaching the Steyer camp. After his arrival in America he was accepted as rabbi of Beth Knesses Agudath Achim in Milwaukee.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz requests US immigration papers
summary_en: In the winter of 5699, the Rebbe Rayatz asked aides to prepare US immigration papers as a precaution.
story_body: Though not yet planning to emigrate, the Rebbe Rayatz instructed his secretariat to begin preparing immigration documents for the United States. Secretary Yechezkel Feigin explained in correspondence that the move was contingent on conditions; if Europe stabilized, no emigration would occur.

title_en: Feigin writes Jacobson about US immigration preparations
summary_en: Secretary Yechezkel Feigin wrote to Israel Jacobson explaining the Rebbe Rayatz's instructions to prepare US immigration papers.
story_body: On 28 Nissan 5699, Feigin conveyed the Rebbe's directive to Jacobson, director of Agudas Chabad in the US. The letter clarified that preparing papers was precautionary against worsening conditions, not yet a firm decision to emigrate.

title_en: Jacobson's yechidus with Rebbe Rayatz in Otwock
summary_en: During mid-Elul 5699, Israel Jacobson met with the Rebbe Rayatz in Otwock, who told him to prepare for the family's arrival in America within six months.
story_body: Jacobson arrived in Otwock with a group of students from New York. In yechidus, the Rebbe Rayatz instructed him to arrange matters in America 'on solid foundations,' saying that within about half a year they would arrive there. By summer's end, the decision to emigrate was final.

title_en: World War II breaks out; Germany invades Poland
summary_en: On 17 Elul 5699, World War II began with the German invasion of Poland, trapping the Rebbe Rayatz and his family in Otwock.
story_body: The outbreak of war drastically changed the situation for the Rebbe Rayatz, who had been staying in Otwock. Within days he and his family would be forced to flee, beginning a four-month ordeal under Nazi occupation in Warsaw.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz leaves Otwock as war engulfs Poland
summary_en: On Tuesday 21 Elul 5699 at 3pm, the Rebbe Rayatz left Otwock weeping, blessing the crowd that gathered to bid farewell.
story_body: As bombings intensified, the Rebbe departed Otwock for Warsaw with deep bitterness on his face. He blessed those gathered, telling them to accept the yoke of Heaven, and that God would protect them and the Rebbe wherever each would be. The original plan to reach Riga proved impossible; the family ended up at the Schmotkin apartment, Muranowska 32, Warsaw.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz flees Schmotkin apartment as bombs fall
summary_en: On Erev Rosh Hashanah 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz and family fled the Schmotkin apartment as German bombs set the building ablaze.
story_body: Just before candle-lighting, a bomb struck the Schmotkin home and the building caught fire. Neighbors screamed and ran toward the gate, while chassidim surrounded the Rebbe to shield him. He sat on a chair murmuring with his lips while a chassid reviewed Mishnayos by heart, with the Rebbe correcting his errors. The family fled to another neighborhood for the High Holy Days.

title_en: Secretary Chaim Lieberman escapes Warsaw to Riga
summary_en: On 8 Tishrei 5700, secretary Chaim Lieberman managed to escape Warsaw to Riga with only twenty minutes to prepare.
story_body: Leaving 'naked and destitute,' Lieberman had no time to gather belongings. From Riga he began the intensive three-month effort to obtain exit permits and US entry visas for the Rebbe Rayatz and his family. The same day, the Rebbe and his family returned to their original Muranowska 32 apartment.

title_en: Heavy Luftwaffe bombing strikes Warsaw on 12 Tishrei
summary_en: On 12 Tishrei 5700, intense aerial bombardment forced the Rebbe Rayatz and his family to take shelter in a basement.
story_body: Telephone lines were cut and water mains broken across the city. The Rebbe descended with his family to a cellar, and on exiting fled from gate to gate. At one point a gate nearly collapsed on Rabbi Dovber Schneerson, who managed to brace it. Massive bombings continued on the eve of Sukkot.

title_en: Pell briefs US ambassador in Berlin on rescue priority
summary_en: State Department representative Robert Pell informed the US ambassador in Berlin of the importance of rescuing the Rebbe Rayatz.
story_body: On October 3, 1939 (20 Tishrei), Pell formally communicated the priority of the rescue mission to the US embassy in Berlin. This initiated months of US-German diplomatic coordination that would ultimately enable the Rebbe's extraction from Warsaw.

title_en: Benjamin Cohen advises Pell on locating the Rebbe
summary_en: On October 26, 1939, advisor Benjamin Cohen informed Robert Pell, on attorney Asher Rabinowitz's behalf, how to locate the hidden Rebbe.
story_body: Because callers seeking the Rebbe Rayatz at Rabbi Tzvi Gurary's home had been turned away by frightened residents, US officials needed help finding him. Cohen's guidance to Pell helped advance the search and eventual rescue effort.

title_en: Lieberman reports Rebbe's hiding address to Jacobson
summary_en: On 4 Kislev 5700, Lieberman informed Jacobson that the Rebbe was hiding at Bonifratrska 29 — the home of Yechiel Tzvi Gurary.
story_body: By November 16, the rescue effort needed a precise address to proceed. Lieberman confirmed the Rebbe's hiding place so the diplomatic and military extraction plan could be set in motion.

title_en: Kirk informs Pell that rescue is feasible
summary_en: On November 25, 1939, US embassy official Alexander Kirk in Berlin notified Pell that the Rebbe had been located and could be extracted around December 1.
story_body: Kirk reported that the German army would assign an officer to travel with the Rebbe and his entourage and ensure the journey. Although the December 1 date slipped, this set the framework for the extraction.

title_en: Max Rhoade updates Kramer on Berlin rescue plan
summary_en: Attorney Max Rhoade informed attorney Sam Kramer that Berlin had prepared a rescue plan, redirecting from Sweden to Riga.
story_body: Rhoade told Kramer the German authorities had a plan to evacuate the Rebbe to Sweden but preferred Latvia (Riga). He expected this to occur within two to three days — which is precisely what happened.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz extracted from Warsaw to Berlin
summary_en: On Thursday 2 Tevet 5700, German Abwehr officers extracted the Rebbe Rayatz and his family from Warsaw to Berlin by train.
story_body: Following coordination by German military intelligence chief Wilhelm Canaris, half-Jewish officer Ernst Bloch and Klaus Schenk escorted the family from the Gurary home in Warsaw to the train station. Despite hostile German soldiers en route, the escort ensured safe passage. They arrived in Berlin that evening and lodged at the Jewish community building.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in Riga from Berlin
summary_en: On Sunday 5 Tevet 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz and his family reached Riga after a Shabbat stopover in Berlin.
story_body: After spending Shabbat at a Berlin hotel arranged through the Latvian consulate, the family traveled onward and arrived in Riga on Sunday evening. The Rebbe immediately wrote a general letter to chassidim announcing his safe arrival, and would remain in Riga for nearly three months.

title_en: US visas confirmed for Rebbe Rayatz and family
summary_en: On 7 Shevat 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote that visas for the United States had been received for the entire family.
story_body: Writing to his son-in-law (the future Rebbe), the Rebbe Rayatz reported that visas had been issued for everyone, including the son-in-law's family. They now needed to coordinate the journey so all could travel together to America.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz breaks his right hand on Shabbos Yisro
summary_en: On Shabbos Parshas Yisro 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz fell and broke a bone in his right hand while walking to make Kiddush.
story_body: The injury required a cast for three weeks and a bandage afterward. Combined with an emergency hernia operation needed by his mother Rebbetzin Shterna Sarah, this delayed the family's planned departure from Riga to the United States.

title_en: Kramer confirms all Riga visas received
summary_en: On February 13, 1940, attorney Sam Kramer informed Henry Butler that all US visas for the rabbis in Riga had been received.
story_body: Kramer relayed news from a cable sent by the Rebbe Rayatz that the visa process was complete. With travel preparations and convalescence still underway, departure was scheduled for early March.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz flies from Riga to Stockholm
summary_en: On Monday 24 Adar I 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz departed Riga by airplane to Stockholm, with thousands gathered at the airport.
story_body: Jews of Riga, chassidim and non-chassidim alike, packed the aerodrome to bid farewell. Chief of Riga's community Mordechai Dubin accompanied the family. The elder Rebbetzin was carried aboard on a stretcher. The Rebbe blessed the Latvian government, its president, and the Jewish community, urging all to join Agudas Yisroel.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz boards ship at Gothenburg for America
summary_en: After a brief stay in Stockholm, the Rebbe Rayatz boarded a transatlantic ship from Gothenburg en route to America.
story_body: From Stockholm the party traveled overnight by train to the port city of Gothenburg, where they were taken directly to the ship as a special exception. The vessel finally departed Thursday morning. During the Stockholm stay, Stockholm Chief Rabbi Yisrael Yaakov Zuber and his family visited the Rebbe.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in New York harbor
summary_en: On Tuesday 9 Adar II 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz arrived at the New York harbor, greeted by thousands.
story_body: Delegations from Agudas HaAdmorim, Agudas HaRabbonim, major yeshivos, communal askanim, and charitable institutions welcomed him. In the harbor's largest hall, he conveyed greetings from European Jewry and urged American Jews to redouble efforts to aid those still trapped overseas. He stayed at the Greystone Hotel for nearly a month.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes thanks to Justice Louis Brandeis
summary_en: On 23 Adar II 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote a letter of thanks to Justice Louis Brandeis for his rescue intervention.
story_body: The Rebbe credited Brandeis with going beyond promises and immediately undertaking decisive action when no one else could have accomplished what he did. Attorney Asher Rabinowitz, son of Rabbi David Meir Rabinowitz, had worked through Brandeis to secure the rescue.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz travels to Lakewood for a month
summary_en: On 8 Nissan 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz moved to Lakewood, New Jersey, where he stayed in a private home for about a month.
story_body: After spending nearly a month at the Greystone Hotel in New York, the Rebbe relocated to Lakewood where a residence was placed at his disposal. He would remain there until returning to New York on 7 Iyar.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz returns from Lakewood to New York
summary_en: On 7 Iyar 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz returned from Lakewood to New York, where he again stayed in a hotel.
story_body: He remained in a New York hotel through the summer months while plans for a permanent residence and headquarters were finalized.

title_en: 770 Eastern Parkway purchased for the Rebbe Rayatz
summary_en: On 12 Menachem Av 5700, the building at 770 Eastern Parkway in Brooklyn was purchased as the Rebbe Rayatz's residence and headquarters.
story_body: The acquisition of 770 Eastern Parkway marked the establishment of what would become the permanent center of Chabad-Lubavitch worldwide. The purchase was completed during the Rebbe's stay at a New York hotel.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz moves into 770 Eastern Parkway
summary_en: On 19 Elul 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz moved into his private residence at 770 Eastern Parkway in Brooklyn.
story_body: The move into 770 marked the formal establishment of the building as the residence of the Rebbe and headquarters of Chabad-Lubavitch. From this address the movement's American rebirth and global expansion would unfold over the coming decades.

title_en: Rabbi Chaim Lieberman flees Warsaw
summary_en: Rabbi Chaim Lieberman (Rachal) left Warsaw on 8 Tishrei 5700, the same day the Frierdiker Rebbe's household began their escape from Nazi-occupied Poland.
story_body: On 8 Tishrei 5700 (Sept 21, 1939), Rabbi Chaim Lieberman left Warsaw separately, having only about twenty minutes to prepare. The Frierdiker Rebbe's son-in-law Rashag had planned to join him but stayed behind because his wife and son refused to leave the Rebbe. Lieberman departed alone with nothing, while the rest of the family would remain in Warsaw until early Teves before traveling together to Riga.

title_en: Future Rebbe submits family birth records for US visas
summary_en: On 28 Tishrei 5700, the future Rebbe wrote from Paris to Israel Jacobson with family birth dates and places to facilitate American visa applications.
story_body: Writing in French to Rabbi Israel Jacobson in New York, the future Rebbe Menachem Mendel Schneerson provided personal details to assist with US visa procurement: Chaya Mushka Schneersohn (b. Aug 13, 1901, Smolensk) and Menachem Mendel Schneersohn (b. Mar 1, 1895, Nikolaev, to Levik and Chana). The application was meant to bring the future Rebbe and Rebbetzin together with the Frierdiker Rebbe's family to America.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe's family arrives in Riga
summary_en: In early Teves 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe's remaining family departed Warsaw together and reached Riga, Latvia, en route to the United States.
story_body: After remaining in Warsaw through the early months of the German occupation, the Frierdiker Rebbe, his family, and son-in-law Rashag traveled together to Riga at the start of Teves 5700 (December 1939). From Riga they would continue to the United States, while the future Rebbe and Rebbetzin remained behind in Paris awaiting their own visas.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe reports US visas approved in Riga
summary_en: On 7 Shevat 5700 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote from Riga that US visas had been received for the entire family, including the future Rebbe in Paris.
story_body: The Frierdiker Rebbe informed his son-in-law in Paris that, thank G-d, all were alive and well, and that American visas had been arranged for the entire family. He proposed planning a joint journey to the United States. In practice, the Paris visas had only been promised, not issued, and the actual struggle to obtain them would continue for over a year.

title_en: Attorney Kremer petitions for future Rebbe's US visa
summary_en: On 4 Adar I 5700, attorney Sam Kremer wrote to attorney Henry Butler in Washington urging that a US visa be secured for Rabbi Mendel Schneerson in Paris.
story_body: Kremer, a member of the Agudas Chabad executive, formally requested Butler's assistance in securing a US visa for Rabbi Mendel Schneerson 'as a member of the leadership of the movement.' This began over a year of intensive correspondence between Chabad's New York lawyers and the State Department to extract the future Rebbe and Rebbetzin from Nazi-controlled Europe.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe departs Riga for America
summary_en: On 24 Adar I 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe left Riga with his family on the final leg of his escape to the United States.
story_body: With Latvia threatened by the war, the Frierdiker Rebbe departed Riga for Stockholm, where he would board a ship to New York. His daughter Chaya Mushka and her husband, the future Rebbe, remained behind in Paris, unable to obtain visas in time. The separation marked the start of more than a year of intense rescue efforts on the family's behalf.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe writes from Stockholm before sailing
summary_en: On 25 Adar I 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote a disguised letter in Russian from Stockholm to the future Rebbe in Paris, fearing censorship.
story_body: Awaiting his transatlantic crossing, the Rebbe Rayatz used Russian to evade wartime censors. He confirmed that $1,000 had been allocated for travel preparations and asked whether Mushka and Mendel could purchase tickets themselves or required them to be forwarded by Jacobson. Coded references and intermediaries became central to the rescue correspondence.

title_en: Gerer Rebbe escapes Poland to Trieste
summary_en: Around Erev Pesach 5700 the Gerer Rebbe (Imrei Emes) escaped Nazi-occupied Poland with 14 followers and reached Trieste, Italy.
story_body: In a letter to attorney Butler on Erev Pesach 5700, Rashag noted that the Gerer Rebbe and 14 of his people had obtained German exit permits and reached Trieste roughly ten days earlier. He urged that the same channel be investigated for his brother-in-law Mordechai Menachem Mendel Horenstein, who was trapped with his wife Sheina in Otwock.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe writes Pidyon Nefesh for daughter trapped in Paris
summary_en: On 21 Iyar 5700, while crossing to America, the Frierdiker Rebbe entered a special Pidyon Nefesh in his diary for his daughter and son-in-law in Paris.
story_body: The prayer asked Heaven to protect Chaya Mushka and Menachem Mendel — the latter not a French citizen and registered for national defense service — and to soften the heart of the American consul to grant their visa. The text was written in the days surrounding the German advance on France, capturing the family's acute fear for the couple stranded in Paris.

title_en: Future Rebbe and Rebbetzin flee Paris to Vichy
summary_en: As the Germans entered Paris, the future Rebbe and Rebbetzin escaped by train to Vichy, arriving Erev Shavuot 5700 toward evening.
story_body: With the Paris train station overwhelmed by Jews fleeing the Wehrmacht, the future Rebbe's enlistment in the French army eased his passage out of the city. The couple reached Vichy on Erev Shavuot and would remain there about two and a half months before continuing south. The Rebbetzin later related these events to the chronicler.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe cables son-in-law about manuscripts
summary_en: On 6 Av 5700 the Frierdiker Rebbe cabled the future Rebbe in Vichy asking about his health and whether he had taken the family's books and manuscripts.
story_body: The cable referred to the trunks of seforim and ksav-yad in the future Rebbe's possession, including his wedding gift books, photographic volumes of the Rebbe Rashab's maamarim, and his own Reshimos. Many of these manuscripts, preserved through the wartime ordeal, are today housed in the Chabad library.

title_en: Future Rebbe and Rebbetzin reach Nice under Italian zone
summary_en: In Av 5700 the future Rebbe and Rebbetzin left Vichy southward for Nice, then under Italian control and a refuge for many Jews.
story_body: After roughly two and a half months in Vichy, it became clear that the German-subordinate Vichy regime was equally dangerous for Jews. The couple moved to Nice, where they would spend 8–9 months while the Frierdiker Rebbe coordinated intensive efforts from New York to secure their visas, travel papers, and basic provisions including matzah and an esrog for Sukkos.

title_en: US visas granted to future Rebbe and Rebbetzin in Marseille
summary_en: On 20 Nissan 5701, after more than a year of effort, the future Rebbe and Rebbetzin received their US visas at the American consulate in Marseille.
story_body: The State Department had cabled the Marseille consulate in mid-March that the Schneersohns qualified for visas under the quota. The Rebbetzin wrote her father on 26 Adar II that the consul had promised the documents. The visas were finally issued on April 17, 1941, paving the way for travel through Lisbon to New York.

title_en: Future Rebbe records 'Reshima' in Lisbon
summary_en: On 16 Sivan 5701 the future Rebbe wrote a Reshima in Lisbon while awaiting transatlantic passage.
story_body: The note, published in Reshimos issue 11, is headed 'Lisbon, 16 Sivan 5701' — documenting that the couple had reached Portugal after the long struggle for Portuguese transit visas and ship tickets. The following day they would board the Serpa Pinta bound for New York.

title_en: Future Rebbe boards Serpa Pinta in Lisbon
summary_en: On 17 Sivan 5701, the future Rebbe and Rebbetzin boarded the Portuguese ship Serpa Pinta in Lisbon, bound for New York.
story_body: The passenger manifest lists Mendel Schneersohn (46, rabbi, Russian refugee, born Nikolaev) and Chaya Mussia Schneersohn (40, Russian refugee, born Smolensk), both with visas issued in Marseille on April 17, 1941, and tickets paid by her father, the Rebbe Rayatz, with destination 770 Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn.

title_en: Future Rebbe and Rebbetzin arrive in New York
summary_en: On 28 Sivan 5701 the future Rebbe and Rebbetzin arrived in New York, ending nearly two years of separation from her father.
story_body: The Frierdiker Rebbe immediately dispatched letters and a cable to Chicago, Baltimore, and elsewhere announcing that 'my daughter and son-in-law have arrived safely.' The day later became one of the most significant in Chabad's modern calendar, marking the future seventh Rebbe's entry to America and the eventual revival of Chabad Lubavitch from 770 Eastern Parkway.

title_en: Rebbetzin Chana Horenstein murdered at Treblinka
summary_en: On 14 Elul 5702, Rebbetzin Chana Mushka Horenstein, mother of Rabbi Mordechai Menachem Mendel Horenstein, was taken to the gas chambers at Treblinka.
story_body: According to the testimony of survivor Mordechai Unrad, who shared a barrack with Rabbi Horenstein at Treblinka, a Kapo brought a note from Sheina informing her husband that his mother had been led to the crematoria on 14 Elul 5702. The Horensteins had been trapped in Otwock since 1939 despite the Frierdiker Rebbe's prolonged efforts to extract them.

title_en: Rebbetzin Sheina Horenstein murdered at Treblinka
summary_en: On the second day of Rosh Hashanah 5703, Rebbetzin Sheina, youngest daughter of the Frierdiker Rebbe, was taken to the gas chambers at Treblinka.
story_body: A Kapo informed the survivor Mordechai Unrad on 3 Tishrei 5703 that Sheina had been led to the crematoria on the second day of Rosh Hashanah. The Frierdiker Rebbe, not yet knowing the details, continued to refer to his youngest daughter and her husband as still being in Otwock in correspondence into Adar II 5703.

title_en: Rabbi Mordechai Menachem Mendel Horenstein murdered at Treblinka
summary_en: On 25 Cheshvan 5703, Rabbi Mordechai Menachem Mendel Horenstein, son-in-law of the Frierdiker Rebbe, was taken from work at Treblinka to the gas chambers.
story_body: Survivor Mordechai Unrad, returning from his work assignment, found that Rabbi Horenstein had been removed from his barrack along with a group of other Jews and led to the crematoria. The Frierdiker Rebbe's nearly four-year rescue effort — visas, exit permits, intermediaries in Italy, Germany, Sweden, and the State Department — had been thwarted at every turn by the Germans' refusal to grant exit permits.

title_en: Chaim Liberman flees Warsaw to Riga
summary_en: The Rebbe's secretary R. Chaim Liberman fled from Warsaw to Riga on 8 Tishrei to organize rescue efforts.
story_body: With the outbreak of WWII, the Frierdiker Rebbe's secretary R. Chaim Liberman escaped Warsaw and reached Riga on 8 Tishrei 5700. From Riga he conducted rescue advocacy for the Rebbe and his family, remaining there until they too were rescued. He later traveled with the Rebbe and his household to the United States.

title_en: Moshe Leib Rotstein marries Kayla Chanovich in Globoke
summary_en: R. Moshe Leib Rotstein married Kayla, daughter of the shochet R. Yisrael Chanovich of Globoke, in 5684.
story_body: In 5684 (1924), R. Moshe Leib Rotstein — born Zusya Shifrin in Russia around 5660 — married Kayla, daughter of R. Yisrael Chanovich, the shochet of Globoke. Rotstein had fled Russia after WWI and the Revolution, adopting a forged identity. His new father-in-law passed away the following year.

title_en: Death of R. Yisrael Chanovich, shochet of Globoke
summary_en: R. Yisrael Chanovich, shochet of Globoke and father-in-law of R. Moshe Leib Rotstein, passed away on 19 Marcheshvan 5685.
story_body: R. Yisrael Chanovich, who served as the shochet of Globoke, passed away on 19 Marcheshvan 5685, one year after his daughter Kayla's marriage to R. Moshe Leib Rotstein. He left behind sons Chaim, Shmuel Avraham, and Gershon, and several daughters.

title_en: Rotstein becomes secretary at Warsaw yeshiva
summary_en: From 5688 onward, R. Moshe Leib Rotstein served as secretary of the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva in Warsaw.
story_body: Beginning in 5688 (1928), R. Moshe Leib Rotstein took up the position of secretary at the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva in Warsaw. He continued in this role for years, serving the institution under the Frierdiker Rebbe's leadership.
