title_en: Rebbe appoints Rotstein as his secretary in Druzgenik
summary_en: During the summer of 5692 at the Druzgenik convalescent home, the Frierdiker Rebbe appointed R. Moshe Leib Rotstein as his secretary.
story_body: In the summer of 5692, R. Moshe Leib Rotstein stayed with the Frierdiker Rebbe at the convalescent home in Druzgenik. It was apparently during this stay that the Rebbe formally appointed him as his secretary, a role he would fulfill in the years to come.

title_en: Rebbe travels to Ludmir with Rotstein as secretary
summary_en: On 23 Menachem Av 5692, the Frierdiker Rebbe traveled to visit Anash in Ludmir with R. Moshe Leib Rotstein as his secretary.
story_body: On 23 Menachem Av 5692, the Frierdiker Rebbe set out from Druzgenik to visit chassidim in Ludmir. In his diary the Rebbe noted that 'the one traveling with me as secretary is the tamim R. Moshe Leib Rotstein,' formalizing the secretarial role.

title_en: Rotstein flees Warsaw with wife before Rosh Hashana
summary_en: R. Moshe Leib Rotstein and his wife fled Warsaw on foot the week before Rosh Hashana 5700, eventually reaching Vilna safely.
story_body: As war broke out, R. Moshe Leib Rotstein and his wife fled Warsaw on foot the week before Rosh Hashana 5700, intending to reach Globoke. Their fate was initially unknown, but it later emerged that they had arrived safely in Vilna, where many Polish yeshiva students had relocated.

title_en: Rotstein meets Rebbe in Riga to report on Vilna yeshiva
summary_en: When the Frierdiker Rebbe arrived in Riga at the beginning of Tevet 5700, Rotstein and R. Shmuel Zalmanov came to report on the yeshiva's reorganization in Vilna.
story_body: At the start of Tevet 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe arrived in Riga. R. Moshe Leib Rotstein traveled there together with R. Shmuel Zalmanov to brief the Rebbe on how the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva had been reconstituted in Vilna after fleeing Poland.

title_en: Rebbe writes letters of thanks for US entry permits
summary_en: After reaching Riga, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote thank-you letters acknowledging US entry permits for himself, his family, and his secretaries.
story_body: Upon arriving in Riga in early 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote several letters of gratitude for US entry permits obtained for himself, his family, and his secretaries Feigin, Liberman, Rotstein, and Rosh Yeshiva Eber. Ultimately only Liberman, Chadakov, and Mindel would accompany the Rebbe and his family to America.

title_en: Skobla reports Rotstein's visa secured
summary_en: On 11 Adar Sheni, R. Chaim Yitzchak Skobla wrote from Riga to the Rashag that R. M.L. Rotstein had received his visa.
story_body: On 11 Adar Sheni 5700, R. Chaim Yitzchak Skobla wrote from Riga to the Rashag — who had just arrived in America with the Rebbe — informing him that R. Moshe Leib Rotstein's visa had been received and that he would soon travel.

title_en: Rebbe instructs loans for rescue travel expenses
summary_en: On 25 Adar Sheni 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe wired instructions to extend interest-free loans to fund travel for Eber, Rotstein, and Zalmanov.
story_body: On 25 Adar Sheni 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to R. Mordechai Chefetz in Riga instructing that gemach loans be given: 2,500 to R. Yehuda Eber, 1,500 to R. Moshe Leib Rotstein, and up to 500 lats to R. Shmuel Zalmanov, all on the Rebbe's account.

title_en: Rebbe instructs delivery of 25 books to Rotstein
summary_en: On 14 Iyar 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe instructed that 25 copies of the Rayatz's sefer be given to R. Moshe Leib Rotstein.
story_body: On 14 Iyar 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to R. Mordechai Chefetz instructing that 25 copies of his sefer be given to R. Moshe Leib Rotstein. The directive was part of ongoing arrangements connected to Rotstein's anticipated departure for the United States.

title_en: Rotstein and Zalmanov depart Riga for America
summary_en: On 19 Elul 5700, R. Moshe Leib Rotstein and R. Shmuel Zalmanov departed Riga for America at 7 PM.
story_body: On 19 Elul 5700, R. Mordechai Chefetz wrote to the Frierdiker Rebbe that he was going to escort R. Moshe Leib Rotstein and R. Shmuel Zalmanov, who were leaving Riga that day at 7 PM en route to America. The journey would take them through Russia and Japan.

title_en: Funds wired for rabbis' Pacific crossing
summary_en: On 21 Elul 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe acknowledged a $500 check from R. Yaakov Katz of Chicago used to fund rabbis' travel.
story_body: On 21 Elul 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to R. Yaakov Katz of Chicago confirming receipt of his $500 check and that arrangements for the two rabbis' travel had been made. A telegram had already confirmed they had set out on their journey.

title_en: Rashag appeals for rescue funds from Chicago
summary_en: On 27 Elul 5700, the Rashag wrote to R. Shalom Posner in Chicago seeking $1,000 in pidyon shvuyim funds to bring two families to America.
story_body: On 27 Elul 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe's son-in-law the Rashag wrote to R. Shalom Posner, the shliach in Chicago. He reported that R. Yitzchak Dov Ushpal had already departed Japan for the US on June 26, while the Zalmanov and Rotstein families had reached Vladivostok needing funds and ship tickets for the next leg.

title_en: Rotstein and Zalmanov travel from Vladivostok to Japan
summary_en: On 4 Tishrei 5701, the Frierdiker Rebbe reported receiving a telegram that Rotstein and Zalmanov had arrived safely in Vladivostok and were traveling to Japan.
story_body: On 4 Tishrei 5701, the Frierdiker Rebbe relayed in a letter that he had received a telegram that day from R. Moshe Leib Rotstein and R. Shmuel Zalmanov, reporting their safe arrival in Vladivostok and their continuing travel to Japan en route to America.

title_en: Rotstein, Zalmanov, and Ushpal arrive in San Francisco
summary_en: In late Tishrei 5701, R. Moshe Leib Rotstein, R. Shmuel Zalmanov, and R. Yitzchak Dov Ushpal arrived in San Francisco from Japan.
story_body: At the end of Tishrei 5701, the three Lubavitch rabbis arrived in San Francisco after their long journey through Russia, Siberia, and Japan. On 29 Tishrei, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to R. Yaakov Katz in Chicago that the three rabbis had safely arrived in America and were traveling on to New York.

title_en: Three Lubavitch rabbis arrive in New York
summary_en: On Friday Parshat Noach 1 Rosh Chodesh Cheshvan 5701, three Lubavitch rabbis arrived in New York and HaKeriah VeHakedusha reported on their rescue.
story_body: On Friday Parshat Noach, 1 Rosh Chodesh Cheshvan 5701, R. Moshe Leib Rotstein, R. Shmuel Zalmanov, and R. Yitzchak Dov Ushpal arrived in New York with their families. The Lubavitch periodical HaKeriah VeHakedusha (issue 2) reported on their rescue from the 'European inferno' through the Pidyon Shvuyim Fund established by the Lubavitcher Rebbe.

title_en: Rotstein appointed to head Agudas Chabad in Chicago
summary_en: Upon arriving in America in late 5701, R. Moshe Leib Rotstein was sent to lead Agudas Chabad in Chicago.
story_body: After arriving in the United States in late Tishrei 5701, R. Moshe Leib Rotstein was dispatched to direct Agudas Chabad in Chicago. He served there before later returning to the Rebbe's secretariat.

title_en: Rotstein returns to serve as Rebbe's secretary
summary_en: In 5706, R. Moshe Leib Rotstein returned to work as secretary to the Frierdiker Rebbe.
story_body: In the year 5706 (1946), R. Moshe Leib Rotstein returned from his post in Chicago to once again serve as secretary to the Frierdiker Rebbe in New York. He would continue this role until the Rebbe's passing.

title_en: Rotstein continues as secretary under the Rebbe
summary_en: After Yud Shvat 5710, R. Moshe Leib Rotstein continued serving as secretary under the Rebbe (Rayatz's successor).
story_body: Following Yud Shvat 5710 and the passing of the Frierdiker Rebbe, R. Moshe Leib Rotstein continued as secretary under the new Rebbe. He served in this capacity for many years thereafter.

title_en: Death of R. Moshe Leib Rotstein
summary_en: R. Moshe Leib Rotstein passed away on 9 Marcheshvan 5728.
story_body: R. Moshe Leib Rotstein, longtime secretary to the Frierdiker Rebbe and the Rebbe, passed away on 9 Marcheshvan 5728. He had served the Lubavitch movement faithfully from his time in Warsaw through his decades in America.

title_en: Feigin reports rescue logistics struggles in Riga
summary_en: On 12 Adar Rishon 5700, R. Yechezkel Feigin wrote that his travel from Riga was still uncertain pending HIAS funding.
story_body: On 12 Adar Rishon 5700, the secretary R. Yechezkel Feigin wrote to his brother-in-law R. Shalom Posner that his travel arrangements were stalled while he sought funding sources. He was in discussion with HIAS and hoped a solution would soon emerge, noting the Rebbe was planning to depart Riga around March 4.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe departs Riga for America
summary_en: On 24 Adar Rishon 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe left Riga on his journey to America.
story_body: On 24 Adar Rishon 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe departed Riga on his journey to the United States. R. Yechezkel Feigin and his family remained behind in Riga, with HIAS funding for their tickets still unresolved.

title_en: Feigin briefs Rebbe on stalled rescue while at sea
summary_en: On 1 Adar Sheni 5700, R. Yechezkel Feigin wrote to the Rebbe — then at sea — explaining HIAS funding confusion delaying his departure.
story_body: On Rosh Chodesh Adar Sheni 5700, with the Rebbe aboard ship bound for America, R. Yechezkel Feigin wrote detailing the obstacles to his family's travel. HIAS New York would not raise the $1,200 ceiling, and confusion arose over whether the Joint had given monetary aid or only endorsement, delaying the matter further.

title_en: Feigin weighs Norwegian vs Swedish ship options
summary_en: On 3 Adar Sheni 5700, Feigin wrote that he was pursuing Norwegian and Swedish transit visas for an April 5 sailing from Bergen.
story_body: On 3 Adar Sheni 5700, Feigin wrote again about logistics. A Norwegian ship would sail from Bergen April 5–8, while a Swedish ship would depart Gothenburg April 13. The Swedish option would mean spending the start of Pesach aboard ship, which he hoped to avoid, especially given his wife's frail health.

title_en: Feigin reports HIAS will cover only 50%
summary_en: On Ta'anit Esther 5700, Feigin wrote that HIAS had agreed to cover only about fifty percent of his travel costs.
story_body: On Ta'anit Esther 5700, R. Yechezkel Feigin reported that Rosenbaum had received a telegram indicating HIAS would participate only at about 50% of the travel costs. With time running short, he was still uncertain how matters would resolve, and Rosenbaum was pushing him toward the April 13 Swedish ship despite the Pesach problem.

title_en: R. Yehuda Eber arrives in Riga from Warsaw
summary_en: On Friday before Purim Sheni 5700, Rosh Yeshiva R. Yehuda Eber arrived safely in Riga from Warsaw.
story_body: Rosh Yeshiva R. Yehuda Eber had failed to depart with the Rebbe in early Tevet. On 12 Adar Sheni 5700, R. Mordechai Chefetz reported he would arrive that Tuesday from Warsaw. On 21 Adar Sheni, Feigin confirmed Eber's safe arrival in Riga the previous Erev Shabbat.

title_en: Rebbe announces Eber's arrival in Riga to Chicago
summary_en: On 3 Nissan 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe informed Agudas Chabad in Chicago that Rosh Yeshiva R. Yehuda Eber had reached Riga.
story_body: On 3 Nissan 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to Agudas Chabad in Chicago that a telegram had arrived from the chief Rosh Yeshiva R. Yehuda Eber confirming his safe arrival in Riga. This was part of efforts to coordinate continued rescue funding from America.

title_en: Eber plans departure via Italy on May 28
summary_en: On 5 Iyar 5700, R. Mordechai Chefetz wrote that R. Yehuda Eber had a permit to travel via Italy and planned to sail May 28.
story_body: On 5 Iyar 5700, R. Mordechai Chefetz reported to the Frierdiker Rebbe that R. Yehuda Eber had received a transit permit through Italy and intended to depart on a ship leaving from there May 28. Two weeks later, however, the route was cut off when no ship was available.

title_en: Italian route blocked for Riga refugees
summary_en: On 18 Iyar 5700, Chefetz reported the Italian sea route had been cut off, stranding the rescuees in Riga.
story_body: On 18 Iyar 5700, R. Mordechai Chefetz wrote that those preparing to travel were ready to leave, but the Italian route had now been suspended with no ship departing. R. Feigin and R. Eber and their families therefore remained stranded in Riga.

title_en: Joint telegram requesting American ship berths
summary_en: On 22 Iyar 5700, Feigin and Eber jointly telegraphed the Rebbe requesting help booking berths on an American ship.
story_body: On 30 May 1940 / 22 Iyar 5700, R. Yechezkel Feigin and R. Yehuda Eber jointly cabled the Frierdiker Rebbe requesting his help to book berths on an American vessel. They asked the shipping company to wire Cook's Riga office authorization to sell them tickets, and sought guidance on whether to try the Italian sailing if it materialized.

title_en: Feigin and Eber appeal for Petsamo route via Rashag
summary_en: On Erev Rosh Chodesh Sivan 5700, Feigin and Eber wrote to the Rashag asking him to pressure Finland to permit the Petsamo route.
story_body: On Erev Rosh Chodesh Sivan 5700, with the Italian route closed, R. Yechezkel Feigin and R. Yehuda Eber wrote a joint letter to the Rashag describing their plight. They had been ready to travel five times already, all foiled. The only remaining option was via Petsamo in Finland, but Finland had refused entry permits; they urged the Rashag to leverage US senators or the Finnish consul to intercede.

title_en: Rashag appeals to Latvian envoy in Washington
summary_en: On 17 Sivan 5700 / June 23, 1940, the Rashag wrote to Latvian envoy Alfred Bilmanis seeking Finnish diplomatic help for the refugees.
story_body: On June 23, 1940 / 17 Sivan 5700, the Rashag wrote to Alfred Bilmanis at the Latvian embassy in Washington following a phone conversation. He listed the Hornstein, Eber, and Feigin families with their dates of birth, noted they held US visas, and asked Bilmanis to request Finland's envoy to instruct his Riga embassy to facilitate transit through Petsamo.

title_en: Riga rescue hopes rise then fall in late summer 5700
summary_en: On 28 Menachem Av 5700, R. Mordechai Chefetz reported hopes that Feigin and Eber would soon receive travel permits.
story_body: On 28 Menachem Av 5700, R. Mordechai Chefetz wrote to the Frierdiker Rebbe expressing hope that R. Yechezkel Feigin would soon receive his travel permit and that R. Yehuda Eber had already obtained his. By 4 Tishrei tash'a, however, both were still waiting in vain for salvation.

title_en: Soviet conquest of Latvia voids exit documents
summary_en: During summer 5700, Latvia was conquered by the Soviets, voiding the refugees' Latvian passports and complicating exit.
story_body: In Sivan 5700, the Soviets conquered Latvia. R. Feigin and R. Eber were Russian citizens whose Latvian-era documents now lost validity. They were forced to re-apply for new Soviet passports — a process taking many months requiring Moscow approval — during which their American visas expired.

title_en: Feigin writes of voided permits and new passport requirement
summary_en: In Tishrei 5701, Feigin wrote that they had been told to reapply for Soviet passports, with a two-month wait for Moscow's reply.
story_body: In Tishrei 5701, R. Yechezkel Feigin wrote to the Frierdiker Rebbe that they had been instructed to submit fresh applications for Soviet passports, with a two-month wait for a Moscow decision. The American consul meanwhile would not renew expired visas without new authorizations from the US, including a new affidavit for their son Shmuel Leib.

title_en: Rebbe responds to Feigin on visa rescue limits
summary_en: On 2 Marcheshvan 5701, the Frierdiker Rebbe replied that everything possible had been done and care had to be taken not to worsen matters.
story_body: On 2 Marcheshvan 5701, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to R. Yechezkel Feigin acknowledging that everything possible had been done. Only one further option remained — asking the local representative to press his superiors — but they feared that pushing too hard might backfire and harm matters.

title_en: Eber's family receives bureaucratic setbacks in Cheshvan
summary_en: In Marcheshvan 5701, R. Yehuda Eber wrote that the prior arrangements were nullified and they had to file fresh autobiographies with the Soviets.
story_body: In Marcheshvan 5701, R. Yehuda Eber wrote that the early Russian envoy's communication had been mistaken; the Russian connection was now entirely voided. They had to file fresh passport applications with detailed autobiographies covering themselves, siblings, and parents from birth. Acceptance of applications had only just begun the previous week.

title_en: Feigin submits Soviet exit application
summary_en: On 9 Marcheshvan 5701, R. Mordechai Chefetz reported that R. Y. Eber had submitted his application and would await an answer in about two months.
story_body: On 9 Marcheshvan 5701, R. Mordechai Chefetz wrote to the Frierdiker Rebbe that R. Yehuda Eber had already submitted his application and was told to expect a response in about two months. R. Yechezkel Feigin had not yet submitted his.

title_en: Rebbe inquires about Feigin's contacts with Soviet relative
summary_en: On 27 Marcheshvan 5701, the Rebbe inquired whether Feigin was in contact with 'R. Nissan,' a coded reference in rescue correspondence.
story_body: On 27 Marcheshvan 5701, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to R. Yechezkel Feigin asking if he was in contact with 'sh'b R. Nissan' and what replies he had received. The cryptic references reflected the wartime need to mask the actual nature of Soviet rescue communications.

title_en: Rebbe writes Feigin about Soviet rescue caution
summary_en: On 15 Kislev 5701, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to Feigin about the difficulty of pressuring Soviet contacts without backfiring.
story_body: On 15 Kislev 5701, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to R. Yechezkel Feigin describing the painful constraints in maneuvering for Soviet exit permits. 'Everyone knows how hard it is to move people whose word is empty,' he wrote, expressing fear that any pressure on the contact might prove counterproductive.

title_en: Eber reports cold rejection on travel
summary_en: In Tevet 5701, R. Yehuda Eber wrote to the Rebbe that the Soviet official had coldly told him no decision was yet made.
story_body: In Tevet 5701, R. Yehuda Eber wrote to the Frierdiker Rebbe that nothing had changed regarding their travel. He had visited the relevant official, who responded coldly that no decision had been made and they would be notified when one was, telling him not to come asking.

title_en: Rebbe writes Eber hoping for travel papers
summary_en: On 7 Shvat 5701, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote praying R. Yehuda Eber would soon receive the necessary papers and travel safely.
story_body: On 7 Shvat 5701, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote to R. Yehuda Eber expressing the prayer that he would soon receive the needed travel documents and that his journey would prove safe and successful in material and spiritual matters.

title_en: Rebbe summarizes Feigin and Eber's situation
summary_en: On 17 Tevet 5701, the Rebbe's secretariat informed R. Yerachmiel Binyaminson that Feigin and Eber remained in Riga unable to obtain exit permits.
story_body: On 17 Tevet 5701, the Rebbe's secretariat wrote to the Gaon HaChasid R. Yerachmiel Binyaminson summarizing the situation: R. Yechezkel Feigin and Rosh Yeshiva R. Yehuda Eber remained in Riga, still unable to obtain exit permits. They prayed for divine mercy on all of them.

title_en: Rebbe writes about Eber's role at Otwock yeshiva
summary_en: On 21 Shvat 5701, the Rebbe wrote that R. Yehuda Eber had been Rosh Yeshiva at Tomchei Temimim in Otwock and was awaiting travel in Riga.
story_body: On 21 Shvat 5701, the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote that R. Yehuda Eber had served as Rosh Yeshiva at Tomchei Temimim in Otwock. He had sent visas for Eber and his family, who were now waiting along the way in Riga.

title_en: Eber's pidyon nefesh from Riga
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Adar 5701, R. Yehuda Eber sent a pidyon nefesh to the Rebbe asking for mercy on his family's rescue.
story_body: On Rosh Chodesh Adar 5701, R. Yehuda Eber sent the Frierdiker Rebbe a pidyon nefesh — the final extant correspondence from him. He asked the Rebbe to arouse mercy for his family, naming each by their mother's name, that the officials should mercifully grant the documents needed to reach America.

title_en: Nazi conquest of Riga
summary_en: In the summer of 5701, Riga was conquered by the Nazis, sealing the fate of its Jewish refugees.
story_body: In the summer of 5701, Riga fell to the Nazis. The Jews there, including R. Yechezkel Feigin, R. Yehuda Eber, and their families — all of whom had spent months trying in vain to escape to America — were unable to flee further. They would be murdered in the months that followed.

title_en: Murder of Riga's Jews by Nazis
summary_en: In Kislev 5702, the Jews of Riga were murdered by the Nazis, including R. Yechezkel Feigin, R. Yehuda Eber, and their families.
story_body: In Kislev 5702, the Nazis murdered the Jews of Riga, including the families of R. Yechezkel Feigin and R. Yehuda Eber, who had spent two years trying to escape to America. According to estimates from survivors of the killing, R. Eber and his family were among the thousands killed al kiddush Hashem.

title_en: Burning of R. Yechezkel Feigin in synagogue
summary_en: On 10 Kislev 5702, the Nazis burned R. Yechezkel Feigin in a synagogue together with chasidim R. Yitzchak Horowitz and R. Eliyahu Chaim Althaus.
story_body: On 10 Kislev 5702, the Nazis burned R. Yechezkel Feigin alive in a synagogue together with the chasidim R. Yitzchak Horowitz (Hamasmid) and R. Eliyahu Chaim Althaus. They were among the many Lubavitch chassidim murdered al kiddush Hashem in occupied Riga.

title_en: Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak arrives in Riga after escaping Warsaw siege
summary_en: On 5 Tevet 5700, the Frierdiker Rebbe reached Riga immediately after the Nazi siege of Warsaw and at once began organizing aid for the chassidim left behind in occupied Poland.
story_body: Having been smuggled out of war-torn Warsaw, the Rebbe arrived in Riga on Sunday, 5 Tevet, and made relief for Polish Jewry his very first order of business. That same day he issued public appeals — one to general Jewry and one to anash worldwide — describing the catastrophic conditions and urging immediate fundraising through the Joint Distribution Committee. The arrival marked the start of a half-year base in Riga from which he would coordinate aid before sailing to America.

title_en: Open letter 'To Our Brethren of Israel' appeals for Polish Jewry via the Joint
summary_en: On the day of his arrival in Riga, the Rebbe published a general letter (Igros V:1132*) calling for a worldwide collection for starving Polish Jewry, with funds to be channeled through the Joint in Warsaw.
story_body: The Rebbe described soup kitchens, hospitals, old-age homes and orphanages running on Joint funding inside Warsaw, and asked Jews of every party affiliation to contribute. A parallel circular addressed to anash and Tomchei Tmimim students worldwide called the health and economic situation 'terrifying' and demanded rapid practical help.

title_en: Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak arrives in New York; addresses thousands at the port
summary_en: On 9 Adar Sheni 5700 the Rebbe landed in New York and immediately addressed a crowd of several thousand in the port hall, conveying greetings from European Jewry and calling for material and spiritual aid.
story_body: Stepping into the largest hall of the harbor, the Rebbe relayed regards from the Jews of Europe and called on American and Canadian Jewry to redouble their relief work and help refugees relocate. The very same day he issued a general letter (Igros V:1165) and within days established the 'Pidyon Shvuyim' fund to rescue chassidim and yeshiva students from occupied Europe.

title_en: 'Pidyon Shvuyim' rescue fund established in New York
summary_en: Shortly after arriving in America in Adar Sheni 5700, the Rebbe founded the Pidyon Shvuyim fund to rescue anash and yeshiva students from Nazi-occupied Europe and support their families.
story_body: From his quarters at the Greystone Hotel, the Rebbe entrusted Rabbi Eliyahu Simpson with the work of registering European families in urgent need. The first list, written on hotel stationery, recorded nearly one hundred families totaling roughly 500 souls across nineteen Lithuanian towns, with parallel lists soon prepared for occupied Poland.

title_en: First $2,000 wartime aid transfer via the Mizrach channel from Riga
summary_en: On 29 Adar Sheni 5700 the wealthy Yehoshua ben Kalman Mizrach handed the Rebbe $2,000 in Riga so that an equivalent sum could later be released in America for rescue work in Poland and Russia.
story_body: Because direct money transfers from the US to occupied Europe were illegal, the Rebbe ran a hidden parallel-payment scheme: Mizrach gave dollars in Riga to R' Mordechai Chefetz, and the Rebbe matched the sum from New York to a beneficiary Mizrach designated. The arrangement was concealed in coded correspondence using terms like 'books,' 'Ben Kalman,' and 'RIVK,' and ultimately moved $5,500 through this single channel.

title_en: Rebbe wires Riga to spend up to 3,000 lats on Pesach matzah and food for Warsaw
summary_en: On 25 Adar Sheni 5700 the Rebbe telegraphed R' Mordechai Chefetz in Riga authorizing shipment of matzah and food packages worth up to 3,000 lats for Pesach relief to anash in Poland.
story_body: Chefetz had reported obtaining a Soviet permit to ship 1,600 kilos of matzah and 1,600 kilos of other foodstuffs to Poland, and was already sending roughly 500 lats' worth to brethren in Russia. The Rebbe authorized expanding the operation, ultimately covering $3,000 personally plus $2,000 via Mizrach, with additional small Pesach shipments bringing the total to 6,000 lats.

title_en: First visa application list for 47 anash families submitted to US government
summary_en: On 22 August 1940 (18 Menachem Av 5700) Agudas Chabad submitted to the US government a first list of 47 visa applications — covering over 100 souls — together with a seven-paragraph petition signed by the Rebbe.
story_body: The petition asked for temporary visas to shelter anash in America until the war ended. It accompanied a separate list of 127 yeshiva-student visas already in process. A second batch of 62 visas covering roughly 200 more souls would follow in November, after which attorney Arthur Rabinowitz filed a consolidated brief through Rashag.

title_en: Second visa list of 62 anash families submitted to US government
summary_en: On 19 November 1940 (18 Cheshvan 5701) Agudas Chabad filed a second list of 62 visa applications covering some 200 anash, accompanied by a brief prepared by Rashag for attorney Arthur Rabinowitz.
story_body: Together with the two student lists and the earlier 47-family list, this submission brought the total to over 100 family-visa applications. The State Department later confirmed it would issue immigration visas for the 75 students and 62 anash on this batch, conditional on affidavits being filed for each applicant.

title_en: Rashag summarizes visa-rescue effort for secretary Roitstein
summary_en: On 7 Shevat 5701 Rashag forwarded to secretary Moshe Leib Roitstein the complete roster of students and anash for whom American visas had been obtained from Lithuania, Latvia and Soviet-occupied Poland.
story_body: He noted that further lists from Warsaw–Otwock and additional applicants were forthcoming, and that the State Department had agreed to convert the second batch from temporary to immigration visas, provided affidavits be supplied. The summary remains the clearest contemporary inventory of the Chabad visa operation just before American consular practice tightened.

title_en: Rebbe describes acute fundraising difficulty in letter to R' Yehoshua Isaac Baruch
summary_en: On 16 Tevet 5701 the Rebbe wrote to R' Yehoshua Isaac Baruch in Lithuania explaining that every dollar of rescue money was being raised as a personal loan and asking that expenses be minimized accordingly.
story_body: The letter (Igros V:1337) noted that he had no fixed source of funds and that the travel costs already sent had required enormous effort to scrape together as gemach loans. He requested that Kovno and Riga representatives keep package costs as low as possible and send detailed accountings of past disbursements.

title_en: Rabbi Yechiel Yaakov Weinberg requests visas for Warsaw rabbis and activists
summary_en: On 25 May 1941 Rabbi Yechiel Yaakov Weinberg, author of Seridei Eish and former director of the Berlin Rabbiner-Seminar, sent the Rebbe's secretariat a list of Warsaw rabbis and communal activists for whom he asked help obtaining American visas.
story_body: Weinberg, then in Warsaw, forwarded names of admorim, rabbis and askanim — but by this date the US government had stopped issuing new visas to European Jews and had revoked many already approved. The list survives in the secretariat archive as documentation of an effort that could no longer succeed.

title_en: Last news from anash in Warsaw reaches the Rebbe's secretariat
summary_en: A 15 Tammuz 5701 secretariat briefing relayed the final updates received from anash in Warsaw, including from R' Shmuel Shmotkin, R' Shneur Zalman Shmotkin, and R' Leib Raskin, confirming receipt of food packages and visa questions.
story_body: Shmuel Shmotkin had received his visa but did not know what to do for his daughters over eighteen or his sons-in-law; Shneur Zalman Shmotkin reported that the packages were a literal lebens-frage and that R' Moshe Schneersohn had been moved from Lublin to Izbica; Leib Raskin thanked the Rebbe for parcels keeping his family alive. After this date contact with Warsaw effectively ceased.

title_en: Riga's Chabad community murdered by the Nazis
summary_en: During Kislev 5702 the anash of Riga — including the families of Feigin, Chefetz, Asheroff, Althaus, Horowitz, Volshanik and others — were murdered by the Nazis.
story_body: Months earlier the Soviet conquest of Latvia had already cut off the package-shipment lifeline from Riga to Poland. With the German occupation that followed Operation Barbarossa, the Chabad community of Riga that had hosted the Rebbe in early 1940 was annihilated; the specific fates would only be confirmed gradually through later correspondence.

title_en: R' Mordechai Dubin released from Soviet prison
summary_en: On 23 Kislev 5702 R' Mordechai Dubin, head of the Riga Chabad community and former Latvian Saeima deputy, was freed from Soviet imprisonment and resettled in Saratov.
story_body: Dubin had been arrested during the Soviet annexation of Latvia and deported into Russia proper. His release left him stranded in Saratov rather than Riga — which in any case had by then been destroyed under Nazi occupation — and he resumed correspondence with the Rebbe in America under heavy censorship.

title_en: Rebbe writes coded inquiry to Dubin about fate of Riga anash
summary_en: On 23 Adar Rishon 5703 the Rebbe wrote to Dubin in Saratov, asking in disguised Yiddish about the welfare of named relatives and chassidim in Riga (Igros XIV:5306).
story_body: Phrased to evade Soviet censors, the letter inquired after Chatche Feigin, Mottel the shochet Chefetz, Avraham Eli Asheroff, Elya Chaim Althaus, Mendel Zak, Avigdor Volshanik and others — all of whom, unknown to the Rebbe at that point, had already perished in the Riga massacres.

title_en: Rebbe relocates from Rostov to Leningrad
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn moved his residence from Rostov to Leningrad (Petrograd).
story_body: In 5684, the Frierdiker Rebbe transferred his seat from Rostov to Leningrad. Soon after the move, the bibliographer Shmuel Wiener approached him with an offer to sell his celebrated private library. This move set the stage for the foundational acquisition of what would become the Lubavitch Library.

title_en: Contract signed to purchase Shmuel Wiener's library
summary_en: The Frierdiker Rebbe signed a written contract to purchase the Wiener library for $5,000 in monthly $50 installments.
story_body: On 8 Cheshvan 5685 the Frierdiker Rebbe and bibliographer Shmuel Wiener executed a signed agreement transferring Wiener's massive bibliographic collection — including some 400 Haggadah editions, 140 Kinnos volumes, sixty Siddur recensions, machzorim, and Yiddish Tchines — to the Rebbe. The purchase price of $5,000 was to be paid in monthly installments of $50 over many years. About 4,000 unbound items came with the collection and would be bound after delivery.

title_en: Wiener library acquired in Kislev 5685
summary_en: In Kislev 5685 the Frierdiker Rebbe formally took possession of the Wiener bibliographic collection, the founding nucleus of the Lubavitch Library.
story_body: Following negotiations begun the previous year, the Rebbe completed the purchase of Wiener's library in Kislev 5685 under terms of long-term monthly payments. The collection had been stored in Wiener's flooded basement and was rescued and dried in the upper floor of a factory rented by R. Eliyahu Chaim Althoz during the Soviet NEP era. The library would become the cornerstone of the future Lubavitch collection.

title_en: Soviet censors approve export of 59 boxes of books
summary_en: Soviet foreign-trade and customs officials in Leningrad personally inspected and sealed 59 boxes of Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak's books for transfer to Latvia.
story_body: On 5 Menachem-Av 5687, representatives A. Feigelstein of the foreign-trade office and G. Alachbrov of the Leningrad customs office signed off on the inspection and official sealing of fifty-nine book boxes belonging to Y. Schneersohn. After initial Soviet refusal to permit export of the library, intercession by Dr. A. Cohen of Berlin and Latvian parliamentarian Mordechai Dubin secured Moscow's order to allow the books out, with the censor instructed to stamp every crate.

title_en: Riga community petitions Soviets to release Rebbe and books
summary_en: The Riga kehillah wrote to the Soviet authorities announcing the Rebbe's appointment as Chief Rabbi of Riga and requesting that he be permitted to bring his ancestors' manuscripts.
story_body: On 23 Menachem-Av 5687 the Riga Jewish community council notified the Soviet regime of the Frierdiker Rebbe's appointment as Chief Rabbi of Riga and pleaded that he be allowed to immigrate with all his family and bring along the writings of his holy forefathers and his own manuscripts. The letter was part of the diplomatic pressure that eventually persuaded Moscow to authorize the export of the library.

title_en: Final Soviet approval to ship 66 book crates to Riga
summary_en: On erev Yom Kippur 5688 the Soviets issued final clearance for sixty-six crates of books and effects to be shipped to Riga.
story_body: Just before the Rebbe's departure, on 5 October 1927, customs and foreign-trade representatives issued the conclusive export authorization covering 66 crates of books and household items destined for Riga. The document noted that the books had been examined and approved for shipment by foreign-ministry officials, completing the long bureaucratic battle to bring the library out of the Soviet Union.

title_en: Rebbe arrives in Riga with library
summary_en: At the start of 5688 the Frierdiker Rebbe left Russia for Riga, bringing the Wiener library and his manuscripts.
story_body: After protracted negotiations and intercession by Dr. Cohen of Berlin and Mordechai Dubin, the Soviet government permitted Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak to emigrate at the beginning of 5688 together with all his printed books and manuscripts. He settled in Riga and began rebuilding his life in exile, still burdened by emigration debts and without permanent quarters.

title_en: Rebbe writes Iyar 5688 letters on building the library
summary_en: On 16 Iyar 5688 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote letters detailing his plan to enlarge the library by soliciting books from authors and dealers worldwide.
story_body: From Riga the Rebbe wrote to bookseller David Frankel of Husiatyn requesting catalogues from booksellers in Yemen, Australia, Africa, France and Italy, and to R. Chaim Hillel Bloch in the Holy Land instructing him to ask authors and Jerusalem institutions to send their publications, forms, calendars and circulars. The strategy aimed to gather books and ephemera cheaply, paying only postage, in order to rebuild the collection lost in Russia.

title_en: Rebbe outlines master plan for an open scholarly library
summary_en: In summer 5688 the Frierdiker Rebbe summoned his librarian Chaim Liberman and outlined a fifteen-year plan to build an open scholarly library at Lubavitch.
story_body: After Liberman's own emigration from Russia in early summer 5688, the Rebbe shared his vision: rather than a closed private collection, the library would be opened to researchers like the seminary or British Museum libraries. He envisioned modest annual book purchases over about fifteen years, eventual cataloging, and a dedicated building — perhaps named for a wealthy donor — to house the future thousands of volumes.

title_en: HaOlam reports on the Rebbe's library in Riga
summary_en: The London weekly HaOlam published a correspondent's report describing the Frierdiker Rebbe's library in Riga as a rich treasury of Jewish antiquities.
story_body: On 22 Elul 5688, HaOlam printed an account by a Yiddishe Shtime correspondent who had visited the library in Riga. The article enumerated such treasures as a 440-year-old manuscript of R. Avraham Saba, a 1475 Venice siddur, 950 Haggadah editions in many languages, 900 selichos volumes, and manuscripts of the Baal Shem Tov and Maggid of Mezeritch, painting a vivid picture of the collection's scope just months after its arrival.

title_en: Rebbe insists books must accompany him out of Russia
summary_en: An Althoz letter from motzaei Rosh Hashana 5690 records that the Frierdiker Rebbe had refused to leave Russia if a single book were left behind.
story_body: Writing in October 1929, R. Eliyahu Chaim Althoz recounted the Rebbe's earlier insistence — delivered while at the ohel in Rostov — that he would not depart if even one volume had to remain. Mordechai Dubin once again traveled to intercede and succeeded in extracting the export concession, a story the chassid R. Y. Jacobson similarly preserved in his memoir Zikaron Livnei Yisrael.

title_en: Library cataloging effort under way in Riga
summary_en: On 29 Tevet 5691 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote that work on cataloging the Wiener-based library was ongoing and a full catalogue was expected within a month.
story_body: Although the Wiener collection had been at the Rebbe's disposal since 1924, no comprehensive list yet existed because the books had been arriving in bundles. In Tevet 5691 the Rebbe wrote that they were finally organizing the holdings and anticipated completing a catalogue within roughly a month, which he hoped to share with correspondents.

title_en: Rebbe details cataloging priorities for the library
summary_en: On 23 Adar 5693 the Frierdiker Rebbe described the library's cataloging order: Yiddish, sacred works, secular Hebrew, broadsides, then catalogues.
story_body: Writing from Riga, the Rebbe acknowledged that comprehensive cataloging remained far off. Only a partial typed inventory existed, prepared by R. Chaim Liberman, used principally to know which holy books still needed acquiring. The Rebbe sketched the planned cataloging sequence by category, reflecting his ongoing struggle to bring scholarly order to the collection.

title_en: Rebbe writes Persitz soliciting books for library
summary_en: On 3 Iyar 5693 the Rebbe wrote to publisher Shoshana Persitz asking that every publisher honor the Lubavitch library with copies of their books.
story_body: The Rebbe explained that he was a collector of everything printed in Hebrew letters regardless of subject, and considered it fitting for publishers to gift the Lubavitch book-collection with their imprints. The note was one of many sent over years in which the Rebbe personally enlisted authors and publishers to enlarge the library at minimal cost.

title_en: Library acknowledges Iyar 5693 book donations
summary_en: On 29 Iyar 5693 the Frierdiker Rebbe confirmed receipt of donated books for the library on its newly printed institutional stationery.
story_body: Using letterhead headed 'Aseifas Sefarim u'Kisvei Yad Lubavitch — temporarily in Riga, Latvia,' the Rebbe acknowledged a recent shipment with thanks. The stationery, envelopes and postcards bearing this header were one of several mechanisms — alongside newspaper advertisements — used to formalize the library as an institution rather than a private collection.

title_en: Rebbe travels to Warsaw and on to Marienbad
summary_en: On 10 Tammuz 5693 the Frierdiker Rebbe departed Riga, stopping at the Warsaw yeshiva on 12 Tammuz and arriving in Marienbad on 13 Tammuz for medical treatment.
story_body: Doctors insisted the ailing Rebbe travel to the Marienbad spa. With great difficulty Lubavitch chassidim raised the funds for the trip. R. Yechezkel Feigin wrote that the Rebbe left Riga on 10 Tammuz, visited the yeshiva in Warsaw on 12 Tammuz, and arrived in Marienbad on 13 Tammuz to begin medical care during the deepest months of the economic depression.

title_en: Rebbe directs library packing for Warsaw move
summary_en: From Marienbad on 3 Menachem-Av 5693 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote his two Riga secretaries with detailed instructions for crating and shipping the library to Warsaw.
story_body: In separate letters to R. Chaim Liberman and R. Moshe Leib Rothstein, the Rebbe specified wooden-box packing, censorship approvals, freight-company arrangements and even the labeling — directing that crates be numbered rather than marked 'Bibliotheca Lubavitch.' A subsequent letter on 22 Av to the Rebbetzin added detailed instructions about manuscript shipment and the yellow case of his father's writings.

title_en: HaPardes advertisement solicits donations for Lubavitch library
summary_en: In Elul 5693 the journal HaPardes carried an advertisement thanking authors and publishers for sending their works to the Lubavitch library and requesting future donations.
story_body: Dictated by the Rebbe himself and signed in the library's institutional name rather than his own, the notice appeared in the American journal HaPardes and listed the Riga address Pulko, Briero 10/5. It instructed rabbis, authors, publishers, and printers to send every imprint — books, broadsides, posters and notices alike — to the library, formalizing its public-institution character.

title_en: Librarian writes David Sassoon requesting Ohel David
summary_en: From Warsaw on 7 Cheshvan 5694, librarian Chaim Liberman wrote collector David Solomon Sassoon asking him to gift his catalogue Ohel David to the Lubavitch library.
story_body: The letter, signed only as 'director of the Lubavitch book and manuscript collection' without mentioning the Rebbe by name, reflected the library's new institutional identity. Liberman cited the precedent of many authors and publishers who had sent their works as gifts and thanked Sassoon in advance for joining them — one of dozens of such solicitation letters dispatched in this period.

title_en: Rebbe summarizes library's growth 5688–5694
summary_en: On 10 Sivan 5694 the Frierdiker Rebbe wrote his son-in-law summarizing that the library had nearly doubled and gained some 700 holy books since the move from Russia.
story_body: Reviewing six years of acquisitions, the Rebbe reported that according to Liberman the collection had grown nearly twofold, with paper and binding alone now worth more than what had been spent, and roughly seven hundred new sefarim added, many donated by authors and publishers. He noted that if Heaven helped him retrieve the Moscow library as well, the combined holdings would constitute an enormous treasure.

title_en: Rebbe directs book purchases from Purkersdorf sanitorium
summary_en: From the Purkersdorf sanitorium in winter 5695 the Frierdiker Rebbe sent funds and detailed purchasing instructions to librarian Chaim Liberman in Warsaw.
story_body: During the Rebbe's winter convalescence in Austria, he and his librarian conducted an active correspondence about acquisitions. Liberman's responses — including 7 Shevat 5695 — describe specific purchases of book lots for 25 to 200 zlotys, queries about exchanges of duplicates, and consultation on individual titles, evidence of the Rebbe's hands-on involvement in every significant decision.

title_en: Researcher Zalman Reisen visits Warsaw library
summary_en: On 27 Adar Sheni 5695 the Yiddish scholar Reisen spent an hour and a half studying Yiddish books and manuscripts in the Lubavitch library in Warsaw.
story_body: Librarian Liberman reported to the Rebbe that Reisen was especially interested in the Yiddish and Ivri-Taytsh divisions and was shown manuscripts and broadsides. Reisen requested permission to publish some items in YIVO's anthologies, asked to borrow others, and inquired whether the library had a room where scholars could work — leaving the visit deeply impressed by holdings he had not expected to find.

title_en: Rebbe moves from Warsaw to Otwock
summary_en: After nearly two years in Warsaw, the Rebbe Rayatz relocated to nearby Otwock in early Tammuz 5695.
story_body: The sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, had lived in Warsaw from Elul 5693 (1933). In early Tammuz 5695 (July 1935) he moved with his household and library to the smaller town of Otwock outside Warsaw, where he would remain for about four years until the end of 5699 (1939). The library was relocated under his oral direction since he was personally present in Warsaw at the time.

title_en: Founding of Agudath Chassidei Chabad in America
summary_en: Agudath Chassidei Chabad of America was founded in 5684 as the principal support organization for Chabad activity in Europe.
story_body: In 5684 (1924) Agudath Chassidei Chabad was established in the United States. It became the primary funder of Chabad's activities in Russia, Riga, and Poland, supporting the network of Tomchei Temimim yeshivos, the Rebbe Rayatz's household and secretariat, and the acquisition of books for the Lubavitch library.

title_en: Future Rebbe writes to R. Eliyahu Simpson about acquiring books
summary_en: On 21 Menachem Av 5696 the Rebbe's son-in-law (later the Rebbe) asked R. Eliyahu Simpson to help collect books in America for the Rayatz's library.
story_body: Writing on 21 Menachem Av 5696 (August 9, 1936), Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson asked R. Eliyahu Simpson, a senior Tomim in America, to organize anash there to send books to the Rebbe Rayatz's library. He specifically requested old siddurim, chumashim, haggadot, machzorim, and any early Hebrew imprints from America.

title_en: Secretary Feigin writes R. Yehuda Shmotkin about library acquisitions
summary_en: On 3 Chol Hamoed Sukkos 5697 the Rebbe's secretary asked R. Yehuda Shmotkin to solicit book donations for the Otwock library.
story_body: On the third day of Chol Hamoed Sukkos 5697 (October 1936), Rabbi Yechezkel Feigin wrote to R. Yehuda Shmotkin in Eretz Yisrael at the Rebbe Rayatz's request. Shmotkin was asked to approach authors and book-buyers to donate copies to the Rebbe's library at his Otwock address (Pruse 6), continuing the established custom of presenting books as gifts to the Lubavitch Bibliothek.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes Simpson about three donated manuscripts
summary_en: On 8 Elul 5697 the Rebbe Rayatz acknowledged three manuscripts sent by R. Eliyahu Simpson, including a Siddur of the Arizal and a Venice machzor.
story_body: Replying to R. Eliyahu Simpson on 8 Elul 5697 (August 15, 1937), the Rebbe Rayatz identified the three manuscripts received as a portion of Sefer HaKavanot, a Siddur of the Arizal, and a handwritten machzor of the type used by Venetian notables on festivals. The Siddur HaArizal is cataloged in the Lubavitch manuscript collection as no. 1991 and the Venice machzor as no. 1996.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes Boston rabbi about cramped library conditions
summary_en: On 18 Tammuz 5698 the Rebbe described his 13,000-volume library as crammed into boxes in his Otwock home.
story_body: Writing to Rabbi David Meir Rabinowitz of Boston on 18 Tammuz 5698 (July 17, 1938), the Rebbe Rayatz lamented that he and his books were 'in an exile of pressure and constraint' without adequate space. He reported owning approximately 13,000 printed volumes of holy books plus several thousand history and related works, only some of which stood on shelves while the rest had been locked in crates for years.

title_en: Feigin urges Jacobson to expedite Agudath Chabad statute for Otwock purchase
summary_en: On 9 Tammuz 5698 secretary Feigin pressed R. Yisrael Jacobson to finalize Agudath Chabad's statute so a building in Otwock could be purchased in its name.
story_body: On 9 Tammuz 5698 (July 8, 1938), Rabbi Yechezkel Feigin wrote to Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson, head of Agudath Chassidei Chabad in America, urgently requesting completion of the organization's official statute. The Rebbe Rayatz had decided that a building in Otwock — to house his residence, library, and the yeshiva — must be purchased in the American organization's name, since the security of Jews and their property in Poland was no longer assured. The lawyer required the statute to explicitly authorize the Aguda to acquire real estate abroad.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz directs registration of Otwock property under American Aguda
summary_en: On 19 Tammuz 5698 the Rebbe instructed Jacobson to secure US and Polish-consular approval of Agudath Chabad's statute so the Otwock building could be acquired.
story_body: Writing on 19 Tammuz 5698 (July 18, 1938), the Rebbe Rayatz personally pressed Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson to obtain governmental and Polish-consular ratification of Agudath Chabad's statute. He asked that the approved document arrive by the end of Menachem Av so the courtyard and building for Yeshivas Tomchei Temimim in Otwock could be purchased in time. The added clauses designated the Rebbe as Honorary President and recorded all real estate as Aguda property.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz flees Otwock for Warsaw as war breaks out
summary_en: On 20–21 Elul 5699 the Rebbe Rayatz left Otwock for Warsaw with his family and secretaries as German forces advanced.
story_body: With the outbreak of World War II in Poland, on 20 or 21 Elul 5699 (around September 4, 1939) the Rebbe Rayatz evacuated Otwock together with his household and secretariat, traveling to Warsaw with the intent of continuing to Riga. Only manuscripts were taken; the entire library of roughly 120 crates and many household effects had to be left behind in Otwock. The party became trapped in the Warsaw siege for four months.

title_en: Librarian Chaim Lieberman escapes Warsaw to Riga
summary_en: On 8 Tishrei 5700 the librarian Chaim Lieberman fled Warsaw for Riga, leaving behind his belongings and Rebbe's effects in his care.
story_body: On 8 Tishrei 5700 (September 21, 1939), librarian R. Chaim Lieberman left Warsaw for Riga with only a summer coat. He later recounted that all his possessions remained behind, including manuscripts of the Rebbe Maharash he had hoped to organize and effects of the Rebbe Rayatz entrusted to him. A suitcase he tried to forward via Zalmanov demanded an exorbitant ransom and was abandoned.

title_en: Lieberman appeals to American Aguda to rescue the Otwock library
summary_en: From Riga between Yom Kippur and Sukkot 5700, Lieberman wrote to Jacobson detailing the library's abandonment in Otwock and urging American intervention.
story_body: Immediately upon reaching Riga, librarian Chaim Lieberman wrote to Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson of Agudath Chassidei Chabad in America. He reported that when they fled Otwock for Warsaw only the manuscripts were taken; the entire library — valued at perhaps thirty thousand zloty — and many household effects remained in Otwock. He warned that with Otwock falling under foreign control all could be lost, urging strong efforts to obtain export permission though prioritizing rescue of lives.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes coded letter from besieged Warsaw
summary_en: By 15 Kislev 5700 Lieberman had received the Rebbe's first letter from Warsaw, written in German to evade censors and signaling the Aguda to reclaim its library.
story_body: In a letter dated 15 Kislev 5700 (around November 27, 1939), Chaim Lieberman quoted the Rebbe Rayatz's first dispatch from besieged Warsaw. Because of heavy censorship the Rebbe wrote in German and in hints, stating he had no apartment and was crowded with his family at a friend's place with no room for the books Agudath Chabad had lent him for study — and would gladly see Agudath Chabad take them back, signaling the American organization to formally petition for the library's return.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz reaches Riga from besieged Warsaw
summary_en: After four months under siege, the Rebbe Rayatz arrived in Riga on 5 Teves 5700 following a major American rescue operation.
story_body: Trapped in besieged Warsaw for four months, the Rebbe Rayatz, his family, and his secretaries were finally permitted to leave following an enormous rescue effort mounted by Agudath Chassidei Chabad in America. On 5 Teves 5700 (December 17, 1939) they reached Riga, where they would remain about two and a half months while preparations were made for the journey to the United States.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes son-in-law of survival of manuscripts and library
summary_en: On 8 Teves 5700 the Rebbe wrote his son-in-law in France that the manuscripts and library were intact, and inquired about photographic copies.
story_body: On 8 Teves 5700 (December 20, 1939), shortly after reaching Riga, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to his son-in-law (the future Rebbe), then in France, reporting that thank God the manuscripts had been preserved and so had the library. Uncertain whether they could yet be extracted from Otwock, he asked for a detailed list of which kisvei kodesh his son-in-law had photographed in prior years, including the small notebooks, letters, and the maamar 'Toldot HaChozrim' he feared had been burned.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz cables Jacobson to extract library from Warsaw
summary_en: In early Adar Sheni 5700 the Rebbe cabled Jacobson from Riga to do everything possible to extract his library and effects from Warsaw.
story_body: In early Adar Sheni 5700 (early March 1940), still in Riga, the Rebbe Rayatz sent a telegram to Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson urgently instructing him to do whatever possible to extract his library and personal effects from Warsaw. He asked Jacobson to also enlist the assistance of Kremer and Kleinfeld in the rescue effort.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz departs Riga for the United States
summary_en: On 24 Adar I 5700 the Rebbe Rayatz left Riga to make his way to America.
story_body: After roughly two and a half months in Riga, the Rebbe Rayatz set out for the United States on 24 Adar I 5700 (March 4, 1940). The relocation marked the transfer of the headquarters of the Chabad movement from war-torn Europe to America, consistent with planning begun in winter 5699.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in New York
summary_en: On 9 Adar II 5700 the Rebbe Rayatz reached New York with his family and secretaries, transferring Chabad's center to America.
story_body: On 9 Adar II 5700 (March 19, 1940), the Rebbe Rayatz arrived in New York with his household and secretariat, completing the rescue from Europe. His arrival formalized the long-planned transfer of Chabad's worldwide headquarters from Eastern Europe to the United States, where Agudath Chassidei Chabad had already been organized since 5684 (1924).

title_en: R' Mordechai Chefetz reports library shipment from Otwock unexpectedly delayed
summary_en: From Riga, R' Mordechai Chefetz writes that the library and manuscripts which had been ready for shipment were suddenly held up, with no explanation given.
story_body: Before the Rebbe Rayatz left Warsaw he had arranged with attorney Aharon Blum to handle export of his library and manuscripts. Under the original plan the books were to leave Otwock through Italy in Adar II 5700. In a letter of 6 Nissan, R' Mordechai Chefetz of Riga — who served as the conduit for correspondence with the Hornstein family in Otwock — reported that shipment had inexplicably stalled.

title_en: Polish authorities revoke library export permit; threat to confiscate Jewish books
summary_en: R' Chefetz writes that the export permit for the library was withdrawn and a new decree threatened confiscation of all Hebrew books in occupied Poland.
story_body: On 13 Nissan, R' Mordechai Chefetz received word — and a confirming visit from the wife and son of R' Shmuel Zalmanov — that the German occupation authorities had revoked the library's export license and issued a general order that all sefarim in Poland would be confiscated. The disclosure put the entire Schneersohn library at imminent risk.

title_en: New opportunity emerges to ship Schneersohn library to USA
summary_en: After months of impasse, attorney Aharon Blum in Warsaw signals via R' Y.L. Blum of Vilna that shipment of the library to America is again possible.
story_body: On 3 Sivan, R' Chefetz reported to the Rebbe Rayatz that R' Yisroel Yaakov Ever had received word from Vilna that Aharon Blum needed an additional 500 sefarim of Rashi (i.e., dollars) to renew the shipment. The Rebbe authorized payment, and R' Ever wrote urgently to Blum to dispatch the library at once.

title_en: Library rerouted via Stettin-Stockholm to evade Soviet-occupied Latvia
summary_en: R' Chefetz telegrams from Riga that the 100 crates en route to him should instead be sent via Stettin to Stockholm rather than reaching Soviet-controlled Latvia.
story_body: By late July the Soviets had annexed Latvia and installed a Communist regime. R' Chefetz — citing his poor health and unable to receive the books in Riga — instructed Schenker shipping to redirect the cargo through Stettin and on to Stockholm, to wait there for transit to New York. The reroute spared the library from Soviet confiscation.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz approves new shipping route in three telegrams
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz cables attorney Blum and the Schenker shipping offices in Warsaw and Berlin authorizing the Stettin-Stockholm route.
story_body: On 26 Tammuz / 1 August 1940, the Rebbe Rayatz dispatched three telegrams instructing that the library be redirected to Eydtkuhnen and on through Stettin to Stockholm, where it would be held until shipment to New York became feasible. R' Chefetz confirmed three days later that the cargo had been halted and rerouted as instructed.

title_en: First railcar with 100 crates of Schneersohn library leaves Stettin for Stockholm
summary_en: Attorney Aharon Blum reports by postcard that a railcar with 100 cases of sefarim has been dispatched from Stettin toward Stockholm.
story_body: On 16 Menachem Av, Blum confirmed that the first transport — 100 cases — was on its way from Stettin to Stockholm. A second railcar with 17 additional cases remained in Warsaw pending further payment. Blum sent repeated reminders through autumn 1940, but the second shipment never left Poland.

title_en: Rashag asks R' Yisroel Chasdan in Stockholm to expedite shipment to New York
summary_en: The Rebbe's son-in-law Rashag writes Chasdan in Stockholm to push Schenker to ship the library and the Jacobson/Hecht manuscripts to the USA without further delay.
story_body: On 26 Shevat the Rashag wrote in English to R' Yisroel Chasdan, asking him to press the Schenker firm to release the Stockholm cargo and to arrange transit via Lisbon for the three crates of manuscripts being held under American Embassy custody in Berlin in the names of Rabbis Jacobson and Hecht.

title_en: R' Yisroel Chasdan secures place for library on freighter from Stockholm
summary_en: Chasdan reports he persuaded the Schenker director in Stockholm to load 12 tons of the Rebbe's library onto a ship sailing the following week.
story_body: On Erev Rosh Chodesh Adar, R' Chasdan replied to the Rashag describing his joy at securing the shipment. He had explained to the Schenker director the long history of the books — through 'Edom' and beyond — and obtained agreement to load 12 tons of sefarim onto a freighter departing Stockholm the next week.

title_en: 100 crates of the Rebbe Rayatz's library arrive in New York
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz announces that part of his library has reached New York, with formal receipt scheduled for the following Monday.
story_body: On 11 Sivan 5701, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote that the first transport of the library had arrived in New York. Secretary R' Chaim Lieberman confirmed on 20 Sivan that about 100 crates of sefarim had been received that week, with roughly 50 more crates plus the manuscripts still in Warsaw.

title_en: 30 crates of sefarim still held by Schenker in Warsaw, Rebbe seeks transit route
summary_en: Rebbe Rayatz reports to R' Chasdan that 100 crates were received but about 30 more crates of his library remain at Schenker's Warsaw office.
story_body: On 9 Cheshvan 5702 the Rebbe wrote that the New York shipment was being unpacked. He noted that among the 100 boxes received were seven of household items of little value, and that some 30 more crates of sefarim remained in Warsaw; he asked Chasdan to find any forwarding firm with a Warsaw connection to retrieve them.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz summarizes: 90 crates of sefarim rescued, 30 still in occupied Poland
summary_en: In a letter of 11 Adar 5703 the Rebbe writes that ninety crates of sefarim have been saved from his former home and roughly thirty crates remain there.
story_body: By early 1943 the Rebbe Rayatz could put a tally to the rescue effort: ninety crates of his library had reached safety, while approximately thirty more crates were still in Poland under Nazi occupation, with no realistic way to extract them while the war raged.

title_en: Final accounting: 100 of 117 crates of library reached USA
summary_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes that of approximately 117 crates of sefarim only 100 reached America; the remaining 17 were lost in Poland.
story_body: In an igeres dated 7 Shevat 5704, the Rebbe noted that not all of his sefarim were saved from Poland: of some 117 crates only 100 had arrived in the USA. R' Chaim Lieberman later told the author that the Germans inspected the first transport and found nothing objectionable, but by the second transport America was already at war; the storehouse holding the remaining books was eventually bombed.

title_en: Bochur Shlomo Zilberberg reports library found in Otwock
summary_en: Holocaust survivor and former bochur Shlomo Zilberberg writes that the library he had packed in Otwock in 1939 has been found.
story_body: On Rosh Hashanah La'ilanot (Tu BiShvat) 5706, Shlomo Zilberberg — who as a young man had packed the library in Otwock in 1939 — wrote that the books had been located, promising precise details to follow. It was the first postwar word that any of the lost crates might be recoverable.

title_en: Pinchas Klein details Schneersohn library remnant found in Warsaw
summary_en: Bochur Pinchas Klein writes from Lodz that a small portion of the Rebbe's library, including manuscripts, has been located at the Jewish Central Committee in Warsaw.
story_body: On 19 Adar I, Pinchas Klein wrote his friend R' A.L. Kramer that, having been in Lodz at the end of the week, he had learned that a small fraction of the Rebbe's library — including many manuscripts and printed sefarim — had been found in Warsaw and was being held by the Historical Department of the Yiddish Central Committee.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz appeals to NY librarians for State Department intervention
summary_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes Alexander Marx and Joshua Bloch asking them to certify to the State Department the historical value of the seized Chabad manuscripts and books.
story_body: On 24 Adar I 5706, after the war's end, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to Alexander Marx of the JTS library and Joshua Bloch of the NY Public Library. He explained that three crates of ancient manuscripts — spanning 150 years of Chabad nesius — together with thousands of rare sefarim from the Shmuel Wiener collection, had been seized by the Nazis from his library in Otwock. The crates had been registered under Rabbis Jacobson and Hecht (US citizens) and were the property of Agudas Chasidei Chabad; he asked the librarians to write the State Department vouching for their scholarly and national-Jewish importance.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz thanks Rashaz Gurevitch for visit to Dr. Kahane on book list
summary_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes R' Shneur Zalman Gurevitch thanking him for visiting Rabbi Dr. Kahane and asking him to expedite the catalog and shipment of the recovered books.
story_body: On 1 Tammuz 5706, the Rebbe acknowledged Rashag's report on Rashaz Gurevitch's visit to Rabbi Dr. David Kahane regarding the books found at the Warsaw Jewish community archive. The Rebbe urged Gurevitch to hurry the cataloging and shipment of the recovered volumes.

title_en: R' Yitzchok Goldin in Poland searches Warsaw cellars for lost manuscripts
summary_en: In the summer of 1947 the Rebbe Rayatz asks his son-in-law (the Ramash) to instruct R' Yitzchok Goldin to search Warsaw cellars for the missing Chabad manuscripts.
story_body: While R' Yitzchok Goldin was in Poland in summer 5707, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote secretary R' Moshe Leib Rodstein asking that his son-in-law the Ramash write Goldin about searching specific Warsaw cellars and other sites where many manuscripts had been gathered. The search produced no results at that time.

title_en: Recovered Warsaw sefarim shipped via Paris to New York
summary_en: Rebbe Rayatz thanks Rashaz Gurevitch via R' Shmuel Zalmanov for shipping the recovered books — including many marked from the Natan of Kremenchug collection — through Paris to New York.
story_body: In winter 5708, R' Shmuel Zalmanov reported that his relative R' Shneur Zalman Gurevitch had finally shipped, together with his own possessions, all the recovered Chabad books obtained from Dr. Kahane at the Warsaw kehilla. On 17 Shevat the Rebbe Rayatz wrote Gurevitch directly to thank him. Whether any of these were among the missing 17 crates remained unverified.

title_en: R' Shlomo Yosef Zevin inquires about identifying rescued sefarim in Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: When many sefarim arrive in Eretz Yisrael from Europe, R' Shlomo Yosef Zevin asks the Rebbe (Ramash) how to identify volumes from the Rebbe Rayatz's library.
story_body: In 5712, with quantities of sefarim arriving in Eretz Yisrael from postwar Europe, R' Shlomo Yosef Zevin asked the Rebbe (Ramash) whether the Rayatz library volumes could be identified. The Rebbe replied — after consulting R' Chaim Lieberman, who had served as the Rayatz's librarian — that there were no library marks, but some volumes bore an inscription identifying them as part of Shmuel Wiener's collection, which he would try to photograph and circulate.

title_en: Lost manuscripts found and returned to Lubavitch
summary_en: The three crates of manuscripts seized by the Nazis from Otwock and considered lost for decades are located and returned in the summer of 5737.
story_body: The three crates of ancient Chabad manuscripts — Torah and correspondence of the Alter Rebbe and the five Chabad Rebbes who followed him — had been held by the American Embassy in Berlin before the US entered the war, then seized when the Germans confiscated embassy property. They were considered lost for decades, until summer 5737, when they were located and returned, as recorded in the 'Sifriyas Lubavitch' chapter 11.

title_en: Author's birth in Zhuravichi
summary_en: Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson, author of the memoirs, was born on 3 Kislev in Zhuravichi.
story_body: Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson was born on 3 Kislev 5656 (corresponding to 1895) in the town of Zhuravichi to his father Reb Yaakov Leib. He descended from four generations of shochtim in Zhuravichi. The family traced its lineage to the Shlah HaKadosh through nine generations.

title_en: Passing of grandfather R. Avraham Shlomo, shochet of Zhuravichi
summary_en: The author's paternal grandfather R. Avraham Shlomo, shochet of Zhuravichi, passed away on 25 Elul.
story_body: R. Avraham Shlomo, who had been a chasid of the Tzemach Tzedek, the Maharash, and the Rashab, passed away on 25 Elul 5661. He had served as shochet in Paritch before being pressed by his family to return to Zhuravichi after his father's death. He left behind his widow Bracha and three sons: Yaakov Leib, Yisrael Yeshaya, and Yosef Hillel.

title_en: Passing of maternal grandfather R. Avraham Nachum of Alkov
summary_en: The author's maternal grandfather R. Avraham Nachum of Alkov passed away on 29 Tammuz.
story_body: R. Avraham Nachum, a well-off villager in Kanave near Zhuravichi who operated a water mill and a wool processing factory, passed away on 29 Tammuz 5665. He left behind his wife Rachel Dvasha, five sons, and one daughter (the author's mother). His will included his son-in-law Yaakov Leib among the heirs, and arrangements for dividing the estate followed.

title_en: Uncles emigrate to America after Shavuos
summary_en: The author's uncles R. Yisrael Yeshaya and R. Yosef Hillel emigrated from Zhuravichi to America after Shavuos 5667.
story_body: After Shavuos of 5667 (1907), uncles Yisrael Yeshaya and Yosef Hillel left Zhuravichi for America, partly to escape Russian army conscription which required a 300-ruble fine for those who emigrated without reporting. They had corresponded with their uncles already in America, who sent them travel tickets and described American prosperity. The family escorted them out of town on the Motzaei Yom Tov following the holiday.

title_en: Author begins studying with Rav Baruch Rabinowitz in Zhuravichi
summary_en: At about age 11, the author began studying Talmud with Rav Baruch Rabinowitz, the Ashkenazi rabbi of Zhuravichi, during the winter of 5667.
story_body: In the winter of 5667 (late 1906 / early 1907), at approximately age 11, the author's father placed him to study with Rav Baruch Rabinowitz, the Ashkenazi rabbi of Zhuravichi. They learned Tractate Bava Basra together, and the rabbi found favor in him. However, lacking a study partner, the need to travel to a yeshiva became clear.

title_en: Departure from Zhuravichi toward yeshiva
summary_en: On Motzaei Shabbos Bereshis, 28 Tishrei 5668, the author and his father left Zhuravichi by wagon to seek a yeshiva.
story_body: On the night of 28 Tishrei 5668, the author and his father set out from Zhuravichi by wagon, first arriving in Rogachev on Sunday morning. That evening they continued by covered wagon some 60 versts to Bobruisk, arriving Monday morning, to consult the father's uncle R. Tuvia the shochet about whether to send the boy to the Lida yeshiva or to Lubavitch.

title_en: Decision to go to Lubavitch instead of Lida
summary_en: En route to Lida yeshiva, the author and his father were dissuaded by two travelers and instead chose Lubavitch.
story_body: While waiting at the Molodechno train station to transfer to Lida, the author's father was approached first by a fundraiser for the Lida yeshiva who warned about lax standards among older students, and later by a venerable bearded man who denounced Rabbi Reines for sharing a stage with a partially uncovered woman and urged: 'If you want your son to remain an honest Jew, take him to Lubavitch.' After much inner turmoil, the boy chose Lubavitch and they boarded the train for Lubavitch instead.

title_en: Author's first entry into the Rashab's chamber
summary_en: On 3 Cheshvan 5668, the author entered the chamber of the Rebbe Rashab in Lubavitch for the first time.
story_body: On Tuesday, 3 Cheshvan 5668 (1907), the young Yisrael Jacobson entered the holy chamber of the Rebbe Rashab in Lubavitch for the first time. Fifty years later, on the corresponding date in 5718, he marked the anniversary by entering the chamber of the Rebbe (Rayatz's successor). It was at that 5718 yechidus that he was directed to begin writing his memoirs.

title_en: Yechidus with the Rebbe and instruction to write memoirs
summary_en: On 2 Marcheshvan 5718, R. Yisrael Jacobson had a yechidus in which the Rebbe instructed him to write his memoirs of Lubavitch.
story_body: On 2 Marcheshvan 5718 (October 1957), R. Yisrael Jacobson entered the Rebbe's chamber for a yechidus, marking the 50th anniversary of his first entry to the Rashab's chamber. During that audience, the Rebbe instructed him to record his memoirs of his time in Lubavitch. He continued writing these memoirs through 5718-5719 and later published selections in the quarterly Di Yiddishe Heim from 5724 until his passing on 17 Sivan 5735.

title_en: Approval to publish Jacobson's memoirs
summary_en: At the start of 5752, the Rebbe gave approval and praise for editing and publishing R. Yisrael Jacobson's memoirs.
story_body: In late 1991 / early 5752, family members proposed editing and publishing R. Yisrael Jacobson's memoirs. They sought the Rebbe's approval, and he responded with not only consent but with strong encouragement, noting that many would learn from the reading, especially regarding authentic Chabad communal activism. Work began first on a separate volume covering events of the winter of 5700 (1939-40) and the rescue of the Rebbe Rayatz from Nazi-occupied Warsaw.

title_en: Passing of R. Yisrael Jacobson
summary_en: R. Yisrael Jacobson, chronicler of Chabad history and longtime communal askan, passed away on 17 Sivan 5735.
story_body: R. Yisrael Jacobson, author of these memoirs and a central figure in Chabad community life in America, passed away on 17 Sivan 5735 (1975). He had continued publishing installments of his memoirs in the quarterly Di Yiddishe Heim from 5724 until his death. His final years included activity in founding Agudas Chassidei Chabad, Agudas HaTmimim, and Achei Tmimim.

title_en: Publication of edited Jacobson memoirs
summary_en: Shalom DovBer Levin completed the editing introduction to Zichron LiBnei Yisrael on 15 Shevat 5756.
story_body: On 15 Shevat 5756 (February 1996), Rabbi Shalom DovBer Levin in Brooklyn, NY, signed off on the foreword to Zichron LiBnei Yisrael, the edited volume of R. Yisrael Jacobson's memoirs. The volume covered Jacobson's years 5667-5699 in Lubavitch, Shchedrin, Kremenchug, Kherson, Homel, and New York. Levin organized the fragmentary original writings into chapters with annotations, photographs, and indexes.

title_en: Author arrives in Lubavitch to begin yeshiva studies
summary_en: The young author arrived in Lubavitch with his father on Wednesday, Rosh Chodesh Marcheshvan 5668, and stayed at the home of his relative, the shochet R. Shlomo Chaim Kutain.
story_body: On Wednesday, the eve of Rosh Chodesh Marcheshvan 5668 (corresponding to early October 1907), the author and his father arrived in Lubavitch. They lodged with their relative R. Shlomo Chaim Kutain, a shochet who trained students in ritual slaughter, including the Rayatz. Roughly ten students at a time learned the craft under him.

title_en: Author's first yechidus with the Rebbe Rashab
summary_en: On Thursday, 2 Marcheshvan 5668, the author entered the Rebbe Rashab's chamber for the first time and was directed to the yeshiva administration.
story_body: On Thursday, 2 Marcheshvan 5668, the author and his father were received in yechidus by the Rebbe Rashab — the author's first encounter with a Lubavitcher Rebbe. The Rebbe instructed that the boy be referred to the yeshiva administration. The next day he was examined by R. Yechiel Komisar and R. Yechezkel Himmelstein and admitted to R. Leib Babin's class.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab delivers maamar in the small zal, Shabbos Noach
summary_en: On Shabbos Parshas Noach 5668, the Rebbe Rashab delivered a maamar of Chassidus in the small zal of the Lubavitch beis medrash.
story_body: After Kabbalas Shabbos on Parshas Noach, the Rebbe Rashab entered the kleiner zal where he then customarily said Chassidus. The Rayatz arrived first in Shabbos garb and shtreimel, and bachurim sang niggunim including the famed Yedid Nefesh of Lubavitch. Sudden silence fell as the Rebbe entered and delivered the maamar — the author's first such experience.

title_en: Fire breaks out in the small zal of Lubavitch yeshiva
summary_en: In mid-winter 5668, a fire erupted in the kleiner zal of the Lubavitch yeshiva and was extinguished by the students with water from courtyard wells.
story_body: During the harsh winter of 5668 (early 1908), sparks were seen escaping the chimney of the heavily stoked stove in the small zal. Within a half hour the fire spread; with no modern firefighting equipment available, the students hauled water in large barrels from two wells in the courtyard and quenched the blaze. For some months afterward davening did not take place in the small zal, and the Rebbe Rashab began saying Chassidus in the large zal.

title_en: Author remains in Lubavitch for Pesach 5668
summary_en: Refused permission to travel home, the young author spent Pesach 5668 in Lubavitch and afterward began receiving yeshiva support as a 'gola' bachur.
story_body: As Pesach 5668 approached, the author wrote home asking for travel funds, but the mashgiach R. Yechezkel Himmelstein denied him leave. After Pesach his father informed him that supporting him was a hardship, and he should seek yeshiva stipends. The Rebbetzin Shterna Sarah's 'krupnik' meals, lodging arrangements, and modest cash from the yeshiva and bachurim's fund began his life as an exile-student.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab delivers Shavuos maamar at Rebbetzin Rivka's home
summary_en: On Shavuos 5668, the Rebbe Rashab said a deep maamar at the seudah held in his mother Rebbetzin Rivka's home in Lubavitch.
story_body: At Rebbetzin Rivka's dining room a long table was set for the Shavuos seudah, with the Rebbe Rashab at its head. Expecting a short, accessible maamar like the prior year's 'Keshe'alah Moshe LaMarom,' students crowded in, but this time the Rebbe delivered a deep maamar continuing the themes of the two days of Yom Tov. Older bachurim teased the younger ones about whether they had managed to follow it.

title_en: R. Elchanan Dov Marozov appointed mashgiach of Chassidus
summary_en: In mid-winter 5668, R. Elchanan Dov Marozov was appointed mashgiach of Chassidus in the large zal of Tomchei Tmimim.
story_body: Earlier in the year R. Shlomo Risin of Rogachov had served as mashgiach of Chassidus in the great hall. Mid-winter 5668 saw R. Elchanan Dov Marozov appointed in his stead. R. Eliezer Kaplan, head of the yeshiva office, came to the large zal to read aloud a letter from the Rebbe Rashab announcing the appointment.

title_en: Author's bar mitzvah in Lubavitch
summary_en: The author marked his bar mitzvah on 3 Kislev 5669 in Lubavitch, having studied a maamar of the Rebbe Maharash with R. Mordechai Leib Rabinowitz.
story_body: On 3 Kislev 5669 the author turned thirteen. His relative R. Mordechai Leib Rabinowitz learned with him the maamar 'Ein HaKadosh Baruch Hu Ba BiTrunya' from 5648, which he reviewed thoroughly.
