R' Zusman was murdered with his sons by the Nazis on 29 Adar 5702.

title_en: Molotov radio broadcast announces Nazi invasion of USSR
summary_en: Soviet Foreign Minister Molotov announced over the radio that Hitler had launched a surprise invasion of the USSR.
story_body: On Sunday at noon, while the author was sitting at home in Moscow doing portrait retouching work, Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov broadcast news that Hitler had begun invading the Soviet Union and had already captured many cities. The announcement upended life for Soviet Jewry instantly — portrait commissions evaporated and within days the Luftwaffe began nightly raids over Moscow, forcing residents into trench shelters dug in their courtyards. Refugees soon poured eastward in masses, and the author would shortly join them.

title_en: Birth of daughter Leah outside Moscow during wartime
summary_en: The author's eldest daughter Leah was born on the night of 12 Menachem Av 5701 in the town of Yegoryevsk, where his wife had relocated to escape Moscow's air raids.
story_body: With Luftwaffe air raids forcing Muscovites into makeshift shelters and many residents fleeing the city, the author's pregnant wife went to stay with her cousin Sterke in Yegoryevsk (116 km from Moscow), beyond the range of the bombers. There their first daughter Leah was born on the night of 12 Av 5701. The author later traveled to retrieve mother and 'new face' back to their home in Cherinya.

title_en: Author and family evacuate from Moscow to Samarkand
summary_en: Facing conscription and the approaching German front, the author closed his Moscow apartment and fled by passenger train through Tashkent to Samarkand.
story_body: Acting on his uncle R' Zusya's counsel to head for a 'Jewish city' rather than join his parents in Mozdok, the author dried bread into rusks, sold his cookware in Yegoryevsk, and on a Thursday in mid-Elul boarded a passenger train for the week-long journey to Tashkent with his wife, infant Leah, and sister Esther. The family spent Shabbat stranded in the Tashkent station park alongside refugees from Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland, then continued the twelve-hour ride to Samarkand. The author records that only in Tashkent did he begin to feel himself a refugee like the rest.

title_en: Author's wife hospitalized with typhus on Purim in Samarkand
summary_en: On Purim 5702 the author's wife fell ill with typhus and was hospitalized; she recovered only just before Passover.
story_body: The first winter in Samarkand brought famine, unusual cold, and a typhus epidemic that filled the city's hospitals to capacity. Returning home from the Purim farbrengen, the author found his wife unwell; the next morning she was taken to hospital with typhus. Fearing the Soviet army press-gangs ('oblavy') that grabbed men off the streets and shipped them to the front, he could not even visit her — his sister Esther served as her contact until she returned home shortly before Passover.

title_en: First 19 Kislev farbrengen in Samarkand and birth of Miriam Reizel
summary_en: Anash held their first large 19 Kislev farbrengen in Samarkand, and that same evening the author's daughter Miriam Reizel was born at home.
story_body: For the first time since arriving in wartime exile, the Chabad chassidim of Samarkand secured a large room and organized a major 19 Kislev farbrengen for 5705. The author hauled his big number-30 kerosene retouching lamp to the venue to illuminate it. Returning home, he ran to fetch a nurse for his wife's labor, but by the time he came back she had given birth on her own to their daughter Miriam Reizel — 'a chassidishe daughter' — at the very hour of the farbrengen.

title_en: Birth of son Gershon in Paris during postwar refugee interlude
summary_en: The author's son Gershon was born in Paris on the eve of Shabbat Vayishlach, 15 Kislev 5708, while the family awaited departure for the United States.
story_body: Holding a U.S. visa but pregnant near term, the author's wife had consulted the Rebbe Rayatz on whether to sail before or after the birth, since trans-Atlantic travel was then by ship. The Rebbe approved their plan to emigrate. On the night entering Friday — erev Shabbat Vayishlach, 15 Kislev 5708 — their son Gershon was born in Paris among the postwar Chabad refugee community.

title_en: Author begins studies at Polotsk Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva
summary_en: The author and his hometown friend Moshe Roxin enrolled for the winter zman at the underground Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva in Polotsk.
story_body: About thirty older bochurim were studying in Polotsk under rosh yeshiva R' Yechezkel Himmelstein (later murdered in Riga) and the celebrated mashgiach R' Shlomo Chaim Kesselman. The author and his fellow townsman Moshe Roxin — son of the Zlobin shochet R' Refoel Eliezer Roxin — were placed in lodgings ('eshel') and joined the shiur on the Bava Metzia mishna 'ha-zahav koneh et ha-kesef.' Two weeks in, the mashgiach told the author he could remain but that Moshe, weaker in learning, must transfer to Vitebsk; the author chose to accompany his friend.

title_en: Soviet authorities expel the Polotsk Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva
summary_en: Mid-winter 5689 Soviet authorities shut down the underground Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva operating in Polotsk.
story_body: The clandestine Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva that had been functioning in Polotsk under R' Yechezkel Himmelstein and R' Shlomo Chaim Kesselman, with about thirty older students, was forcibly closed by Soviet authorities mid-winter. The author had already transferred to the Vitebsk branch a short time earlier, which he later recorded as providential. He completed the winter zman at Vitebsk under R' Gavriel Kagan without disturbance.

title_en: Author begins serving as ba'al koreh in Vitebsk
summary_en: Studying at the Vitebsk Tomchei Tmimim, the author began chanting the weekly Torah portion in a local minyan starting from Parashat Bo.
story_body: Lodging in the same apartment building as rosh yeshiva R' Gavriel Kagan, with R' Tzemach (son of R' Yitzchak the masmid) serving as mashgiach, the author followed a schedule of Gemara until 8 PM and a half-hour of Tanya. Beginning with Parashat Bo and continuing through Yitro and the rest of the year, he reviewed each parsha after the evening seder and chanted it the next Shabbat at a nearby minyan, training himself into the role of ba'al koreh he would carry for life.

title_en: Ireland offers thousands of tons of kosher meat to the Yishuv
summary_en: The Irish government offered the Jewish settlement in the Holy Land thousands of tons of meat to be made kosher, prompting a major shechita operation organized from Paris.
story_body: After the war, the Irish government proposed gifting thousands of tons of meat — kashered on site and canned — to the Jewish settlement in the Holy Land, an undertaking requiring shochtim, menakrim, supervising rabbis, and laborers. The Union of Refugee Rabbis in Paris, headed by the author's uncle R' Chaim Leib, judged the project beyond its capacity and referred it to R' Benyamin Gorodetzky's bureau, which obtained the Rebbe Rayatz's approval to take it on. Gorodetzky drew up a roster of avreichim who had studied shechita in Pocking, the author among them, though by then his U.S. visa was already in hand.

title_en: First printing of Kitzurim v'Hearos al Tanya at Gertz Brothers press
summary_en: The memoirist typeset and printed the first edition of Kitzurim v'Hearos al Tanya (by the Tzemach Tzedek) at the Gertz Brothers press in 5708/1948.
story_body: The Rebbe (then Ramash) handed the memoirist successive manuscript fascicles of the Tzemach Tzedek's Kitzurim v'Hearos al Tanya to typeset, until a small kuntres grew into a full book. When the Gertz print shop's vacation ended before the book was finished, the brothers gave him a key so he could work alone until midnight to complete it. The first edition's colophon reads 'Printed at the Gertz Brothers Press.'

title_en: Reprint of Kitzurim v'Hearos al Tanya for Tzemach Tzedek bicentennial
summary_en: In late Elul 5749 (September 1989), Kitzurim v'Hearos al Tanya was reissued in an enlarged edition to mark 200 years since the birth of the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: For the bicentennial of the Tzemach Tzedek's birth, the work was reprinted in an enlarged edition, though without the 'Gertz Press' attribution of the original. When the memoirist passed by during the Rebbe's distribution of the volume, he told the Rebbe that this was the first book he had ever printed, and the Rebbe responded with a smiling face.

title_en: Memoirist begins typesetting at Modern Linotype on Eastern Parkway
summary_en: After completing Kitzurim v'Hearos al Tanya, the memoirist arranged to use Yechiel Shapira's 'Modern Linotype' shop on Eastern Parkway and St. Johns each evening to typeset further works for the Rebbe.
story_body: With no equipment of his own, the memoirist arranged through the Gertz brothers to work at R' Yechiel Shapira's Modern Linotype shop each evening from dusk until 10 p.m., paying Shapira for use of the machine. The Rebbe gave him manuscripts to typeset, including Ohr HaTorah on Shemos, Mafteach Ma'amarei Admur Maharashab, and the kuntresim for each chag and mo'ed.

title_en: End of World War II in Europe
summary_en: The Second World War ended in the summer of 5705 (1945), prompting the Chabad refugee community in Samarkand to begin planning their departure.
story_body: Even before the war ended, the material and spiritual situation among the Lubavitcher refugees in Samarkand had improved — life became more cheerful and bachelors began marrying. But everyone understood they would not remain in Samarkand once the war ended, which it did in the summer of 1945.

title_en: Polish repatriation office opens in Samarkand
summary_en: In the winter of 5706 (early 1946), the Polish government's representation in Samarkand opened a repatriation office issuing Polish passports to former Polish nationals.
story_body: After the war, Poland's representation in Samarkand announced that Poles wishing to return to their homeland could register. By winter 5706 an office opened where anyone presenting some 'paperel' showing Polish birth could obtain (after a few months) a Polish passport allowing emigration to Poland — and from Poland onward, to the free world. Many Lubavitchers obtained such passports despite confusion over what the Frierdiker Rebbe wanted them to do.

title_en: Wedding of Golda Schusterman and Nechemia Nodel in Samarkand
summary_en: The memoirist's sister Golda married Nechemia Nodel, son of a chassidic shochet from the Kherson colonies, in Samarkand around 5706.
story_body: R' Tzemach HaLevi Horowitz proposed the match between Golda and Nechemia Nodel, a young man recently returned wounded from the front. He was described as 'a very refined bachelor,' and the wedding took place in good fortune. The match later kept the memoirist's parents from emigrating with him, since Nechemia's elderly parents were staying behind.

title_en: Arrest of Yeshiva Rosh R' Yitzchak Kopelman
summary_en: After Polish Jews left Samarkand in summer 5706, Soviet authorities openly arrested Rosh Yeshiva R' Yitzchak Kopelman and interrogated other Chabad rabbinic figures.
story_body: Once Polish-Jewish refugees emptied out of Samarkand in summer 1946, the atmosphere grew colder for those who remained. The famed Rosh Yeshiva R' Yitzchak Kopelman was arrested in broad daylight, and the memoirist's uncle R' Chaim Leib Zaks, rabbi of Uzda, was called for interrogation. R' Chaim Stein of Telshe, who had married into the Zaks family, fled by truck to Tashkent in the dead of night after being inquired about.

title_en: Departure from Samarkand to Lemberg via Moscow
summary_en: In late Tammuz 5706 (July 1946), the memoirist left Samarkand with his wife and two daughters for Lemberg, traveling via Moscow alongside the Kalmanson family.
story_body: After packing the household belongings, the memoirist boarded the train at Samarkand with the Kalmanson family. Parting from his elderly parents at the platform, he sensed he would never see them again. The Polish passport, held by his father, was swapped to him only at the moment of boarding the train.

title_en: R' Dovber Lebertov warns memoirist to leave Moscow immediately
summary_en: Stopping in Moscow en route to Lemberg, the memoirist was told by R' Dovber Kobeliaker (Lebertov) to flee the city at once rather than spend Shabbos there.
story_body: Arriving in Moscow on a Thursday, the memoirist intended to spend Shabbos with relatives. When he told R' Dovber Kobeliaker of his plan, R' Dovber sharply commanded him to leave immediately, knowing how dangerous the city had become. The memoirist left the next day; R' Dovber was later repeatedly summoned by the GPU, ultimately arrested and exiled, dying in the wilds.

title_en: Setting type for Hachaltzu 5659 in late summer 1948
summary_en: In late summer 5708 (1948), the memoirist typeset the Hachaltzu 5659 ma'amar, though the kitzurim had not yet been provided.
story_body: Late in the summer of 1948, the Rebbe gave the memoirist the Hachaltzu 5659 ma'amar to typeset. The kitzurim accompanying the ma'amar were only delivered after Sukkos, allowing publication of the full version with corrections.

title_en: Thirty copies of Hachaltzu printed overnight for 50th anniversary
summary_en: On the night of Hoshana Rabbah 5709 (24 October 1948), the memoirist and R' Tzvi Gansburg worked through the night to print 30 copies of Hachaltzu 5659 for its 50th anniversary on Simchas Torah.
story_body: On Chol HaMoed Sukkos close to Hoshana Rabbah, the Rebbe told the memoirist that the Frierdiker Rebbe wished a small printing of Hachaltzu to mark its 50th anniversary on Simchas Torah. With time short, the memoirist and Bochur Tzvi Gansburg worked through Hoshana Rabbah night — in place of Tikkun — typesetting and producing thirty stapled copies, which were handed to the Rebbe the next morning.

title_en: Asterisk footnote convention introduced in Kuntres 2 Nissan 5709
summary_en: Just before printing the Kuntres of 2 Nissan 5709 (1 April 1949), the Frierdiker Rebbe required asterisks be added in the body of the ma'amar to mark Ramash's footnotes — a convention used in all subsequent kuntreisim.
story_body: After the lead pages of the 2 Nissan 5709 kuntres had already gone to the Manhattan press, R' Chadakov telephoned: the Frierdiker Rebbe had asked why no marker in the body of the ma'amar indicated the Ramash's marginal notes. The memoirist set new lines with asterisks, rushed them to the press at dawn, and replaced the old slugs. From that kuntres onward, asterisks marked the Ramash's marginal notes throughout the chassidus kuntreisim.

title_en: Reprint of Hachaltzu for 127th birthday of the Rebbe Rashab
summary_en: On 20 Cheshvan 5748 (12 November 1987), Hachaltzu was reissued in a special edition marking 127 years since the birth of the Rebbe Rashab.
story_body: For the 127th birthday of the Rebbe Rashab, the Hachaltzu kuntres was reprinted in a special edition. During its distribution to chassidim, the memoirist had time only to tell the Rebbe, 'This is also the first kuntres I printed,' before R' Leibel Groner urged him along to avoid holding up the long line.

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe directs memoirist to buy a Linotype machine
summary_en: In a yechidus with the Frierdiker Rebbe, the memoirist was told to purchase a Linotype machine to print the chag-and-mo'ed kuntreisim — replacing the cumbersome Shulsinger workflow.
story_body: The Frierdiker Rebbe knew the memoirist had begun printing the kuntresim and was paying others for typesetting. In yechidus he instructed him to purchase a Linotype machine. When the memoirist objected that the $3,000 price (an enormous sum at the time) was beyond him, the Rebbe answered, 'You don't need to pay it all — a bit on the mountain and a bit on the worry!'

title_en: Memoirist travels to teach at Cherson yeshiva
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Cheshvan 5690 (3 November 1929) the memoirist set out from Zlobin to teach at the Chabad yeshiva in Cherson, only to find on arrival that the staff and students had been arrested.
story_body: The memoirist boarded the train Sunday morning on Rosh Chodesh Cheshvan 5690 with fellow Zlobin native Dovber HaLevi Gurevitch, arriving in Cherson 36 hours later. The R'M R' Yosef Himelstein's wife met them outside in tears: her husband, the mashgiach, and all the students had been arrested. Too frightened to take them in, the residents sent the pair back, and a non-Jewish wagon driver sheltered them overnight before they returned to Kremenchug.

title_en: Arrest of Cherson Tomchei Tmimim faculty and students
summary_en: In autumn 5690 (1929), Soviet authorities in Cherson arrested R' Yosef Himelstein, the mashgiach R' Tzemach Gurevitz, and the entire student body of the Tomchei Tmimim branch.
story_body: The Chabad yeshiva in Cherson was opened by R' Yosef Himelstein and the mashgiach R' Tzemach HaLevi Gurevitz for the winter term. Before the new arrivals from Zlobin reached the city, the entire faculty and student body had been arrested. They were eventually released under condition not to leave Cherson — and immediately fled the city the moment they were freed.

title_en: Death of Shaina (Sania) Schusterman in Zlobin
summary_en: The memoirist's sister Shaina (Sania) died young in summer 5687 (1927), prompting his parents to move to a new house in the center of Zlobin.
story_body: After Shaina's untimely death in summer 1927, the memoirist's mother no longer wished to remain in the family home. The father bought a larger house in the center of Zlobin and went into debt as a result, leaving the family in difficult straits when the memoirist later took ill with pleurisy.

title_en: Yezhov takes over NKVD and Great Terror peaks
summary_en: In 5698 (1938), Yezhov became NKVD chief and the wave of nighttime arrests in the Soviet Union reached its peak — the Hebrew letters of the year forming the word 'tirtzach' (murder).
story_body: The Soviet situation deteriorated steadily, and in 5698 it became so murderous that the Hebrew letters of the year spelled 'murder.' Plain-clothed 'visitors' came in the dead of night to drag people from their homes on no charge, and Jews would ask each other every morning whom the GPU had taken the night before.

title_en: Arrest of R' Avraham Sverdlov in Leningrad
summary_en: In 5698 (1938) the chassidic scholar R' Avraham Sverdlov, a co-leader of the Chabad yeshiva in Odessa, was arrested in Leningrad and never heard from again.
story_body: Sverdlov had been one of the directors of the underground Tomchei Tmimim branch in Odessa, an unusually broad talent — a master of nigleh and chassidus, a brilliant darshan, a first-rate ba'al koreh. He was arrested in Leningrad in 1938; no trace of him was found thereafter, Hashem yikom damo.

title_en: Mass arrests of Lubavitcher activists in Leningrad
summary_en: On the same winter 5698 (early 1938) night that arrests occurred in Zlobin, R' Elchanan Dov Morozov, R' Yitzchak Raskin, and R' Shmuel Nimaytin were arrested in Leningrad.
story_body: On the Thursday night that seven 'shul-Jews' were arrested in Zlobin, the NKVD in Leningrad simultaneously arrested R' Elchanan Dov Morozov, R' Yitzchak Raskin, R' Shmuel Nimaytin, and others. When the memoirist himself fled to Leningrad days later, he learned of the parallel arrests.

title_en: Memoirist and father flee Zlobin to Zhitomir
summary_en: On a Friday night in Shvat or Adar 5698 (early 1938), warned by a contact in the NKVD that more arrests were imminent, the memoirist and his father fled Zlobin for Zhitomir.
story_body: A woman who worked at the bread shop and was friendly with the NKVD secretary tipped the memoirist off that another round of arrests was planned that very night. Knowing his father and himself were on the list, the memoirist made hurried arrangements and that Friday night the two boarded a train for Zhitomir. From there the memoirist continued to Gomel, then to his brother Zev in Leningrad, until the danger passed.

title_en: Family crosses Soviet border from Lemberg to Poland on 15 Av 5706
summary_en: On 15 Menachem Av 5706 the narrator and Reb Yisrael Shimon, with their families, boarded a train from Lemberg and crossed the Soviet-Polish border using a passport whose photograph the narrator had affixed and stamped himself by candlelight.
story_body: Because Yisrael Shimon's purchased passport lacked a photograph and Polish border crossing required one, the narrator forged a Samarkand police seal onto an affixed photo using ink-pencil tools acquired in Lemberg. Anash including R. Yehuda Leib Matzkin and R. Yaakov Yosef Raskin examined and approved the forgery. The train passed through the border station Medyka, and a Soviet officer accepted the doctored passport, allowing the families to reach Przemyśl on the Polish side.

title_en: Shabbat Mevorchim Elul 5706 spent near Polish-Czech border before Bricha crossing
summary_en: On the last Shabbat of Menachem Av 5706, near the Polish-Czech border in a town the narrator recalls as Kliatzk, Anash held a farbrengen where R. Nissan Nemenov declared that they were leaving a 'true world' under Soviet persecution for a 'false world' where Torah brought honor and money.
story_body: The Anash group waited at this settlement near the Polish-Czech border for the Bricha to move them onward. At the Shabbat Mevorchim Elul farbrengen, one of the participants — likely R. Nissan Nemenov — observed that in Russia Yiddishkeit had been authentic precisely because Torah-learning and Shabbat brought five-year prison sentences, while in the West religious life would be cheapened by ease. On motzaei Shabbat they were told to prepare to cross the border that night.

title_en: Bricha crossing from Poland into Czechoslovakia by night, late Av 5706
summary_en: After motzaei Shabbat Mevorchim Elul 5706, the narrator, his wife, and daughters Miriam and Leah climbed mountains by night with a Bricha guide and reached a DP camp on Czech soil by dawn.
story_body: The Bricha was an underground operation run by young Eretz Yisrael emissaries in coordination with the Joint and the American Vaad Hatzalah, smuggling Soviet refugees on foot across borders into Czechoslovakia, Austria, and Germany. The narrator carried two suitcases while his wife held the 1½-year-old Miriam and led five-year-old Leah by the hand. From the Czech DP camp they were transferred to Vienna and housed in the former Rothschild Hospital.

title_en: Ketubah d'irkesa written in Vienna on 1 Elul 5706
summary_en: Having left their original ketubah in Moscow, the narrator arranged a replacement ketubah d'irkesa dated Wednesday, 1 Rosh Chodesh Elul 5706, while housed in Vienna's former Rothschild Hospital.
story_body: Because halacha forbids living without a ketubah even for an hour, once the family reached the relative safety of Vienna the narrator commissioned a replacement ketubah arranged by R. Avraham Eliyahu Plotkin. The witnesses were R. Moshe Binyamin Kaplan and R. Menachem Mendel Raskin. The document confirms the family was already in Austria by Rosh Chodesh Elul 5706.

title_en: Train ride from Vienna toward Steyr stalled in Soviet zone, Erev Shabbat Elul 5706
summary_en: Traveling by freight train from Vienna to the Austrian town of Steyr in late Av 5706, the refugees were stalled for many hours when Soviet zone authorities refused passage; the train finally moved overnight and arrived in Steyr on Shabbat morning.
story_body: Post-war Austria and Germany were divided into American, British, French, and Soviet occupation zones, and the Soviet zone authorities held the freight cars indefinitely. The travelers sat in darkness without food in cattle wagons, and the narrator gave R. Avraham Eliyahu Plotkin a piece of bread for kiddush. They were instructed to identify themselves as Greek nationals if questioned. The train finally rolled overnight and reached Steyr by Shabbat dawn, where the Joint and Vaad Hatzalah received them.

title_en: Shabbat Slichot 5706: refugees arrive at Pocking DP camp
summary_en: By Shabbat Slichot 5706, the last Shabbat of the year, the Anash refugee group had reached the Pocking DP camp in Germany, completing roughly two months of travel from Samarkand.
story_body: Pocking, a former wartime airbase converted into a vast refugee camp, housed many factions — Hungarian, Polish, right-wing, left-wing, Betar, Hashomer Hatzair — each in separate barracks. Anash received five or six barracks, with one set aside as a Tomchei Temimim yeshiva and another as a beit knesset. R. Nissan Nemenov organized a full daily seder of Tehillim, tefillah, and learning from dawn through ma'ariv, and arranged a group to study sh'chita; the narrator received his sh'chita certification later in Paris.

title_en: Family departs Pocking DP camp on forged Prague passports, end of Iyar 5707
summary_en: At the end of Iyar 5707, after eight months in Pocking, the narrator's family left Germany on passports arranged by the Rebbe Rayatz's Paris lishka, ostensibly traveling from Prague to Paris via Germany.
story_body: The Paris lishka headed by R. Benyamin Gorodetzky supplied Pocking refugees with passports lacking the required Czech-German border stamps because the bearers had never actually been in Prague. Boarding the train at Munich, the family was discovered by a strict American military conductor who put them off at Karlsruhe, the last station before the French border. After hours of uncertainty, a station official ruled the documents valid and they continued on the next train to Paris, ending the Pocking-Germany chapter that had spanned late Elul 5706 through late Iyar 5707.

title_en: Narrator reads Torah for Rebbe Rayatz on Shabbat HaChodesh 5709 at 770
summary_en: On Shabbat Mevorchim Nisan 5709 (Parshat HaChodesh), the narrator was unexpectedly called to read the Torah upstairs at 770 in the presence of the Rebbe Rayatz, who took the maftir aliyah from his wheelchair.
story_body: R. Yitzchak Dzikobson brought the narrator to 770 hoping merely to observe the Rebbe's maftir aliyah on this last Shabbat before Beis Nisan, the Rashab's yahrtzeit. Because the regular ba'al korei R. Yochanan Gordon was occupied downstairs at the aufruf of his future son-in-law Shimon Goldman, Dzikobson sent the narrator upstairs to lein for the Rebbe. The Rebbe Rayatz, seated in his wheelchair, signaled with his head the moment the reader accidentally voiced a stray 'beit' from 'bnei Yisrael' that does not appear in the verse — a final demonstration of his exacting attention to leining. This was the Rebbe's last Beis Nisan in this world.

title_en: Daughter Feigel born to narrator on last day of Pesach 5709
summary_en: On the last day of Pesach 5709 — 22 Nisan — a daughter was born to the narrator and named Feigel after his wife's mother, who had perished in the Shoah.
story_body: The narrator had begun serving as shamash at his East Flatbush shul at the start of Pesach and walked home on the final yom tov evening to discover the news. Feigel was the first child they named after his murdered mother-in-law, once they had confirmed she did not survive. Their son Gershon was similarly named after the wife's brother Gershon, hy'd.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz provides $500 'shlissel-geld' through Ramash for narrator's apartment, Nisan 5709
summary_en: In Nisan 5709 the Rebbe Rayatz, through his son-in-law the Ramash, advanced the narrator $500 in 'shlissel-geld' to secure a scarce apartment near his East Flatbush shul.
story_body: Apartments in East Flatbush were so scarce that an under-the-table $500 key-fee was required. When the narrator asked the Ramash to consult the Rebbe Rayatz, the Rebbe answered that he must take the apartment but asked where such a sum would come from. The Ramash replied that he himself would supply the money, and the next day at 770 he counted out $500 for the narrator. The narrator repaid the full sum once his financial situation improved.

title_en: Yom Kippur Mincha 5710: narrator leins for Ramash while Rebbe Rayatz takes maftir Yonah
summary_en: At Mincha of Yom Kippur 5710 the narrator, having come to 770 from his East Flatbush post, leined the Torah for the Ramash in the upstairs minyan as the Rebbe Rayatz, seated in the adjacent room, took maftir Yonah.
story_body: On yom tov a second minyan was held upstairs in 'the Alte Rebbetzin's room,' where the chazan stood and the leining took place, with the door to the Rebbe Rayatz's office open so he could hear the davening. Arriving from his East Flatbush shamash duties for Mincha, the narrator was asked by the Ramash to lein; a Torah scroll was placed on a small table in the corridor near the dining room. The Ramash himself received maftir Yonah at this minyan.

title_en: 19 Kislev 5710 farbrengen with Rebbe Rayatz upstairs at 770
summary_en: The narrator attended the Yud-Tes Kislev 5710 farbrengen — believed to be the Rebbe Rayatz's last — held upstairs in 770's dining room with the Rebbe presiding at the head of the table in his shtreimel.
story_body: Festival farbrengens were held on the second floor of 770, with the Rebbe Rayatz at the head of the table flanked by his sons-in-law and senior chassidim; the door was opened to admit guests but closed before start time due to the Rebbe's weakness. When R. Nissan Telushkin was admitted as an honored guest, additional chairs had to be brought near the Rebbe's seat. When fewer were produced than he had asked for — out of deference to crowding him — the Rebbe declared, 'Why so few? Yidden don't crowd me — I was raised on Jewish sweat!'

title_en: R. Yerachmiel Binyaminson leads minyan to Rebbe Rayatz's tziyun on 15 Elul 5710 to plead for Ramash to accept nesius
summary_en: On 15 Elul 5710, R. Yerachmiel Binyaminson of Montreal hired two taxis to bring a minyan to the Rebbe Rayatz's tziyun and left a pidyon pleading that his son-in-law the Ramash accept the nesius of Chabad.
story_body: Binyaminson, an elder of the chassidic rabbinate, had personally pressed the Ramash to take the leadership, telling him 'the older generation is one thing, but the young chassidim need a Rebbe' — to which the Ramash replied 'I have never withheld myself from the young.' On 15 Elul — the founding date of Tomchei Temimim — Binyaminson assembled a minyan including the narrator and R. Yisrael Shimon Kalmenson and laid a written pidyon at the kever asking Heaven to move the Ramash to accept the nesius. Upon returning, he handed the pidyon to the Ramash, who, the narrator recalls, received it with quiet satisfaction — unlike a similar attempt by another askan some time earlier which had drawn only an indifferent reaction.

title_en: R. Yerachmiel Binyaminson niftar on Rosh Chodesh Shevat 5715
summary_en: R. Yerachmiel ben Avraham Yehuda Leib Binyaminson, the elder Lubavitcher rabbinic figure of Montreal, passed away on Rosh Chodesh Shevat 5715 and was buried close to the Rebbe Rayatz's tziyun.
story_body: Binyaminson, a venerable Chabad rabbi who had previously brought a minyan to plead at the Rebbe Rayatz's kever for the Ramash to accept the nesius, came regularly from Montreal to New York and lodged with the narrator or with his sister. His passing on Rosh Chodesh Shevat 5715 was honored with burial adjacent to the Frierdiker Rebbe at the Old Montefiore section that would later become known as the Ohel.

title_en: Merkos becomes one-third partner in Empire Press (Ezra) by directive of the Rebbe
summary_en: By directive of the Rebbe, Merkos L'inyonei Chinuch was made a one-third profit-sharing partner of the narrator's Ezra print shop, registered with the authorities as a tax-exempt department of Merkos.
story_body: The Rebbe pressed the narrator's partner R. Tzvi on why Merkos was not yet a partner in the press; when the partners and R. Chadakov disagreed about whether Merkos should join — Chadakov insisting Merkos should not be in partnership at all — the Rebbe overruled all of them, ruling that the partners would draw a worker's salary and that Merkos would receive one-third of the profits when there were any. The print shop opened a 'Ezra–Merkos L'inyonei Chinuch' bank account signed by Chadakov or Shusterman. The narrator did not insist on a formal contract — a decision he later regretted on the advice of the Merkos bookkeeper Mr. Telushkin, son of R. Nissan Telushkin.

title_en: Eliyahu Shusterman born in Lohin, Volhynia
summary_en: Eliyahu ben Achiezer Shusterman, father of the author, was born in 5641 in the small town of Lohin near Korosten in the Volhynia region.
story_body: Eliyahu Shusterman, the author's father, was born in the year 5641 (1880/1881) in the small Volhynian town of Lohin, near Korosten in the Berdichev region. He later studied in Vyetka near Homel, a town known as a seat of sharp Talmudic scholars. His Yiddish accent remained 'Litvish' from his upbringing in Belorussia, unlike his brother David who spoke in a 'Polish' Volhynian dialect.

title_en: Eliyahu Shusterman travels to Rebbe Rayatz in Leningrad
summary_en: For Shavuot 5685, Eliyahu Shusterman traveled to the Rebbe Rayatz in Leningrad intending to leave his shamash position in Zhlobin, but was instructed to remain.
story_body: For Shavuot 5685 (1925) — the 'matzaim' holiday — Eliyahu Shusterman traveled from Zhlobin to Leningrad to see the Frierdiker Rebbe. He intended to leave his post as shamash and relocate to Kharkov. The Rebbe did not agree and instructed him to continue in the shamash role at the Karmer Shul in Zhlobin.

title_en: Epidemic in Zhlobin disrupts yeshiva studies in Surazh
summary_en: At the end of summer 5687 a contagious disease in Zhlobin prevented the author and other boys from returning to the yeshiva ketana in Surazh founded by R. Moshe Axelrod.
story_body: When R. Moshe Axelrod moved to Surazh and established a yeshiva ketana there, Eliyahu Shusterman had taken his son's entire class — seven boys, all under bar-mitzvah age — and brought them to study and board in Surazh. At the end of summer 5687 (1927) a contagious disease spread through Zhlobin and the boys could not return; they remained in Zhlobin, where Rabbi Binyaminsohn taught them Bava Metzia and the elderly R. Yitzchak Matles taught them Tanach and Hebrew grammar in the evenings.

title_en: Kiddush in Zhlobin marking first anniversary of Rayatz's liberation
summary_en: On 12 Tammuz 5688 the Shusterman home in Zhlobin hosted a kiddush marking the first anniversary of the Rebbe Rayatz's liberation, attended by R. Tzemach Horowitz.
story_body: On 12 Tammuz 5688 (June 30, 1928), the first anniversary of the Frierdiker Rebbe's liberation, the Shusterman family hosted a kiddush in their Zhlobin home. The chassid R. Tzemach Horowitz, then serving as a mashpia in Zhlobin, participated. The author recalled the event still vividly decades later.

title_en: Author becomes shamash at Yeshivat R. Meir Simcha HaKohen shul in Brooklyn
summary_en: In Nissan 5709 the author began serving as shamash at the Yeshivat R. Meir Simcha HaKohen shul in East Flatbush alongside Rabbi J.J. Hecht.
story_body: In Nissan 5709 (April 1949), the author began a four-year tenure as shamash at the Yeshivat R. Meir Simcha HaKohen shul in East Flatbush. He worked alongside Rabbi J.J. Hecht, the shul's rav, in friendship and harmony. The shul's contract had to be renewed annually around Pesach.

title_en: Father Eliyahu Shusterman dies in Samarkand
summary_en: Eliyahu ben Achiezer Shusterman of Zhlobin died in Samarkand on 18 Elul 5711, with news reaching the author the same day by telegram.
story_body: On 18 Elul 5711 (September 19, 1951), the author received a telegram from his sister Golda in Samarkand reporting their father Eliyahu Shusterman's death after a prolonged illness. The author immediately sat shiva in New York. Eliyahu is buried in the Samarkand cemetery alongside chassidim R. Eliyahu Levin (Pechicer), R. Yerachmiel Chadash, and R. Bentzion Geisinsky.

title_en: Memorial kuntres for Rebbe Rayatz published with dedication to Eliyahu Shusterman
summary_en: The kuntres released for Rosh Hashana 5712, near the conclusion of the author's shiva, carried a dedication to the memory of his father Eliyahu Shusterman.
story_body: The kuntres that appeared for Rosh Hashana 5712 (autumn 1951) — published close to the conclusion of the author's shiva for his father — included a dedication for the elevation of the soul of Eliyahu ben Achiezer Shusterman. This was the first of several kuntresim he sponsored in his father's memory.

title_en: Tzvi Gansburg marries in Montreal and leaves printing partnership
summary_en: In spring 5712 the author's printing partner Tzvi Gansburg married the daughter of R. Yeshayahu Denberg of Shchedrin in Montreal and left the Brooklyn print shop.
story_body: In spring 5712 (1952), the author's printing partner Tzvi (Hershel) Gansburg married the daughter of R. Yeshayahu Denberg of Shchedrin in Montreal, with the author's teacher Rabbi Binyaminsohn serving as shadchan. Hershel remained in Montreal, lured by a wealthy relative's unfulfilled promises, and left the printing house. The author was deeply unhappy, but the two remained loyal friends.

title_en: First yahrzeit kuntres dedication for Eliyahu Shusterman
summary_en: The kuntres appearing for 18 Elul 5712, the first yahrzeit of Eliyahu Shusterman, again carried a dedication to his memory.
story_body: On the first yahrzeit of his father, 18 Elul 5712 (September 8, 1952), the author again included a memorial dedication in the kuntres that appeared at that time. He also completed learning the entire Shisha Sidrei Mishnah during the year of mourning.

title_en: Sukkot tension at shul exposes author's split focus
summary_en: On Sukkot 5713 in the shul sukkah, the author declared he had not come to the shul to make a living, sparking the gabbaim's decision to push him out.
story_body: On Sukkot 5713 (October 1952), at a kiddush in the shul sukkah in East Flatbush, the author told the balebatim that he had not come to the shul to 'make a living' but to accomplish something in Yiddishkeit. The gabbaim later quoted him as saying he could manage without them. Combined with their discovery of his work at the print shop, this set the stage for his departure.

title_en: Daughter Nechama Shusterman born
summary_en: On 4 Kislev 5713 the author's daughter Nechama was born, named after his wife's brother Nechemia who perished in the Shoah.
story_body: On 4 Kislev 5713 (November 22, 1952), the author and his wife had a daughter, Nechama. She was named for his wife's brother Nechemia, who was murdered in the Shoah.

title_en: R. Sh.D.B. joins author's printing house as partner
summary_en: In Shevat 5713 R. Sh.D.B. became a partner in the author's printing house after about eighteen months of the author working alone.
story_body: In Shevat 5713 (January 1953), after roughly eighteen months working without a partner, the author brought R. Sh.D.B. into the printing house. The author had invested $14,000; the new partner had promised $5,000 but produced only $1,500 in cash, which the author accepted because he wanted a working partner more than capital. The funds were transferred to R. Tzvi Gansburg for his share.

title_en: Author's contract as shamash not renewed
summary_en: In Nissan 5713 the East Flatbush shul declined to renew the author's contract; Rabbi Avigdor Miller protested and the chevra mishnayos honored him with five hundred dollars and silver candlesticks.
story_body: In Nissan 5713 (April 1953), the East Flatbush shul did not renew the author's contract as shamash, ending his four-year tenure. Rabbi Avigdor Miller, mashgiach of Yeshivat Rabbi Chaim Berlin, banged the table in protest, ceased davening there, and gathered neighborhood signatures protesting to the absent president in Florida. When the balabatim later invited the author back for lesser duties, the Rebbe responded 'avekgegangen iz avekgegangen' — once gone, gone. The chevra mishnayos he had led gave him their entire $500 treasury and presented silver candlesticks his wife still uses.

title_en: R. Yekutiel Zusman 'Zushya' Paz dies in Moscow
summary_en: R. Yekutiel Zusman ben Moshe Leib 'Zushya' Paz, longtime shamash of the Marina-Roshcha shul in Moscow, died on 2 Cheshvan 5714 and was buried in Malachovka.
story_body: R. Yekutiel Zusman Paz, the legendary shamash of the Marina-Roshcha shul in Moscow, died on 2 Cheshvan 5714 (October 11, 1953) and was buried in Malachovka. Every night after maariv he would pretend to evict homeless mispalelim so the Gentile watchman Simon would lock up and leave, then quietly readmit them through a side door. During the war he reached Samarkand, where he served as shamash on Khodzhum Street and ran an unpaid cheder.

title_en: Mother Rachel Shusterman dies in Tashkent
summary_en: On 4 Tevet 5714 Rachel bat Aharon Tzvi Shusterman died in Tashkent; news was withheld from the author in New York for a year and a half.
story_body: On 4 Tevet 5714 (December 10, 1953), the author's mother Rachel bat Aharon Tzvi died in Tashkent. Because of the climate of fear in the Soviet Union, the family did not inform the author for a year and a half; he therefore sat no shiva and recited no kaddish. His brother Yosef said kaddish in Tashkent and arranged a minyan there with great mesirat nefesh.

title_en: Daughter Zissel Shusterman born
summary_en: On 14 Tevet 5714 the author's daughter Zissel was born, named for his father-in-law Zussman ben Gershon who was killed by the Nazis on 28 Adar 5702.
story_body: On 14 Tevet 5714 (December 20, 1953), the author and his wife had a daughter, Zissel. She was named for the author's father-in-law, R. Zussman ben Gershon, who was murdered by the Nazis on 28 Adar 5702 (March 17, 1942).

title_en: Father-in-law Zussman ben Gershon murdered in the Shoah
summary_en: The author's father-in-law R. Zussman ben Gershon was murdered by the Nazis on 28 Adar 5702.
story_body: R. Zussman ben Gershon, the father of the author's wife, was murdered by the Nazis on 28 Adar 5702 (March 17, 1942). His granddaughter Zissel, born in 5714, was named after him.

title_en: Shusterman family moves into Crown Heights home at 1717 President Street
summary_en: On Erev Purim 5715 the Shusterman family moved into 1717 President Street in Crown Heights with the Rebbe's blessing to buy rather than rent.
story_body: On Erev Purim 5715 (March 7, 1955), the author's family moved into their newly purchased Crown Heights home at 1717 President Street, beside the shul of Rabbi B.Z. Frankel with its mikveh. Earlier the author had asked the Rebbe about renting a Crown Heights apartment; the Rebbe replied that smaller people than him had managed to buy. The doubled 'tov' in the number 1717 was taken as a good sign.

title_en: Sheina Paz dies in Moscow
summary_en: Sheina bat Mordechai, wife of R. Zushya Paz, died on 28 Tammuz 5721 and was buried beside him in Malachovka.
story_body: Sheina bat Mordechai, the wife of the Marina-Roshcha shamash R. Yekutiel Zusman 'Zushya' Paz, died on 28 Tammuz 5721 (July 12, 1961). She was buried beside her husband in Malachovka outside Moscow. Their daughter, who lived in a village near Moscow, had supplied chalav yisrael to the shul daily from her cow.

title_en: Author's first pilgrimage to parents' graves in Samarkand and Tashkent
summary_en: In Elul 5753 the author traveled for the first time to Samarkand and Tashkent to visit his parents' graves and arrange for repairs and a new matzevah.
story_body: In Elul 5753 (August/September 1993), the author traveled for the first time to Samarkand to visit his father Eliyahu's grave and to Tashkent to visit his mother Rachel's grave. He left funds in Samarkand for restoration of the matzevah and arranged for a new matzevah in Tashkent. For decades earlier he had relied on shluchim traveling to the Soviet Union to bring back photographs of the gravestones.

title_en: Author moves to Crown Heights and becomes regular at 770
summary_en: The author moved to Crown Heights before Pesach 5715 and became a regular Shabbat worshipper at 770.
story_body: Before Pesach 5715 (April 1955) the author relocated from East Flatbush to Crown Heights, becoming a fixed Shabbat mispallel at 770. The gabbai Reb Yochanan Gordon, who had been the regular baal korei for the Rebbe Rayatz, began calling him up each week to read from the Torah.

title_en: Author begins regular Torah reading at 770
summary_en: Around mid-5715 the author became the regular baal korei at 770 after Reb Yochanan Gordon told him to come up on his own.
story_body: After a year of being called up each Shabbat by Reb Yochanan Gordon, the elderly gabbai told the author, 'How long must I call you each week? Go up on your own!' From mid-5715 (1955) onward the author served as the regular baal korei at 770.

title_en: Ezra & Balshan press buys 480 Sutter Avenue building
summary_en: In 1956 the Ezra & Balshan printing house bought a building at 480 Sutter Avenue in Brownsville to accommodate its expansion.
story_body: The Ezra & Balshan print shop had outgrown its original premises at 238 Belmont Avenue. In 1956 the partners purchased a building at 480 Sutter Avenue in the Brownsville section of Brooklyn, moved all the machinery there, and added new equipment.

title_en: Wedding of Leah to Yerachmiel Binyamin Klein
summary_en: On 21 Adar 5721 the author's daughter Leah married Yerachmiel Binyamin Halevi Klein at the Melrose-Chateau hall in Brownsville.
story_body: The wedding was celebrated on 21 Adar 5721 (March 9, 1961) at Melrose-Chateau in Brownsville. Since Kollel Avreichim did not yet exist, the Rebbe instructed the chatan to specialize in the laws of mikvaot, which he learned with the Rav of Norolsk. A few months later the couple was sent on shlichus by Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch to Australia.

title_en: Yechidus on Alter Rebbe's 150th yahrzeit and bochurim's roles
summary_en: At his Erev R"Ch Elul 5722 yechidus the Rebbe asked the author to publish unpublished manuscripts for the Alter Rebbe's 150th yahrzeit year and to revive bochurim's leining and davening at the amud.
story_body: On Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5722 (August 30, 1962) the author entered yechidus for his birthday. The Rebbe noted that this was the 150th year since the Alter Rebbe's passing and asked for a list of unpublished manuscripts at the print shop to release that year. He also pressed the author to resume the Torah-reading dikduk shiur for bochurim and to have bochurim daven before the amud on weekday Mincha.

title_en: Wedding of Miriam Reizel to Moshe Nemenov
summary_en: On 23 Kislev 5724 the author's daughter Miriam Reizel married Moshe Nemenov at Grand-Paradise Hall in Williamsburg.
story_body: The wedding took place on 23 Kislev 5724 (December 9, 1963) at the Grand-Paradise Hall in Williamsburg, joining the families of two Zlobin natives. On the Rebbe's instruction, sheva brachos were held in Cleveland — first at the shul of Reb Zalman Kaizen and then at the home of Reb Chaim Stein, mashgiach of Telshe Yeshiva, where the Telshe roshei yeshiva attended.

title_en: Wedding of Feigel to Menachem Mendel Wolf
summary_en: On 15 Kislev 5730 the author's daughter Feigel married Menachem Mendel (Mani) Wolf at the Menorah hall in Boro Park.
story_body: The match was arranged by son-in-law Binyamin Klein, who proposed Feigel to the Wolfs while they were waiting for yechidus; in the yechidus the Rebbe himself raised the same suggestion. The wedding was on 15 Kislev 5730 (November 24, 1969) at the Menorah hall in Boro Park, and the couple later settled in Nachalat Har Chabad in Eretz Yisrael.

title_en: Hemshech 5666 typesetting begins by Rebbe's instruction
summary_en: On 2 Nisan 5725, after returning from the Ohel, the Rebbe directed Kehot to begin typesetting Hemshech Yom Tov shel Rosh Hashanah 5666 that same evening.
story_body: On the night of 2 Nisan 5725 (April 4, 1965) Rabbi Chadakov phoned to relay that the Rebbe, on returning from the Ohel, ordered typesetting of the Hemshech Yom Tov shel Rosh Hashanah Tarsa"v to begin immediately and that the most corrected manuscript be sought. Reb Baruch Sholom Shvei went to the press that very night and began setting the type. On the following motzaei Acharon Shel Pesach the Rebbe gave the author a bottle of wine 'for the Samach-Vov.'

title_en: Yechidus where Rebbe revisits Hemshech 5666 printing
summary_en: On Erev R"Ch Elul 5730 the Rebbe asked the author about the status of Hemshech 5666 and blessed Rabbi Rudshtein for advising the press to keep typesetting.
story_body: At his Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5730 (August 31, 1970) birthday yechidus, the Rebbe asked, 'What is happening with the Samach-Vov?' The author explained that after the initial halt they had quietly continued, on the advice of the late Rabbi Mordechai Leib Rudshtein, to set another fifty galleys. The Rebbe exclaimed, 'Tavo alav berachah!'

title_en: Hemshech 5666 published bound
summary_en: At the beginning of 5731 the bound volumes of Hemshech 5666 were finally received from the binder.
story_body: At the start of 5731 (fall 1970) Kehot received the bound copies of the long-delayed Hemshech 5666. The author distributed the bottle of wine the Rebbe had given him in 5725 to all the workers involved and gave each a bound copy. The Rebbe responded via Rabbi Chadakov, 'Their merit is very great; may it stand for them in this world and the next, I will mention them at the Tziyun.'

title_en: Wedding of Nechama and Shmuel Greisman
summary_en: On 6 Kislev 5735 the author's granddaughter Nechama married Shmuel Greisman at the Jewish Center in Brooklyn.
story_body: The wedding took place on 6 Kislev 5735 (November 20, 1974) at the Jewish Center in Brooklyn. The young couple was later among the first shluchim the Rebbe sent to Eretz Yisrael in 5736 to establish the Chabad community in the holy city of Tzfat.

title_en: First Rebbe-sent shluchim to Eretz Yisrael settle Tzfat
summary_en: In 5736 the Rebbe sent his first group of shluchim to Eretz Yisrael, including the Greismans, to found the Chabad neighborhood in Tzfat.
story_body: In 5736 (1975–76) the Rebbe dispatched his first wave of shluchim to Eretz Yisrael. Among them were Shmuel and Nechama Greisman, who were sent to establish the Chabad community in the holy city of Tzfat.

title_en: Death of printing partner Reb Shalom Dov Ber Pevzner
summary_en: During Iyar 5747 the author's printing partner Reb Shalom Dov Ber Pevzner died suddenly after collapsing at work.
story_body: In Iyar 5747 (May 1987), while the author was attending a wedding in Cleveland, his longtime printing partner Reb Shalom Dov Ber Pevzner — who had suffered for years from ulcers — went to the press despite feeling ill, collapsed, and died before an ambulance could help. The author completed all outstanding contracts alone, sharing the profits with the widow and with Merkos, which had been a one-third partner in the business.

title_en: Fiftieth wedding anniversary celebration
summary_en: On 9 Tammuz 5750 the author marked fifty years since his marriage in Moscow with an intimate family gathering hosted by his daughter Leah.
story_body: On 9 Tammuz 5750 (July 2, 1990) the family marked fifty years since the author's 5700 wedding in Moscow with a small jubilee gathering at his daughter Leah's home. The author repeated themes from the maamar 'Kol Hamaarich Be'echad' that the Frierdiker Rebbe had said on 12 Tammuz 5700 in New York during the week of his sheva berachos, and made a siyum on Maseches Nedarim.

title_en: Settlement check sent to Merkos over old partnership
summary_en: In 5752 the author sent a $500 check to Merkos via Rabbi Krinsky as a halachic settlement of any unintended discrepancies in the long-running printing partnership.
story_body: Citing Rambam's halachot of partners — that when partners separate each must swear about possible inadvertent overcharges — the author in 5752 (1992) wrote out a $500 check to Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch. He delivered it to Rabbi Yehuda Krinsky, his liaison to Rabbi Chadakov, asking him to verbally mochel on behalf of Merkos any sums that may have remained with the partners contrary to din.

title_en: Rebbe gives dollar with blessing for long life on Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul
summary_en: On Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5751, during the dollar distribution, the Rebbe gave the writer a birthday blessing and an additional dollar for success.
story_body: The author marks his birthday on Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5751 by receiving dollars from the Rebbe, who blessed him with long and good years. The Rebbe then handed an additional dollar and added a blessing for success 'like the king who read the Torah before all the people,' with good timing and health.

title_en: Rebbe gives extra dollar for tzedakah before family's trip to Israel
summary_en: On 12 Marcheshvan 5752, before the family's three-week trip to Eretz Yisrael, the Rebbe gave an additional dollar to be donated as tzedakah in the Holy Land.
story_body: Before traveling to Israel on Sunday, 12 Marcheshvan 5752, the family received dollars from the Rebbe, who added an extra dollar for tzedakah in Eretz Yisrael. With a smile he remarked that surely they had arranged who would read from the Torah, to which the writer's wife replied 'certainly!' — and the Rebbe blessed them with great success.

title_en: Wedding of Rachel Klein and Mendel Gordon
summary_en: On 3 Shevat 5742, the author's granddaughter Rachel Klein married Mendel Gordon, who would serve as a ram in the Lubavitch yeshiva of London.
story_body: Rachel, daughter of the author's daughter Leah and her husband Yerachmiel Binyamin HaLevi Klein, married Mendel Gordon on 3 Shevat 5742. The couple settled in London, where Mendel Gordon serves as a ram in the mesivta.

title_en: Wedding of Feigel Klein and Levi Yitzchak Sudak
summary_en: On 1 Adar 5743, Feigel Klein married Levi Yitzchak Sudak, future director of the Chabad House in Edgware, England.
story_body: Feigel, daughter of the author's daughter Leah and Yerachmiel Binyamin HaLevi Klein, married Levi Yitzchak Sudak on 1 Adar 5743. Levi Yitzchak Sudak became the director of the Chabad House in Edgware, England.

title_en: Wedding of Chana Klein and Levi Yitzchak Gurelik
summary_en: On 3 Adar 5745, Chana Klein married Levi Yitzchak Gurelik, who would serve as a ram in New York.
story_body: Chana, daughter of Leah and Yerachmiel Binyamin HaLevi Klein, married Levi Yitzchak Gurelik on 3 Adar 5745. Levi Yitzchak Gurelik serves as a ram in New York.

title_en: Wedding of Sterna Sarah Klein and Levi Yitzchak Krinsky
summary_en: On 17 Sivan 5746, Sterna Sarah Klein married Levi Yitzchak Krinsky, future director of the Chabad House in Manchester, New Hampshire.
story_body: Sterna Sarah, daughter of Leah and Yerachmiel Binyamin HaLevi Klein, married Levi Yitzchak Krinsky on 17 Sivan 5746. Levi Yitzchak Krinsky serves as director of the Chabad House in Manchester, New Hampshire.

title_en: Wedding of Esther Klein and Pinchas Tziment
summary_en: On 8 Elul 5750, Esther Klein married Pinchas Tziment, future director of the Chabad House in Little Rock, Arkansas.
story_body: Esther, daughter of Leah and Yerachmiel Binyamin HaLevi Klein, married Pinchas Tziment on 8 Elul 5750. Pinchas Tziment serves as director of the Chabad House in Little Rock, Arkansas.

title_en: Wedding of Levi Yitzchak HaLevi Klein and Rivka
summary_en: On 23 Sivan 5751, Levi Yitzchak HaLevi Klein married Rivka; he would serve as director of the Chabad House in Memphis, Tennessee.
story_body: Levi Yitzchak HaLevi Klein, son of Leah and Yerachmiel Binyamin HaLevi Klein, married Rivka on 23 Sivan 5751. He serves as director of the Chabad House in Memphis, Tennessee.

title_en: Wedding of Rivka Klein and Mordechai Grossbaum
summary_en: On 19 Adar II 5754, Rivka Klein married Mordechai Grossbaum, a member of the kollel in New York.
story_body: Rivka, daughter of Leah and Yerachmiel Binyamin HaLevi Klein, married Mordechai Grossbaum on 19 Adar 5754. Mordechai Grossbaum is a member of the kollel in New York.

title_en: Wedding of Chana Nemenov and Mendel Moskowitz
summary_en: On 13 Tammuz 5745, Chana Nemenov married Mendel Moskowitz, future melamed at Cheder Lubavitch in Chicago.
story_body: Chana, daughter of the author's daughter Miriam Reizel and Moshe Nemenov, married Mendel Moskowitz on 13 Tammuz 5745. Mendel Moskowitz serves as a melamed at Cheder Lubavitch in Chicago.

title_en: Wedding of Sterna Sarah Nemenov and Yosef Yitzchak Paltiel
summary_en: On 6 Kislev 5750, Sterna Sarah Nemenov married Yosef Yitzchak Paltiel, who serves as a ram at Tomchei Temimim in Brooklyn.
story_body: Sterna Sarah, daughter of Miriam Reizel and Moshe Nemenov, married Yosef Yitzchak Paltiel on 6 Kislev 5750. Yosef Yitzchak Paltiel serves as a ram in the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva in Brooklyn.

title_en: Wedding of Batya Nemenov and Shneur Zalman Marcus
summary_en: On 5 Tammuz 5753, Batya Nemenov married Shneur Zalman Marcus, a member of the kollel in New York.
story_body: Batya, daughter of Miriam Reizel and Moshe Nemenov, married Shneur Zalman Marcus on 5 Tammuz 5753. Shneur Zalman Marcus is a member of the kollel in New York.

title_en: Wedding of Eli Wolf and Nechama Dina
summary_en: On 13 Elul 5753, Eli Wolf married Nechama Dina; the couple is associated with the Gutnick Center in Jerusalem.
story_body: Eli, son of the author's daughter Feigel and Mendel Wolf, married Nechama Dina on 13 Elul 5753. The couple is associated with the Gutnick Center in Jerusalem.

title_en: Avraham Meir Pinchas Rodes founds evening kollel for working avreichim
summary_en: In 5748 (1988), Avraham Meir Pinchas Rodes founded an evening kollel for working avreichim who learn Torah Monday through Thursday evenings at the Frenkel shul.
story_body: Starting in 5748, Avraham Meir Pinchas Rodes established an evening kollel for avreichim whose Torah study is not their primary occupation. The participants gather at Rabbi Frenkel's shul from Sunday through Thursday evenings until late. From an initial group of ten regular avreichim, additional neighborhood participants joined, growing the program into a 'torch of light.'

title_en: Birth of Yisrael Yehuda Levin in Zhivotov
summary_en: Yisrael Yehuda Levin, author of the memoir Zichronotai, was born on Shabbat 7 Tammuz 5672 in Zhivotov, Ukraine.
story_body: Levin was born to Ephraim Shmuel ben Yosef and Leah Beila (daughter of the Dashov shochet Yisrael Bilenki) in the small town of Zhivotov in Vinnitsa province. His memoir, written across 35 years beginning around 1960, would document his life under Soviet rule and his eventual escape. The town was a religious community where his father served as a melamed.

title_en: Father drafted to World War I army
summary_en: Levin's father Ephraim Shmuel was conscripted into the army in the middle of World War I, leaving the mother to support the family.
story_body: During the height of World War I, Ephraim Shmuel was taken to the front, forcing Leah Beila to run their small shop and continue the children's education on her own. She was unusually learned for a woman of her region, having attended cheder herself, and taught the children Hebrew reading, Tanach, grammar, and arithmetic. Ephraim Shmuel returned home in 1918 and reopened his cheder.

title_en: Father released from army, reopens cheder in Zhivotov
summary_en: Ephraim Shmuel returned from military service in 1918 and reopened his Torah school for children and youth in Zhivotov.
story_body: After his release following the fall of the Tsar, Ephraim Shmuel resumed teaching Torah to the youth of Zhivotov. The political climate had changed dramatically: Russia was now a republic, parties were forming, and secular movements were drawing young Jews away from religion. The first public political address in the synagogue by a young woman shocked the elders and ignited communal conflict.

title_en: Haidamak pogroms reach Zhivotov
summary_en: At the start of summer 1919 Haidamak pogromist bands arrived in Zhivotov, beginning a long campaign of robbery, forced labor, and murder.
story_body: Petliura and Denikin forces were fighting their civil war across Ukraine, and successive bands of pogromists — including those of Tyutyunyk and Sokolov — passed through the area. They imposed taxes on the Jewish community, conscripted men like Ephraim Shmuel to dig defensive trenches, and increasingly turned to murder. Local Ukrainian peasants joined the violence as the months wore on.

title_en: Massacre at Tetiev synagogue burning
summary_en: In winter 1920 the Jews of nearby Tetiev (Titov) were gathered into their synagogue and burned alive by pogromists, reducing the community of 8,000 to under 2,000.
story_body: While fleeing Zhivotov through the fields, the Levin family watched a column of smoke rising from Tetiev in the distance. They later learned that pogromists had locked the Jews of Tetiev inside the synagogue and set it on fire. Tetiev was a deeply religious Chernobyl chassidic town of about 8,000 souls; fewer than 2,000 survived, most of them young orphans.

title_en: Pogromist Sokolov extorts Zhivotov, kills ten
summary_en: The pogromist Sokolov entered Zhivotov in late winter 1920, demanded tribute, and had ten Jews killed including the rabbi's wife.
story_body: When Sokolov's band approached Zhivotov, the town's elders went out to greet him with bread, water, and a Torah scroll, begging him to restrain his men. He agreed but said ten Jews would die regardless. Among the dead was the wife of the town's rabbi, Reb Chaim. The town considered itself spared compared to neighboring Tetiev.

title_en: Levin family flees Zhivotov for Lipovets
summary_en: After Purim 5680 the Levin family hired a wagon and fled Zhivotov for Lipovets, arriving just before Pesach.
story_body: The roads were thick with mud, forcing the family to repeatedly dismount and help push the wagon. They traveled several days, sleeping at the wagon-driver's village home along the way. All six members of the family arrived safely in Lipovets days before Passover 1920, where Rabbi Shlomo Sternberg and shochet Reb Levi helped them settle.

title_en: Polish-Bolshevik war reaches Lipovets
summary_en: In summer 1920 Polish troops occupied Lipovets, demanding flour and lodging from Jewish residents before being driven out by the advancing Soviet army.
story_body: Unlike the pogromists, the Polish soldiers did not murder, but they demanded that locals bake bread for them and house their men. The Levin family hosted a Polish soldier and baked from flour the army provided. Soviet forces eventually captured the Poles or drove them back, and Lipovets quieted from major fighting.

title_en: Levin parents recover from typhus
summary_en: Late in summer 1920 Ephraim Shmuel and Leah Beila contracted typhus along with all their children; only eight-year-old Yisrael Yehuda remained well, and the family recovered by Tishrei 5681.
story_body: With both parents and siblings bedridden, the young Yisrael Yehuda was the family's only able body, though he was too small to help much. The parents nevertheless fasted on Yom Kippur despite their weakness. By the end of the High Holidays the family had recovered completely.

title_en: Ephraim Shmuel opens large cheder in Lipovets
summary_en: After Simchas Torah 5681 the family moved into a three-room apartment in Lipovets and Ephraim Shmuel opened what became the town's largest cheder.
story_body: The new apartment was rented from the widow of the melamed Reb Gedalyahu Shmuel. Ephraim Shmuel taught Chumash with Rashi to a large group of children, and Leah Beila assisted by teaching them Hebrew writing and arithmetic. This was the largest cheder in Lipovets.

title_en: Levin leaves to learn at Kiev yeshiva
summary_en: In summer 1927 the fifteen-year-old Yisrael Yehuda Levin traveled to Kiev to study in yeshiva, where he first learned of the underground Tomchei Tmimim network.
story_body: This trip marked the start of a decade of wandering through Soviet underground yeshivos. Levin would move between Vitebsk, Pereyaslav, Kiev, Baku, Kutaisi, Kulashi, Moscow, Chernigov, Malachovka, Leningrad, Voronezh, Krivoy Rog, and Kharkov as yeshivos were repeatedly shut down by the secret police. He lived without proper papers or with forged ones.

title_en: Death of Ephraim Shmuel Levin in Lipovets
summary_en: Ephraim Shmuel ben Yosef, the author's father, died on 15 Shevat 5693 in Lipovets, leaving his widow Leah Beila to support four orphans.
story_body: Ephraim Shmuel had taught Torah in Lipovets with great devotion, refusing to allow his daughters to attend Soviet schools even under threat of fines. His widow Leah Beila was sickly with heart disease and struggled to support the younger children Sarah, Rivka, and Freide. The eldest son Yosef was then nearing twenty-five and Yisrael Yehuda was about twenty-one.

title_en: Levin writes to Rebbe Rayatz from Lipovets
summary_en: In Iyyar 5694 Yisrael Yehuda Levin wrote to Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn describing his late father's mesirus nefesh in raising the children as Torah-observant.
story_body: The letter recounted that Ephraim Shmuel had insisted his daughters not attend the Soviet school despite repeated official demands and threats of fines. Levin listed his mother and three younger sisters by name and age, noting his mother's heart disease prevented her from earning a living. The letter was preserved in the Rebbe's archive.

title_en: Leah Beila Levin writes memoir-letter to Rebbe Rayatz
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Tammuz 5694 Leah Beila Levin sent the Rebbe Rayatz a detailed account of her family history and her late husband's piety from Lipovets.
story_body: The letter described her descent from Reb Avraham Yehuda of Linets and the Kosover-Berditchev rabbinic line, her childhood in Dashov, and her marriage to Ephraim Shmuel of Zhivotov. It detailed how their small shop and his teaching supported the family, and how she herself sometimes taught the children of his cheder. The letter is preserved in the Lubavitch library archive.

title_en: Levin reports for army induction in Moscow
summary_en: On 11 Tishrei 5696 Yisrael Yehuda Levin was required to appear for army induction in Moscow, weeks after the senior Lubavitchers there had been arrested and exiled.
story_body: Levin had no proper identity papers and a record of arrests, and his classmates warned that the secret police were inquiring about a young man matching his description. The Rebbe Rayatz instructed him to put on eyeglasses, and miraculously he received a total exemption from military service. He immediately fled Moscow for Voronezh.

title_en: Levin marries in Kharkov
summary_en: Yisrael Yehuda Levin married in Kharkov in late winter 5698, ending a decade of wandering between underground yeshivos.
story_body: After running an underground yeshiva branch in Krivoy Rog for over a year, Levin married and settled in Kharkov. His army exemption obtained through the eyeglasses miracle remained valid until World War II, when the Soviets stopped honoring such exemptions and drafted virtually every young man with hands and legs. Many of his friends were taken to the front and never returned.

title_en: Death of Levins' only son in Samarkand
summary_en: The Levins' two-and-a-half year old son, their only child, died upon their arrival in Samarkand after a three-week train journey fleeing the war.
story_body: When the Eastern Front reached Kharkov, the Levins fled with thousands of other Jews to Central Asia. The grueling three-week journey in a freight car proved fatal for their young son, who died soon after they reached Samarkand. The couple would not have more children until after leaving the Soviet Union.

title_en: Levin escapes Soviet Union as Polish refugee 'Naftali Bat'
summary_en: In summer 1946 Levin used forged Polish refugee documents in the name Naftali Bat to leave the Soviet Union among the first wave of Anash to escape.
story_body: Unable to renew his army exemption in Samarkand, Levin had gone underground using papers identifying him as a Polish refugee not yet drafted. He could not work openly under this name without Polish-language skills, so he worked under his wife's name. The same Polish papers eventually allowed both of them to leave Russia, with his wife re-registered as having remarried a Pole named Naftali Bat.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz instructs Anash to record Soviet-era memoirs
summary_en: After Chassidim began leaving the Soviet Union in 1946-1947, the Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn directed them to write down their memories of clandestine activity and the names of those involved.
story_body: The Rebbe specifically asked that participants record everything they could remember about underground religious work, the names of fellow Chassidim and students, and the places and times of their activities. Reb Bentzion Shemtov was charged with coordinating the collection. The instruction launched a tradition of Chabad memoir writing that produced major historical sources including Reb Meir Gurkov's Sefer HaZichronot.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes to Shemtov about memoir collection
summary_en: On 18 Tevet 5709 the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to Reb Bentzion Shemtov about coordinating the collection of memoirs from Anash and the temimim in Eretz Yisrael.
story_body: The letter, published as Iggros Kodesh vol. 10, no. 3365, directed Shemtov to correspond with Anash and Tomchei Tmimim alumni in Eretz Yisrael and elsewhere, gather their memoirs, and forward everything to the Rebbe. The Rebbe assigned a specific editor to organize the incoming material. This launched the project that produced multiple memoir volumes.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz follow-up letter on memoir project
summary_en: On 24 Shevat 5709 the Rebbe Rayatz thanked Reb Bentzion Shemtov for taking up the task of organizing alumni of the underground yeshiva to record their experiences.
story_body: Published as Iggros Kodesh vol. 10, no. 3398, the letter expressed deep satisfaction with Shemtov's decision to enlist the temimim and Anash in writing memoirs of their clandestine Torah work in their homeland. The Rebbe blessed the participants with material and spiritual success.

title_en: Levin family arrives in Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: After three years of wandering since leaving the Soviet Union, the Levins reached Eretz Yisrael in early summer 5709 and settled in Kfar Chabad.
story_body: Their post-Soviet journey had taken them through Lodz, the Föhrenwald-area DP camps including Pocking, and Paris. Settlement in the newly established Chabad village proved difficult; the family lived in hardship until the new permanent homes were built in 1957.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz acknowledges Meir Gurkov's memoir
summary_en: On 22 Marcheshvan 5710 the Rebbe Rayatz confirmed receipt of Reb Meir Gurkov's memoir manuscript and urged senior temimim to follow his example.
story_body: The letter, published as Iggros Kodesh vol. 10, no. 3612, thanked Gurkov for the kuntres of memories he had submitted in response to the Rebbe's earlier instruction. The Rebbe stated that all senior temimim should similarly record what was worth remembering. Gurkov's memoir was later published as Sefer HaZichronot Divrei HaYamim.

title_en: New homes constructed in Kfar Chabad
summary_en: In 5717 new permanent homes were built in Kfar Chabad, finally allowing families like the Levins who had immigrated from the Soviet Union to settle properly.
story_body: The years preceding the new construction had been very hard for the Russian Anash who had arrived in 1948-1949. The new housing project marked a turning point that enabled families to stabilize and resume normal communal life. Yisrael Yehuda Levin began preparing for his first trip to the Rebbe in New York soon after.

title_en: Levin's first trip to the Rebbe for Tishrei 5723
summary_en: In late Elul 5722 Yisrael Yehuda Levin traveled from Kfar Chabad to New York for his first visit to the Rebbe Menachem Mendel Schneerson.
story_body: Levin had hoped for this meeting through years of underground religious work in the Soviet Union. He spent the entire month of Tishrei 5723 with the Rebbe, attending farbrengens, yechidus, and the Sukkos and Simchas Torah celebrations at 770. The memoir ends with the description of this Tishrei month.

title_en: Publication of Sefer HaZichronot Divrei HaYamim
summary_en: Reb Meir Gurkov's memoirs of underground Chabad activity in the Soviet Union were published in 5736 in New York as Sefer HaZichronot Divrei HaYamim.
story_body: Gurkov was the father-in-law of Yisrael Yehuda Levin and one of the first Anash to comply with the Rebbe Rayatz's 1946-1949 directive to record memoirs of Soviet-era religious work. His volume became a foundational primary source for the history of Chabad in the Soviet Union.

title_en: Publication of Toldot Chabad in Soviet Russia
summary_en: Rabbi Shalom Dovber Levin's Toldot Chabad B'Russia HaSovietit was published by Kehot in 5749, drawing in part on his father's then-unpublished memoirs.
story_body: Shalom Dovber Levin, son of Yisrael Yehuda Levin and longtime librarian of the Central Lubavitch Library, used excerpts from his father's accumulating memoir notes in this historical work. The full memoir Zichronotai was prepared for publication separately and signed by the author in Elul 5755.

title_en: Yisrael Yehuda Levin completes memoir introduction
summary_en: On 18 Elul 5755 in Kfar Chabad, Yisrael Yehuda Levin signed the introduction to his memoir Zichronotai, completing 35 years of writing.
story_body: Levin had begun writing his memories around 1960 and added to them periodically through the 1990s. His son Shalom Dovber and grandson Yosef Yitzchak Keller edited the manuscript for publication. The memoir covers his life from the 1919-1920 pogroms in Zhivotov through his first month with the Rebbe in Tishrei 5723.

title_en: Anti-religious Chanukah parade mocks Avraham Hanoch's cheder in Lipovets
summary_en: On Chanukah 5681, Soviet activists led a public parade through Lipovets caricaturing the author's father teaching Torah and ridiculing Chanukah lights and his cheder.
story_body: Yevsektsiya operatives marched students and elders wearing red ties through the streets in an anti-Jewish demonstration, drawing cartoons of the father instructing his pupils and mocking the family cheder. The author's family experienced for the first time a threat aimed not only at their bodies but at their souls. The mother responded that being publicly linked with G-d and Torah was a great merit.

title_en: Family moves near the kloiz at the Bashtun in Lipovets
summary_en: In early winter 5683 the family relocated next to the Bashtun kloiz, where the father resumed teaching a large group of children in the home.
story_body: A G-d-fearing cooper was their neighbor at the new dwelling. More observant parents who still clung to Yiddishkeit entrusted their sons to the author's father, and a sizable cheder gathered in a large room of the home. The move offered modest stability during the worsening Soviet anti-religious climate.

title_en: Brothers light menorah and play Chanukah kvitlach in Lipovets
summary_en: During Chanukah 5683 the author and his older brother prayed Hallel daily, lit the menorah with their father, and played kvitlach at night.
story_body: Each day of the festival the boys walked to shul together to daven and recite Hallel. In the evenings, after their father kindled the lights and their mother fried latkes, they played the traditional Chanukah kvitlach game, providing a small island of warmth amid the harsh anti-religious environment.

title_en: Famine and Joint-supplied food relief reach Lipovets
summary_en: In 5683 a terrible famine struck and the Soviet government distributed cooked food and bread, almost certainly supplied by the Joint Distribution Committee.
story_body: Residents stood on long queues to receive a portion of cooked food, bread and meat from a local official. Because the official's sons studied in the family's cheder, the author and his brother were able to obtain the bread ration with little waiting. The episode reflects the dire hunger gripping Ukrainian shtetls during this period.

title_en: Bar mitzvah of Rabbi Shlomo Sternberg's only son in Lipovets
summary_en: In the summer of 5683 the only son of Rabbi Shlomo Sternberg of Lipovets celebrated his bar mitzvah, with the author's brother and their melamed seated alongside the celebrant.
story_body: The author's brother Yosef had befriended Mordechai, son of Rabbi Sternberg, and a private melamed was teaching the two boys Gemara with Rashi and Tosafot. At the bar mitzvah seudah the brother sat beside the bar mitzvah boy together with their teacher, a rare moment of communal Jewish celebration in the increasingly hostile shtetl.

title_en: Trotsky leadership conflict briefly eases anti-religious persecution
summary_en: Toward the end of 5684, internal Communist Party strife around Trotsky temporarily quieted the campaign against Jewish religious life in Lipovets.
story_body: The author attributes a noticeable lull in anti-religious pressure to factional struggles at the top of the Communist Party. The respite was short-lived, but it gave families like his room to breathe and to resume modest Torah study at home. The episode illustrates how Kremlin politics directly affected daily Jewish life in the shtetls.

title_en: Visit to the Lipovets Jewish cemetery on Tisha B'Av 5684
summary_en: On Tisha B'Av 5684 the author, his brother and Rabbi Sternberg's son walked the rural roads outside Lipovets to visit the town's Jewish cemetery.
story_body: Reaching the beit hachaim required a long trek along village roads far from town. The author later recalled it as the first and only outing he ever took with religious boys his age. The episode evokes the shrinking circle of observant peers available to him as Soviet pressure mounted.

title_en: Rabbi of Lipovets relocates to Kiev
summary_en: At the end of 5685 the rabbi of Lipovets moved to Kiev, after which the local dayan filled the rabbinic role and the Yevsektsiya intensified its work.
story_body: With the rav gone, a less stalwart replacement appeared in public debates with Yevsektsiya activists, and the position of religious Jewry in Lipovets weakened sharply. The Yevsektsiya summoned the new rabbinic representative to a public disputation in the town club, where he conceded much of the anti-religious argument. The author, then a youth, attended and was deeply shaken.

title_en: Family moves to Rabbi Levi the shochet's house in Lipovets
summary_en: For the winter of 5686 the family moved into the home of R' Levi the shochet, filling its cellar with potatoes to last through Pesach.
story_body: The cellar storage of their potato harvest from the small plot they had worked outside town secured the family's food supply through winter and Pesach. The move also provided the moral support of living beside an observant shochet at a time when religious neighbors were increasingly rare in Lipovets.

title_en: Author's brother begins studying at Rabbi Morgenstern's yeshiva in Kiev
summary_en: In the summer of 5686 Yosef left Lipovets for the Morgenstern yeshiva in Kiev, after his friend Mordechai Sternberg wrote that the yeshiva accepted bachurim from age 18.
story_body: The yeshiva was headed by Rabbi Morgenstern under the oversight of Kiev's chief rabbi, Rav Chaim Matasov, and admitted only older bachurim. Yosef boarded with R' Shlomo Telingator in Podol, a Boyan chassid and old friend of the author's father. Soon a Komsomol infiltrator with a fake beard arrived at the (Litvish) yeshiva to corrupt the students.
