story_body: Approaching Rosh Hashana 5710, Levin received a personal greeting from the Rebbe Rayatz blessing him and his family within the broader community of Israel and Anash. The letter again featured the emphasized yud in the signature that had become Rayatz's custom.

title_en: Levin learns of Rayatz's passing en route to Bnei Brak
summary_en: On Sunday 11 Shevat 5710 Levin saw a newspaper report at the Tel Aviv central bus station announcing the histalkus of the Rebbe Rayatz.
story_body: Levin had been working at the matzah bakery in Pardes Katz under Rabbi Yaakov Landa's supervision during late winter 5710. On 11 Shevat, while traveling to Bnei Brak, he saw a newspaper at the central bus station with the news of the Rayatz's passing the day before. He arrived at work, asked someone to perform kriah for him, and sat on the floor in mourning.

title_en: First letter from the Rebbe (Menachem Mendel) to Levin
summary_en: Between Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur 5711, Levin received his first letter from the future Rebbe responding to a pan and asking for an update on the month of Tishrei.
story_body: Before Rosh Hashana 5711 Levin sent a pan to be read at the Rayatz's ohel. The reply, dated 'between kesseh and asor' 5711, confirmed it was read on the ohel and in the heichal, noted that 'a tzaddik who has departed is present in this world more than during his lifetime,' and asked Levin to report on developments during Tishrei. This was the first of many letters Levin would receive from the next Rebbe.

title_en: Levin recovers from illness in Sarafand
summary_en: In summer 5711 Levin fell seriously ill in Sarafand, and the Rebbe responded with instructions and blessings for recovery.
story_body: Worn down by hard labor and poverty, Levin became gravely ill in summer 5711. R' Shlomo Kesselman wrote to the Rebbe about him, and the reply urged Levin to strengthen his observance of the three daily shiurim and the takanot concerning Tehillim, expressing confidence that he would soon report improving health.

title_en: Chanukat habayit of the Lod yeshiva in the pardes
summary_en: By Chai Elul 5711 Levin had recovered and was present at the chanukat habayit of the Lod yeshiva in the pardes.
story_body: Following the Rebbe's blessing during his illness, Levin recovered in time to attend the dedication of the new Lod yeshiva building in the pardes on 18 Elul 5711. The occasion marked both his personal recovery and a milestone for Chabad institutions in Eretz Yisrael.

title_en: Kfar Chabad residents move into newly built homes
summary_en: In 5717 the Levin family and other Kfar Chabad residents moved from abandoned Arab homes into newly built dwellings constructed for them in the village.
story_body: For eight years after their arrival in 5709, the Levins lived in the abandoned Arab homes that had been allocated to settlers of Kfar Chabad. In 5717 new houses built specifically for the residents were finally ready, and the families moved into the new dwellings.

title_en: Levin's first flight to the Rebbe via charter from Lod
summary_en: On Tuesday 26 Elul 5722 Levin flew from Lod via Paris to New York on a charter flight to spend Tishrei with the Rebbe for the first time.
story_body: After years of yearning, Levin joined a charter flight at the end of Elul 5722 for his first trip to the Rebbe. The plane departed Lod at noon, stopped two hours in Paris where Chassidim could see them only through a thick glass partition (only R' Raphael Wilshansky was allowed in), then continued to New York. The Rebbe was waiting at 770 and emerged from his room to daven Maariv when the group arrived.

title_en: Erev Rosh Hashana 5723 farbrengen on Tzemach Tzedek's birthday
summary_en: On the night of 29 Elul 5722, the birthday of the Tzemach Tzedek, the Rebbe led a farbrengen with women in the ezrat nashim and spoke on hachnasat orchim.
story_body: On Thursday night, the eve of 29 Elul 5722 — the birthday of the Tzemach Tzedek — the Rebbe held a farbrengen at 770 with a microphone since it was the night before Rosh Hashana. The ezrat nashim was filled with women and the Rebbe addressed a sicha to them. He spoke about the mitzvah of hachnasat orchim being greater than receiving the Divine Presence, embracing the assembled guests.

title_en: Rebbe receives pidyonot on Erev Rosh Hashana 5723
summary_en: On Erev Rosh Hashana 5723 the Rebbe led Selichot, performed hatarat nedarim, received pidyonot, and the Vaad HaMesader presented a collective pan.
story_body: Early Friday morning of Erev Rosh Hashana 5723, the Rebbe led Selichot and Shacharit before a large crowd of Tishrei guests. He performed hatarat nedarim before a minyan of elder Chassidim, then received personal pidyonot at his hand. The Vaad HaMesader and elder Anash then brought a collective pan, with each signer giving a dollar. The Rebbe then traveled to the Ohel to read and tear the pidyonot.

title_en: Rebbe called for maftir on first day of Rosh Hashana 5723
summary_en: On Shabbat, first day of Rosh Hashana 5723, the Rebbe was called to the Torah for maftir and read the haftarah of Chana with great emotion.
story_body: Because the first day of Rosh Hashana 5723 fell on Shabbat there was no shofar blowing. Levin pushed his way onto the bima next to baal koreh R' Mordechai Shusterman to hear the maftir from the Rebbe. The Rebbe read the haftarah of Chana with such inner weeping and sweetness that Levin had to cover his face with his tallit to muffle his sobs.

title_en: Rebbe blows shofar on second day of Rosh Hashana 5723
summary_en: On the second day of Rosh Hashana 5723 the Rebbe blew shofar, led Tashlich, and delivered the maamar 'Yivchar Lanu Et Nachalateinu.'
story_body: Levin again ascended the bima and unexpectedly received the honor of gelilah. The Rebbe covered the bundled pidyonot with his tallit, wept, and blew only the first tekiah. After Mincha the Rebbe led the entire crowd to Tashlich along Eastern Parkway in remarkable order, with even non-Jewish onlookers watching with reverence. The maamar 'Yivchar Lanu Et Nachalateinu' was delivered at the farbrengen that followed.

title_en: Kfar Chabad delegation presents Rebbe with the village's etrog
summary_en: On the night of 4 Tishrei 5723, representatives of Kfar Chabad delivered the village's etrog to the Rebbe, who blessed them in return.
story_body: Members of Anash from Kfar Chabad presented the Rebbe with the etrog grown in the village. The Rebbe blessed them that just as the etrog has both taste and fragrance — symbolizing all qualities — so should all Israel, Anash, and Kfar Chabad in particular be granted matters of taam and reach throughout the entire year.

title_en: Levin's first yechidus with the Rebbe
summary_en: On the night of 6 Tishrei 5723, just before 3am, Levin entered yechidus with the Rebbe for the first time and recited Shehecheyanu.
story_body: After a lifetime of hoping for this moment, Levin entered the Rebbe's room for his first yechidus in the early hours of 6 Tishrei 5723. He recited Shehecheyanu and presented a long written tzettel of questions. The Rebbe answered each one in depth, and when Levin failed to grasp a detail, the Rebbe patiently repeated his words verbatim.

title_en: Levin davens before the amud on Shabbat Shuva 5723
summary_en: On 8 Tishrei 5723 (Shabbat Shuva and his mother's yahrzeit), Levin led prayers at the Rebbe's beit midrash and was called up for shevii.
story_body: On 8 Tishrei 5723, the yahrzeit of his mother (Hashem yikom damah), Levin davened all the Shabbat tefillot before the amud in the Rebbe's beit midrash, with the gabbai R' Yochanan Gordon pushing him toward the amud for Musaf. He stood beside the Rebbe for maftir. Before the Shabbat, an Anash printer had given him a galley of the Tzemach Tzedek's maamar 'V'chol Adam' brought from Russia, which the Rebbe delivered at the farbrengen that day.

title_en: Lekach distribution before Yom Kippur 5723
summary_en: On Erev Yom Kippur 5723 Levin received lekach from the Rebbe and also obtained lekach from Rebbetzin Chana.
story_body: Levin waited in line to receive lekach from the Rebbe, who gave him a piece for his daughter as well. He also visited Rebbetzin Chana with his host's family — R' Berl Yunik's family — and received lekach and a blessing from her. She remembered Levin from Pocking, where he had stayed with Michoel Teitelbaum.

title_en: Levin blesses on the Rebbe's etrog on Sukkot 5723
summary_en: On the second day of Sukkot 5723 Levin entered the Rebbe's sukkah and blessed on the Rebbe's arba minim.
story_body: After the first day of Sukkot fell on Shabbat, Levin waited in line on the second day to enter the Rebbe's sukkah and bless on his arba minim. The Rebbe stood in a corner holding a sefer and watched Levin throughout, who silently prayed not to fumble the brachah from the intensity of the moment.

title_en: Hoshana Rabbah 5723 hakafot mission and 770 farbrengen
summary_en: On Erev Shabbat Hoshana Rabbah 5723, Chassidim were dispatched to distant shuls to lead hakafot, then converged at 770 for the Rebbe's farbrengen.
story_body: On Erev Shabbat Hoshana Rabbah 5723, Levin and others were sent according to a list to far-away shuls to gladden Jews with hakafot. They later gathered at Rabbi Yaakov Hecht's shul for kiddush and walked together with song and dance back to 770. At the farbrengen the Rebbe asked all those who had gone to gladden others to say l'chaim and recite Atah Hareita and the hakafot — a peak of joy as the Rebbe danced with the Rashag during the first and seventh hakafot.

title_en: Simchat Torah 5723 hakafot and 'Stav Ya Pitu' niggun
summary_en: On Simchat Torah night 5723 the Rebbe taught the Russian niggun 'Stav Ya Pitu' for the first time at 770.
story_body: After the late-night hakafot of Simchat Torah 5723, Chassidim waited as the Rebbe was set to distribute mashke. The Rebbe recounted the story behind the niggun 'Stav Ya Pitu' and began to sing it. Standing right beside the Rebbe, Levin watched as the Rebbe repeated the Russian-lyric melody many times until R' Yoel Kahn finally picked it up — since the wave of bochurim from Russia had not yet arrived.

title_en: Rebbe calls Israeli army veterans up at Motzaei Simchat Torah farbrengen
summary_en: At the Motzaei Simchat Torah 5723 farbrengen the Rebbe asked all Israeli army or reserve veterans to ascend the table and say l'chaim, hinting at the Cuban missile crisis.
story_body: Toward the end of the Motzaei Simchat Torah farbrengen the Rebbe unexpectedly invited all those from Eretz Yisrael who had served in the army or miluim to come up on the table and say l'chaim, then led the singing of 'V'haya Machanecha Kadosh' and 'Shalom Al Yisrael.' He said cryptically 'one should fulfill it with the fear,' which Chassidim later interpreted in light of Soviet missiles approaching Cuba. Levin received kos shel bracha and was called back to receive a bottle of wine to distribute in Eretz Yisrael.

title_en: Levin's second yechidus on Rosh Chodesh Cheshvan 5723
summary_en: On the night of Rosh Chodesh Cheshvan 5723 Levin had a second yechidus, during which the Rebbe instructed him to establish a yahrzeit for the martyred R' Yona Cohen.
story_body: On his second yechidus, just before 10pm on the night of Rosh Chodesh Cheshvan 5723, Levin handed in a lengthy tzettel and mentioned the kadosh R' Yona Cohen. The Rebbe asked for his mother's name and his date of death and instructed Levin to fix a yahrzeit, say kaddish, and learn mishnayot. Levin later confirmed with R' Elya Chaim Roitblat (R' Yona's brother-in-law) that the date was 22 Shevat and the mother's name was Frade, and conveyed the information to R' Chadakov.

title_en: Vasili III signs treaty transferring Lubavitch to Poland
summary_en: Vasili III of Russia signed an agreement transferring several towns in the Smolensk region, including Lubavitch, to Poland.
story_body: The first known documentary mention of the town of Lubavitch appears in this 1521 treaty. At that time, Lubavitch sat near the contested border between Russia and Poland, an area subject to repeated wars and shifting sovereignty. The Smolensk region towns named in the agreement included Lubavitch among them.

title_en: Ivan the Terrible signs treaty affecting Smolensk-region towns
summary_en: Ivan the Terrible signed an agreement similar to the 1521 treaty involving the Smolensk-area towns near Lubavitch.
story_body: A second documentary reference places Lubavitch within the contested Russian-Polish frontier zone during the mid-16th century. The agreement reaffirmed the ongoing diplomatic tensions over towns in the Smolensk area. These early documents form part of the small surviving record of the town's pre-Chassidic existence.

title_en: List of approximately fifty Jewish families in Lubavitch recorded
summary_en: A roster of roughly fifty Jewish families then residing in Lubavitch was recorded in 1784.
story_body: This list, later published by Hendel Deutsch in his 1994 Russian booklet on Lubavitch, gives a snapshot of the town's Jewish community in the era of the Alter Rebbe's youth. It documents the modest scale of the settlement before Lubavitch became a movement headquarters. Around this period the future Alter Rebbe studied Torah in Lubavitch with Rabbi Yissachar Ber.

title_en: Birth of Rabbi Menachem Mendel (Tzemach Tzedek) in Liadi
summary_en: Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn, later the third Chabad Rebbe known as the Tzemach Tzedek, was born on Erev Rosh Hashanah 5550 in Liadi.
story_body: Born on the eve of Rosh Hashanah 5550, the future Tzemach Tzedek would later become both nephew and son-in-law of the Mittler Rebbe. He would assume Chabad leadership in 1827 and guide the movement from Lubavitch for nearly four decades. His birth in Liadi predates the relocation of the Chabad center to Lubavitch.

title_en: Passing of the Alter Rebbe in the village of Piena
summary_en: Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, founder of Chabad Chassidus, passed away on 24 Tevet 5573 in the village of Piena while fleeing the Napoleonic invasion.
story_body: Forced to flee Liadi during Napoleon's 1812 campaign, the Alter Rebbe was carried from town to town and village to village for several months. His soul departed on 24 Tevet in the village of Piena. His passing set the stage for his son the Mittler Rebbe to relocate the Chabad center to Lubavitch later that year.

title_en: Mittler Rebbe settles in Lubavitch, establishing it as Chabad center
summary_en: Rabbi Dovber, the second Chabad Rebbe, settled in Lubavitch in late summer 5573, inaugurating the town's century as Chabad world headquarters.
story_body: Following the close of the Napoleonic War, the Mittler Rebbe returned to White Russia and chose Lubavitch as his residence. He purchased a wooden house from the estate owner Krouyer and began building a large wooden synagogue in the courtyard. This move opened the 102-year period during which Lubavitch served as the movement's worldwide center.

title_en: Construction of large wooden synagogue begins in Lubavitch
summary_en: The Mittler Rebbe began building a large wooden synagogue in the Lubavitch courtyard in 5574, taking one to two years to complete.
story_body: The synagogue measured roughly 21 by 13 meters with a vestibule open on two sides and a central bimah. According to investigator Korbitzky's 1826 court report, the building also housed Torah scrolls written by the Yanovich scribe, menorahs ordered from Petersburg, and a library of 611 books kept in four cabinets and available for lending.

title_en: Passing of the Mittler Rebbe in Nezhin
summary_en: Rabbi Dovber, the second Chabad Rebbe, passed away on 10 Kislev 5588 in Nezhin while returning from a visit to his father's resting place in Haditch.
story_body: At the start of 5588 the Mittler Rebbe traveled to prostrate himself at the grave of his father the Alter Rebbe in distant Haditch. On the return journey he stopped in Nezhin, where he passed away on the tenth of Kislev. He is buried there, and his son-in-law the Tzemach Tzedek subsequently assumed the leadership of Chabad.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek accepts Chabad leadership in Lubavitch
summary_en: Following the passing of the Mittler Rebbe in 5588, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn accepted the leadership of Chabad and continued the movement from Lubavitch.
story_body: The Tzemach Tzedek, both nephew and son-in-law of his predecessor, would lead the movement for nearly forty years from Lubavitch. In his early years he regularly toured Chassidic communities, having visited more than thirty towns by 5597. Lubavitch under his leadership became the cornerstone to which all Chabad communities turned.

title_en: Rabbi Yissachar Ber Halevi Horowitz appointed Rabbi of Lubavitch
summary_en: Rabbi Yissachar Ber Halevi Horowitz began serving as Rabbi of the town of Lubavitch in 5592.
story_body: Horowitz served as town rabbi during much of the Tzemach Tzedek's leadership era. He was followed in the position by Rabbi Avraham son of Avigdor Hakohen. These local rabbinic appointments operated alongside the Chabad leadership presence in the town's main courtyard.

title_en: Maskilim inform on Tzemach Tzedek; police search his home
summary_en: Maskilim denounced the Tzemach Tzedek to the Russian government in 5601 for opposing forced Haskalah education of Jewish children, leading to a police search of his Lubavitch home.
story_body: A special police officer came to Lubavitch to interrogate the Rebbe and search his home, and the Tzemach Tzedek fell ill from the shock. The incident triggered ongoing secret surveillance by the Russian secret police, which continued until the spring of 5607. The denunciation was part of a broader Haskalah-driven government effort to compel Jewish children into state-run secular education.

title_en: Rabbinic Vaad on Jewish education convenes in Russia
summary_en: A government-convened conference on Jewish education met during the summer of 5603, with the Tzemach Tzedek among the participating rabbinic leaders.
story_body: The maskilim had proposed the conference to pressure rabbinic leaders into agreeing to open Haskalah schools for Jewish youth. Initially the Tzemach Tzedek declined to attend due to ill health following the 5601 search, but it was ultimately decided that his presence was crucial to prevent harmful resolutions. Following the conference the Russian government issued him a certificate of honored citizenship for his descendants.

title_en: Government removes secret surveillance from Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: In the spring of 5607 the Russian authorities concluded there was no fault in the Tzemach Tzedek's conduct and lifted the secret surveillance imposed on him.
story_body: The continuous secret-police watch had begun after the 5601 denunciation by maskilim and continued for some six years. After concluding no improper conduct, the government discontinued the surveillance. Documentation of the episode was later published in Pardes Chabad volume 4.

title_en: Birth of Rebbe Maharash (Rabbi Shmuel) in Lubavitch
summary_en: Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn, the future fourth Chabad Rebbe known as the Maharash, was born on 2 Iyar 5594 in Lubavitch.
story_body: The Maharash is the only Chabad Rebbe to have been born, lived his entire life, and passed away in Lubavitch. He would assume Chabad leadership in 5626 following the passing of his father the Tzemach Tzedek. His birth in the town further entrenched Lubavitch as the dynastic seat of the movement.

title_en: Passing of the Tzemach Tzedek in Lubavitch
summary_en: Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn, the Tzemach Tzedek, passed away on 13 Nisan 5626 in Lubavitch, the first Chabad Rebbe buried there.
story_body: He had instructed in his will that no structure of brick or wood be built over his grave. Out of concern that gentiles might dig the grave searching for buried gold, an ohel of high walls without a roof was constructed around the resting place. A study hall was later added on the southern side, making the spot a place of study and prayer.

title_en: Rebbe Maharash accepts Chabad leadership
summary_en: Following the passing of his father in 5626, Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn became the fourth Chabad Rebbe.
story_body: The Maharash's leadership continued the Chabad center in Lubavitch and saw major rebuilding of the courtyard after the 5628 fire. He would lead until his own passing in 5643. His era saw significant expansion of structures in the Lubavitch courtyard, including a large new hall and additional family residences.

title_en: Fire destroys the Lubavitch courtyard
summary_en: In the summer of 5628 fire again consumed the entire Lubavitch courtyard and all the buildings standing upon it.
story_body: Just two years into the Maharash's leadership, the wooden buildings of the Rebbe's courtyard were destroyed. The disaster forced major rebuilding decisions, including whether the Maharash could lawfully build his residence on the site of his father's home given the Tzemach Tzedek's will against such use. The rebuilding produced the large hall and new family residences that would characterize the courtyard for the remaining decades.

title_en: Maharash builds large hall in Lubavitch courtyard
summary_en: In 5632 the Maharash erected a large hall of roughly 21 by 21 meters on the site of his father's former residence in the Lubavitch courtyard.
story_body: The hall featured an unusually high ceiling and tall, wide windows on three sides. It was used for High Holiday prayers and large farbrengens whenever sizable crowds of Chassidim came to Lubavitch. It later hosted major family celebrations including the 5652 Hornstein wedding, the 5653 bar mitzvah, and the 5657 wedding of the Frierdiker Rebbe.

title_en: Wedding of Rabbi Zalman Aharon Schneersohn (Raza) in Lubavitch
summary_en: The wedding of the Maharash's son Rabbi Zalman Aharon, the Raza, was celebrated at the start of 5634 in the small hall of the Lubavitch courtyard.
story_body: Because the wedding fell in winter and the large hall was unheated, the celebration meal was held in the heated small hall instead. The Maharash had reserved the right to use the small hall for any purpose at his discretion. This was the first major family celebration in the rebuilt Lubavitch courtyard.

title_en: Birth of Rebbe Rashab in Lubavitch
summary_en: Rabbi Shalom Dovber Schneersohn, the future fifth Chabad Rebbe known as the Rashab, was born on 20 Marcheshvan 5621 in Lubavitch.
story_body: The Rashab was born to the Maharash and Rebbetzin Rivkah. He would later found the Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva in Lubavitch in 5657 and lead the movement through the upheavals of World War One. His birth in the courtyard further confirmed Lubavitch as the dynastic center.

title_en: Passing of Rebbe Maharash in Lubavitch
summary_en: Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn, the Maharash, passed away in Lubavitch on 13 Tishrei 5643.
story_body: He was buried in the ohel that had been constructed for his father the Tzemach Tzedek in the Lubavitch cemetery. The Maharash was the only Chabad Rebbe to live his entire life in the town. His passing brought his son the Rashab to the leadership of Chabad.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab accepts Chabad leadership
summary_en: Some time after the passing of his father in 5643, Rabbi Shalom Dovber Schneersohn assumed the leadership of Chabad.
story_body: The Rashab's leadership inaugurated the final phase of Lubavitch as Chabad's world center. His most lasting institutional contribution was the founding of Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva in Lubavitch in 5657. He would lead the movement through the trauma of forced exile from Lubavitch in World War One.

title_en: Wedding of Chaya Mushka Hornstein in Lubavitch
summary_en: The Maharash's daughter Chaya Mushka Hornstein was married in the large hall of the Lubavitch courtyard in the summer of 5652.
story_body: This was among the major family celebrations held in the great hall the Maharash had erected in 5632. The large hall, with its high ceiling and wide windows, served as the venue for Chabad's most significant communal occasions when large crowds gathered in Lubavitch. The 5652 wedding was followed a year later by the bar mitzvah of the Frierdiker Rebbe in the same hall.

title_en: Bar Mitzvah of the Frierdiker Rebbe in Lubavitch
summary_en: The bar mitzvah celebration of the future Frierdiker Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was held in the great hall of the Lubavitch courtyard in the summer of 5653.
story_body: The celebration brought a large gathering of Chassidim to Lubavitch and used the same large hall that had hosted the 5652 Hornstein wedding. Four years later in 5657 the same hall would host the future Frierdiker Rebbe's wedding. This event marked the coming of age of Chabad's next generation of leadership.

title_en: Wedding of the Frierdiker Rebbe in Lubavitch
summary_en: The wedding of the future Frierdiker Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was celebrated in the great hall of the Lubavitch courtyard in the summer of 5657.
story_body: This wedding coincided with the founding of Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva in the same summer. The great hall again served as the venue for one of the dynasty's central family events. Together, the founding of the yeshiva and the marriage of the heir-apparent made the summer of 5657 a pivotal moment in Lubavitch history.

title_en: Tomchei Tmimim classes move to renovated great hall
summary_en: By 5661 the growing enrollment of Tomchei Tmimim required relocating classes into the great hall, which was being renovated for year-round yeshiva use.
story_body: The great hall, originally built only for summer use, lacked heating and had simple wooden walls that had deteriorated. Renovation began with installation of stoves, new foundations and flooring, and new windows, continuing until 5663. Eighteen large tables seating up to ten students each filled the hall, with a central bimah holding two tables for the mashgichim.

title_en: Kitchen and dining hall built for Tomchei Tmimim students
summary_en: In 5662 a kitchen and dining facility was built in the Lubavitch courtyard to serve the students of Tomchei Tmimim.
story_body: The growing yeshiva required dedicated food-service infrastructure within the courtyard. The kitchen and dining hall sufficed for several years until further expansion forced construction of a larger building. The expanded yeshiva also accommodated cheder students who had come to study in Lubavitch.

title_en: Renovations of great hall completed for Tomchei Tmimim
summary_en: The multi-year renovation of the great hall in the Lubavitch courtyard for year-round yeshiva use was completed in 5663.
story_body: Stoves had been installed, foundations and flooring renewed, and new windows fitted to make the building usable in winter. The renovated hall could now host the yeshiva's growing enrollment around its eighteen large study tables. The project transformed what had been a summer-only celebration space into the daily home of Chabad's flagship yeshiva.

title_en: Major donation received for Tomchei Tmimim expansion
summary_en: An important donation arrived in 5666 to fund expansion of the Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva facilities in Lubavitch.
story_body: The donation enabled construction over subsequent years of two brick buildings in the eastern portion of the courtyard. These housed a study hall for the lower shiurim, a special dining hall for Passover, and a tea station for the yeshiva students. The expansion accommodated both the growing enrollment of Tomchei Tmimim and the cheder students who studied alongside them.

title_en: Passing of Rebbetzin Rivkah in Lubavitch
summary_en: Rebbetzin Rivkah, wife of the Maharash, passed away in 5674 and was buried beside her husband in the Lubavitch ohel.
story_body: Her resting place was placed adjacent to the Maharash's grave alongside the ohel originally built for the Tzemach Tzedek. The Lubavitch cemetery also contained a separate ohel for the Chabad rebbetzins, including the wives of the Alter Rebbe, the Mittler Rebbe, and the Tzemach Tzedek. Her passing came on the eve of the upheavals that would soon end Lubavitch's role as Chabad's center.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab flees Lubavitch as German army advances
summary_en: In the autumn of 5676 the Rashab and his family were forced to flee Lubavitch as the German army approached during World War One, eventually settling in Rostov-on-Don.
story_body: After several weeks of travel they reached Rostov-on-Don, deep in the Russian interior far from the front. The Frierdiker Rebbe later recorded their hope to return to Lubavitch the following summer once the war ended. They never returned, and the departure proved to be the effective end of Lubavitch's century as Chabad's center.

title_en: Manuscripts taken to Rostov; library left in Moscow warehouse
summary_en: When the Rashab fled to Rostov in 5676 he took the manuscripts of the Chabad Rebbes with him but left the large book collection in 35 crates in the Moscow warehouses of Zalkind Persitz.
story_body: Thousands of books and hundreds of manuscript volumes were stored in Persitz's Moscow warehouses pending the family's intended return. The books were later seized and transferred to the Moscow public library, where they remain in exile to this day. The fate of these volumes would become a major decades-long campaign of the Chabad movement.

title_en: Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva relocates from Lubavitch to Kremenchug
summary_en: After two and a half years operating without the Rebbe in residence, Tomchei Tmimim relocated from Lubavitch to Kremenchug in late summer 5678.
story_body: The final students dug deeply into the cellar of the Rebbe's residence to hide possessions before departing. They gathered for a bitter farbrengen marking their separation from Lubavitch, still hoping the move was temporary. With the Soviet anti-religious campaign that followed, the yeshiva eventually retreated underground across dozens of Russian towns.

title_en: Passing of Rebbe Rashab in Rostov
summary_en: Rabbi Shalom Dovber Schneersohn, the Rashab, passed away on 2 Nisan 5680 in Rostov-on-Don and is buried there.
story_body: He had been forced from Lubavitch four and a half years earlier by the German advance in World War One. His passing in Rostov marked the definitive end of the Lubavitch era of Chabad. His son the Frierdiker Rebbe assumed the leadership under the increasingly hostile conditions of early Soviet Russia.

title_en: Entire Lubavitch courtyard burns down
summary_en: At the start of Nisan 5681 fire destroyed the entire Lubavitch courtyard of the Rebbes, ending the town's role as Chabad's center.
story_body: The fire came one year after the passing of the Rashab in Rostov and three years after the yeshiva's departure for Kremenchug. With the courtyard gone and the Rebbe's family long departed, the town ceased to function as the movement's headquarters. The buildings of the great hall, the small hall, the residences, and the yeshiva facilities all perished.

title_en: Lubavitcher Rebbe sends delegation to Russia for redemption of books
summary_en: In 5751 the Lubavitcher Rebbe sent a four-member delegation to Russia regarding the redemption of the Chabad books and manuscripts seized in 5676.
story_body: The Rebbe appointed the four delegates to lead the newly formed Agudas Chabad in Russia and later in the Commonwealth of Independent States. The delegation met with the Russian government to discuss the books still held in the Moscow public library. The government subsequently sent a recommendation to the leadership of the Smolensk region, which includes Lubavitch, to assist with related plans including the future museum project.

title_en: Hendel Deutsch publishes Russian documentary booklet on Lubavitch
summary_en: In 5754 Hendel Deutsch published a small Russian-language booklet titled Lubavitch - Center of Chabad Chassidus: A Documentary Description.
story_body: Deutsch collected documents and general information about the town across its centuries of history. The booklet included material such as a 5544 list of approximately fifty Jewish families living in Lubavitch. It served as a key reference work for the contemporary effort to recover and document the town's Chabad history.

title_en: Eliyahu Segal purchases first portion of Lubavitch courtyard
summary_en: In 5756 the philanthropist Eliyahu Segal purchased the first portion of the original Lubavitch courtyard for the museum project being led by Rabbi Nosson Gourary.
story_body: The purchase was the first step in reassembling the historic courtyard for use as a Chabad museum. Rabbi Nosson Gourary, the Rebbe's emissary to Buffalo, had been negotiating with the Russian government on the project since the opening of the Iron Curtain. The Rebbe had repeatedly urged him to bring the plan to fruition.

title_en: Second portion of Lubavitch courtyard acquired
summary_en: In 5758 Eliyahu Segal purchased an additional portion of the original Lubavitch courtyard for the museum project.
story_body: The acquisition continued the multi-year effort to reassemble the courtyard plot under the museum's ownership. The work was coordinated by Agudas Chasidei Chabad of the CIS together with Rabbi Nosson Gourary. Each phase brought the project closer to enabling construction of the museum at the original site.

title_en: Final portion of Lubavitch courtyard acquired
summary_en: In 5760 the third and final portion of the original Lubavitch courtyard was purchased by Eliyahu Segal, completing the site assembly for the museum.
story_body: With the full courtyard now under museum ownership, construction of the museum building could proceed at the center of the historic site. The acquisitions had taken four years across three transactions. The completed assembly enabled immediate construction work to begin.

title_en: Lubavitch Museum opens in original Chabad courtyard
summary_en: The Lubavitch Museum, operated by Agudas Chasidei Chabad of the CIS, opened to the public on 3 Nisan 5761 at the historic courtyard.
story_body: The opening commemorated 80 years since the 5681 fire that destroyed the courtyard and 81 years since the passing of the Rashab in Rostov. The museum building had been constructed at the center of the courtyard reassembled through purchases in 5756, 5758, and 5760. It is administered by Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Aharonov, Rabbi Shalom Dovber Levin, and Rabbi Nosson Gourary.

title_en: Birth of Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn in Lubavitch
summary_en: The future sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe, Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, was born on 12 Tammuz in the town of Lubavitch.
story_body: Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak (the Rayatz) was born on 12 Tammuz 5640 in Lubavitch, the town that gave Chabad its name. He was the only son of the Rebbe Rashab and would later succeed him as the sixth Rebbe of Chabad-Lubavitch. The date of his birth would later become doubly significant as the same date on which he was released from Soviet imprisonment in 1927.

title_en: Bar Mitzvah of the future Rayatz in Lubavitch
summary_en: In the summer of 5653 the Bar Mitzvah of the future Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak was held in the great hall of the Rebbes' courtyard.
story_body: In the summer of 5653 (1893), the Bar Mitzvah of the future Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak was celebrated in the large hall of the courtyard of the Rebbes in Lubavitch, the same hall used for the large communal gatherings of Chabad. The event is documented in Sefer HaMaamarim 5711.

title_en: Wedding of the future Rayatz in Lubavitch
summary_en: At the end of 5657, the wedding of the future Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak was held in the great hall of the Lubavitch courtyard.
story_body: At the end of 5657 (1897), the wedding of the future Rayatz was celebrated in the great hall of the courtyard of the Rebbes in Lubavitch. After the wedding an additional room was built onto his father's house for the couple, and he later moved into the adjacent house in the southwestern corner of the courtyard.

title_en: Tomchei Temimim opens; Yosef Yitzchak appointed director
summary_en: Following his wedding, the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva opened in Lubavitch and the future Rayatz was appointed as its director.
story_body: Shortly after his wedding, the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva was opened in Lubavitch under his father the Rebbe Rashab, and the future Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak was appointed to serve as its director. The yeshiva offices occupied the front of his new residence facing the courtyard. This appointment launched his lifelong leadership of Chabad's educational network.

title_en: Last Tomchei Temimim students leave; municipality seizes the Lubavitch courtyard
summary_en: At the end of 5678 the last yeshiva students departed Lubavitch, and the municipality took over the courtyard of the Rebbes for civic uses.
story_body: At the end of 5678 (1918), the last students of the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva left Lubavitch. The local municipality then seized the courtyard of the Rebbes: the great hall became the municipal theater, the Rashab's house became the courthouse, the Rebbe Maharash's rooms housed the municipal leadership committee, the Rayatz's rooms became the municipal officials' building, and the stone house was turned into the city school.

title_en: Fire destroys the houses of the Lubavitch courtyard
summary_en: At the beginning of Nissan 5681, fire consumed all the houses in the courtyard of the Rebbes in Lubavitch within half an hour.
story_body: At the beginning of Nissan 5681 (1921), one year after the passing of the Rebbe Rashab, a fire from heaven destroyed all the houses in the courtyard of the Rebbes in Lubavitch within half an hour. Whatever was stored in the cellars was looted and broken by non-Jews. The physical heart of Chabad's home town was effectively erased.

title_en: Rayatz sends funds to repair the Lubavitch mikvah
summary_en: At the start of 5682 the Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak sent money to the remaining Jews of Lubavitch to rebuild the destroyed mikvah.
story_body: After the fire destroyed the courtyard and the mikvah, some members of Anash still living in Lubavitch relocated the synagogue into the stone house. At the start of 5682 (1921), the Rayatz sent them a sum of money to repair the mikvah, as documented in Igrot Kodesh vol. 14.

title_en: Rayatz's only return visit to Lubavitch as Rebbe
summary_en: On Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5682, the Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak traveled to Lubavitch to pray at the Ohel of his predecessors.
story_body: On Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5682 (1922), the Rayatz traveled to Lubavitch to prostrate himself at the Ohel of his predecessors. While there he delivered a Chassidic discourse in the synagogue that had been relocated to the stone house. This was the only time he visited Lubavitch after assuming the leadership of Chabad.

title_en: Rayatz works to repair the Lubavitch Ohel
summary_en: In 5684 the Rayatz worked to arrange repairs to the destroyed Ohel of the Rebbes in Lubavitch.
story_body: When the courtyard was destroyed, the Ohel covering the Rebbes' graves was also destroyed, the attached study hall was ruined, and non-Jews stole the stones of the surrounding fence. In 5684 (1924), the Rayatz worked to arrange repairs to the Ohel, as recorded in Igrot Kodesh vol. 1. The overall situation, however, continued to deteriorate.

title_en: Rayatz writes to his uncle about Ohel repairs
summary_en: At the start of 5689 the Rayatz wrote to his uncle Rabbi Moshe Leib Ginzburg about ongoing efforts to repair the Lubavitch Ohel.
story_body: At the beginning of 5689 (1928), the Rayatz wrote a letter to his uncle Rabbi Moshe Leib Ginzburg discussing efforts to make repairs at the Ohel in Lubavitch. The correspondence is preserved in Igrot Kodesh vol. 15. Soviet conditions made such practical work extremely difficult.

title_en: Rayatz inquires from 770 about Lubavitch and the Ohel
summary_en: In 5709, while living at 770 in New York, the Rayatz inquired into the state of Lubavitch and the feasibility of repairing the Ohel.
story_body: In 5709 (1949), in his final years from his residence at 770 Eastern Parkway in New York, the Rayatz sought information on the condition of the town of Lubavitch and the Ohel of his predecessors and explored whether any repair work could be undertaken. The political conditions of the time made it impossible for Jews to travel to Lubavitch for such purposes.

title_en: Germans capture the town of Lubavitch
summary_en: In the summer of 5701 the German army captured the town of Lubavitch.
story_body: In the summer of 5701 (1941), as part of the German invasion of the Soviet Union, German forces conquered the town of Lubavitch. The occupation set the stage for the destruction of the town's remaining Jewish community a few months later.

title_en: Massacre of the 483 Jews of Lubavitch
summary_en: On November 4, 1941 (Cheshvan 5702), the Germans murdered all 483 Jews of Lubavitch.
story_body: On November 4, 1941, corresponding to Cheshvan 5702, German forces murdered all 483 Jews remaining in the town of Lubavitch, Hashem yikom damam. The massacre effectively ended Jewish presence in the town that had given Chabad its name. Russian-language documents preserve the historical record.

title_en: First post-war visit of Anash to Lubavitch; gravestones restored
summary_en: In 5726, Rabbi Dovid Gurevitz traveled from Samarkand to Lubavitch and re-erected the destroyed gravestones of the Tzemach Tzedek and Rebbe Maharash.
story_body: In 5726 (1966), for the first time since the war, members of Anash found an opportunity to come to Lubavitch. Rabbi Dovid Gurevitz traveled from distant Samarkand all the way to Lubavitch, where he re-erected the destroyed gravestones of the Tzemach Tzedek and the Rebbe Maharash. This visit marked the beginning of efforts to restore the holy site.

title_en: Ohel of the Rebbes in Lubavitch rebuilt
summary_en: In 5749, Rabbis Dovid Nachshon and Avi Taub rebuilt the Ohel of the Rebbes in Lubavitch.
story_body: In 5749 (1989), Rabbi Dovid Nachshon and Rabbi Avi Taub rebuilt the Ohel of the Rebbes in Lubavitch over the graves of the Tzemach Tzedek and Maharash. From that point onward, Anash began traveling regularly to Lubavitch to visit the courtyard of the Rebbes and pray at the Ohel. The restoration coincided with the opening of the Soviet Union.

title_en: Beit Chabad established in Lubavitch
summary_en: In 5749, a courtyard and house were purchased in Lubavitch and turned into a Beit Chabad to host visitors to the Ohel.
story_body: In 5749 (1989), a courtyard with a house was acquired in Lubavitch and converted into a Beit Chabad. The house serves as a gathering point for travelers visiting the Ohel: there they write their pidyon notes before walking to the holy gravesite.

title_en: Rebbe dispatches Russia delegation for redemption of seforim
summary_en: In 5751 the Rebbe sent a special delegation to Russia regarding the redemption of the Schneersohn library and appointed its members to lead Agudat Chabad in Russia.
story_body: In 5751 (1991), the Rebbe sent a special delegation to Russia to address the redemption of the Schneersohn family seforim, and appointed its four members as the leadership of Agudat Chabad in Russia (and later in the CIS). The delegation met with the Russian government, which then sent a recommendation to the Smolensk regional authorities to assist with Chabad's plans for the town of Lubavitch. Following the meeting, the chairman of the Council of Ministers wrote to Agudat Chabad proposing that a Chabad representative work directly with the Smolensk leadership on the project.

title_en: Eli Segal purchases first portion of the Lubavitch courtyard
summary_en: In 5756 the philanthropist Eli Segal bought the first portion of the courtyard of the Rebbes in Lubavitch for the planned museum.
story_body: In 5756 (1996), the philanthropist Mr. Eli Segal joined the long-running effort to build a museum on the site of the courtyard of the Rebbes in Lubavitch, purchasing the first portion of the courtyard. The initiative built on years of negotiation by Rabbi Natan Gurary with the Russian government following the opening of the Iron Curtain, in response to repeated encouragement from the Rebbe.

title_en: Eli Segal purchases second portion of the Lubavitch courtyard
summary_en: In 5758 Eli Segal acquired an additional portion of the courtyard of the Rebbes in Lubavitch for the museum project.
story_body: In 5758 (1998), Mr. Eli Segal acquired a further portion of the courtyard of the Rebbes in Lubavitch. This was the second of three stages by which he was assembling the historic site for the construction of a Chabad museum at its center.

title_en: Final portion of the Lubavitch courtyard purchased; museum built
summary_en: In 5760 Eli Segal purchased the third and final portion of the courtyard of the Rebbes, completing the site for the Chabad museum which was then built and opened.
story_body: In 5760 (2000), Mr. Eli Segal purchased the third and final portion of the courtyard of the Rebbes in Lubavitch. Construction of the museum building began immediately at the center of the courtyard, and by the beginning of Nissan the museum was completed and opened to the public.

title_en: Fire at Alter Rebbe's home destroys Shulchan Aruch manuscript
summary_en: A fire at the Alter Rebbe's home in Liadi consumed his autograph manuscript of the Shulchan Aruch he had authored.
story_body: In 5570 (1810), a fire broke out at the home of Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, the founder of Chabad. The blaze destroyed the autograph manuscript of his Shulchan Aruch HaRav, the legal code he had composed. It was the first of two devastating fires that struck his household in his final years.

title_en: Alter Rebbe flees Liadi during Napoleon's invasion of Russia
summary_en: At the end of 5572 the Alter Rebbe fled his home in Liadi as Napoleon's forces advanced through Russia.
story_body: During the French invasion of Russia in 1812, Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi abandoned his home and possessions and joined the retreating Russian populace. A second fire struck the household during these upheavals. The Alter Rebbe was carried from place to place along the way, never to return home.

title_en: Passing of the Alter Rebbe, Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, founder of Chabad, passed away on 24 Tevet 5573 while in flight from Napoleon's army.
story_body: On Motzaei Shabbat, 24 Tevet 5573, after months of displacement following his flight from Liadi, the Alter Rebbe passed away at the age of 66. He was buried in the town of Haditch. Communities of his followers everywhere observed deep mourning.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe settles in the town of Lubavitch
summary_en: Rabbi Dovber, the Mitteler Rebbe, settled in the town of Lubavitch in late 5573 and built a home, large synagogue, and library there.
story_body: Following the passing of his father in early 5573, the Mitteler Rebbe took up the leadership of Chabad. At the end of that same year (1813) he settled in the small town of Lubavitch. There he constructed a home, a large beit knesset, and a library that became the new center of the movement.

title_en: Tsarist search at Mitteler Rebbe's home documents 611-volume library
summary_en: A house search by Russian authorities at the Mitteler Rebbe's home in Lubavitch in 5586 recorded a library of 611 volumes in four cabinets.
story_body: In 5586 (1826) Tsarist authorities conducted a search of the Mitteler Rebbe's home in Lubavitch. Their detailed inventory recorded a personal library of 611 books arranged in four cabinets. This document provides the earliest concrete glimpse of the size of the Chabad library in its second generation.

title_en: Passing of Rabbi Yehuda Leib of Yanovich, brother of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: Rabbi Yehuda Leib of Yanovich, the Alter Rebbe's brother and author of Shearit Yehuda, passed away in winter 5586.
story_body: Rabbi Yehuda Leib, brother of the Alter Rebbe and rabbi of Yanovich, passed away in the winter of 5586 (1826). He was the author of Shearit Yehuda and had served as a senior halachic authority in Chabad. His passing is noted in the introductions to the Tzemach Tzedek's responsa.

title_en: Publication of Shivchei HaRav, early biography of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: Shivchei HaRav, an early printed biography of the Alter Rebbe, was published in Lvov in 5624.
story_body: In 5624 (1864) the small biographical work Shivchei HaRav appeared in Lvov. It collected and edited oral traditions about the life of the Alter Rebbe that Chasidim had long preserved in private manuscripts. It became one of the foundational printed sources for the Alter Rebbe's biography.

title_en: Toldot Amudei HaChabad published in Königsberg
summary_en: Michael Levi Radkinson's Toldot Amudei HaChabad, a biographical work on the Chabad Rebbes, was published in Königsberg in 5636.
story_body: In 5636 (1876), the writer Michael Levi Radkinson published Toldot Amudei HaChabad in Königsberg. The book gathered and reworked the existing biographical traditions of the Chabad Rebbes for a wider reading public. It served as a precursor to later, more rigorous works such as Beit Rebbi.

title_en: Rebbe Maharash travels to Switzerland for medical treatment
summary_en: Rabbi Shmuel of Lubavitch, the Rebbe Maharash, traveled to Switzerland in autumn 5640 on doctors' orders for his health.
story_body: On the instruction of his physicians, the Maharash departed Lubavitch in Tishrei 5640 (October 1879) and traveled westward through Europe. He stayed in Vevey until 19 Cheshvan, then moved to Montreux on Lake Geneva. In a letter to the chasid Shmuel Dovber of Borisov dated 27 Cheshvan, he reported that the climate was helping him and that he planned to continue to Biarritz before returning home via Paris.

title_en: Publication of Beit Rebbi, comprehensive Chabad biographical history
summary_en: Rabbi Chaim Meir Hillman's Beit Rebbi, the major early biographical work on the Chabad dynasty, was published in Berditchev in 5662.
story_body: In 5662 (1902) Rabbi Chaim Meir Hillman published Beit Rebbi in Berditchev. The work greatly expanded earlier accounts of the lives of the Chabad Rebbes and drew on many oral and written sources. It became the standard reference for Chabad biographical history for generations.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrested, exiled, and forced to leave Soviet Russia
summary_en: In 5687 Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested by Soviet authorities, sentenced to exile, released, and forced to leave Russia.
story_body: In 5687 (1927) the sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, was arrested by the Soviet GPU for his work to preserve Jewish life under communism. After being sentenced, his sentence was commuted and he was eventually freed and ordered out of the country. He refused to leave without his library, and only after firm insistence was he permitted to take his collection with him as he relocated the center of Chabad to Riga.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz escapes Nazi-occupied Warsaw
summary_en: In late winter 5700 the Rebbe Rayatz was rescued from Nazi-occupied Warsaw along with members of his household and secretaries.
story_body: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn had been in Warsaw when Nazi Germany invaded Poland at the start of 5700. After several months under occupation, a coordinated rescue effort succeeded in extracting him along with family members and secretaries in late winter 5700 (early 1940). They first traveled to Riga and from there continued onward to New York.

title_en: The Rebbe arrives in New York
summary_en: Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, the future seventh Rebbe, arrived in New York in summer 5701.
story_body: After fleeing wartime Europe, the future seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe arrived in New York in the summer of 5701 (1941). His father-in-law, the Rebbe Rayatz, immediately appointed him to head Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch, the educational arm of the movement. He soon began assembling a working library to support its activities.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz library collection arrives in New York
summary_en: After eighteen months of clandestine transit through occupied Europe, the Rebbe Rayatz's library reached New York in late 5701.
story_body: When the Rebbe Rayatz was rescued from Warsaw in early 1940 his book collection remained behind in Nazi-occupied Poland. For a year and a half emissaries worked to move the collection through occupied Europe in stages. In late 5701 (1941) it finally arrived in New York and was housed on the ground floor of the newly acquired Chabad center at 770 Eastern Parkway.

title_en: Passing of the Rebbe Rayatz on Yud Shevat
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, the sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe, passed away on 10 Shevat 5710.
story_body: On 10 Shevat 5710 (28 January 1950), the Rebbe Rayatz passed away in Brooklyn. The leadership of Chabad subsequently passed to his son-in-law, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, who formally accepted the nesius a year later. Yud Shevat became one of the central dates on the Chabad calendar.

title_en: Library building adjacent to 770 purchased
summary_en: In 5727 the building adjacent to 770 Eastern Parkway was purchased to house the Rebbe's growing library collection.
story_body: By 5727 (1967) the Rebbe's working library, built up since 1941 through emissaries around the world, had outgrown its space. The building next to 770 Eastern Parkway was purchased to house it. From then until 1985 two parallel libraries existed at the Chabad headquarters — the Rayatz's collection in 770 and the Rebbe's collection next door.

title_en: Shalom Dovber Levine appointed director of the Chabad Library
summary_en: Rabbi Shalom Dovber Levine was appointed to direct the Chabad Library in 5737.
story_body: In 5737 (1977) Rabbi Shalom Dovber Levine was appointed director of the library of Agudas Chasidei Chabad at 770. From that year onward he began publishing serialized articles drawn from the library's collections — first in Yagdil Torah and later in Kfar Chabad, Heoros U'Biurim, Heichal HaBesht and other journals. These articles later formed the basis of his book MiBeit HaGenazim.

title_en: Chabad manuscript collection returned from Warsaw to New York
summary_en: In early 5738 the manuscript collection of the Chabad Rebbes, lost in occupied Warsaw since 1939, was returned to the central Chabad library in New York.
story_body: When the Nazis occupied Warsaw at the start of 5700, the precious manuscript collection of the Chabad Rebbes was lost for thirty-eight years. It was eventually located in a library in Warsaw. At the beginning of 5738 (late 1977) the collection was returned to the central Chabad library at 770 in Brooklyn, rejoining the corpus from which scholars continue to edit and publish the Chasidic teachings of the Rebbes.

title_en: Rebbe begins efforts to recover Chabad library from Moscow
summary_en: From 5741 onward the Rebbe directed emissaries to work for the return of the Chabad library held in Moscow since World War I.
story_body: When the Rebbe Rashab fled Lubavitch in World War I, he placed the family library in storage in Moscow with the intention of retrieving it after the war. After the Soviet takeover, the books were nationalized and moved into the Russian State Library, where they remain. Beginning in 5741 (1980), the seventh Rebbe sent dedicated emissaries to Russia and pursued every avenue to secure their return, an effort that continues today.

title_en: Didan Notzach library trial begins in U.S. federal court
summary_en: In 5745 a U.S. federal lawsuit was filed by a grandson of the Rebbe Rayatz claiming personal ownership of part of the Chabad library.
story_body: In 5745 (1985) a grandson of the Rebbe Rayatz initiated proceedings claiming that a portion of the central Chabad library belonged to him personally. The case became known among Chasidim as the 'sefarim trial.' It was litigated through 5747 and centered on whether the Rebbeim had owned the books personally or as trustees of the movement.

title_en: Didan Notzach — Chabad Library trial concludes in favor of Agudas Chassidei Chabad
summary_en: In 5747 the U.S. court ruled that the entire library belongs to Agudas Chassidei Chabad and not to any individual heir.
story_body: In 5747 (1987) the court issued its ruling: the Rebbeim had not held the library as personal property and the entire collection belonged to Agudas Chassidei Chabad. Following the verdict, the Rebbe launched a massive book-donation campaign and ordered the two parallel libraries — the Rayatz's and his own — to be merged into a single central library of Agudas Chassidei Chabad. The day of the verdict, 5 Tevet, entered the Chabad calendar as 'Didan Notzach.'

title_en: Rebbe orders expansion of central Chabad Library building
summary_en: In 5749 the Rebbe directed the renovation and expansion of the library building physically connected to 770.
story_body: Following the consolidation of the library after the 1987 verdict, the Rebbe in 5749 (1989) instructed that work begin on enlarging and renovating the building that housed the library and connected it to 770 Eastern Parkway. The work was intended to make the unified collection accessible to scholars and researchers.

title_en: Chabad Library exhibition hall opens to the public
summary_en: In 5754 the exhibition hall of the Chabad Library was opened to the general public.
story_body: In 5754 (1994) a dedicated exhibition hall within the Chabad Library was opened to the public. It displays rotating selections of rare books, manuscripts, photographs, objects, and artwork drawn from the library's collections, with a new thematic exhibit chosen roughly every year or two by the library's administration.

title_en: Letter from Rebbe Maharaitz of Ovruch to his brother Maharash
summary_en: Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak of Ovruch wrote to his brother Rebbe Maharash about the latter's health and gifts purchased for the betrothed children Maharashab and Sterna Sarah.
story_body: In the summer of 5630 (1870), Yosef Yitzchak of Ovruch sent a letter to his brother Maharash of Lubavitch inquiring about his health, his milk-drinking and gymnastics regimen, the status of the shadarim collecting funds for Eretz Yisrael and Maamad, and the progress of printing the Tzemach Tzedek responsa. He also asked Maharash to deliver, on his behalf, a gift he had bought in Petersburg to his son Maharashab (then nine years old), and to send a gift to his betrothed Sterna Sarah.

title_en: Attached letter to Avraham Zalman Ginzburg of Vitebsk for tea from Moscow
summary_en: Yosef Yitzchak of Ovruch asked the wealthy Avraham Zalman Ginzburg to order Gulubkov tea from Moscow for him, since he could not drink the Kiev tea.
story_body: On 27 Tammuz 5630 (26 July 1870), in Ovruch, the Rebbe of Ovruch wrote to the philanthropist R' Avraham Zalman Ginzburg of Vitebsk asking him to arrange that four pounds of Gulubkov tea be shipped from Moscow to Ovruch. He explained that although tea was available in nearby Kiev, he could not drink that tea. Ginzburg would later become a mechutan of Maharash when his son married Devorah Leah.

title_en: Engagement of Maharashab to Sterna Sarah finalized by the Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: The shidduch between the four-and-a-half-year-old Maharashab and Sterna Sarah, daughter of the Rebbe of Ovruch, was finalized by the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: In 5625 (1865), the Tzemach Tzedek finalized and signed the tenaim between his grandson Sholom DovBer (Maharashab), then aged four and a half, and Sterna Sarah, daughter of his son Yosef Yitzchak, Rebbe of Ovruch. The agreement stipulated that the wedding would take place ten years later in 5635 (1875).

title_en: Wedding of Moshe Aryeh Leib Ginzburg and Devorah Leah, daughter of Maharash
summary_en: Moshe Aryeh Leib Ginzburg, son of Avraham Zalman Ginzburg of Vitebsk, married Devorah Leah, daughter of Rebbe Maharash.
story_body: In the summer of 5632 (1872), R' Moshe Aryeh Leib Ginzburg, son of the philanthropist Avraham Zalman Ginzburg of Vitebsk, married Devorah Leah, daughter of the Rebbe Maharash of Lubavitch. The match sealed a family connection between the Schneersohn dynasty and a leading Vitebsk merchant family.

title_en: Maharash travels to Marienbad for health treatment
summary_en: Due to his fragile health, Maharash traveled to the healing springs of Marienbad on doctors' recommendation.
story_body: Already in 5628 (1868), Rebbe Maharash was very weak and traveled to Marienbad and other curative springs. Physicians instructed him to engage in physical exercise and manual work, regimens that continued for years afterward and were the subject of his brother's solicitous inquiries in correspondence.

title_en: First volume of Shu"t Tzemach Tzedek printed in Vilna
summary_en: The first volume of the Tzemach Tzedek's responsa was published in Vilna after years of editorial work.
story_body: After the Tzemach Tzedek's passing, his manuscripts were entrusted to two Chabad rabbis, R' Chaim Yaakov Widrevitz and R' Shimon ben Dovid, to prepare the responsa and novellae for publication. They worked on the material for several years, and the first volume was finally printed in Vilna in 5631 (1871).

title_en: Cantonist conscription law begins for Russian Jewry
summary_en: The Tsar's cantonist decree imposed conscription quotas on Jewish communities, sending young boys to the Russian army for 25 years.
story_body: From 5587 (1827) onwards, the cruel cantonist law forced Jewish communities to supply fixed quotas of Jewish children — sometimes as many as 30 per thousand Jews — who were dispatched to the army for 25 years and completely cut off from their parents and Jewish life. When communities could not meet the quotas, khappers were sent to seize Jewish children from the streets amidst the cries of children and parents.

title_en: Russian universal military conscription law published
summary_en: The Russian government published the Ustav (decree) on military obligation, requiring every young Jewish male to serve four years in the army.
story_body: In 5634 (1874), the Russian government issued a booklet titled 'Der Ustav (gezetz) vegen militer pflicht', instituting universal conscription. Every Jewish youth was required to serve four years in the Russian army, prompting widespread Jewish efforts to obtain exemptions and triggering periodic crackdowns when the authorities discovered such efforts.

title_en: Maharashab receives permanent exemption from Russian military service
summary_en: At age 18, Maharashab was registered for the 1877 conscription cohort, examined, and ruled permanently unfit for military service.
story_body: On 25 July 1879, during the summer of 5639, the Vitebsk Gubernia conscription office issued certificate no. 1645 to 'the Vitebsk merchant's son Sholom Berke Shmuilov Schneersohn', recording that he had presented himself for service under the 1877 draft. Following medical examination he was declared wholly unfit for military service and granted a permanent exemption. He was registered as a Vitebsk resident — likely to ease obtaining the exemption — reflecting his father's property holdings in that city.

title_en: Arrests of Rabbi Meshulam Zalman Neimark and Starodub Jews
summary_en: Rabbi Meshulam Zalman Neimark and many Jews of Starodub were arrested for helping evade conscription and imprisoned for two full years.
story_body: In 5641 (1881), the Russian authorities discovered the conscription-evasion efforts of Rabbi Meshulam Zalman Neimark along with many Starodub Jews. They were arrested and held in custody for two full years, an episode documented in the Igrot Kodesh of the Maharash.

title_en: Arrest of R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum in Pleshchenitsy
summary_en: Chassid R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum was arrested in Pleshchenitsy for involvement in evading conscription and imprisoned for three years.
story_body: In 5648 (1888), the chassid R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum was arrested in Pleshchenitsy for helping Jews evade Russian military conscription. He remained in custody for three years, his ordeal recorded in 'Toldot Avraham Chaim'.

title_en: Russian internal passport issued to Maharashab
summary_en: The Orsha district police issued Maharashab an internal Russian passport recording his status as a hereditary honorary citizen and second-guild merchant.
story_body: On 2 January 1903 (16 Tevet 5663), the Orsha district police of Mogilev Gubernia issued Sholom Berke ben Shmuel Schneersohn an internal Russian passport. The document recorded him as a hereditary honorary citizen and second-guild merchant of Orsha, aged 48, residing permanently in the town of Lubavitch. The passport's validity was restricted to the Pale of Settlement and would document his subsequent travels through 1917.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Vitebsk
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Vitebsk on 4 Shevat 5663.
story_body: Two and a half weeks after his passport was issued, on 19 January 1903 (4 Shevat 5663), Maharashab's internal Russian passport was stamped in Vitebsk, his first recorded trip on this document.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Petersburg
summary_en: Maharashab traveled to Petersburg, his passport recording the stamp dated 8 Kislev 5665.
story_body: On 3 November 1904 (8 Kislev 5665), Maharashab's passport was stamped in Petersburg. Petersburg lay outside the Pale of Settlement, and his repeated visits there reflect his merchant status that allowed him such travel.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Moscow
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Moscow on 2 Adar 5666.
story_body: On 14 February 1906 (2 Adar 5666), Maharashab's internal Russian passport was stamped in Moscow, documenting one of his several trips to the imperial cities outside the Pale of Settlement.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Moscow
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Moscow on 11 Iyar 5668.
story_body: On 29 April 1908 (11 Iyar 5668), Maharashab traveled again to Moscow, where his internal Russian passport received an entry stamp.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Vilna
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Vilna on 12 Iyar 5669.
story_body: On 20 April 1909 (12 Iyar 5669), Maharashab visited Vilna, the great Lithuanian center of Jewish learning, with his passport stamped there.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Petersburg
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Petersburg on 28 Adar I 5670.
story_body: On 24 February 1910 (28 Adar I 5670), Maharashab arrived in Petersburg, the first of three trips he would make to the capital that year.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Petersburg
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Petersburg on 16 Iyar 5670.
story_body: On 12 May 1910 (16 Iyar 5670), Maharashab returned to Petersburg, with his internal passport receiving another official stamp.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Petersburg
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Petersburg on 16 Cheshvan 5671.
story_body: On 5 November 1910 (16 Cheshvan 5671), Maharashab travelled to Petersburg for the third time that calendar year, with his passport again stamped at the capital.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Moscow
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Moscow on 20 Elul 5671.
story_body: On 31 August 1911 (20 Elul 5671), shortly before Rosh Hashanah, Maharashab traveled to Moscow, the visit documented by a passport stamp.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Petersburg
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Petersburg in late 5673.
story_body: On 22 November 1912, Maharashab's internal passport was stamped in Petersburg during one of his trips to the Russian capital.

title_en: Maharashab and family leave Lubavitch for Rostov
summary_en: On Sunday 16 Cheshvan 5676, Maharashab departed Lubavitch with his entire household amid the upheavals of World War I.
story_body: On Sunday, 16 Cheshvan 5676 (October 1915), Maharashab left Lubavitch together with his entire family. Earlier accounts based on Chanoch L'Naar and the Rebbe Rayatz's letters had suggested they reached Rostov around mid-Kislev, but the dated passport stamps reveal a much shorter journey of less than two weeks.

title_en: Maharashab arrives in Rostov-on-Don
summary_en: Maharashab and his family arrived in Rostov-on-Don on Friday 28 Cheshvan 5676, establishing the new Chabad headquarters there.
story_body: On Friday 28 Cheshvan 5676 (23 October 1915), Maharashab's passport was stamped in Rostov-on-Don, documenting the precise date the Rebbe and his household reached their new home in exile. The discovery of this passport stamp corrected earlier estimates and confirmed the family's testimony that the journey from Lubavitch to Rostov took less than two weeks.

title_en: Maharashab travels from Rostov to Petersburg
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Petersburg on 18 Adar II 5676.
story_body: On 10 March 1916 (18 Adar II 5676), several months after settling in Rostov, Maharashab traveled to Petersburg, with his internal passport stamped accordingly.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Petersburg
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Petersburg on 7 Iyar 5676.
story_body: On 27 April 1916 (7 Iyar 5676), Maharashab returned to Petersburg, marking his second wartime visit to the Russian capital from Rostov.

title_en: Maharashab visits the mineral baths at Slavyansk
summary_en: Maharashab traveled to the mineral baths at Slavyansk on 14 Sivan 5676.
story_body: On 2 June 1916 (14 Sivan 5676), Maharashab traveled to the Slavyansk mineral baths, continuing the family tradition of seeking healing waters that his father had begun at Marienbad decades earlier.

title_en: Maharashab returns to Rostov
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped on his return to Rostov on 14 Tishrei 5677.
story_body: On 28 September 1916 (14 Tishrei 5677), just before Sukkot, Maharashab's internal passport was stamped in Rostov, recording his return to the family's wartime base.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Petersburg
summary_en: Maharashab's passport was stamped in Petersburg on 29 Tevet 5677.
story_body: On 10 January 1917 (29 Tevet 5677), just weeks before the February Revolution, Maharashab visited Petersburg, his passport receiving another stamp at the capital.

title_en: Maharashab travels to Moscow
summary_en: Maharashab's final recorded passport stamp was issued in Moscow on 26 Menachem Av 5677.
story_body: On 1 August 1917 (26 Menachem Av 5677), in the volatile months between the February and October Revolutions, Maharashab's internal Russian passport received its final recorded stamp, in Moscow. This visit marked the last documented journey in this passport during the closing months of imperial and revolutionary Russia.

title_en: Maharaitz's diary: outbreak of World War I observed at Zaalshe
summary_en: Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak began a diary at the Zaalshe summer retreat covering the outbreak of the First World War.
story_body: Beginning 13 Menachem Av 5674 (August 1914), while staying with his father at the Zaalshe summer retreat, Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak recorded daily entries about the outbreak of World War I. Maharashab followed the news closely through newspapers and visitors, expressed wonder at Germany's audacity to fight several nations at once, and refused to share his own opinions on the conflict.

title_en: Maharashab and Maharaitz travel from Zaalshe to Lubavitch
summary_en: On 24 Menachem Av 5674, Maharaitz traveled to Lubavitch on Tomchei Temimim business and Maharashab joined him for the trip.
story_body: On 24 Menachem Av 5674, Maharaitz set out from Zaalshe for Lubavitch to attend to yeshiva matters; Maharashab unexpectedly decided to accompany him. They arrived at 9:30 at night. Early the next morning Maharashab visited the great hall where the temimim slept and was deeply moved by their condition. He prayed for hours, visited the ohel of his ancestors, and returned to Zaalshe that afternoon, exhausted from the visit.

title_en: Maharashab speaks on yeshiva reform and balancing Torah with prayer
summary_en: On 28 Menachem Av 5674, Maharashab discussed at length how the yeshiva must balance Talmudic study with avodah of prayer.
story_body: On 28 Menachem Av 5674, Maharashab walked with his son and discussed the Tomchei Temimim yeshiva, including the dormitory conditions and the need for students to study Nigleh. He explained that although many bochurim who came to him wished to devote themselves more to prayer, he typically refused: both Torah and prayer were essential, and the leader needed wisdom to keep the matter pure of intent.

title_en: Reports reach Lubavitch of German atrocities at Kalisz
summary_en: Maharashab expressed astonishment at reports of the German massacre of civilians in conquered Kalisz.
story_body: Newspapers and private reports brought news of German army conduct in conquered territory, especially in the city of Kalisz where civilians, women and children had been slaughtered. Maharashab marveled at this, suspecting initially that the reports might be war propaganda to inflame hatred, but added a teaching that kings face stricter judgment in the heavenly court because rulers stand higher in matters of providence.

title_en: Maharaitz visits Lubavitch on yeshiva business
summary_en: On 9 Elul 5674, Maharaitz travelled alone to Lubavitch for Tomchei Temimim matters and stayed until 11 Elul.
story_body: On Monday, 9 Elul 5674, Maharaitz set out for Lubavitch to attend to the affairs of Tomchei Temimim. He remained in the town until the afternoon of Wednesday 11 Elul, when he returned to the family's summer retreat at Zaalshe.

title_en: 39th wedding anniversary of Maharashab and Rebbetzin Sterna Sarah
summary_en: 12 Elul 5674 marked the 39th wedding anniversary of Maharashab and Rebbetzin Sterna Sarah.
story_body: On 12 Elul 5674, the 39th anniversary of the wedding of Maharashab and Sterna Sarah, Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak recorded a heartfelt blessing in his diary that they should be granted length of days and years in pleasantness, true health, and great nachas from their children.

title_en: 17th wedding anniversary of Maharaitz and Rebbetzin Nechama Dina
summary_en: 13 Elul 5674 marked Maharaitz's 17th wedding anniversary, with prayers for a son after three daughters.
story_body: On 13 Elul 5674, the 17th anniversary of his own wedding, Maharaitz recorded a prayer for length of days, nachas from his three daughters, and a son who would be a yarei shamayim, a chassid, a great scholar, and successful in all his affairs. At the time he had only daughters; the diary entry reflects his deep yearning for a male heir.

title_en: Maharashab teaches Chassidus on Parshat Eikev
summary_en: On Shabbat Parshat Eikev 5674, Maharashab delivered a maamar on 'V'haya Eikev Tishmaun' connected to the ongoing series.
story_body: On Shabbat Parshat Eikev 5674, Maharashab delivered a discourse beginning 'V'haya Eikev Tishmaun' as part of an ongoing series explaining the union of Or (light) and Keilim (vessels) — that the connection occurs specifically in the inner aspect of the vessels.

title_en: Maharashab teaches Chassidus on Parshat Re'eh
summary_en: On Friday before Parshat Re'eh 5674, Maharashab delivered a maamar continuing his series on the union of Or and Keilim.
story_body: On the Friday of Parshat Re'eh 5674, Maharashab delivered a discourse beginning 'Re'eh Anochi Notein Lifneichem... et HaBrachah Asher Tishmeun' as part of his ongoing series on the union of light and vessels, including the exchange of their natures whereby the speaker draws downward and the vessel becomes elevated and attached.

title_en: Council in Lubavitch over whether to leave the war zone
summary_en: Family and close chassidim convene in Lubavitch for a five-hour deliberation on whether and where the Rebbe Rashab should evacuate.
story_body: On 10 Marcheshvan 5676, R. Shmuel Michel Trainin and R. Shmuel Gourary arrived from Petrograd and met in the Rebbe Rashab's room with him, the Rebbetzin Shterna Sarah, and the Rayatz. They debated whether to remain in Lubavitch, move to a major city, or travel to the Caucasus health resorts. After about five hours it was resolved that the whole family would travel together, though the destination was still undecided.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab visits the graves of his ancestors before departing Lubavitch
summary_en: Before leaving Lubavitch, the Rebbe Rashab spends about four hours at the gravesites of his Chabad predecessors.
story_body: On Thursday, 13 Marcheshvan 5676, the Rebbe Rashab traveled to the resting places of the previous Chabad Rebbes in Lubavitch. He remained there for roughly four hours and returned with eyes red from weeping, traces of which were still visible the following day. That night he told the Rayatz of his hope that the German army would not reach Lubavitch.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab leaves Lubavitch for the last time
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab, his family, and 97 puds of luggage depart Lubavitch by train, never to return.
story_body: On Sunday, 16 Marcheshvan 5676, at 11:00 a.m., the Rebbe Rashab left Lubavitch as the German advance pressed eastward. Students of Tomchei Temimim, the staff, the town rav, townspeople, and even non-Jewish neighbors gathered in the courtyard to take leave of him. The stationmaster at Rudnya personally supervised the loading of the family's 97 puds of luggage onto the train.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab arrives in Orel
summary_en: After about 29 hours on a crowded train, the Rebbe Rashab reaches Orel and is hosted by R. David Fradkin.
story_body: On Monday evening, 17 Marcheshvan 5676, the Rebbe Rashab's party arrived in Orel at 7:00 p.m. after a tightly packed journey of roughly twenty-nine hours. Unable to find suitable lodgings, they stayed in three rooms at the home of R. David Fradkin while sharing a common dining room. Despite efforts by R. Yaakov the shochet, no permanent residence in Orel could be secured.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab leaves Orel for Rostov-on-Don
summary_en: After eight days in Orel, the Rebbe Rashab boards an express train direct to Rostov-on-Don.
story_body: On Tuesday, 25 Marcheshvan 5676, the Rebbe Rashab left Orel after eight days of cramped lodging. With R. David Fradkin's help, tickets were obtained on the express train running straight to Rostov-on-Don, and the family's luggage traveled with them. Fradkin himself accompanied them to see them off.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab moves into apartment on Pushkinskaya Street, Rostov
summary_en: After nine days at the Hotel Petrograd, the Rebbe Rashab settles into a six-room rented flat at 166 Pushkinskaya Street.
story_body: On Friday, 5 Kislev 5676, the Rebbe Rashab moved his household into a rented apartment at 166 Pushkinskaya Street in Rostov. The previous tenant had only vacated at 2:00 p.m., furniture had not yet arrived, and the electric wiring was unfinished, yet the Rebbe insisted on moving in before Shabbat. A telephone (number 19-89) was installed in the following days as the family adjusted to urban Rostov life.

title_en: First Yud-Tes Kislev farbrengen in Rostov
summary_en: Chassidim converge on Rostov for the Rebbe Rashab's first Yud-Tes Kislev in the city, where he delivers the maamar 'Padah Beshalom.'
story_body: On 19 Kislev 5676 (Friday), chassidim arrived in waves at the Rebbe Rashab's new home in Rostov, with delegations from Kharkov, Homel, Minsk, Kremenchug, and elsewhere. On Thursday evening the Rebbe delivered the maamar 'Padah Beshalom Nafshi' lasting over an hour, and on Friday evening, despite displeasure that so many had come during wartime, he said the maamar 'Karov Havayah Lechol Korav.' The Shabbat meal continued for two hours of Torah and inspiration, and a closing Sunday meal stretched until 7:00 p.m.
