During this period he could no longer hold full audience and answered questions submitted through his attendants on small notes, replying briefly in person or in writing. Manuscripts in his hand from these years are scarce and show a trembling script.

title_en: Sons of Tzemach Tzedek announce family unity pact
summary_en: In summer 5626, the sons of the Tzemach Tzedek issued a public letter committing to peace and joint custody of their father's manuscripts.
story_body: After the Tzemach Tzedek's passing earlier that year, his sons issued a circular letter to chassidim describing their pact of peace and a weekly gathering in their father's birth-room. They explained that the surviving forty manuscript volumes — twenty in nigleh and twenty in chassidus — could not be divided, because the nigleh works were destined for printing. The Rebbe Maharash twice added a personal note saying he strongly wished all the writings to be printed and his father's wellsprings to spread outward, citing the Baal Shem Tov's famous letter.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's house in Lubavitch burns
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek's house in Lubavitch burned in 5628 (1868), two years after his passing.
story_body: The home of the Tzemach Tzedek burned in 1868, two years after his death. The manuscripts of his Torah writings survived because they had been moved to and preserved in the home of his son the Rebbe Maharash. The fire is mentioned in Igros Kodesh of the Rebbe Maharash, letter 41.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's responsa begin publication
summary_en: Editing and printing of the Tzemach Tzedek's responsa began in 5631 (1871) and continued through 1884.
story_body: Following the brothers' 1866 commitment to publish their father's manuscripts, the Tzemach Tzedek's responsa were sent to editors and printed serially from 1871 through 1884. His chassidic discourses were not printed in this period; they only appeared many years later in the Ohr HaTorah series.

title_en: Eshel Avraham first edition printed in Lvov
summary_en: Mahadura kamma of Eshel Avraham by R. Avraham David of Buchach was published in Lvov in 5646 (1886).
story_body: The first edition of Eshel Avraham — chiddushim on Shulchan Aruch by R. Avraham David of Buchach — appeared in Lvov in 1886, forty-five years after the author's passing. The manuscripts had been preserved by his great-grandson R. Yisrael Aryeh Leib Wahrman, who copied them in unsystematic order.

title_en: Eshel Avraham second edition printed in Buchach
summary_en: Mahadura tinyana of Eshel Avraham was published in Buchach in 5666 (1906).
story_body: A second edition of Eshel Avraham appeared in Buchach in 1906, twenty years after the Lvov first edition. Much later, a third edition drawn from the surviving manuscripts in the Chabad library was progressively printed in the Shulchan Aruch HaShalem of Machon Yerushalayim.

title_en: Manuscript volume sent to Chabad library for review
summary_en: On 27 Nisan 5721 (1961), librarian R. Chaim Lieberman responded to R. Shmuel Ber Leikin describing the contents of a buch he had sent in for review.
story_body: R. Shmuel Ber Leikin sent a manuscript volume to the Chabad library asking what it contained. On 27 Nisan 5721 Lieberman replied that the volume held copies of chassidic discourses plus three original pages: two by the Tzemach Tzedek and one by the Rebbe Maharash — a letter to R. Chaim Yaakov Widrewitz. The original three pages later disappeared from the volume, and locating them became a decades-long search.

title_en: Mondshine searches Touro library for missing Maharash letter
summary_en: In 5748 (1988), R. Yehoshua Mondshine traveled to Touro College in New York seeking the missing Maharash letter among Leikin's books.
story_body: Researcher R. Yehoshua Mondshine traced Leikin's library to Touro College in New York and visited there in 5748 looking for the lost manuscript pages, including the Maharash letter to R. Chaim Yaakov Widrewitz. After being passed between librarians, clerks, and managers, he left empty-handed. The search continued unresolved for over a decade more.

title_en: Lost Maharash letter rediscovered as photo in geniza
summary_en: On 27 Elul 5759 (1999), a photocopy of the missing Rebbe Maharash letter to R. Chaim Yaakov Widrewitz surfaced in a municipal library geniza.
story_body: After nearly forty years of unsuccessful searches, R. Shaul Vilhelm called from Detroit on 27 Elul 5759 to report that Yosef Levin had found a photocopy of the lost buch in a public library's geniza. The photocopy contained the long-sought Maharash letter to R. Chaim Yaakov Widrewitz, in which the Rebbe acknowledged receiving Widrewitz's kuntress and promised to set aside time to study it despite poor health and many demands.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab flees Lubavitch for Rostov
summary_en: Rebbe Rashab fled Lubavitch with his family during WWI and settled in Rostov, taking manuscripts and ~100 books while leaving most of his library in Moscow.
story_body: At the start of 5676 (autumn 1915), as World War I disrupted Lubavitch, the Rashab moved his household to Rostov. He could not carry his entire library, so most books were stored in a Moscow warehouse (where they remained for decades). He brought along the manuscript collection and about one hundred books, including a Jerusalem Talmud printed in Zhitomir with his handwritten glosses.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz moves from Rostov to Leningrad
summary_en: Rebbe Rayatz relocated from Rostov to Leningrad, bringing the family library and manuscripts.
story_body: In 5684 (1924), the Rebbe Rayatz emigrated from Rostov to Leningrad, taking with him the books and manuscripts inherited from his father the Rashab. This was the first of a series of moves that carried the Lubavitch library across Europe before it eventually reached New York.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz emigrates from Russia to Riga
summary_en: Rebbe Rayatz left Soviet Russia for Riga in 5688, bringing the family library with him.
story_body: Following his arrest and release, the Rayatz emigrated from the Soviet Union to Riga, Latvia, in 5688 (late 1927). He carried with him the books and manuscripts saved from Rostov and Leningrad, continuing to safeguard the inheritance of the Chabad Rebbeim through political upheaval.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz moves from Riga to Warsaw
summary_en: Rebbe Rayatz relocated from Riga to Warsaw in 5693, again moving the library with him.
story_body: In 5693 (1933), the Rebbe Rayatz left Riga for Warsaw, Poland. The cherished books and manuscripts of the Chabad Rebbeim accompanied him on this next stage of his wanderings, an exile that would continue as conditions in Europe deteriorated.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz moves from Warsaw to Otwock
summary_en: Rebbe Rayatz left Warsaw for Otwock in 5695, where Tomchei Temimim's central yeshiva would be based.
story_body: In 5695 (1935), the Rebbe Rayatz moved from Warsaw to the resort town of Otwock, Poland. There the central yeshiva of Tomchei Temimim continued under his leadership, and his library remained with him until the outbreak of war forced its dramatic rescue from occupied Poland.

title_en: Chabad library rescued from occupied Poland to New York
summary_en: In 5701 the library of Rebbe Rayatz was rescued from Nazi-occupied Poland and brought to New York.
story_body: After the German invasion of Poland and the Rayatz's own escape, his library and manuscript collection were extracted from occupied territory in 5701 (1940-1941) and shipped to New York. From that point forward the books rested in the Rebbe's quarters at 770 Eastern Parkway, where they have remained the heart of the Chabad library.

title_en: First wall calendar of Chabad customs by R. A.C. Naeh
summary_en: The earliest extant Chabad wall calendar edited by R. Avraham Chaim Naeh and issued by Kollel Chabad is from 5699.
story_body: R. Avraham Chaim Naeh authored a calendar of synagogue laws and Chabad customs, initially as a booklet and later as a wall calendar. The oldest wall-calendar copy preserved in the library is from 5699 (1938-1939), published by Kollel Chabad — beginning an annual tradition that continued under his son R. Baruch Naeh and beyond.

title_en: Earliest extant Naeh booklet calendar (5692)
summary_en: The oldest surviving copy of R. A.C. Naeh's annual calendar of customs is the 5692 booklet edition.
story_body: Before Kollel Chabad began publishing R. Naeh's calendar, he printed it himself as a booklet sent to overseas supporters. The library's earliest preserved copy is titled 'Luach for the year 5692 with the laws and customs of the year, by Rabbi Avraham Chaim Naeh, Jerusalem,' carrying his New Year greeting to donors.

title_en: Rebbe edits Kollel Chabad calendar for 5713
summary_en: At the end of 5712 R. A.C. Naeh sent his draft 5713 wall calendar to the Rebbe, who edited dozens of Chabad customs into it.
story_body: Late in 5712 (1952), R. Avraham Chaim Naeh sent the Rebbe a proof of the wall calendar he was preparing for 5713. The Rebbe added and corrected dozens of details of Chabad practice, and from then on the published Kollel Chabad calendar reflected his revisions. The surviving Tishrei-to-Kislev sheet of the edited calendar is preserved in the library archive, with the glosses published in Kerem Chabad vol. 1.

title_en: R. Yosef Hatzaddik of Posen passes away
summary_en: R. Yosef 'Hatzaddik' ben Pinchas, son-in-law of the Nodah BiYhudah and Av Beit Din of Posen, died on 5 Adar 5561.
story_body: Born in Zolkov in 5486 (1726), R. Yosef Hatzaddik served as rabbi in Witkow, Skole, Yavorov and finally Posen, and was deeply praised by his father-in-law the Nodah BiYhudah. He died on 5 Adar 5561 (18 February 1801) and is buried in Posen; his book Zikhron She'erit Yosef was printed in Kolomea in 5642.

title_en: Louis Lamm acquires R. Akiva Eiger oil portrait
summary_en: Amsterdam dealer Louis Lamm purchased the oil portrait of R. Akiva Eiger from the Eiger family inheritance for 25 marks in 1913.
story_body: Louis Lamm, an Amsterdam book dealer and publisher, acquired the oil portrait of R. Akiva Eiger — said to originate from Russia and from the Eiger family inheritance — in 1913 for 25 Reichsmark. He kept it for over two decades before it was sold to the Rayatz in 1936, eventually entering the Chabad library archive.

title_en: Louis Lamm receives the Dr. Baer estate of calendars
summary_en: After the death of grammarian Dr. Seligman Isaac Baer in 5657, his book-bound estate of calendars passed to Louis Lamm.
story_body: Dr. Seligman Isaac Baer of Biebrich, the renowned masoretic scholar, died in 5657 (1897). Following his death, his bound estate of calendars came into the possession of Louis Lamm of Amsterdam. Part of the Chabad library's collection of ancient calendars — over a thousand items in some four hundred varieties — traces back to this Baer estate via Lamm.

title_en: Lamm letter to Rayatz on portrait sale
summary_en: On 19 August 1936 (Rosh Chodesh Elul 5696) Louis Lamm wrote to the Rebbe Rayatz detailing the provenance of oil portraits and 31 additional prints he sold him.
story_body: In a German letter dated 19 August 1936, Amsterdam dealer Louis Lamm wrote to the Rebbe Rayatz about the sale of two oil portraits — R. Yosef Hatzaddik of Posen (obtained from Dr. Calvary of Posen in a barter for 60 Reichsmark in books) and R. Akiva Eiger (acquired from the Eiger family in 1913 for 25 Reichsmark) — along with 31 additional prints. Decades later this letter, found by R. Yitzchak Wilhelm during the archiving of the Rayatz's papers, finally identified the provenance of the portraits and many old calendars in the library.

title_en: First lithograph of the Tzemach Tzedek portrait approved by Vilna censor
summary_en: The earliest printed portrait of the Tzemach Tzedek, a lithograph by N. Metz, received Vilna censor approval on 30 October 1886.
story_body: In the winter of 5647, N. Metz of Vilna issued the first widely distributed lithograph of the Tzemach Tzedek, captioned in Hebrew 'Tzaddik for an everlasting memory: portrait of the holy gaon Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch' and in Russian as 'Portrait of the Lubavitcher rabbi Mendel Schneersohn.' Censor approval was granted in Vilna on 30 October 1886. It became the basis for many subsequent reproductions of the Tzemach Tzedek's likeness.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek portrait printed in Keneset Yisrael (Warsaw)
summary_en: An engraving of the Tzemach Tzedek signed by artist Z. Schatz appeared in the journal Keneset Yisrael, vol. 3 (Warsaw 5648).
story_body: In 5648 (1888), the Warsaw journal Keneset Yisrael reproduced a portrait of the Tzemach Tzedek in its third volume (cols. 215-216), signed by the artist Z. Schatz. This version differs noticeably from the original painting and from the Metz lithograph, and the author of the present study judges it an unsuccessful attempt unworthy of further analysis.

title_en: First written account of the Tzemach Tzedek's portrait
summary_en: Alexander Zisskind Rabinowitz published the earliest account of the Tzemach Tzedek's surreptitious portrait in HaAsif 5649.
story_body: In the 5649 (1889) volume of HaAsif (p. 167), Alexander Zisskind Rabinowitz wrote that the portrait of R. Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch was widespread, having been made by a photographer who stole into his room against the Tzemach Tzedek's will — for Chassidic rebbes refused to leave images of themselves to posterity. This is the earliest published version of the famous tradition about the painting's origins.

title_en: Vilna-censored Warsaw print of Tzemach Tzedek portrait
summary_en: A Warsaw-printed copy of the Tzemach Tzedek portrait carrying a Vilna censor approval dated 26 January 1889 is preserved at the National Library in Jerusalem.
story_body: The National Library in Jerusalem holds a Warsaw-printed copy of the Tzemach Tzedek portrait stamped with a Vilna censor's permit dated 26 January 1889. It is one of several variants of the portrait circulating after the original Metz lithograph of 1886.

title_en: Rayatz receives Tzemach Tzedek portrait from R.M.A. Stillerman
summary_en: On 4 Shevat 5684 the Rebbe Rayatz received a printed Tzemach Tzedek portrait from R.M.A. Stillerman.
story_body: On 4 Shevat 5684 (10 January 1924), R.M.A. Stillerman gave the Rebbe Rayatz a print of the Tzemach Tzedek's portrait. The print is one of the earliest preserved in the Chabad library and exhibits more of the Rebbe's chair, feet and bookcase than the well-known Metz lithograph, suggesting both derive from a still-earlier original.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek portrait on the Remigalski Riga calendar
summary_en: The 5689 calendar published by Remigalski in Riga featured the Tzemach Tzedek's portrait on its cover, and was also issued as a Shanah Tovah card.
story_body: In 5689 (1928-29), the Remigalski publishing house in Riga produced a yearly calendar with the Tzemach Tzedek's portrait on the title page; a copy is in the Chabad library. The same image was distributed as a New Year greeting card, reflecting how widely circulated the Tzemach Tzedek's image had become by the interwar period.

title_en: Kehot reissues the Tzemach Tzedek portrait
summary_en: In 5713 Kehot reprinted the Tzemach Tzedek's portrait, deliberately flipping the plate so the coat overlap and the held book read right-to-left.
story_body: In 5713 (1953), Kehot Publication Society reissued the Tzemach Tzedek's portrait. The plate was intentionally reversed so the right side of the coat would lie over the left (as Jewish custom dictates) and so that the book held in his hand would open from the right like a Hebrew text — corrections to the original gentile artist's depiction discussed in Chabad tradition.

title_en: Rabbinical Conference in Korosten
summary_en: The first rabbinical conference of the Korosten, Zhitomir and Shepetovka districts met in Korosten on 18-20 Cheshvan 5687 (26-28 October 1926).
story_body: From 26 to 28 October 1926 (18-20 Cheshvan 5687), seventy-two Soviet-era rabbis convened in Korosten with about thirty additional unofficial participants — 101 men in all are numbered in the surviving group photograph. The official list of delegates includes communal rabbis from Malin, Korosten, Zhitomir, Ovruch, Berdichev and other towns, with guests from Kiev, Leningrad, Odessa, Vinnitsa and elsewhere; the photograph was first published by the author in 1989 in 'Toldot Chabad B'Russia HaSovietit.'

title_en: Photograph of Rayatz with future Rebbe before wedding
summary_en: A photograph from 5689, evidently taken shortly before the Rebbe's wedding, shows the future Rebbe standing beside his seated father-in-law at a dining-room table, likely in Riga.
story_body: Among the library's photographs is one from 5689 (1929), evidently taken close to the Rebbe's wedding — perhaps when he was already a chassan. The future Rebbe stands while his future father-in-law, the Rayatz, sits and holds his hand, beside the dining-room table that was apparently in Riga. A companion image from the same session shows the Rayatz seated at the same table beside his wife Rebbetzin Nechama Dina, studying a book.

title_en: Photograph of Rayatz with the Rebbe at Pirkersdorf
summary_en: On 25 Adar I 5695 the Rayatz was photographed with the Rebbe standing among the trees at the Pirkersdorf convalescent resort.
story_body: On 25 Adar I 5695 (28 February 1935), at the Pirkersdorf convalescent resort where the Rayatz had gone for medical treatment, the Rayatz was photographed standing among the trees together with the Rebbe. Two further photographs from the same session show the Rayatz alone among the trees.

title_en: Annual Tomchei Temimim celebration in New York
summary_en: On Erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz 5702, the annual celebration of Merkos HaYeshivos Tomchei Temimim featured the Rayatz speaking while the Rebbe supported him with both hands.
story_body: On Erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz 5702 (14 June 1942), the central yeshiva organization Tomchei Temimim held its annual celebration in New York. A photograph captures the Rayatz speaking while standing, with the Rebbe physically supporting him with both hands. Also present in the images are Dr. Leo Jung, the Rashag, R. Joseph B. Soloveitchik, R. Dovber Chaskind and others.

title_en: Rebbe describes how Rebbetzin Chana made ink in exile
summary_en: At the farbrengen of 20 Menachem-Av 5723, the Rebbe recounted how his mother improvised colored inks from grasses so his father could write glosses on a Zohar in Soviet exile.
story_body: On 20 Menachem-Av 5723 (10 August 1963), the yahrzeit of his father R. Levi Yitzchak Schneerson, the Rebbe told that when his father was in Soviet exile, he eventually received some books — including a Zohar — but no paper, so he wrote his Kabbalistic glosses in the margins. He also lacked ink, so Rebbetzin Chana learned to manufacture ink from grasses; lacking expertise, her batches came out red, green or black, accounting for the varied colors visible in the manuscript glosses later published as Likutei Levi Yitzchak.

title_en: Author first views original Tzemach Tzedek portrait in Moscow
summary_en: On Issru Chag Pesach 5751 the author visited Yehuda Leib Ginzburg in Moscow and saw the original Tzemach Tzedek oil painting on his wall.
story_body: On Issru Chag Pesach 5751 (7 April 1991), the librarian visited the Moscow home of Yehuda Leib Ginzburg — a great-grandson of R. Shlomo Zalman of Kapust (the Magen Avot), himself a grandson of the Tzemach Tzedek — and saw on the wall a vivid colored portrait of the Tzemach Tzedek. Years of attempts to obtain the painting or a photo for the Chabad library followed; eventually R. Baruch Gorin succeeded in securing a copy of this rare and beautiful image.

title_en: Tziyun HaMetzuyenes published
summary_en: In Iyar 5753, R. Yosef Menachem Weiss published Tziyun HaMetzuyenes, documenting the graves of the Nodah BiYhudah and his family in Prague.
story_body: In Iyar 5753 (May 1993), R. Yosef Menachem Weiss published the book Tziyun HaMetzuyenes about the graves of the Nodah BiYhudah and his family in the Prague cemetery, with documents, photographs and biographies — including an entry on the Nodah BiYhudah's distinguished son-in-law R. Yosef Hatzaddik of Posen.

title_en: Tomchei Tmimim children's parade from 770 courtyard
summary_en: A parade for the Tomchei Tmimim Lubavitch chadarim children set out from the 770 courtyard on 9 Iyar 5705.
story_body: Rebbe Rayatz's network of Tomchei Tmimim chadarim in America held a children's gathering in the 770 courtyard, where the synagogue was later built. On 9 Iyar 5705 a parade was organized for them, departing from the courtyard. Surviving photographs from that period show R' Yitzchak Dovber Ushpal, R' Shneur Zalman Gourary, and R' Shmuel Isaac Popack with the children at the Eastern Parkway entrance.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's sons write R' Aharon Lifshitz on the clothing decree
summary_en: On 24 Tammuz 5605 the three sons of the Tzemach Tzedek wrote R' Aharon Lifshitz of Belinitch about the Tsarist clothing decree.
story_body: Tsar Nicholas I's 1845 decree forced Jews to abandon traditional garb, with a transitional tax (korobka) levied on those still wearing long coats. Because the Tzemach Tzedek was under secret-police surveillance, his sons — the future rebbes of Kopust, Liadi, and Niezhin — wrote to R' Aharon Lifshitz, dayan of Belinitch, asking how the tax collection there with the Mohilev governor's office had been handled, hoping to learn from it for Lubavitch.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz received Maharash's kippah from R' Shneur Tzvi Schneersohn
summary_en: On 3 Elul 5688 Rebbe Rayatz received the white silver-threaded mitznefet of his grandfather the Maharash as a gift.
story_body: A handwritten note by Rebbe Rayatz, later discovered in a Russian archive, recorded that the mitznefet (kippah) of his grandfather the Maharash was given to him as a gift by his relative R' Shneur Tzvi Schneersohn, grandson of R' Chaim Avraham, on 3 Elul 5688. The kippah, woven with silver threads and bearing a small tail, eventually entered the Chabad library's artifact archive after the 'didan notzach' books trial of 5746–47.

title_en: The Rebbe acknowledges Slavita brothers' cane from R' Shmuel Aba Shapira
summary_en: On 16 Iyar 5717 the Rebbe wrote R' Shmuel Aba Shapira thanking him for the cane of the holy Slavita brothers.
story_body: The Rebbe's letter, printed in Igros Kodesh vol. 15 (#5452), thanked R' Shmuel Aba Shapira for sending 'a cane from a holy place.' The accompanying note explained the cane had belonged to R' Pinchas of Slavita, passed via his only son R' Heshel and his daughter-in-law Treina, who had carried it to the brothers' Moscow prison and broken it in the mud. A Polish prince repaired it with a new handle; the cane is catalogued in the library archive as item 5186.

title_en: Rayatz at Tomchei Tmimim annual celebration holding London cane
summary_en: Rebbe Rayatz appears holding his metal-handled London cane at the annual Tomchei Tmimim celebration on 7 Adar II 5703.
story_body: A photograph from the annual fundraising celebration for the Tomchei Tmimim Lubavitch yeshivos, held on 7 Adar II 5703, shows Rebbe Rayatz holding the cane catalogued as library item 5188, whose metal handle is engraved 'LONDON SOLID S K.' Several other canes from his estate, including one purported to belong to R' Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, are preserved in the library archive.

title_en: Rabbi Chaim Kavash passes away in Samarkand
summary_en: Rabbi Chaim Kavash, rabbi of Yochavitch who fled the Nazi advance to Samarkand, died there on 24 Iyar 5703.
story_body: Born in Vyetka in 5649, Chaim Kavash studied at Tomchei Tmimim in Lubavitch and in 5686 became rabbi of Yochavitch in the Polotsk district. As Soviet persecution of rabbis intensified he fled to Nevel; when the Germans invaded he escaped further east to Samarkand among Anash, dying there on 24 Iyar 5703. His estate included several heirloom vessels, including a spoon attributed to the Baal Shem Tov and a cup of R' Mordechai of Lechovitch.

title_en: Passing of Rebbe Rayatz
summary_en: Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn passed away on 10 Shevat 5710.
story_body: Rebbe Rayatz's histalkus on 10 Shevat 5710 ended his nesius and the era in which the second-floor room at 770 served as his yechidus room. According to his secretary R' Nissan Mindel, Rayatz used a single mechanical pencil to answer thousands of letters in special numbered notebooks for several consecutive years until his passing on that date.

title_en: The Rebbe writes R' Yosef Chaim Rosenfeld accepting the Bezpaloff cane
summary_en: On 13 Kislev 5720 the Rebbe acknowledged receipt of the second Bezpaloff cane sent by R' Yosef Chaim Rosenfeld.
story_body: R' Shneur Zalman Bezpaloff had originally brought two silver-handled canes to Rebbe Rayatz, who kept one; Bezpaloff later moved to San Francisco. When the shliach R' Yosef Chaim Hakohen Rosenfeld visited him there, Bezpaloff gifted him the second cane, which Rosenfeld then forwarded to the Rebbe. The Rebbe's reply (Igros Kodesh vol. 18 #6612) noted his habitual avoidance of gifts and enclosed a check in exchange.

title_en: Rebbetzin Rivka gives Maharash's leather portfolio to grandson Rayatz
summary_en: In winter 5648 Rebbetzin Rivka gave her grandson, the future Rebbe Rayatz, the leather paper-portfolio that had belonged to her father-in-law the Maharash.
story_body: Rebbe Rayatz inscribed a note documenting that the leather portfolio used for holding papers, from the estate of his great-grandfather the Maharash, was given to him as a gift by his grandmother Rebbetzin Rivka in the winter of 5648. The portfolio is preserved with his inscription identifying its provenance.

title_en: Rayatz instructs Atkin to send the Kavash vessels via the Rebbe
summary_en: On 29 Iyar 5707 Rebbe Rayatz wrote R' Meir Atkin to hand the holy vessels from R' Chaim Kavash's estate to R' Benjamin Gorodetsky.
story_body: Having fled the Soviet Union, R' Meir Atkin offered Rebbe Rayatz the heirloom vessels he had purchased from the estate of R' Chaim Kavash — including a spoon attributed to the Baal Shem Tov and a cup of R' Mordechai of Lechovitch. Rayatz replied on 29 Iyar 5707 directing him to entrust them to R' Benjamin Gorodetsky for safekeeping. Atkin, however, ultimately handed them to the Ramash (the future Rebbe) in Paris on 25 Sivan, before the Rebbe's return to New York.

title_en: The Rebbe travels to Paris to bring his mother Rebbetzin Chana
summary_en: In 5707 the Rebbe traveled to Paris to bring his mother Rebbetzin Chana, who had been rescued from Russia, to America.
story_body: While in Paris in 5707 the Rebbe also received from Mrs. Chana Uzerman — the granddaughter of R' Menachem Mendel of Paris, son of the Maharash — a mosaic-style table built by the Maharash himself. The collapsible table had passed from the Maharash to his youngest son and then to Uzerman after R' Menachem Mendel's death during WWII. The Rebbe reassembled it in his 770 yechidus room, where it has remained ever since.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in the United States
summary_en: At the end of Sivan 5701 Rebbe Rayatz arrived in America and began using the second-floor 770 room as his yechidus room.
story_body: From his arrival at the end of Sivan 5701 until his histalkus in the winter of 5710, Rebbe Rayatz used the second-floor room at 770 as his yechidus chamber, where he also delivered maamarim. After his passing the same room became the Rebbe's and Machneh Israel's office until the office layout was reorganized.

title_en: R' Yisrael Poizner brings Baal Shem Tov kettle to the Rebbe
summary_en: Around 5730 R' Yisrael Poizner of Klimovitch brought to the Rebbe a small kettle attributed to the Baal Shem Tov.
story_body: R' Yisrael Poizner had purchased the small kettle in Samarkand in 5726 from a member of Anash, who said it was among the vessels left by R' Chaim Kavash and was used by the Baal Shem Tov. In 5729 the kettle was smuggled across the Soviet border to Eretz Yisrael via R' Avraham Leib Godin of Riga, and around 5730 Poizner presented it to the Rebbe with an accompanying letter of provenance.

title_en: Library books trial: artifact collection transferred to library archive
summary_en: Following the 5746–47 books trial, the artifact collection from Rayatz's wall cabinet was transferred to the Chabad library archive.
story_body: Rebbe Rayatz's yechidus room had contained a wall cabinet holding inherited holy objects, several without provenance markings. After the conclusion of the books-trial saga in 5746–47, this collection — including a much-used black silk sleeve attributed to the Tzemach Tzedek and a silver atarah likely traced to the Chernobyl–Cherkas families — was moved into the library's artifact archive for cataloguing and preservation.

title_en: Kehot publishes Sefer HaToldot Admur Maharash
summary_en: In 5707 Kehot published Sefer HaToldot Admur Maharash, including a photograph of one page of the megillah he wrote.
story_body: The biography described how the Maharash, on doctors' orders for physical activity, produced craftworks including a man-height menorah, mosaic tables, sifrei Torah, megillos, and mezuzos. While the household vessels were lost in transit out of Russia, the megillah and one of the tables survived; Kehot's 5707 edition reproduced one of its pages, and a clearer reproduction appeared in Igros Kodesh Admur Maharash in 5753.

title_en: Igros Kodesh Admur Maharash published
summary_en: In 5753 the Igros Kodesh of Rebbe Maharash was published, including clearer reproductions of the megillah he wrote.
story_body: The 5753 volume of Rebbe Maharash's letters included higher-quality photographs of several pages of the megillah he wrote in his own hand, which had been mentioned in earlier sources as having been distributed among his sons. The original megillah is preserved in the Chabad library archive.

title_en: Rebbe uses the third amud at 770 by Tishrei 5712
summary_en: By Tishrei 5712 the Rebbe was already using the low, slanted amud in the southeast corner of the small upstairs beis medrash.
story_body: In the early years of his nesius the Rebbe refused a special chair and amud, sitting on the regular bench at the regular table for tefillah on weekdays. By Tishrei 5712 a low slanted amud had been built in the southeast corner for Shabbos Shemoneh Esreh. R' Moshe Herlig recalled that on Yom Kippur of that year the Rebbe brought his bundle of pidyonos and asked Herlig to guard the amud's lid against anyone opening it during the break.

title_en: Fourth amud for the Rebbe built at Kfar Chabad trade school
summary_en: In 5722 a fourth amud for the Rebbe was constructed at the Kfar Chabad trade school for shipment to 770.
story_body: The fourth amud was built in 5722 at the Beis Hasefer Le'Mlacha trade school in Kfar Chabad, modeled on the wide and elegant third amud already in use at 770, with two small doors and a fold-out shelf. The new amud differed in having a thin dividing column between the two doors — a detail that mattered for Yom Kippur, when the Rebbe used to place his hat inside the amud during the Minchah-Maariv break.

title_en: Kfar Chabad delegation brings new amud to the Rebbe on Erev Rosh Hashanah
summary_en: On Or L'Erev Rosh Hashanah 5723 a delegation from Eretz Yisrael presented the Kfar Chabad-built amud to the Rebbe.
story_body: A chartered flight brought a group from Eretz Yisrael for the Tishrei holidays of 5723, and R' Chaim Schneur Zalman Lipsker carried the new amud with them. He and R' Dovber Teichman presented it at the special farbrengen held Or L'Erev Rosh Hashanah 5723, after which the Rebbe delivered a sicha explaining the inner meaning of the 'shtender' and recounted the Mitteler Rebbe's exchange with the Alter Rebbe about davening 'with the shtender.'

title_en: Rebbe permanently positions the new amud in the upstairs beis medrash
summary_en: During Pesach 5723 the Rebbe instructed R' Chadakov to permanently place the new amud upstairs in the small beis medrash.
story_body: After the new amud spent more than half a year in the Rebbe's room, the downstairs courtyard shul at 770 was already serving for Kabbalas Shabbos, Shacharis, and Mussaf, while Minchah on Erev Shabbos and Shabbos remained upstairs — requiring staff to carry the third amud up and down. On Pesach 5723 the Rebbe told R' Chadakov to leave the older amud downstairs permanently and bring the new amud up to the small beis medrash as its fixed amud.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek released from secret-police surveillance
summary_en: In Nisan 5607 the Tzemach Tzedek's secret-police surveillance, in place during the clothing-decree period, came to an end.
story_body: During the years surrounding the 1845 clothing decree the Tzemach Tzedek lived under the watch of the Tsarist secret police and feared writing letters in his own name on sensitive halachic matters, leaving such correspondence to his sons. The surveillance ended in Nisan 5607, after which he could resume more open conduct of his nesius.

title_en: R' Chaim Kavash receives rabbinic appointment in Yochavitch
summary_en: In 5686 R' Chaim Kavash, a Tomchei Tmimim Lubavitch alumnus, became rabbi of Yochavitch in the Polotsk district.
story_body: After studying in Tomchei Tmimim in Lubavitch, R' Chaim Kavash was appointed rabbi of Yochavitch in the Polotsk district in 5686. As Soviet pressure on rabbis in small towns mounted, he fled first to Nevel and, when the Germans invaded, deeper into Russia to Samarkand.

title_en: R' Chaim Kavash born in Vyetka
summary_en: R' Chaim Kavash was born in Vyetka in 5649.
story_body: Born in Vyetka in 5649, Chaim Kavash went on to study in the Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva in Lubavitch and to serve as a rabbi in Yochavitch and a refugee community leader in Samarkand. His estate preserved several artifacts of disputed but reputed Baal Shem Tov and early-chassidic provenance.

title_en: Rabbinical assembly in Paks to strengthen Orthodox observance
summary_en: Leading Hungarian rabbis convened in Paks to coordinate opposition to the Reform movement and the planned modernist seminary.
story_body: On 3 Elul 5604, prominent Hungarian rabbis gathered in Paks to strengthen Orthodox observance against the inroads of the Reform movement. Among the issues debated was the proposed founding of a modernist rabbinical seminary promoted by the reformers, which the Ksav Sofer later reported had been successfully blocked. In follow-up correspondence, the Ksav Sofer counseled that ongoing resistance to the reformers should be conducted discreetly rather than through further public assemblies.

title_en: R. Binyamin Wolf Loew of Verbov writes to Maharia Asad on religious decline
summary_en: R. Binyamin Wolf Loew, av beis din of Verbov, wrote to R. Yehuda Asad lamenting the breaches in Jewish observance and seeking guidance.
story_body: In a letter dated to the week of Parshas Nitzavim 5603, R. Binyamin Wolf Loew of Verbov poured out his anguish to R. Yehuda Asad over the spread of Reform and the loss of an older generation of rabbinic leaders who had stood in the breach. He confessed that the situation pained him daily and pressed Asad to share any practical strategy he might have for resisting the modernist breach-makers. The letter is the earliest of three surviving responses to Asad's outreach campaign for strengthening religious life in Hungary.

title_en: Ksav Sofer writes to Maharia Asad about the Paks assembly's outcome
summary_en: The Ksav Sofer reported to R. Yehuda Asad that the threat of a modernist seminary had been quashed and counseled discreet ongoing resistance.
story_body: Writing from Pressburg on 5 Cheshvan 5605, R. Avraham Shmuel Binyamin Sofer (Ksav Sofer) updated R. Yehuda Asad on developments since the Paks assembly. He confirmed that the magnates had withdrawn support for the reformers' seminary and the danger had passed, crediting community askanim who had worked tirelessly to defeat it. He recommended against convening a further public rabbinical council in Pressburg, urging that resistance proceed quietly until the controversy subsided.

title_en: R. Yechezkel Banet of Neitra writes to Maharia Asad on monitoring reformers
summary_en: R. Yechezkel Banet of Neitra told R. Yehuda Asad that he had posted watchers to detect new modernist moves before the government committee.
story_body: In a letter dated the 6th day of Chanukah 5605 from Neitra, R. Yechezkel Banet expressed pain over the continuing troubles being caused to Torah scholars by the reformers. He informed R. Yehuda Asad that he had stationed informants to alert him the moment any modernist proposal was placed before the government committee, at which point he would dispatch a special messenger so that a coordinated response could be prepared. The letter reflects the underground intelligence network the Hungarian rabbinate maintained in the wake of the Paks assembly.

title_en: Vitebsk cheder teachers petition Petersburg conference against secular studies
summary_en: Fifteen Vitebsk cheder teachers and principals petitioned the Petersburg rabbinical conference to bar secular studies for children under thirteen.
story_body: On 17 Adar Sheini 5670, fifteen melamdim and principals of cheders in Vitebsk signed a letter, led by R. Dov Nachman Horowitz, to the rabbis assembled in St. Petersburg. They warned from experience that exposing young children to Russian-language schoolbooks and gymnasium classes hollowed out their faith and led them to reject Chassidus and prayer. They proposed barring admission to Russian-language schools before age thirteen, requiring melamdim to teach mussar works approved by rabbis, and ensuring religious instruction in state schools be given only by Orthodox rabbis. The letter was conveyed to the conference through Vitebsk's rabbi, R. Shmaryahu Yehuda Leib Medalia.

title_en: Petersburg rabbinical conference debates rabbinic credentials and chinuch
summary_en: A government-convened rabbinical conference in St. Petersburg debated requiring secular-education certificates for rabbis and reforming cheder studies.
story_body: In Adar 5670, leading rabbis of the Russian Empire assembled in St. Petersburg for a rabbinical conference whose agenda included the proposed requirement that rabbis hold a secular-education certificate, the future of the kazyonny (crown) rabbinate, and the place of secular studies in the cheder system. The Rebbe Rashab invested years of preparation in shaping the lineup of attendees and their positions, urging opposition to mandatory secular credentials and to the modernist reforms championed by the maskilic attorney Henry Slosberg. Communities such as Vitebsk and Romen submitted petitions backing the Rashab's positions, several of which were preserved in his archive.

title_en: R. Shmaryahu Yehuda Leib Medalia appointed rabbi of Vitebsk
summary_en: R. Shmaryahu Yehuda Leib Medalia was appointed rabbi of Vitebsk in Tishrei 5669.
story_body: R. Shmaryahu Yehuda Leib Medalia took up the rabbinate of Vitebsk in Tishrei 5669, with his appointment documented in correspondence of the Rebbe Rashab. Within roughly a year and a half he would serve as Vitebsk's delegate to the 1910 St. Petersburg rabbinical conference, where he carried the city's anash petitions on chinuch and rabbinic credentials. Medalia would later become one of the most prominent Chabad rabbinic figures of the Soviet period.

title_en: R. Chaim Yeshaya Schneersohn becomes rabbi of Romen
summary_en: R. Chaim Yeshaya Schneersohn, great-grandson of the Tzemach Tzedek, was installed as rabbi of Romen in 5661.
story_body: R. Chaim Yeshaya Schneersohn — son of the rebbe of Retchitsa, grandson of the Kapuster rebbe R. Yehuda Leib, and great-grandson of the Tzemach Tzedek — assumed the rabbinate of Romen in 5661 (1900/1901). He would serve the town for over twenty-five years and was among the senior anash figures in the city who endorsed the local petition to the 1910 St. Petersburg rabbinical conference. He held the position until his passing in late 1927.

title_en: Passing of R. Chaim Yeshaya Schneersohn, rabbi of Romen
summary_en: R. Chaim Yeshaya Schneersohn, longtime rabbi of Romen and descendant of the Tzemach Tzedek, passed away on 15 Kislev 5688.
story_body: R. Chaim Yeshaya Schneersohn passed away on 15 Kislev 5688 after more than a quarter-century as rabbi of Romen. A direct descendant of the Tzemach Tzedek through the Kapuster and Retchitsa branches of the dynasty, he had been a leading anash figure in the city during the late Tsarist period. His signature stands at the foot of the 1910 Romen petition to the St. Petersburg rabbinical conference preserved in the Rebbe Rashab's archive.

title_en: R. Shmaryahu Mekler elected Vitebsk delegate to the Moscow conference
summary_en: The Vitebsk philanthropist R. Shmaryahu Mekler was chosen in 5677 as the city's representative to the rabbinical conference held in Moscow.
story_body: In 5677, in the upheavals surrounding the Russian Revolution, the Vitebsk askan and gevir R. Shmaryahu Mekler was elected as the city's delegate to the rabbinical conference held in Moscow. He had earlier been among the lay leaders who backed the 1910 cheder-teachers' petition to the St. Petersburg conference, and his role in 1917 marks the continuity of anash communal organizing into the revolutionary period.

title_en: R. Zalman Butman sends coded report from Riga to Rebbe Rayatz on arrests
summary_en: R. Zalman Butman smuggled a coded report through Riga to the Rebbe Rayatz listing Chabad chassidim arrested or executed by the Soviets.
story_body: On 1 Adar Aleph 5701 (27 February 1941), R. Yehuda Eber forwarded from newly Soviet-occupied Riga a letter that R. Shneur Zalman Butman had smuggled out of the USSR to the Rebbe Rayatz in America. The body of the letter, encoded in 'ksav stam' lettering and other cryptic devices to evade NKVD censorship, named anash arrested and executed by the Soviets in recent years, those who had been released, conditions of shechita and food in Moscow and Leningrad, and the impossibility of writing openly abroad. Eber, who had escaped Warsaw to Riga but was unable to obtain US visas, would be murdered together with the rest of Riga's Jews after the German conquest later that year.

title_en: German conquest of Riga and murder of R. Yehuda Eber and family
summary_en: After the German conquest of Riga in summer 1941, R. Yehuda Eber — a Warsaw refugee who had been seeking US visas — was murdered together with his family.
story_body: The Chassidic scholar R. Yehuda Eber had fled Nazi-occupied Warsaw to Riga, where in early 1941 he served as the conduit for R. Zalman Butman's coded reports to the Rebbe Rayatz in New York. Eber and his household were unable to obtain travel permits from Riga to the United States before the German army overran the city later in 1941. He and his family perished along with the rest of Riga's Jews in the subsequent Nazi massacres.

title_en: R. Moshe Yisrael sent on Safed mission to North Africa
summary_en: R. Moshe Yisrael departed Jerusalem on a fundraising mission for the holy city of Safed to the lands of North Africa.
story_body: Born in Jerusalem around 1680 and son-in-law of R. Moshe ibn Habib, R. Moshe Yisrael was dispatched as an emissary (shadar) of Safed to North Africa in 1710. He remained on this mission until 1713, traveling through Moroccan communities including Meknes and Fez. During this period he corresponded with fellow emissary R. Nissim Avraham Hakohen regarding the collection of pledged donations.

title_en: R. Eliezer Behlul composes Mareh Einayim in Meknes
summary_en: R. Eliezer Behlul, one of the sages of Meknes, composed a manuscript book of sermons titled Mareh Einayim.
story_body: R. Eliezer Behlul of Meknes wrote his homiletical work Mareh Einayim in 1712, which remained in manuscript form. The book incorporated novel teachings he heard from the visiting emissaries R. Moshe Yisrael and R. Nissim Avraham Hakohen, who were then traveling through Morocco on Land of Israel missions.

title_en: R. Moshe Yisrael becomes rabbi of Rhodes
summary_en: R. Moshe Yisrael was accepted as the rabbi of the Jewish community of Rhodes in eastern Greece.
story_body: After completing his North African emissary mission in 1713, R. Moshe Yisrael was appointed rabbi of Rhodes in 1714. He served the community there until 1736, with an interruption between 1727 and 1731 when he undertook a Jerusalem emissary mission to Italy and Holland.

title_en: R. Yom Tov Crispo begins Jerusalem mission to North Africa
summary_en: R. Yom Tov Crispo departed Jerusalem as an emissary to the communities of North Africa.
story_body: R. Yom Tov Crispo was sent in 1718 on a Jerusalem emissary mission to North Africa, beginning with the towns of Morocco. The mission continued for four years until 1722, during which he traveled through Algeria, Tunisia, and Egypt. In Fez he was assisted by R. Yaakov ibn Tzur in raising support both locally and in surrounding towns.

title_en: R. Yaakov ibn Tzur becomes rabbi of Meknes
summary_en: R. Yaakov ibn Tzur was appointed rabbi of Meknes in the middle of summer 1718.
story_body: After serving as a judge in Fez, R. Yaakov ibn Tzur (the Ya'avetz), author of Mishpat U'Tzedaka B'Yaakov, was accepted as rabbi of Meknes in the summer of 1718. He served there until 1729, when he returned to Fez. Following the death of his teacher R. Yehuda ibn Atar, he served as head of the Fez rabbinical court until his death in 1753.

title_en: Crispo writes from Fez to ibn Tzur on new Meknes post
summary_en: Crispo wrote ibn Tzur on 13 Av 1718 about overseeing the collection of pledges in Fez and surrounding towns after the latter's move to Meknes.
story_body: On 13 Av 1718, R. Yom Tov Crispo wrote from Fez to R. Yaakov ibn Tzur, who had just been appointed rabbi of Meknes. The letter expressed joy at the appointment and asked ibn Tzur to oversee the collection from a distance of the various pledges promised in Fez, Taza, Debdou, and other communities for the Jerusalem mission.

title_en: R. Moshe Yisrael's Jerusalem mission to Italy and Holland
summary_en: R. Moshe Yisrael departed on a Jerusalem emissary mission to Italy and Holland.
story_body: In 1727, while serving as rabbi of Rhodes, R. Moshe Yisrael was dispatched as a Jerusalem emissary to the communities of Italy and Holland. He remained on this mission for four years until 1731, when he returned to Rhodes. During this period his rabbinical post in Rhodes was temporarily vacated.

title_en: R. Yom Tov Crispo's second mission from Hebron to Europe
summary_en: R. Yom Tov Crispo departed on a Hebron emissary mission to the lands of Europe.
story_body: In 1727, R. Yom Tov Crispo was sent on a second emissary mission, this time on behalf of Hebron to the European Jewish communities. The mission lasted four years until 1731. Some years earlier he had returned from his first Jerusalem mission to North Africa.

title_en: R. Moshe Yisrael prints Mishat Moshe in Constantinople
summary_en: R. Moshe Yisrael printed the first two volumes of his responsa work Mishat Moshe in Constantinople.
story_body: Between 1734 and 1735, R. Moshe Yisrael printed the first two parts of his responsa collection She'elot U'Teshuvot Mishat Moshe in Constantinople. The third volume was later printed posthumously by his son R. Avraham in 1742, and his sermons were collected and published as Apei Moshe in Livorno in 1828.

title_en: R. Moshe Yisrael dies in Alexandria
summary_en: R. Moshe Yisrael, former rabbi of Rhodes and Jerusalem emissary, died in Alexandria, Egypt.
story_body: Around 1737 R. Moshe Yisrael moved from Rhodes to Alexandria, Egypt, and died there in 1740. His third responsa volume was printed posthumously by his son R. Avraham in Constantinople in 1742, while his collected sermons appeared as Apei Moshe in Livorno in 1828.

title_en: Apei Moshe printed in Livorno
summary_en: The collected sermons of R. Moshe Yisrael were printed posthumously in Livorno under the title Apei Moshe.
story_body: Nearly ninety years after his death in Alexandria, the sermons of R. Moshe Yisrael were gathered and published in Livorno in 1828 under the title Apei Moshe. The book was one of three posthumous publications of his work, alongside his responsa Mishat Moshe printed in Constantinople.

title_en: R. Shmuel Segal of Rogatchov listed in Alter Rebbe's charity assessment
summary_en: R. Shmuel Segal, moreh tzedek of Rogatchov, was first mentioned in a charity assessment signed by the Alter Rebbe.
story_body: In the winter of 1810, R. Shmuel Segal was first recorded as 'moreh tzedek of the community of Rogatchov' in a charity assessment signed by the Alter Rebbe. He served as moreh tzedek in Rogatchov for some fifteen years before making aliyah to the Land of Israel in 1824.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe letter to Meisels and Itinga on aliyah plans
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe wrote to R. Moshe Meisels and R. Baruch Mordechai Itinga advising against their planned aliyah at that time.
story_body: Around 13 Iyar 1814, the Mitteler Rebbe wrote a counsel-letter to two prominent Vilna chassidim, R. Moshe Meisels (author of Shirat Moshe) and R. Baruch Mordechai Itinga (son-in-law of the Vilna av beit din), advising them against their plan to ascend to the Land of Israel. He warned that they would not enjoy long life there, citing reasons known to him. He added that if they nevertheless decided to settle, they should choose Jerusalem rather than Safed or Tiberias, and that the chassidic fund would allocate fifty gold coins annually for their support.

title_en: R. Moshe Meisels makes aliyah to Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: R. Moshe Meisels, longtime trustee of the Vilna community, immigrated to the Land of Israel.
story_body: Around 1816, R. Moshe Meisels, author of Shirat Moshe and former trustee of the Vilna kehilla, ascended to the Land of Israel. Although the Mitteler Rebbe had earlier advised against this move, in 1816-1817 he instructed several of his chassidim to make aliyah. When the Mitteler Rebbe later founded the Chabad community in Hebron, Meisels became one of its leading members and signed most communal documents between 1827 and 1844.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe founds Chabad settlement in Hebron
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe established the Chabad community settlement in Hebron.
story_body: Between 1816 and 1819, in response to deepening tensions that had developed since 1805 between the general chassidic community of Safed and Tiberias and the local Chabad chassidim, the Mitteler Rebbe founded a separate Chabad yishuv in Hebron. Until this settlement was established, the Mitteler Rebbe had counseled chassidim planning aliyah to settle in Jerusalem instead.

title_en: R. Shmuel Segal makes aliyah from Rogatchov to Hebron
summary_en: R. Shmuel Segal, the longtime moreh tzedek of Rogatchov, immigrated to Hebron and became a leader of the Chabad community there.
story_body: In 1823-1824, R. Shmuel Segal left his fifteen-year post as moreh tzedek of Rogatchov and ascended to the Land of Israel. He settled in Hebron and became rabbi, maggid mesharim, and first appointed leader of the Chabad community established there by the Mitteler Rebbe. The Mitteler Rebbe wrote to chassidim of Rogatchov and surrounding towns requesting an annual stipend of thirty gold coins to support him.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe requests stipend for R. Shmuel Segal's aliyah
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe wrote to chassidim of Rogatchov and neighboring towns requesting an annual stipend of thirty gold coins for R. Shmuel Segal's aliyah.
story_body: Around 1823, as R. Shmuel Segal prepared to leave Rogatchov for Hebron, the Mitteler Rebbe addressed a letter to the chassidim of Rogatchov, Bobruisk, Paritch, Zhlobin and their surrounding settlements. He requested they collectively pledge an annual stipend of thirty gold coins — ten from Rogatchov, five from Zhlobin, three from Stareshin, and ten from Bobruisk-Paritch — to enable Segal to devote himself to Torah and divine service in the Land of Israel.

title_en: R. Yissachar Ber Horowitz asks halakhic question of MaHaRIL
summary_en: R. Yissachar Ber Horowitz of Rogatchov submitted a halakhic query to the MaHaRIL mentioning Segal's two-week absence in Mohilev seeking a passport for aliyah.
story_body: In the summer of 1823, R. Yissachar Ber Horowitz of Rogatchov — who would later serve as moreh tzedek in Lubavitch — sent a halakhic question to the MaHaRIL. The question mentioned that R. Shmuel Segal had already been away two weeks in Mohilev attempting to obtain a passport for travel to the Land of Israel and had been preparing for nearly a year for the journey.

title_en: R. Shmuel Segal departs Hebron on emissary mission
summary_en: After settling in Hebron, R. Shmuel Segal departed on an emissary mission abroad.
story_body: Following his 1824 aliyah to Hebron, R. Shmuel Segal was sent abroad on an emissary mission in 1826-1827 on behalf of the Chabad community. He resumed his communal leadership in Hebron upon his return, where he served for decades and signed nearly all communal documents from 1830 onward.

title_en: R. Baruch Mordechai Itinga settles in Jerusalem
summary_en: After many years serving as rabbi of Bobruisk, R. Baruch Mordechai Itinga ascended to the Land of Israel and settled in Jerusalem.
story_body: Around 1851, more than thirty-five years after the Mitteler Rebbe had advised against his aliyah, R. Baruch Mordechai Itinga finally ascended to the Land of Israel and settled in Jerusalem. He had served for an extended period as rabbi of Bobruisk in the intervening years. He died in Jerusalem just over a year later, on 14 Elul 1852.

title_en: R. Baruch Mordechai Itinga dies in Jerusalem
summary_en: R. Baruch Mordechai Itinga, son-in-law of the av beit din of Vilna, died in Jerusalem on 14 Elul 1852.
story_body: On 14 Elul 1852, R. Baruch Mordechai Itinga passed away in Jerusalem, just over a year after settling there. He had been a prominent Vilna chassid and son-in-law of R. Shmuel, av beit din of Vilna, and served as rabbi of Bobruisk for many years before his aliyah.

title_en: Letter of Rabbi Yisrael Dov Twersky of Vilednik to Rabbi Aharon Lifshitz
summary_en: Rabbi Yisrael Dov of Vilednik writes to Rabbi Aharon Lifshitz of Belinitz on a Tuesday of Parashat Vayishlach 5605.
story_body: In a letter dated Tuesday of Parashat Vayishlach 5605, the Rebbe of Vilednik acknowledges Rabbi Aharon Lifshitz's letter about a marital question. He declines to rule and directs the questioner to 'the great rabbi of Lubavitch' — the Tzemach Tzedek — instead, illustrating how Ukrainian chasidic rebbes referred difficult halakhic cases to Lubavitch.

title_en: Letter from Maharchash"z of Lyady on 24 Nisan 5622
summary_en: Rabbi Chaim Schneur Zalman of Lyady writes from Lyady asking Reb Aba Pershan of Krasłowa to organize support, on 24 Nisan 5622.
story_body: This letter, one of seven from Rabbi Chaim Schneur Zalman of Lyady — son of the Tzemach Tzedek — was written while his father was still alive but in great weakness. It asks longtime supporters in Krasłowa, through Reb Dan and Rabbi Shneur Zalman, to repeat their previous year's fundraising effort on his behalf.

title_en: Wedding of Nachum Mordechai of Chortkov in Potik
summary_en: Rabbi David Moshe of Chortkov's son Nachum Mordechai marries the daughter of Rabbi Shalom Yosef of Sadigura on the Shabbat after Shavuot 5622.
story_body: Rabbi David Moshe of Chortkov, son of the Ruzhiner Rebbe, sent a circular letter from Potik in 5622 announcing the wedding of his son Nachum Mordechai to his niece, daughter of his brother Rabbi Shalom Yosef of Sadigura. The wedding was scheduled for the Shabbat after Shavuot, and the letter — addressed to chasidim in Kalisz, Kotarid, Miyaskovke, Krati, Nemirov, and Krasna — requested contributions to defray its substantial costs.

title_en: Maharash of Lubavitch begins his nesi'ut
summary_en: Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn (Maharash) becomes Rebbe of Lubavitch in 5626.
story_body: Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn, son of the Tzemach Tzedek, began leading as Rebbe of Lubavitch in 5626 and continued until his passing in 5643. His tenure is referenced in a recommendation letter from Rabbi Mordechai of Loyev that mentions a 'great rabbi of Lubavitch' (either the Maharash or his son the Rashab) who interceded on behalf of a chasid seeking to settle in the Land of Israel.

title_en: Death of Rabbi Menachem Nachum Twersky of Loyev
summary_en: Rabbi Menachem Nachum Twersky of Loyev, a Chernobyl dynasty rebbe, passes away in 5636.
story_body: Rabbi Menachem Nachum of Loyev, father of Rabbi Mordechai of Loyev, died in 5636. After his passing, his son Mordechai signed letters as 'son of the deceased Menachem Nachum,' a signature change that helps date the surviving correspondence of the Chernobyl-Rachmistrivka rabbinic family.

title_en: Death of Rabbi Yitzchak Yosef Twersky of Ovrutch
summary_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Yosef of Ovrutch, son-in-law of the Tzemach Tzedek, passes away in 5636.
story_body: Rabbi Yitzchak Yosef Twersky of Ovrutch, son-in-law of the Tzemach Tzedek of Lubavitch, died in 5636. He was succeeded by his son Nachum Dov ('Maharanad'), who led the Ovrutch chasidic court until his own death in 5654 and was also the brother-in-law of the Rebbe Rashab.

title_en: Wedding of Chaim Meir Yechiel in Sadigura
summary_en: Grandson of Rabbi Avraham Yaakov of Sadigura marries the daughter of Rabbi Yitzchak of Bohush on the Shabbat after Shavuot 5640.
story_body: Rabbi Avraham Yaakov of Sadigura, son of the Ruzhiner, sent a circular letter from Sadigura in 5640 announcing the wedding of his grandson Chaim Meir Yechiel — son of his son-in-law Rabbi Aviezri Zelig — to Bat-Sheva, daughter of his nephew Rabbi Yitzchak of Bohush. The letter was carried by emissaries Reb Gedalia the shochet and Reb Chaim Kwashis of Kamenetz, who invited chasidim to attend.

title_en: Death of Rabbi Yeshaya Meshulam Zusya Twersky
summary_en: Rabbi Yeshaya Meshulam Zusya Twersky, son of Rabbi Aharon of Chernobyl, passes away in 5641.
story_body: Rabbi Yeshaya Meshulam Zusya of the Chernobyl dynasty died in 5641. Letters he co-signed with his brother Baruch Asher and his nephew Mordechai of Loyev are therefore dateable to the window 5636–5641 — after Menachem Nachum of Loyev's death but before his own.

title_en: Rabbi Yochanan of Rachmistrivka endorses Rabbi Eliyahu Posek's appointment in Ravna
summary_en: Rabbi Yochanan of Rachmistrivka writes to the community of Ravna in 5647 endorsing their selection of Rabbi Eliyahu Posek as rabbi.
story_body: Dated Sunday of Parashat Behaalotecha 5647, the letter expresses joy that the Ravna community accepted Rabbi Eliyahu Posek — author of Mor V'Ohalot — as rabbi without controversy. Rabbi Yochanan urges holdouts to add their signatures and instructs the community to pay both the rabbi and the shochet on time so the rabbi can study undisturbed.

title_en: Rabbi Eliyahu Posek leaves Ravna to become rabbi of Alapolia
summary_en: After only one year in Ravna, Rabbi Eliyahu Posek accepts the rabbinate of Alapolia in 5648.
story_body: Rabbi Eliyahu Posek's tenure in Ravna proved short-lived; in 5648 he moved to serve as rabbi in Alapolia. He was the author of Mor V'Ohalot and many other works, and Rabbi Yochanan of Rachmistrivka had publicly endorsed his earlier appointment in Ravna the previous year.

title_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Shlomo Yoel Sherman appointed rabbi of Ravna
summary_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Shlomo Yoel Sherman, later author of Pitchei Shearim, becomes rabbi of Ravna in 5648.
story_body: After Rabbi Eliyahu Posek left Ravna for Alapolia in 5648, the community appointed Rabbi Yitzchak Shlomo Yoel Sherman in his place. He later became known as the author of Pitchei Shearim, published in London in 5720 (1960).

title_en: Death of Rabbi Nachum Dov Twersky of Ovrutch
summary_en: Rabbi Nachum Dov of Ovrutch ('Maharanad'), brother-in-law of the Rebbe Rashab, passes away in 5654.
story_body: Rabbi Nachum Dov Twersky of Ovrutch, son of Rabbi Yitzchak Yosef of Ovrutch and brother-in-law of the Rebbe Rashab of Lubavitch, died in 5654. Surviving correspondence with chasidim such as Reb Yaakov Ayerov of Kovel includes a letter pleading on behalf of a man whose only son had been taken — likely conscripted into the Russian army.

title_en: Letter of Rabbi Menachem Nachum of Tolna for a blind chasid
summary_en: The Tolna Rebbe writes to Rabbi Avraham Yechezkel Orlozarov of Kharkov on behalf of Tzvi Surkes, who lost his sight.
story_body: Dated Thursday of Parashat Chayei Sarah 5655 in Tolna, the letter introduces Tzvi Surkes — a man who had always supported himself by his own labor until suddenly going blind. The Tolna Rebbe asks Rabbi Orlozarov, a chasid of the Rebbe Rashab, to help Surkes both financially and in securing a consultation with a professor in Kharkov.

title_en: Death of Rabbi Yochanan Twersky of Rachmistrivka
summary_en: Rabbi Yochanan of Rachmistrivka, son of Rabbi Mordechai of Chernobyl, passes away in 5655.
story_body: Rabbi Yochanan of Rachmistrivka died in 5655. After his death, his son Rabbi David of Zlatopol no longer signed letters as 'son of the master, may he live,' a change that allows researchers to date a surviving emissary-letter of his to before 5655.

title_en: Rabbi Yisrael Shalom Yosef of Mezhibuzh appoints Asher Zelig Muterperel as rabbi of Michelfaliye
summary_en: From Mezhibuzh, Rabbi Yisrael Shalom Yosef writes to the leaders of Michelfaliye endorsing Asher Zelig Muterperel as their new rabbi.
story_body: Dated Parashat Acharei 5658 in Mezhibuzh, the letter approves Asher Zelig Muterperel — son of Rabbi Shalom of Ba'ar — to succeed his late father-in-law as rabbi of Michelfaliye. The rebbe instructs the community to support him generously so 'no stranger shall sit on his throne' and so he can devote himself to study.

title_en: Death of Rabbi Mordechai Twersky of Loyev
summary_en: Rabbi Mordechai of Loyev, son of Rabbi Menachem Nachum, dies in 5671.
story_body: Rabbi Mordechai of Loyev died in 5671, providing the latest possible date for his surviving letter of recommendation on behalf of a chasid seeking to settle in the Land of Israel. That letter, addressed to communities including Brahin, Layev, Mazyr, Rechitsa, and Bobruisk, also references the 'great rabbi of Lubavitch' (Maharash or Rashab) who interceded for the petitioner.

title_en: Mordechai Perl delivers Ruzhin family letters to the Lubavitcher Rebbe
summary_en: In 5751, Mordechai Perl brings the Lubavitcher Rebbe a cache of letters from the Ruzhiner and his descendants, carried from Moscow.
story_body: In 5751 (1991), Mordechai Perl carried from Moscow to the Lubavitcher Rebbe a letter of Rabbi Yisrael of Ruzhin together with letters from his sons and grandsons — the rebbes of Chortkov, Sadigura, Husiatyn, and Mezhibuzh. Perl had inherited the letters from his father Yitzchak Dov Muterperel and grandfather Rabbi Asher Zelig Muterperel, rabbi of Michelfaliye.

title_en: Rebbe Maharash sends business and shidduch advice via secretary Levi Yitzchak Idelevitz
summary_en: On 17 Av 5639, the Rebbe Maharash dictated a reply through his secretary to the chassid R' Yaakov Ayerov, endorsing a proposal from the town of Kalk and reporting on his improving health.
story_body: The Rebbe Maharash often communicated with chassidim through his secretary R' Levi Yitzchak Idelevitz. In this letter, written on Wednesday 17 Menachem Av 5639 (1879), the Rebbe advises Yaakov Ayerov — likely on a match for one of his sons — that the proposal from Kalk seems good and that he should look into it carefully. The note also reports that the Rebbe's health has improved, helping fix the dating to 5639.

title_en: Rebbe Maharash advises chassid Shmuel Dovber of Borisov on Pleshchenitz trade
summary_en: During Chanukah 5633, the Rebbe Maharash, through his secretary, instructed the chassid R' Shmuel Dovber of Borisov (the Reshadam) to travel to Pleshchenitz and proceed with a merchandise purchase.
story_body: The Reshadam had written to ask whether to travel to Pleshchenitz to buy goods at a favorable price. The Rebbe's reply, sent through Levi Yitzchak Idelevitz on the 7th day of Chanukah 5633 (December 1872), told him to set the merchant's letter aside and make the trip. The exchange shows how the Maharash gave concrete commercial guidance to chassidim engaged in trade.

title_en: Reshadam writes Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum of Pleshchenitz about a halachic question
summary_en: On 6 Tevet 5633, R' Shmuel Dovber of Borisov wrote R' Avraham Chaim Rosenbaum of Pleshchenitz to reconcile a written Pesikta source with an oral ruling Rosenbaum had transmitted.
story_body: Writing on motzaei Shabbat, 6 Tevet 5633 (December 1872), the Reshadam tells Rosenbaum that the Pesikta passage just received from the post and an oral ruling reported in Rosenbaum's name appear to contradict one another. He treats the printed source as 'halacha v'ein morin kein' because of the risk involved, and asks for a clear practical clarification before an awaited visitor arrives for the last days of Chanukah.

title_en: Rebbe Maharid of Ladi writes Avraham Avli Person on business and family
summary_en: On 12 Kislev 5624, R' Yitzchak Dovber of Ladi, son of R' Chaim Shneur Zalman and grandson of the Tzemach Tzedek, wrote to the chassid Avraham Avli Person with business counsel and family news.
story_body: The future Admor Maharid of Ladi, author of Siddur Maharid, encouraged Person to keep faith despite slow earnings and to actively seek commissions. He recounted a visit from R' Moshe and his only son, who agreed to set up a shop, and asked Person to send him a commission. He also reported that the Tzemach Tzedek and his own father R' Chaim Shneur Zalman were both in good health.

title_en: Russian Jewish statute of 1804 permits chassidim to build separate synagogues
summary_en: The 1804 Russian Jewish statute, in §53, allowed a faction within a community that could not coexist with the other in one synagogue to build its own and appoint its own rabbis.
story_body: Following years of informing against the chassidim that culminated in the Alter Rebbe's arrest, the imperial Jewish statute of 5564 (1804) codified the right of a divided community to split. Chassidim used §53 to found their own minyanim across many towns; the same paragraph was later cited in denunciations against the Alter Rebbe. In Pleshchenitz, for example, chassidim long blocked from a separate shul finally invoked this right to build a chassidisher shtibl.

title_en: Mittler Rebbe urges Mordechai and Yehuda to help build a chassidic shul in their town
summary_en: The Mittler Rebbe wrote two chassidim to join R' Yehuda Leib in handling synagogue construction and other community needs so that the latter could resume Torah study and avodah.
story_body: Anash in one town had loaded the entire burden of building their new chassidic synagogue and managing communal affairs onto R' Yehuda Leib, leaving him no time for learning. The Mittler Rebbe asked R' Mordechai and R' Yehuda to take a share of the work, promising that the merit of the public would stand them in good stead. The undated letter belongs to the years after the 1804 statute opened the way for separate chassidic shuls.

title_en: Pinkas of the Malbish Arumim clothing-the-poor society renewed in Lubavitch
summary_en: On 18 Marcheshvan 5620 in Lubavitch, a fire-damaged clothing-the-poor society was reconstituted with a new ledger, endorsed by the Tzemach Tzedek and pledged to by his sons and grandsons.
story_body: An earlier Malbish Arumim chevra in Lubavitch had collapsed after fire destroyed its pinkas, ending weekly donations that had clothed poor children, especially those attending cheder. On 18 Cheshvan 5620 (November 14, 1859), townsmen reorganized the society in a new pinkas, with the Tzemach Tzedek adding his haskama and his sons and grandsons — including R' Menachem (son of Maharash), R' Baruch Shalom, R' Yehuda Leib of Kopust, R' Chaim Shneur Zalman of Ladi and others — pledging annual contributions.

title_en: R' Avraham Dovid Lavut moves from Romanovka to Nikolaev
summary_en: In 5616, the chassidic scholar R' Avraham Dovid Lavut — later the Rebbe's grandfather — left Romanovka, where he had run a yeshiva and talmud Torah, to take up the rabbinate of Nikolaev.
story_body: Lavut, author of Kav Naki, headed a yeshiva and talmud Torah in Romanovka and was its mora d'asra. A surviving letter of support signed by the Tzemach Tzedek's sons R' Chaim Shneur Zalman, R' Yehuda Leib and R' Yisrael Noach urging anash to back this yeshiva must therefore date between 5605 and 5615. In 5616 (1856) Lavut relocated to Nikolaev, a move that brackets the latest possible date of the letter.

title_en: Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva founded in Lubavitch
summary_en: Tomchei Tmimim was founded in Lubavitch in 5657, soon developing departments for younger bachurim and for advanced avreichim training to be poskim.
story_body: Established by the Rebbe Rashab, Tomchei Tmimim quickly gathered cohorts of select bachurim and provided their full upkeep, including clothing and footwear for poor students. A later department for outstanding avreichim — men close to receiving semicha for hora'ah — was added, with the institution also covering their families' needs. Letters of support from the rabbis of Nikolaev, including the Rebbe's maternal grandfather R' Meir Shlomo Yanovsky, were solicited as enrollment grew and resources tightened.

title_en: Apatov chassidic shul founded in Vilna
summary_en: The Apatov synagogue at 21 Vilenskaya Street in Vilna was founded around 5610.
story_body: Apatov served as a Chassidic house of prayer in Vilna for decades before it was acquired by Chabad. Its existence within a city long associated with the misnagdim made it a logistical anchor for Chabad activity in Lithuania. The shul would later host both a major rabbinical conference and a branch of Tomchei Tmimim.

title_en: Chabad chassidim in Vilna purchase the Apatov synagogue
summary_en: In the winter of 5669, Chabad chassidim in Vilna bought the Apatov synagogue at 21 Vilenskaya Street.
story_body: The purchase gave Vilna's Chabad community a permanent base and is documented in a letter of Rebbe Rayatz (Igrot Kodesh vol. 1, letter 25). The same building would later host the Vilna branch of Tomchei Tmimim. Its acquisition came just months before a major rabbinical conference convened in the city.

title_en: Rabbinical conference convenes in Vilna in Iyar 5669
summary_en: A rabbinical conference was held in Vilna from 12 to 20 Iyar 5669, with the Rebbe Rashab among its conveners and leading participants.
story_body: The Rebbe Rashab was one of the conveners and chief figures of the gathering, whose details are recorded in Igrot Kodesh of the Rashab (vol. 4, letter 1029, with introduction p. 26). Beyond formal sessions, the visit brought the Rebbe Rashab into the newly acquired Apatov shul on Lag BaOmer, where he delivered a chassidic discourse.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab visits the Apatov shul in Vilna on Lag BaOmer 5669
summary_en: On Lag BaOmer 5669, while in Vilna for the rabbinical conference, the Rebbe Rashab visited the Apatov shul and delivered a maamar there.
story_body: The visit is recorded in a letter of the Rebbe Rayatz (Igrot Kodesh vol. 1, letter 171). Coming during the Iyar 5669 rabbinical conference, it strengthened the standing of the newly acquired Chabad synagogue in Vilna. The discourse left a lasting impression on the local Chabad community.

title_en: Anash in Vilna establish a Tomchei Tmimim branch at the Apatov shul
summary_en: In early spring 5687, chassidim in Vilna moved to found a branch of Tomchei Tmimim inside the Apatov synagogue.
story_body: The initiative is described in HaTamim issue 2, p. 133. It was driven by local Chabad askanim and would be staffed in time by figures including Eliyahu Weitz, Shneur Zalman Zeligson, Moshe Katzenelson and Chaim Shpreiregen. The Rebbe Rayatz responded with a letter of encouragement weeks after the project was launched.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes encouragement letter to the new Vilna yeshiva branch
summary_en: On 27 Nisan 5687, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote a letter of encouragement and blessing to the chassidim founding the Vilna branch of Tomchei Tmimim.
story_body: Published in Igrot Kodesh of the Rayatz (vol. 1, letter 323), the letter responded to the spring 5687 effort by Vilna anash to launch the yeshiva at the Apatov shul. It set the institution on its formal footing under the central Tomchei Tmimim network. The branch's office was eventually housed not in the shul itself but in the office of the I. V. Levin company at 15 Kolejowa Street.

title_en: Vilna Tomchei Tmimim management issues first preserved letter
summary_en: On 4 Nisan 5689 the management of the Vilna branch of Tomchei Tmimim issued a letter signed by its committee — Weitz, Epstein, Aronowitz, Lueyev, Minkov, secretary Kapelyuvits, and Reltsnik.
story_body: The signed letter, on yeshiva letterhead and stamped with the institution's seal, documents the working committee a few years into operations. Eliyahu Weitz served as director, with a multi-member board overseeing the branch from the Levin company offices on Kolejowa Street. The branch was already a recognized communal institution, supported by monthly donations from Vilna and the region and even by an allocation from R' Chaim Ozer Grodzinski's Vaad HaYeshivos.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz appoints Yehuda Eber as spiritual director of Tomchei Tmimim Vilna
summary_en: On 19 Marcheshvan 5691, the Rebbe Rayatz sent Yehuda Eber — a Tomchei Tmimim director recently extracted from Soviet Russia — to lead the Vilna branch.
story_body: Eber, brother of the well-known R' Eliyahu of Krasnoluki, had himself been a senior figure inside the Soviet Tomchei Tmimim network before escaping with his family. The Rayatz's letter (Igrot Kodesh vol. 2, letter 498) introduces him to the Vilna leadership as a great talmid chacham and gifted young man. He served in Vilna until 5693, when he was reassigned as spiritual director of the central yeshiva in Warsaw.

title_en: Yehuda Eber transferred from Vilna to Tomchei Tmimim Warsaw
summary_en: In 5693 R' Yehuda Eber was appointed spiritual director of the central Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva in Warsaw, ending his tenure in Vilna.
story_body: Eber had run the Vilna branch since his appointment in 5691. His move to Warsaw placed him at the head of Tomchei Tmimim's flagship institution in interwar Poland. The Vilna branch continued under Eliyahu Weitz and the local committee.

title_en: Rayatz writes Vilna students after Warsaw and Polish branches flee to Vilna
summary_en: On 20 Tevet 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote to Tomchei Tmimim students newly arrived in Vilna from Warsaw and other Polish branches, urging them to recognize their situation as one of transition.
story_body: After the German invasion of Poland, students of the Warsaw yeshiva and other Polish branches fled to Vilna, joining the existing branch there. In his letter (Igrot Kodesh vol. 5, letter 1141), the Rayatz acknowledged a report relayed by R' Shmuel Zalmanov and R' M. L. Rodshtein on the temporary arrangements. He told the talmidim to internalize that the yeshiva was in a state of relocation, not stable settlement.

title_en: Rayatz writes that some Polish talmidim remain stranded in Poland
summary_en: On 17 Adar Sheni 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz wrote that part of the Polish Tomchei Tmimim talmidim were already in Vilna but others remained in Poland and would still need to be brought across.
story_body: The letter (Igrot Kodesh vol. 12, letter 4362) describes an operation still very much in progress — moving students from German-occupied territory into Vilna. It reflects the patchwork rescue of yeshiva students in the months following the invasion. The Rayatz's concern was both logistical and pastoral.

title_en: Rayatz responds to Yehoshua Isaac Baruch on Vilna talmidim and Lithuanian anash
summary_en: On 14 Sivan 5700, the Rayatz wrote R' Yehoshua Isaac Baruch acknowledging his detailed report on the Tomchei Tmimim talmidim studying in Vilna and on anash in Lithuania.
story_body: The mashpia R' Yehoshua Isaac Baruch was on the ground with the talmidim and corresponded directly with the Rayatz about their condition. The Rebbe's reply (Igrot Kodesh vol. 12, letter 4408) expresses satisfaction at the fullness of the information. Over the following year the Rayatz wrote frequently about the talmidim's situation and their eventual rescue.

title_en: Tomchei Tmimim Vilna closes; talmidim scattered or rescued via Japan
summary_en: The Vilna branch of Tomchei Tmimim ceased to exist in 5701 as some talmidim were rescued via Russia, Japan and Shanghai while others were murdered or sent to Nazi labor camps.
story_body: Across 5700–5701 the Rebbe Rayatz worked to obtain visas and travel papers for the Vilna talmidim, routing many through the Soviet Union to Japan, on to Shanghai, and ultimately to the United States and Canada. Some talmidim perished in the Shoah and others were swept into Nazi labor camps, surviving only by the end of the war. The branch that had taken root in the Apatov shul thirty-two years earlier closed with the broader destruction of Lithuanian Jewry.

title_en: Birth of R' Yochanan Gordon in Dokshitz
summary_en: R' Yochanan Gordon, who would later serve for many years as the gabbai of 770, was born on 23 Iyar 5654 in Dokshitz to R' Yisrael and Esther.
story_body: R' Yochanan Gordon, future longtime gabbai of 770 Eastern Parkway, was born in the town of Dokshitz to his father R' Yisrael and mother Esther. He recorded his birthdate of 23 Iyar 5654 himself on a 'Sefer HaChassidim' registration card filled out 17 Tevet 5723. He would go on to study at Tomchei Tmimim in Lubavitch and become a central figure in Chabad communal life in America.

title_en: R' Yochanan Gordon studies at Tomchei Tmimim Lubavitch
summary_en: R' Yochanan Gordon entered Tomchei Tmimim in Lubavitch in 5669, where he studied for eight years until 5677.
story_body: According to a self-recorded registration card, R' Yochanan Gordon learned in the Lubavitcher yeshiva Tomchei Tmimim from 5669 through 5677. This placed him at the central Chabad yeshiva during the final years of Rebbe Rashab's leadership and into the turbulent World War I period.

title_en: Founding of Gemach Shomrei Shabbos in New York
summary_en: The 'Shomrei Shabbos' free-loan society was founded in the year 5670, with its office at the Tzemach Tzedek shul on 184 Henry Street in New York.
story_body: The Shomrei Shabbos gemach (free-loan society) was established in 5670 and based at the Tzemach Tzedek synagogue at 184 Henry Street, a three-story stone building in a Jewish neighborhood of New York. Although little is known of its earliest years, the institution's location at the Chabad shul suggests it may have been founded from the outset as a Chabad chassidic gemach. R' Gershon Simson served as its first chairman.

title_en: R' Yochanan Gordon emigrates to New York
summary_en: After living in Dokshitz until 5692, R' Yochanan Gordon emigrated with his family to New York, where he established himself as a shochet u'bodek.
story_body: In 5692, R' Yochanan Gordon left his hometown of Dokshitz with his family and emigrated to New York. He set himself up in his new country as a shochet u'bodek (ritual slaughterer and inspector), a trade he had presumably been trained in earlier. This move placed him among the growing community of Lubavitcher chassidim taking root in America.

title_en: R' Yisrael Jacobson founds students' minyan in New York
