summary_en: In 5694 R' Yisrael Jacobson founded a minyan for his students, with R' Yochanan Gordon teaching Chassidus before davening and serving as baal korei.
story_body: R' Yisrael Jacobson established a minyan in New York in 5694 for the young men he was teaching. R' Yochanan Gordon played a central role: he learned Chassidus with the students before davening and served as the Torah reader. This represented one of the early efforts to transplant Lubavitcher chinuch and chassidic practice to American soil.

title_en: Founding of Achos Tmimim in New York
summary_en: The Achos Tmimim women's organization was founded in New York in 5698, with a three-man va'ad overseeing it.
story_body: In 5698 the Chabad women's organization Achos Tmimim was founded in New York. R' Yochanan Gordon learned Chassidus with the members and led farbrengens for them. The Rebbe Rayatz appointed a va'ad of three to oversee the group: Rabbi Yisrael Jacobson, Rabbi Shlomo Aharon Kazarnovsky, and R' Yochanan Gordon.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in New York and founds Agudas Chasidei Chabad
summary_en: In 5700 the Rebbe Rayatz arrived in New York and established Agudas Chasidei Chabad, with R' Yochanan Gordon appointed as one of the founding members of its hanhalah.
story_body: The Rebbe Rayatz reached New York in 5700 after his escape from Nazi-occupied Europe, and shortly thereafter founded Agudas Chasidei Chabad to organize the chassidic community in America. R' Yochanan Gordon was appointed as one of the members of its founding management. This event marked the formal beginning of organized Chabad institutional life in the United States.

title_en: Letter from Shainin in Dokshitz during wartime
summary_en: On 2 Rosh Chodesh Adar II 5700, Rabbi Aryeh Leib Shainin of Dokshitz wrote a coded letter to R' Yochanan Gordon describing wartime suffering and asking for support.
story_body: From within Nazi-shadowed Dokshitz at the height of winter 5700, Rabbi Aryeh Leib Shainin sent a disguised letter to his former townsman R' Yochanan Gordon in New York. Writing as 'Uncle Yaakov Leib Glaz,' Shainin reported that he and his wife were severely ill and begged for material support. Shainin, who had been sent to serve as rabbi of Dokshitz by the Rebbe Rayatz in 5683, would later perish in the Holocaust.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz founds Bikur Cholim department of Machne Israel
summary_en: In the summer of 5704 the Rebbe Rayatz founded the Bikur Cholim department of Machne Israel and appointed R' Yochanan Gordon as its chairman.
story_body: In summer 5704 the Rebbe Rayatz established a Bikur Cholim (visiting the sick) division within his Machne Israel organization. He appointed R' Yochanan Gordon as its chairman, leveraging Gordon's communal credibility and pastoral disposition. This was one of several institutional building blocks the Rebbe Rayatz put in place during his early American years.

title_en: Passing of R' Tzvi Hirsh Padnes, treasurer of Shomrei Shabbos
summary_en: R' Tzvi Hirsh Padnes, treasurer of the Shomrei Shabbos free-loan society, passed away on 11 Shevat 5705 and was buried the following day.
story_body: R' Tzvi Hirsh Padnes, who served as treasurer (gizbor) of the Chabad Shomrei Shabbos gemach in New York, passed away on 11 Shevat 5705 and was buried on 12 Shevat. R' Yochanan Gordon wrote a touching biographical letter about him to the Rebbe Rayatz, describing how Padnes had been orphaned young in Russia, served four years in the Russian army at Libau, fled the Russo-Japanese War to America, and spent his evenings emptying Rabbi Meir Baal HaNess pushkas for Chabad and visiting the sick. The Rebbe Rayatz responded with letters of consolation (Igros Kodesh vol. 8, nos. 2630-2631).

title_en: Passing of Rabbi Avraham Zev Sharfstein
summary_en: Rabbi Avraham Zev Sharfstein, who had served on the Shomrei Shabbos gemach management since 5707, passed away on 21 Kislev 5714.
story_body: Rabbi Avraham Zev Sharfstein, who had joined the management of the Shomrei Shabbos free-loan society in 5707 to fill R' Tzvi Hirsh Padnes's place, passed away on 21 Kislev 5714. After his death, R' Yochanan Gordon ran the gemach kupah by himself until his own final day on Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5729.

title_en: Passing of R' Yochanan Gordon
summary_en: R' Yochanan Gordon, longtime gabbai of 770 and director of the Shomrei Shabbos gemach, passed away on Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5729.
story_body: R' Yochanan Gordon, the longtime gabbai of 770 Eastern Parkway and a fixture of Chabad communal institutions in New York, passed away on Erev Rosh Chodesh Elul 5729. After his death, leadership of the Shomrei Shabbos gemach he had directed alone since 5714 passed to his son-in-law R' Shimon Goldman, who continued its work for many years thereafter.

title_en: Ancient ketubah from Crimea
summary_en: A ketubah dated 21 Av 5440 from Krasov in Crimea records the marriage of Menachem ben Yosef to Sara bat Gershon Ashkenazi, with a dowry of 49,148 lakhans.
story_body: Among the more than fifty ancient ketubot in the Lubavitcher library archive is one from Krasov (Karasubazar) in Crimea, dated 21 Av 5440. The document records the union of Menachem ben Yosef Walid with Sara bat Gershon Ashkenazi; her dowry — including gold jewelry, silverware, garments listed in Tatar, copper vessels, and bedding — totaled 44,680 lakhans, to which the groom added 4,468 for a total of 49,148 lakhans in the coin of Murat Giray. The ketubah reached the Rebbe Rayatz in 5685 through the bibliographer R' Shmuel Wiener.

title_en: Ancient Moroccan ketubah
summary_en: A decorated parchment ketubah dated 8 Cheshvan 5420, apparently from Morocco, records the marriage of Avraham to Esther bat Massoud ibn Attiyah.
story_body: A second ancient ketubah in the Lubavitcher archive, discovered inside the binding of an old library book, is written on parchment in square and Sephardic Rashi script with decorative ornamentation. Dated 8 Cheshvan 5420 (with the place name partially damaged but appearing to be in Morocco), it records the wedding of a groom named Avraham to the maiden Esther bat Massoud ibn Attiyah.

title_en: Tnaim signed between Rebbe Rashab and Rebbetzin Sterna Sara
summary_en: On 10 Sivan 5625 the engagement contract was written between the four-and-a-half-year-old Rebbe Rashab and his cousin Sterna Sara, with the Tzemach Tzedek personally inscribing the opening line and a financial pledge.
story_body: On 10 Sivan 5625, while the future Rebbe Rashab was just four and a half years old, his tnaim were signed with his cousin Sterna Sara, daughter of the Admor Maharin of Ovruch. The Tzemach Tzedek — grandfather of both bride and groom and just ten months before his own passing — personally inscribed the opening blessing on both copies and added on the reverse a pledge to give the couple 50 rubles every year, totaling 500 rubles. The contract stipulated that the wedding itself would take place in Jerusalem in the summer of 5635.

title_en: Wedding of Rebbe Rashab in Ovruch
summary_en: On Motzaei Shabbos 11 Elul 5635, the Rebbe Rashab married Rebbetzin Sterna Sara in Ovruch rather than the originally planned Jerusalem.
story_body: Although the tnaim of 5625 had set the wedding for Jerusalem in summer 5635, the actual wedding of the future Rebbe Rashab to Rebbetzin Sterna Sara took place on Motzaei Shabbos 11 Elul 5635 in the city of Ovruch. The Rebbe Maharash did not attend, for various reasons; he was known to have wanted the wedding held specifically in Lubavitch, arguing that if not Jerusalem as stipulated, then Lubavitch.

title_en: Wedding invitation from the Chiddushei HaRim
summary_en: On 7 Adar Sheni 5624 the Chiddushei HaRim of Ger married his grandson Pinchas Menachem Mendel of Pilcz to his granddaughter Hendel Leah (sister of the Sfas Emes).
story_body: From Gur on Rosh Chodesh Adar II 5624, the Chiddushei HaRim wrote a wedding invitation for the union of his grandson Pinchas Menachem Mendel of Pilcz to his granddaughter Hendel Leah, sister of the future Sfas Emes. The invitation was addressed to R' Meshulam Reich, who was a son-in-law of the Rebbe Rashab the elder (son of the Tzemach Tzedek) and later served as a shadar of Kolel Chabad — through whom the letter eventually reached the archive of the Lubavitch rebbeim.

title_en: Wedding of Rachel Leah of Kopust
summary_en: On Friday 9 Tamuz 5653, R' Yaakov Halevi Vishelitzky married Rachel Leah, daughter of the Admor Maharshaz of Kopust (author of Magen Avos).
story_body: On Friday 9 Tamuz 5653 in the town of Kopust, R' Yaakov ben Avraham Yeshaya Halevi Vishelitzky married Rachel Leah, daughter of the Admor Maharshaz of Kopust — the author of Magen Avos and the senior leader of the Kopust branch of Chabad. The surviving ketubah was witnessed by Shneur Zalman David ben Moshe and Binyamin ben Shimon.

title_en: Wedding of the Lubavitcher Rebbe and Rebbetzin Chaya Mushka in Warsaw
summary_en: On Tuesday 14 Kislev 5689 the future Lubavitcher Rebbe Menachem Mendel Schneerson married Chaya Mushka, daughter of the Rebbe Rayatz, in Warsaw.
story_body: On Tuesday 14 Kislev 5689 in Warsaw, the future seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe Menachem Mendel Schneerson married Chaya Mushka, daughter of the Rebbe Rayatz. R' Yochanan Gordon recalled in a later letter that the Rebbe Rayatz had urged guests to attend by saying, 'Imagine such a wedding where the Rebbe my father will surely be present, and the Maharash and the Tzemach Tzedek and the Mitteler Rebbe and the Alter Rebbe — and perhaps the Baal Shem Tov.'

title_en: Sefer Ohr HaMeir presented to the Rebbe at his wedding
summary_en: At the Rebbe's wedding on 14 Kislev 5689 in Warsaw, Rabbi Meir Shapiro presented his responsa work Ohr HaMeir inscribed as a 'drasha gift.'
story_body: At the Rebbe's wedding in Warsaw on 14 Kislev 5689, Rabbi Yehuda Meir Shapiro — founder of Yeshivas Chachmei Lublin and originator of the Daf Yomi — presented his responsa work Ohr HaMeir as a drasha gift. He inscribed it: 'A drasha gift to the choicest of vines, sons of holy supernal fathers, on the wedding day, 3 Vayishlach 5689, in Warsaw.' The Rebbe Rayatz directed his son-in-law to engage Rabbi Shapiro in Torah discussion at the wedding.

title_en: Sefer Ohr Sameach presented to the Rebbe at his wedding
summary_en: The Gaon R' Meir Simcha HaKohen of Dvinsk presented his Ohr Sameach commentary on the Rambam to the Rebbe at his wedding on 14 Kislev 5689.
story_body: Among the books the Rebbe received at his wedding on 14 Kislev 5689 was the Ohr Sameach commentary on the Rambam by R' Meir Simcha HaKohen of Dvinsk. The Rebbe himself inscribed the title page: 'From the books of Menachem Schneersohn, 14 Kislev 5689.'

title_en: Rebbetzin Sterna Sara's letter from Riga about the impending wedding
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Kislev 5689 from Riga, Rebbetzin Sterna Sara wrote to Rabbi Eliezerov about the family's difficult years in Russia and her impressions of her future grandson-in-law.
story_body: On Rosh Chodesh Kislev 5689 from Riga, Rebbetzin Sterna Sara wrote in Yiddish to her relative Rabbi Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov, describing the hardships the family had endured in Soviet Russia and the joyous transition to her granddaughter Chaya Mushka's upcoming wedding. She told him she had recently had the opportunity to meet his nephew the chosson Menachem Mendel and found him 'a quite distinguished young man,' inviting Eliezerov to share in the simcha even from afar.

title_en: Wedding of Sheina daughter of the Rebbe Rayatz
summary_en: On Tuesday 10 Sivan 5692, Sheina daughter of the Rebbe Rayatz married her cousin R' Menachem Mendel HaKohen Horenstein, both later murdered in the Holocaust.
story_body: On Tuesday 10 Sivan 5692, Sheina daughter of the Rebbe Rayatz married her cousin R' Menachem Mendel HaKohen Horenstein, son of R' Moshe HaKohen Horenstein who had been a son-in-law of the Rebbe Maharash. Their tnaim had been written several weeks earlier on Lag B'Omer of that year, in the Rebbe Rayatz's own hand. Sheina and her husband would later be murdered in the Holocaust, Hashem yikom damam.

title_en: Tnaim of Sheina written in Rebbe Rayatz's own hand
summary_en: On Lag B'Omer 5692, the Rebbe Rayatz personally wrote the text of the tnaim for his daughter Sheina's engagement to R' Menachem Mendel Horenstein.
story_body: On Lag B'Omer 5692, several weeks before his daughter Sheina's wedding, the Rebbe Rayatz personally wrote the precise text of her tnaim — modeled on those of his daughter Chana — and handed it to the scribe to copy out fair. The original autograph version survives, along with the witnessed scribal copy signed by R' Yaakov Halevi Horowitz of Riga and the Rayatz's secretary R' Yechezkel Feigin (later murdered by the Soviets).

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz sends R' Aryeh Leib Shainin to Dokshitz
summary_en: In 5683 the Rebbe Rayatz dispatched R' Aryeh Leib Shainin — a top student of Tomchei Tmimim — to serve as rabbi and mashpia in Dokshitz.
story_body: In 5683 the Rebbe Rayatz sent R' Aryeh Leib Shainin to the town of Dokshitz to serve as its rabbi and mashpia. Shainin had been one of the most outstanding talmidim of Tomchei Tmimim in Lubavitch — the Rebbe Rashab reportedly said that the entire founding of Tomchei Tmimim had been worthwhile for him alone. Shainin lived in Dokshitz until the Second World War and was murdered there in the Holocaust.

title_en: Krasov ketubah enters the Rebbe Rayatz's archive
summary_en: In 5685 the bibliographer R' Shmuel Wiener transmitted the 5440 Krasov ketubah to the Rebbe Rayatz, where it was added to the library archive.
story_body: In 5685, the bibliographer R' Shmuel Wiener — known for his scholarly catalogues of Jewish manuscripts — transmitted an extraordinary ketubah from 5440 Crimea to the Rebbe Rayatz. It eventually became part of the Lubavitcher library's collection of more than fifty antique ketubot of over a century in age.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz sends letter of encouragement to Shomrei Shabbos gemach
summary_en: In 5702 the Rebbe Rayatz sent a letter of encouragement together with a check to the Shomrei Shabbos free-loan society, asking to participate in their good works.
story_body: The earliest documented contact between the Rebbe Rayatz and the Chabad Shomrei Shabbos gemach is a 5702 letter in which the Rebbe sent encouragement together with a check, asking 'to participate with them in their good actions.' This was during the Rebbe Rayatz's early American years and the height of World War II.

title_en: Passing of the Maharshaz of Kopust, author of Magen Avos
summary_en: The Admor Shlomo Zalman of Kopust, author of Magen Avos and son of the Admor Maharil of Kopust, passed away in the year 5660.
story_body: The Admor Shlomo Zalman of Kopust, son of the Admor Maharil and grandson of the Tzemach Tzedek, lived until 5660. Known for his work Magen Avos, he had assumed his father's place in Kopust from 5627 onward and was the senior figure of the Kopust branch of Chabad.

title_en: Passing of the Maharshan of Bobruisk
summary_en: The Admor Shmaryahu Noach of Bobruisk, who had succeeded his brother as leader of the Kopust line, passed away in 5683.
story_body: The Admor Shmaryahu Noach of Bobruisk, brother of the Maharshaz of Kopust, took his brother's place after the latter's passing in 5660 and continued to lead until his own death in 5683. He represented the Bobruisk-Kopust continuation of the Tzemach Tzedek's offspring dynasty alongside the main Lubavitcher line.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz announces Torah scroll to greet Moshiach
summary_en: At the Simchat Torah 5702 farbrengen, the Rebbe Rayatz declared his decision to begin writing a Torah scroll with which to greet Moshiach.
story_body: On Simchat Torah 5702 (October 1941), the Frierdiker Rebbe, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, announced his decision to commission the writing of a Sefer Torah 'to greet Moshiach with.' After the holiday he publicized the initiative to chassidim across the world so that anyone who wished could take part in purchasing letters. This was launched amid the devastation of World War II as a call to spiritual mobilization and faith in the imminent redemption.

title_en: Rabbi Shila Eliezerov notifies Rabbi Zevin of Moshiach Torah scroll
summary_en: Rabbi Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov informed Rabbi Shlomo Yosef Zevin by letter of the Rebbe Rayatz's telegram about the Moshiach Torah scroll.
story_body: Shortly after Simchat Torah 5702, Rabbi Shlomo Yehuda Leib Eliezerov (Shila), the Rebbe's representative in the Land of Israel, wrote to Rabbi Shlomo Yosef Zevin notifying him of a telegram received from the Frierdiker Rebbe announcing his decision to write a Torah scroll to greet Moshiach. Anash in Eretz Yisrael immediately began purchasing letters in the scroll, and the Kollel secretary recorded 156 buyers in a special ledger. Among the registrants were Rabbi A.C. Naeh, Rabbi Yaakov Landau of Bnei Brak, Rabbi Yaakov Yisrael Kanievsky, and Rabbi Zevin himself.

title_en: Completion of the Moshiach Sefer Torah
summary_en: The writing of the Sefer Torah to greet Moshiach, begun by the Rebbe Rayatz in 5702, was completed on Erev Shabbos, 10 Shevat 5730.
story_body: On Friday, 10 Shevat 5730 (January 16, 1970), nearly 28 years after the project was launched by the Frierdiker Rebbe in 5702, the writing of the Sefer Torah to greet Moshiach was finally completed. The date coincided with the yahrzeit of the Rebbe Rayatz, whose initiative it had been. The siyum marked the conclusion of a worldwide undertaking in which chassidim from many lands had purchased letters.

title_en: Lubavitch Library exhibition hall opens
summary_en: The exhibition hall of the Library of Agudas Chassidei Chabad opened to the public on Chai Elul 5754.
story_body: On Chai Elul 5754 (August 1994) the Lubavitch Library inaugurated its exhibition hall in Brooklyn, opening selected treasures from the archive to the broader public. The library had previously been intended only for researchers, rabbis and authors, but the Rebbe had earlier approved opening an exhibition once a suitable space became available. The first exhibit, which ran until Erev Rosh Chodesh Kislev 5755, featured items connected to each of the Chabad Rebbes and to every area of Chabad activity.

title_en: First Library exhibition closes
summary_en: The inaugural Lubavitch Library exhibition closed on Erev Rosh Chodesh Kislev 5755.
story_body: The first exhibition of the Lubavitch Library, which opened on Chai Elul 5754, closed on Erev Rosh Chodesh Kislev 5755 (early November 1994). It had displayed items linked to each of the Chabad Rebbes and to every sphere of Chabad activity. The exhibit established what would become a regular practice of mounting themed exhibitions every year or two.

title_en: Exhibition on Chabad in the World and Torah Giants
summary_en: The Library's second exhibition, on Chabad worldwide and Torah and Chassidic leaders, ran from Rosh Chodesh Sivan through after 3 Tammuz 5755.
story_body: Opening on Rosh Chodesh Sivan 5755 and continuing past the yahrzeit of the Rebbe on 3 Tammuz, this exhibition focused on the Rebbe, the Chabad Rebbes, and gedolei Yisrael, alongside the spread of Chabad activity around the world. It emphasized the leadership era of the Rebbe Rayatz and the early years of the Rebbe's nesius, when Chabad activity expanded globally. Items included photographs, letters, signs and artifacts from Chabad centers in Russia, Eretz Yisrael, Europe, America and beyond.

title_en: Exhibition of Haggadot in the Library
summary_en: The Library mounted an exhibition of Passover Haggadot in spring 5756.
story_body: In the spring of 5756 (1996), the Lubavitch Library presented an exhibition devoted to the collection of Passover Haggadot held in its archive. It was the third themed exhibition since the hall opened in 5754. The display drew on the library's rare-book holdings of early and unusual printed editions of the Haggadah.

title_en: Exhibition of Rabbeinu Nesieinu (1996)
summary_en: An exhibition devoted to the Chabad Rebbes was held at the Library in late 5756.
story_body: Toward the end of the year 5756 (1996), the Lubavitch Library held an exhibition focused on the Chabad Rebbes. It was the fourth in the series of themed exhibitions launched after the hall opened in 5754. The display drew on manuscripts, photographs and personal items connected to each successive Rebbe.

title_en: Exhibition on Chabad, Shlichus and the Mivtzaim
summary_en: The Library's summer 5757 exhibition focused on Chabad activity, shlichus and the mitzvah campaigns.
story_body: In the summer of 5757 (1997), the Lubavitch Library presented an exhibition on Chabad's worldwide activity, the work of shluchim, and the Rebbe's mivtzaim—campaigns to spread observance of mitzvos such as tefillin, mezuzah, Shabbos candles, kashrus and the four species. The exhibit displayed candle-lighting sets, tzedakah boxes, menorahs, mivtza tanks' keys and other items sent to the Rebbe from Chabad centers around the world.

title_en: Exhibition of Chassidus
summary_en: The Library held an exhibition devoted to Chassidus in summer 5758.
story_body: The summer 5758 (1998) exhibition at the Lubavitch Library was dedicated to the broader Chassidic movement. It was the sixth in the rotation of themed exhibitions begun in 5754. The display drew on the library's holdings of early Chassidic books, manuscripts and related artifacts.

title_en: Exhibition on the Alter Rebbe's 200th liberation anniversary
summary_en: The Library mounted an exhibition marking 200 years since the Alter Rebbe's liberation, in winter 5759.
story_body: In the winter of 5759 (1998–99), the Lubavitch Library presented an exhibition marking the 200th anniversary of the liberation of the Alter Rebbe, Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, from Czarist imprisonment on Yud Tes Kislev. Exhibits included items associated with the Alter Rebbe, such as a first edition of his Shulchan Aruch (Kapust 5574) and the first edition of Tanya (Slavita 5557), as well as a handwritten letter.

title_en: Exhibition on the Rebbe Rayatz
summary_en: The Library's summer 5760 exhibition was devoted to the Rebbe Rayatz.
story_body: In the summer of 5760 (2000), the Lubavitch Library held an exhibition dedicated to the sixth Rebbe, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn (Rayatz). Exhibits drew on his manuscripts, the spodik he wore, his writing implements and items from his secretariat. It was the eighth in the library's series of themed exhibits.

title_en: Exhibition of the Rebbeim's books
summary_en: The Lubavitch Library held an exhibition of books authored by the Chabad Rebbes in 5762.
story_body: During the year 5762 (2001–02), the library displayed first editions and other significant printings of works authored by the Chabad Rebbes. The exhibit included items such as the first edition of Maggid Devarav LeYaakov (Koretz 5541), Imrei Binah (Kapust 5581) and Tzemach Tzedek (Vilna 5631). It was the ninth themed exhibit since the hall opened in 5754.

title_en: Exhibition of certificates of honor to the Rebbe
summary_en: The Library mounted an exhibition of honorary certificates given to the Rebbe in spring 5765.
story_body: In the spring of 5765 (2005), the Lubavitch Library held an exhibition focused on the honorary certificates, keys, medals and scrolls of honor presented to the Rebbe by heads of state, mayors, military commanders and institutional leaders. It was the tenth themed exhibit since the hall opened in 5754.

title_en: MiBeis HaGenazim exhibition and album
summary_en: The Library held the 'MiBeis HaGenazim' exhibition in winter 5770 and printed an accompanying album of 154 archive items.
story_body: In the winter of 5770 (2009–10), the Lubavitch Library presented its eleventh exhibition, titled 'MiBeis HaGenazim,' surveying treasures held in the archive. A printed album of the same name accompanied the exhibit, documenting 154 special items preserved in the library's collection. The volume later served as a model for a successor work compiled in 5778.

title_en: Exhibition of keys and certificates of honor
summary_en: The Lubavitch Library held an exhibition of keys and certificates of honor in summer 5773.
story_body: In the summer of 5773 (2013), the Lubavitch Library presented an exhibition focused on keys and honorary certificates given to the Rebbe. It was the twelfth themed exhibition in the hall since 5754. Items displayed included tokens sent by municipalities, governments and institutions around the world.

title_en: Exhibition of book treasures
summary_en: The Library mounted a 'Treasures of Books' exhibition in summer 5774.
story_body: In the summer of 5774 (2014), the Lubavitch Library held an exhibition of rare books and bibliographic treasures from its collection. It was the thirteenth themed exhibit since the hall opened in 5754. The library's holdings include some 200,000 books, many of them incunabula and first editions.

title_en: Exhibition on the Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: The Library held an exhibition on the Tzemach Tzedek in winter 5776.
story_body: In the winter of 5776 (2015–16), the Lubavitch Library presented its fourteenth themed exhibit, devoted to the third Chabad Rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn, the Tzemach Tzedek. The display drew on his manuscripts, his Tanach (used for reading the Haftarah), his siddur and the first edition of his responsa work, Tzemach Tzedek (Vilna 5631).

title_en: Exhibition of Rabbeinu Nesieinu (2017)
summary_en: The Library's spring 5777 exhibition was devoted to the Chabad Rebbes.
story_body: In the spring of 5777 (2017), the Lubavitch Library held its fifteenth themed exhibit, again focused on the Chabad Rebbes. The display included manuscripts in the handwriting of each successive Rebbe, personal items such as the Mitteler Rebbe's tefillin pouch and the Rebbe Rashab's passport, and selected first editions of their works.

title_en: Sequel to 'MiBeis HaGenazim' published
summary_en: A sequel volume to 'MiBeis HaGenazim' was completed by Rabbi Shalom Dovber Levin in Brooklyn on 5 Teves 5778.
story_body: On 5 Teves 5778 (December 2017), Rabbi Shalom Dovber Levin, director of the Lubavitch Library, signed the preface to a new book continuing the work of the earlier album 'MiBeis HaGenazim,' which had accompanied the winter 5770 exhibition. The new volume collected the guide booklets the library had printed for each exhibition since 5754, together with summaries of those exhibits for which no booklet had been printed. Together the book documented 15 exhibitions across more than two decades.

title_en: Rebbe calls for women and girls to light Shabbos candles
summary_en: Toward the end of 5734 the Rebbe issued a special call for every Jewish woman and girl of educational age to light Shabbos and Yom Tov candles.
story_body: From the latter part of 5734 (1974), the Rebbe began issuing a special public call that every Jewish woman and girl light Shabbos and Yom Tov candles, including unmarried girls from the age of chinuch. The campaign produced candlesticks, explanatory literature in many languages, and outreach materials distributed by Chabad centers worldwide. It became one of the Rebbe's signature mitzvah campaigns.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab founds Tomchei Temimim Yeshiva
summary_en: In 5657 the Rebbe Rashab founded the Tomchei Temimim Lubavitch yeshiva.
story_body: In the year 5657 (1897), Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn (the Rebbe Rashab) founded the yeshiva 'Tomchei Temimim Lubavitch.' Over subsequent years it expanded to dozens of branches across Russia, operating openly at first and then underground after Soviet persecution intensified. The yeshiva became the backbone of Chabad's educational network in Russia.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab's public letter in Iyar 5677
summary_en: In Iyar 5677, during the Kerensky era in Russia, the Rebbe Rashab published a general letter.
story_body: In Iyar 5677 (May 1917), during the brief Kerensky government in revolutionary Russia, Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn (the Rebbe Rashab) issued a general public letter, later printed in his Igros Kodesh, vol. II, no. 469. The letter addressed his Chassidim during a turbulent period preceding the Bolshevik takeover.

title_en: Chassidim in Russia begin sending photos to Rebbe Rayatz
summary_en: In summer 5693 Chassidim in Russia began the practice of sending personal photos to the Rebbe Rayatz.
story_body: In the summer of 5693 (1933), several years after the Rebbe Rayatz was forced to leave Russia and settled in Riga, a custom arose among anash in Russia of sending personal photographs to the Rebbe. Persecution of Chabad in Russia was intensifying, and the Rebbe encouraged the practice in a general letter (Igros Kodesh II, no. 633), writing that seeing the families' faces brought him great joy.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab's passing on 2 Nissan 5680
summary_en: Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn, the Rebbe Rashab, passed away on 2 Nissan 5680.
story_body: Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn, the fifth Lubavitcher Rebbe known as the Rebbe Rashab, passed away on 2 Nissan 5680 (March 21, 1920). His son, the Rebbe Rayatz, subsequently recorded a chart of all the Chabad Rebbeim's lifespans and resting places. He had marked the place where he had stopped learning in a sefer some ten days before his passing.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz stays in Otwock for Tishrei 5691
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz stayed in Otwock during Tishrei 5691, as reported in the local press.
story_body: During Tishrei 5691 (autumn 1930), Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn (the Rebbe Rayatz) stayed in the Polish town of Otwock, as reported by the local 'Otwocker Tzeitung.' The visit drew significant local attention. The Library preserves a copy of the newspaper edition reporting on his stay.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz passes away on 10 Shevat 5710
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, the Rebbe Rayatz, passed away on 10 Shevat 5710.
story_body: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, the sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe, passed away on 10 Shevat 5710 (January 28, 1950). The pencil he used continuously in his final years was preserved by his secretary, Rabbi Nissan Mindel. His son-in-law, the Rebbe, wrote in a letter dated 20 Shevat 5710 that the loss had left Chassidim stunned but resolved to continue with even greater strength.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's first edition published in Vilna
summary_en: The first edition of the responsa work 'Tzemach Tzedek' was published in Vilna in 5631.
story_body: In 5631 (1871), the first edition of the responsa work 'Tzemach Tzedek' by Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn was published in Vilna. The book gathered the halachic responsa of the third Chabad Rebbe. A copy of this first edition is preserved in the Lubavitch Library.

title_en: Likkutei Torah with Rebbe Maharash's annotations published
summary_en: Likkutei Torah on three parshiyos with annotations of the Rebbe Maharash was printed in Vilna in 5644.
story_body: In 5644 (1884), an edition of Likkutei Torah on three parshiyos was printed in Vilna incorporating annotations of Rabbi Shmuel Schneersohn, the Rebbe Maharash. The Lubavitch Library preserves a copy of this edition. The work transmits Chassidic discourses of the Alter Rebbe with later commentary.

title_en: Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch first edition
summary_en: The first edition of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch was published in Kapust in 5574.
story_body: In 5574 (1814), the first edition of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch was published in Kapust. The work compiles Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi's revised rulings on Jewish law. The Lubavitch Library preserves a copy of this edition.

title_en: Tanya first edition printed in Slavita
summary_en: The first edition of the Tanya by the Alter Rebbe was printed in Slavita in 5557.
story_body: In 5557 (1797), the first edition of the Tanya, the foundational work of Chabad Chassidic thought by Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, was printed in Slavita. The Lubavitch Library preserves a copy of this first edition. The book is one of Chabad's central canonical texts.

title_en: Imrei Binah first edition published in Kapust
summary_en: The first edition of Imrei Binah by the Mitteler Rebbe was published in Kapust in 5581.
story_body: In 5581 (1821), the first edition of Imrei Binah by Rabbi Dovber Schneuri, the Mitteler Rebbe, was published in Kapust. The book is a major Chassidic discourse work by the second Chabad Rebbe. A copy is preserved in the Lubavitch Library.

title_en: Maggid Devarav LeYaakov first edition published in Koretz
summary_en: The first edition of Maggid Devarav LeYaakov by the Maggid of Mezeritch was published in Koretz in 5541.
story_body: In 5541 (1781), the first edition of Maggid Devarav LeYaakov by Rabbi Dovber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, was published in Koretz. The work transmits Chassidic teachings of the Maggid, successor to the Baal Shem Tov. A copy is preserved in the Lubavitch Library.

title_en: Keser Shem Tov first edition published in Zolkiew
summary_en: The first edition of Keser Shem Tov, teachings of the Baal Shem Tov, was published in Zolkiew in 5554.
story_body: In 5554 (1794), the first edition of Keser Shem Tov, a collection of teachings of Rabbi Yisrael Baal Shem Tov, was published in Zolkiew. The Lubavitch Library preserves a copy of this first edition. The book is among the earliest printed sources for the Baal Shem Tov's teachings.

title_en: Hayom Yom first edition published
summary_en: The first edition of Hayom Yom, compiled by the Rebbe, was published in New York in 5703.
story_body: In 5703 (1942–43), the first edition of Hayom Yom was published in New York. Compiled by Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, the future Rebbe, the daily-calendar book gathers Chassidic teachings, customs and stories. The Lubavitch Library preserves a copy of this first edition.

title_en: Rebbe's Haggadah with Likkutei Minhagim first edition
summary_en: The Rebbe's Haggadah with Likkutei Minhagim u'Ta'amim was first published in New York in 5706.
story_body: In 5706 (1946), the Rebbe's Haggadah of Passover with Likkutei Minhagim u'Ta'amim was first published in New York. The work compiles Chabad customs and reasons accompanying the Pesach Haggadah. The Lubavitch Library preserves a copy of this first edition.

title_en: Kalligrapher Chaim ben Asher Anshil begins illuminated Haggadah work in Kitzee
summary_en: The famed calligrapher Chaim ben Asher Anshil began producing illuminated Haggadot and prayer books in Kitzee near Pressburg in 5501.
story_body: Between 5501 and 5542 (1741–1782), Chaim ben Asher Anshil worked as a calligrapher and illustrator in Kitzee, near Pressburg. During this period he wrote and decorated Haggadot, Birkat HaMazon booklets, and prayer texts that became prized manuscripts.

title_en: First Haggadah printed in Zhovkva
summary_en: The first Haggadah was printed in Zhovkva (Galicia) in 5510, bound with the commentary Shimon v'Levi.
story_body: In 5510 (1750), the first Haggadah of Zhovkva was printed together with the commentary Sefer Shimon v'Levi by Shimon ben Kadish HaLevi. It marked the beginning of Haggadah printing in this important Galician printing center.

title_en: Kitzee illuminated Haggadah manuscript completed
summary_en: Chaim ben Asher Anshil completed the famous illuminated Kitzee Haggadah manuscript on parchment in 5520.
story_body: In 5520 (1760), the calligrapher Chaim ben Asher Anshil of Kitzee, near Pressburg, completed his ornate manuscript Haggadah on parchment. Twenty-two leaves of square Hebrew text and Yiddish ritual instructions in tzena u'rena script were enhanced with elaborate illustrations.

title_en: First Haggadah printed in Livorno
summary_en: The Chida's Simchat HaRegel — the first Haggadah printed in Livorno — was issued in 5542.
story_body: In 5542 (1782), the Chida's commentary Simchat HaRegel was printed in Livorno by Avraham Yitzchak Estilo and Eliezer Sadoun. It was the first Haggadah ever printed in Livorno, which would become a major center of Sephardi printing.

title_en: First Haggadah printed in Hrodna
summary_en: An early Russian-imprint Haggadah with Yiddish translation in tzena u'rena script appeared in Hrodna in 5551.
story_body: In 5551 (1791), one of the first Haggadot ever printed in the Russian Empire was issued in Hrodna by the HaMelech press. It presented Hebrew text alongside a Yiddish translation in tzena u'rena script, side by side, marking an early Russian milestone in Haggadah printing.

title_en: First Haggadah printed in Warsaw
summary_en: The first Haggadah ever printed in Warsaw appeared in 5589 with the commentary Birkat HaShir.
story_body: In 5589 (1829), the first Haggadah in Warsaw was printed with the commentary Birkat HaShir by Rabbi Aryeh Leib Zintz, issued from the press of Avigdor ben Yoel Lebensohn. Warsaw would later become one of the major centers of Hebrew printing in the world.

title_en: First Haggadah printed in Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: The first Haggadah printed in the Land of Israel was issued in Jerusalem in 5602.
story_body: In 5602 (1842), the first Haggadah ever printed in the Land of Israel was issued in Jerusalem. It included necessary laws for the Seder night, the Ma'ariv prayer, and the order of counting the Omer.

title_en: First Haggadah printed in the United States
summary_en: One of the earliest American Haggadot, with English translation, was printed in New York in 5617.
story_body: Around 5617 (1857), Henry Frank printed one of the first Haggadot in the United States, in New York. The 72-page volume featured an English translation opposite the Hebrew and included illustrations.

title_en: Chabad expansion across Europe begins after Russian pogroms
summary_en: Following the pogroms in Russia from 5640 onward, Chabad began spreading across European countries.
story_body: Beginning in 5640 (1880), as a result of pogroms in Russia, Chabad communities began establishing footholds in countries across Europe. This was the first significant wave of Chabad expansion beyond the Russian Empire.

title_en: Death of Rabbi Yehuda Tzvi of Rozdol
summary_en: Admor Yehuda Tzvi Eichenstein of Rozdol, of the Kaliver chassidic dynasty, passed away in 5646.
story_body: Rabbi Yehuda Tzvi ben Shlomo Eichenstein of Rozdol, a Kaliver rebbe, passed away in 5646 (1886). He had famously prayed from a siddur once owned by the Baal Shem Tov, an inscription on which dates it to before his death.

title_en: Wiener's bibliography of Haggadot published in St. Petersburg
summary_en: Shmuel Wiener published his pioneering bibliography of 909 Haggadot in St. Petersburg in 5661.
story_body: In 5661 (1901), the bibliographer Shmuel Wiener published in Petersburg his Reshimat Haggadot-Pesach Shenidpesu B'Khol Artzot Tevel — a list of 909 editions of the Haggadah printed worldwide between 1500 and 1900. It became the foundational bibliographic reference for the Haggadah.

title_en: Tomchei Tmimim Yeshiva founded in Hebron
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab established the Torat Emet yeshiva in Hebron in 5672, dispatching a mashpia and top Lubavitcher students.
story_body: In 5672 (1911/12), the Rebbe Rashab founded the Torat Emet yeshiva in Hebron, sending a special mashpia and several outstanding students from Tomchei Tmimim Lubavitch to lead it. The yeshiva would later close during the deportations of World War I.

title_en: Tomchei Tmimim Yeshiva founded in Warsaw
summary_en: The Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva was founded in Warsaw in 5681, eventually growing to ten branches across Poland.
story_body: Tomchei Tmimim was established in Warsaw in 5681 (1921). Over the next 19 years it expanded to ten branches throughout Poland, until it was destroyed during the Holocaust.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz reopens Torat Emet yeshiva in Jerusalem
summary_en: In 5682, the Rebbe Rayatz re-established the Torat Emet yeshiva in Jerusalem after its closure in WWI.
story_body: After the Torat Emet yeshiva of Hebron had closed during World War I, the Rebbe Rayatz reopened it in Jerusalem in 5682 (1922). It has continued to operate there to the present day, with a branch also opened at the time in Jaffa.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz acquires Shmuel Wiener's collection
summary_en: In Kislev 5685, the Rebbe Rayatz purchased Shmuel Wiener's collection of about 5,000 rare books, including roughly 400 Haggadot.
story_body: In Kislev 5685 (December 1924), the Rebbe Rayatz acquired the collection of bibliographer-collector Shmuel Wiener. The acquisition of approximately 5,000 rare books — including some 400 Haggadot — formed a cornerstone of the Lubavitch library's renowned holdings.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz leaves Russia
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz was forced to leave the Soviet Union at the beginning of 5688, settling first in Riga.
story_body: At the start of 5688 (late 1927), the Rebbe Rayatz was compelled to leave the Soviet Union. He resided for several years in Riga before later relocating his household to Warsaw and then Otwock.

title_en: Anash families begin leaving Russia for Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: Between 5693 and 5698, many Anash families succeeded in leaving Russia for the Land of Israel, settling mainly in Tel Aviv.
story_body: During the years 5693–5698 (1933–1938), many Lubavitcher families managed to leave the Soviet Union and immigrate to the Land of Israel. They settled mainly in Tel Aviv, where they founded a cheder and a Tomchei Tmimim Lubavitch yeshiva.

title_en: First Haggadah printed in South America (Buenos Aires)
summary_en: The first Haggadah ever printed in South America was issued in Buenos Aires in 5694 by Yekutiel Weiss.
story_body: In 5694 (1934), Yekutiel Weiss issued the first Haggadah printed in South America, in Buenos Aires. Titled Bonah Zeret, it featured his commentary Yeku L'Or alongside the laws of Passover from the Derech HaChaim.

title_en: First Haggadah printed in Morocco
summary_en: Ya'ish Krispin's Rakik Echad — the first Haggadah printed in Morocco — appeared in Casablanca in 5695.
story_body: In 5695 (1935), the first Haggadah ever printed in Morocco was issued in Casablanca by the press of Y. Razon. The volume, titled Rakik Echad, was written by Ya'ish Krispin and was bound together with his commentary Anaf Shoshan on Pirkei Avot.

title_en: Chaim Liberman publishes list of 32 unknown Haggadot
summary_en: Chaim Liberman, librarian of the Lubavitch library, published a bibliographical list of 32 previously unknown Haggadot in 5698.
story_body: In 5698 (1938), Chaim Liberman — then director of the Rebbe's library in Warsaw — published in Kiryat Sefer (vol. 15, p. 258) a list of 32 editions of the Haggadah unknown from any other source. The Haggadot had been acquired by the Rebbe Rayatz between 5660 and 5698.

title_en: Last pre-war European Haggadah printed in Munkacs
summary_en: The Tov Devarcha Haggadah by Rabbi Shaul Brach was among the last Haggadot printed in Europe before WWII, in Munkacs in 5700.
story_body: In 5700 (1940), Rabbi Shaul Brach's son Shmuel published his father's Haggadah Tov Devarcha at the Grafia press in Munkacs. With the war engulfing Europe, it became one of the last Haggadot printed there before printing in Europe ground to a halt.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz escapes Nazi-occupied Warsaw and reaches the United States
summary_en: In the winter of 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz was miraculously rescued from Nazi-occupied Warsaw and arrived in the United States.
story_body: During the winter of 5700 (1940), the Rebbe Rayatz was miraculously saved from Nazi-occupied Warsaw and reached the United States. He spent the final ten years of his life — from 5700 to 5710 — in America, where he established institutions across the country.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz launches Pidyon Shvuyim rescue fund
summary_en: Upon arrival in the United States in 5700, the Rebbe Rayatz immediately launched a Pidyon Shvuyim fund to rescue Tmimim and Anash from Nazi-occupied Europe.
story_body: Immediately upon his arrival in the U.S. in 5700 (1940), the Rebbe Rayatz established a dedicated fund called Pidyon Shvuyim aimed at rescuing Tmimim and Anash trapped in Nazi-occupied Europe. A group of more than thirty students was eventually routed through Russia, Japan, and Shanghai to safety.

title_en: Mimeographed Haggadah produced in occupied Nice
summary_en: In 5701, a hand-written, mimeographed Haggadah following the Rambam's text was produced in Nazi-occupied Nice by Agudat HaRabbanim of Paris.
story_body: During the wartime spring of 5701 (1941), with France under Nazi occupation and printing impossible, the rabbinic association of Paris (then exiled in Nice) produced a Haggadah by hand and duplicated it on a mimeograph. The Lubavitcher Rebbe and Rebbetzin were among the Jews who had taken refuge in Nice that Passover.

title_en: Tomchei Tmimim Yeshiva established in Montreal
summary_en: In early 5702, students rescued via Russia, Japan, and Shanghai founded the Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva in Montreal.
story_body: In early 5702 (late 1941), some of the more than thirty students rescued from Nazi-occupied Europe via Russia, Japan, and Shanghai arrived in Montreal. They immediately founded the Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva there, with the rescued students themselves later becoming its leaders.

title_en: First Haggadah printed in the Far East (Shanghai)
summary_en: A Haggadah containing 238 commentaries was printed in Shanghai in 5705, the first ever in the Far East.
story_body: In 5705 (1945), a remarkable Haggadah was printed in Shanghai, containing 238 commentaries and supplementary materials. It was the first Haggadah ever printed in the Far East, produced amid the displaced Jewish community there during World War II.

title_en: First post-war Haggadah printed in Föhrenwald DP camp
summary_en: A photo-offset Haggadah was printed in the Föhrenwald DP camp in liberated Germany in 5705 for survivors.
story_body: In 5705/5706 (1945–1946), the first Haggadah in liberated Europe was printed in Föhrenwald as a photo-offset reproduction of a Warsaw edition. Produced by the YPA publishing house, it was intended for the She'erit HaPleita displaced-person camps in Germany and was supplemented with illustrations taken from other Haggadot.

title_en: First Haggadah printed in Central America (Mexico)
summary_en: The first Haggadah printed in Central America, with a Spanish translation by Z. Shipmanovich, was issued in Mexico in 5706.
story_body: In 5706 (1946), the first Haggadah ever printed in Central America was issued in Mexico City. Sponsored by Yitzchak Krochmalnik and his wife Sarah, it featured a Spanish translation by Z. Shipmanovich and was illustrated.

title_en: Mass escape of Anash from the Soviet Union
summary_en: Around 1,000 Anash succeeded in escaping the Soviet Union across the border into liberated Europe in 5706–5707.
story_body: With the end of World War II in 5706–5707 (1946–1947), a large group of about one thousand Lubavitcher chassidim managed to smuggle themselves across the Soviet border into liberated Europe. The Rebbe then asked these refugee chassidim to send him their photographs as a record of their rescue.

title_en: Lubavitcher refugee yeshivot founded in DP camps
summary_en: Refugee Anash settled in DP camps in Pocking and Steyr in 5706–5707, immediately establishing yeshivot for surviving students.
story_body: Following the mass escape from the Soviet Union in 5706–5707 (1946–1947), several hundred refugee families settled in displaced-persons camps in Pocking, Germany and Steyr, Austria. Upon arrival they founded yeshivot for the surviving students.

title_en: Lubavitchers regroup in Paris and found Brunoy yeshiva and Beis Rivka
summary_en: In 5708, most refugee Anash regrouped in Paris and founded the Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva in Brunoy and the Beis Rivka school in Yerres.
story_body: In 5708 (1948), the bulk of the Lubavitcher refugees from the DP camps gathered in Paris and then dispersed across France. They immediately founded the Tomchei Tmimim yeshiva in Brunoy and the Beis Rivka girls' school in Yerres, both of which have continued to grow until today.

title_en: R. Bentzion Shemtov dispatched to lead Chabad institutions in England
summary_en: In 5708, Rabbi Bentzion Shemtov was sent to direct Chabad educational institutions in England.
story_body: In 5708 (1948), Rabbi Bentzion Shemtov was dispatched to manage Chabad's educational institutions in England. About ten years later, his son-in-law Rabbi Nachman Sudak joined him to help with the leadership of the British Chabad institutions.

title_en: Major Aliyah of Lubavitch refugees to Eretz Yisrael
summary_en: In 5709, the bulk of Lubavitcher refugees who had escaped the Soviet Union finally reached the Land of Israel.
story_body: In 5709 (1949), a major portion of the chassidim who had fled the Soviet Union in 5706–5707 finally arrived in the Land of Israel after extensive wanderings in Europe. The yeshiva students from Tel Aviv moved to Lod, where several Anash families had settled, and reopened the yeshiva.

title_en: Kfar Chabad founded with 70 families
summary_en: Kfar Chabad was founded in 5709 by 70 families of Lubavitch refugees from the Soviet Union, settling in abandoned Arab houses.
story_body: In 5709 (1949), the majority of the Lubavitch refugees arriving in the Land of Israel settled in the newly established village of Kfar Chabad. Beginning with 70 families occupying abandoned Arab homes, the village grew over time to become the central hub of Chabad activity in Israel.

title_en: First Lubavitch families settle in Australia
summary_en: In 5709, the first Lubavitcher families from the Soviet Union exodus settled in Australia and were instructed to open educational institutions immediately.
story_body: In 5709 (1949), several Lubavitcher families from among those who had escaped the Soviet Union in 5706–5707 settled in Australia. The Rebbe instructed them to immediately establish educational institutions, and over time he dispatched additional shluchim from New York to strengthen the work.

title_en: Rebbe launches global Shluchim campaign
summary_en: Upon accepting the leadership in 5710, the Rebbe immediately began dispatching shluchim to open Chabad centers worldwide.
story_body: Immediately upon accepting the leadership of Chabad in 5710 (1950), the Rebbe began sending shluchim to establish Chabad centers in every possible city and country. During the first decade of his leadership (5710–5720), shluchim were dispatched to North Africa, Italy, England, Brazil, Argentina, Australia, the Far East, and many cities in the Land of Israel and the United States.

title_en: Vienna Haggadah with Italian translation in Latin characters
summary_en: The first Haggadah with the Italian translation printed in Latin characters was issued in Vienna in 5611 by Meir Ranbarger.
story_body: In 5611 (1851), a Haggadah with an Italian translation in Latin script, printed opposite the Hebrew, was issued in Vienna by Meir Ranbarger. Earlier Haggadot had printed the Italian translation in Hebrew characters, making this a milestone in vernacular Haggadah typography.

title_en: Yaari's comprehensive Haggadah bibliography published in Jerusalem
summary_en: Avraham Yaari's comprehensive Haggadah bibliography listing 2,717 editions was published in Jerusalem in 5721.
story_body: In 5721 (1960/61), Avraham Yaari published in Jerusalem his Bibliografia Shel Haggadot Pesach, listing 2,717 editions of the Haggadah from the dawn of printing through 5720. The bibliography drew in part on the descriptions of Haggadot in the Lubavitch library that had been sent to him by librarian Chaim Liberman.

title_en: Theodore Wiener publishes supplements to Yaari's Haggadah bibliography
summary_en: Theodore Wiener published supplements to Yaari's bibliography in Studies in Bibliography and Booklore in 5725.
story_body: In 5725 (1965), Theodore Wiener published bibliographical supplements to Avraham Yaari's Haggadah bibliography in Studies in Bibliography and Booklore, vol. VII (Cincinnati, 1965, p. 90). The supplements further refined the bibliographic record of printed Haggadot.

title_en: Mass Soviet Jewish exodus begins
summary_en: Beginning in 5726, the great exodus of Jews from the Soviet Union began, restoring contact between Russian Anash and the outside world.
story_body: Following the post-WWII period during which Russian Anash had been nearly completely cut off from those outside the Soviet Union, the great Jewish exodus from Russia began in 5726 (1966). Before this point, Chabad activity in Russia had been entirely underground, conducted via the Rebbe's secret shluchim, with photographs and printed announcements forbidden.

title_en: Haggadah with Yiddish Kabbalistic commentary printed in Frankfurt an der Oder
summary_en: A Passover Haggadah with Yiddish translation and Kabbalistic commentary was printed in Frankfurt an der Oder.
story_body: In 5549 (1789), Itzik son of Aharon Zelig, typesetter and printer, produced a Haggadah in Frankfurt an der Oder that featured the original Hebrew alongside a Yiddish translation in parallel columns. Beneath these, a Kabbalistic commentary was printed in square Hebrew letters. The final page additionally contained a Yiddish commentary on Chad Gadya in Tzene-Rene script.

title_en: First Haggadah printed with literal German translation in Cologne
summary_en: The first Haggadah with a literal German translation was printed in Cologne, including musical notation at the end.
story_body: In 5598 (1838), a Haggadah with a German translation rendered word-for-word was printed in Cologne. The 91-page volume marked a milestone as the first appearance of the Haggadah with this style of vernacular German translation. Musical notation for the Seder songs was appended at the end of the work.

title_en: Dutch translation of Sephardic Haggadah 'Kol Yaakov' printed in Amsterdam
summary_en: Jacob Lopes Cardozo published a Sephardic-rite Haggadah translated into Dutch with notes in Amsterdam.
story_body: In 5619 (1859), Jacob ben David Lopes Cardozo published 'Sefer Kol Yaakov' in Amsterdam, a Sephardic-custom Haggadah newly translated into Dutch with annotations. The 53-page edition served the Dutch-speaking Sephardic community of the Netherlands. It represented a fresh translation effort aimed at making the Seder accessible in the local vernacular.

title_en: Hungarian translation Haggadah printed in Vienna
summary_en: An illustrated Haggadah with Hungarian translation in parallel pages was printed in Vienna.
story_body: Around 5646 (1886), a Haggadah was issued in Vienna with a Hungarian translation displayed page-by-page opposite the Hebrew original. The volume included illustrations, with the laws printed in Yiddish using Tzene-Rene script and in Ladino in square letters. The 31-page edition catered to the multilingual Jewish communities of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

title_en: Ladino Haggadah 'Hamon Chogeg' by Elisha Chabilyo printed in Livorno
summary_en: Elisha Chabilyo published 'Sefer Hamon Chogeg', a Haggadah with Ladino translation and two Hebrew commentaries, in Livorno.
story_body: In 5554 (1794), Elisha Chabilyo authored 'Sefer Hamon Chogeg' which was printed in Livorno, Italy. The work presented the text of the Haggadah alongside a Ladino translation, with two Hebrew commentaries — one based on the plain meaning and the other on ethical instruction. The Hebrew original and Ladino translation were printed in vocalized square letters, passage by passage.

title_en: Latin translation of the Haggadah printed in Frankfurt
summary_en: A Haggadah with a Latin translation and musical notation for liturgical poems was printed in Frankfurt.
story_body: In 5458 (1698), a Haggadah was published in Frankfurt featuring the Hebrew text alongside a parallel Latin translation. The Hebrew was printed without vowel points, and the edition included musical notation for the songs 'Ki Lo Naeh' and 'Adir Hu'. The 70-page work made the Seder text accessible to Latin-reading scholars of the era.

title_en: Judeo-Arabic Haggadah 'Chukat HaPesach' printed in Livorno
summary_en: The 'Chukat HaPesach' Haggadah, with laws and instructions in Egyptian Judeo-Arabic, was printed in Livorno.
story_body: In 5619 (1859), 'Chukat HaPesach' was published in Livorno by Agudat Ezov, organized into three sections containing legal novellae, the Haggadah with Seder laws in Egyptian-dialect Judeo-Arabic, and a new commentary on Pirkei Avot called 'Avot u'Gevurot'. The 202-page volume also included readings for Rosh Chodesh Nissan, the offerings of the tribal princes, and the burning of leaven. It served the Arabic-speaking Sephardic communities of North Africa.

title_en: Arabic-script Haggadah translated by Hillel Farchi printed in Egypt
summary_en: Hillel Farchi published a Sephardic-custom Haggadah with an Arabic translation in Arabic script in Egypt.
story_body: In 5677 (1917), Hillel Farchi produced a Haggadah following Sephardic customs accompanied by an Arabic translation rendered in Arabic letters. Printed by Reuven Muskovitch in Egypt, the 42-page edition aimed to make the Seder accessible to Egyptian Jews more familiar with Arabic script than with Hebrew transliteration. The work reflected the linguistic realities of early 20th-century Egyptian Jewry.

title_en: Polish translation of the Haggadah by Fabius Strauch printed in Warsaw
summary_en: Fabius Strauch's Polish translation of the Haggadah was printed in Warsaw.
story_body: Around 5641 (1881), Fabius Strauch's translation of the Haggadah into Polish was issued in Warsaw. The 96-page volume made the Seder ritual accessible to Polish-speaking Jews who had become more integrated with the local language. It represented part of the broader 19th-century movement to render Jewish liturgical texts into local European languages.

title_en: Persian translation Haggadah 'Chukat HaPesach' for Bukharian Jews printed in Jerusalem
summary_en: Shimon Hakham translated the 'Chukat HaPesach' Haggadah into Persian to serve the Bukharian Jewish community of Jerusalem.
story_body: In 5664 (1904), 'Chukat HaPesach' was printed in Jerusalem by Shmuel HaLevi Zuckerman, featuring readings for the entire month of Nissan, the Korban Pesach with an extract from Shimshon of Ostropoli, and a Persian translation of the Haggadah by Shimon Hakham. The 68-page work also included tales and songs related to Pesach intended to benefit the Bukharian Jewish community. A separately titled Persian translation of Shir HaShirim was appended at the end.

title_en: Czech translation of the Haggadah by Dr. Gustav Weiner printed in Prague
summary_en: Dr. Gustav Weiner's Czech translation of the Haggadah was printed in Prague.
story_body: Around 5658 (1898), Dr. Gustav Weiner's translation of the Haggadah into Czech was published in Prague. The 79-page volume served the Czech-speaking Jewish community of Bohemia. It reflected the late 19th-century integration of Central European Jewry with the surrounding national languages.

title_en: French translation of the Haggadah by David Drach printed in Metz
summary_en: David Drach's French translation of the Haggadah, following both Ashkenazic and Sephardic customs, was printed in Metz.
story_body: In 5579 (1819), David Drach's French translation of the Haggadah was issued in Metz, following both Ashkenazic and Sephardic customs. The Hebrew original and French translation were printed page-by-page, with a separate French title page. The 127-page work served the French-speaking Jewish community emerging in post-revolutionary France.

title_en: Romanian translation of the Haggadah by Avraham Shlomo Gold printed in Craiova
summary_en: The third revised edition of Avraham Shlomo Gold's Romanian translation of the Haggadah, with musical notation, was printed in Craiova.
story_body: Around 5662 (1902), Avraham Shlomo Gold issued the third revised edition of his Romanian translation of the Haggadah, with many additions, in Craiova. The 83-page work included annotations and musical notation. It served the Romanian-speaking Jewish community of the Balkans.

title_en: Russian translation of the Haggadah by Moshe Goldstein printed in Vilna
summary_en: Moshe ben Yaakov Goldstein's Russian translation of the Haggadah was printed in Vilna.
story_body: Around 5630 (1870), Moshe ben Yaakov Goldstein produced a Russian translation of the Haggadah, accompanied by annotations in Russian, printed in Vilna. The 70-page work featured the original Hebrew and Russian translation page-by-page. It marked an early example of a Russian-language Haggadah for the Russian Empire's Jews.

title_en: Illustrated Abarbanel Haggadah printed in Amsterdam by Shlomo Proops
summary_en: Shlomo Proops printed an illustrated Haggadah in Amsterdam featuring the Abarbanel and other commentaries.
story_body: In 5472 (1712), Shlomo Proops issued a richly illustrated Haggadah in Amsterdam with commentaries by Don Isaac Abarbanel, Ma'aseh Hashem, Mateh Aharon, and Chevel Bnei Yehudah, alongside abridgments of other commentators. The work included an engraved map showing all the Israelite wanderings in the desert, etched on copper plates. The 31-leaf folio became an iconic illustrated edition of the era.

title_en: Haggadah with commentary of Eliyahu ben Todros Broda printed in Prague
summary_en: A Haggadah with a Yiddish translation by Eliyahu ben Todros Broda was printed in Prague by Shlomo Proops.
story_body: In 5473 (1713), Shlomo Proops printed a Haggadah in Prague featuring a Yiddish translation by Eliyahu ben Todros Broda. The 16-leaf folio edition served the Yiddish-speaking Jewish community of Bohemia. The surviving copy in the library is missing its title page and possibly its opening section.

title_en: Wandsbeck Haggadah printed by Yisrael ben Avraham
summary_en: A small-format Haggadah was printed in Wandsbeck by Yisrael ben Avraham.
story_body: In 5493 (1733), Yisrael ben Avraham produced a small-format Haggadah in Wandsbeck (Germany), bearing the Yiddish title noting this 'great mitzvah of telling'. The 24-leaf miniature edition included the Akdamut at its conclusion. It served the Yiddish-speaking Ashkenazic communities of Northern Germany.

title_en: Illustrated Abarbanel Haggadah with Yiddish translation printed in Fürth
summary_en: An illustrated Abarbanel Haggadah with Yiddish liturgical translations was printed in Fürth.
story_body: Around 5510 (1750), an ornate folio Haggadah was printed in Fürth (Furth, Bavaria) containing the commentary of Don Isaac Abarbanel together with a Kabbalistic commentary. Yiddish translations of the liturgical poems appeared in Tzene-Rene script, and illustrations were placed below the Hebrew text and commentaries. The 16-leaf folio also exists in a variant dated 1757.

title_en: Tzli Esh Haggadah by Yehuda Aryeh of Modena printed in Amsterdam
summary_en: The illustrated 'Tzli Esh' Haggadah by Yehuda Aryeh of Modena, with full Yiddish translation, was printed in Amsterdam.
story_body: In 5525 (1765), an illustrated Haggadah was printed in Amsterdam featuring the 'Tzli Esh' commentary by Yehuda Aryeh of Modena, an abridgment of his earlier work 'Zevach Pesach'. The 32-leaf quarto edition included a complete Yiddish translation of the Haggadah in Tzene-Rene script. The work became a popular Amsterdam edition of the Italian-influenced Haggadah tradition.

title_en: Bet Chorin Haggadah with commentaries printed in Metz
summary_en: The 'Bet Chorin' Haggadah, with Alshich, Gevurot Hashem, and Olelot Efraim commentaries, was printed in Metz.
story_body: In 5527 (1767), the 'Bet Chorin' Haggadah was issued in Metz, France, with commentaries by Moshe ben Chaim Alshich, the Maharal's 'Gevurot Hashem', and 'Olelot Efraim'. The 30-leaf quarto edition included beautiful illustrations and concluded with a map of the Land of Israel in vernacular language. It exemplified the French-printed Haggadah tradition of the late 18th century.

title_en: Illustrated Italian-translation Haggadah printed in Trieste
summary_en: An illustrated Haggadah with an Italian translation was printed in Trieste.
story_body: Around 5624 (1864), a 66-page illustrated Haggadah with Italian translation was issued in Trieste. The folio volume served the Italian-speaking Jewish community of the Habsburg port city. It represented the Italian-Jewish tradition of richly produced Haggadot.

title_en: Ladino Haggadah with Hebrew commentary printed in Livorno
summary_en: An illustrated Ladino-translation Haggadah, including Maariv prayers and Shir HaShirim, was printed in Livorno.
story_body: In 5664 (1904), Shlomo Belforte & Co. printed a Haggadah in Livorno with Ladino translation and several illustrations. Maariv prayers were appended along with Shir HaShirim. The 42-leaf volume served the Ladino-speaking Mediterranean Sephardic community.

title_en: Facsimile of Moshe ben Natan HaKohen's Haggadah for the Chatam Sofer published in Berlin-Leipzig
summary_en: A facsimile of the manuscript Haggadah created in 1816 for the Chatam Sofer by Moshe ben Natan HaKohen was published in Berlin-Leipzig by B. Cohen.
story_body: In 5684 (1924), B. Cohen published in Berlin-Leipzig a precise facsimile reproduction of an illustrated Haggadah manuscript originally created in 1816 by Moshe ben Natan HaKohen for the renowned halakhic authority Moshe Sofer, the Chatam Sofer. The 19-leaf quarto reproduction featured colorful illustrations alongside the Yiddish translation in Tzene-Rene script. The work was printed by B.G. Teubner.

title_en: Berlin Haggadah illustrated by Y. Liberman published by Gunzer and Levin
summary_en: An illustrated Haggadah by Y. Liberman was published by Gunzer and Levin's bookstore in Berlin.
story_body: Around 5685 (1925), the book firm of Gunzer and Levin issued an illustrated Haggadah in Berlin with art by Y. Liberman. Printed by Rudolf Grätz, the 48-page folio included a special German title page but no German translation. The Yiddish translation occupied a separate 23-page section.

title_en: Jerusalem Haggadah illustrated by A. El-Hanani
summary_en: A Haggadah illustrated by A. El-Hanani was printed in Jerusalem.
story_body: In 5690 (1930), an illustrated Haggadah by A. El-Hanani was printed by Lipschitz in Jerusalem. The 37-page edition included musical notation. It represented the developing Yishuv artistic tradition of Haggadah illustration in pre-state Palestine.

title_en: Illustrated Haggadah with hand-written text printed in New York
summary_en: An illustrated Haggadah with text hand-written by the artist was published in New York.
story_body: Around 5709 (1949), a 58-page Haggadah was printed in New York featuring colorful illustrations and the text itself hand-lettered by the artist. The quarto edition exemplified the mid-20th-century trend of artist-designed liturgical works. It served the American Jewish community of the post-war period.

title_en: Shulsinger Brothers Haggadah with English translation by Abraham Regelson
summary_en: The Shulsinger Brothers published a Haggadah in New York with English translation by Abraham Regelson and color illustrations by Siegmund Forst.
story_body: In 5710 (1950), the Shulsinger Brothers issued a second edition Haggadah in New York with English translation by Abraham Regelson printed in parallel columns. Sigmund Forst contributed color illustrations, Yehoshua Weisser provided musical notation, and Sh. B. Honig and Michal Yehoshua Shulsinger compiled a Yalkut for the Festival of Freedom appended in Hebrew and English. The 64-plus-80-page folio edition became a notable American Haggadah.

title_en: Tel Aviv Haggadah illustrated by Y. Zimberknopf (Zim)
summary_en: Y. Zimberknopf (Zim) illustrated and decorated a Haggadah printed in Tel Aviv.
story_body: In 5712 (1952), an illustrated and decorated Haggadah by Y. Zimberknopf, known as Zim, was published in Tel Aviv. The 88-page folio edition reflected the burgeoning Israeli Haggadah tradition in the early years of the state. It demonstrated the visual style that emerged in the new Hebrew-speaking artistic culture.

title_en: Tel Aviv Haggadah illustrated by Gad Ullman from Massada Press
summary_en: Gad Ullman wrote and illustrated a Haggadah published by Massada Press in Tel Aviv.
story_body: In 5724 (1964), Massada Press in Tel Aviv issued a Haggadah whose calligraphy and illustration were both executed by Gad Ullman. The 20-leaf landscape edition (12x34 cm) showcased Ullman's artistic approach to the Haggadah text. It reflected the developing Israeli book arts tradition of the mid-1960s.

title_en: Yossi Rosenstein illustrated Haggadah with English translation published in Jerusalem
summary_en: Yossi Rosenstein illustrated a Haggadah with English translation that was printed in Jerusalem.
story_body: In 5746 (1986), an illustrated Haggadah by Yossi Rosenstein was printed in Jerusalem with an English translation. The 142-page duodecimo edition served both Hebrew- and English-speaking audiences. It reflected the late 20th-century Israeli tradition of producing bilingual illustrated Haggadot.

title_en: Haggadat Am published by Adamah with English translation by Mordechai HaCohen
summary_en: Adamah Press published 'Haggadat Am' with English translation by Mordechai HaCohen and illustrations by Chaim Ron.
story_body: In 5747 (1987), Adamah Press in the Holy Land issued 'Haggadat Am', translated and commented in English by Mordechai HaCohen and illustrated by Chaim Ron. The 184-page folio edition served the modern Israeli-American Jewish audience. It represented contemporary Israeli liturgical publishing aimed at a bilingual market.

title_en: Fenton Haggadah illustrated and designed by Zvi Fenton in London
summary_en: Zvi Fenton's illustrated and designed 'Fenton Haggadah' was published in London with a supplementary English translation booklet.
story_body: In 5748 (1988), 'The Fenton Haggadah' was published in London, designed and illustrated by Zvi Fenton. The 64-page quarto edition was accompanied by a separate 26-page booklet containing an English translation. It served the English-speaking Jewish community of Britain.

title_en: Tel Aviv Haggadah illustrated by Bilha Krieger Barzel
summary_en: An illustrated Haggadah by Bilha Krieger Barzel was printed in Tel Aviv.
story_body: In 5748 (1988), an illustrated Haggadah by Bilha Krieger Barzel was published in Tel Aviv. The 56-page octavo edition exemplified contemporary Israeli Haggadah artistry. It contributed to the rich late 20th-century tradition of Israeli illustrated Passover texts.

title_en: Facsimile of the first printed Haggadah from Guadalajara published in Jerusalem
summary_en: A facsimile of the first printed Haggadah (Guadalajara, c. 1482) was published in Jerusalem from the National Library's unique copy.
story_body: In 5721 (1961), a facsimile edition of the earliest printed Haggadah, originally produced around 1482 in Guadalajara (Wadi al-Hagara), was published in Jerusalem. The 12-leaf folio reproduction was made from the unique copy preserved in the National Library of Israel's Jewish National and University Library. It appeared as an appendix to the 'Bibliography of Passover Haggadot'.

title_en: Facsimile reproduction of the Soncino Haggadah published in Leipzig
summary_en: A facsimile reproduction of the c. 1485 Soncino Haggadah was published in Leipzig with illustrations supplied by Albert Frisch.
story_body: Around 5683 (1923), a facsimile reproduction of the Haggadah extracted from the c. 1485 Soncino Machzor was issued in Leipzig. Illustration plates were supplied by Albert Frisch, with the title and printing notes hand-lettered by Franziska Baruch. Two copies were produced, one on slightly larger paper.

title_en: Shulsinger Brothers facsimile of Gershom Cohen's Prague Haggadah
summary_en: The Shulsinger Brothers reissued in New York a facsimile of Gershom Cohen's 1527 Prague Haggadah.
story_body: In 5724 (1964), the Shulsinger Brothers issued in New York a facsimile reproduction of the Haggadah printed at the press of Gershom Cohen in Prague in 1527. The 42-leaf folio edition revived one of the most influential early printed Haggadot for modern audiences. It was a key contribution to mid-20th-century Hebrew bibliophilic publishing.

title_en: Facsimile of the Venice 1609 Italian-Hebrew Haggadah published in Jerusalem
summary_en: A facsimile of the 1609 Venice Haggadah with Italian translation in Hebrew letters was published in Jerusalem with an introduction by Bezalel Narkiss.
story_body: In 5734 (1974), a facsimile of the 1609 Venice Haggadah was issued in Jerusalem, vocalized and featuring an Italian translation rendered in Hebrew letters, with an introduction by Professor Bezalel Narkiss. The reproduction was made from a special copy printed on parchment in honor of Gershon Printz. The 70-page folio was titled 'Ma'aleh Bet Chorin'.

title_en: Jerusalem facsimile reissue of the Vienna 1813 Alshich Haggadah
summary_en: A facsimile of the 1813 Vienna Haggadah with commentaries by Alshich, Maharal, and Olelot Efraim was published in Jerusalem.
story_body: In 5735 (1975), a facsimile reproduction of the 1813 Vienna Haggadah was issued in Jerusalem with commentaries by Moshe Alshich, Yehuda Loew (Maharal) of Prague's 'Gevurot Hashem', and 'Olelot Efraim'. The 52-leaf folio came with an accompanying introduction. It made classical Ashkenazic exegesis on the Haggadah more accessible to modern readers.

title_en: Tel Aviv facsimile of the Altona 1738 manuscript Haggadah by Yosef ben David of Leipnik
summary_en: A facsimile of the 1738 Altona manuscript Haggadah by Yosef ben David of Leipnik was published in Tel Aviv with Abarbanel's commentary.
story_body: In 5747 (1987), a facsimile edition of a manuscript Haggadah from the Rosenthaliana Library, written in Altona in 5498 (1738) by Yosef ben David of Leipnik, was published in Tel Aviv. The volume included Don Isaac Abarbanel's commentary, a brief Kabbalistic commentary, Seder instructions in Yiddish and Ladino, and illustrations. A separate booklet contained an English description by Emile Schrijver translated into Hebrew by Shlomo Zucker, with a Haggadah translation by Aharon Asher Green.

title_en: Facsimile of the Kaufmann Haggadah published in Budapest
summary_en: A facsimile of the 14th-century Kaufmann Haggadah, held by the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, was published in Budapest.
story_body: Around 5750 (1990), the Hungarian Academy of Sciences Library's Oriental Collection sponsored the publication of a facsimile of the 14th-century illuminated 'Kaufmann Haggadah' in Budapest. Limited to 1,000 copies, the 60-page facsimile was accompanied by a separate English introductory booklet by Gabriel Sed-Rajna. The featured copy was number 21 of the print run.

title_en: Belgrade facsimile of the Sarajevo Haggadah
summary_en: A facsimile of the 14th-century Sephardic Sarajevo Haggadah from the Bosnian National Museum was published in Belgrade.
story_body: In 5745 (1985), Belgrade published a facsimile reproduction of the famous Sarajevo Haggadah, a Spanish manuscript from the second half of the 14th century preserved at the National Museum of Bosnia in Sarajevo. The 34-plus-104-leaf facsimile was accompanied by a Hebrew introduction by Shlomo Zucker (Tel Aviv 1986) and an English introduction by Hoger Werber (Belgrade 1985).

title_en: Tel Aviv facsimile of the Copenhagen Haggadah by Uri Feivush ben Yitzchak
summary_en: A facsimile of the 1739 Copenhagen Haggadah by Uri Feivush ben Yitzchak Segal was published in Tel Aviv by Nahar and Steimatzky.
story_body: In 5746 (1986), Nahar and Steimatzky publishers in Tel Aviv issued a facsimile of the Copenhagen Haggadah, a manuscript written by Uri Feivush ben Yitzchak Segal in Altona-Hamburg in 1739. The 34-leaf folio facsimile featured the Abarbanel commentary, Kabbalistic notes, Seder laws in Hebrew, Yiddish, and Ladino, and full illustrations. It included a six-leaf bilingual Hebrew-English introduction by Chaya Benjamin.

title_en: Leipzig facsimile of the Darmstadt Haggadah manuscript
summary_en: A facsimile of the Darmstadt Haggadah manuscript was published in Leipzig with a separate text volume edited by Bruno Italianer.
story_body: In 5687 (1927) and 5688 (1928), a facsimile of the Darmstadt Haggadah manuscript was issued in Leipzig in two volumes. The text-volume — featuring introduction and German commentary by Bruno Italianer — was 313 pages, while the facsimile-volume issued the following year reproduced 56 leaves of the original manuscript. Together they constituted one of the major early 20th-century scholarly publications of an illuminated medieval Haggadah.

title_en: Italian facsimile of the 15th-century Yoel ben Shimon Haggadah from the British Library
summary_en: A facsimile of a 15th-century Haggadah manuscript by Yoel ben Shimon Feibush from the British Library was published in Italy.
story_body: In 5745 (1985), a facsimile of a 15th-century Haggadah manuscript was published in Italy. The original — held at the British Library — was written and illustrated by Yoel ben Shimon Feibush HaAshkenazi, with a commentary drawn from the school of Rabbi Eleazar of Worms. The 49-plus-40 leaf folio included an introduction, notes, and French transcription by David Goldstein.

title_en: Pereshel facsimile of Netanel ben Aharon Segal's 1771 Haggadah manuscript
summary_en: Tuvia Pereshel published a facsimile of Netanel ben Aharon Segal's 1771 manuscript Haggadah in New York.
story_body: In 5731 (1971), Tuvia Pereshel published in New York a facsimile of a manuscript Haggadah by Netanel ben Aharon Segal from the year 5531 (1771). The 24-leaf octavo edition included an introduction by Pereshel. It inaugurated his annual project of publishing facsimiles of rare Haggadot before each Passover.

title_en: Pereshel facsimile of Netanel ben Aharon Segal's 1772 Haggadah manuscript
summary_en: Tuvia Pereshel published a facsimile of a 1772 manuscript Haggadah by the scribe Netanel ben Aharon Segal in New York.
story_body: In 5732 (1972), Tuvia Pereshel published in New York a facsimile of a manuscript Haggadah by the soferet Netanel ben Aharon Segal dated 5532 (1772). The 32-leaf octavo edition came with an introduction by Pereshel. It continued his annual series of rare Haggadah reproductions.

title_en: Pereshel facsimile of the 1782 Kitse manuscript Haggadah
summary_en: Tuvia Pereshel published a facsimile of an illustrated 1782 Kitse-community manuscript Haggadah in New York.
story_body: In 5735 (1975), Tuvia Pereshel published in New York a facsimile of a manuscript Haggadah produced in the community of Kitse in 5542 (1782). The 28-page octavo edition included an English introduction by Pereshel. It was part of his ongoing series of rare Haggadah reproductions for the Passover season.

title_en: Pereshel reproduction of the Fürth 1741 Haggadah
summary_en: Tuvia Pereshel issued in New York a facsimile of the Fürth 1741 Haggadah with Yiddish translation.
story_body: In 5736 (1976), Tuvia Pereshel published in New York a facsimile reproduction of the 1741 Fürth Haggadah, which included a Yiddish translation. The 16-leaf octavo edition came with bilingual English and Hebrew introductions by Pereshel. It continued his annual project of resurrecting rare printed Haggadot.

title_en: Pereshel facsimile of Aharon Schreiber Erlangen's 1751 Vienna Haggadah
summary_en: Tuvia Pereshel published in New York a facsimile of the 1751 Vienna manuscript Haggadah by Aharon Schreiber Erlangen.
story_body: In 5738 (1978), Tuvia Pereshel published in New York a facsimile of a Haggadah manuscript written in Vienna in 5511 (1751) by Aharon Schreiber Erlangen. The 32-page octavo edition included Pereshel's bilingual English-Hebrew introduction. It was part of his ongoing facsimile-of-rare-Haggadot project with Munish Weintraub.
