title_en: Alter Rebbe revises Tanya and sends to press
summary_en: In 5556, the Alter Rebbe revised the Tanya anew and sent it to the printer.
story_body: In 5556 (1796), Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi revised and completed the Tanya, then sent it to the press in Slavuta. The printing was completed on 20 Kislev 5557 (1796).

title_en: First printing of Tanya completed in Slavuta
summary_en: The first printing of the Tanya was completed on 20 Kislev 5557.
story_body: The first printing of the Tanya — comprising Likutei Amarim and Sha'ar HaYichud VeHa'emunah — was completed on 20 Kislev 5557 (December 1796) in Slavuta. The book was eagerly received by chassidim and reprinted at least six times in its first decade.

title_en: Informer denounces Alter Rebbe to Russian authorities
summary_en: On 4 Sivan 5558 (8 May 1798), a Vilna informer submitted a denunciation accusing the Alter Rebbe of supporting the French Revolution.
story_body: On 4 Sivan 5558 (8 May 1798), an informer from Vilna submitted a denunciation to the Russian authorities accusing Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi of organizing a conspiracy, gathering rebellious youth, supporting the French Revolution, and recommending exile to Siberia. This denunciation initiated the legal case against the Alter Rebbe.

title_en: Second denunciation against Vilna authorities filed on Shavuot
summary_en: On 6 Sivan 5558 (10 May 1798), Shavuot, a follow-up denunciation was filed against Vilna's officials.
story_body: On 6 Sivan 5558 (10 May 1798) — the first day of Shavuot — a second denunciation was filed, this one against the Vilna municipal authorities. The fact that it was composed on Shavuot and bore a distorted Hebrew signature suggests the actual author was not Jewish.

title_en: Case against Alter Rebbe formally opened
summary_en: On 10 Elul 5558 (11 August 1798), the General Procurator presented the denunciation to the Tsar, opening the case.
story_body: On 10 Elul 5558 (11 August 1798), the General Procurator of Russia formally presented the denunciation to Tsar Paul I, opening an official file against the Alter Rebbe and the chassidic movement.

title_en: Tsar orders investigation of denunciation against Alter Rebbe
summary_en: On 13 Elul 5558 (14 August 1798), the Tsar ordered investigation of the denunciation's content.
story_body: On 13 Elul 5558 (14 August 1798), Tsar Paul I issued an order to investigate the contents of the denunciation against Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi. The General Procurator passed the order to the civil governor of Lithuania two days later.

title_en: Lithuanian governor recommends arrest of Alter Rebbe
summary_en: On 29 Elul 5558 (30 August 1798), Lithuania's civil governor recommended arresting the Alter Rebbe and chassidic leaders for interrogation.
story_body: On 29 Elul 5558 (30 August 1798), the civil governor of Lithuania recommended that the Alter Rebbe and the heads of chassidic communities in Lithuania be taken into custody for interrogation.

title_en: Tsar orders arrest of Alter Rebbe
summary_en: On 13 Tishrei 5559 (12 September 1798), the Tsar ordered the arrest of the Alter Rebbe and chassidic leaders.
story_body: On 13 Tishrei 5559 (12 September 1798), Tsar Paul I ordered that Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi and the leading chassidim be arrested and brought to Petersburg for interrogation. The order arrived during the holiday season of Sukkot 5559.

title_en: Arrest of Alter Rebbe at end of Sukkot 5559
summary_en: At the end of Sukkot 5559, officers arrived to arrest the Alter Rebbe and transport him to Petersburg.
story_body: In the last days of Sukkot 5559 (autumn 1798), Russian officers came to arrest Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi and transport him to Petersburg for interrogation, in execution of the Tsar's order. He was sent under guard of an officer and two soldiers.

title_en: Alter Rebbe arrives at Peter-Paul Fortress in Petersburg
summary_en: On 8 MarCheshvan 5559 (7 October 1798), the Alter Rebbe arrived in Petersburg and was imprisoned in the Peter-Paul Fortress.
story_body: On 8 MarCheshvan 5559 (7 October 1798), the General Procurator notified the governor of Belorussia that Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi had arrived in Petersburg and was incarcerated in the Peter-Paul Fortress, where he remained during the investigation.

title_en: Liberation of the Alter Rebbe — Yud-Tes Kislev
summary_en: On 19 Kislev 5559 (16 November 1798), the Tsar ordered the release of the Alter Rebbe from prison.
story_body: On 19 Kislev 5559 (16 November 1798), Tsar Paul I ordered the release of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi from imprisonment in Petersburg. The day became known as Yud-Tes Kislev, celebrated annually as the 'Rosh Hashanah of Chassidut' marking the vindication of chassidic teachings.

title_en: Alter Rebbe receives release certificate
summary_en: On 20 Kislev 5559 (17 November 1798), the Alter Rebbe was issued a release certificate.
story_body: On 20 Kislev 5559 (17 November 1798), the General Procurator issued an official release certificate to Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi and notified the governor of Belorussia of his liberation.

title_en: Belorussia notifies Vitebsk to allow chassidim to continue
summary_en: On 18 Tevet 5559 (15 December 1798), the governor of Belorussia informed Vitebsk officials of the Alter Rebbe's release and order to leave the chassidic community in peace.
story_body: On 18 Tevet 5559 (15 December 1798), the governor of Belorussia notified the Vitebsk authorities of the Alter Rebbe's release and conveyed the Tsar's order that the chassidic community be allowed to continue its existence undisturbed.

title_en: Lithuanian chassidim leaders released on 5th night of Chanukah
summary_en: Twenty-two leading Lithuanian chassidim arrested with the Alter Rebbe were released by lighting time of the fifth Chanukah candle 5559.
story_body: Parallel to the arrest of the Alter Rebbe, twenty-two leading chassidim of Lithuania had been detained in early Cheshvan 5559 for interrogation. On 19 Kislev the Tsar ordered all of them released; the order reached Lithuania on 28 Kislev, and they were freed to their homes by the time of lighting the fifth Chanukah candle.

title_en: Tsar reaffirms right of chassidim to exist
summary_en: On 20 Kislev 5560 (7 December 1799), the General Procurator confirmed the Tsar's order that the chassidic movement be allowed to exist.
story_body: On 20 Kislev 5560 (7 December 1799), the General Procurator replied to the governor of Lithuania that, in accordance with the Tsar's order, the chassidic movement must be allowed to continue. This reaffirmation came in response to renewed denunciations by opponents of the chassidim.

title_en: Avigdor of Pinsk denounces Alter Rebbe to Tsar
summary_en: On 10 Iyar 5560 (23 April 1800), Avigdor of Pinsk submitted a lengthy denunciation against the Alter Rebbe to the Tsar.
story_body: On 10 Iyar 5560 (23 April 1800), Avigdor, formerly rabbi of Pinsk and then residing in Vilna, submitted to the Tsar a lengthy denunciation against Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi and the chassidic movement. He attacked Tzava'at HaRivash, argued the movement was a continuation of Sabbatianism, and complained that chassidim had caused his dismissal from the Pinsk rabbinate.

title_en: Second arrest of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: On 4 Kislev 5561 (9 November 1800), the Alter Rebbe was arrested again and sent to Petersburg.
story_body: On 4 Kislev 5561 (9 November 1800), Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi was arrested for a second time and sent under police escort to Petersburg, despite the Belorussian governor's findings that there was no basis for the accusations against him.

title_en: Order issued to search Alter Rebbe's home
summary_en: On 11 Kislev 5561 (16 November 1800), an order was issued to search the Alter Rebbe's home and seize his documents.
story_body: On 11 Kislev 5561 (16 November 1800), the General Procurator ordered the governor of Belorussia to conduct a search of the Alter Rebbe's home, seize manuscripts and documents, and forward them to Petersburg for examination.

title_en: Tsar orders Senate to investigate Alter Rebbe's case
summary_en: On 21 Kislev 5561 (26 November 1800), the Tsar ordered the case transferred to the Senate for further investigation.
story_body: On 21 Kislev 5561 (26 November 1800), after reviewing the Alter Rebbe's written replies, Tsar Paul I ordered the case transferred to the Senate, which then assigned the investigation to the Senate's Third Department (the secret police).

title_en: Tsar orders Alter Rebbe released on bail
summary_en: On 23 Kislev 5561 (28 November 1800), the Tsar ordered the Alter Rebbe released from prison on condition he remain in Petersburg.
story_body: On 23 Kislev 5561 (28 November 1800), Tsar Paul I ordered Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi released from his second imprisonment on bail, with the condition that he remain in Petersburg until permitted to leave. This date is observed by Chabad as a secondary day of redemption.

title_en: Search of Alter Rebbe's home in Liozna
summary_en: On 24 Kislev 5561 (29 November 1800), Russian officials searched the Alter Rebbe's home and confiscated his books and manuscripts.
story_body: On 24 Kislev 5561 (29 November 1800), Russian officials carried out the search of the Alter Rebbe's home in Liozna. Books and manuscripts were taken, and the lay leaders of the community signed a document acknowledging the confiscation and the sealing of the house.

title_en: Confiscated books and manuscripts delivered to Senate
summary_en: On 18 Tevet 5561 (22 December 1800), the seized books and manuscripts from the Alter Rebbe's home were delivered to the Senate.
story_body: On 18 Tevet 5561 (22 December 1800), the books and manuscripts taken from Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi's home were delivered to the Senate, accompanied by a list of 14 manuscripts and 103 books.

title_en: Avigdor files additional denunciation citing Tanya
summary_en: On 24 Tevet 5561 (28 December 1800), Avigdor filed an additional denunciation citing passages from the Tanya about the souls of the nations.
story_body: On 24 Tevet 5561 (28 December 1800), Avigdor of Pinsk submitted yet another denunciation, copying out passages from the Tanya concerning the souls of the nations and arguing that the chassidic movement was harmful to the state. He proposed that the leaders of the chassidim be arrested and interrogated.

title_en: Assassination of Tsar Paul I
summary_en: On 9 Nissan 5561 (11 March 1801), Tsar Paul I was assassinated and his son Alexander succeeded him.
story_body: On 9 Nissan 5561 (11 March 1801), Tsar Paul I of Russia was assassinated, and his son Alexander I ascended to the throne. The change of regime would directly affect the Alter Rebbe's case still pending before the Senate.

title_en: Tsar Alexander orders Alter Rebbe's full release
summary_en: On 19 Nissan 5561 (21 March 1801), Tsar Alexander I ordered the Alter Rebbe released to return home.
story_body: On 19 Nissan 5561 (21 March 1801), the newly enthroned Tsar Alexander I ordered Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi released from his bail conditions in Petersburg and permitted to return home. A formal notice was sent to the White Russian authorities on 27 Nissan.

title_en: Notice of release and freedom to spread chassidut
summary_en: On 27 Nissan 5561 (29 March 1801), Petersburg notified White Russia of the Alter Rebbe's release and full license to spread chassidut.
story_body: On 27 Nissan 5561 (29 March 1801), Petersburg sent notification to the governor of White Russia confirming the Alter Rebbe's release and granting him full permission to continue spreading chassidut throughout the White Russian district without any interference.

title_en: Alter Rebbe moves from Liozna to Liadi
summary_en: Following his release, the Alter Rebbe left Petersburg and settled in Liadi rather than returning to Liozna.
story_body: Around Elul 5561 (1801), Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi left Petersburg following his second release. Rather than return to his former home in Liozna, he settled in the town of Liadi, which would lend his name and that of his dynasty its lasting designation.

title_en: Tsar Alexander signs Jewish Statute including section 53
summary_en: On 18 Tevet 5565 (9 December 1804), Tsar Alexander signed the Jewish Statute granting chassidim the right to build their own synagogues.
story_body: On 18 Tevet 5565 (9 December 1804), Tsar Alexander I signed the Russian Jewish Statute. Section 53 granted that wherever a community split such that one party did not want to share a synagogue with the other, either party could build its own synagogue and appoint its own rabbis — formally protecting the chassidim from interference by mitnagdim.

title_en: Passing of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi passed away on 24 Tevet 5573 in Piena.
story_body: Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, founder of Chabad chassidut, passed away on 24 Tevet 5573 (1812) in the town of Piena during the flight from Napoleon's invading army. He was succeeded by his son, Rabbi Dov Ber, the Mitteler Rebbe.

title_en: Great fire at the Alter Rebbe's home in Liadi
summary_en: A major fire struck the Alter Rebbe's home in Liadi in 5570, evidently destroying his original manuscript of the Tanya.
story_body: In 5570 (1810), a great fire struck Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi's home in Liadi. The original manuscript of the Tanya is believed to have been consumed in this fire, though a corrected manuscript of Iggeret HaTeshuvah in his hand survived in the Chabad library archives.

title_en: Sons of Alter Rebbe publish expanded Tanya
summary_en: In 5574, after the Alter Rebbe's passing, his sons published an expanded edition of the Tanya adding Iggeret HaKodesh and Kuntres Acharon.
story_body: In 5574 (1814), one year after the passing of the Alter Rebbe on 24 Tevet 5573, his holy sons published a new edition of the Tanya. They added two additional sections: Iggeret HaKodesh and Kuntres Acharon. From this edition onward, all printings of the Tanya have contained these five parts.

title_en: Exhibit marking 200 years since Alter Rebbe's liberation
summary_en: In 5759 the Chabad library held an exhibit marking 200 years since the Alter Rebbe's liberation on 19 Kislev 5559.
story_body: On Tuesday, 19 Kislev 5759 (1998), 200 years had passed since the liberation of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi from his first imprisonment. The Chabad library mounted an exhibit running through 11 Nissan 5759 (1999), displaying first editions of the Alter Rebbe's works, original handwritten manuscripts, ancient copies, sacred artifacts, and portraits.

title_en: Maggid of Mezeritch issues approbation for Halacha Pesuka
summary_en: Rabbi Dov Ber of Mezeritch granted his only known approbation, for the work Halacha Pesuka printed in Turka.
story_body: The 1765 Turka edition of Halacha Pesuka carries what is regarded as the sole approbation ever issued by the Maggid of Mezeritch. It survives as a rare textual witness to the Maggid's personal endorsements during the early diffusion of Chassidism.

title_en: Alter Rebbe begins composing the Shulchan Aruch under the Maggid
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi began drafting his Shulchan Aruch while studying under the Maggid of Mezeritch around 1770.
story_body: According to the preface written by his sons, the Alter Rebbe began the Shulchan Aruch while "sitting under the wing of Tachkemoni" with the Maggid in Mezeritch, around 5530 (1770). He started with Orach Chaim, completing that section within about two years, and continued reworking the code for over forty years.

title_en: Maggid of Mezeritch's Maggid Devarav L'Yaakov printed in Korec
summary_en: The first edition of the Maggid of Mezeritch's classic Maggid Devarav L'Yaakov was published in Korec in 1781.
story_body: This Korec printing was one of the earliest Chassidic books to be published, presenting the Maggid's teachings to a wider readership. It would become foundational reading for Chassidic disciples for generations.

title_en: Alter Rebbe publishes Hilchos Talmud Torah in Shklov
summary_en: The Alter Rebbe released Hilchos Talmud Torah in Shklov in 1794, his first published work, with approbations but without naming the author.
story_body: This 35-folio Shklov edition was the first book the Alter Rebbe sent to press—more than two years before his Tanya appeared. He had it published anonymously, with approbations from other authorities, foreshadowing the pattern of his later halachic publications.

title_en: Keter Shem Tov first edition printed in Zolkva
summary_en: The first edition of Keter Shem Tov, an anthology of teachings of the Baal Shem Tov, was published in Zolkva in 1794.
story_body: The 1794 Zolkva edition gathered teachings attributed to the Baal Shem Tov into one of the early printed Chassidic anthologies. It remains a foundational source for Baal Shem Tov's Torah and a benchmark text in the early Chassidic library.

title_en: Manuscript of Tanya copied with colophon Tammuz 1796
summary_en: A manuscript volume containing an early version of the Tanya was completed in Tammuz 5556 (1796).
story_body: This manuscript, held as collection no. 268 in the library, contains an early recension of the Tanya alongside discourses of the Alter Rebbe and the Mitteler Rebbe. Its colophon dates the copying to Tammuz 5556, predating the printed first edition by roughly a year.

title_en: First printed edition of Tanya issued in Slavita
summary_en: The Tanya was first printed in Slavita in 5557 (1797), marking the foundational publication of Chabad chassidic thought.
story_body: The 86-folio Slavita edition is the first printed Tanya and the first to publicly transmit the Alter Rebbe's systematic work on chassidic psychology and avodah. Within the next decade the book would be reprinted at least six more times in Zhalkva, Shklov, and elsewhere.

title_en: Second edition of Tanya printed in Zhalkva
summary_en: The Tanya was reprinted in Zhalkva in 5559 (1799), one of several early reprints within a decade of its first edition.
story_body: This 74-folio Zhalkva octavo edition is among the very earliest reprints of the Tanya. Such Galician printings helped spread Chabad chassidic thought beyond White Russia in the years following the first 1797 Slavita edition.

title_en: Alter Rebbe's Hilchos Talmud Torah reissued in Lvov
summary_en: An edition of the Alter Rebbe's Hilchos Talmud Torah was issued in Lvov in 1799 with fresh approbations and now attributed to the author of the Tanya.
story_body: Unlike the anonymous 1794 Shklov first edition, the Lvov 5559 (1799) printing identifies the work as having been authored by "the author of the Tanya." The 34-folio duodecimo carried new approbations and helped circulate the Alter Rebbe's Torah-study halachot in Galicia.

title_en: Luach Birkat HaNehenin published in Shklov
summary_en: The Alter Rebbe's Luach Birkat HaNehenin was first printed in Shklov in 1800.
story_body: This first printing of the Luach Birkat HaNehenin appeared in 5560 (1800) in Shklov, well before the full Shulchan Aruch reached press. It transmitted an early recension of the Alter Rebbe's halachot of blessings on food and remained a separate booklet alongside later expanded versions.

title_en: Luach Birkat HaNehenin reprinted in Zhalkva
summary_en: The Alter Rebbe's Luach Birkat HaNehenin was reprinted in Zhalkva in 1801.
story_body: The 27-folio Zhalkva 5561 (1801) duodecimo carried the first recension of the Alter Rebbe's halachot of blessings. Multiple parallel printings in Russia-Poland and Korec followed in the early 1800s before the second recension superseded it in the 1803 siddur.

title_en: Alter Rebbe sends his Siddur Nusach Ari to press in Shklov
summary_en: The Alter Rebbe published his Siddur arranged according to the Arizal's nusach in Shklov in 5563 (1803), with appended laws and customs.
story_body: Tradition records that the Alter Rebbe examined some sixty existing siddurim before fixing his own nusach, and that on his deathbed he counted the formulation of this nusach as one of his three lifetime achievements. The siddur also incorporated his collected halachot and customs—the second recension of Birkat HaNehenin—and shaped Chabad davening to this day.

title_en: Tanya reprinted in Zhalkva
summary_en: The Tanya was again reprinted in Zhalkva in 5565 (1805).
story_body: The 73-folio Zhalkva 5565 edition is another in a series of early Galician reprints that diffused the Tanya across Eastern Europe in the decade following the 1797 Slavita first edition.

title_en: Sixth edition of Tanya printed in Shklov with revised Igeret HaTeshuva
summary_en: The Shklov 1806 edition of the Tanya included the Alter Rebbe's revised Igeret HaTeshuva, also issued separately as its own booklet.
story_body: For this 5566 (1806) Shklov printing—the sixth edition within roughly a decade—the Alter Rebbe re-edited Igeret HaTeshuva and entrusted it to press together with the Tanya. The reworked Igeret HaTeshuva also appeared as a 20-folio standalone booklet in Shklov the same year.

title_en: Fire destroys Alter Rebbe's home in Liadi
summary_en: A large fire struck the Alter Rebbe's home in Liadi in 5570 (1810).
story_body: According to his sons' later account, this blaze together with a second fire in 1812 consumed the Alter Rebbe's own holograph manuscripts of the Shulchan Aruch. The disasters meant the eventual printed Shulchan Aruch had to be reconstructed from disciples' copies.

title_en: Second fire destroys manuscripts as Alter Rebbe flees Napoleon
summary_en: A second fire late in 5572 (1812), during the Alter Rebbe's flight from Napoleon's advance, destroyed remaining Shulchan Aruch manuscripts.
story_body: As the Alter Rebbe fled with his household during the Napoleonic invasion, fire consumed what remained of his autograph Shulchan Aruch manuscripts. Only copies in students' hands survived, becoming the basis for the eventual posthumous printed edition.

title_en: Passing of the Alter Rebbe on 24 Tevet 5573
summary_en: Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi, the Alter Rebbe of Chabad, passed away on 24 Tevet 5573, corresponding to January 1813.
story_body: The Alter Rebbe died on 24 Tevet 5573 while in flight from the Napoleonic war, leaving his Shulchan Aruch still unprinted. Leadership of Chabad passed to his son, the Mitteler Rebbe, who would oversee posthumous publication of his father's halachic and chassidic works.

title_en: Tanya reprinted in Shklov by the Alter Rebbe's sons with new sections
summary_en: In 1814 the Alter Rebbe's sons reprinted the Tanya in Shklov, adding Igeret HaKodesh and Kuntres Acharon for the first time.
story_body: This 5574 (1814) Shklov edition, prepared by the author's sons after his death, established the canonical five-part structure—Tanya, Shaar HaYichud VehaEmuna, Igeret HaTeshuva, Igeret HaKodesh, and Kuntres Acharon—that all subsequent Tanya editions would follow.

title_en: First volumes of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch printed in Shklov-Kapust
summary_en: The first edition of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch began appearing across 1814–1816 in six volumes printed in Shklov and Kapust.
story_body: Roughly a year after the Alter Rebbe's passing, his sons brought the long-awaited Shulchan Aruch to press, drawing on student manuscripts to replace the holograph copies lost in the fires. The first volumes, including hilchot Pesach and the laws of niddah, appeared in 5574 (1814).

title_en: Standalone teshuva of the Alter Rebbe published in Kapust
summary_en: A standalone responsum of the Alter Rebbe was issued as a separate Kapust booklet in 1815.
story_body: The 10-folio Kapust 5575 (1815) quarto presented one of the Alter Rebbe's responsa on its own, alongside other teshuvot that would be embedded into the Shulchan Aruch volumes. It would later be regathered into the Zhitomir 1847 responsa collection.

title_en: Final volumes of Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch issued in Kapust
summary_en: The first edition of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch was completed in 1816 with further Kapust volumes covering Orach Chaim.
story_body: By 5576 (1816), the Kapust press had issued the additional Orach Chaim, hilchot Shabbat, and hilchot Eruvin volumes that completed the six-part first edition of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch begun two years earlier.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe prints Siddur Im Da"Ch and Biurei HaZohar in Kapust
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe issued in Kapust in 1816 his father's siddur supplemented with chassidic discourses, alongside the first edition of Biurei HaZohar.
story_body: Following his father's passing, the Mitteler Rebbe brought to press in Kapust the Siddur Im Da"Ch—pairing the Alter Rebbe's siddur with related chassidic discourses—and the 139-folio first edition of Biurei HaZohar. These two volumes anchored the early posthumous publication of the Alter Rebbe's chassidic teachings.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe publishes Ner Mitzvah u'Torah Or in Kapust
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe issued the first edition of his Ner Mitzvah u'Torah Or in Kapust in 5580 (1820).
story_body: This 1820 Kapust printing was among the first books of the Mitteler Rebbe's own discourses to reach press. It would be followed in the next two years by Ateret Rosh, Imrei Bina, and Sha'arei Orah, all printed in Kapust.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe's Ateret Rosh and Imrei Bina printed in Kapust
summary_en: First editions of the Mitteler Rebbe's Ateret Rosh and Imrei Bina were published in Kapust in 5581 (1821).
story_body: These two volumes appeared together in 1821 as part of the Mitteler Rebbe's intensive publication campaign at the Kapust press, expanding the printed corpus of Chabad chassidic discourses well beyond what the Alter Rebbe had issued in his lifetime.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe's Sha'arei Orah published in Kapust
summary_en: The first edition of the Mitteler Rebbe's Sha'arei Orah was published in Kapust in 5582 (1822).
story_body: Sha'arei Orah completed an extraordinary three-year run of major chassidic works issued by the Mitteler Rebbe at the Kapust press between 1820 and 1822.

title_en: Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch reprinted in Sudilkov
summary_en: The Alter Rebbe's complete Shulchan Aruch was reissued as a unified six-part series in Sudilkov in 1826.
story_body: This 5586 (1826) Sudilkov printing was the first to bring the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch out as a single complete series, departing from the volume-by-volume issuance of the 1814–1816 first edition.

title_en: Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch reissued in Sudilkov
summary_en: Another full edition of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch appeared in Sudilkov in 1831.
story_body: By the early 1830s the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch was well-established across White Russia and Poland, prompting repeated reprints such as this 5591 (1831) Sudilkov edition.

title_en: Russian government closes nearly all Jewish presses
summary_en: In 1837 the Russian authorities shut down nearly every Jewish printing house in the empire, leaving only one operating press in Vilna.
story_body: The 5597 (1837) decree halted Hebrew publishing in Russia and forced Chabad and other publishing efforts abroad—notably to Warsaw. The lone Vilna press could not keep up with demand, opening the way for the Zhitomir chassidic press a decade later.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's Torah Or completed and printed in Kapust
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek completed editing the first volume of his grandfather's discourses—the Torah Or on Bereishit and Shemot—and printed it in Kapust in 5597 (1837).
story_body: After gathering and selecting from many copies of the Alter Rebbe's discourses, the Tzemach Tzedek prepared the Torah Or volume covering Genesis and Exodus and brought it to press in Kapust in 1837. The intended second volume was delayed when Russia shut down its Jewish presses that same year.

title_en: Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch reprinted in Warsaw
summary_en: A Warsaw edition of the Alter Rebbe's Shulchan Aruch was published between 1838 and 1840 by Rabbi Avraham Mordechai Alter, son of the Chiddushei HaRim of Gur.
story_body: With Russia's Jewish presses shuttered, the Alter Rebbe's halachic code was reprinted in Warsaw during 5598–5600 (1838–1840), notably edited by a future Gerrer rebbe. The edition reflected the spread of the Alter Rebbe's halachic authority into Poland.

title_en: Zhitomir edition of Shulchan Aruch published with sons' approbations
summary_en: A re-edited Shulchan Aruch with additional material and a preface by the Alter Rebbe's son R. Chaim Avraham was issued at the newly opened chassidic press in Zhitomir from 1847.
story_body: When Russia's second Jewish press—the chassidic Zhitomir house—opened in 5607, the Tzemach Tzedek's circle entrusted it with a new Shulchan Aruch edition. The 1847–1848 Zhitomir printing added newly discovered material, a preface by R. Chaim Avraham, and approbations from the senior Chabad rabbis.

title_en: First responsa collection of the Alter Rebbe issued in Zhitomir
summary_en: The Alter Rebbe's previously scattered responsa were gathered into a single booklet appended to the 1847 Zhitomir Shulchan Aruch.
story_body: For the Zhitomir 5607 (1847) Shulchan Aruch edition, all the Alter Rebbe's known responsa—previously printed in their respective halachic contexts—were recollected and issued as a standalone 44-folio supplement. The collection was reprinted with every subsequent Shulchan Aruch edition.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek issues Likutei Torah in Zhitomir
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek published the second volume of his grandfather's chassidic discourses—renamed Likutei Torah—at the Zhitomir press in 5608 (1848).
story_body: A decade after Russian censorship had blocked the planned sequel to Torah Or, the Tzemach Tzedek brought the Vayikra–Devarim and Shir Hashirim volume to the new Zhitomir chassidic press. Censorship constraints required a name change—Likutei Torah—and the two volumes thereafter circulated as a paired set.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's responsa printed in Vilna
summary_en: The first edition of the Tzemach Tzedek's responsa, Tzemach Tzedek, was printed in Vilna in 1871.
story_body: This 5631 (1871) Vilna printing brought the third Chabad rebbe's halachic correspondence into print, anchoring his halachic legacy alongside his already-published chassidic and kabbalistic works.

title_en: Birth of Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn (the Rebbe Rayatz)
summary_en: The sixth Chabad rebbe, Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, was born in 5640 (1880).
story_body: The Rebbe Rayatz, who would lead Chabad through the Soviet repression and the Holocaust era and eventually settle the movement in New York, was born in 5640. His 120th birth-anniversary in summer 2000 prompted a dedicated library exhibition of his belongings and writings.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe's Shnei HaMeoros published in Lvov
summary_en: Shnei HaMeoros, a collection of the Alter Rebbe's discourses transcribed by the Mitteler Rebbe, was printed in Lvov in 1882.
story_body: The 48-folio Lvov 5642 (1882) edition presented hanachot—written transcriptions—of the Alter Rebbe's chassidic discourses as recorded by his son and successor, expanding the documented corpus of the Alter Rebbe's Torah.

title_en: Likutei Torah on three Parashiyos printed in Vilna
summary_en: An edition of Likutei Torah on three Parashiyos was issued in Vilna in 1884, associated with the Rebbe Maharash.
story_body: This 5644 (1884) Vilna printing was among the chassidic works connected to the Rebbe Maharash, the fourth Chabad rebbe, and broadened distribution of the Alter Rebbe's discourses on these portions.

title_en: First print of a portrait of the Alter Rebbe
summary_en: The first printed image of the Alter Rebbe's likeness, taken from a painted portrait, was issued in 5649 (1889).
story_body: This 1889 reproduction is the earliest known printed portrait of the Alter Rebbe; later painters would render new images based on it, several of which the seventh Rebbe received and the library preserves.

title_en: Rabbi A.D. Lavut re-edits and prints the Siddur Torah Or in Vilna
summary_en: Rabbi A.D. Lavut reissued the Alter Rebbe's siddur as Siddur Torah Or in Vilna in 1887, scrubbing later printing errors.
story_body: By 5647 (1887), various siddur reprintings had accumulated textual corruptions. Rabbi Lavut's Vilna edition restored the nusach to its early Shklov-Kapust form and added Shaarei Tefillah, a commentary explaining the precise wording. The edition was reprinted multiple times in 1889, 1890, and 1892.

title_en: Siddur Im Shaar HaKollel edition published in Vilna
summary_en: A reworked Chabad siddur edition with Shaar HaKollel was published in Vilna in 5656 (1896).
story_body: This 1896 Vilna printing reorganized Rabbi Lavut's earlier edition and added Shaar HaKollel, becoming a long-influential template for subsequent Chabad siddur printings.

title_en: Seder HaAvodah siddur issued in Vilna
summary_en: The Seder HaAvodah Chabad siddur was issued in Vilna in 5671 (1911).
story_body: This 1911 Vilna siddur would later serve as the photographic base for the first 1945 Tehillas Hashem edition, with corrections directed by the Rebbe Rayatz.

title_en: Meah Shearim published in Berditchev
summary_en: Meah Shearim, a collection of one hundred discourses and letters of the Alter Rebbe, Mitteler Rebbe, and Tzemach Tzedek, was published in Berditchev in 1913.
story_body: The 5673 (1913) Berditchev printing bundled chassidic discourses and correspondence of the first three Chabad rebbes with the Alter Rebbe's siddur, giving the latter the popular name Siddur Meah Shearim.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab issues general letter to Chassidim
summary_en: The Rebbe Rashab printed a general letter to chassidim in 1917, on the eve of revolutionary upheaval in Russia.
story_body: The 5677 (1917) general letter was issued by the fifth Chabad rebbe during a turbulent year that included Russian revolution and the relocation of his court. Printed exemplars are preserved in the library exhibition.

title_en: Rostover Siddur printed in Rostov
summary_en: The Rostover Siddur, an edition of Tehillas Hashem incorporating corrections directed by the Rebbe Rashab, was printed in Rostov in 5678 (1918).
story_body: Photographed from the earlier Tefillas Kol Peh, the Rostov 1918 siddur incorporated many revisions ordered by the Rebbe Rashab and would later serve as the photo-master for the 1947 New York Tehillas Hashem.

title_en: Boneh Yerushalayim published in Jerusalem
summary_en: Boneh Yerushalayim, a collection of the Alter Rebbe's discourses, was published in Jerusalem in 1926.
story_body: The 180-page Jerusalem 5686 (1926) printing extended publication of the Alter Rebbe's chassidic teachings to the Land of Israel.

title_en: Liberation of the Rebbe Rayatz on 12 Tammuz
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was freed from Soviet imprisonment and exile on 12 Tammuz 5687 (July 1927), the Chabad festival of liberation.
story_body: Arrested for his work sustaining Jewish life under Soviet repression, the Rebbe Rayatz was released on 12 Tammuz 5687. The date became a major commemorative occasion in Chabad, marked in 2000 by a library exhibition honoring his 120th birth-year and 73 years since his liberation.

title_en: Maamar written in the Rebbe Rayatz's handwriting in 5700
summary_en: A chassidic discourse written in the Rebbe Rayatz's own handwriting dates to the year 5700 (1940).
story_body: Among the exhibition holdings is a maamar in the Rebbe Rayatz's hand from 5700, the year of his escape from Nazi-occupied Europe and arrival in the United States.

title_en: First edition of Hayom Yom published by Kehot
summary_en: The first edition of Hayom Yom, a daily Chabad almanac compiled by the future Rebbe, was published by Kehot in 5703 (1943).
story_body: Hayom Yom was compiled by Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson at the request of his father-in-law the Rebbe Rayatz, with each calendar day pairing a teaching, custom, or anecdote. Kehot's 1943 first edition made it a daily companion across Chabad households.

title_en: First edition of Tehillas Hashem siddur published in New York
summary_en: The first edition of the Tehillas Hashem siddur was published in New York in 5705 (1945) by the Central Organization for Jewish Education.
story_body: Largely a photographic reissue of the 1911 Vilna Seder HaAvodah with corrections, the 1945 New York Tehillas Hashem became the most widely used Chabad siddur of the modern era, eventually printed in close to one hundred subsequent editions.

title_en: First edition of the Chabad Haggadah with Likkutei Taamim u'Minhagim
summary_en: Kehot published the first edition of the Chabad Haggadah with Likkutei Taamim u'Minhagim in 5706 (1946).
story_body: The Haggadah's commentary, gathering sources and customs, was the future Rebbe's compilation. Its 1946 first edition became the standard Chabad Haggadah used at seder tables for generations.

title_en: Thinner-format Tehillas Hashem siddur issued in New York
summary_en: A second, thinner-format edition of Tehillas Hashem was published in New York in 1947, photographed from the 1918 Rostover Siddur.
story_body: The 5707 (1947) New York edition reproduced the Rostov 1918 siddur, itself based on the Tefillas Kol Peh corrected under the Rebbe Rashab. Issued alongside the thicker 1945 edition, it gave Chabad davveners two parallel formats.

title_en: Seventh Rebbe issues new Tanya edition with index and printing list
summary_en: In 5714 (1954) the Rebbe sent a new edition of Tanya to press, adding a topical index, list of corrections, and printing history.
story_body: From this 1954 edition forward, every printing of the Tanya included the Rebbe's added apparatus—index, errata, and a record of prior editions. Over the next two decades the Tanya would be reprinted more than thirty further times in this enhanced format.

title_en: New edition of Hilchos Talmud Torah with sources and notes
summary_en: Rabbi Nissan Mangel produced a new edition of the Alter Rebbe's Hilchos Talmud Torah in 1965, complete with source references and footnotes.
story_body: The 5725 (1965) Mangel edition added marginal notes and sources to the Alter Rebbe's halachot of Torah study. It became the standard, photo-reproduced in countless later printings and embedded into subsequent Shulchan Aruch editions.

title_en: Alter Rebbe's tefillin brought from Russia to the Rebbe
summary_en: Tefillin attributed to the Alter Rebbe were brought from Russia in 5726 (1966) and placed for viewing on the bima at 770.
story_body: On their 1966 arrival the Rebbe directed that the tefillin be set on the synagogue bima so that those who had immersed in the mikveh could file by to see them. They remain part of the library's object collection (#6104).

title_en: Rebbe launches expansion of Chabad houses on 11 Nisan 5732
summary_en: On his seventieth birthday, 11 Nisan 5732, the Rebbe called on his shluchim to establish 71 new institutions in the year ahead.
story_body: Rejecting the suggestion of retirement at seventy, the Rebbe applied the verse "I will come in the gevuros of Hashem" to his own work and asked shluchim to launch seventy-one new institutions during the year. The initiative kicked off the era's dramatic expansion of Chabad houses worldwide.

title_en: Rabbi Shlomo Cunin presents album of 71 new California institutions
summary_en: On 11 Nisan 5733 (1973) Rabbi Shlomo Cunin presented the Rebbe with a silver-bound album of new Chabad institutions established that year in California.
story_body: The album's silver cover read: "71, dedicated to the Rebbe, 11 Nisan 5733, the year of the Rebbe's seventy-first year." It documented the rapid expansion of Chabad's California network in direct response to the Rebbe's prior-year call.

title_en: Rebbe launches Maamarei Admur HaZaken editing project on Shavuos 5738
summary_en: At a Shavuos 5738 (June 1978) farbrengen the Rebbe announced the founding of a system to edit and publish the rebbes' discourses from manuscript.
story_body: The Rebbe's Shavuos announcement gave rise to a long-running editorial enterprise whose first major output was the multi-volume series Maamarei Admur HaZaken. Over the following years more than twenty volumes appeared, mostly arranged by the year each maamar was originally said.

title_en: Rebbe issues call to print Tanya in every Jewish locale, Eikev 5738
summary_en: In a special talk on Motzei Shabbos Parshas Eikev 5738 (August 1978) the Rebbe directed that the Tanya be printed in every locality where Jews live.
story_body: The Rebbe's directive launched what became a global mivtza of Tanya printing. By the time of writing, the Tanya had been printed more than five thousand times—often by mobile presses brought to distant cities—each printing carrying the imprimatur of the local Jewish community.

title_en: Rebbe reaffirms mivtza Tanya on 3 Shvat 5744
summary_en: On Shabbos Parshas Bo, 3 Shvat 5744 (January 7, 1984), the Rebbe again called for the worldwide printing of the Tanya in a special talk.
story_body: The 3 Shvat 5744 sicha reignited mivtza Tanya several years after its 1978 launch and brought renewed momentum to local Tanya printings in cities around the globe.

title_en: Certificate of honor for the Rebbe from US president and Congress, 11 Nisan 5743
summary_en: For the Rebbe's 11 Nisan 5743 birthday in 1983, the US president, senators, and members of Congress signed a certificate of honor naming the day a national Day of Education.
story_body: Coordinated annually in Washington by shliach Rabbi Avraham Shemtov, the 1983 certificate paired with Congressional Record speeches and a presidential greeting letter, anchoring the recurring 11 Nisan Day of Education in the United States.

title_en: Alter Rebbe's responsa issued as a standalone volume
summary_en: Rabbi Levi Bistritsky's edition of the Alter Rebbe's responsa was published as a freestanding 494-page volume in New York in 1988.
story_body: The 5748 (1988) New York edition pulled the Alter Rebbe's previously appended responsa into a dedicated volume, expanded with added material, source references, and cross-citations prepared by Rabbi Bistritsky.

title_en: US Congress awards the Rebbe a Congressional Gold Medal
summary_en: The US Congress presented the Rebbe with a gold medal of honor on the occasion of his 90th birthday, 11 Nisan 5752 (April 1992).
story_body: The 1992 award marked the Rebbe's ninetieth birthday and stood out among the many official tributes from American officials over the years.

title_en: Gold medal "L'taken Olam" issued in honor of the Rebbe
summary_en: A specially minted gold medal bearing the Rebbe's likeness, the image of 770, and the inscription "L'taken Olam" was issued in 5754 (1994).
story_body: The 1994 medal carried the Rebbe's portrait on one side and the iconic facade of 770 Eastern Parkway on the other, along with the Hebrew motto "L'taken Olam" and the English values Benevolence, Ethics, Leadership, and Scholarship.

title_en: Library opens Rebbe Rayatz exhibition on 12 Tammuz 5760
summary_en: The Chabad library opened a major exhibition of the Rebbe Rayatz's possessions, manuscripts, and books around 12 Tammuz 5760 (July 2000).
story_body: Marking the 120th anniversary of the Rebbe Rayatz's birth and 73 years since his Soviet liberation, the exhibition displayed his shtreimel, kittel, walking staff, passport, diaries, and chassidic manuscripts. It ran through the jubilee 50th yahrzeit period ending 10 Shvat 5761.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz exhibition closes on jubilee yahrzeit, 10 Shvat 5761
summary_en: The Rebbe Rayatz exhibition concluded on 10 Shvat 5761, marking the fiftieth-year jubilee of his passing and of the Rebbe's assumption of Chabad leadership.
story_body: The 10 Shvat 5761 close date matched the half-century since the Rebbe Rayatz's 1950 passing and the seventh Rebbe's acceptance of the Chabad nesius. The yom hilula remains the central Chabad date for the seventh Rebbe's leadership.

title_en: Library opens exhibition of certificates of honor to the Rebbe
summary_en: On 11 Nisan 5765 (April 20, 2005) the library opened an exhibition of medals, keys, and certificates given to the Rebbe by heads of state and city governments.
story_body: Exhibition Yud featured items presented to the Rebbe by world leaders and municipal authorities, alongside keys to Chabad houses and mitzvah tanks from his shluchim around the globe.

title_en: Library opens "Keys and Certificates of Honor" exhibition in Elul 5773
summary_en: A library exhibition of keys and honor certificates given to the Rebbe opened in Elul 5773 (August/September 2013).
story_body: Exhibition Yud-Beis displayed medallions, mitzvah-tank keys, and Chabad-house keys gathered by the Rebbe over the decades, illustrating his global network of shluchim and official ties with heads of state and municipal authorities.

title_en: Shulchan Aruch printed in Venice
summary_en: Rabbi Yosef Karo's Shulchan Aruch was printed in Venice in 5334 (1574).
story_body: Among the early Venetian printings of the Shulchan Aruch, this 1574 edition helped fix Karo's halachic code as the central reference work of Jewish law.

title_en: Ancient ketuba dated 5420
summary_en: A ketuba dated to 5420 (1660) is preserved in the Chabad library's manuscript collection.
story_body: Among the library's ancient ketubot is this 1660 marriage contract, witnessing Jewish family life of the mid-seventeenth century.

title_en: Amsterdam Haggadah printed with map of the Land of Israel
summary_en: A Pesach Haggadah was printed in Amsterdam in 5455 (1695) accompanied by a map of the Land of Israel.
story_body: The 1695 Amsterdam Haggadah included one of the early printed maps of the Holy Land bound with a Pesach service, a notable example of early modern Jewish cartography.

title_en: Ketuba from Finale dated 5496
summary_en: A ketuba from Finale, Italy, dated 5496 (1736) is among the library's manuscript holdings.
story_body: The 1736 Finale ketuba represents the rich Italian-Jewish tradition of decorated marriage contracts displayed in the library's exhibition.

title_en: Ketuba from Fez dated 5559
summary_en: A ketuba from Fez, Morocco, dated 5559 (1799) is preserved in the library's collection.
story_body: The 1799 Fez ketuba documents Sephardic-Moroccan marriage practice at the close of the eighteenth century and complements the library's other antique ketubot.

title_en: Y.Y. Benyamin publishes a map of the Land of Israel
summary_en: Y.Y. Benyamin issued a map of the Land of Israel in 5615 (1855).
story_body: Among the antique maps of the Holy Land preserved in the library is this 1855 production by Y.Y. Benyamin, a mid-nineteenth-century traveler-cartographer.

title_en: Warsaw map of the Land of Israel printed
summary_en: A map of the Land of Israel was printed in Warsaw in 5641 (1881).
story_body: The 1881 Warsaw map is part of the library's collection of antique Holy Land cartography spanning the seventeenth through nineteenth centuries.

title_en: Rebbe's 91st birthday celebrated with kos shel berachah
summary_en: On 11 Nissan 5753, Rabbi Yitzchak Kaduri sent a kos shel refuah blessing for the Rebbe's 91st birthday.
story_body: On 11 Nissan 5753 (April 2, 1993), Rabbi Yitzchak Kaduri sent a 'cup of healing' inscribed with a blessing for the Lubavitcher Rebbe Menachem Mendel Schneerson on his 91st birthday. The cup carried the inscription invoking blessings for the Rebbe, son of Chana, and is preserved among the personal items associated with the Rebbe.

title_en: Kiryat Gat mayor sends Rebbe key of the city — first such gift
summary_en: In Elul 5722, the mayor of Kiryat Gat became the first mayor to honor the Rebbe by sending him the key to the city.
story_body: In Elul 5722 (August–September 1962), the mayor of Kiryat Gat in Israel became the first municipal head to express appreciation for Chabad by sending the Rebbe the key of the city. He entrusted the key to Rabbi Yaakov Peles, who later delivered it. This precedent led many other mayors to follow suit through their local shluchim.

title_en: Rebbe receives Kiryat Gat's key at Erev Rosh Hashana farbrengen
summary_en: On Erev Rosh Hashana 5723, Rabbi Yaakov Peles handed Kiryat Gat's city key to the Rebbe at the welcome farbrengen for guests.
story_body: On the night of Erev Rosh Hashana 5723 (September 18, 1962), Rabbi Yaakov Peles delivered Kiryat Gat's city key to the Rebbe during the welcome farbrengen for visiting guests in 770. The Rebbe responded with a sicha explaining the symbolism of a city key — that it opens and closes the city gates to protect it from outside threats (Toras Menachem Hisvaaduyos vol. 34, p. 324).

title_en: São Paulo mayor sends Rebbe the city key
summary_en: On 10 Shevat 5730, the mayor of São Paulo, Brazil sent the Rebbe the key of the city through Rabbi David Rosen.
story_body: On 10 Shevat 5730 (January 17, 1970), the mayor of São Paulo, Brazil sent the Rebbe the city key through Rabbi David Rosen. The Rebbe himself wrote a note in his handwriting recording the date and origin of the gift. The key and note are displayed in the library exhibition's South America section.

title_en: NYC Mayor Abraham Beame presents Rebbe certificate for 25 years of leadership
summary_en: On 10 Shevat 5735, NYC Mayor Abraham Beame presented the Rebbe a certificate of honor marking 25 years of his leadership.
story_body: On 10 Shevat 5735 (January 22, 1975), New York City Mayor Abraham Beame presented the Lubavitcher Rebbe with a certificate of honor commemorating the 25th anniversary of his assumption of the Chabad leadership. The certificate is displayed in the library exhibition's New York case.

title_en: NYC Mayor Beame presents Rebbe city medallion shaped as a cup
summary_en: On 11 Nissan 5737, NYC Mayor Abraham Beame presented the Rebbe a city medallion shaped like a cup.
story_body: On 11 Nissan 5737 (March 30, 1977), New York City Mayor Abraham Beame presented the Rebbe with a medallion of the city, fashioned in the shape of a cup. The Rebbe himself wrote the date on an accompanying note, and the medallion and note are now displayed in the New York case of the library exhibition.

title_en: Chabad Library begins annual themed exhibitions
summary_en: Starting in 5754, the Chabad Library at 770 began mounting a new themed exhibition every one to two years.
story_body: In 5754 (1993–1994), the Agudas Chasidei Chabad – Ohel Yosef Yitzchak – Lubavitch Library at 770 Eastern Parkway began its tradition of mounting themed exhibitions of rare items from its archives. Over the years more than ten exhibitions have been organized, each dedicated to a different theme such as rare manuscripts, Chabad Rebbeim, Haggadot, or the bicentennial of the Alter Rebbe's liberation.

title_en: Library opens 13th exhibition of rare incunabula on 20th yahrzeit
summary_en: On 3 Tammuz 5774, the library opened its 13th exhibition, displaying rare books printed in the first century of Hebrew printing.
story_body: On 3 Tammuz 5774 (July 1, 2014), marking the 20th yahrzeit of the Lubavitcher Rebbe, the Chabad Library opened its 13th exhibition — Ta'aruchat Ginzei Sefarim. The exhibition displays incunabula and rare books printed in the first 100 years of Hebrew printing (1475–1574), along with rare manuscripts, broadsides and posters. A guide booklet was prepared by Rabbi Shalom DovBer Levin and R. Moshe Heller.

title_en: Pesaro Hebrew press founded by Gershom Soncino
summary_en: In 5267 (1507), Gershom Soncino founded the Hebrew printing house in Pesaro.
story_body: In 5267 (1507), Gershom Soncino founded the Hebrew printing house in Pesaro, Italy. Over the next twenty years he printed more than fifty books there, including half the tractates of the Talmud, issued between 5269–5279 (1509–1519).

title_en: Tractate Eruvin printed in Pesaro by Gershom Soncino
summary_en: In 5271 (1511), Gershom Soncino printed Tractate Eruvin at his Pesaro press.
story_body: In 5271 (1511), Gershom Soncino printed Tractate Eruvin as part of his Pesaro Talmud series. The tractate is part of his run of more than two dozen tractates issued there between 1509 and 1519.

title_en: First printing of Ba'al HaTurim on the Torah in Constantinople
summary_en: In 5274 (1514), the commentary of the Ba'al HaTurim on the Torah was printed for the first time in Constantinople.
story_body: In 5274 (1514), the first edition of Rabbi Yaakov Ba'al HaTurim's commentary on the Torah — containing notes on masorah, gematria, and homiletics — was printed in Constantinople. Excerpts of this commentary later became a standard component of printed Chumashim.

title_en: Kitzur Piskei HaRosh printed in Constantinople
summary_en: In 5275 (1515), Kitzur Piskei HaRosh — Rabbi Yaakov Ba'al HaTurim's abridgement of his father's halachic rulings — was printed in Constantinople.
story_body: In 5275 (1515), Kitzur Piskei HaRosh was printed as a standalone book in Constantinople. Composed by Rabbi Yaakov Ba'al HaTurim as a digest of his father the Rosh's rulings, it was later usually printed bound with the Rosh itself.

title_en: Fez Hebrew printing house founded
summary_en: In 5276 (1516), refugees from Spain established a Hebrew printing press in Fez, Morocco.
story_body: In 5276 (1516), Sephardic refugees who had settled in Fez, Morocco established a Hebrew printing house there. The press operated only a few years but produced several volumes, including an edition of the Arba'ah Turim in 5280 (1520).

title_en: Rabbeinu Yerucham's Toldot Adam ve-Chava printed in Constantinople
summary_en: In 5276 (1516), Rabbeinu Yerucham's halachic compendium Toldot Adam ve-Chava was printed for the first time in Constantinople.
story_body: In 5276 (1516), Rabbeinu Yerucham ben Meshullam's Toldot Adam ve-Chava was printed for the first time, in Constantinople. Rabbeinu Yerucham was a student of the Rosh from Provence, and his halachic compendium is among the foundational pre-Tur codes.

title_en: Daniel Bomberg founds Hebrew press in Venice
summary_en: In 5277 (1517), Daniel Bomberg founded the largest Hebrew printing house of the era in Venice.
story_body: In 5277 (1517), the Christian printer Daniel Bomberg founded his Hebrew printing house in Venice — the largest Hebrew press of the era. Over the next three decades he printed numerous editions of the Bible and the complete Talmud, setting the standard page layout still used today.

title_en: Teshuvot HaRambam printed in Constantinople
summary_en: In 5277 (1517), a collection of Rambam's responsa and letters was printed in Constantinople.
story_body: In 5277 (1517), a collection of Rambam's responsa, queries, and letters was printed in Constantinople. It was among the first published anthologies of Maimonidean correspondence.

title_en: Responsa of the Rosh printed in Constantinople
summary_en: In 5277 (1517), the responsa of Rabbeinu Asher (the Rosh) were printed in Constantinople, organized into 108 thematic sections.
story_body: In 5277 (1517), the responsa of Rabbeinu Asher (the Rosh) were printed in Constantinople. They were arranged in 108 thematic 'kelalim,' with each kelal containing multiple responsa, and became a foundational responsa collection.

title_en: Megillat Esther with Akedat Yitzchak commentary printed in Constantinople
summary_en: In 5278 (1518), Shmuel Nachmias printed Megillat Esther with Rabbi Yitzchak Arama's Akedat Yitzchak commentary in Constantinople — his last imprint.
story_body: In 5278 (1518), Shmuel Nachmias, son of David Nachmias, printed his final book — Megillat Esther with the commentary of Rabbi Yitzchak Arama (Akedat Yitzchak), one of the Spanish exiles. The Nachmias brothers had founded the first Hebrew press in Constantinople after the 1492 expulsion.

title_en: Bomberg prints Tehillim-Iyov in Venice
summary_en: In 5278 (1518), Daniel Bomberg printed a Tehillim-Iyov volume in Venice.
story_body: In 5278 (1518), Daniel Bomberg printed a Tehillim and Iyov volume at his Venice press. It formed part of his early Bible output, which he produced in multiple editions over the following years.

title_en: Responsa attributed to Ramban printed in Venice
summary_en: In 5279 (1519), a collection of 288 responsa was printed in Venice under the (mistaken) attribution to Ramban.
story_body: In 5279 (1519), a volume titled 'Teshuvot leRabbeinu Moshe ben Nachman' containing 288 responsa was printed in Venice. The responsa were actually those of the Rashba but had been mistakenly attributed to Ramban; the volume is counted as part 8 of the Rashba responsa series.

title_en: Responsa of Maharik printed in Venice
summary_en: In 5279 (1519), the responsa of Rabbi Yosef Colon (Maharik) were collected and printed in Venice.
story_body: In 5279 (1519), the responsa of Rabbi Yosef Colon (Maharik), one of the leading 15th-century Italian poskim, were printed in Venice. The volume gathered his halachic rulings for the first time in print.

title_en: Gershom Soncino founds Rimini press
summary_en: In 5280 (1520), Gershom Soncino founded a Hebrew printing house in Rimini.
story_body: In 5280 (1520), the wandering printer Gershom Soncino established a new Hebrew printing house in Rimini, Italy. Six years later he would print there the Sefer Ha-Agur of Rabbi Yaakov Landau.

title_en: Bomberg prints first complete Talmud in Venice
summary_en: Between 5280–5283 (1520–1523), Daniel Bomberg printed the first complete edition of the Talmud in Venice — setting the standard page layout used ever since.
story_body: Between 5280 and 5283 (1520–1523), Daniel Bomberg produced the first complete printed edition of the Babylonian Talmud at his Venice press, including Rashi and Tosafot on every page. This edition established the standard pagination of the Talmud, which has been retained by virtually every subsequent edition; standard citations of folio and side derive from it.

title_en: Tur printed in Fez, Morocco
summary_en: In 5280 (1520), the Arba'ah Turim was printed at the Hebrew press in Fez, Morocco.
story_body: In 5280 (1520), the Arba'ah Turim of Rabbi Yaakov ben Asher was printed at the Hebrew press in Fez, Morocco. Several leaves of this Fez edition, recovered from book bindings, survive in the Chabad Library archive.

title_en: Bomberg prints Rif with commentaries in Venice
summary_en: In 5281 (1521), Daniel Bomberg printed the Rif in Venice with its commentaries and the Mordechai and Tosefta appended.
story_body: In 5281 (1521), Daniel Bomberg printed an edition of the Hilchot Rav Alfas (Rif) in Venice. The multi-volume edition included the commentaries on the Rif, with the Mordechai and Tosefta appended at the end of each tractate.

title_en: Bomberg prints Rambam's Mishneh Torah in Venice
summary_en: In 5284 (1524), Daniel Bomberg printed an edition of Rambam's Mishneh Torah with commentaries in Venice.
story_body: In 5284 (1524), Daniel Bomberg printed an edition of Rambam's Mishneh Torah in Venice, accompanied by its standard commentaries. The edition was part of the Venice press's run of major rabbinic works in the 1520s.

title_en: Bomberg prints Mikraot Gedolot Torah in Venice
summary_en: In 5285 (1525), Bomberg printed a Mikraot Gedolot Torah volume in Venice with multiple commentaries and the Greater and Lesser Masorah.
story_body: In 5285 (1525), Daniel Bomberg printed a volume of the Torah as part of the Mikraot Gedolot series at his Venice press. The volume included multiple commentaries together with the Greater and Lesser Masorah.

title_en: Sefer Ha-Agur printed in Rimini by Gershom Soncino
summary_en: In 5286 (1526), Gershom Soncino printed Rabbi Yaakov Landau's halachic work Sefer Ha-Agur in Rimini.
story_body: In 5286 (1526), Gershom Soncino printed Sefer Ha-Agur of Rabbi Yaakov Landau at his Rimini press. Landau, a German halachist who had earlier served as proofreader at the Naples press, had first issued the book in Naples; the Rimini edition followed.

title_en: First complete Rif edition with commentaries printed in Constantinople
summary_en: The first complete edition of the Rif with commentaries and the Mordechai was printed in Constantinople in 5269.
story_body: In 5269, the first complete printed edition of Hilchot Rav Alfas (Rif) — Rabbi Yitzchak Alfasi's foundational digest of Talmudic law — was issued in Constantinople, accompanied by its commentaries and the Mordechai appended at the end. Several portions of this edition are preserved in the Chabad Library archive.

title_en: Krakow Hebrew printing house founded
summary_en: In 5290 (1530), a Hebrew printing house was established in Krakow, Poland, which printed the Tur among its first books.
story_body: In 5290 (1530), Jews who had settled in Poland after the Iberian expulsions established a Hebrew printing house in Krakow. Among its first publications was an edition of the Arba'ah Turim, which was reprinted there in 5299 (1539).

title_en: Sefer Ha-Tania (Rabbati) printed in Mantua
summary_en: In 5274 (1514), Rabbi Yechiel ben Yekutiel's halachic compendium Sefer Ha-Tania (Tania Rabbati) was printed in Mantua.
story_body: In 5274 (1514), Rabbi Yechiel ben Yekutiel ben Binyamin Harofeh's halachic compendium Sefer Ha-Tania — later called Tania Rabbati to distinguish it from the Alter Rebbe's Tanya — was printed in Mantua. The work collects rulings and customs for the entire year.

title_en: Sefer Ha-Mitzvot of Rambam printed in Constantinople
summary_en: In 5270 (1510), Rambam's Sefer Ha-Mitzvot was printed in Constantinople.
story_body: In 5270 (1510), Rambam's Sefer Ha-Mitzvot — his enumeration and explanation of the 613 commandments — was printed in Constantinople. It joined a small but growing body of pre-Shulchan Aruch halachic literature being issued by the Ottoman Sephardic presses.

title_en: Tur reprinted in Krakow
summary_en: In 5299 (1539), the Arba'ah Turim was reprinted in Krakow.
story_body: In 5299 (1539), the Arba'ah Turim of Rabbi Yaakov ben Asher was printed for the second time at the Krakow Hebrew press, nearly a decade after the press was founded. The volume is preserved in the Chabad Library exhibition.

title_en: Tosafot Chagigah copied by hand in Egypt
summary_en: In 5349 (1589), a portion of Tosafot to Tractate Chagigah was copied by hand in Egypt onto a blank page of the Wadi al-Hijara Talmud.
story_body: In 5349 (1589), a rabbi in Egypt who owned a Spanish-edition Talmud — which had been printed with Rashi but without Tosafot — copied a portion of the Tosafot on Tractate Chagigah by hand into a blank leaf at the start of his copy. The page is preserved in the Chabad Library archive.

title_en: Tur with Beit Yosef first printed in Venice
summary_en: In 5310 (1550), the Arba'ah Turim was printed for the first time alongside Rabbi Yosef Karo's Beit Yosef commentary in Venice.
story_body: In 5310 (1550), the Arba'ah Turim was printed in Venice together with Rabbi Yosef Karo's Beit Yosef commentary for the first time. This edition would establish the standard pairing of the Tur and Beit Yosef in subsequent printings.

title_en: Bragadin and Justinian Rambam controversy in Venice
summary_en: In 5310 (1550), competing Venice printers Bragadin and Justinian issued rival editions of Rambam, igniting a fierce controversy and a cherem from the Rema.
story_body: In 5310 (1550), the rival Venetian printers Bragadin and Justinian both issued editions of Rambam's Mishneh Torah. Bragadin's edition included new glosses by Maharam of Padua; Justinian pirated those glosses, reprinted them, and undersold his competitor. The dispute convulsed the Jewish world, and the Rema (R. Moshe Isserles) issued a cherem against anyone who purchased the Justinian edition.

title_en: Bragadin Rif printed in Venice
summary_en: In 5312 (1552), the Bragadin press in Venice printed an edition of the Rif — its last Venetian edition.
story_body: In 5312 (1552), the Bragadin press in Venice printed what would be the last Venetian edition of the Rif. The Chabad Library copy bears many marginal Italian-script glosses by an unidentified annotator.

title_en: Tuviah Foa founds Sabbioneta Hebrew press
summary_en: In 5311 (1551), Tuviah Foa established the Hebrew printing house in Sabbioneta, Italy.
story_body: In 5311 (1551), the printer Tuviah Foa founded the Hebrew printing house in Sabbioneta, Italy. Two years later it began printing the Talmud with additions and annotations, a project halted by the 1553 papal decree to burn the Talmud.

title_en: Pope orders burning of the Talmud across Italy
summary_en: In 5313 (1553), an apostate-driven denunciation led the Pope to decree that all copies of the Talmud in Italy be burned, with harsh penalties for possession.
story_body: In 5313 (1553), apostates denounced the Talmud to the Pope, who decreed that all copies of the Talmud in every Italian state be burned, with severe penalties for anyone retaining tractates. The decree halted the Sabbioneta Talmud project and forced Italian Jews to substitute study of the Rif — which presents the Talmud's halachic conclusions — in place of the Talmud itself.

title_en: Sabbioneta prints Moreh Nevuchim
summary_en: In 5313 (1553), Tuviah Foa's Sabbioneta press printed Rambam's Moreh Nevuchim.
story_body: In 5313 (1553), the Sabbioneta press of Tuviah Foa printed Rambam's philosophical magnum opus, Moreh Nevuchim. The volume appeared the same year that the papal decree forced the Italian presses to abandon Talmud production.

title_en: Sabbioneta prints Rif with Shiltei HaGiborim
summary_en: In 5314 (1554), Tuviah Foa's Sabbioneta press issued an edition of the Rif with Rabbi Yehoshua Boaz's Shiltei HaGiborim.
story_body: In 5314 (1554), with Talmud printing forbidden by papal decree, Tuviah Foa's Sabbioneta press shifted to printing the Rif. The edition was edited by Rabbi Yehoshua Boaz and included his newly composed Shiltei HaGiborim along with substantial marginal additions.

title_en: Cremona Hebrew press founded; prints Shu"t Maharil
summary_en: In 5316 (1556), Vincenzo Conti founded the Hebrew printing house in Cremona, and printed Shu"t Maharil there that same year.
story_body: In 5316 (1556), Vincenzo Conti established the Hebrew printing house in Cremona, Italy. That same year he printed Shu"t Maharil — the responsa of Rabbi Yaakov Halevi Molin, the leading Ashkenazi halachist and arbiter of customs in his generation.

title_en: Riva di Trento Hebrew press founded
summary_en: In 5318 (1558), Rabbi Yosef Ottolenghi and Rabbi Yaakov Marcaria founded the Hebrew printing house in Riva di Trento; its first book was the Rif.
story_body: In 5318 (1558), Rabbi Yosef Ottolenghi and Rabbi Yaakov Marcaria founded the Hebrew printing house in Riva di Trento, Italy. It operated for four years; its first imprint was an edition of the Rif in a smaller format than the preceding Sabbioneta edition.

title_en: Sefer Sha'arei Dura printed in Venice
summary_en: In 5308 (1548), Sefer Sha'arei Dura — the medieval halachic compendium on the laws of forbidden mixtures — was printed in Venice.
story_body: In 5308 (1548), Sefer Sha'arei Dura was printed in Venice. The work, a medieval Ashkenazic compendium primarily on the laws of forbidden mixtures and ritual matters, was widely used by halachic decisors.

title_en: Responsa of Mahari Weil printed in Venice
summary_en: In 5309 (1549), the responsa of Rabbi Yaakov Weil (Mahari Weil) were printed in Venice.
story_body: In 5309 (1549), the responsa of Rabbi Yaakov Weil (Mahari Weil), one of the foremost halachic decisors in 15th-century Ashkenaz and a student of the Maharil, were collected and printed in Venice.

title_en: Justinian Rambam printed in Venice (pirated edition)
summary_en: In 5310 (1550), Justinian published a competing, pirated Rambam edition in Venice, copying Maharam Padua's glosses and undercutting Bragadin's price.
story_body: In 5310 (1550), as Bragadin began printing his edition of Rambam in Venice, the rival printer Justinian copied Maharam of Padua's glosses without authorization and rushed out his own edition at a lower price. The dispute became one of the most consequential printing controversies of the era and prompted the Rema's cherem against purchasing the pirated edition.

title_en: Rabbi Yosef Karo brings new Rambam edition to press in Venice
summary_en: In 5334 (1574), after a twenty-year hiatus following the 1550 controversy, Rabbi Yosef Karo issued a new edition of Rambam in Venice with his Kessef Mishneh commentary.
story_body: In 5334 (1574), after more than twenty years in which no Rambam was printed in the wake of the Bragadin–Justinian controversy, Rabbi Yosef Karo (author of the Shulchan Aruch) brought a corrected edition of Rambam's Mishneh Torah to press in Venice. The edition included his commentary Kessef Mishneh, and several copies are preserved in the Chabad Library.

title_en: Small-format Shulchan Aruch printed in Venice
summary_en: In 5334 (1574), a small octavo-format edition of the Shulchan Aruch was printed in Venice.
story_body: In 5334 (1574), a small octavo (8°) format edition of Rabbi Yosef Karo's Shulchan Aruch was issued in Venice, alongside the larger Rambam edition published that year. The small format was intended for portable personal use.

title_en: Compact pocket Tanakh printed in Paris by Robert Estienne
summary_en: Between 5304–5305 (1544–1545), the printer Robert Estienne (Robertus Stephanus) produced a compact pocket Tanakh in Paris.
story_body: Between 5304 and 5305 (1544–1545), the Paris printer Robert Estienne (Robertus Stephanus) produced a small-format pocket edition of the Tanakh, without translation or commentary. It was issued in parallel to the larger Mikraot Gedolot editions then being produced in Italy.

title_en: Manuscript of Darkei Moshe and Maharshal's glosses copied in Szydłów
summary_en: In 5401 (1641), a manuscript volume containing the long Darkei Moshe of the Rema and the Maharshal's glosses on the Tur was completed in Szydłów.
story_body: In 5401 (1641), a scribe in Szydłów, near Krakow, completed copying a manuscript volume containing two works of glosses on the Tur and Beit Yosef: the long recension of Rema's Darkei Moshe, and Maharshal's glosses on the Tur (which were never independently printed but were later incorporated into the Derisha, Perisha, and Bach).

title_en: Shu"t HaRashba printed in Bologna
summary_en: In 5299 (1539), the first volume of Shu"t HaRashba — containing 1,255 responsa — was printed in Bologna.
story_body: In 5299 (1539), a volume of 'Teshuvot She'elot' by Rabbi Shlomo ibn Aderet (Rashba) containing 1,255 responsa was printed in Bologna. It became part 1 of the Rashba responsa series, joining the body of his thousands of rulings on questions sent to him from across the Jewish world.

title_en: Sefer HaMitzvot first printed in Constantinople
summary_en: Maimonides's Sefer HaMitzvot was first printed in Constantinople in 1510.
story_body: Maimonides composed Sefer HaMitzvot in his youth in Arabic, and it was translated into Hebrew during his lifetime by R. Avraham ibn Chasdai, R. Shlomo ibn Ayyub, and R. Moshe ibn Tibbon. The work catalogs the 613 commandments and serves as a preface to his Mishneh Torah. Its first printing appeared in Constantinople in 1510.

title_en: SMaK parchment manuscript purchased
summary_en: A parchment manuscript of Sefer Mitzvot Katan with Rabbenu Peretz's glosses was purchased on 26 Shevat 5305 (1545).
story_body: The library preserves an early Ashkenazi parchment copy of R. Yitzchak of Corbeil's SMaK (Amudei Golah) together with the glosses of his student R. Peretz of Corbeil. An owner inscription records its purchase on 26 Shevat 5305 (February 1545). It is catalogued as archive manuscript 1956.

title_en: Vincenzo Conti opens Hebrew press in Cremona
summary_en: Vincenzo Conti opened his Hebrew printing house in Cremona in 1556, issuing the SMaK that same year.
story_body: In 5316 (1556) Vincenzo Conti established the Hebrew press in Cremona. In its inaugural year the house produced an edition of Sefer Mitzvot Katan, beginning a printing program that would soon include the celebrated Cremona Zohar.

title_en: Azharot of ibn Gabirol first printed in Constantinople
summary_en: Solomon ibn Gabirol's Azharot, with Rashbatz's Zohar HaRakia commentary, was first printed in Constantinople in 1515.
story_body: R. Shlomo ibn Gabirol of Spain (c.1020-1057) composed the Azharot, a poetic enumeration of the commandments. R. Shimon b. Tzemach Duran (Rashbatz, Algeria 1361-1444) wrote on it the commentary Zohar HaRakia, and the two were issued together in their first edition in Constantinople in 5275 (1515).

title_en: Sefer HaIkkarim printed in Rimini
summary_en: R. Yosef Albo's Sefer HaIkkarim was printed in Rimini in 1522.
story_body: R. Yosef Albo, who lived in Spain in the second century of the sixth millennium, composed Sefer HaIkkarim, a systematic exposition of Jewish dogmatic principles. The Rimini edition of 5282 (1522) is among the early printings preserved in the library.

title_en: Rosh Amana by Abrabanel printed in Constantinople
summary_en: Don Yitzchak Abrabanel's Rosh Amana on principles of faith was printed at the Nachmias press in Constantinople in 1505.
story_body: Several years after his exile from Spain, Abrabanel delivered to print his Rosh Amana, devoted to the foundational tenets of Jewish belief. It was issued by the Nachmias press in Constantinople in 5265 (1505).

title_en: Kad HaKemach first printed in Constantinople
summary_en: Rabbenu Bachya b. Asher's Kad HaKemach was first printed in Constantinople in 1515.
story_body: R. Bachya b. Asher of Spain (1255-c.1340), in addition to his Torah commentary, composed Kad HaKemach, alphabetically arranged homilies on the principles of Torah and the commandments. Its first edition appeared in Constantinople in 5275 (1515).

title_en: Derech Emunah by Avraham Bibago printed in Constantinople
summary_en: R. Avraham Bibago's philosophical treatise Derech Emunah was printed in Constantinople in 1522.
story_body: R. Avraham Bibago lived in Spain in the years preceding the expulsion and authored Derech Emunah, philosophical investigations into matters of faith and religion. The work was printed in Constantinople in 5282 (1522).

title_en: Torah Or by ibn Yachya printed in Bologna
summary_en: R. Don Yosef ibn Yachya's Torah Or was printed in Bologna in 1538.
story_body: Don Yosef ibn Yachya, an exile of the 1497 expulsion from Portugal, composed Torah Or on the soul's ultimate felicity and on the doctrines of Gan Eden, Gehinnom, and the World to Come. It was printed in Bologna in 5298 (1538).

title_en: First printing of the Zohar in Mantua
summary_en: The first edition of the Zohar was printed in Mantua between 1558 and 1560.
story_body: The Zohar of Rashbi was first printed in 5318-5320 (1558-1560). The Mantua edition was produced at the press of R. Meir b. Efraim of Padua and R. Yaakov b. Naftali of Gazzuolo, and it became the textual basis for most subsequent printings of the Zohar.

title_en: Cremona printing of the Zohar
summary_en: A parallel edition of the Zohar was printed at Vincenzo Conti's press in Cremona in 1558.
story_body: Concurrent with the Mantua edition, the Zohar was printed at the Cremona house of Vincenzo Conti in a larger format with textual variants from the Mantua text, known as the Zohar Gadol. This Cremona text was reprinted twice more, in Lublin (1623-4) and Sulzbach (1684).

title_en: Lublin reprint of the Cremona Zohar
summary_en: The Cremona-text Zohar Gadol was reprinted in Lublin in 5383-5384 (1623-1624).
story_body: The large-format Cremona edition of the Zohar was reissued in Lublin in 5383-5384 (1623-1624), continuing the textual tradition distinct from the Mantua line.

title_en: Sulzbach reprint of the Cremona Zohar
summary_en: The Cremona-text Zohar Gadol was reprinted in Sulzbach in 5444 (1684).
story_body: The Sulzbach edition of 5444 (1684) was the second reprint of the Cremona Zohar Gadol, preserving the variant text of Vincenzo Conti's 1558 edition.

title_en: Maarechet HaElokut printed in Ferrara
summary_en: Maarechet HaElokut with R. Yehuda Chayyat's Minchat Yehuda commentary was printed in Ferrara in 1558.
story_body: R. Peretz HaKohen of Spain (1305-1370), a Talmudic commentator and kabbalist, authored Maarechet HaElokut. R. Yehuda Chayyat, an exile of the Spanish expulsion who helped disseminate Kabbalah in Italy, wrote the commentary Minchat Yehuda upon it. The combined work was printed in Ferrara in 5318 (1558).

title_en: Maarechet HaElokut printed in Mantua
summary_en: Maarechet HaElokut was also printed in Mantua the same year, 1558.
story_body: Parallel to the Ferrara edition, Maarechet HaElokut with Minchat Yehuda was issued in Mantua in 5318 (1558).

title_en: Machzor according to the Roman rite printed in Bologna
summary_en: A Roman-rite machzor with R. Yochanan Treves's Kimcha De'avishuna commentary was printed in Bologna in 1540.
story_body: Early printers issued machzorim with distinct texts for each community. The Bologna edition of 5300 (1540) followed the Roman rite (k"k Roma) and included the Kimcha De'avishuna commentary of R. Yochanan Treves.

title_en: Mantua machzor printing begins
summary_en: Printing of a Roman-rite machzor began in Mantua in 5317 (1557).
story_body: The Mantua edition of the Roman-rite machzor was a multi-year project, beginning in 5317 (1557) and finishing only in 5320 (1560).

title_en: Mantua machzor printing completed
summary_en: The Mantua Roman-rite machzor was completed in 5320 (1560).
story_body: Begun in 1557, the Mantua edition of the Roman-rite machzor was completed in 5320 (1560).

title_en: Machzor printed in Salonika
summary_en: A machzor was printed in Salonika in 5310 (1550).
story_body: Among the early machzorim preserved in the library is the Salonika edition of 5310 (1550), representing the rite of one of the Ottoman Jewish communities.

title_en: Machzor printed in Venice
summary_en: A machzor was printed in Venice in 5328 (1568).
story_body: The Venice edition of 5328 (1568) is one of the early machzorim preserved in the library's collection.

title_en: Leshon Limudim printed in Constantinople
summary_en: Leshon Limudim was printed in Constantinople in 5266 (1506).
story_body: The Hebrew grammar Leshon Limudim was issued in Constantinople in 5266 (1506).

title_en: Sefer HaAruch printed in Pesaro
summary_en: R. Natan of Rome's Sefer HaAruch was printed in Pesaro in 5277 (1517).
story_body: R. Natan b. Yechiel of Rome (c.1035-1110) compiled the Aruch, an alphabetical dictionary of difficult Talmudic terms. The Pesaro edition of 5277 (1517) is preserved in the library.

title_en: Aruch HaKatzar printed in Constantinople
summary_en: An abridged Aruch was printed in Constantinople in 5271 (1511).
story_body: The Aruch HaKatzar, an abridged version of R. Natan of Rome's Talmudic dictionary, was printed in Constantinople in 5271 (1511).

title_en: Concordance Meir Nativ printed in Venice
summary_en: R. Yitzchak b. Kalonymus Natan's Meir Nativ concordance was first printed in Venice in 1524.
story_body: The Hebrew biblical concordance, also called Meir Nativ, was compiled by R. Yitzchak b. Kalonymus Natan to index Hebrew word-roots with their Tanach references. Its first edition was issued at Daniel Bomberg's Venice press in 5284 (1524).

title_en: Hebrew grammar printed in Basel
summary_en: A Hebrew grammar was printed in Basel in 5285 (1525).
story_body: Among the early grammar works in the library is the Basel printing of 5285 (1525).

title_en: Machbarot Imanuel printed in Constantinople
summary_en: Machbarot Imanuel was printed in Constantinople in 5295 (1535).
story_body: The poetic Machbarot Imanuel of Immanuel of Rome was issued in Constantinople in 5295 (1535).

title_en: Yosef Schneur founds Hebrew press in Furth
