summary_en: The Furth Hebrew printing house was established by Yosef Schneur in 5451 (1691).
story_body: The printer Yosef Schneur founded the Furth press in 5451 (1691). He died shortly afterwards, but the house continued to operate under his name.

title_en: Furth press notice of printed books
summary_en: In 5452 (1692) the Furth press printed an announcement of the books issued in its house.
story_body: The Furth press of the late Yosef Schneur printed a broadside in 5452 (1692) advertising 'the books printed in the holy community of Furth in the excellent press of the eminent Yosef Schneur z"l.' Such notices are exceptionally rare survivals from this period.

title_en: Amsterdam Haggadah desert-journey map printed
summary_en: A fold-out map of the Israelites' desert journeys was printed in Amsterdam in 5455 (1695) for inclusion in a Passover Haggadah.
story_body: Early printers sometimes issued large broadsheets meant to be folded and bound into a book. The Amsterdam map of the journeys of the Children of Israel through the wilderness was produced in 5455 (1695) for binding into the Amsterdam Haggadah of that year.

title_en: Chevrat Mishmeret HaBoker veHaErev founded in Mantua
summary_en: On 1 Nisan 5462 (March 1702) the Mantua society for early-morning and late-Shabbat Torah study was founded.
story_body: On Rosh Chodesh Nisan 5462 (March 1702) the 'Chevrat Mishmeret HaBoker veHaErev' was established in Mantua for those who would rise early and remain late on Shabbat for Torah study. Thirteen years later the society celebrated its founding.

title_en: Mantua society marks 13th anniversary
summary_en: On 1 Nisan 5475 (April 1715) Mantua's Chevrat Mishmeret marked its 13th anniversary with a printed Shir LaMaalot.
story_body: Thirteen years after its founding, the Mantua Chevrat Mishmeret HaBoker veHaErev celebrated 'the birthday of the chevrah' on 1 Nisan 5475 (April 1715), and printed a Shir LaMaalot poem in honor of the occasion.

title_en: Mantua Pragmatica sumptuary regulations renewed
summary_en: On 29 Cheshvan 5483 (November 1722) the Mantua community renewed its Pragmatica sumptuary regulations for six years.
story_body: Mantua's community ordinances, known as the Pragmatica, restricted royal dress, jewelry, and dancing so that Jews would not stand out before the gentile population. On 29 Cheshvan 5483 (November 1722) the regulations were renewed for six years, from Rosh Chodesh Adar Sheni 5483 through Erev Rosh Chodesh Adar 5489, signed by Rabbi David Pinzi and the scribe R. Shimshon Moron.

title_en: Mantua prayer for excessive rain printed
summary_en: A 'prayer for excessive rains that damage crops' was printed in Mantua in 5489 (1729).
story_body: Following the halachic ruling in Shulchan Aruch (OC 576:11) that one prays when excessive rains cause distress, Mantua's community printed a sheet of prayers for excessive rains that were damaging the grain harvest in 5489 (1729).

title_en: Wedding poem printed for R. Yitzchak Marini in Mantua
summary_en: In 5492 (1732) R. Yeshayahu Bassan printed a praise-poem for the Mantua wedding of R. Yitzchak Marini and Yudita.
story_body: The 5492 (1732) wedding of R. Yitzchak Marini and his bride Yudita in Mantua was honored with a printed poem of praise by R. Yeshayahu Bassan, author of Lechmei Todah. A companion sheet preserved in the library archive bears a poem by his son R. Yisrael Binyamin Bassan for the wedding of Ben-Tzion Ashkenazi and his bride Brachah.

title_en: Florence prayer printed for Reggio plague
summary_en: In 5495 (1735) a 'prayer for many illnesses' was printed at Shmuel Falasos's Florence press during a plague in Reggio.
story_body: When a plague struck Reggio in northern Italy in 5495 (1735), a 'tefillah leribbui chalaim' was composed and printed at the Florence press of Shmuel Falasos to be recited during the outbreak.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek born on Erev Rosh Hashanah
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek (R. Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch) was born on Erev Rosh Hashanah 5550 (September 1789).
story_body: R. Menachem Mendel Schneersohn, later known as the Tzemach Tzedek, was born on Erev Rosh Hashanah 5550. On that very day his grandfather the Alter Rebbe began delivering the lengthy discourse 'Mashbiim Oto,' whose content forms the first three chapters of Tanya.

title_en: Rebbetzin Devorah Leah passes on Tzom Gedaliah
summary_en: Rebbetzin Devorah Leah, daughter of the Alter Rebbe, passed away on Tzom Gedaliah 5553 (September 1792).
story_body: When the Tzemach Tzedek was three years old, on Tzom Gedaliah 5553, his mother Rebbetzin Devorah Leah, daughter of the Alter Rebbe, passed away. From that point he was raised in the household of his grandfather the Alter Rebbe.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek begins recording hanachot
summary_en: Around 5566 (1805) the fifteen-year-old Tzemach Tzedek began recording hanachot from his grandfather the Alter Rebbe's chassidic discourses.
story_body: At about age fifteen, the future Tzemach Tzedek began writing down hanachot of the discourses he heard from his grandfather the Alter Rebbe. Manuscript 1116 in the library archive contains his hanachot of an Alter Rebbe maamar 'Shema Yisrael' delivered in 5566 (1805-1806), preserved in his youthful handwriting.

title_en: Mittler Rebbe's passing and Tzemach Tzedek's nesius
summary_en: On 9 Kislev 5588 (November 1827) the Mittler Rebbe passed, and the Tzemach Tzedek accepted the Chabad nesius for the next 38 years.
story_body: Following the passing of his father-in-law the Mittler Rebbe on 9 Kislev 5588 (November 1827), R. Menachem Mendel Schneersohn assumed the leadership of Chabad chassidut. He served as Rebbe for 38 years, until his own passing on 13 Nisan 5626 (1866).

title_en: Torah Or printed in Kopust
summary_en: The Alter Rebbe's discourses were issued as Torah Or in Kopust in 5597 (1837), edited by the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: The Tzemach Tzedek collected and edited an anthology of his grandfather the Alter Rebbe's chassidic discourses, which was published as Torah Or in Kopust in 5597 (1837). A teshuvah preserved in manuscript 227 discusses the preparation of this volume.

title_en: Likutei Torah printed by the Tzemach Tzedek
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek published the Alter Rebbe's Likutei Torah in 5608 (1848), with his own appended glosses.
story_body: In 5608 (1848) the Tzemach Tzedek brought to press Likutei Torah, his curated anthology of his grandfather the Alter Rebbe's chassidic discourses. He added two manuscript volumes of his own hagahot (manuscripts 1101-1102) supplementing the printed text.

title_en: R. Issachar Ber Hurwitz appointed Rav of Lubavitch
summary_en: R. Issachar Ber HaLevi Hurwitz served as Rav of Lubavitch from 5592 to 5603 (1832-1843), working closely with the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: From 5592 to 5603 (1832-1843), R. Issachar Ber HaLevi Hurwitz held the rabbinate of Lubavitch. He maintained close halachic contact with the Tzemach Tzedek, frequently routing inquiries to him and binding the resulting responsa into volumes preserved in the library.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's good-conduct resolutions
summary_en: Between 5601 and 5603 (1841-1843) the Tzemach Tzedek recorded a list of personal good-conduct resolutions, written under Russian secret-police surveillance.
story_body: Manuscript 1124 preserves a list of 'good practices' the Tzemach Tzedek set for himself, addressed in the style of a man speaking to himself. Internal evidence places it in 5601-5603 (1841-1843), a period during which he was subjected to surveillance by the Russian secret police, which deeply affected his health.

title_en: Pinkas Malbish Arumim opened in Lubavitch
summary_en: The Lubavitch society Malbish Arumim opened its ledger in 5620 (1860) with the Tzemach Tzedek's signed endorsement.
story_body: The Pinkas of the Malbish Arumim chevrah in Lubavitch dates its founding to 5620 (1860). It records the establishment of the society, includes a written endorsement and signature from the Tzemach Tzedek, and bears annual pledges signed by his sons and grandsons.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's letter to Avrutch
summary_en: In 5614 (1854) the Tzemach Tzedek wrote a letter to his son, the future Rebbe of Avrutch.
story_body: Among the Tzemach Tzedek's preserved correspondence is a 5614 (1854) letter to his son R. Yisrael Noach, later Rebbe of Avrutch. It was published as Igeret 58 in the Tzemach Tzedek's Igrot Kodesh.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's testament to the Rebbe Maharash
summary_en: In 5626 (1866) the Tzemach Tzedek wrote a testament instructing his son the Rebbe Maharash on guiding chassidim and reviewing chassidut.
story_body: In the final year of his life, the Tzemach Tzedek addressed a testament to his son R. Shmuel, the future Rebbe Maharash, directing him to listen to chassidim, advise them, and review chassidic discourses before them. It appears as Igeret 78 in the Tzemach Tzedek's Igrot Kodesh and offers a sample of his handwriting in its final form.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek's passing on 13 Nisan
summary_en: The Tzemach Tzedek passed away on 13 Nisan 5626 (March 30, 1866) in Lubavitch.
story_body: After 38 years of Chabad leadership, the Tzemach Tzedek passed away on 13 Nisan 5626 (March 30, 1866). He was succeeded as Rebbe of Lubavitch by his son R. Shmuel, the Rebbe Maharash.

title_en: Rebbe Maharash receives Tzemach Tzedek manuscript as gift
summary_en: In 5638 (1878) the Rebbe Maharash gifted a Tzemach Tzedek chiddushim manuscript to his son, the future Rebbe Rashab.
story_body: Manuscript 226, containing the Tzemach Tzedek's chiddushim and Even HaEzer responsa, was given by the Rebbe Maharash to his son, the future Rebbe Rashab, in 5638 (1878). A gold-tooled inscription on the binding records the gift.

title_en: Rebbe announces 100-year hilula initiatives
summary_en: On Rosh Chodesh Elul 5725 (August 1965) the Rebbe announced fundraising and learning programs for the Tzemach Tzedek centennial.
story_body: At the farbrengen of Rosh Chodesh Elul 5725, the Rebbe announced that, in connection with the centennial of the Tzemach Tzedek's hilula, every chassid should contribute 100 coins toward printing his works. He reiterated the call at the Shabbat Nitzavim (28 Elul) farbrengen and added a directive to study the first three chapters of Tanya on Erev Rosh Hashanah, the Tzemach Tzedek's birthday.

title_en: Rebbe issues centennial klalli letter
summary_en: On 8 Nisan 5726 (March 29, 1966) the Rebbe's office issued a klalli letter to Chabad institutions worldwide for the Tzemach Tzedek's 100-year hilula.
story_body: The Rebbe's secretariat sent a klalli letter on 8 Nisan 5726 to 'Chabad organizations and institutions in every locality,' authorizing them as the Rebbe's shluchim to receive special hilula-day donations to a 'Keren HaMeah' for the printing of the Tzemach Tzedek's writings. The letter is published in Igrot Kodesh vol. 24, p. 113.

title_en: Rebbe leads 100-year hilula farbrengen
summary_en: On the eve of 13 Nisan 5726 (April 3, 1966) the Rebbe held a special farbrengen marking the Tzemach Tzedek's 100-year hilula.
story_body: On the eve of 13 Nisan 5726, the Rebbe held a dedicated farbrengen elucidating teachings of the Tzemach Tzedek and again repeating his maamar 'HaChodesh HaZeh Lachem,' said by the Tzemach Tzedek shortly before his own passing. At the close he again urged participation in Keren HaMeah, with joy.

title_en: Baal Shem Tov passes away on Shavuot
summary_en: The Baal Shem Tov, founder of Chassidism, passed away on Shavuot 5520.
story_body: Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov founded the Chassidic movement and gathered a circle of disciples who carried his teachings forward. He passed away on Shavuot 5520 (1760). Over the next two generations his students collected the stories about him, eventually published as Shivchei HaBaal Shem Tov.

title_en: Alter Rebbe travels to Mezeritch to study Kabbalah
summary_en: At about age 20, Rabbi Shneur Zalman left Vitebsk for Mezeritch to study Kabbalah under the Maggid.
story_body: The young Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, then about twenty years old, traveled from Vitebsk to Mezeritch to learn the foundations of Chassidic teachings and conduct. As he later wrote in his own hand, he began studying Kabbalah there under Rabbi Dov Ber. He also studied halacha with the Maggid during this period.

title_en: Alter Rebbe studies halacha with the Maggid in Rovno
summary_en: In the summer of 5532, Rabbi Shneur Zalman discussed a halachic pilpul with the Maggid in Rovno.
story_body: In his own writing the Alter Rebbe records that during summer 5532 (1772) he was in the home of the Maggid of Mezeritch in Rovno. They discussed a halachic question concerning shechita, and the Maggid concurred with his ruling. The episode reflects the close halachic training he received.

title_en: Maggid of Mezeritch passes away on 19 Kislev
summary_en: Rabbi Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezeritch, passed away on 19 Kislev 5533.
story_body: The Maggid of Mezeritch led the Chassidic movement after the Baal Shem Tov's passing. He died on 19 Kislev 5533 (1772). Over the next eight years his students compiled his teachings into Maggid Devarav L'Yaakov, first printed in Koretz in 1781.

title_en: Toldot Yaakov Yosef printed in Koretz
summary_en: Rabbi Yaakov Yosef HaKohen of Polonne's Toldot Yaakov Yosef was printed in Koretz in 5540.
story_body: Rabbi Yaakov Yosef of Polonne, one of the Baal Shem Tov's foremost students, published Toldot Yaakov Yosef in Koretz in 1780. The book quotes hundreds of teachings he heard directly from the Baal Shem Tov. It was the very first Chassidic book to appear in print.

title_en: Maggid Devarav L'Yaakov first printed in Koretz
summary_en: The teachings of the Maggid of Mezeritch first appeared in print as Maggid Devarav L'Yaakov in Koretz, 5541.
story_body: Eight years after the Maggid's passing, his disciples compiled his teachings and published them as Maggid Devarav L'Yaakov in Koretz, 1781. The book went through several editions in quick succession over the next decade.

title_en: Tzofnat Paneach printed in Koretz
summary_en: Rabbi Yaakov Yosef of Polonne's Tzofnat Paneach appeared in Koretz in 5542.
story_body: The third of Rabbi Yaakov Yosef's Chassidic works, Tzofnat Paneach, was printed in Koretz in 1782. Together with Toldot Yaakov Yosef and Ben Porat Yosef, it formed the trio of the earliest published Chassidic books quoting the Baal Shem Tov.

title_en: Maggid Devarav L'Yaakov reprinted in Koretz
summary_en: A second edition of the Maggid's teachings appeared in Koretz in 5544.
story_body: Three years after its first appearance, Maggid Devarav L'Yaakov was reprinted in Koretz in 1784, attesting to the demand for the Maggid's teachings.

title_en: Maggid Devarav L'Yaakov printed in Lvov
summary_en: A third edition of Maggid Devarav L'Yaakov was issued in Lvov in 5552.
story_body: The Maggid's collected teachings appeared again in 1792, this time in Lvov. The book had now spread well beyond its original Volhynian center.

title_en: Keter Shem Tov volume 1 printed in Zolkiew
summary_en: The first volume of Keter Shem Tov, the main anthology of Baal Shem Tov teachings, appeared in Zolkiew in 5554.
story_body: Keter Shem Tov, the principal anthology of teachings attributed to the Baal Shem Tov, was first published in Zolkiew in two parts. Volume one appeared in 1794, drawing on earlier printed Chassidic works.

title_en: Hilchot Talmud Torah printed in Shklov
summary_en: The Alter Rebbe's Hilchot Talmud Torah was printed in Shklov in 5554.
story_body: Before publishing the Tanya, the Alter Rebbe issued several of his halachic works. Hilchot Talmud Torah, his treatise on the laws of Torah study, was printed in Shklov in 1794.

title_en: Keter Shem Tov volume 2 printed in Zolkiew
summary_en: The second volume of Keter Shem Tov was printed in Zolkiew in 5555.
story_body: The companion volume to Keter Shem Tov part one appeared in Zolkiew in 1795. Together the two volumes became the standard collection of the Baal Shem Tov's recorded teachings.

title_en: Tanya first edition printed in Slavita
summary_en: The first edition of the Tanya was completed in Slavita on 20 Kislev 5557.
story_body: Printing of the foundational Chabad text, the Tanya, began in Elul 5556 (Aug 1796) in Slavita and concluded on 20 Kislev 5557 (Dec 19, 1796), at which point a short list of corrections was appended. Two surviving copies bear witness to this first printing.

title_en: Approbation of Maharil printed in Tehillim, Shklov
summary_en: Maharil, brother of the Alter Rebbe, gave an approbation to a Tehillim printed around 5576 in Shklov.
story_body: Rabbi Yehuda Leib of Yanovich (Maharil), the Alter Rebbe's brother, was author of She'erit Yehudah. Among his approbations is one to a Tehillim with anthologized commentaries and Zohar selections, printed in Shklov around 1816. He wrote that he was lending his name 'to strengthen those who hold fast to G-d's Torah.'

title_en: Sha'ar HaTeshuvah printed in Shklov
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe's Sha'ar HaTeshuvah V'HaTefilah appeared in Shklov in 5577.
story_body: After issuing his father's works in his first years of leadership, the Mitteler Rebbe began printing his own writings. Sha'ar HaTeshuvah V'HaTefilah was published in Shklov in 1817, the first of nearly a yearly publication schedule.

title_en: Derech Chayim printed in Kopust
summary_en: Derech Chayim by the Mitteler Rebbe was printed in Kopust in 5579.
story_body: Derech Chayim V'Tochachat Mussar HaSechel, an ethical-Chassidic work by the Mitteler Rebbe, appeared in Kopust in 1819. It opened a long series of Mitteler Rebbe publications issued from Kopust.

title_en: Ner Mitzvah V'Torah Or printed in Kopust
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe's Ner Mitzvah V'Torah Or was printed in Kopust in 5580.
story_body: Continuing the steady stream of his published works, the Mitteler Rebbe issued Ner Mitzvah V'Torah Or in Kopust in 1820.

title_en: Imrei Binah and Ateret Rosh printed in Kopust
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe published both Imrei Binah and Ateret Rosh in Kopust in 5581.
story_body: In 1821 the Mitteler Rebbe issued two volumes from the Kopust press: Imrei Binah, a major Chassidic treatise, and Ateret Rosh. They were part of his prolific publication output during his sixteen years of leadership.

title_en: Shaarei Orah printed in Kopust
summary_en: The Mitteler Rebbe's Shaarei Orah appeared in Kopust in 5582.
story_body: Shaarei Orah, a discourse on Chanukah and Purim themes, was published by the Mitteler Rebbe in Kopust in 1822.

title_en: Torat Chayim printed in Kopust
summary_en: Torat Chayim by the Mitteler Rebbe was printed in Kopust in 5586.
story_body: Torat Chayim, a collection of the Mitteler Rebbe's discourses on Genesis and Exodus, was published in Kopust in 1826, two years before his passing.

title_en: Mitteler Rebbe passes away on 9 Kislev
summary_en: Rabbi Dov Ber of Lubavitch, the Mitteler Rebbe, passed away on 9 Kislev 5588.
story_body: The Mitteler Rebbe led Chabad for fifteen years, from 1813 until his passing on 9 Kislev 5588 (1827). His tenure was marked by an extraordinary publication output, with nearly one volume issued each year.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek sends Torah Or to print
summary_en: In 5597 the Tzemach Tzedek sent Torah Or, the Alter Rebbe's discourses, to press.
story_body: In 1837 the Tzemach Tzedek sent Torah Or to the printer, having edited his grandfather the Alter Rebbe's discourses for the volume. Printing began but was halted when government decrees closed many presses in Russia, leaving the second part unprinted at that time.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek summoned to Petersburg rabbinic conference
summary_en: In the summer of 5603 the Tzemach Tzedek was summoned to a rabbinic conference in Petersburg.
story_body: In summer 1843 the Tzemach Tzedek was called by the Russian government to a rabbinical conference in Petersburg, where he stayed several months. He took along a list of books for study during free time; some volumes still contain blank pages he had inserted to record new chiddushim.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek adds discourses to Likutei Torah
summary_en: In 5611 the Tzemach Tzedek issued additional discourses for Likutei Torah.
story_body: Continuing to edit his grandfather's discourses, the Tzemach Tzedek published a set of supplements to Likutei Torah in 1851.

title_en: Rebbe Maharash begins recording his father's discourses
summary_en: Rebbe Maharash recorded hanachot of his father's discourses in 5614.
story_body: Few people wrote down hanachot of the Tzemach Tzedek's discourses because he generally recorded them himself. Among those who did was his son the future Rebbe Maharash, whose 1854 transcript survives in the library archive.

title_en: Loan note to Tzemach Tzedek due 5 Tevet
summary_en: A loan note from Rabbi Yitzchak Chaim Dov Ber Wilensky and Aryeh Leib was due to the Tzemach Tzedek by 5 Tevet 5618.
story_body: Two prominent Chassidim signed a debt obligation to the Tzemach Tzedek with a repayment date of 5 Tevet 5618 (Dec 22, 1857). The note may have covered either a personal loan from the Rebbe or a commitment of maamad support.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek adds more discourses to Torah Or
summary_en: Additional discourses for Torah Or were issued by the Tzemach Tzedek in 5622.
story_body: In 1862 the Tzemach Tzedek issued a supplement containing additional discourses on Genesis and Exodus, including selections for Chanukah, Purim and Pesach, expanding Torah Or further.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab's engagement signed on 10 Sivan
summary_en: The engagement contract of Rebbe Rashab was signed on 10 Sivan 5625.
story_body: On 10 Sivan 5625 (June 4, 1865), when Rebbe Rashab was four and a half years old, his tenaim were written. The Tzemach Tzedek personally added the opening line and a closing line of obligation, signing 'Menachem Mendel,' less than a year before his own passing.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek passes away on 13 Nisan
summary_en: Rabbi Menachem Mendel, the Tzemach Tzedek, passed away on 13 Nisan 5626.
story_body: The Tzemach Tzedek led Chabad for nearly four decades. He passed away on 13 Nisan 5626 (March 29, 1866). His sons divided several of his personal effects, including a black sirtuk whose surviving portion is preserved in the library archives.

title_en: Or HaGanuz printed with Tzemach Tzedek approbation
summary_en: Or HaGanuz by Rabbi Yehuda Leib HaKohen of Anipoli was issued in 5626 with a rare approbation from the Tzemach Tzedek.
story_body: Or HaGanuz appeared in 1866 with an unusual haskama from the Tzemach Tzedek and his sons. It is the only book to which the Tzemach Tzedek lent his name—he made the exception because the author's grandfather, Rabbi Yehuda Leib, had given an approbation to the Alter Rebbe's Tanya.

title_en: Rebbe Maharash hanachot from 5641
summary_en: A bound volume of Rebbe Maharash's 5641 discourses survives in his own handwriting.
story_body: Rebbe Maharash's manuscripts include a volume of discourses he composed in 1881, three years before his passing. These hanachot remain in the library archive.

title_en: Rebbe Maharash passes away; Rashab begins delivering maamarim
summary_en: After Rebbe Maharash's passing in 5643, his son Rebbe Rashab began delivering and writing Chassidic discourses.
story_body: Rebbe Maharash passed away in 1883. Although Rebbe Rashab did not formally accept the Chabad leadership until 1894, he began saying and writing Chassidic discourses immediately. A volume of his discourses from this first year, 5643, survives.

title_en: First lithograph portrait of Tzemach Tzedek approved by censor
summary_en: On October 30, 1886, the Russian censor in Vilna approved the first lithograph of the Tzemach Tzedek's portrait.
story_body: The lithographer N. Metz in Vilna produced the first printed portrait of the Tzemach Tzedek, captioned in Hebrew and Russian. The censor's approval is dated October 30, 1886, and the print appeared the following year as part of an exhibit of the Rebbe in his white garment.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek portrait reissued in Knesset Yisrael
summary_en: A version of the Tzemach Tzedek's portrait was published in Warsaw's Knesset Yisrael 1888 anthology.
story_body: Knesset Yisrael, third volume (Warsaw 1888), included a portrait of the Tzemach Tzedek signed by the engraver Z. Shatz. It reproduced an earlier lithograph distributed by Shmaryahu Schneersohn.

title_en: Rabbanit Rivka gifts a leather case to her grandson
summary_en: In winter 5648, Rabbanit Rivka gave Rebbe Rayatz a leather paper case that had belonged to Rebbe Maharash.
story_body: Rebbe Rayatz inscribed that the leather case for papers in the archive was from his grandfather Rebbe Maharash. He received it as a gift from his great-grandmother Rabbanit Rivka in the winter of 1888.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab formally accepts Chabad leadership
summary_en: Rebbe Rashab formally assumed the Chabad leadership in 5654.
story_body: Although he had been delivering discourses since 1883, Rebbe Rashab only officially accepted the Chabad leadership in 1894. Throughout his tenure he was unable to publish Chassidic books in Russia, due to Tsarist censorship; his discourses circulated in handwritten and mimeographed copies.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab's internal Russian passport issued
summary_en: Rebbe Rashab's internal Russian passport, recording his travels from 5663 onward, is preserved in the archive.
story_body: An internal Russian passport belonging to Rebbe Rashab survives in the library archive, documenting his travels within Russia from 1903 onward.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab's 5666 maamarim circulated
summary_en: Discourses of Rebbe Rashab from 5666 circulated in handwritten and mimeographed copies.
story_body: Two editions of Rebbe Rashab's 1906 (5666) discourses are exhibited—one mimeographed, the other handwritten by the well-known Chassid R. Zalman Idel Zislin. Tsarist restrictions prevented formal publication, so discourses circulated in multiple copies among Chassidim.

title_en: Rebbe Rashab photographed for emigration passport
summary_en: After the Bolshevik takeover, Rebbe Rashab permitted a photograph for a passport in 5678.
story_body: In 1918, following the Bolshevik conquest of Russia, Chabad leaders worried they might be forced to emigrate. For passport purposes, Rebbe Rashab permitted a photograph of himself seated in his yechidus room in Rostov. It remains the only photograph of him.

title_en: Final volume of Rebbe Rashab's discourses
summary_en: Rebbe Rashab's last year of recorded discourses is 5680.
story_body: A volume of Rebbe Rashab's discourses from 1920—his final year—is preserved in the archive. It marks the close of nearly four decades of teaching.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz's 5683 maamar circulated by mimeograph
summary_en: A maamar from 5683 was distributed by mimeograph among Chassidim.
story_body: During the early Soviet years Rebbe Rayatz transmitted his discourses by mimeograph rather than print. A 1923 maamar circulated in this fashion and is preserved in the exhibit.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes a postcard from prison
summary_en: During his summer 5687 imprisonment, Rebbe Rayatz was allowed to send one censored postcard home.
story_body: While held in his Soviet prison cell in summer 1927, Rebbe Rayatz was permitted to send a single postcard home in Russian, after censorship review. The card survives in the library archive.

title_en: Rebbe corresponds with the Rogatchover on 22 Shevat
summary_en: On 22 Shevat 5688 the future Rebbe wrote a halachic question to the Rogatchover Gaon.
story_body: On 22 Shevat 5688 (Feb 13, 1928), the future Lubavitcher Rebbe wrote a halachic letter to the Rogatchover Gaon. The Rogatchover replied on 24 Shevat, and the Rebbe wrote back again on 21 Adar of that year. The Rebbe later copied the exchange in his Reshimot, notebook 33.

title_en: Rogatchover replies to the Rebbe on 24 Shevat
summary_en: The Rogatchover Gaon replied to the Rebbe on 24 Shevat 5688.
story_body: Two days after the Rebbe's question, on 24 Shevat 5688 (Feb 15, 1928), the Rogatchover Gaon sent his response. The exchange formed part of a brief halachic correspondence later recorded by the Rebbe.

title_en: Rebbe writes again to the Rogatchover on 21 Adar
summary_en: On 21 Adar 5688 the Rebbe sent a second letter to the Rogatchover Gaon.
story_body: Completing their exchange, the future Rebbe wrote back to the Rogatchover Gaon on 21 Adar 5688 (March 13, 1928). The full set of letters was later published in his Reshimot.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz arrives in Riga and begins publishing kuntreisim
summary_en: From 5688 onward, Rebbe Rayatz published his maamarim as Kuntreisim and his sichot as Likutei Dibburim in Riga.
story_body: Following his release from Soviet captivity, Rebbe Rayatz settled in Riga in 1928. There he established a publishing program of maamarim in the Kuntres series and sichot in Likutei Dibburim. The Riga period continued through 1933.

title_en: Lubavitch calendar issued by Remigalsky in Riga
summary_en: The 5689 luach published by Remigalsky in Riga featured a Tzemach Tzedek portrait.
story_body: In 1929 the Remigalsky publishing house in Riga issued an annual luach whose cover bore a portrait of the Tzemach Tzedek, one of many adaptations of the famous 1886 lithograph.

title_en: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson begins exile glosses
summary_en: From 5699 onward, Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson wrote glosses on the Zohar during Soviet exile.
story_body: After being exiled by the Soviet government as punishment for spreading religion, Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson—Yekaterinoslav rabbi and father of the Rebbe—wrote Kabbalistic glosses on the few books he had with him from 1939 to 1944. He also sent his son letters and kuntreisim on Chassidut and Kabbalah from exile.

title_en: Rebbe's first publication: Luach 5703 in English
summary_en: The Rebbe's first publication, an English Luach for 5703, appeared in the United States.
story_body: After settling in New York, the Rebbe was appointed by his father-in-law to head Machne Israel, Merkos L'Inyonei Chinuch, and Kehot. His first published work, in 1942/43, was an English-language Luach for 5703 with laws, customs and information for young students.

title_en: Luach HaYom Yom published by Kehot
summary_en: Luach HaYom Yom was issued by Kehot in 5703.
story_body: The Rebbe compiled and edited Luach HaYom Yom, a calendar with daily teachings of the Chabad Rebbes, published by Kehot in 1942/43.

title_en: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson passes away in exile
summary_en: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson passed away on 20 Av 5704 in Alma-Ata.
story_body: After Soviet exile in Chiili (Kazakhstan), Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson was eventually permitted to move to Alma-Ata, where he passed away on 20 Av 5704 (Aug 9, 1944). His wife Rabbanit Chana had sent him the Tehillim he recited tearfully in his final years; she later brought it out of Russia.

title_en: Haggadah with Likutei Minhagim u'Taamim published
summary_en: The Rebbe's annotated Haggadah was issued by Kehot in 5706.
story_body: Kehot issued the Rebbe's Haggadah with Likutei Minhagim u'Taamim in 1946. It collected Chabad customs and reasons for the seder, including the note that 'in the Rebbe's house the matzot are arranged on a cloth, not a plate—except the Rebbe himself, who arranges them on a silver tray.'

title_en: First small stender used by the Rebbe
summary_en: From 5711 to about 5715 the Rebbe prayed at a small, simple stender.
story_body: When the Rebbe assumed leadership in 1951 he initially refused a separate stender from the Chassidim. He eventually agreed to a small, plain stender, though it was rather low and uncomfortable. He used it for his first roughly four years.

title_en: Tzemach Tzedek portrait reprinted by Kehot
summary_en: Kehot printed a mirrored version of the Tzemach Tzedek's portrait in 5713.
story_body: In 1953 Kehot reissued the Tzemach Tzedek portrait, reversing the engraving plate so the right side of the garment lapped over the left and the book in his hands would open to the right.

title_en: Second stender built for the Rebbe
summary_en: A taller stender with a hinged top was built for the Rebbe around 5716.
story_body: Around 1956 a more comfortable stender was constructed for the Rebbe with a hinged top that opened to hold his siddur during prayer. He used it from then on for daily prayer.

title_en: Walking stick of Berditchev and Slavita sent to the Rebbe
summary_en: In 5717, R. Shmuel Aba Shapira sent the Rebbe a family walking stick tied to Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev.
story_body: In 1957 R. Shmuel Aba Shapira sent the Rebbe a walking stick that had belonged to the family—linked through marriage to Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev and the Slavita brothers (R. Pinchas and R. Shmuel Aba). The stick had survived seizures by the Bolsheviks and Hitler; it broke en route to a Moscow prison and was repaired by a Polish prince who fashioned the current handle.

title_en: Stender built in Kfar Chabad for the Rebbe
summary_en: In 5722 students at the Kfar Chabad trade school built a stender for the Rebbe.
story_body: In 1962 the trade school in Kfar Chabad, Israel, constructed a stender for the Rebbe. It was carried by air with the group of Chassidim who chartered a flight to spend Tishrei 5723 with the Rebbe in New York.

title_en: Stender presented to the Rebbe at erev Rosh Hashana farbrengen
summary_en: On the eve of Rosh Hashana 5723 the Kfar Chabad stender was presented to the Rebbe at a special farbrengen.
story_body: On the night of erev Rosh Hashana 5723 (1962), the Rebbe held a farbrengen for the Israeli Chassidim who came for the month of Tishrei. The new stender was presented, and the Rebbe spoke about its significance, recounting the Mitteler Rebbe's question to his father, the Alter Rebbe, on what he had prayed with on Rosh Hashana—answered with 'with the stender,' since 'all is G-dliness, He alone exists.'

title_en: Rabbanit Chana passes away on 6 Tishrei
summary_en: The Rebbe's mother, Rabbanit Chana, passed away on 6 Tishrei 5725.
story_body: After leaving Russia, Rabbanit Chana continued reciting her husband's Tehillim daily until her passing in New York on 6 Tishrei 5725 (Sept 12, 1964). She had recorded on its flyleaf the story of how the Tehillim had been brought to her late husband in Soviet exile.

title_en: Rashab purchases rare books for Lubavitch library
summary_en: In a July 1908 letter, the Rashab describes purchasing four rare books that summer for his library.
story_body: Rabbi Sholom Dovber Schneersohn (the Rashab) actively expanded his library throughout his life. A letter from July 1908 documents the purchase of four rare books that summer that did not appear on the earlier 1905 catalog, evidence later used to argue the collection had grown to roughly 7,000 titles by 1915.

title_en: Rebbe Rayatz writes about Yevsektsia bid for library
summary_en: On 21 Tevet 5687 the Sixth Lubavitcher Rebbe wrote about reports the Yevsektsia in Belarus had been granted the Schneersohn library.
story_body: Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn (the Rayatz) addressed rumors that the Yevsektsia—the Jewish section of the Communist Party in Belarus—had received ownership of the Lubavitch library. He insisted the books were still held in Moscow and instructed his followers to keep pressing for their return.

title_en: Rayatz letter to R' Eliyahu Simpson about library
summary_en: In December 1926 the Rayatz wrote to Rabbi Eliyahu Simpson in New York reporting the books were still in the church building beside the former Rumyantsev (Lenin) Museum.
story_body: Writing to a leader of the Lubavitch community in New York, the Rayatz confirmed the books were lodged in the ex-church annex of what had been the Rumyantsev Museum—now the Lenin Library—and that the Yevsektsia had failed to take them. He laid out a strategy for lobbying the Soviet government from the United States to compel their return.

title_en: Soviet search at Rayatz's Leningrad home
summary_en: On 14 Sivan 5687, Soviet authorities searched the Rayatz's residence but took only papers of no value.
story_body: According to the Rayatz's own contemporaneous notes, agents who entered his home on 14 Sivan 5687 left with only worthless papers. A separate summer 1927 search in Rostov, however, confiscated a collection of his writings from 1921.

title_en: Lenin Library again refuses to return Schneersohn books
summary_en: In February 1927 the Lenin Library denied a formal request to return the Schneersohn books, despite an authorized return permit.
story_body: After lawyer Orinson prepared a formal certificate authorizing the books' return on the grounds they had been improperly seized, the library claimed the document had been lost and refused to act on it. The Rayatz reported the rejection in correspondence to followers in New York.

title_en: Rayatz arrested in Leningrad; manuscripts hidden by chassidim
summary_en: During his 1927 arrest in Leningrad, the Rayatz distributed bundles of chassidic manuscripts to his followers for safekeeping.
story_body: When Rabbi Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn was arrested by Soviet authorities in 1927, he entrusted manuscript bundles (bichlach) to several chassidim to conceal until the danger passed. The Seventh Rebbe later clarified that the manuscripts were returned almost immediately and that authorities had not, in fact, formally confiscated them.

title_en: Levi Yitzchak Schneerson arrested in Dnepropetrovsk
summary_en: The Rebbe's father, Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson, was arrested in Dnepropetrovsk in 1939.
story_body: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak Schneerson—chief rabbi of Dnepropetrovsk and father of the seventh Lubavitcher Rebbe—was arrested by Soviet authorities in 1939. The Seventh Rebbe later denied that his father's writings had been confiscated at the time of arrest, but still directed the 1988 mission to inquire about related papers held in Dnepropetrovsk.

title_en: Rebbe initiates Hammer/Weintraub channel for library
summary_en: In summer 5741 the Rebbe summoned R' Baruch Shlomo Kunin and directed him to engage Jerry Weintraub and Armand Hammer to approach the Kremlin about the library.
story_body: The Rebbe called the head Chabad shliach to California, Rabbi Baruch Shlomo Kunin, and instructed him to recruit Jerry Weintraub and Armand Hammer—both of whom maintained ties with senior Soviet officials. Hammer subsequently approached Moscow authorities asking them to locate and return the Schneersohn collection.

title_en: Krinsky tells Levin a Russia delegation is being assembled
summary_en: In early Kislev 5748, Rabbi Krinsky informed Rabbi Levin that a special delegation would soon travel to Russia to search for the library.
story_body: Rabbi Yehuda Krinsky, the Rebbe's secretary, told Rabbi Shalom DovBer Levin that within several weeks a delegation would travel to Moscow. It was to include Rabbi Baruch Shlomo Kunin (head shliach in California), Rabbi Nissan Mindel (the Rebbe's English-language secretary), and Rabbi Levin himself.

title_en: First letter to Rebbe outlining trip questions
summary_en: On 15 Kislev 5748 Rabbi Levin wrote his first detailed letter to the Rebbe asking how broadly to search.
story_body: Levin asked whether manuscripts brought from Leningrad by Prof. A.I. Katz indicated more items still lay there, whether to chase materials seized in 1927, and whether to extend the search to Rostov and Dnepropetrovsk. The Rebbe answered tersely—'Why shouldn't they search there?!'—and refused conditional limits.

title_en: Second letter detailing four-city work plan
summary_en: On 9 Tevet 5748 Rabbi Levin submitted a fuller work plan for searches in Moscow, Leningrad, Kiev/Minsk, and Dnepropetrovsk.
story_body: The plan laid out what to look for in each target city, and the Rebbe edited it line by line. He struck out conditional phrasing—'if not found there'—and insisted searches happen everywhere regardless, including for items belonging to chassidim like the Rebbe's own father.

title_en: Rebbe's Shemot farbrengen frames mission as pidyon shevuyim
summary_en: On Shabbat Parshat Shemot 5748 the Rebbe publicly framed the upcoming mission as 'pidyon shevuyim'—redeeming captives—applied to a tzaddik's books.
story_body: Without naming the delegation, the Rebbe told his Shabbat farbrengen that one must redeem the books, manuscripts and possessions of righteous leaders from captivity with self-sacrifice. He invoked the Tzemach Tzedek's principle that an emissary is empowered to make on-the-spot decisions, and afterward instructed the three delegation members to say l'chaim on a full cup.

title_en: Yechidus and departure of Chabad library delegation
summary_en: On 20 Tevet 5748—Maimonides' yahrzeit—the Rebbe held yechidus with the three delegates before their departure for Moscow.
story_body: Speaking in Yiddish, the Rebbe described the trip as 'one unified shlichus' that should function 'like a single body,' gave them three multiples of chai dollars for charity in Russia, and told them to treat every doubt leniently. He concluded: 'I am not thanking you—the greatest thanks will come from the books themselves.'

title_en: Chabad delegation arrives in Moscow
summary_en: The delegation landed in Moscow on Monday evening, 21 Tevet 5748, and walked to the Lenin Library to scout its buildings.
story_body: The plane arrived at 4:30 PM and the team reached the Hotel Intourist by 7. Realizing the library housing the Schneersohn collection was only a few blocks away, they walked over to inspect its three buildings—the Rumyantsev wing, the Muzei Knigi where the first books had been located, and the high-rise stacks—so they would recognize them in negotiations to come.

title_en: First negotiating day at the Lenin Library
summary_en: On 22 Tevet 5748 the delegation met Lenin Library PR director Olga Diakonova, who refused to admit outside experts to the stacks.
story_body: Through Armand Hammer's Moscow office head Nina Vlasova and Deputy Culture Minister Litvinov, the delegation gained a 90-minute meeting at the library. Diakonova rejected their request to search alongside library staff, insisting outsiders had never been permitted into the holdings, and asked them to hand over their lists for internal review. The delegation supplied 12 representative titles and pressed for a reversal.

title_en: Library director appeals to Soviet Culture Minister to block search
summary_en: On 23 Tevet 5748 the library director wrote to the Soviet Culture Minister opposing Chabad's search request; the delegation visited the Marina Roscha shul.
story_body: Diakonova's written objection prompted Nina Vlasova to suggest Hammer escalate directly to Culture Minister Vasily Zakharov. While waiting, the delegation drafted a formal memorandum with Mindel and Hammer's chief aide Jacobs, visited the Marina Roscha synagogue (where they immersed in the mikveh for the Alter Rebbe's yahrzeit), and reported the impasse back to the Rebbe's office in New York.

title_en: Hammer and Kunin meet Soviet Culture Minister Zakharov
summary_en: On the Alter Rebbe's yahrzeit, R' Kunin accompanied Armand Hammer to meet Soviet Culture Minister Vasily Zakharov.
story_body: On 24 Tevet 5748—the yahrzeit of the founder of Chabad—the delegation finalized a supplemental memorandum laying out the documentary case that the Schneersohn collection had grown to roughly 7,000 titles by 1915. R' Kunin then joined Hammer for the high-level meeting with the Culture Minister, the escalation toward which the impasse had been pointing.

title_en: Rebbe's secretariat writes to Shvadron about library effort
summary_en: The Frierdiker Rebbe's secretariat wrote to Shvadron with cautious optimism about retrieving the Chabad library, saying 'hope appears for the good.'
story_body: Efforts to recover the Chabad library held by Soviet authorities continued throughout the late 1920s. In 1929, the Frierdiker Rebbe's secretariat sent a letter to Shvadron stating that 'hope appears for the good' regarding the library. The letter is documented in the Rebbe Rayatz's published correspondence (vol. 1, p. 538).

title_en: Frierdiker Rebbe writes about Senator Borah's library intervention
summary_en: The Frierdiker Rebbe wrote about US Senator Borah's intervention to recover the Chabad library from the Soviets.
story_body: In August 1932, the Frierdiker Rebbe (Rayatz) wrote a letter discussing efforts by US Senator William Borah to recover the Chabad library held by Soviet authorities. The letter appears in his published correspondence (vol. 11, letter 3881). Borah was known for raising religious freedom issues regarding the USSR.

title_en: Russian rabbi writes to Rebbe about library in Leninsky Museum
summary_en: A rabbi in Russia wrote to the Frierdiker Rebbe describing ongoing efforts to retrieve the library still held at the Leninsky Museum.
story_body: In October 1934, one of the rabbis of Russia wrote to the Frierdiker Rebbe about the continuing effort to recover the Schneersohn library, which was still housed in the Leninsky Museum. The letter is documented in the Rebbe Rayatz's published correspondence (p. 182).

title_en: Starakova publishes Russian article mentioning Schneersohn archive
summary_en: Soviet scholar Starakova published a Russian-language article referencing a 'Schneersohn archive' held in Leningrad.
story_body: In 1974, scholar Starakova published a Russian-language article that referenced a 'Schneersohn archive' held in a Leningrad library. This article would later become a key lead for Chabad emissaries searching for the lost Chabad archive in 1991.

title_en: French translation of Starakova's Schneersohn-archive article
summary_en: Starakova's article describing the Schneersohn archive was published in French translation.
story_body: Two years after the original Russian publication, Starakova's article was translated and published in French in 1976. This French version was the one Chabad emissaries cited when searching for the lost Schneersohn archive in Leningrad in 1991.

title_en: Imperial Russian library founded with legal-deposit law
summary_en: The major Russian imperial library (later Saltykov-Shchedrin) was founded, with a legal-deposit law requiring every printed book to be sent there.
story_body: In 5578 (1818), the major Russian imperial library was founded in St. Petersburg, later renamed Saltykov-Shchedrin. From the date of its founding, Russian law required every published book in the empire to be deposited at the library. This made it a near-complete repository of Hebrew printings, including early Chabad publications that emissaries searched there in 1991.

title_en: Wiener buys handwritten Tanya manuscript in Borisov
summary_en: Shmuel ben Yermiyahu Wiener purchased a handwritten manuscript of the Tanya in the town of Borisov.
story_body: In 5639 (1879), bibliophile Shmuel ben Yermiyahu Wiener acquired a handwritten Tanya manuscript in Borisov. The manuscript was missing its first page and conclusion, containing only up to chapter 37. Wiener's inscription on the inner cover documented the purchase. The manuscript was found in 1991 by Chabad emissaries in Leningrad's Asiatic Institute, in the Friedland collection.

title_en: Tanya manuscript catalogued in Wiener private collection
summary_en: The Tanya manuscript bought in 1879 was catalogued as item 225 in Wiener's private collection.
story_body: In 1918, the Tanya manuscript Wiener had purchased decades earlier in Borisov was catalogued as item 225 in his personal collection. This cataloguing inscription remained visible to Chabad emissaries who examined the manuscript at the Asiatic Institute in Leningrad in 1991.

title_en: Wiener transfers his private library to the Frierdiker Rebbe
summary_en: Shmuel Wiener handed over his entire private library to the Frierdiker Rebbe.
story_body: In 1924, Shmuel Wiener transferred his entire personal collection of books and manuscripts to the Frierdiker Rebbe (Rayatz), making them part of the Chabad library. One Tanya manuscript was apparently not transferred and remained behind, later showing up in the Friedland collection in Leningrad.

title_en: Tanya manuscript catalogued in Friedland collection
summary_en: The Tanya manuscript previously in Wiener's collection was catalogued as item 177 in the Friedland collection.
story_body: In 1935, the handwritten Tanya manuscript that had passed through Wiener's hands was catalogued as item 177 in the Friedland collection at the Asiatic Institute in Leningrad. This inscription was still visible when Chabad emissaries examined the manuscript on their 1991 mission to locate Chabad manuscripts in Soviet collections.

title_en: Wiener buys 1490 Soncino Rambam in Yekaterinoslav
summary_en: Shmuel Wiener purchased a 1490 Soncino incunabulum Rambam in Yekaterinoslav.
story_body: In the summer of 5647 (1887), Shmuel Wiener acquired a precious Soncino 1490 incunabulum edition of the Rambam in Yekaterinoslav (now Dnipro). His inscription documented the purchase. The book was located by Chabad emissaries in 1991 in the Asiatic Institute's collection, which holds roughly 60 incunabula.

title_en: Venice edition of Rambam printed
summary_en: A Venice edition of the Rambam was printed in 5334.
story_body: In 5334 (1574), a Venice edition of the Rambam was printed. A surviving copy bearing the stamp of R' Avraham Klatzkin, the Chabad rabbi of Lozna, turned up in the Polyakov collection (originally the Schneersohn collection) at the Lenin Library in Moscow when Chabad emissaries searched it in 1991, helping confirm the collection's true origin.

title_en: Polyakov-Schneersohn collection survey at Moscow Lenin Library
summary_en: The Chabad delegation cross-referenced 87 cards in the Polyakov collection against the Lubavitch library list at the Lenin Library in Moscow.
story_body: On Sunday, 5 Shevat 5750 (January 31, 1990), Rabbi Shlomo Cunin and his colleagues spent two and a half hours in the rare books reading room of the Moscow library identifying books from the Polyakov collection that matched the Lubavitch inventory. The Polyakov collection contained over 8,000 books numbered up to 8,577, while the Lubavitch list compiled around 1906 recorded 5,642 books. The discrepancy reflected both multi-volume works counted separately and post-1906 acquisitions never catalogued in the original Lubavitch list.

title_en: Official meeting with Lenin Library archivists on Schneerson manuscripts
summary_en: The delegation met Medvedev and archive directors at the Lenin Library, clarifying that the manuscript holdings included roughly 30 volumes of Chabad Chassidus.
story_body: On Tuesday, 7 Shevat 5750 (February 2, 1990), Rabbi Nissan Mindel, Rabbi Shlomo Cunin and Rabbi Berel Levine met with Medvedev, department head Dyragin and his deputy Midovich at the Lenin Library. Through pointed questioning they established that only part of the manuscript holdings came from the Ginzburg collection and that some 30 volumes of Chabad Chassidus were among the manuscripts. The meeting marked progress after a frustrating day of bureaucratic obstacles in arranging onward travel to Ukraine.

title_en: Delegation flies from Moscow to Kiev to search for the lost library
summary_en: Accompanied by Soviet escort Andrei Kasianenko, the Chabad delegation flew from Moscow to Kiev to begin searching Ukrainian libraries for the lost Yiddish Cultural Institute collection.
story_body: On Thursday, 9 Shevat 5750 (February 4, 1990), the eve of the Frierdiker Rebbe's yahrzeit, Rabbi Shlomo Cunin and Rabbi Berel Levine flew from Moscow to Kiev together with their assigned Soviet librarian-escort Andrei Kasianenko. Their visas, hotel bookings and tickets had been obtained only after days of bureaucratic struggle, including a night spent crowded into Rabbi Mindel's single hotel room. They arrived in Kiev around 12:40 PM and immediately began arranging meetings with library officials to locate the confiscated Yiddish Cultural Institute library.

title_en: Meeting with Ukrainian Academy of Sciences library in Kiev
summary_en: The delegation met Kiev Academy of Sciences scholarly secretary Ivanchenko Vasilyevna and located two Hebrew incunabula traced to the lost Yiddish Cultural Institute library.
story_body: On 9 Shevat 5750 (February 4, 1990), Rabbi Berel Levine and Rabbi Shlomo Cunin met with the scholarly secretary of the Kiev Academy of Sciences library. Levine explained how the books of the Institute for Jewish Culture had been seized by the Yevsektsiya from synagogues, confiscated by the Soviet government in 1949, and stored in two cellars. They located two Hebrew incunabula (Abudraham, Lisbon 1491, and a Shorashim from Naples 1491) bearing the stamp of the Institute, suggesting that the rest of the lost collection might also have ended up at the Academy.

title_en: Pechersk Lavra library search reveals 1960 manuscript fire
summary_en: Inquiries at Kiev's Pechersk Lavra revealed that confiscated Hebrew books had been stored in the bell tower until a 1960 fire at the Vodavitsky monastery destroyed part of the collection.
story_body: On Friday, 10 Shevat 5750 (February 5, 1990), the yahrzeit of the Frierdiker Rebbe, Rabbi Berel Levine's delegation visited three libraries at Kiev's Pechersk Lavra complex. A veteran librarian named Tsedenko revealed by telephone that book treasures had been stored in the Lavra's bell tower since 1951, transferred to the Vodavitsky monastery building around 1960, and that a fire that same year had destroyed part of the collection. Surviving books had reportedly been returned to the Academy of Sciences library, suggesting the lost Institute collection might still lie in unsorted storage there.

title_en: Night train from Kiev to Dnepropetrovsk to continue library search
summary_en: After Shabbos, the Chabad delegation took an overnight train from Kiev to Dnepropetrovsk to continue searching for the lost Schneerson and Jewish library holdings.
story_body: On Motzaei Shabbos Beshalach, 11 Shevat 5750 (February 10, 1990), having exhausted leads in Kiev, Rabbi Shlomo Cunin's delegation boarded an overnight sleeper train to Dnepropetrovsk. Their Soviet escort Kasianenko had secured the tickets after multiple ticket offices initially refused. They arrived the next morning at 9:45 AM and immediately surveyed three Dnepropetrovsk libraries — the university library, the public library, and the historical museum — though most were closed for the day.

title_en: Schneersohn library confiscated by Soviet government
summary_en: The Soviet government nationalized the Schneersohn library of Lubavitch rebbes' books and manuscripts.
story_body: In 1921 the Russian government confiscated the Schneersohn library, which would later become the focus of decades-long Chabad efforts to recover the texts. Culture Minister Gubenko cited this 1921 nationalization in his December 1990 letter refusing to return the collection to Agudas Chassidei Chabad. The confiscation set the stage for the Didan Notzach campaign decades later.

title_en: Rebbe announces Soviet recognition of Agudas Chassidei Chabad
summary_en: At a Shabbat Vayishlach farbrengen the Rebbe announced that the Soviet authorities had recognized Agudas Chassidei Chabad and agreed to return the rebbes' library.
story_body: On Shabbat Vayishlach 5751 the Lubavitcher Rebbe declared at a farbrengen that the Soviet government had officially recognized Agudas Chassidei Chabad as a separate entity, provided it with a building, and committed to return the seforim, manuscripts, and correspondence of the Chabad rebbes. He compared the return to retrieving a pledge and urged that pikuach nefesh of pidyon shvuyim justified non-Jewish officials working on the matter even on Shabbat. The announcement framed the Moscow mission's pursuit of the Schneersohn collection.

title_en: Chabad delegation buys Moscow office near Kremlin
summary_en: The Chabad delegation paid a $300 deposit on a small room in a historic building near Gorky Street and the Kremlin to serve as Agudas Chassidei Chabad's Moscow office.
story_body: During the special mission to Moscow the delegation acquired a 15-by-15-foot room in a historic building near Gorky Street and the Kremlin, paying a $300 down payment. They placed a set of Rambam in the office and started a library with the three volumes of Toldos Chabad, holding a siyum and hatchalah on the Rambam study. The Rebbe approved hanging a Beis Agudas Chassidei Chabad sign in Hebrew and Russian on the door and affixing a mezuzah.

title_en: Culture Minister Gubenko refuses to sign book-return order
summary_en: Soviet Culture Minister Gubenko refused to sign the document returning the Schneersohn library to Chabad, deferring it to the Supreme Soviet.
story_body: On 16 Kislev 5751 the Chabad delegation, with Veronika as their advocate, brought a prepared memo to Culture Minister Nikolai Gubenko for signature. Gubenko refused to sign, claiming the matter required the Supreme Soviet, and at first refused even to meet them. After pressure he met the delegation with deputies Zolotov and Babushkin and ultimately agreed to instruct the Lenin Library director to draft a fresh memo distinguishing duplicates so a final approval could be issued.

title_en: Veronika summoned by KGB at Gorbachev's office
summary_en: Veronika, the delegation's advocate, was summoned by the KGB office of Gorbachev's staff and questioned about the Chabad delegation's activities.
story_body: On 17 Kislev 5751 Veronika was called in by the KGB section attached to Gorbachev's office and questioned about the Chabad mission and its members. She left the encounter satisfied and rejoined the delegation at the Lenin Library, where they were meeting with director Grigorov and manuscripts librarian Medvedev about the Schneersohn collection.

title_en: Yeltsin signs order to return Schneersohn collection
summary_en: Russian Federation President Boris Yeltsin signed a directive to transfer the Schneersohn collection to Chabad.
story_body: On 18 Kislev 5751 the Chabad delegation worked with Yeltsin's staff on memos and received an initial promise, then word, that the Russian Federation president had signed an order to give them the Schneersohn library. Yeltsin's office asked Chabad to organize broad press coverage and senatorial thank-you letters for a ceremonial transfer the next day on Yud-Tes Kislev.

title_en: Yeltsin reneges, defers Schneersohn books to Gorbachev
summary_en: On Yud-Tes Kislev Yeltsin canceled the planned ceremonial book transfer and told Chabad the matter depended only on Gorbachev.
story_body: On 19 Kislev 5751, after Chabad arrived for the promised ceremonial handover, Yeltsin had press coverage canceled and told the delegation that returning the books was up to Gorbachev, not him. The reversal coincided with a long Yeltsin-Gorbachev meeting that day in which Deputy Prime Minister Ryzhkov was sidelined and Yeltsin and Gorbachev publicly closed ranks. Veronika assessed that Yeltsin had originally planned a publicity move against Gorbachev but switched to a unity stance once the leaders aligned.

title_en: Foreign Ministry meeting with Deputy Minister Petrovsky
summary_en: Chabad met for hours with Soviet Deputy Foreign Minister Vladimir Petrovsky, who promised to escalate the book issue to Foreign Minister Shevardnadze.
story_body: On 19 Kislev 5751 at 4:30 PM the delegation met with Deputy Foreign Minister Petrovsky and three aides. Petrovsky promised to speak with Gubenko and to seek 'other means' if no positive decision came. By night the case was being routed via Foreign Minister Shevardnadze, who was asked to deliver a Chabad file to Gorbachev.

title_en: Russian Federation approves Poliakov Synagogue for Chabad
summary_en: The Russian Federation Council of Ministers approved transferring the historic two-story Poliakov Synagogue in central Moscow to Chabad.
story_body: On 20 Kislev 5751 the Council of Ministers of the Russian Federation approved giving Chabad the Poliakov Synagogue, a handsome two-story building in central Moscow. The delegation toured the building and was deeply impressed, although it remained temporarily occupied by another office. Local leaders planned to relocate the yeshiva and Tzeirei Agudas Chabad activities there from the Marina Roshcha synagogue.

title_en: Chabad delegation visits Lubavitch town graves
summary_en: The Moscow delegation drove overnight to the town of Lubavitch to pray at the graves of the Chabad rebbes and visit the original courtyard site.
story_body: Late on 21 Kislev 5751 the delegation left Moscow by car with Veronika's driver, arriving in Lubavitch at 8 AM on 22 Kislev. They prayed at the ohel for the success of their mission, visited the Chabad house and the site of the courtyard, and observed that only a well — and perhaps the surrounding trees — remained as physical markers of the rebbes' era. They departed at 10 AM and returned to Moscow that night.

title_en: Gubenko letter formally refuses Schneersohn library return
summary_en: Soviet Culture Minister Gubenko's office sent a formal letter to Dr. Armand Hammer refusing to return the Schneersohn collection, citing its 1921 nationalization.
story_body: On 23 Kislev 5751 a reply from Culture Minister Gubenko to Dr. Armand Hammer's appeal arrived at Hammer's office, announcing the decision not to return the Schneersohn-Agudas Chassidei Chabad collection because it had been nationalized in 1921. Veronika dismissed it as a personal opinion lacking response to Hammer's letter to Gorbachev and continued working through the Foreign Ministry. Copies of the letter were taken in Russian and English and delivered to the Foreign Ministry the same afternoon.

title_en: Gorbachev declines to meet Chabad delegation
summary_en: After Gubenko warned Gorbachev against returning the books, the Soviet president's office informed Chabad that no meeting or decision was possible.
story_body: On the first day of Chanukah 5751 (25 Kislev) the delegation was told that Culture Minister Gubenko had personally warned Gorbachev against returning the Chabad library. Gorbachev's office informed Chabad that the inter-ministerial disagreement left him unable to decide and a planned meeting — at which Chabad had hoped to present a special menorah — would not take place. Veronika immediately began preparing a legal brief and worked through the night with a partner attorney to build a court-ready dossier.

title_en: James Baker asks Shevardnadze to return Chabad library
summary_en: U.S. Secretary of State James Baker formally requested that Soviet Foreign Minister Shevardnadze approve the return of the Schneersohn library to Chabad.
story_body: During Chanukah 5751, through Baruch Hecht and producer Jerry Weintraub, U.S. Secretary of State James Baker submitted a request to Soviet Foreign Minister Eduard Shevardnadze that Chabad's request for the rebbes' library be granted. The intervention was part of broader pressure from American officials, senators, and press as the delegation pushed through the Soviet Foreign and Culture ministries.

title_en: Large public Chanukah menorah lighting in central Moscow
summary_en: Chabad in Moscow organized its first major public Chanukah menorah lighting near the Hammer Center, with extensive Soviet TV coverage.
story_body: During Chanukah 5751 Rabbi Moshe Chaim Levin and Veronika arranged a large public menorah on a Moscow square. After protests over a Manezh Square site near monasteries, the menorah was relocated near the Hammer Center on the riverfront. Busloads of children from the Chabad school, the Chernobyl children's camp, and the Sunday school attended with dancing, a play, and the twelve pesukim, and Soviet television gave the event wide coverage.

title_en: Russian White House backs Chabad property requests
summary_en: Yeltsin's office at the Russian White House issued letters supporting Chabad's plans in Lubavitch, the Poliakov Synagogue, and a Maimoni center in Moscow.
story_body: On Shabbat Miketz 5751 (4th Chanukah) the delegation met with four of Yeltsin's officials at the Russian government's White House. The officials agreed to write supportive letters on three Chabad initiatives — construction in Lubavitch town, the Poliakov Synagogue, and a Maimoni Center — addressed to the Smolensk city council and the Moscow city council under Deputy Mayor Muzykantsky. Copies were dispatched to each jurisdiction and to the delegation as confirmation.

title_en: Gubenko delivers formal rejection of Chabad library petition
summary_en: Soviet Culture Minister Nikolai Gubenko issued a written letter rejecting the Chabad delegation's petition, claiming the Schneersohn library was ownerless when nationalized and had become state property.
story_body: On Zos Chanukah (2 Tevet 5751) the Chabad delegation in Moscow received Gubenko's formal rejection of their request to repatriate the Lubavitcher Rebbes' library held by the Lenin Library. The letter argued the books had become national property when nationalized in 1918–1919 and offered at most to provide copies after further consultation with jurists and scholars. The delegation immediately escalated through American senators, an Inyurkollegia legal opinion contradicting Gubenko, and outreach to Russian Federation officials, while continuing their hunger strike.

title_en: Chabad delegation meets new Soviet Justice Minister Lushchenkov
summary_en: After the Soviet Justice Minister was replaced, the new minister Lushchenkov received Veronika and instructed his deputies to study the Chabad library case in depth.
story_body: On 3 Tevet 5751 Veronika met briefly with the newly appointed Soviet Justice Minister Lushchenkov, who directed her to brief his deputies in detail and scheduled a full delegation meeting before Shabbat. Lushchenkov later told the delegation that Gubenko's refusal did not accord with Soviet law and pledged to back their effort, though formal action would await the conclusion of the Congress of People's Deputies. The change of minister was viewed as providential after weeks of stalemate at the Ministry of Culture.

title_en: Chabad delegation expelled from Moscow hotel, shelters at Chernobyl camp
summary_en: After OVIR attempted to invalidate the delegation's visas, the Chabad emissaries left their hotel and spent Shabbat Vayigash at a recuperation camp for Chernobyl children outside Moscow.
story_body: On Friday 4 Tevet 5751, hotel staff abruptly demanded the delegation's passports for visa stamping while OVIR moved to nullify their recently extended visas. A parallel five-week visa had been issued by the Russian Federation Foreign Ministry, sidestepping the central Soviet authorities. Veronika urged the group to leave the hotel for safety, and they spent Shabbat with roughly seventy children at a Chernobyl recovery camp, davening, learning, and discovering descendants of the chossid R. Shmuel Dobruskin among the staff.

title_en: Soviet police arrest R. Yitzchak Kogan en route to Chernobyl camp
summary_en: Soviet police halted a car carrying R. Yitzchak Kogan five kilometers from the Chernobyl children's camp and detained him as collateral while ordering the rest of the group back to Moscow.
story_body: In the early hours of Sunday 6 Tevet 5751 a car carrying R. Yitzchak Kogan, R. Yisroel Aronov, Kogan's eldest daughter, and Veronika's driver was stopped by Soviet police outside the children's camp. After a prolonged exchange the police held R. Kogan as a pledge and forced the others to return to the capital, ostensibly because the delegation's visas were restricted to Moscow. The incident was understood as retaliation by Gubenko's faction, and prompted Veronika to escalate the matter to the Russian Federation Foreign Ministry.

title_en: Chabad delegation meets Soviet political adviser Yuli Gelman
summary_en: Returning from the Chernobyl camp, the Chabad delegation met with Soviet adviser Gelman, who urged them to focus their lobbying on cultural-collections expert Dmitry Likhachov.
story_body: On the evening of 6 Tevet 5751 the delegation moved into Hotel Ukraina and traveled to Yuli Gelman, who advised that the decisive figure was now Dmitry Likhachov, the Russian Federation's chief authority on rare collections. Gelman, then in Moscow for the Congress of People's Deputies, said Likhachov was open to meeting before returning to Leningrad. He also pledged to lobby Jewish deputies at the Congress and to seek a meeting with Gorbachev after the Congress closed.

title_en: OVIR apologizes to Chabad delegation for visa incident
summary_en: Soviet migration office OVIR apologized to the Chabad delegation, claiming it had been unaware of the mission's status, while the Mossoviet signaled it intended to return the Polyakov Synagogue.
story_body: On 7 Tevet 5751 Veronika met with OVIR officials who apologized for the Friday hotel incident, blaming their ignorance of the delegation's diplomatic status. The same day R. Kogan met with Mossoviet officials about the Polyakov Synagogue and Chabad's building needs, hearing that a positive decision was pending final approval. The delegation also began coordinating to send the rescued books out through the upcoming Chernobyl children's charter flight to Israel.

title_en: Breakthrough meeting with Dmitry Likhachov on Schneersohn library
summary_en: The delegation persuaded Dmitry Likhachov, the Soviet government's chief expert on rare collections, that the Schneersohn library must be returned, and he committed to writing Gorbachev in support.
story_body: On 8 Tevet 5751 the delegation met Dmitry Likhachov, the renowned Leningrad scholar overseeing the Russian Federation's rare cultural collections. Initially favoring a general principle of state custodianship, Likhachov was won over by Rabbi Shlomo Cunin and R. Kogan's exposition of the library's history and meaning. He attempted to call Gubenko on the spot and then drafted letters to Gorbachev and Justice Minister Lushchenkov recommending the books be returned. The night before, the delegation had also consulted journalist Viktor Louis, who counseled sustained pressure backed by the threat of litigation.

title_en: Likhachov dispatches letter to Gorbachev backing Schneersohn return
summary_en: Word reached the Chabad delegation that Likhachov had already forwarded his recommendation to Gorbachev and the Justice Minister, while a Moscow district leader offered land for a Chabad-affiliated Maimoni medical-educational center.
story_body: By 9 Tevet 5751 the delegation learned that Likhachov had sent his letter to Gorbachev and Lushchenkov backing the return of the Schneersohn library, with plans to follow up with Gubenko the next day. The same evening they met with the head of a Moscow suburban district who offered land for a Maimoni Center — a Veronika-led medical and educational complex including schools. Authorities had renewed their inquiries about the delegation's status, and two letters arrived from the Russian Federation government supporting their visas.

title_en: Asara b'Tevet diplomacy day for Chabad mission in Moscow
summary_en: On the fast of 10 Tevet the Chabad delegation packed in meetings on the Schneersohn library, the Polyakov Synagogue, the Chernobyl airlift, and US diplomatic support.
story_body: On 10 Tevet 5751 the delegation met Moscow deputy mayor Muzykantsky regarding restitution of the Polyakov Synagogue (still partly occupied by a choir); the US ambassador Maxwell at his residence; American philanthropist Tom Ferris on medical aid; and Israeli consular officials to finalize the next-morning Chernobyl children's airlift. News came that Likhachov had spoken with Gorbachev and Supreme Soviet chairman Lukyanov to recommend return of the books and that Lushchenkov was preparing to issue a binding decision.

title_en: Chernobyl children airlift departs Moscow for Israel
summary_en: A Chabad-organized charter flight carrying Chernobyl-affected children and their families departed Moscow for Israel, with the delegation seeing them off at the airport.
story_body: On Friday 11 Tevet 5751 the delegation accompanied Chernobyl children and their families to the Moscow airport for the Chabad-coordinated airlift to Eretz Yisrael, which lifted off before Shabbos and landed in Israel on schedule. The same day Veronika met with the Justice Minister, who confirmed that a special government commission under Lukyanov had been convened to decide the library question. The successful airlift removed a parallel concern that the library campaign might endanger the children's evacuation.

title_en: Gorbachev and Lukyanov approve return of Schneersohn library
summary_en: On Motzei Shabbos Vayechi the Chabad delegation received word that Mikhail Gorbachev and Supreme Soviet chairman Anatoly Lukyanov had signed approval for the Schneersohn library to be returned.
story_body: Motzei Shabbos Vayechi 12 Tevet 5751 brought the long-sought message: Gorbachev and Lukyanov had signed off on returning the books, and the file had been forwarded to Culture Minister Gubenko for implementation. Lukyanov's commission concluded the books should be returned without a public government ceremony. Likhachov warned obstacles from Gubenko's office were still likely, gave Veronika his private Leningrad number, and instructed her to call immediately if problems arose.

title_en: Gubenko televised speech prompts new Chabad appeal
summary_en: After Culture Minister Gubenko called the Ministry of Culture 'a ministry of kindness' on Soviet television, the Chabad delegation drafted a new appeal quoting his words and delivered it at his office before 9am.
story_body: On the evening preceding 13 Tevet 5751 Gubenko appeared on Soviet television describing the Ministry of Culture as 'a ministry of kindness' whose central mission was 'to open the soul'. Veronika proposed turning his own words against him; R. Kogan drafted the letter overnight at Armand Hammer's Moscow office and presented it to the Ministry of Culture before 9am on 13 Tevet. The maneuver came as Gorbachev and Lukyanov's decision was being slowly implemented over Gubenko's continued resistance.

title_en: Kogan meets Russian State Library deputies on Schneersohn collection
summary_en: R' Yosef Kogan met with deputies and staff at the Russian State Library, who claimed the Schneersohn books would be returned.
story_body: On 13 Tevet 5751 Director Gubinko was unavailable, but his deputies and the adviser Yefimovich told R' Yosef Kogan the books would be returned and asked him to leave his letter with them. Yefimovich said a committee had been convened and a response was promised on Wednesday, November 2. Later Lichachev told Veronika that Gubinko had promised return but suggested waiting until after the Russian holiday.

title_en: Chabad ships Ezras Achim food packages to eight Russian cities
summary_en: The mission packed and dispatched food packages by rail from Moscow to eight Russian Jewish communities.
story_body: On 14 Tevet R' Yosef Kogan and R' Shlomo Cunin packed Ezras Achim food parcels at Marina Roshcha for distribution to eight Russian towns. The delegation held an internal meeting with R' Moshe Chaim Levin and R' Dovber Lazar on Chabad work in Moscow and Aguch oversight. After Maariv the parcels were sent by train.

title_en: Rebbe declines proposal to name Aguch representative in Russia
summary_en: After the mission proposed an Aguch representative in Russia to coordinate Chabad institutions, the Rebbe told them not to intervene.
story_body: On 15 Tevet the delegation faxed R' Yehuda Leib Groner a proposal that Aguch appoint a representative in Russia to coordinate all Chabad institutions there. Groner replied that he had already raised the idea with R' Cunin and that the Rebbe had instructed not to intervene in such matters. The same day Veronika reported that Lichachev and Shenazara, a Gorbachev adviser, had pressed Gubinko to release the library.

title_en: Chabad winter camp opens for Moscow children during school break
summary_en: A two-week Chabad winter camp ran in a vacant state school building for about 60 children of the Moscow Chabad school.
story_body: On 17 Tevet R' Shalom Dovber Levin visited a Chabad winter camp where roughly 60 pupils from the Moscow Chabad school spent two weeks of school break living in a Jewish environment. The camp ran in a state school building empty for the holiday and was run by R' Moshe Chaim Levin and R' Zalman Korbsky. The visit also covered the new Aguch office obtained from the Mossoviet.

title_en: Soviet law signed returning religious books and objects to faith bodies
summary_en: R' Refael relayed that a Soviet law had been signed Friday evening returning to religious institutions the books and objects nationalized in Soviet times.
story_body: On 20 Tevet morning the delegation learned from the local press that a law had been signed Friday evening to return to religious institutions books and objects nationalized under Soviet rule. R' Levin assessed that the law did not cover the Schneersohn case, since Chabad sought the books for its headquarters abroad rather than for a Russian institution. The delegation continued pressing for an exception, as Lichachev had previously conceded the Chabad case warranted unique treatment.

title_en: Chabad delegation rents Moscow apartment near Marina Roshcha
summary_en: The mission rented a year-long apartment near Marina Roshcha at $150 a month and began moving out of the hotel.
story_body: On 21 Tevet R' Cunin signed a one-year lease at $150 a month, replacing the hotel's $340 a day rate. The team prepared the apartment overnight and packed to move. The day was quiet because Russian Orthodox Christmas (25 December Julian) closed Soviet offices.

title_en: Mayor Popov writes Rebbe; Gorbachev orders Schneersohn books returned
summary_en: Moscow Mayor Gavriil Popov sent a letter to the Rebbe, and that evening Gorbachev's office reported he had ordered Gubinko to return the books.
story_body: On 22 Tevet R' Kogan brought back Mayor Popov's letter to the Rebbe, thanking him for help with Chernobyl children and Jewish education in Moscow and signaling the return of the Polyakov synagogue to Chabad. That evening Veronika called to report that Gorbachev's office had dispatched a government message to Gubinko ordering the Schneersohn library returned. The delegation broke into dance and l'chaim while R' Yehuda Leib Groner was still on the second telephone line.

title_en: Alter Rebbe yahrzeit farbrengens held in Moscow amid Gubinko backlash
summary_en: On 24 Tevet, the Alter Rebbe's yahrzeit, Gubinko went to Gorbachev to challenge the order to return the books while Chabad farbrengens were held in Moscow.
story_body: On 24 Tevet 5751 Gubinko told Gorbachev that Arthur Schneier, Adolph Shayevitch and Edgar Bronfman opposed returning the library, prompting the delegation to spend the night chasing rebuttals via Bronfman's deputy Israel Singer at the Savoy hotel. Rosh Yeshiva R' Uri Kamishov hosted a farbrengen at Marina Roshcha that R' Levin then continued at the Aguch office until 11:30 pm, reviewing the Alter Rebbe's biography on his yahrzeit. The delegation returned to the apartment around 2 am.

title_en: Pidrubsky meeting and Israeli consulate inauguration in Moscow
summary_en: The delegation met Rabbi Pidrubsky of the Choral Synagogue and attended the inauguration of the Israeli consulate in Moscow.
story_body: On 25 Tevet R' Kogan, R' Cunin and R' Levin met Pidrubsky at the Arkhipova Choral Synagogue, who wrote a letter to Gubinko stating that anything tied to the Rebbe must be returned immediately.
