He inspected the Great Synagogue's matzah bakery — far from satisfactory — and Chief Rabbi Lewitas asked him to supervise the baking of 5 tons of shemurah flour. The author insisted Krovliak would supervise but he would not certify the matzot as fully proper. He gave a shiur on Passover halacha to the elders, visited a children's garden in the city, and discussed the rabbinic position offered to him by Lewitas.

title_en: Pesach shiurim across Petersburg shuls and yeshiva
summary_en: On 10 Nisan 5752, the author taught Pesach halachos across Petersburg's synagogues, yeshiva, and parent groups during his special shlichus mission to Russia.
story_body: Based in Petersburg ahead of Pesach 5752, the author records giving shiurim before Kabbalat Shabbat in the small shul, before Musaf in the great shul, and again in the small shul; speaking at a post-tefillah farbrengen about yetzias mitzrayim in our times; teaching a parents' group of day-school children on Sunday afternoons; and learning with yeshiva students from 5 to 8 pm. Alongside the classes he handled chametz sales using forms specially printed by Kuritz and fielded live halacha questions throughout the day, noting deep satisfaction with the output of the learning.

title_en: Pesach visit to Peter and Paul Fortress, site of Alter Rebbe's imprisonment
summary_en: On 1st day Chol HaMoed Pesach 5752, the author visited Petersburg's Peter and Paul Fortress and the wooded grove marking where the prison that held the Alter Rebbe once stood.
story_body: During Chol HaMoed Pesach 5752 the author crossed into the Peter and Paul Fortress on Petersburg's Neva island and toured its prison cells. Guides explained that the current prison post-dates the Alter Rebbe — they pointed to a sparse grove not far from the present building where the older prison had stood before being demolished when the current one was built. Afterwards he toured the nearby palace housing the Asian Institute, where Shimon Yakerson showed him rare books and incunabula from the institute's collection and heard updates on the campaign to recover the Schneersohn library.

title_en: Major diplomatic push for return of Schneersohn library
summary_en: On 15 Iyar 5752 several parallel meetings on the Schneersohn library converged: Aharonov and Cunin met Vorontsov in NY; Yeltsin summoned culture minister Sidorov; Strauss met Yeltsin; and Veronika met PM Gaidar.
story_body: After a long lull the books issue exploded into activity. Rabbi Yosef Yitzchok Aharonov flew to New York and, through Mr. Fishman, arranged a meeting between himself, Rabbi Shlomo Cunin, and Vorontsov — Yeltsin's deputy, in NY for the UN. Yeltsin called culture minister Sidorov for a report; Robert Strauss was to meet Yeltsin on the library that day; Aubrey at the US embassy summoned Mr. Weissman for a briefing; and Veronika was scheduled to meet Prime Minister Gaidar. Veronika also received a copy of a letter from Mr. Philipov to the Rebbe stating that beyond the 2,000 books previously identified, the library had now found Schneersohn-collection markings on another 700 volumes, with months of identification work still ahead.

title_en: Rebbe's first post-stroke visit to the upstairs shul at 770
summary_en: On Monday 15 Iyar 5752 the Rebbe visited the upstairs shul at 770 for the first time since his stroke, marking another step in his gradual recovery.
story_body: In the weeks following his stroke on Purim 5752 the Rebbe gradually resumed public activities. The diary notes that on the Monday before Lag BaOmer the Rebbe was brought upstairs to visit the shul at 770 for the first time. The next day he would tour the library; both visits were framed as part of a slow return that those close to him hoped would lead to full recovery.

title_en: Rebbe tours all floors of Schneersohn library at 770
summary_en: On Tuesday 16 Iyar 5752 the Rebbe was brought through every floor and department of the Schneersohn library at 770, then sat on the roof terrace, answering written questions by nodding.
story_body: Doctors had encouraged the Rebbe to go up to the roof terrace to enjoy the warm weather. Before reaching the terrace the Rebbe toured every floor and department of the library — pushed in his wheelchair by his three secretaries Yitzchok Wilhelm, Moshe Klein, and Yengi Bistritzky. On the terrace he sat for tea while Rabbi Leibel Groner read aloud the contents of submitted questions; the Rebbe responded with nods of his head. The library visit lasted roughly half an hour, and the terrace visit another half hour.

title_en: Lag BaOmer parade through Moscow with cruise to river island
summary_en: On Lag BaOmer 5752, hundreds of children and adults paraded with a band and signs from Moscow's great shul to the river, then boarded two cruise boats to an island.
story_body: Lag BaOmer 5752 in Moscow opened with a parade from the great synagogue to the riverbank, drawing several hundred children and adults marching with a band and placards. Participants then boarded two cruise ships out to an island on the river. The author returned to Marina Roshcha to daven, then drove with Rabbi Ariel Chaikin — back from inspecting the mikveh under construction in Kharkov — to catch the last leg of the boat trip to the island. They addressed the gathered children briefly before returning.

title_en: Wedding of Chaim Tolochinsky at Moscow Aguch shul
summary_en: On Lag BaOmer night 5752, Chaim Tolochinsky — the first top student of the Moscow yeshiva and institute to marry through the shlichus mission — was wed at the Aguch shul.
story_body: The wedding was prepared by Rabbi Yitzchok Kogan, Rabbi Berel Lazar, and Rabbi Daniel Edri, with Rabbi Ariel Chaikin serving as mesader kiddushin. The author escorted the chossen to the Aguch shul and managed proceedings throughout the evening, returning home at 1 am. He records that this was the first time one of the top talmidim of the Moscow yeshiva and institute had married under the mission's auspices, calling the chuppah very beautiful and joyous.

title_en: Shloshim for traveling shliach R. Avraham Yitzchok Glick in Stamford Hill
summary_en: On the evening of 2 Sivan 5752, a large London crowd gathered at the Stamford Hill shul for the shloshim of the traveling shliach R. Avraham Yitzchok Glick.
story_body: Stopping in London en route from Moscow to New York, the author found a packed shul at Stamford Hill assembled for the shloshim of R. Avraham Yitzchok Glick, a longtime traveling shliach. The elder Rabbi Padwa, Rabbi Ashkenazi, and other senior figures spoke in his memory. Spotting the author as he entered, the organizers seated him at the head table and asked him to say a few words. The evening concluded with maariv.

title_en: Rebbe appears publicly in wheelchair after Shavuot tahalucha
summary_en: On motzaei Shavuot 5752, after the tahalucha, the Rebbe was brought to the entrance of 770 in a wheelchair to see the assembled crowd for about four minutes.
story_body: On the evening following the Shavuot tahalucha of 5752 the Rebbe was brought to the 770 entrance in his wheelchair to see the assembled crowd. He stayed outside for roughly four minutes; when asked if he wished to go back inside he nodded yes. The author, standing in the corridor as the Rebbe emerged from his room, noted that the Rebbe's face appeared almost as usual but that he looked only straight ahead at the crowd. Some reported the Rebbe slightly inclined his head toward Rabbi Yoel Kahan.

title_en: Baker to deliver 100-senator letter demanding return of Schneersohn library
summary_en: Around 7 Sivan 5752, Secretary Baker was to hand Foreign Minister Kozyrev a letter from 100 US senators demanding Yeltsin honor his promise to return the Schneersohn library.
story_body: Rabbi Shlomo Cunin assembled signatures from 100 US senators demanding that Yeltsin honor his commitment to Baker to return the Schneersohn library. Baker was to deliver the letter and signatures to Foreign Minister Kozyrev, who had come to Washington to prepare the Bush–Yeltsin summit. The author judged Yeltsin unlikely to ignore it, since he was hoping for major US aid and could not afford bitterness from senators and the administration. The pressure was compounded by separate leverage over the Smolensk archive — three million documents whose return to Russia President Bush had paused pending release of the Schneersohn collection.

title_en: Bush–Yeltsin summit: Bush raises Schneersohn library; Yeltsin silent
summary_en: At the Washington summit in mid-June 1992 Bush raised the Schneersohn library with Yeltsin and received no answer, reportedly because Yeltsin lacked authority to commit.
story_body: Around 1 Tammuz 5752 the author noted that for the two weeks since the Bush–Yeltsin summit there had been no news from Washington on the library. Reports filtered back that Bush had raised the books issue with Yeltsin during the summit but Yeltsin had not responded — apparently because he wanted to release the collection but had not been authorized internally, and rather than admit that publicly chose to stay silent. Soon after, a fax from Devorah Rochel reported fresh movement on the library issue and urged immediate return to Moscow.

title_en: Completion of first edit of Igrot Kodesh volume 20
summary_en: On 29 Sivan 5752 the author completed the first editing pass of Igrot Kodesh volume 20.
story_body: Back in New York between trips to Russia, the author spent two weeks editing Igrot Kodesh volume 20, finishing the first pass on Tuesday afternoon 29 Sivan 5752. He noted the absence of news from Washington in the wake of the recent Bush–Yeltsin summit. The next morning a fax arrived from Devorah Rochel in Moscow reporting renewed movement on the library and urging the delegation's immediate return.

title_en: Chabad delegation hands Yeltsin appeal for Schneersohn library at Munich G7
summary_en: On 6 Tammuz 5752 the Chabad delegation greeted Yeltsin on his arrival at Munich's Marriott during the G7 summit with 'Davai knigi Schneersohn!' — and Yeltsin replied 'Skoro' (soon).
story_body: Having transferred from the Arabella to the Marriott — where Yeltsin and his government were staying — the delegation was on hand when Yeltsin arrived in the evening. Rabbis Cunin and Aharonov shook his hand and said 'Davai knigi Schneersohn!' (Give us the Schneersohn books!). Caught off guard, Yeltsin had no real answer; pressed by Aharonov 'Kogda?' (When?), he replied 'Skoro' (Soon). The next morning the delegation approached him again, and Rabbi Yitzchok Kogan gave him a Chitas as a segulah for success. The shliach Rabbi Diskin took members of the delegation to meet US official Spakoyne, who promised to push Helmut Kohl to raise the library with Yeltsin.

title_en: Levin writes letter expressing crisis about abandoning book restitution mission
summary_en: Rabbi Shalom Dovber Levin wrote to Yosef Yitzchak Aharonov, agonizing over whether he could ethically abandon the mission to recover the Schneerson library books from Moscow.
story_body: After a discouraging phone call, Levin fell into depression questioning his role in Moscow. Concluding he was too personally invested to judge alone, he consulted three uninvolved advisors per the Rebbes' guidance. Most agreed he must continue the effort and travel at least briefly to publicly demonstrate the demand for the books' return.

title_en: Russian Ministry of Culture grants permission to inspect Schneerson books
summary_en: Shortly before Purim 5753, the Russian Ministry of Culture notified the Chabad delegation that they would be permitted to view and inspect the disputed library books.
story_body: After prolonged negotiations, the Russian authorities granted limited access to inspect the Schneerson collection. Levin, then in New York, viewed this skeptically as a distraction tactic from the real goal of returning the books. He wrote to Aharonov questioning the purpose of merely viewing the books rather than receiving them.

title_en: Levin protests inspection-only access as distraction from book return
summary_en: Levin wrote in distress to Aharonov, arguing that the offer to merely inspect the books was a Russian tactic to deflect pressure for actual restitution.
story_body: Levin questioned what value there was in just viewing books in the library. He pointed out a pattern: whenever the Russians felt pressure to return the books, they introduced a distraction to silence the demand. The only proper response, he insisted, was to declare this is not what was requested.

title_en: Levin suspects librarians of forging collection markings on the books
summary_en: Examining inspection notes faxed by Chaim Eliezer Ashkenazi, Levin concluded the librarians were actively forging markings to obscure that Polyakov-collection books were really Schneerson books.
story_body: Levin noted that on several books the 'P' mark for Polyakov coexisted suspiciously with an 'S' for Schneerson freshly written on the card. He suspected the librarians were systematically erasing 'P' marks and adding 'S' marks to hide the books' true provenance. He urged Ashkenazi to keep checking discreetly since the Russians would block Levin himself.

title_en: Levin writes to Moscow librarian Goldenberg requesting Polyakov book list
summary_en: Levin sent a diplomatic letter to librarian Shmuel Goldenberg asking him to provide the list of Polyakov collection books in the Muzey Knigi to verify Schneerson provenance.
story_body: Thanking Goldenberg for helping his colleagues view books, Levin asked for the list of over 100 Polyakov books in the rare-books museum so he could compare them to the Schneerson catalogue. He framed this as a small first step before tackling the larger collections of 2,000 books in Moscow and 10,000 in the Khimki depot.

title_en: Librarian confirms forgery markings then receives orders to stop showing books
summary_en: Ashkenazi confirmed nearly every catalogue card showed a 'P' mark overwritten with 'S', and the very next day Russian inspectors were told the operation was over.
story_body: Ashkenazi reported that without exception the old cards revealed a 'P' (Polyakov) had been overwritten by an 'S' (Schneerson). When confronted, Goldenberg deflected, saying what mattered was that they had the books. The next day access was cut off, having lasted only one day.

title_en: Russians propose exchanging Schneerson collection for substitute books
summary_en: Rabbi Yisroel Kogan phoned Levin reporting that Russian officials offered to return the Schneerson collection if Chabad provided substitute books of equivalent value.
story_body: Kogan also reported receiving the full archive file on the books, including over ten previously unseen documents. Levin rejected the exchange concept outright, predicting it would lead to endless demands for matching books, hidden payments, and ultimately government-funded receptions before any real return. He insisted the books must be returned unconditionally.

title_en: Russian Culture Minister presents first returned Tanya to Vice President Gore
summary_en: On Zos Chanukah 5754, Russian Culture Minister Yevgeny Sidorov hosted Vice President Al Gore at the Moscow public library and handed him a 1900 Tanya from the Schneerson collection.
story_body: Sidorov showed Gore twelve books from the Schneerson collection and gave him one: a Tanya printed in 5660 by the Rebbe Rashab through Tomchei Tmimim. A special leather-bound copy inscribed as a gift 'to the head of Tomchei Tmimim, the Rebbe Yosef Yitzchak' was the actual volume transferred. Vice President Gore handed it to Rabbi Boruch Shlomo Cunin to deliver to the Lubavitcher Rebbe.

title_en: Special delegation brings the first returned Tanya to the Lubavitcher Rebbe
summary_en: On Erev Shabbos Vayigash, the special delegation including Cunin, Aharonov, Kogan, and Levin presented the recovered 1900 Tanya to the Rebbe at 770.
story_body: At 3:20 PM the entire delegation, with attorney Devorah Rachel Kogan and supporter Albi Rozhouse, approached the Rebbe at the entrance to his room. Cunin placed the Tanya on the table; the Rebbe raised his eyes and gazed at each person passing before him. The delegation then sang and danced in the Gan Eden HaTachton for about an hour.

title_en: Seven additional Schneerson books transferred to US government as temporary loan
summary_en: Beyond the gifted Tanya, Russia transferred seven more books from the Schneerson collection to the US government as a temporary loan, which Cunin brought directly to the Rebbe.
story_body: These seven books were framed as a borrowed loan to the American administration rather than a return. Rabbi Cunin carried them straight to the Rebbe's room and placed them on his table. They became the focal point of the IFLA complaint that followed when they were not returned.

title_en: Russian official Shvydkoy visits Levin to pitch loan-language compromise
summary_en: Russian deputy culture minister Mikhail Shvydkoy and two colleagues brought Levin a letter from Filipov proposing Chabad officially request the books as a loan.
story_body: Levin refused firmly but gently to sign anything framed as conceding the books did not belong to Chabad. Shvydkoy described plans to allocate buildings at Chekhova 18 or Mokhovaya 6 for a special center housing the collection. Levin objected that participating in such a center would imply Chabad accepted the books were not theirs.

title_en: Russia files IFLA complaint demanding return of seven loaned books
summary_en: When the April 19 return deadline arrived for the seven loaned books, Moscow library immediately filed a formal complaint to the IFLA international library association.
story_body: The original loan deadline had been described as a mere formality, but the Russians used it as a trap. Upon the deadline passing, the Moscow library filed an official grievance with IFLA over the unreturned books. Chabad received the complaint letter in early winter 5755 and after deliberation decided not to respond.

title_en: Former librarian Goldenberg visits Levin in Brooklyn after leaving Russia
summary_en: Shmuel Goldenberg, the former Moscow librarian who had moved to Brighton Beach, visited Levin and disclosed details about Schneerson book quantities and markings.
story_body: Goldenberg revealed he had been ordered to separate marked books at the Khimki depot, selecting 3,500 of 8,000 books and transferring them to the Moscow library's restricted basement. He claimed most of the remaining 4,500 in Khimki also bore identifying marks but he was instructed not to be thorough. He confirmed 750 of the 2,000 books at the main library bore Schneerson marks, plus nearly 100 at the Muzey Knigi.

title_en: Levin travels to Moscow for Agudas Chabad conference around Yud Shevat
summary_en: Levin flew from New York to Moscow for an Agudas Chabad conference organized by Rabbi Yisroel Kogan around Yud Shevat 5757.
story_body: Levin arrived Monday afternoon for the conference at Agudas Chabad's Moscow center. Aharonov also flew in Thursday afternoon. Conference attendees were invited to visit the library to view 16 Schneerson books prepared in a new wing, but Levin refused to formally request fuller access and left publicly to avoid legitimizing the new wing concept.

title_en: Levin issues open letter rejecting Moscow Schneerson wing proposal
summary_en: On 7 Av 5757, Levin published an open letter to Anash explaining why reports of a planned Schneerson wing at the Moscow library were misleading and contrary to the Rebbe's wishes.
story_body: Levin cited the Rebbe's 5751 ruling that opening a Chabad library in Russia would only fuel arguments against the books' return. He argued the 12,000-book collection was not particularly rare, with a market value under a quarter-million dollars, and held only sentimental value. He warned that sensational press coverage misled the Russians into thinking they had something marketable, undermining return efforts.

title_en: Devorah Rachel Kogan writes Rebbe about opening Chabad library in Moscow
summary_en: In early Sivan 5751, attorney Devorah Rachel Kogan wrote to the Rebbe about establishing a Chabad library in Moscow, separate from the Schneerson collection question.
story_body: The Rebbe responded that opening a new Chabad library in Russia could provoke opponents to argue the Schneerson books should stay in Russia rather than leave it. He framed the argument as so distorted yet predictable that Chabad should avoid raising any such ideas. This ruling guided Levin's opposition to subsequent wing proposals for years afterward.

title_en: Levin records detailed diary entry about renewed Moscow library negotiations
summary_en: After years of silence in his diary, Levin resumed writing on 17 Kislev 5760 after receiving a formal invitation from the Moscow library to inspect the books.
story_body: Levin noted nothing had moved on the books for years. The new invitation asked him to join a special commission to discuss the books. He accepted and prepared to fly to Moscow in two weeks, motzei Shabbos Zos Chanukah, viewing it as a rare opportunity to actually check the books one by one.

title_en: Levin replies to Aharonov on commission letter, eve of Rosh Hashanah 5760
summary_en: On erev Rosh Hashanah 5760, Levin wrote to Aharonov rejecting Russian library proposals for an international commission funded by Agudas Chabad.
story_body: Library Eastern department head Mira Trifonenko proposed an international commission to identify Polyakov collection ownership, with Chabad covering all expenses. Levin suspected this would lead to hundreds of thousands of dollars in costs for hostile commission members while never actually allowing real inspection. Still, he offered to travel personally if needed, but only with a precise agenda.

title_en: Mira Trifonenko confirms Levin's solo inspection visit to Moscow library
summary_en: On 2 Kislev 5760, Levin received Trifonenko's reply approving his plan to come for a week of book inspection without waiting for the commission's formation.
story_body: Mira welcomed the proposal that Levin alone visit on Agudas Chabad funding, rather than convening the full commission. She asked him to indicate his preferred dates. Levin offered November 21–26 or December 12–17 and outlined a three-list inspection plan: marked Schneerson books, books in the 1914 Lubavitch catalogue, and unmarked unlisted books.

title_en: Levin sends detailed Moscow library inspection plan by fax
summary_en: On 14 Kislev 5760, Levin faxed Trifonenko a detailed work plan covering each library department he would inspect with a day-by-day schedule.
story_body: Mira quickly confirmed his visa was arranged for pickup at the embassy on December 3 and accepted his agenda and department list. Levin finalized his departure for motzei Shabbos Zos Chanukah and planned to start work the morning of 4 Tevet. He remained undecided whether to stay one or two weeks, depending on his access.

title_en: Levin arrives in Moscow at Hotel Minsk to begin library inspection
summary_en: Levin arrived in Moscow the morning of 4 Tevet 5760, stopping at the Agudas Chabad center on Bolshaya Bronnaya before settling at Hotel Minsk.
story_body: His original plan had been to start work the same day, but Mira had warned by fax that a Russian national holiday closed the library. He spent the day at the Agudas Chabad center conversing with Rabbi Yisroel Kogan and Boruch Gorin, then returned to his hotel to rest and pray. He scheduled the first inspection day for the morning of 5 Tevet, 'didan natzach' day.

title_en: First day Levin permitted to fully inspect Schneerson collection
summary_en: On 5 Tevet 5760, the Didan Natzach anniversary, Levin was granted unprecedented access to inspect the Schneerson collection book by book at the Moscow library.
story_body: Mira Trifonenko, head of the Eastern books department, told Levin all 110 rare-museum books were confirmed Schneerson. The Polyakov collection was split into four parts: 110 rare museum books, 2,300 old books, 8,350 books from 17th–18th centuries at the Khimki depot, and 280 manuscripts known as the Schneerson archive. Levin began his planned categorization of marked, catalogued, and unmarked unlisted books.

title_en: Library staff identify 3,000 books from Schneersohn collection
summary_en: Russian State Library staff identified 3,000 volumes as belonging to the Schneersohn (Lubavitch) collection within the larger Polyakov holdings.
story_body: In 5752 (1992), librarians at the Russian State Library sorted through the Polyakov collection and identified clear markings on 3,000 volumes as belonging to the Schneersohn library — 700 in the main building and 2,300 in the Khimki warehouse. These were consolidated on the 11th floor of the main building. The Chabad emissary was not permitted to participate, leaving the identification incomplete.

title_en: Seven Lubavitch books loaned to Rabbi Cunin via US government
summary_en: Seven books from the Schneersohn collection were given to Rabbi B.S. Cunin as a two-month loan arranged through US government channels and never returned.
story_body: In 5754 (1994), Rabbi B.S. Cunin signed for seven books from the Schneersohn collection as a two-month loan, the transaction mediated through the US government. He was told his signature was a mere formality and the books would not need to be returned; they were given to the Rebbe and placed sealed in his study. The Moscow Library subsequently filed a claim at the International Court of Justice in The Hague.

title_en: Didan Notzach farbrengen at Moscow's Agudas Chabad synagogue
summary_en: About fifty Chabad community members in Moscow gathered on 5 Tevet to mark Didan Notzach, the anniversary of the Lubavitch library court victory.
story_body: On the night of 5 Tevet 5760, the diarist joined a Didan Notzach gathering at the Agudas Chabad synagogue in Moscow with roughly fifty Anash members and yeshiva students. He spoke in Hebrew while Rabbi M. Hochberg translated to Russian. He also joined a live broadcast to a parallel farbrengen at Beis Rivka in New York to report progress in identifying Schneersohn books that day.

title_en: First inspection of Schneersohn books at Khimki warehouse
summary_en: The Chabad emissary was first permitted to examine the 6,000 Polyakov-collection volumes stored in Khimki, identifying about 70 of 250 sampled as Lubavitch books.
story_body: On 6 Tevet 5760, the emissary traveled with librarian Oleg to the Russian State Library's Khimki branch. After being required to obtain a special permit on site, he was allowed onto the 10th floor for the first time, where 6,000 unsorted Polyakov-collection volumes were kept. He recorded about 250 volumes and identified roughly 70 as bearing clear Lubavitch markings.

title_en: Meeting with US embassy representative Mary Dietrich on the books
summary_en: A 2.5-hour meeting between the emissary, US embassy representative Mary Dietrich, and library department head Mara Trifonenko outlined a Russian proposal for returning the Lubavitch library.
story_body: On 7 Tevet 5760, the emissary met with US embassy representative Mary Dietrich and Russian State Library Oriental Books department head Mara Trifonenko for over two hours. Trifonenko detailed a four-stage plan involving a committee, duplicate-checks, and a new building before any books could be returned. The emissary argued the plan was unrealistic and would take decades, but provided a list of 100 books for the librarians to verify.

title_en: 'Lubavitch Collection' labeling of Polyakov books begins in Khimki
summary_en: On a second Moscow visit, the emissary began affixing 'Lubavitch Collection' stickers — prepared himself in New York — onto Polyakov-collection books identified as Schneersohn library volumes.
story_body: On 8 Tammuz 5760, the emissary arrived in Moscow with 3,000 self-printed 'Lubavitch Collection' stickers, having distrusted the library's offer of blank labels. Working with librarians Oleg and Lena on the 10th floor in Khimki, he passed over about 2,500 books and identified 263 as bearing clear Lubavitch markings, which they immediately labeled.

title_en: Meeting at US embassy in Moscow with deputy ambassador John Ordway
summary_en: A two-hour meeting at the US embassy with deputy ambassador John Ordway and aide Howard Solomon to discuss returning the Lubavitch library.
story_body: On 9 Tammuz 5760, after a morning session with Mara Trifonenko, the emissary went to the US embassy for a two-hour meeting with deputy ambassador John Ordway and his aide Howard Solomon. He argued the Russian side had no real intention of returning books, using duplicate-checks and a committee to stall indefinitely. He proposed starting returns with the 500+ books the librarians had already verified, but was refused.

title_en: Identification of 845 new Lubavitch books in Moscow library
summary_en: The emissary finished examining the 1,500 unidentified books on the 12th floor of the main library, bringing his total newly identified Lubavitch volumes to about 845.
story_body: On 16 Tammuz 5760, the emissary completed sorting through the 1,500 unidentified volumes in the main building, identifying an additional 74 Lubavitch books and bringing his two-visit total to about 845. The team also began affixing 'Lubavitch Collection' stickers to the 3,000 books originally identified by library staff in 5752, completing 825 of them that day.

title_en: Final labeling of 4,354 books as 'Lubavitch Collection' in Moscow
summary_en: The emissary completed labeling 4,354 identified Schneersohn-collection volumes in the Russian State Library with 'Lubavitch Collection' stickers, finishing his identification mission.
story_body: On 17 Tammuz 5760, the labeling project was completed: 4,354 books in the public library bore 'Lubavitch Collection' stickers — 770 in the Khimki branch and the rest in the main building. The emissary estimated roughly 2,500 additional Lubavitch volumes remained mixed in the Polyakov collection without identifying marks, alongside 110 rare books in the museum and 280 manuscripts outside Trifonenko's jurisdiction.
